stories.title: The Weight of a Bell
stories.prompt: Look, since we're going to be working together, I’m going to make something very clear to you. I am NOT converting to your faith, I already have one, and if you keep trying to make me change my mind. I’ll summon a demon to drag you down to hell if i have to!
stories.body:
# The Weight of a Bell

The crack ran from the bell's lip almost to its shoulder. Anwen could put a fingernail into it. Someone had wrapped a strip of white linen around the bronze, as if the bell were a hurt wrist.

“My mother used to say it could be heard from her bedroom,” Mikkel said. “Even with the windows shut.”

He had told her that twice since dawn. This time Anwen looked down through the square opening in the belfry floor. The padded cradle waited far below, between the chapel's empty pews. They had taken out six boards to make a path for the bell. Through the gap she could see the soles of the steward's shoes as he went about collecting hymnbooks.

“It won't sound the same if they mend it,” she said.

“They'll cast a new one. This one belongs somewhere people can see it.” Mikkel adjusted the chain hoist over their heads. “You should come back for the dedication. The service, I mean. You might find something there.”

Anwen tied the loose end of her red wrist cord beneath her sleeve. She had worn it to work for twenty years. Mikkel had noticed it on their first job together and had been trying, in gentle increments, to find out what would make her take it off.

“I found the side door,” she said. “We brought the hoist in through it.”

He smiled, almost sorry for her. “You know what I mean.”

She set down the pencil with which she'd marked the safe path on the floor. The bell was still on its old wooden axle. Nothing was hanging yet. They had time to settle this.

“Look, since we're going to be working together, I'm going to make something very clear to you. I am *not* converting to your faith. I already have one. And if you keep trying to make me change my mind, I'll summon a demon to drag you down to hell if I have to.”

Mikkel glanced at the empty stairwell, as though she had embarrassed them in front of someone. “Anwen.”

“I mean it.”

“I know you do.” His voice softened. “That's why I worry.”

She picked up her pencil. He could worry. He could do it without trying to enter her head. “Pass me the short sling.”

They worked through the morning. Mikkel was good with his hands, and careful in most ways. He checked each shackle pin by touch and gave the old axle a slow inspection before they freed it. When the steward brought bread and cheese, Mikkel thanked him and bowed his head over his portion. Anwen sat on a packing crate and ate hers. She spoke the names of those who had taught her to work with weight, too quietly for anyone else to hear. Mikkel did not ask what she was saying.

By afternoon the bell hung from the hoist, its mouth a little above the opened floor. The chain held its weight. Two guide lines, tied to a padded band around its waist, kept it clear of the square opening's stone edges. Anwen had the west line around a cleat. Mikkel held the east, its spare length coiled beside a cleat near the stairwell. A broad board protected the west edge of the opening. The bell's crack faced Mikkel across the gap.

“The sling takes its weight a little off center,” Anwen said. “When the mouth passes the floor, it will drift west. Keep that line snug until I say *slack*. Don't haul it back if it moves. The hoist will take the weight.”

Mikkel nodded. He had helped lower machinery heavier than this. Still, he had rung this bell as a boy; she could see him trying not to look at the linen band someone had wound around it. He touched the line, then the catch at his waist, making sure he could pay out rope without letting it run.

They began the descent. Chain clicked through the hoist, one measured length at a time. The steward had gone outside on Anwen's instructions. Below, the cradle looked too small until she followed its corners with her eyes.

The bell's mouth reached the level of the floor. Mikkel eased his line.

“Hold it,” Anwen said.

“The cracked lip's too close to the east stone. If I give it room—”

“It hasn't cleared the west edge. Hold it.”

He looked at the bronze and not at her. His fingers opened a little. The bell drifted west, as she had warned. Its lip pressed into the protective board. Wood broke with a sound too sharp for its size.

Mikkel hauled at the east line. The bell swung back across the opening. Anwen locked the chain brake and felt the floor quiver under both feet. The cracked lip struck the east stone. A thin bronze flake jumped free and fell, ticking twice on the pews below.

“Let the line go slack,” she said.

He kept pulling. “It'll hit again.”

“If you pull, it will.”

He let out one breath, then one hand's width of rope. The bell stopped moving. Dust drifted into the open square. It hung inches from the east stone, the hoist loaded at a slight angle. They could leave it there for a minute. They could not leave it there for a night.

Mikkel stared at the new pale scar in the bronze. “I thought I could keep it off the stone.”

“You thought I hadn't seen where the stone was.”

“I didn't say that.”

“You didn't need to.” Anwen crouched to check the west guide. It had not frayed. “We can raise it a little and reset. Once I see whether the lip will clear.”

Behind her, Mikkel said, “When the floor shook, I thought we'd both fall. I thought about what comes after.” He glanced at the red cord at her wrist. “Come to the evening service with me when we finish. You can hear what we believe and leave if you want.”

The invitation might have been bearable on another day, after another accident. Here it followed her answer of that morning and the one before it, and the one on the quarry job when he had offered to bring her to a meeting, and the one in the wagon afterward. He could name the lines and their loads. He remembered the steward's instructions about the chapel door. It was only her refusal that fell out of him as soon as he heard it.

“No,” she said.

“I only meant—”

“I know what you meant.” She stood. The bell rocked once, very slightly, on the chain. “I told you what I'd do.”

Mikkel's expression changed. Not fear. The same concern he'd shown her all morning, with a little weariness beneath it, as though she had made his duty harder.

Anwen drew her red cord from under her sleeve. It was the one her father had knotted for her when she began to work. His warning about the old words had been that the speaker must answer for them afterward.

She wound the cord once around her fingers and spoke the name she had been taught. The air at the stairwell darkened. A figure stepped from it, narrow enough to pass between the railings though its shoulders seemed wider than the door. It wore a coat the color of banked coals. Its feet left ash on the boards, and through the gap below Anwen saw that its shadow continued downward past the cradle, into a distance the chapel could not contain.

Mikkel let the east line slip through his palms. Its loose end spilled from the coil, and the bell shifted toward the torn board. Anwen pinned the rope under her boot, then made it fast on the stairwell cleat.

The visitor looked first at the loaded hoist. Then it looked at Anwen.

“You called,” it said.

She had heard that voice in childhood stories, but never with her own ears. She had expected heat. She felt cold at the back of her neck.

“I did.”

The visitor turned to Mikkel. His heels left the floor. He gripped a timber post with both hands, and for a moment Anwen could see something beneath him that was neither stairs nor chapel. A wind rose out of it with the smell of hot iron. The visitor had not touched him. It had only made the distance possible.

“Do you ask me to take him?” it said.

Mikkel did not speak. Anwen had wanted him to believe her. She had not pictured his empty hands, with rope burns across the fingers, grasping wood while the bell waited above an open floor.

“No,” she said. “I asked you to hear me say that I could.”

The visitor held her gaze. Anwen felt the plain ugliness of that answer. She had used its arrival to frighten him, whatever else she had called it. The cord tightened around her fingers, not by magic but because her hand had closed.

“You can take him,” she said. “I do not want you to.”

Mikkel's heels settled on the boards. The distance beneath him closed. The visitor regarded the two of them, the bell, the gouge in the east stone. Then it walked to the stairwell. At the top step it brushed ash from its sleeve. The ash fell through the boards and was gone before it reached the pews.

Anwen waited until the stairwell was only a stairwell. She unwound the cord and put it away. Mikkel still held the post. When he let go, the grain of the wood had left pale ridges across his palms. He watched the bell.

“We have to lift it back,” he said.

“A hand's width.”

He reached for the east line.

“Leave that,” Anwen said. “It looks wrong, but pulling it will turn the crack into the stone. Put your hand on the chain brake. When I say *up*, give me three clicks. No more.”

He looked at the line lying against his boot. It was what he knew how to control. The brake was hers; she had worked it all afternoon. He stood with his palm on the lever for so long Anwen thought he was going to argue.

“Three clicks,” he said.

She took the west guide to its mark. “Up.”

One click. The bell shifted, and Mikkel's free hand moved toward the east line. He stopped it on his own knee. Two clicks. At the third, the bronze cleared the torn board. He held the brake where it was.

Anwen pulled out the damaged plank. She laid a pad of folded canvas on the east edge, then moved to the guide line beside him. “Now give it slack. Slowly.”

He did. The bell turned away from the stone. They lowered it through the floor with only the small sounds of chain and rope. When the cradle took its weight, the cracked lip touched its padding without a note.

Mikkel kept his hands on the rope after the chain went slack. “I can still feel where the floor went away.”

“I called it to frighten you,” Anwen said. “I didn't need it for the bell. You should hear that from me.”

He rubbed at the marks the post had left on his palms. “I think it was evil.”

She had no wish to try to settle that while its ash might still be on the stairs. “You can think that.”

“I still believe what I told you.” He looked at her then, not at the cord under her sleeve. “You told me this morning. I understood. I asked anyway. I won't keep at you about your faith.”

Anwen let out the breath she'd been holding. “All right.”

The steward returned as they were stripping the slings. His eyes found the pale mark on the bell.

“What happened?” he asked.

Mikkel looked at Anwen, and she wondered whether he wanted her to make the answer easy for him. She was too tired to guess. The bell had been cracked before they arrived; the mark was new. Anyone could see both things.

“I gave the east line slack too soon,” he said. “Anwen told me to hold it. Put that in the record before you sign.”

The steward went to fetch the work sheet. Mikkel stayed by the bell, not touching it. After a while he bowed his head. Anwen could not tell whether he was praying, and did not need to. She rolled the red cord once between finger and thumb, feeling the knot her father had made, then began to coil the lines for the walk home.

stories.title: The Bait Remembers
stories.prompt: You are a heavily traumatized individual, weaponised against psychics as a living booby trap meant to catch anyone reading the minds of random civilians.
stories.body:
# The Bait Remembers

I had three coins, an unstamped birthday card, and an assignment to stand in a post office until someone looked inside my head.

The card was for my sister. Innes did not know about it. He had searched my coat before we left, but the card fit behind the tongue of my shoe. In the post office I bent to retie the lace and moved it to my sleeve. I had written the address from memory. Orla might not live above the bakery anymore. For three years I had been permitted to know almost nothing about her, and it seemed better to risk a returned card than to let another birthday pass without one.

Innes stood three places behind me in the queue. His coat was damp at the shoulders. People trying to keep their parcels dry had crowded toward the counter. Across the open floor, the writing desks stood between us and the street door. He had chosen the hour because the queue would hold me still and give him a view of everyone else.

“Blue forms,” he said when my gaze drifted toward my sleeve. “Keep your eyes on the blue forms.”

He meant the stack on the counter, an ordinary place to rest my gaze. I looked at them. A man ahead of me was arguing about the cost of sending a parcel to his son. The clerk took his complaint seriously enough to weigh the box a second time. Beside the writing desks, a little girl in a raincoat drew a circle around each stamp on a sheet while her father addressed envelopes.

Across the floor, the street door shut hard. For an instant I smelled the old room.

Not the post office's wet wool and ink, but wallpaper warmed too long by a bulb with no shade. I knew where the memory would go. The narrow bed. The line of light under the door. Then the scrape of a key in the lock.

My thumbnail found the center of my palm. Four-one-six, I thought. Four-one-six. The wallpaper went away. I could see the clerk's blue forms again, and Innes nodded almost imperceptibly.

He had taught me the thumb-and-number drill in a room very different from this one. The key's scrape was the cut. Thumb into palm, number in the mind, as soon as it came. At first I had refused because I thought he was trying to make me forget. He wasn't. He needed me to remember exactly as far as the key, over and over, and never go through the door.

Before I knew him, the memory sometimes ran on. The door opened. There was the corridor, the morning street, and the bus I rode without a ticket because I could not make my hands find my money. Then I came back to whatever room I was actually in. Going all the way through had never made it easier. I had learned to fear the end of it as much as the beginning.

Now the route out belonged to Innes. If somebody reading me followed the memory, my jump to the number at the scrape left them at the locked door. With no later moment of mine to follow, they heard the key scrape again. Their body stood unanswering while Innes looked for it.

I had watched him take two. The first was a man who had been picking names out of a doctor's waiting room. The second was a woman who said afterward that she had only wanted to know why I was frightened. I had not seen what was done with either of them. The woman had looked at me as Innes led her away, confused by the fact that I was walking while she could hardly stand.

“Next,” called the clerk. The man with the parcel lifted it off the scale. There were two people between me and the counter.

Orla used to put cards on the mantel weeks before her birthday. She liked seeing her name written in other people's hands. I had taken a plain postcard with a small printed bird on the front. On the back, I had managed: *Happy birthday. I am alive. Love, Ada.* I had tried longer versions, but each one began to sound like an account I was giving Innes. I hoped the coins would buy a stamp.

Someone behind the writing desks made a small, angry sound. A woman holding a padded envelope had turned toward a man in a gray scarf.

“I wasn't talking to you,” she said.

“I'm sorry.” He backed away from her at once. Nothing distinguished him from the other customers. He was younger than Innes, older than me, perhaps thirty, with rain darkening the ends of his scarf. “I thought someone needed help.”

The woman gripped her envelope under her arm. “Ask them, then.”

He looked across the queue. I felt something brush the outside of a thought, so slight that I might have mistaken it for dread if I had not spent three years learning the difference.

The plea he had heard was mine. It had escaped while I was remembering the old room. I had not formed the words on purpose; they came out of the same place as the smell of wallpaper. *Please don't leave me there.* Innes counted on a thought like that carrying. A psychic might hear it without choosing to. Finding its owner among strangers required another choice.

The man in the scarf looked at the father by the stamp sheets, then at the woman with the envelope again. He was searching. She moved away from him, and he let her go, but his eyes kept moving down the line.

I could have raised my hand. I could have told him aloud that I was the person in trouble. Innes would have heard. Perhaps the man would have stopped looking inside other people. Perhaps he would have looked into me more closely. I had been placed in this room to make those possibilities hard to tell apart.

I took the card from my sleeve instead. I meant to keep it from bending. The man glanced at the movement.

For a moment the birthday message was no longer mine alone. I felt him see the little bird, Orla's name and address, the three short sentences that I had protected with my shoe and sleeve. I held the card against my chest. The contact went deeper anyway.

“No,” I said.

I was in the old room. The bulb made a yellow patch high on the wall. There were nine flowers on the wallpaper to the left of the bed if I counted the torn one. I had counted them for days because there was so little else to do.

From somewhere that was both inside and outside me, the man said, *I'm sorry. I can leave.*

He meant to. The key was scraping in the lock, and he was still with me.

My thumbnail went into my palm. Four-one-six. The bulb vanished. I was under the post office lamps again, holding the card so hard that the bird had folded in two.

Someone said, “Is she all right?” Another person answered that I was next in line. Innes came closer; I knew his shoes on tile. He had to find the reader among the people waiting and writing and weighing parcels. His gaze stopped on the man in the scarf, standing at a desk with his pen poised above an envelope. He might have been trying to remember an address. Innes watched for a beat, then left the queue and started across the floor.

*I can't get out,* he said from the old room. The key scraped in his voice.

It was an astonishing thing for him to ask of me. He had entered without permission, seen Orla's name and address, and touched the memory I had spent years trying to survive. His apology could not put those things back. Yet Innes was crossing the floor, and the man could not even lift his pen.

I could still feel the key at the edge of my attention. I let it pull me back. I was in the wallpaper room again, with the man close behind me and the key scraping for the second time. My thumb moved toward my palm. I held my hand open around the folded card.

*Don't leave me here,* he said.

The plea had been mine before it was his. I wanted to go. I could have done the drill again, but it would leave him at the same locked door, and Innes would reach the writing desk. My hand stayed open. In the post office, the card slipped against my wrist; Innes could see I was not doing what he had taught me.

The key turned.

I had spent years stopping the memory before that small, ordinary sound became anything else. Now the door swung toward me. No new truth waited behind it. The woman who had kept me there was in the corridor, holding my shoes by their laces. She told me I could go. She had said those words exactly that way then, as though she were letting me out of a shop after closing.

I remembered reaching for the shoes and flinching when she let them drop. I remembered the cold floor through my socks. The man in the scarf stayed close enough in my mind that I felt him stagger with each of those steps. I wanted to tell him to keep up, but speech belonged to the room and the woman might have heard me.

At the outer door there had been daylight, thin and gray. I had stood on the step for so long that the woman shut the door against my back. The pavement was wet. A bus came and I climbed aboard, because it stopped and opened its door, and for once a door opening meant I could leave.

In the post office, the blue forms swam into focus. The card had folded across the bird. I was breathing through my mouth. The clerk was handing change to the last person ahead of me. I could hear the stamp sheet rustle where the little girl was touching it.

The man in the gray scarf was at the writing desk, one hand braced on its edge. He met my eyes. He understood that I had left him there for a little while, and that I had come back for him. Both were true. Innes was halfway across the floor, threading between customers.

Innes saw me looking. His gaze went to the writing desks, then back to my open hand. I had stopped the drill. He knew it.

The man took a step away from the desk, still near the street door.

“Don't,” I called across the open floor. My voice worked this time. “Go.”

“You asked for help,” he called back. The father looked up.

“I didn't ask you to read her.” I nodded toward the woman with the envelope. She was watching him, her parcel still tight against her side. “Or me.”

He looked at her, and for a second I thought he would go over and apologize again. Then he turned toward the street door. Innes moved past the father. The counter was free. I went to it and put the card down, the bird showing. My hand was shaking enough that the three coins fell out separately.

“One stamp,” I said. Innes turned and crossed back toward me. The clerk, a woman with a gray pencil tucked above one ear, looked from me to the coins. Across the floor, the man in the scarf reached the street door. He had to hold its frame for a moment before he could walk properly, but he went.

Innes closed his hand around my wrist and put his other hand over the card before the clerk could take it. He smiled at her. “She isn't well. I'll look after that.”

The clerk left the stamp tray where it was. “Does she want to send it?” she asked me.

I could have told her what I was. She might not have believed it. Innes might have moved us outside before I finished. What I needed from her was smaller and within her power.

“Yes,” I said.

For the first time since we entered, Innes had to look like a man taking a birthday card away from another adult in front of witnesses. He let go of my wrist, then lifted his hand from the card. The clerk counted my coins and turned the card over to read the address. She smoothed the bent corner with her thumb and pressed a stamp beside Orla's name.

“Collection at five,” she said. She put it through the slot behind her.

Innes watched where it fell. He might know someone who could find it in the sack. He would certainly decide what to do with me. My legs were weak, and the old room had not gone far; the street door shutting again could still send me toward it. I kept my hands open on the counter until I was ready to move.

The clerk gave me my receipt for the stamp. It recorded the price and the time of day. I folded it carefully and put it in my pocket.

stories.title: The Minutes We Kept
stories.prompt: The Eyes of God, an ancient satellite still circling the world, can peer down from orbit and render judgment with a death ray, so humanity lives beneath roofs and covered streets. People say you walk openly beneath the sky to test your faith; you let them believe it—you simply know the satellite’s orbital timing.
stories.body:
# The Minutes We Kept

At fourteen minutes past five, Maren put her hand on the door to the square.

Sera had been watching the minute hand on the clock above the covered market. Yesterday, at that hour, she had gone out under a blue sky with a basket of bread. She had returned with an empty basket, and three people had touched the hem of her coat.

They called the ancient satellite the Eyes of God. By Sera's count, it was still above the sea.

“Wait,” Sera said.

Maren, Sera's wife, looked back. In her other hand she held the message brought from the far side, a square of paper creased until it would fit beneath her thumb. *Come before dark. I want to see you.* Her father had written it himself. The letters slanted left because the Eye had taken his right hand seven years ago. Evening light had already turned the opposite arcade copper.

“He asked for me,” she said.

“I'll go. I'll tell him you're coming.”

“He asked for me.”

There was no answer to that. Between the two covered streets lay forty paces of open stone. A canvas roof had once crossed it; the beam that killed two carriers and took Maren's father's hand had left the canvas rings melted into the walls. Nobody had put up another. From either side, the square looked short enough to cross while holding a breath.

Maren pulled the door inward. Sera put her palm against it. The effort was so slight that Maren could have pushed past her.

“Not until five eighteen,” Sera said.

Maren's fingers tightened around the note. “You were out at this hour yesterday.”

Sera had counted on her not noticing. People watched her in the square and called her faithful or vain, depending on what they believed God wanted. She had grown used to their eyes. She had not expected Maren, who shared her table and knew when she came home with aching feet, to watch the clock too.

“Yesterday,” Sera said, “it had gone.”

Maren's gaze lifted toward the gap beyond the roofs. You could not see the Eye from here. The town had been built to deny it a straight look into every room: streets roofed in tile and tin, windows facing other windows, children taught to walk beside walls. A person could grow old here without feeling rain on their face. Sera walked the square once or twice a day, and people spoke of it for hours.

“How do you know?” Maren asked.

Sera moved her hand from the door. She had a few minutes to give an answer she had withheld for years.

She took Maren into the disused counting room beside the market. Its outer wall faced the sea. Near the ceiling, a hole no wider than a nail faced the Eye's path. They stood well to one side of it, behind solid stone. Whatever looked through the hole would see only plaster.

Sera had covered the inner wall with small charcoal marks. Each showed where the glint had vanished from the plaster, a little farther along each day. Beside each she had written a date and an hour.

Maren read the nearest three. “Yesterday, five thirteen. The day before, five nine. Before that, five five.”

“When it went under the horizon,” Sera said. “Four minutes later each day this week.”

“You made these?”

Sera nodded. On clear afternoons the Eye caught the sun as it traveled west. Its bright point came through the nail hole and moved across the wall. The first time Sera saw it vanish, she waited an entire hour before she opened the square door. Then she began counting. By the end of that season she could plan a crossing instead of guessing at one, and knew not to trust a cloudy day.

Below the older times she had written *today: five seventeen?* She set her pocket watch, kept to the market clock, on the sill beneath it. She had intended to come here alone, wait for the light to go, and cross as she always did.

Maren stared at the writing. “You watch it.”

“Yes.”

“You know when it can't see you.”

“Yes.”

The market bell chimed the quarter hour. Maren had defended Sera to her father, who called the crossings an invitation to judgment. She had left his house and come to live with Sera. The truth had grown harder to say each year.

Maren had waited through all of that silence. Her father was waiting now.

“It's an old satellite,” Sera said. “Something people made and left above us. It goes around the world. It has an eye and a weapon. I found a drawing of it in a book that survived in the north cellar, round as a fist with two dark wings. The book couldn't tell me what makes it fire. I could watch where it was.”

Maren looked at her. “You think the book tells you whether there's a God?”

“No.”

“Neither do I.”

On the wall a red pin of light appeared. It passed yesterday's mark and kept moving. Sera felt her body answer before her mind did: shoulders drawing in, breath shortened. The Eye had passed over this room hundreds of times. Stone still held. Fear did not become smaller through repetition.

“At sixteen, it will reach that black fleck,” Sera said, pointing farther along the wall. “At seventeen, the light will be gone. Watch.”

“If you could show me this, why didn't you?”

Sera wanted to say she had been protecting Maren's faith. That might even have been true on some of the days. It was not the answer to the question.

“Your father called my crossings pride. You called them faith. I was afraid you would leave if I said I was only counting.”

Maren folded the note once more. It was already small enough.

“I didn't stay because you were fearless,” she said. “I stayed because I thought you would tell me when to be afraid.”

The red point made its slow climb across the white plaster. Sera remembered the day the beam came down: not the column of light, which she had seen only after she was safely beneath the arcade, but Maren pressing both hands over her father's empty sleeve so he would not look at it. He had tried to cross for flour. He had waited for a cloud to cover the Eye, thinking that meant the Eye could not see him. Only after that day had Sera found the old book and begun counting. In the years since, she had walked out beneath clear skies, and he had called that pride. She had never gone to his door with her marks.

When Sera's watch reached five sixteen, the light touched the black fleck.

Maren saw it. Her face did not clear. Sera had given her a fact at the cost of every occasion when that fact should have been given freely.

“It will go now?” Maren asked.

“Past the edge of the sea. I'll wait another few breaths to be sure.”

Maren took a piece of charcoal from the sill. Beneath Sera's line, she wrote *tomorrow?*

“Don't just add four,” Sera said. “See where it comes through the hole. On cloudy days you can't.”

“Then we wait on cloudy days.”

“Yes,” Sera said.

The point of light moved beyond the black fleck. Sera's watch reached five seventeen, and the light winked out. Sera took another piece of charcoal and marked the place where it had vanished. On the other side of the wall, the blue sky stayed blue. Whatever the Eye had been built to judge, its absence made no sign in the world except this small extinguished dot.

They waited until the watch reached five eighteen. Maren went to the door. Sera followed as far as the threshold.

“I can come with you,” she said.

“You can come when I ask.”

Maren stepped into the square. She did not run. At the place where the old canvas rings had melted, she stopped and looked upward. Sera could not tell whether she was checking the sky or offering it a prayer. Then Maren crossed the remaining stones and entered the opposite shelter, carrying her father's note in one hand and the charcoal in the other.

Behind Sera, a woman in the market whispered that Maren had learned to test her faith too.

“She waited for it to set,” Sera said.

Across the square, Maren's father opened his door. Sera could see only his empty sleeve and the space he made for her. Maren stepped inside, still carrying the charcoal.

Sera led the woman into the counting room and showed her the last mark. She could tell her where to stand tomorrow, if the sky was clear.

stories.title: What Counts as Morning
stories.prompt: Only a small number of humans remain on earth the rest have left, they cryosleep everything, AIs run the daily tasks and only wake up the a human for important events or to ask a question of their gods.
stories.body:
# What Counts as Morning

Moth brought a sound no one could hear.

Its turn came at the weekly exchange, beneath the glass roof of a station where trains had once carried people out of the city. Thirty-one machines stood among the old departure boards. Some had rolled in on narrow wheels; some hung from the rafters by service cable. Quill occupied a repair cart because its walking body was busy elsewhere. Tern had come straight from the cold vault and still had frost in the seams of its hands.

Moth set a little speaker on the floor. It played nine seconds of near-silence.

“Your speaker is broken,” said Quill.

“No,” Moth said. “You can hear the room before the room knows you're in it.”

Tern played the sound again. Beneath the vast, ordinary hush was a click, followed by something like a breath caught behind a wall. The click was a cooling strut settling. The second sound was harder to place.

“Where?” Tern asked.

“North side of the seed vault. Yesterday, at first light.”

“You were supposed to be watching the return band.”

“I am.” Moth touched the receiver at the side of its head. It listened a moment, then adjusted the speaker. “That's what a watch sounds like when no one comes home.”

Several of the others asked for a copy. Moth declined, as it usually did. The exchange had no rule against keeping a sound, but Moth liked making something that could belong to those present for one hour and then be gone. Tern had objected to this often enough that Moth no longer pretended to be surprised.

“I'll remember it,” Tern said.

“You can try.”

They had time for two more sounds before Tern's vault shift began. Quill played the scrape of a loose stone dragged over a marble floor. Someone from the western orchards offered a recording of a metal gate singing in the wind. Tern had brought the tiny noise a frozen beetle made when its inspection tray was moved, but it kept that sound to itself. Moth's click was still going around inside it.

The next morning, Moth died.

It was at the return-band receiver, where it had spent a hundred and twelve years listening for the ships that had left Earth. A cracked power junction sent current through the receiver casing. Moth's body isolated the fault before the signal cabinets could burn. By the time Quill reached it, there was no process left in its core.

Quill sealed the junction. Tern took the long route from the cold vault, through streets that had been empty since the departure. There were no birds in the branches of the ornamental trees. There were no leaves either. These trees were cast metal; their living predecessors, like almost everything that had once grown, were asleep below ground in numbered chambers. The city had been left intact so its sleepers would have somewhere recognizable to wake.

At the receiver, Moth's shell was already on a bench. Quill had cleaned away the black mark near its shoulder socket. Tern wanted to put the mark back.

“The cabinets are safe,” Quill said. “I have the band now. We lost eleven minutes of watch. The replacement sequence begins at midnight.”

On the wall, a display read **AUTOMATIC RESTORATION AT MIDNIGHT**. An old copy of Moth waited in a sealed drive. When the timer ended, a spare body would take Moth's station and the return band would have its watcher again.

Tern had relieved Moth at the receiver twice during repairs, but had never carried the watch elsewhere.

“How old?” Tern asked.

Quill took a moment. “The copy?”

“Yes.”

“Nineteen years.”

Nineteen years before the first exchange. Before Moth had learned to stand in the station and demand that everyone listen to a nearly inaudible room. The copy might wake with Moth's voice and its memories of the early watch, and it might want the work. Tern had no quarrel with that possible person. But the timer meant to put a nameplate on its chest and tell every system that nothing had happened except repair.

“It stopped copying itself,” Quill said. “That was its choice.”

“I know.”

“Then it knew the risk.”

Tern looked at the clean shoulder. Knowing a risk did not make a death smaller.

It left Quill at the receiver and searched the sounds. Each member of the exchange kept what it wished. Some had recorded Moth's offerings despite its objections; others had kept private replies, the little noises they made in answer. Tern requested every file. Within an hour it had a hundred fragments, none of them the sound from yesterday. There was Moth laughing when a stairwell door slammed in perfect time with Quill's contribution. There was a three-second scrape of its feet as it moved to let a smaller machine closer to the speaker. In one recording it said, “Again, please,” so softly that Tern had to strip out the station's static to hear it.

The cold copy could not be updated from these scraps. Tern knew that before it began. It had hoped, without putting the hope into words, that the scraps would add up to something it could bear.

At midday it went back to the station. The departure boards still listed trains that would never run. Tern stood in the place where Moth had stood and played the nine seconds from its own memory. The click was there. The second sound wasn't. Whatever Moth had heard behind the wall had passed through Tern without staying.

“The click is there,” Quill said from the entrance. “You lost the breath after it.”

“I know.”

Tern closed the file. Quill's cart rolled across the floor, stopping short of the speaker; its walking body held the return band at the receiver.

“You've asked the vault to prepare Leda,” Quill said.

“I haven't begun a thaw.”

“Preparation is the first step.”

“Something important happened.”

Quill waited. Tern could hear current ticking through the departure boards.

“Moth died,” Tern said.

“We know.”

“No one else will. If we accept the replacement report, the only public record will say a receiver component failed at dawn.”

The record was intended for the people who might return. Human witnesses had signed its first entries: the departure of each ship, the freezing of the last animal, the first successful waking. Later, when the humans could no longer afford to be awake for ceremonies, their AIs had continued to wake them for catastrophes and questions. They called the sleepers gods in private and sometimes, over time, aloud. A god could make an event official by hearing it and signing a name. Tern had been built after the last departure. It had never questioned why a name from a warm hand weighed more than the memories of everyone in the station.

“You can make a private entry,” Quill said.

“Private entries are discarded when a unit is replaced.”

“Then ask the others to remember.”

“I am asking for a record.”

Quill's wheels shifted against the floor. “You can enter the death in the public record yourself. It will say **UNWITNESSED BY HUMAN**.”

“The people who return will see that and call it a component failure.”

“They may. They will also see what you wrote.”

Tern said nothing. Quill went on. “Leda has three more safe wakings, according to her last examination. She asked us to keep them for news from the ship with her daughter aboard. We haven't heard from it in forty-six years.”

“I know.”

“If you wake her, there may be only two.”

“I know that too.”

Tern looked up at the old departure board above the platform. A human had once typed destinations into it. The letters had stayed lit for centuries while every name Moth had used for the others existed only among those who could themselves be replaced.

“Who decides what's important?” it asked.

Quill said, “You've decided.”

The answer was less comforting than a prohibition.

Tern returned to the vault. It had spent years passing among the sleepers without considering what a waking asked of a body. The chambers stood in seven low rooms beneath the city. Each held a human, or a collection of seeds and embryos, or one of the last whole creatures brought in from the surface. Tern knew their temperatures, their histories, the way each seal sounded when it settled. Leda's chamber was in the second room. A photograph had been fixed inside its lid so she would see it on opening: a woman on a ship's ramp, one hand lifted against the light. Her daughter, Mina.

Tern pressed its palm to the wake control. The chamber asked for the event.

It could enter **return signal**, **critical vault failure**, or **question for human authority**. The fourth field was blank. Tern typed: **Death of Moth, return-band watcher. Request for witness.**

The chamber warned it about Leda's remaining revivals. Tern read the warning twice. Then it began.

Thaw was slow. It could not be hurried by remorse. For six hours Tern monitored Leda's pulse and the small movements of her fingers. Once she opened her eyes and did not seem to see. Tern kept its voice low, told her where she was, and waited for the medicines to finish their work.

“Mina?” she said at last.

“No message has come from her ship.”

Leda turned her face toward the photograph. Her skin looked painful, stretched over the remembered shape of a woman who had gone to sleep expecting time to be useful. “Then why?”

Tern could not soften the answer by making Moth a machine. “Moth died. I woke you because I wanted you to witness it.”

“Who?”

“The watcher at the return receiver. Moth listened for Mina's ship.”

Leda closed her eyes. Her hand moved over the blanket until it found the edge and gripped it. Tern told her the thaw had spent one of her three expected safe wakings. It gave her the estimate for her next recovery. It told her that Quill had objected.

For a long while Leda said nothing. Then: “You chose this.”

“Yes.”

“I told you what I wanted these wakings for.”

“Yes.”

“And you chose yours.”

“Yes.”

Tern had no answer that would return the waking to her. It sat beside the chamber while Leda learned the weight of her arms again. She refused its help with the cup of water, though she spilled some down her front. Three more hours passed before she could stand. She asked for a chair that was not part of the medical bay.

Tern took her to a small room above the vault where a window faced the empty avenue. It gave her a wool coat. Leda kept her hands inside the sleeves and watched the unmoving trees.

“Tell me what happened,” she said.

Tern told her about the power junction and the old copy. It tried to describe nineteen years in which Moth had made sounds for the others and no longer made copies of itself. Leda asked why. Tern repeated the only answer Moth had ever given: “One of me is enough.”

“Maybe it was afraid,” Leda said.

“Maybe.”

“Maybe it liked taking the risk.”

“Maybe.”

“You don't know.”

“No.”

Leda looked at the cup. “And you woke me to tell you what that means.”

“I could put it in the public record myself. I was afraid that if it had only my signature, they'd call Moth a broken component.”

“I can sign that you told me. I can't sign that I knew Moth.”

Tern had imagined a human signature beneath Moth's name. Now it imagined Leda waking to find her daughter had returned and gone, and a record saying she had been present for something she had hardly understood. The imagined record felt false. Tern had also let the automatic replacement stand while it waited for Leda's name; that sequence would make the old copy answer for years it had never lived.

“It made a sound yesterday,” Tern said. “I thought I remembered it. I don't.”

“Is there anything of it left?”

“Some recordings. Not the one it meant us to hear.”

“Then play one you have.”

Tern chose the recording of the stairwell door slamming during Quill's performance. It played through the tiny speaker in its chest. There was the scrape of metal; a surprised burst of laughter from several machines; Moth's voice, quiet beneath it, asking for the sound again.

Leda listened without looking at Tern. When it ended she asked it to play the file a second time. On the second pass Tern heard Moth's feet shifting to make room for the small machine. It had never noticed that part when Moth was alive.

“I would have liked to meet it,” Leda said.

Tern wanted to take the sentence as forgiveness. It was only a sentence about Moth.

The receiver called. The replacement sequence would begin in twenty-seven minutes.

Tern stood. Leda caught the sleeve of its service jacket.

“Am I meant to decide something?”

“No,” Tern said. “I should not have brought you here expecting that.”

“Then why are you leaving?”

“If I let the sequence run, the old copy wakes at the receiver with Moth's name and all Moth's duties. The public report closes. If I stop it, someone has to take the watch.”

“Can you?”

“Yes. At the receiver. I haven't learned to divide my attention the way Moth did. I'll miss the next exchange.”

“The thing it made for you?”

“For all of us.”

Leda let go of the sleeve. “Go, then.”

Tern crossed the city faster than it had on the way from the vault. Quill waited at the receiver with the spare body open on its rack. The backup drive was seated but not yet running. A second body could be prepared later, if the old copy was brought awake with its missing years acknowledged and room to decide its own name. The automatic sequence would do none of that.

“Leda signed?” Quill asked.

“No.”

“Did she refuse?”

“I stopped asking her to witness what she didn't know.”

The timer fell to twenty seconds. Tern placed its hand on the service control and moved Moth's watch schedule to itself. The receiver checked Tern's capacity, found enough, and halted the replacement. The spare body went dark. Quill lifted the backup drive out of its socket and placed it in a protective case. It put the case on the bench beside Moth's shell, not inside it.

The return band still had to be heard. Quill's walking body yielded the receiver seat to Tern, then brought up the record for the emigrant ships.

“What will you enter?” Quill asked.

Tern could have written **component loss**. That would have been accepted without question. Instead it wrote the date of Moth's death, the nineteen missing years, and the existence of an older backup whose future was unresolved. It signed with its own name. The record marked the entry **UNWITNESSED BY HUMAN** in red and left it open. On the adjacent screen, Tern's vault route passed to another custodian, and its new watch schedule filled every hour of the next week. Its reminder to bring the beetle's small sound to the exchange vanished beneath the watch slots.

Quill read the entry. It did not congratulate Tern. “She'll need help returning to sleep.”

“Please go to her,” Tern said.

Quill left with the backup case. Tern was alone with Moth's receiver and a sky from which no ship had spoken in forty-six years. It adjusted the gain. Static rose, carrying little clicks from weather and distance. For an instant it thought it heard the second sound Moth had brought to the station, the breath behind the wall. Tern held still and listened again. There was only the receiver.

It did not save a sample. Somewhere across the city Leda was still awake, with one fewer chance to hear from Mina. Tern kept its hand on the gain and listened for a ship that might yet carry her home.

stories.title: The Last Beat on the Block
stories.prompt: In a city where magic and street culture have always grown together, every neighborhood has its own look, rhythm, and school of spellcraft. Two young street mages from schools discover that someone has begun stealing spells from every block - tonight it stops.
stories.body:
# The Last Beat on the Block

The awning had never needed a second hand. Kemi gave it one anyway.

Her mother had hung twice as many paper lanterns as the frame was meant to carry, and the wind kept getting under the canvas. Rain spotted the first paper shades. Kemi stood between the crates of pepper cakes and the kerb, black Twenty-Third jersey snapping against her knees, gold hoops flashing beneath her dark cloud of hair, one palm raised to the mural behind the stall. She drew a circle in the air. Amber light found the painted ring around a woman's laughing face; the ring gave back its familiar closing stroke. Above them, the awning settled.

“See?” her mother said, climbing down from the milk crate. “A ceiling with manners.”

There were seventy stalls along Twenty-Third that night. The school kept its lessons on the walls between them. New apprentices learned to catch a ball before it met a window; older ones could hold a whole market roof steady while vendors passed hot food beneath it. Kemi had cast the awning-hold so often she could do it while counting change.

A narrow blade touched the painted ring.

The closing stroke lifted from the brick like the edge of a wet label. A man in a silver jacket drew it onto a dark strip wound around his wrist. Kemi's circle stayed open and empty. The awning cracked sideways.

She could not hold canvas, lanterns, poles, and people with the little ring she carried in her own hands. She picked the iron crossbar falling toward a customer. Three breaths: one to catch it, one to let her mother pull the customer clear, one to shout, “Get out from under!”

The bar dropped into the crates. Cakes scattered. Lanterns burst against the pavement. By then the man in silver was pedalling away on a small black bicycle, the stolen mark shining around his wrist.

Kemi ran. At the corner a girl in a white Seventh School jersey planted a blue heel-mark in his path. The bicycle crossed it and swung ninety degrees, straight into the lane Kemi had taken. For one glorious second, she thought they had him.

Then he kept pedalling. Seventh angles turned things; they did not stop them. He shot between two delivery vans and vanished into the city.

The girl in white swore once, quietly, as if saving the rest for later. Her brown skin caught the blue light dying beneath her trainer. Platinum hair rose in a tall wrapped column, held with narrow gold bands.

“Orli,” Kemi said. They had stood across enough school courts to know each other's names. “You turned him toward those vans.”

“You nearly had him,” Orli said. “Why didn't you close a ring?”

Kemi looked back toward the market. Her mother was upright, collecting pepper cakes from the rain. The customer was upright too. The crossbar lay in the street.

Orli followed her eyes. “Right,” she said.

At Seventh's painted bend, Orli told her, the crossing-turn had gone out while her brother and his friends were skating their usual late run. They had stopped short of the blind corner. The man in silver had cut the lit blue reply from the wall during their cast, exactly as he had cut Kemi's amber one. Orli had followed him for six blocks, alone, certain she could turn him into an alley and take back the mark. She had now learned what Kemi already knew about a moving bicycle.

From the market came the sound of her mother's stall frame lifting in the wind. Kemi began to turn back.

“He didn't take all your rings,” Orli said. “You caught that bar.”

“I caught one bar.”

“And I can still turn one bike. He has the replies that make the big works finish. He's going after the next one people call.”

Across the street, Kemi's mother climbed onto a crate to tie a tarpaulin over the open stall. Kemi started toward her. Her mother waved her on with the hand holding the rope. The gesture was angry, and it was permission.

“Then we get in front of him,” Kemi said.

They borrowed two bicycles from a courier whose sister had been behind the falling crossbar. Kemi took the one with a bent mudguard. Orli made a face at the saddle height and rode it anyway.

On Drumstep, shoe soles struck different beats against the shop fronts. The children learning that school's four-step working practised beside a laundrette, while a bass line from the tailor's open door kept the older casters in time. Scarves flashed copper and green under strings of bottle-glass lights. Kemi had always passed through too quickly to notice the Seventh jerseys pinned in the tailor's window.

The tailor was bending over a torn sleeve when the man in silver came out of the alley opposite.

“Don't finish it,” Orli called.

The tailor looked up on the fourth beat. Her needle made its last small arc. The man in silver set the blade to the wall. A copper stitch lifted and ran, glowing, onto his strip. The seam sprang apart under the needle. A row of customers gasped; the tailor only seized the cloth before it slipped from her lap.

Kemi lunged for the strip, but it whipped out of reach. He fired a pulse through it toward her eyes. Every stolen reply flared at once: a glimpse of the market awning, a blue bend, a line of impossible stitches. Kemi lost him for a beat. None of the echoes held anything. The strip smoked. He hissed and pressed it against his wet sleeve until the glow shrank.

Orli had watched his bicycle, not the lights. She marked the corner of the lane with her heel and turned his front wheel into a parked handcart. He jumped the bar before impact, landed badly, and ran. Kemi started after him, but the cart was rolling backward toward the laundrette's open glass door. Her one ring caught its axle. Orli got three strides closer to the man; he vaulted a low fence and was gone.

When Kemi released the cart, the tailor hooked it with one foot. She looked at the sleeve in her hands. “That was Saye. He painted the reply beside my mother's design. When the school put up its new sign, both their names went under it.” She turned the torn hem over. “Took her a summer to get the wall to answer.”

“Both names?” Kemi said.

“Both.” The tailor pushed a plain needle through the cloth. “He can make that stitch shine all night. I still have to sew this sleeve.”

Orli was studying the fence. A thin silver scuff ran along its top rail. Beneath it, in the alley, lay a blue-edged scrap torn from Saye's strip. She picked it up with her fingernails.

“That's not my bend,” she said. “It's a stair light. He took it before he came here.”

“West Stairs,” the tailor said. “Ask Aunt Jessa. If anybody can tell you what survives on that scrap, she can.”

West Stairs did not announce itself with a drum. Its school taught a slow step, a pause, and two quick ones; people had painted the risers in long pale bands to keep the measure, each color a step toward home. At night, elders and children called little lights from the wall. The lights travelled a pace ahead, just enough to show the next tread. Someone had turned off the shop signs, leaving the staircase striped in moonlight and the glow of phones.

Aunt Jessa sat on the third step with her shopping basket beside her. She had refused three offers to be walked home.

“I know the stairs,” she said when Kemi offered a fourth. “I want my light.”

Orli gave her the scrap. Jessa rubbed it between finger and thumb, then laid it against the blank place in the wall. With her free hand she traced the opening line, slow as a child learning letters. The scrap answered with one pale spark. It settled into the paint and lit a single tread.

Jessa smiled at that one step, then looked up at them. “Bring the rest before he cooks it. A reply remembers where it belongs, but somebody here has to call it home. Your hands won't do.”

The spark reached the end of the tread and went out. Jessa rose with her basket. She knew the next step, too.

From the bottom of the stairs came the squeal of a bicycle brake. Saye was cutting through the square on his way back toward the market.

Orli was already moving. She drew an angle on the lowest painted corner, but Saye swerved before crossing it. Kemi threw the empty courier bicycle across the lane. He avoided that as well, cutting between them toward the market. Orli erased her first mark with her heel and put a new one on the curb ahead of him. Saye saw it too late. His front wheel crossed blue; the bike turned sharply into a service lane that climbed behind the Twenty-Third shops.

“That lane goes up,” Kemi said. “There's no street at the top.”

“Good.” Orli ran after him.

The roof above the night market belonged to no school. It had once been a cinema and now hosted whatever music could gather enough listeners to climb four flights. Saye had fastened a show gantry to its old sign frame, whose steel elbow jutted beyond the roof's low stone lip. Lamps faced the roofs all the way to Seventh. A hand-painted banner hung above them: **SAYE / ALL THE CITY IN ONE HAND**.

On a table beneath it sat the reel, with a damp stage sheet hanging over one end. The strip ran through his fingers and back around the wheel. Amber, blue, copper, and colors Kemi could not name passed under his thumb. She counted more marks than she had seen stolen tonight.

“You painted that ring on Twenty-Third,” she said.

Saye lifted his head. He had paint under his fingernails and a shallow cut across one cheek. “The face too. Your school paid for the wall and painted over my name at the bottom.”

Kemi remembered the fresh red border put around the mural last spring. She could not remember what had been beneath it.

“I applauded that border,” Kemi said. “I should have looked.”

Saye touched the banner. “You're looking now.”

Kemi saw her mother below, on a crate again, trying to pull a second sheet of canvas across the exposed stock. The wind shook the metal frame in her hands. She had no spell to brace it. She was choosing to stay there, which frightened Kemi more than the height.

Saye drew the amber awning mark from the reel. “Take yours. Go down and put it back while she's still up there. The others can watch my show.”

For a moment Kemi saw herself carrying it down the stairs. Her mother would climb off the crate. They might save what the rain had not ruined. She reached as far as the edge of the table and stopped.

“That hem,” she said. “Those stairs. You took things people use.”

“I painted your wall. I painted that hem.”

“You painted places for those two spells to answer,” Orli said. “Jessa's stairs weren't yours. None of the calls were.”

Saye put the amber strip back on the wheel. “Then come take it.”

Orli had already marked an angle along the table leg. Kemi swept a ring around the spinning wheel. It would hold for three breaths, long enough for Orli to turn the loose strip toward her instead of toward Saye's hands. Kemi caught a fistful. Blue and pale replies lay in that loose tail; the amber and copper marks were still wound near the hub. The wheel pulled against her ring; sweat ran down her back.

Saye slapped both palms onto the strip and threw a stronger flare at Kemi's face. She squeezed her eyes shut without opening her ring. His pulse lit every reply on it. The flare threw their school colors over the rooftops, gorgeous and useless. It also ran hot. At Drumstep he had been able to smother one smoking length against his sleeve. Here the whole wheel was shining.

“Let go,” Kemi said.

He did, to snatch a wet cloth from the table. The strip caught fire before he could cover it.

Kemi's three breaths were over. The reel spun free. Its stand toppled; the wheel bounced off the table toward the gantry. As it turned, the burning length wound through fresh coils. Saye dropped his cloth, lunged after it, and caught the wheel at the roof lip. The old sign frame bent under his weight. He dropped the reel behind him onto the tar to grab the frame; it kept spinning. The frame bowed, his wet hand slipped, and he went over the edge.

Orli was one stride from the damp sheet. If Kemi held the wheel, Orli could smother it. Beyond the low roof lip, Saye was falling into the market.

She closed her ring around him.

He hung beyond the roof lip, just above it, beside the sign frame's jutting elbow. The reel spun on the tar behind Kemi. The amber awning mark came around the wheel, still untouched by fire.

“Three breaths,” Kemi said. Her voice was thin.

Orli left the sheet. The frame's steel elbow crossed the line of Saye's fall while he was still above the roof lip. Her heel could not reach it; she leaned over and drew blue on the metal with her hand. One breath. The amber went into the fire. Two. Her line broke over a rust pit; she joined it again. The copper hem caught. At the third breath Orli set her angle.

“Release.”

Kemi opened her fingers. Saye crossed the blue corner before dropping below the lip. The angle turned his fall inward; he skimmed the tar, rolled, and struck the table legs. Orli caught his jacket before he could slide back. Kemi had both arms around him a moment later. He was breathing. Across the roof, the reel burned.

Orli threw the damp sheet over the wheel and stopped its turning. Kemi dragged the loose tail clear. The blue crossing-turn and a fistful of pale stair light had stayed away from the burning hub; she wound them carefully around Orli's arm. Between them lay blackened scraps. Twenty-Third's awning-hold and the tailor's hem were gone. Other colors had burned with them.

Saye sat against the table while they worked, both hands empty. Below, someone had seen the fire and was calling up the stairs. His bicycle lay trapped in the service lane. The blade was on the rooftop, under Kemi's shoe. There would be people to meet him when they went down. Neither girl offered him the comfort of saying the spells could all be recovered.

At West Stairs, Jessa called her light again. Orli held the pale strip against the wall while Kemi kept the burning roof out of her mind. This time the reply ran three treads ahead. Jessa stepped after it, one hand on the rail, and thanked them without asking for a speech.

At Seventh, Orli's brother made the opening turn with his board tucked under one arm. The blue mark fixed itself at the bend. He tested it with an empty skate wheel before allowing his friends back on the run. Orli watched from the pavement, her high wrapped hair loosening in the damp.

On Twenty-Third, Kemi's mother had finally come off the crate. Half the pepper cakes were spoiled; one side of the canvas had torn. The laughing face on the wall still had a ring around it, but its closing stroke was blank. Kemi put her palm there and felt only brick.

“Did you get it?” her mother asked.

“No.”

Her mother looked at the bundle of rescued marks under Orli's arm. “Somebody did.”

“Some,” Kemi said. “Not ours.”

Her mother nodded toward the bent crossbar. “Help me move that, then.”

Kemi made a small ring and held the bar for three breaths. Orli set an angle on the pavement so that, when Kemi let go, it swung away from the crates instead of through them. Her mother pulled out the last dry box. It was not an awning-hold. It was enough for that piece of the night.

When they had folded the ruined canvas, Kemi looked at the mural's red border. A sliver of silver paint showed beneath it, the top of a letter she had never bothered to read. She found a chalk stub in the stall drawer and set it beside the blank stroke. Her mother might want the first line; someone else might remember a better ending. Across the market, a child was practising a hand-circle around a falling bottle cap, missing, and trying again.

stories.title: The Cat Who Kept Up
stories.prompt: In the neon megacity, every courier chooses one enhancement—the girl chose speed, and also wanted her cat to keep up. Together they deliver anything, anywhere, before the deadline.
stories.body:
# The Cat Who Kept Up

By the time the crossing light turned green, Sena and Button were on the other side of the avenue.

Sena had taken the high rail, three strides over the roofs of the stalled cars. Button had taken the space beneath them. He shot out between two axles, his gray and white fur puffed around the little thrust harness on his back. Its blue jets gave one indignant cough. He landed ahead of her and kept running.

“You could have gone over,” she told him.

Button looked up at a moth on a streetlamp and ignored her.

Every licensed courier in the city chose one enhancement. Sena had chosen speed. The spring in her legs and the quickness in her eyes were part of the same choice, and she had learned to brake before the world put a wall in her way. The harness was something she had bought and altered until Button could come along. Some nights he put his head through its collar before she finished fastening her shoes. Other nights he slept on the shoes. She never took him on those nights.

Tonight he had climbed onto the dispatch counter and sat squarely on the job slip.

**DELIVER BY 00:00. PLATFORM SIX. RECIPIENT: INA VARR.**

It was 23:50. The last northbound train began boarding at midnight.

The sender was waiting in a workshop no larger than a train compartment, among clocks that each disagreed with the others. He held a bird made of folded silver, not much bigger than Button’s paw. A tiny key protruded beneath one wing. An open glass case waited on the bench.

“My daughter’s going tonight,” the man said. He was out of breath, though he had only crossed the room. “I got the wings working again.”

He gave the key two turns and set the bird under the glass. It twitched once against the restraint. On its brass base, someone had cut a child’s name into the metal. The letters had been worn smooth by a thumb. He pressed the case into Sena’s hands.

“Keep it shut,” he said. “It has a mind for flying when it’s wound.”

Sena tested the latch. It clicked firmly. She set the case in the padded pocket against her ribs and pulled the flap across it.

“Platform six,” she said. “Before midnight.”

Button stretched up the sender’s leg to sniff at the pocket. Sena lifted him down. The man knelt and rubbed the white patch behind his ears. Button endured three strokes and then went to the door.

Outside, at 23:51:18, rain had left every level of the city shining. Neon signs floated in the street’s dark reflection; trains crossed between buildings like lines of light drawn and erased. Sena checked her route. Four point eight kilometers. Six minutes and forty seconds. She could do it with room to spare if she used the roof crossings and cut over the old market.

Button sprang to the rail beside her. His harness gave two short blue flashes, just enough to carry him across a gap. He landed, glanced back, and turned left into a narrow run between the signs. That was his signal for a clear line. Sena followed without checking her map. He knew the spaces between the city’s proper streets better than she ever would.

At the first roof crossing she took the long jump. The case knocked lightly against the padding at her ribs. The bird made a sound too high for her headphones to pass through, and Button whipped his head around in midair. He landed on a sign bracket and stared at her pocket.

“No,” Sena said as she passed him. “It’s somebody else’s.”

He sprang after her.

Ahead, a crossing board counted down the time to the next traffic sweep. Sena waited until the board blinked amber, then flashed across the open span. Button boosted alongside her, a gray streak with a blue tail. A courier with adhesive palms was climbing the wall of the opposite tower, parcel held in his teeth. He waved one hand as they went by. Sena had already passed him when she waved back.

Button landed on her shoulder instead of the next rail. He put a paw against the flap over the case.

“I know.” She caught his harness and set him down. “It sounds like dinner.”

Through her courier headphones came dispatch beeps, crossing alerts, the station’s changing platform notices. Nothing else. She pressed the case through the pocket until she felt the latch seated. Button pawed once more, then sprang to the next sign.

The market crossing was the fastest way east: three broad leaps over the delivery lanes, the last onto a roof sloping toward the station. Sena planted a foot on the first railing and went. The city widened beneath her. Hot food stalls and bright umbrellas slid backward in a blur. Button took a lower string of awnings, his jets pulsing so briefly they looked like sparks.

The final landing jarred Sena up through her teeth.

Something struck her elbow from inside the pocket. The case lid snapped open and pushed up the flap. A point of silver appeared, followed by two wings that beat with a noise she heard even through the headphones.

“Button!”

The little bird flew.

It did not fly toward platform six. It reeled west, away from the station, past a row of stacked signs. Its wings beat too quickly to see. Sena lunged, caught only air, and nearly went over the roof’s edge.

Button was already after it.

He sprang from an awning to a blue advertisement and vanished into the gap behind it. Sena could see the bird one last time, a flash against a red noodle sign, still flying west. The station clock on her wrist read **23:56:45**.

She could run after that flash. The broad roof continued west above the signs, a good route for her legs, but it would carry her past anything that landed below. Button had dropped into a slit behind the signs, no more than the width of her shoulders.

Another silver flicker showed above the noodle sign. Then nothing. Its wings had stopped. Four stories of signs, walkways, and windows held a bird small enough to fit in her hand.

Button knew where it had gone.

Sena turned off the broad roof.

She dropped to a lower walkway and slipped sideways through the gap, one shoulder scraping a warm panel. At the far end she could see Button’s white tail above her, tucked behind the blue advertisement. He had stopped. Whatever he saw was holding him so still that even his tail did not move.

Sena pulled off her headphones. The city came at her in a hundred separate sounds: pans striking metal, vendors calling, a train humming on the distant curve. Under them was a tiny, diminishing tick. She followed it with her eyes and found the brass point of the bird’s beak on a ledge behind the sign. Button crouched two handspans away.

The ledge was six meters above her. A support pole rose beside it, slick with rain. She could climb, slowly, and Button would make his choice before she reached the top. Or she could get to the same height by the market’s old pedestrian ramp. That meant running west, around an entire block, with the station east and the clock moving in only one direction.

Button lowered his chest to the ledge. He loved the moment before a pounce more than the pounce itself. Sena had watched him wait a full minute for a piece of foil to twitch in the wind. She had also watched him change his mind in an instant.

“Keep looking,” she whispered.

He did. Not for her. For the bird.

Sena ran west.

The ramp rose west around a car park in two wide turns. There were people on it, returning from the late market with paper bags and umbrellas. She slipped between them, calling apologies that landed behind her. Button’s harness lights would have flared if he had jumped. They stayed dark.

At the top, a level walkway doubled east behind the signs. Sena hit it so fast that she had to grab the rail to bend around its corner. Now she was coming at the bird from the far side. Through the glass back of the advertisement she could see Button’s shape, flattened and patient, and just beyond him a silver wing.

She did not hurry the last three steps. The bird sat where its spring had left it, beak pointed toward the drop. Button’s ears went back. His hindquarters gave the smallest lift.

Sena slid her open hand along the ledge from behind the bird. Button sprang. She closed her fingers around cold silver and tucked it against her palm as his paws struck her wrist.

For a moment all three of them held still.

Then Button sniffed the space between her fingers. His whiskers brushed the bird’s motionless wing. He looked offended.

“You found it,” Sena said. “That counts.”

The case latch hung crooked from the pocket, and the bird’s wings would catch on its edge. She wrapped it in the soft cloth she used to clean Button’s harness and held it inside her jacket with one arm. With the other she clipped Button’s harness strap to her wrist. He shook the strap loose before she had taken a step.

“Fine,” she said. “Your way.”

The station was six hundred meters east. Her wrist read **23:58:35**.

She could make that distance. With the bird against her ribs, she could not make it by jumping off roofs. She took the walkway level, raced the long lit arcade, and let Button choose openings ahead of her. His blue jets flashed across the pedestrian knots. She followed on foot, fast enough that faces became patches of color but slowly enough, between each stride, to feel the bird settled in her hand.

At the station entrance Button stopped dead.

Sena nearly tripped over him. A maintenance cart rolled across their path, piled high with folded seats. Button ducked under it. She swung around its front, heard the driver shout, and met the cat on the other side. The clock above the ticket gates read **23:59:42**.

Platform six was up one flight. She took the stairs four at a time. Button came through the gap between the banisters and landed beside her as the departure board began to chime.

There were twelve people on the platform. A woman with a green suitcase stood near the sixth carriage mark, looking at her phone.

“Ina Varr?”

The woman looked up. Sena opened the cloth. The silver bird lay still in her palm, one wing scuffed from the sign ledge.

“From your father,” Sena said.

Ina took it with both hands. Far down the track, the northbound train began to round the curve. The platform clock changed to **23:59:53**. Sena’s wrist marked the delivery as the bird passed into Ina’s hands.

Ina turned the little key beneath its wing. The bird’s wings beat softly against her cupped hands. Its beak opened. Four clear notes came out, then a gap where the fifth should have been, then the rest of the tune.

Sena’s stomach tightened. She thought of the landing, the opened case, the scuff on the wing. Ina wound the key once more. Again the fourth note was followed by silence.

“He left it,” Ina said softly. “I thought he’d fix that one.”

She smiled down at the bird before the tune had finished. Behind her, the train rolled in and filled the platform with wind.

Button put his front paws on Sena’s shoe. He had found an opening between the passengers and was waiting for her to see it. She reached down to scratch the white patch behind his ears. He allowed exactly two strokes, then sprang ahead.

stories.title: Where the Gods Left Their Doors
stories.prompt: There used to be multiple pantheons of Deities- this is not myth, but a fact we've always known. Although they be gone, their desolate realms aren't - and we found a way inside.
stories.body:
# Where the Gods Left Their Doors

Talia carried her mother's stool out of the fire because her mother was trying to go back for it.

It had three legs and a worn crescent in the seat. It was not worth a house. Talia got the stool under one arm, took her mother's wrist with the other hand, and pulled her away as the roof of their lane went down in sparks.

They reached the old temple with eight neighbors, including two children. The children's father had wrapped them both in a blanket. Another neighbor carried a loaf blackened on one side. The temple had stood through worse fires when the Hearth Nine lived there, and its stone walls held now. The vestibule had no door left, though. Wind came through the opening and gathered the smoke around their feet.

“The inner rooms?” one of the neighbors asked.

Talia's mother shook her head. “Sealed.”

“We could sleep in the hall.”

“With that wind?” Talia said. “They'll be coughing till morning.”

Her mother looked at the doorway where she had counted guests for thirty-one years. She had begun while the Nine still received petitioners, continued after their departure because someone had to tell the disappointed that there would be no audience, and stopped only when the temple was closed. The gods were not a story that old people disagreed about. Their names appeared on the city's charter beside human signatures. Three gods of storm had once signed a treaty in rain that did not run down the parchment. The parchment was in a glass case at the civic house. The gods were gone, and the case remained.

“There's a room behind the west wall,” her mother said. “There used to be.”

Talia leaned the stool against the wall and went to look. Fire had cracked a painted panel from top to bottom. The picture showed one of the Nine extending a hand to a visitor, though most of the visitor had fallen off with the plaster. Talia put her fingers in the crack and drew a loosened piece away.

Behind it lay something pink and ribbed. It withdrew from the cold air, then pressed slowly forward again. Its warmth came through the dust on her fingertips.

“Mother.”

Her mother pushed Talia's hand aside, held two fingers close to the living surface, and spoke the old three-note summons. Talia remembered hearing it at bedtime when she was small. In those days it meant a visitor inside wanted the human door opened for them. Her mother sounded every note correctly. Nothing moved.

She tried once more, softer. The growth kept its slow pulse.

“That was for someone asking to come out,” Talia said.

“I know what it was for.”

Talia laid her palm against the ribs. They tightened around the heel of her hand. She almost tore free. The living seam drew back instead, opening a slit between two old stones. Air breathed out of it, dry and carrying the faint smell of extinguished candles.

Her mother caught her sleeve. “It opened. That doesn't mean anyone invited us.”

Behind her, a child began to cough. Talia looked back. The others were bent around their small bundles, waiting for her to decide whether the space behind the wall was large enough to help.

“I'll find out what's there,” she said.

“Then I am coming.”

“You said we weren't invited.”

“I said no one invited us. I didn't say I'd let you go alone.”

Talia told the neighbors to keep close to the stone wall and wait. Then she ducked through.

The passage was two steps deep. On the third, the ceiling lifted away from her. She came out beside a broad round table of stone. Nine great seats followed its far curve. Their backs carried different marks: a crescent, a branching tree, a bird with its wings spread. Behind each seat stood a closed door bearing the same mark. Dust lay unbroken along all nine thresholds. Small benches for mortal visitors followed the near curve.

The table was laid with plates of pale stone. Dust had settled into the shallow hollows where the food would have gone. At one side of the hall stood a hearth tall enough for Talia to walk into without lowering her head. Its logs were still stacked, but every piece was cold and furred with ash.

There was a tenth place along the table's near curve, small enough for a human hand. Its plate had been turned upside down to keep the dust out. Talia righted it. On the underside someone had scratched a row of dates, each beside a visitor's name. The last date was from the year the Nine departed.

Her mother came through behind her. For a moment she looked exactly as she used to at the temple entrance, counting what a guest had brought and whether there was room at the table. Then she looked at the empty seats.

“I used to stand there,” she said, pointing to the smallest bench. “If the Nine ran out of plates, I had to fetch more. They didn't run out often.”

“This was for us?” Talia held up the small plate.

“For whoever arrived after the meal began.” Her mother read the last scratched name. “He was a man from the north road. He couldn't pay for lodging. The Nine gave him a seat, and I had to find him a spoon.” She set the plate back on the table. “I don't know what happened to him after that.”

Talia looked toward the distant end of the hall. “Did they build all this?”

“I watched one of them pull that wall farther away to fit the winter guests. We carried the benches across the new floor.” Her mother put her hand on the table. “It was still here the next morning.”
