I let that sit. I didn't want to force her into showing me something she had not offered, and the question had already cost a line at her wrist. Then she held up her hand where I could see it over the board.

"Would it help to watch?"

"If you want me to."

A thread of red appeared between her finger and thumb. She pulled it through the air as if drawing silk from a spool. Blue and green followed it; under her moving fingertips the threads bent into the shape of a tiny horse, jointed legs poised without a surface beneath them. Its colors touched the table and lit my charcoal sticks. A child passing the stall cried out and reached through the horse's flank. Her hand met empty air. The horse took three steps across the air, climbed nothing, and disappeared when Auvet lowered her fingers.

The child protested. Auvet gave her a small bow. "More in the square."

She wasn't speaking to me. I had opened the covered eye without noticing, pushing the rag aside with my brow. Auvet's inner light came at me all at once, much stronger than the little horse had looked to anyone else. I couldn't say whether the two sights had any relation. I only knew that my own marks on the paper disappeared in the glare. I drew the rag back into place.

"It walked," I said.

"Only three steps." She held up the fingers she'd used, checking a charcoal smudge left when she had touched my table. "I'm still learning the legs."

I glanced at the tabletop below where the horse had walked. There was no mark on the wood. "Could you make one hold still long enough for me to copy?"

"I tried. It goes when I stop." Auvet turned her hand palm up, then let it rest on her knee. "Can you draw from that?"

"From memory, perhaps. But I need your face first."

"Then hurry."

The music in the square had become a pattern rather than a test, with a flute taking up the space between drumbeats. I moved the board so the lamp shone across the paper instead of into my right eye. Auvet leaned forward to inspect a few lines. I asked her to sit back; she did, but she reached across and indicated the end of the eyebrow with one finger.

"There. You missed the gap."

"I see it."

"You didn't the first time."

I cut the notch into the dark line. She watched, then nodded. We worked that way for the next minute. She told me the lower edge of her coat was frayed, not embroidered. I had mistaken a loose thread in the lamplight. She said the left side of her hair was shorter because she'd cut it in a hurry, and no, she did not want it evened out on paper. She could be still only until the flute reached the familiar rising phrase; then one foot started moving under the chair. I drew it as far as the page allowed.

Auvet broke the end off a charcoal stick as she tried to turn it between her fingers. "Sorry."

"That's the short piece. I use it for darks."

"You're welcome, then." She set both pieces down. "May I see?"

I held the board so she could look without standing. Her face on the page was smaller than in the first drawing. The nose turned as it did when she faced me, the eyelid on the lamp side lowered a little, the mouth almost forming a word. The coat showed its worn cuff, not the shining folds I'd invented around the first figure. I had put more care into the gap in her eyebrow than into any surrounding shadow.

She looked at it for a long time, considering the paper at several angles. "My chin is sharper than that."

"A little." I made the correction while she held the pose.

"And that mark beside my mouth goes all the way to the corner when I smile."

"You're not smiling."

"I will be, when I see the person this is for. If you can catch a little of it."

I asked her to smile so I could see it. She obliged too broadly. We both knew it, and it fell away. The line remained for a breath. I marked its course, then rubbed the end gently with a clean thumb so it belonged to the face in front of me.

"Better," she said. "What's this space?" She pointed to the blank beside her hand.

"I meant to ask." I pulled the rag clear of my left eye to look at her, not at the page. The gold-white center crowded back into view. "Do you want any of what I see in the drawing? I have chalk."

She studied the empty space. "If it's all around my head, no. The person getting this has heard me describe the show often enough, but hasn't seen it. Could you put the horse there? In my hand?"

"A small one. You made it above the table, though."

"Put my hand higher, then. It was there for a moment." She raised it to the height where the horse had walked. "I won't ask you to invent the legs. You've seen how bad mine are."

I steadied the second portrait on the board and moved her drawn arm, only a little; the old line disappeared under the heel of my hand, leaving a grey seam in the sleeve. Auvet checked it before I continued. With the right eye I could remember the horse's red spine, its blue belly, the green steps that had fallen through air. I laid three short chalk strokes over the charcoal, then added a fourth where its foreleg should have bent. In the page it rested just above her fingers. It wasn't a likeness of the bright center I saw with my left eye. It was something she had made while I watched, and she had chosen its place.

"It needs the back leg," she said.

"I only saw three."

"Fair." She took the board and angled it toward the lamp. The little shape caught the light before the rest of the drawing did. "The face is right now."

The flute stopped; applause came from the square. Auvet rose, tucking the bundle under her arm, and reached for her purse. She paid the price we'd agreed on, plus the small difference between her offer and mine. When I held the extra coin out, she closed my fingers around it.

"For the second sheet," she said.

"The first was my mistake."

"Then for the chalk."

I tucked the coin into the tin. She looked once more at the notch in the eyebrow and touched the paper below it, where no mark could smudge. Then I slipped a clean sheet over the portrait so the chalk wouldn't brush against her sleeve and rolled both pages into a tube.

"Is it dry?" she asked.

"The chalk may still come off if you rub it. Hold the tube by the ends."

She did. The applause was thinning. Auvet backed into the moving people, gave me a quick nod, and turned toward the square. I could see her pale hair for three steps. My left eye found the flare twice more between passing bodies, then a high-sided delivery cart crossed the street and hid her completely.

The first drawing lay face down where I'd left it. I picked it up by the corners. The paper still held my thumbprint at the edge of the great bright head. I put it under the board before the night air could lift it away. From the square came the sharp slap of a drum, then a ripple of voices answering something I couldn't see.

stories.title: The Place Laid for Her
stories.prompt: "No weapons allowed in this establishment, ma'am." "My consciousness is in the sword, the humanoid body you're looking at is a glamoured mannequin I'm puppeting."
stories.body:
# The Place Laid for Her

“No weapons allowed in this establishment, ma'am.”

“My consciousness is in the sword, the humanoid body you're looking at is a glamoured mannequin I'm puppeting.”

The host of the Ousel Room looked down at the sword, then up at the woman holding it. Ildesse had given the mannequin dark eyes, a long nose, and a mouth that looked well in repose. At present the mouth was doing a smile she had rehearsed for somebody else.

“Would you be willing to have the scabbard tied shut?” he asked.

“Yes, certainly.”

He fetched a silk cord from beneath his desk. She held herself out horizontally in the mannequin's two hands while he wound it between the guard and the scabbard buckle. It was a very pretty scabbard, pale green leather tooled with leaves, selected to suit her dress rather than her blade. The dress was copper silk. Its skirt required a generous interpretation of doorways.

“And the reservation?” he asked the pommel.

“Ildesse.” Her voice came, as usual, from the mannequin. “It's still this end for conversation.”

“Of course. Two at eight. Your gentleman hasn't arrived.”

She had intended to arrive three minutes after Brevot, giving him time to sit down and begin wondering whether the copper dress appearing between the curtains could possibly be for him. To accomplish this, she had come early to ascertain the arrangement of the room. The host was now tying a second knot. Above his head, the clock began striking eight.

“Not over the little cap, please.”

He moved the cord. The pommel's feeding cap had loosened in the carriage; with one wooden fingertip she pressed it home. Beneath it, a wet wick nourished the warm, pulsing thread that ran down through the tang into the blade. Her living flesh was narrow, delicate, well protected, and presently cross. The magic that moved her mannequin and dressed its plain head in features came from there. She could send that body six paces from herself, but not a seventh; the sword had no means of following. Being put in a cloakroom would have made an exceptionally short evening.

The host tested his knot, offered her the cord's two ends for inspection, and showed her in.

There was a banquette against the wall, a chair opposite it, candles, small glasses, folded napkins. Her flowers had arrived. The musician stood near the far curtain with his fiddle under his arm; he caught her eye and raised two fingers. Two pieces, as agreed, beginning with the first course. She acknowledged him with a small nod, the sort that looked discreet unless one was wearing three copper feathers in one's hair.

Forty-three years old, and she had spent most of the afternoon choosing those feathers. She would have done it again. In the long mirror beside the curtain, her skirt moved like an expensive liquid.

She was laying the sword along the banquette, behind the place where she meant to sit, when a man said, “Ildesse?”

Brevot had arrived without waiting for her entrance.

“Yes. Just a moment.”

The point of the scabbard was on her wrap. She lifted it, freed the wrap, and discovered that the mannequin's elbow had caught the flowers. Brevot steadied the vase. Now they were both holding things and looking at each other across an extraordinarily large white bouquet.

“Shall I put this somewhere?” he asked.

“In the middle. No, nearer the wall.”

He put it nearer the wall.

“There,” she said, and stood properly. “Good evening.”

“Good evening.” He smiled, and she was glad she had bought the feathers.

His portrait had been done by a friend who disliked noses, but otherwise it had prepared her. He was handsome in a worn, uneven way, with a broad mouth and gray beginning above his ears. Thirty-eight, he had written; vain about his hair and helpless before a well-turned ankle. She had been considering that last confession for eleven days.

“I nearly wore my other coat,” he said. “Then I remembered telling you how much I hated this one. I thought you might like to see what all the fuss was about.”

“The buttons do look distressed.”

“It's the left sleeve. Watch.”

He reached for his chair. The sleeve rode halfway up his forearm, and a bright inch of lining protruded from the cuff.

She laughed. His answering grin was immediate and unceremonious. There he was: the man who had sent her four pages about his landlord's campaign against pigeons and then, in the margin, admitted to feeding them.

They sat down.

“You look—” he began.

“The complete supper for two?” asked a server at his shoulder.

“Yes, please,” Ildesse said. “As I ordered.”

The server departed. Brevot looked at the unused plates before her, then toward the entrance.

“Are we expecting someone?”

“No.”

“I thought you couldn't eat.”

“I can't.”

He looked back at the plates.

“I ordered supper for two,” she said. “That is how they sell it.”

“Ah.”

The menu had described a procession of little dishes brought beneath silver covers. When reserving, she had pictured the lifting of those covers, the steam, his delighted surprise. She hadn't pictured having to account for the second quail.

“You needn't eat all of it.”

“I probably shall. I missed lunch.”

She had hoped for something less hungry, though she couldn't reasonably have said what. She arranged her hands on the table. He glanced at them, at the slim gloves with their pearl buttons. The mannequin could return touch as well as sight and hearing; if he put his hand over hers, she would feel it. His fingers were broad, with an ink stain just beneath one nail.

He reached into his coat.

“I brought you something.”

“Did you?”

A narrow parcel emerged, wrapped in blue paper. For the instant before he unfolded it, she let it be earrings.

“It's a poem,” he said.

She kept smiling while he opened it. “A new one?”

“Finished this morning. I wanted you to be the first to hear it.”

Four months ago she had sent a letter to the review in which his verse appeared, objecting to its editor's habit of cutting out the funny stanzas. Brevot had written back. Since then there had been books, arguments, the pigeons, accounts of parties they separately refused to attend. She had praised two of his poems extravagantly and found fault with the rest. He said hers were the only letters he opened before breakfast.

“It's for you,” he said.

This was better than earrings. Possibly. She folded her hands together to keep them from making any premature decision.

He took out three sheets, smoothed them, and moved the flowers an inch to the left.

“It's called ‘The Unsheathed Heart.’”

Behind her, silk cord held her firmly shut. She did not mention it.

Brevot began softly. His reading voice was lower than his speaking voice, and slower. She liked hearing him take care over something. In the first stanza a blade rested among lilies; in the second it remembered the men who had carried it; by the third, a battlefield had appeared. The grass of that battlefield was compared to young hair.

She tried to keep hold of the pleasure of being written for. He had worked on this at his desk, thinking of her. He had bought blue paper.

“Before the field remembers grass,” he read, “she dreams its brief red flowering—”

The server appeared at the far curtain with two covered bowls. The fiddle began immediately behind Brevot's left ear.

He flinched, lost his place, and turned. The musician smiled at Ildesse over the instrument. She had asked for the old air with the long rising phrase, the one in which a lover arrived beneath a window and insisted that being married to somebody else was no great impediment. Without its words it was perfectly respectable. With its words it was one of her favorites.

“Could you wait?” Brevot asked.

The musician stopped with his bow lifted.

“Just until I've finished,” Brevot added.

“I asked him to play,” Ildesse said.

“Oh. Sorry.” He set the poem down. “Yes. Of course.”

The musician looked from one to the other. “Shall I start again?”

“Please,” she said.

He started again.

Ildesse put one hand beside Brevot's, close enough that he could take it without reaching. He watched the musician. She could not decide whether he was listening intently or waiting for it to be over. The server arrived with the bowls and tried to catch her eye. Ildesse gave a small shake of the head. Just until the rising phrase was over. Then the covers could come off.

It was not a short air. She had liked that about it when choosing.

Brevot smiled at her once, apologetically. She smiled back. He looked down at the soup cooling in the server's hands. She could have dismissed the musician, but they were approaching the part for which she had hired him. By the time they reached it, she had to count the phrases to make herself listen.

The last note lingered. Brevot applauded too soon, then again when the bow came down.

“Beautiful,” Ildesse said. “Thank you.”

The soup was set before them. Brevot picked up his spoon.

“And the second piece, madam?”

“In a little while.”

“I'm engaged at the other end of the room in a little while.”

She had paid to interrupt the regular program. He had explained the arrangement clearly in his note. The whole evening had looked much more spacious on paper.

“Then now, please.”

Brevot lowered his spoon.

“You can eat,” she told him.

“I don't want to be rude.”

“It doesn't trouble me,” said the musician, and began the second piece.

This one was quicker. Brevot ate his soup. With no spoon to occupy her, Ildesse held her hand on the table until it began to look as though she were waiting to have it examined. She brought it back into her lap.

When the music ended, Brevot thanked the player with evident feeling. Ildesse watched him go to a table where three women were happily shouting over one another. None of them stopped when he began to play.

“You don't like music,” she said.

“I do. Sometimes. I never know where to look when somebody's playing it at me.”

“I thought it would be lovely.”

“It was well played.”

“Yes.”

He glanced at the pages beside his bowl. “Should I leave this?”

“No, go on.” She meant it. Something might yet happen in the poem that would bring the evening round. The blade might be taken dancing.

He finished the third stanza and read two more. There were banners, a dead king, and a final image of the sword laid across the knees of a man too weary to lift it. That last stanza was good. She could see the man in the dark, his legs cramped under the cold weight, ashamed to wake his companions and ask for help. Unfortunately, she could see nothing in it that resembled their correspondence.

Brevot lowered the pages.

“Well?”

“The end is very good.”

He waited.

“The man in the last stanza. I like him.”

“But?”

“Must there be a but?”

“There always is in your letters.” His thumb rubbed the edge of the paper. “I'd rather have it.”

She looked at the little ink stain. “It's a great deal of war to give someone over dinner.”

“I thought you'd enjoy a proper attempt. After all those dreadful epics we've been sending each other.”

“I enjoy being rude about them. I don't wish I were in one.”

“It's not meant as a portrait.”

“You said it was for me.”

“It is for you. That doesn't mean every line describes you.”

No, it didn't. She knew that perfectly well. She had defended poets against precisely this complaint, in print, and at considerable length.

“I'm sorry,” she said. “I expected something different.”

“What?”

She made the mannequin pick up her glass. It was an old social trick: the little pause, the excuse to look down. She could not drink from it, and he knew that, and now she had a glass in her hand.

“Something amorous.”

He looked at her for so long that she put it down again.

“It is amorous.”

“Is it?”

“The lilies. The entire first stanza.”

She remembered the lilies. They had lain on the blade and withered because it dreamed of battle. Oh, dear.

“I thought the flowers were a reproach,” she said.

“They are. Rather.”

He looked past her at the large bouquet, then quickly back at his poem. She had selected every stem herself.

“May I?” The server held a plate of quail at Brevot's elbow.

Ildesse made room. The server replaced both soup bowls and brought potatoes, a sauceboat, two more knives. Brevot folded the poem in half before a dish could be put on it.

For a time he ate and she watched candlelight collect in the untouched sauce on her plate. She had paid for a real dress because no glamour could give her the drag and whisper of its silk. Its bodice fitted the mannequin beautifully. Beneath the table, a wooden knee pressed against a crosspiece; she adjusted it, hearing the small click through the room's talk.

“Would you like my quail?”

“Not yet, thank you.”

He cut a potato. She let herself stop smiling.

“I was nervous,” he said eventually. “About reading it. That's why I started so soon.”

“I didn't mean to arrange an interruption.”

“No. I know.”

She moved her plate toward him, just a little, ready for later. He asked whether she had finished the novel they had been discussing. This was familiar ground. Yes, she had finished it; she had stayed up until three.

“Worse than the second volume?” he asked.

“Much better. She goes back for him.”

“Surely not.”

“Yes. After the duel.”

“Then he hasn't died? What was the point of forty pages of his dying?”

“I liked those pages.”

He laughed. She didn't.

“Oh,” he said. “You really did?”

“I like a long death scene. You can settle into it.”

“But you called the second volume indefensible.”

“It is. I read it twice.”

“I thought you hated it.”

“I thought you'd laugh at the bit I copied out.”

“I did.”

She remembered lying awake after writing that letter, inventing things he might say in reply. His answer had arrived with a parody of the dying man's speech. She'd laughed so much her concentration had gone and her mannequin's eyebrows had disappeared. It had been a very happy morning.

“I thought you liked it too,” she said.

“The things you wrote about it.”

“Oh.”

He put his knife down. “Tell me what you liked about the ending.”

She began. At first he listened; then he asked why the woman hadn't simply sent a servant to find out whether the man was alive. It was a sensible question. It had an answer, something to do with the woman's brother, but she couldn't recall it under his attention. She tried explaining the scene at the staircase instead, the wounded man coming down because he couldn't bear to wait for her to come up. Halfway through, she heard herself apologizing for the stairs.

“Never mind,” she said.

“I didn't mean to spoil it.”

“You haven't. I shall read it again.”

He nodded. She sat with her bare disappointment, which had no particular facial expression she wanted to give it. The mannequin looked peacefully attentive.

“I should have suggested somewhere simpler,” he said. “I don't do very well with all this.”

“I like all this.”

“Yes. I can see that.”

She looked at the flowers he had shifted, her place laid with things she couldn't use, the beautiful room in which she had placed him. He hadn't asked for any of it. She had hoped he would arrive and know what to do.

“You wouldn't have liked the other song either,” she said.

“Was there another?”

“Only one I decided against.”

“Ah.” He took a little more sauce. “No, probably not.”

She nearly laughed, but didn't feel obliged to help him enjoy saying it.

Dessert came in two shallow dishes. She asked for the bill before he had finished his. He looked up, spoon still in hand, and then nodded.

When the bill arrived he reached for it. “Let me.”

“Half the supper.”

“I ate nearly all of it.”

“I ordered it. Half, please.”

He considered her, then counted out his coins. She paid for the flowers and the music and her half of the food. The number looked startling even though she had known it beforehand. Brevot left something extra for the server and wrapped his poem again. The blue paper made a loud, fussy noise.

“Would you like to keep it?” he asked.

She wanted to say yes for the man who had spent his morning finishing it. But she would have to open the parcel at home. She could already feel how it would be to read those lilies again.

“No, thank you.”

He pressed the fold flat. “All right.”

They stood. He offered her the wrap, and she bent her head while he laid it around her shoulders. His fingers briefly touched the back of her neck. She felt their warmth, and the care with which he avoided the feathers. For a moment she wanted to turn and try the whole evening again, starting here.

Then he stepped away to retrieve his coat.

Ildesse lifted the sword from the banquette and tucked it under her arm. She looked at the flowers, then asked the server to keep them.

At the curtains Brevot stopped. “Your dress is wonderful, by the way. I was trying to say so when we sat down.”

“Thank you.”

“I should have said it again.”

She smoothed a fold in the copper silk. “I would have liked that.”

He looked as though there were several things he might say next, and she waited. Then he wished her good night. She returned it. He went out first, taking the poem with him, and she stood by the host's desk while a carriage was called.

The host offered to cut the cord, but she could undo it herself at home. It did no harm where it was.

Outside, her skirt took up most of the pavement until she gathered it. She climbed into the carriage with the sword held close and settled among the rustling folds. The tallest feather brushed the carriage roof. She reached up to take it out, then stopped.

She had imagined asking Brevot to take them out. All afternoon she had been imagining it. She lowered her hand and left the feathers where they were.

stories.title: A Curse Before Breakfast
stories.prompt: You’re older sister is a witch, and you have a massive test tomorrow that you forgot to study for, so you beg her to curse you with a sudden illness so you can stay home from school to study.
stories.body:
# A Curse Before Breakfast

At eleven thirty I turned a page in my pirate novel and found the notice about the mathematics examination. I had been using it as a bookmark.

The examination was tomorrow. It covered the entire term, lasted two hours, and accounted for a third of our final mark. I knew all this because I had written it on the notice myself, underneath the teacher's printed instructions, and boxed it twice.

I opened my mathematics book. There were triangles in it that I remembered liking. There were other things I had apparently done in my own handwriting. For perhaps three minutes I tried to work out how much I could revise before morning. Then I went to wake my sister.

Coris answered her bedroom door with the blanket still round her. Her hair was caught under one armpit.

"I need a favor," I whispered.

"Tomorrow."

"It has to be before tomorrow. Could you curse me?"

She stopped shutting the door.

"With an illness," I said. "A sudden one. I've got the whole-term test and I forgot to study. If I stay home tomorrow, I'll have a whole extra day."

She looked at the book under my arm.

"That's pirates."

I had brought the wrong book. "Yes. That's partly how it happened."

She took it from me, checked my place, and held it out again. "You were nearly finished."

"I know."

"Awful."

I put my foot against the door before she could close it. She was twenty-one and a witch, but there were still things she had to do with a door like everybody else.

"Please, Coris. Nothing serious. Just enough to get me off school. Something where I can eat."

"You could pretend."

"Mum always catches me. This way, when she rings, you can tell her I'm ill. You can tell the school too. There wouldn't have to be any pretending."

"Except about how you got it."

"They don't ask that."

She leaned her forehead on the doorframe. I could see the warm hollow she had left in her bed. Her room smelled of the dried orange peel she kept in little cloth bags among her clothes. I had always thought that was witchcraft until I tried it with my socks and she told me to wash them.

"I'll swap you," she said. "My ghost-show seat for yours."

"No."

She lifted her head.

"I've got the front row," I explained, as if she didn't know. "That's where the head comes down."

The travelling ghost show was here on Saturday. In the last act, according to the poster, the beheaded duke floated his head along the front row and asked somebody to hold it. I had queued before breakfast for my ticket. Coris had stayed in bed and bought hers that afternoon. From her seat she would mostly see the back of a pillar.

"Then move your foot."

"You weren't even going until you saw my ticket."

She pushed the door against my toes. I withdrew them and spoke through the narrowing gap.

"I'll do your washing."

"You shrink things."

"I'll stop borrowing your headphones."

The door opened again, a little. "You've got my headphones?"

It cost me the headphones just to continue negotiating. I brought them from my room and held them out with both hands. She inspected the cord, wound it round her fingers, and waited while I said please again. This time I left the arrangements to her. I was fifteen; I could still make my voice do something embarrassing if I needed to.

"I can't learn it all tonight," I said. "I did understand it in class. I just need to go over it. Please. I'll leave you alone after this."

Coris rubbed one eye with the heel of her hand.

"I can give you a day ague. Fever, sneezing, green spots. It isn't catching. It'll end at sunset."

"Could you leave out the fever?"

"Not with the one I know."

"Could you do it for an hour? Just while you telephone?"

"Sunset, Philip. Once I've put it on you, I can't change the symptoms or shorten it. I could draw it back into myself, but then I'd be the one with the ague. On my day off. So don't count on that."

I considered green spots. They sounded convincing. I had been sick before, and the parts I chiefly remembered were toast in bed and being allowed to read.

"Sunset's fine."

"You will actually feel ill."

"Yes. I understand."

"Go to bed, then. I'll do it after Mum leaves. And if you wake me again before that, I'm having the ticket."

I went away before she could improve the terms.

* * *

At seven the next morning Coris sat on the edge of my bed and asked whether I still wanted it. Downstairs, Mum had left a note about leftovers and remembering to lock the back door. Her early shift had saved us an audience.

I had put my exercise books on the desk in the order I intended to conquer them. There was a clean stack of paper beside them, two pencils, and a biscuit on a saucer. The biscuit was for after algebra.

"Do it," I said.

Coris put her warm palm against my forehead. With her other hand she held my wrist. She took a breath, paused with her lips parted, and let it out through her teeth. Something cool seemed to gather under her palm. It went through my scalp and down behind my eyes.

"That's a horrible feeling."

"Hold still."

She breathed out again, this time with a low humming sound that made my teeth ache. When she lifted her hand, a green spot had appeared on the bridge of my nose. I could just see its edge if I went cross-eyed.

"Mirror."

She passed me the little mirror from my desk. Five more spots were coming up, round and unmistakable, as if someone had pressed peas under the skin. I turned my head to admire the ones on my cheek. Then I sneezed into the mirror.

Coris took it away.

The next sneeze folded me almost in half. I pulled the duvet up. A moment earlier the room had been warm enough; now cold kept finding bits of me I hadn't tucked in properly. My knees hurt. I touched my forehead and found it hot, which was unfair when the rest of me was freezing.

"School," I reminded her.

"I'm going."

"Could you bring the thick blanket?"

She fetched it before taking the telephone into the hall. Through my open door I heard her give my name, say she was my sister, and describe my symptoms with none of the pleasure I had put into imagining them.

"Yes, a day ague. No, it isn't contagious. Yes, I'm staying with him."

There was a pause. I clutched the blanket under my chin. The school might say I could do the test at home. They might send somebody round with it.

"Tomorrow morning," Coris repeated. "At the usual time? I'll tell him. Thank you."

She came back, picked up my biscuit, and took a bite.

"That's my reward."

She put the rest back on the saucer.

"You can do the examination tomorrow. Different paper, same topics. Your teacher said to rest today."

"Put the algebra book here."

She put it on the bed, along with what was left of my reward.

For the first ten minutes everything went reasonably well. I recognized the first example. I understood why the brackets were there. Then I sneezed just as I was writing an equals sign, which became a long accusing scratch across the page. I started again. By the fourth attempt I no longer knew what I was trying to make equal to what.

Coris appeared with tea and toast. She was dressed now, in her loose striped trousers, with her hair twisted up round a pencil.

"How's it going?"

"Can I have another pillow?"

She wedged one behind me. I slid down it. She pulled me up by the shoulders, and for a second I wanted to lean against her and stay there. Instead I pointed out that she had trapped my sleeve.

"Sit forward a bit."

I sat forward. She freed it, put the toast within reach, and opened my pirate novel. She had read it twice already.

"You can't read that here."

"Why?"

"I'm trying to concentrate."

"I'll read quietly."

She settled in the chair. She really did read quietly, which meant I could hear the little snort she made when she reached something funny.

"What?" I said.

"Nothing."

"Which page?"

She showed me. I hadn't got that far.

I returned to the algebra. The toast smelled good until I bit it. Then it seemed to consist entirely of corners. I chewed one mouthful for so long that Coris looked up and asked if I was going to finish it. I said yes and made her go downstairs.

Without her there, the room was boring as well as unpleasant. I read the same example three times. I couldn't remember the first line by the time I got to the last. At nine fifteen I had used six tissues and completed half a question, incorrectly.

I called her back.

"It's too much," I said.

She felt my forehead. "That's about right for it."

"Too much illness. Not enough studying. Can you stop the sneezing?"

"I told you. I can't alter it now."

"There must be something you can do."

"I can get you more tissues."

"I mean with magic."

She stood with the empty tissue box in her hand until I remembered what she had said outside her room.

"You could take it."

"I could."

"It's not that bad."

Her eyes went to the six tissues on the duvet, then back to me. I sneezed again. She handed me a corner of the sheet.

After she brought the new box, I tried to work. I really did. I moved to the desk, thinking bed was the problem, then moved back because I was cold. I took off the thick blanket because I was hot. Coris found me trying to drag it off the floor without putting my feet out.

"Help."

She picked it up and spread it over me.

"I haven't done anything," I said.

She moved the book out from under the blanket. "I can see."

I shut my eyes. The test would be starting now. Everybody else would be turning over the first page. My clean stack of paper still had square edges, apart from the top sheet where I had dribbled tea.

"I can't do this all day."

Coris stopped folding the corner under my feet.

"Well, neither can I."

For a while she stayed on the bed without offering anything else. I lay there holding the edge of her trouser leg, which I hoped she would take for an accident. Her knee was conveniently warm.

"You could have the ticket," I said.

She looked down at me.

"We swap. You take the ague and I'll take your seat behind the pillar."

"Beside the pillar."

"Fine. Beside it."

She put her fingers against one of the green spots. She didn't look as pleased as I'd expected.

"There's most of the day left."

"I'll bring you things. Like you brought me. And you can have the sofa."

"The quilt from your bed."

I nodded. It was the good quilt, with the soft lining.

"And you don't get to moan when I ask for things."

I hesitated. "Some things. I do have to study."

She thought about this, stroking a crease in the blanket with her thumbnail.

"Drinks. Food. Pillows. Ordinary sick things."

"Yes."

"Fetch the tickets first."

* * *

We sat facing each other on the sofa with the tickets on the little table. Coris had examined my front-row one for damage, although I had scarcely dared touch it since I bought it. The printed duke was holding his head out of the corner of the picture. Even the tiny version looked worth holding.

She took my wrists.

"I'm drawing back what's left," she said. "It still ends this evening. This isn't another whole day."

"Are you going to be able to stop halfway if you hate it?"

"No. Don't wriggle."

This time she breathed in. Her hands tightened on my wrists. The coolness behind my eyes came forward so suddenly that I blinked, and a green stain spread across the back of her hand. It divided into round spots. My nose cleared. I could breathe through both sides at once.

Coris let go and sneezed all over her lap.

"Oh," she said. "Oh, I don't like that."

She sank sideways against the arm of the sofa. The blotch on my nose had gone. Hers appeared while I watched, followed by three on her cheek. For the first time that morning, I felt hungry.

"Quilt," she said.

I ran upstairs for it. When I returned, she was curled up with her feet tucked under her and my ticket in her fist.

"You don't have to hold it."

She slipped it inside the pillowcase. I tucked the quilt round her and offered to make tea.

"And toast. With butter right to the edges."

I made four slices, two for her and two for me. She ate one corner and left the rest. I asked whether she wanted it cut smaller. She shook her head, then changed her mind, and I brought the plate back to the kitchen.

I set my books out on the table. The page hadn't become easier, exactly, but the first line remained in my head while I read the second. I did a question. The answer agreed with the one in the back. I put a small tick beside it and went on before anything could happen.

"Philip."

I closed my eyes.

"What?"

"My feet are cold."

I fetched her socks.

"The thick ones."

I fetched the thick ones. When I returned she was attempting to blow her nose without taking her arms out of the quilt. I held the box for her until she managed it.

Three questions later she wanted the curtains half closed. Then the book. Then the tea she had left on a side table six inches beyond her fingers. I moved the table closer. She watched this with the air of somebody who had been waiting for me to show a little intelligence.

At lunchtime I heated the leftovers. Coris said the smell was horrible. I took her portion back to the kitchen, ate mine standing up, and brought her a plain biscuit instead.

"On a plate."

"It's one biscuit."

"There'll be crumbs in your quilt."

I got a plate.

She asked me to put the telephone within reach, in case Mum called, and to take the other end of the sofa so she wouldn't have to keep shouting. I brought my geometry there. For nearly half an hour she let me work. Once she reached over and ran a hot finger along the seam of my sleeve, a little way up and down. I left my arm where it was.

Then she began turning from side to side. Her pillow thumped against my elbow.

"What's wrong now?"

"I'm uncomfortable."

"You're taking up most of the sofa."

"I know. I can't get comfortable on it."

She sat up, cross and flushed, and tried to move the quilt out from under herself. I was about to say she was making a performance of it when she sneezed three times without quite getting a breath between. Tears spilled from her eyes. She looked at me, startled and miserable, with a tissue stuck to her lip.

I moved my books and helped her sit forward. I shook the quilt out, put her pillow at the other end, and let her lie with her feet against my thigh.

"Better?"

"Don't move yet."

I stayed. After a while I pulled the geometry back onto my knee.

The afternoon went in pieces: a page of examples, a drink; another page, a search for the softer tissues; one long problem about a cone while Coris complained that the people in my pirate novel should put on dry clothes. I had attended the lessons. Under the panic and the sneezing, some of the work was still there. The pieces began fitting together, although one sort of equation kept coming out wrong and I had to go back two chapters to find out why.

Coris fell asleep with the book open on her stomach. I slid a finger between the pages as I lifted it, then caught myself beginning to read. I closed it, keeping her place with the examination notice.

By five I had filled nine sheets. There were things I hoped wouldn't be on the test. There were also things I hoped would, which was new.

Mum rang to say she was going to be late. Coris, awake again, told her I was improving and asked if we could have money for a takeaway. She didn't mention whose forehead was hot now. When she put down the telephone, she gave me a weak thumbs-up from under the quilt.

Near sunset I sat on the floor with the last of the revision questions. Coris had begun watching the window. The room darkened gradually, then a spot on her wrist shrank to a pinprick and disappeared. She threw the quilt off.

"Finally."

She sat up slowly, testing it, and rubbed her bare cheek. Then she stood and stretched with an enormous, ordinary yawn.

"I want chips."

"Your toast's still there."

She looked at the cold plate and began hunting inside the pillowcase for the ticket.

* * *

Next morning I came down dressed for school, with two sharpened pencils and a reasonable chance of knowing what to do with them. Coris sat at the kitchen table in her dressing gown. There were green spots on her cheeks.

I stopped in the doorway.

She coughed a little and pointed at the bread. "Toast?"

"It ended. I saw it end."

"I may be having complications."

One of her spots was an oval. Another had a scratchy tail. On the table, beside her cup, lay the green pencil she used for drawing on her eyelids.

I picked it up.

"That was here already," she said.

"You missed a bit." I held the pencil out to her. "Under your nose."

She reached for it. When she saw my face, she pulled her hand back. I put it down and lifted my schoolbag onto my shoulder.

"I was very ill yesterday," she said.

"So was I."

"I took yours."

"And my seat."

She looked at the bread again. "One slice. I'm already sitting down."

I took a slice from the bag and put it in her hand.

"You haven't toasted it." She took a bite anyway.

"You haven't sneezed."

She tried, immediately and unconvincingly, with her mouth full of bread. I was still laughing when she threw the crust.

stories.title: A Busy Year for Dying
stories.prompt: As an immortal you have to periodically disappear and restart your life, lest people get suspicious. You thought that the post-apocalyptic wasteland would make your life easier, but so far you've had to fake your death more often than ever before.
stories.body:
# A Busy Year for Dying

Kelro was still waiting for his left leg to straighten when somebody claimed his coat.

"Leave it," said another voice above the rubble. "We might get him out."

An iron bar scraped along the stone over his head. Kelro held his breath, although that was hardly necessary. A little gravel ticked against his cheek; then the bar withdrew and boots retreated across the scree. The quarry had been shedding pieces of itself all afternoon. Now even the men who had come to steal the cutting machinery were prepared to respect it.

"When we come back," the first man said. "I'm saying I want the coat."

Kelro closed his eyes. It was excellent wool, red outside, quilted within, with enough room in the shoulders to wear two shirts underneath. He had acquired it during a particularly good marriage eighty years ago. His body repaired itself. His possessions required looking after.

This was his fifth death that year.

Before the cities fell, he had generally managed thirty years between deaths. He would put on spectacles, acquire a slight stoop, complain about his knees, and eventually go on a journey from which he failed to return. Once he had left an entire shipping business to himself. There had been solicitors. He missed solicitors. A solicitor might remember a face for thirty years, but he would not follow it across a continent carrying its boots.

The collapse had seemed promising. Records burned; borders ceased to matter. Kelro had expected to keep one name for a century. Instead, everyone who remained traveled between the same few places, and they watched one another with the attention once reserved for royalty and public executions.

Yesterday a fragment of brittle metal had caught him across the forehead. The man in the yellow scarf had seen blood running into Kelro's eyebrow. A few minutes later, when Kelro forgot himself and wiped his face, the man had come close and pushed back his hair.

"Where's the cut?"

An ordinary question, and usually the beginning of trouble. Kelro had spent eleven months of an earlier life shut in a wealthy man's house while people argued about whether his blood would benefit their employer. They had fed him very well and refused to let him leave.

So this afternoon, when everyone ran from the groaning quarry face, Kelro had made sure they saw him hesitate in his red coat. He had stepped into the descending dust. Getting underneath a rock had been an unwelcome addition to the performance.

By dusk his leg would bear him. He worked free of his coat, which the fallen stone had caught by the hem, and crawled through a gap toward the far end of the quarry. Nothing but a sleeve was visible from above. They would have to shift a considerable weight to recover the rest.

On the ridge he looked back once. Then the cold got through his shirts, and he found it necessary to walk faster.

* * *

As Jalmot he lasted a fortnight.

He attached himself to Ruldo's wagon, which carried lamp oil, salt, six travelers, and a fiddle nobody could play. They stopped at a camp in the shell of a freight yard to trade for winter food. Kelro helped unload. When he complained about the questions people asked in the crowded tents, Ruldo found him an empty signal hut on a strip of cinders beyond the tents and lent him a blanket.

It was almost a home. The door latched. There was a shelf at the correct height for a cup.

On the ninth day Glessa arrived with a cart of clothes. His coat hung from the highest rail, shaking its empty sleeves in the wind. He went straight to it.

"That patch pulls," he said.

Glessa turned it around. She had a long pin between her lips and several shorter ones stuck in the cuff of her own coat.

"It's a large hole."

"You could have taken cloth from inside the pocket. Nobody would have seen it."

She removed the pin. "You can mend it how you like after you buy it."

The lining still had its small scorch mark beside the inner breast pocket. He touched it with a thumb.

"Two tins of fat," she said.

"For something pulled off a dead man?"

"I washed it."

"It used to have horn buttons."

Glessa looked at him. He let go of the lining.

"Coats of this quality generally did," he added.

"Then you'll know what they cost."

He had one tin of fat. She put the coat back on its rail.

Three days later he cut his wrist on torn metal beneath Ruldo's wagon. He clapped his other hand over it before Ruldo could look and accepted a strip of cloth. By supper he had thrown away the bandage and forgotten the injury. Ruldo noticed the bare wrist while passing him a bowl.

"Let me see that."

Kelro obediently held out the bowl.

"Your hand."

There was no mark. Ruldo turned it over once, looking for the injury that had soaked Kelro's sleeve.

"You heal quick."

"Always have."

"My sister has a sore on her leg. Nothing closes it. When we get north, could you have a look?"

Kelro drew his hand back. He had nothing to offer the sister. He could not even decide which parts of himself to repair; the little nick in his ear had healed six times after six attempts to look different.

"I'm no physician."

"I didn't say you were. Something you eat, perhaps."

"Whatever you put in that bowl."

Ruldo waited. Kelro ate, although the beans had burned to a black crust on one side. For years after the collapse he had expected hunger to become less offensive through familiarity. It hadn't.

Two nights later a gale tore a sheet of roofing loose from the signal hut. The sheet struck his lamp. He woke to heat and orange light, with his blanket burning at the foot of his bed.

By the time Ruldo shouted from the cinder strip, Kelro had reached the broken rear window. He could have answered. He could have climbed out and joined the men dragging the nearest tent farther away. Instead he left through the darkness behind the hut, crouched beyond the railway embankment, and kept going.

The burning blanket had been Ruldo's. That troubled him more than he cared to examine. His feet troubled him too; he had not found both boots. The next morning his remaining tin of fat bought a boot that was too big.

* * *

Orvett was clean-shaven, quiet, and going south. After eighteen days of abandoned camps and roads buried in ash, he came north again. The only pass still usable before snow delivered him to a trading gathering beside a broken freight engine.

Kelro counted the wagons. Twelve. There had been a town here, once, and twelve wagons would scarcely have supplied one street. Now they made a crowd he hoped to disappear into.

A man was trying to juggle three tin cups beside the engine. He caught two, picked up the third, and asked for contributions. Nobody moved. Farther along, a woman gave off little blue sparks between her palms to light a customer's pipe. The customer paid her with a button.

Kelro had just decided to spend his last beans on something hot when he saw the coat.

Glessa had mended the patch again. It hung straight now. He crossed to her cart before caution could remind him what coats had cost him lately.

"Better," he said.

She followed his gaze. "Still two tins."

She remembered the customer but apparently hadn't heard about the fire. He let his rehearsed story about a lost brother go unused.

Then Ruldo came around the engine with a sack over his shoulder.

He stopped. Set down the sack. Walked up to Kelro and touched his sleeve, lightly at first, as if confirming the presence of cloth.

"Jalmot?"

"Orvett," Kelro said. "My brother was Jalmot."

Ruldo kept hold of the sleeve.

"He mentioned you," Kelro added, which he regretted immediately.

"Did he? When?"

"Before we parted."

"I only met him five weeks ago."

"A different Ruldo, then."

Glessa had stopped rearranging her stock.

Ruldo said, "I haven't told you my name."

Kelro looked past his shoulder. The man in the yellow scarf was approaching them, smiling with the peculiar delight of someone who had recognized an acquaintance and did not yet remember why he shouldn't.

"Kelro! We thought you were under the quarry. How did you get out?"

Ruldo turned to him. "You know this man?"

"He was with us three weeks. That's his coat."

Glessa took it down from the rail and folded it over her arm.

"I bought it," she said.

"Nobody's disputing that," Kelro said, although he was. "There has been considerable confusion."

"We went back," said the man in the scarf. "We pulled out your coat. Couldn't find anything else."

"Thank you for trying."

"You could have come and told us."

Ruldo released the sleeve. He took a spoon from his pocket, a bent thing with a bit of cloth wrapped around its handle.

"This was outside your hut. I found it in the morning. Been carrying it because I didn't like to throw it away."

Kelro reached for the spoon. Ruldo closed his hand.

"I sat out there all night. Thought you might call from underneath. By morning we could get near enough to lift the roof."

"I wasn't underneath."

"I can see that now."

Kelro could usually meet displeasure with an account of difficult circumstances. Nothing he could safely say explained why he had heard Ruldo shouting and chosen to stay silent. He stood with his hand still extended until he noticed it and lowered it.

The juggler came over, carrying his cups. So did two women who had been sorting engine parts. Kelro wished the juggler success in a distant location.

"We had a drink for you," Ruldo said. "I told them you were coming north to help my sister."

"You asked me to look at her leg. I never promised I could cure it."

Ruldo regarded him.

"So we're finished with the brother?"

"Yes," said Kelro.

Glessa laid the coat inside her cart. "And the wound on your head? Yellow scarf here told me there was blood all over you, then nothing."

"There was," the man said. "No cut when I looked."

"His wrist, too," said Ruldo. "Wouldn't let me look at it until later."

The small audience grew quiet. Kelro felt the old, familiar calculation begin around him: what he might be worth, what he might be made to do. The woman with the pipe-lighting sparks had only a threadbare shawl. Magic was common enough to be badly paid, but his particular variety attracted people with rooms that locked from outside.

Glessa looked from his unmarked forehead to his empty hands.

"Were you begging? Pretending you were hurt?"

The opening was so unexpected that he nearly denied it.

"No," he said carefully. "I did used to perform."

That, at least, was true. There had been a theater, two hundred years ago, where he had been responsible for assassinations and very minor kings.

"Paint?" Glessa asked. "On your skin?"

He allowed her a small, reluctant nod.

The man in the scarf said, "What about the quarry?"

"You found an empty coat."

"But we saw you go in."

"And then you couldn't see anything. Dust everywhere."

That was true as well. Kelro almost felt honest.

Ruldo put the spoon away. "You did it on purpose. The hut. You meant us to think you were dead."

"The fire was an accident."

"You could still have called out."

"Yes," Kelro said.

Ruldo waited for more. Kelro looked at the spoon's outline in Ruldo's pocket and said nothing. It was preferable to being kept as a remedy. He could feel himself choosing that preference again.

Glessa reached into her cart and brought out a cracked tin of red lip salve.

"Show us."

* * *

The salve was stiff with cold. Kelro warmed a little between his fingers and put it across his brow. From three paces away, with his hand over it and the appropriate expression, it looked very well. He dipped a rag into Glessa's cup and wiped it off.

The man in the scarf stepped closer.

"You made a noise when it hit you."

"I said I used to perform."

Somebody laughed. Kelro hoped the laugh would spread. It did, but Ruldo stayed beside the cart, his sack at his feet.

"Could you do the quarry again?" Glessa asked.

"Here?"

"There's old canvas. Plenty of things to fall over."

"I hardly need to demonstrate every possible disappearance."

"You said you could perform."

He looked toward the pass. A half-day's walk through the wind would take him out of sight of this gathering, after which there would be more wind, no food, and no new face waiting for him. Beside him was the cart with his winter coat. Behind it, the juggler had begun practicing with two cups instead of three.

"A brief demonstration," he said. "If someone can lend me a screen."

Glessa immediately began asking for payment from the people nearest her. When one protested that he had already seen the trick, she said the man was going to be buried alive next.

"Nothing heavy," Kelro told her.

"Empty tins," she said, pointing to a stack beside the engine.

Two clothes rails and a piece of canvas made the screen. Kelro arranged empty packing tins behind it, and the juggler lent him a straw-filled sack that ordinarily cushioned the cups. It would make a tolerable body if nobody insisted on knowing it personally. He drew trousers over the bottom and reached for his coat.

Glessa held it away.

"No."

"They saw the red coat in the quarry. That's the point."

"It's not going under those tins. I've mended it twice."

She made him wrap the tins' bent edges in scraps of cloth, watched him cover the sack, and only then allowed him to dress it. He caught himself worrying about the new patch. She was being quite reasonable.

By the time he stepped in front of the canvas, the juggler was collecting contributions with all three cups.

Ruldo came up beside him.

"First you tell them."

"I'm going to explain the illusion."

"Tell them who you are. What you did."

Kelro glanced at the spectators. The two women had brought their engine parts to sit on. Someone had found a length of dry sausage. There was room for anger to become a great deal worse with an audience.

"My name is Kelro," he said. "Recently I traveled under the name Jalmot."

"And Orvett," Glessa called, remembering.

"Briefly."

"He let me sit beside his burnt hut until morning," Ruldo said. "Thought he was in there."

There were no laughs. Kelro waited while Ruldo looked at the people in front of him, making sure they had heard. Then Ruldo took up a place at the side of the screen.

Kelro bowed. It was a poor beginning, but in his experience there were few beginnings that a sufficient quantity of movement could not improve.

He went behind the canvas, put on a battered hat, and reappeared with the solemn gait of a man approaching unstable rocks. He had meant to give a short account of the dangers. The man in the scarf interrupted.

"We ran. You just stood there."

"I shall stand there presently."

"You were scratching your neck."

Kelro scratched his neck. This received more appreciation than his bow.

He retreated behind the screen. The tins fell with a splendid crash. A red sleeve flopped out at the foot of the canvas. Kelro left the dummy there and, doubled up behind the screen, made for the other end.

"He's down there," said a woman at the side.

"You can't stand there," he told her from his crouch.

"You didn't say."

"Nobody was standing at the back of the quarry!"

"There was a cliff," said the man in the scarf.

They moved her to the front. Kelro dragged the sack out, reset the tins, and began again. This time, when he emerged on the far side and dusted himself off, people clapped. They knew where he had gone. He was giving them the pleasure of catching him at it.

He held up the sack. "You recognize a hat and a coat. You think you've seen a man. By the time you can look properly, he's somewhere else."

"We never saw a body," the man in the scarf said to his neighbor. "Only the sleeve."

Kelro bowed again. The juggler's cups rattled. Glessa came forward and removed the coat before he could devise anything further for it to suffer.

"Now the burning," somebody called.

"I have no intention of setting fire to anything," Kelro said.

Glessa was already bringing him an orange shawl. She shook it. The loose fringe flickered in the light.

He looked at the shawl, the two rails, the sack sprawled at his feet. For a moment he was back in a theater that no longer existed, watching an audience settle for a burning city represented by three boys and a length of silk. They had enjoyed themselves. He had too, until the leading actor's grandchildren began asking questions.

"We'll need someone to wave that," he said.

* * *

After the second performance Glessa counted the takings on the folded canvas. There were beans, buttons, a tin of fat, and half the sausage. Kelro sat on a crate in his red coat. She had let him put it on while they discussed terms.

"Food, a place on the cart, and you keep the coat," she said. "Until the thaw. Two performances at each stop."

"One."

"They paid for two."

"They paid to watch an argument. The performances were incidental."

"Then we'll have an argument at each stop."

He tucked his hands under his arms. The coat was warming through. Across the gathering, Ruldo was showing the spoon to someone and pointing toward him. Kelro would have to become accustomed to accounts of his conduct delivered without consultation.

"No actual fire," he said. "No real stones. And I don't perform before breakfast."

Glessa gave him a piece of sausage. "Until the thaw?"

He chewed. Swallowed. "Until the thaw."

She went to settle with the juggler. Kelro had eaten the rest of his sausage when a fresh party arrived from the north. Glessa met them, pointed at the canvas, and returned with a pleased expression.

"Jalmot first this time. They heard about the fire on the way here."

He was already getting to his feet. "The quarry makes a better beginning. I have an entrance."

Ruldo had come to collect his sack. He stopped beside the crate.

"You were asleep in the hut," he said. "Start there."

Kelro considered explaining the difficulty of opening a performance with an unconscious protagonist. Then he looked at Ruldo and thought better of it. He went behind the canvas, lay down in the warm coat, and began to snore.

stories.title: The Credit Book
stories.prompt: In the city-state built across the great river, your grandmother’s cookshop has fed dockworkers, caravan drivers, and penniless traders for forty years—whether they could pay or not. When the merchant guild buys the wharf and orders her out, she hands you her old credit book. “Find these people,” she says. “Tell them I need a favour.”
stories.body:
# The Credit Book

The guild's man had to wait while Orlena found a bowl for a customer who had brought his own spoon and nothing else.

“There's bread under that cloth,” she told the customer. Then she turned back. “Say it again.”

He laid the notice beside the bread. The merchant guild had bought the wharf. It wanted the cookshop for storage, along with the sheds on either side, and would take possession at sundown the day after tomorrow.

Lutrel put down the onions she was peeling. “We can pay more.”

Her grandmother looked at her. They could not pay much more. Behind the guild's man, three carters were sharing two portions of beans, and Orlena had already sent Lutrel to give them a third.

“They won't renew at any price,” he said. “The carts need to come straight from the boats.”

“Our customers come straight from the boats,” Lutrel said.

“I know.” He drew the notice away from a spreading patch of gravy. “I'm sorry. I'll be back for the keys.”

Lutrel followed him out. Beyond his shoulder the great arches of Kelvra crossed the river, carrying whole streets towards the green opposite bank. Sun caught the windows of houses stacked above houses. There had to be somebody in all those rooms who could stop this.

The man gave her the guildhall's address, though she knew it, and repeated that the purchase was complete.

By the time she returned, Orlena was serving beans. Lutrel served beside her, watching her grandmother's hands: the old burn, the bent finger, the portion of bread left beside a bowl where someone could take it without asking. Forty years of this, and a man could arrive before lunch and tell them to leave.

After the customers had gone, Orlena reached beneath the counter. She brought out a book so swollen that the string round it would no longer tie.

“Find these people,” she said. “Tell them I need a favour.”

Lutrel opened it. Names, meals, tiny sums; a pressed leaf; an address crossed out three times. Beside one entry Orlena had written *wife called him something else*. Lutrel had worked beside her grandmother for twelve years, but most of these names were strangers to her. Some had eaten here before she was born.

“How much do they owe you?”

“I don't know. Some brought things. I never put those down.”

There was a woman who had eaten here through a winter with a broken leg, a caravan driver who had lost his wagon, traders whose stock had been stolen or spoiled. Lutrel found Brisken beneath a greasy thumbprint. She knew him; he worked the grain boats now.

Farther back, *Dorbett: nine suppers, boots by the fire* had been underlined twice.

“Dorbett too?”

Orlena took the onion bowl. “Start with whoever's nearest.”

Brisken was buying boots beside the lower stair. One new boot was on his foot; the other hung from the seller's hand. When Lutrel opened the book, he began pulling the new one off.

“No,” she said quickly. “It's not a bill.”

He stopped with his heel caught. “Then why have you brought it?”

She explained the notice, and the wharf, and the storage carts, and asked whether he knew anyone in the guild who might speak for them. She could hear herself giving him too many things to answer.

“Your gran sent you?”

Lutrel nodded.

Brisken looked towards the cookshop, though the stair tower stood between them and it. “She fed me for eleven weeks when they dropped that bale on my leg. You were little. Used to bring me the pepper and then stand there till I sneezed.”

“I don't remember doing that.”

“I do.” He thumped his heel into the boot. “Where are you moving?”

“We aren't. I mean, we haven't anywhere. I thought perhaps you could help us stay.”

“I can carry your tables.”

The seller bent to feel the boot across his toes. Brisken waved him away, then apologised and stood still. His purse lay open on the stool, with scarcely enough in it for the boots.

“That's kind, but until we know—”

“My eldest has a cart. Tomorrow at noon, before our shift. I'll get the boys.”

“Tomorrow may be too soon.”

“Day after's too late to start.” He paid, picked up his old boots and hurried away in the new ones, walking as if he distrusted the ground.

Lutrel wrote *noon* beside his name. It was the first mark she had made in the book. She stared at it for a moment before climbing the stairs.

She spent the rest of that afternoon following addresses. A knife-grinder had gone upriver. At a lodging under the high crossing, a woman answered through the door that her husband still had no money. Lutrel couldn't make her hear the rest. A woman in a shuttered spice stall read her mother's name, held the book for a while and returned it with three small coins tucked inside. Lutrel tried to explain that she had come to ask after her mother.

“I understood,” the woman said.

At dusk a cloth seller told her Fodric had his own shop now, up beside the crossing, and opened early.

She returned with the coins, sore calves, and four promises to visit. Orlena had saved her supper in the oven. Lutrel ate standing up while she described the unsuccessful calls; her grandmother listened until she said that no one important had been at home.

“Did you find Brisken?”

“Yes.”

“Well, then.” Orlena pushed a stool against the backs of her knees.

By morning Lutrel had decided what to say to Fodric. She forgot most of it when she entered his shop. Bolts of cloth stood shoulder-high against the walls, and he was showing a length of blue wool to two customers in fur-trimmed coats.

“My grandmother's Orlena. From the wharf.” She opened the book at his name. “You ate with us when—”

“Yes. Yes, I remember.” He laid the wool down and came out from behind his counter. “Let's go through here.”

He took her into a back room so narrow that they could not stand facing each other without trapping the door. There was a heel of bread on his desk, still wrapped from breakfast.

“I would have paid her,” he said.

“That's not why I'm here.”

“She wouldn't take it. I had to buy stock, she said. Then I stopped coming. It's a long way down for lunch.” He looked at the book. “How is she?”

“Being put out.”

This time she told it briefly. Fodric listened with his thumb pressed into the blue chalk stain on his cuff.

“I can't get them to give up warehouse space. But there's a dining room to let up here. You'd need a loan. I could manage one, if she agreed to charge properly.”

“She does charge.”

“Everyone, I mean. You couldn't fill it with men waiting for work. The rent's too high.”

Lutrel looked through his window. Between the projecting houses she could see a patch of the river, very far below, with a loaded boat turning slowly in the current. An hour for lunch, if you were lucky. You could spend half of it climbing here.

“They wouldn't come,” she said. “And she wouldn't.”

“Then I don't know what to suggest,” Fodric said.

“I know. I'm sorry. I'm asking badly.” She moved aside so one of his assistants could squeeze through for the measure hanging on the wall. The girl glanced at Fodric's untouched bread.

“What if we brought lunch here?” Lutrel asked. “For your people. Would you pay ahead?”

“How far ahead?”

“Ten days. Six bowls a day?”

“Eight. The lads downstairs eat too.”

They worked out a sum at Orlena's usual price. Lutrel would bring two covered pots before the dockworkers' rush, and his lads would return them at closing. She could accept the advance without agreeing to turn anyone away. Fodric would pay as soon as they had a place to cook. When she asked about rooms near the wharf, he pointed down through the window.

“Dorbett has the old bakehouse under her rooms, below the tower. I sell her curtain cloth. Your grandmother knows her.”

“They had a falling-out.”

“Go all the same. She asks after her.”

Dorbett was beating a rug outside the bakehouse when Lutrel arrived. Beyond her, boats passed under an arch so high that their sails looked like scraps caught between its stones. She stopped with the stick raised.

“Is your gran ill?”

“No. It's the shop.”

Lutrel told her. Dorbett let the stick hang against her skirt.

“And she sent you?”

“She gave me this.” Lutrel showed her the book.

Dorbett searched for her name with a cracked fingernail. “Nine suppers. I was stranded near a month.”

“Perhaps you paid for the others.”

“Perhaps.” She read the line again. “Boots by the fire. My feet were in a terrible state that winter.”

Lutrel waited. When Dorbett said nothing more, she asked about the bakehouse.

“It's empty. The baker moved to his son's. Hearth's sound.”

“Would you let it to us?”

“I'd let it to a tenant who paid the rent.”

“She always pays rent.”

“I know she does. Come and look.”

The room was smaller than the cookshop and smelled of cold flour. An oven filled one corner; beside it stood a hearth broad enough for Orlena's cauldron. Dorbett knelt with a grunt, lit a twist of paper and held it inside. Smoke rose cleanly. Lutrel found herself measuring the walls with her strides.

Outside, the public cart road curved past the wharf entrance towards the lower houses. Four minutes from the old shop, perhaps five carrying bowls; no tower steps, no toll, no guild gate to pass. A boatman could see the door as he left work. Lutrel walked as far as the wharf entrance and back. She was almost afraid to go inside and ask the price.

“How much?”

Dorbett named a monthly rent a little below their old one. She needed it; the baker's last payment had gone on winter fuel. She usually asked a quarter in advance. For Orlena, one month would do, but she could not give them the room.

Lutrel counted silently. Half Fodric's advance must stay aside for ingredients. With what remained, the spice woman's coins and their own small reserve, they could pay the first month and still buy firewood. After that they would need their paying customers back.

“She'll take it,” Lutrel said.

Dorbett brushed ash off her skirt. “Will she?”

The card-game quarrel had been three years ago. Lutrel remembered the cards scattered across a wiped supper table, Dorbett saying Orlena had counted a trick twice, Orlena telling her to empty her sleeves. They had managed thirty years of rough friendship before that evening and not one civil word since.

“I'll bring her to look.”

“Do that.” Dorbett held out the book. “And don't tell me she sent her love. I won't believe you.”

At the cookshop Brisken and his sons had lifted the longest table on to their cart. Six customers were eating from bowls balanced on their knees.

“We needed that,” Lutrel said.

“We'll need it at the other end,” said Brisken. “Where are we going?”

“Nowhere yet. Gran, there's a room—”

“Whose?” Orlena asked.

“Dorbett's.”

“Put the table back.”

Brisken's sons looked at their father. He looked at Lutrel, who nodded. They unloaded it in silence except for the scrape of wood.

Orlena began collecting bowls. Lutrel followed her behind the counter, furious with the weight of the book under her arm and with everyone who expected her to know what happened next.

“I've been all over Kelvra. Fodric will pay us ahead for lunches. The room's near enough for everyone. I can't get us the wharf back.”

“I didn't ask you to.”

“Then what am I supposed to do with her offer?”

Orlena set a bowl inside another. “I told that woman I'd never take anything from her again.”

Lutrel nearly said something about a stupid game of cards. Then she saw that her grandmother was fitting the bowls into the shelf by touch, looking instead at the row of marks cut into the counter's end. Lutrel's height, summer by summer, until she had grown taller than the counter. Orlena had never let anyone plane them out.

“I want this room too,” Lutrel said.

Orlena rubbed a thumb along the counter. Outside, Brisken was loudly telling his sons that nobody could carry a table like them, even if they did have to carry it twice.

“We could look,” Orlena said. “After the washing-up.”

They went at four. Lutrel expected Dorbett to make her grandmother ask, but she simply unlocked the door and stood aside. Orlena inspected the hearth, the oven, the cupboards and the back room where they could keep provisions. Then she went out and walked towards the wharf until Lutrel could no longer see her. Dorbett leaned against the doorpost and waited.

When Orlena came back, she asked the rent. Dorbett gave the same figure.

“You'd want that at the beginning of every month?”

“Yes.”

“And you wouldn't object to the people I feed?”

“If they break a window, you'll mend it. The rest's your business.”

Orlena looked up at the bare nail over the door where the baker's board had hung. “We'll need the key tonight.”

Dorbett unhooked it from her belt. Orlena held out her hand. For a moment neither of them let go.

“I didn't have a card up my sleeve,” Dorbett said.

“I saw you put your hand there.”

“Yes. I was scratching.”

Orlena gave the key a tug, and Dorbett released it.

That evening Lutrel went up to Fodric's again and came down with the advance tied inside her coat. She kept the provision money separate before paying Dorbett. Brisken promised the cart again for the following afternoon. Other people arrived with sacks, old packing cloths, a promise of bread. Lutrel stopped trying to refuse offers before she knew what they were.

On the third morning Orlena served everything that would not travel. The man who had brought his own spoon returned with two baskets, and stayed to wrap bowls. One of the drivers Lutrel had failed to find arrived with a cousin and a sack of turnips. Someone wanted to know whether there would still be cabbage on the day he liked it. Lutrel stood in the doorway, repeating the directions until she began to give them to people who were bringing things back from the bakehouse.

At noon Brisken came back and announced that his feet were bleeding. His sons put him on the cart beside the flour and told him to hold the sacks. He directed the entire move from there, audible above the wheels.

The longest table caught in the new doorway. It had to go in on its side, with one of the sons crawling underneath to keep its legs clear, and by the time it was down everyone involved had a different account of whose idea that had been. Orlena carried the cauldron herself with Lutrel at the other handle. They stopped twice along the road; neither suggested putting it on the cart among the shifting furniture.

Back at the old shop, Lutrel took the last jars from the high shelf. Her hand went automatically to the warm patch of wall beside the oven. It was cooling. She had leaned there every winter morning of her working life.

Orlena stood in the doorway until she was ready. Then they took the book and went out together.

The guild's man was waiting. Lutrel handed him the keys. Already two carts of baled wool stood behind him, their drivers eyeing the cleared floor. She turned away before the first bale went in.

At the bakehouse someone had hung the old sign crookedly. Lutrel left it. Smoke was coming from the chimney; she could smell onions, and something sweet beneath them.

Inside, the tables were set. The spice seller's daughter had come with a pot. Fodric's two lads had carried down bread after closing and were eating the ends. Dorbett stood beside the oven in the patched apron she had worn driving caravans through Kelvra.

“What's all this?” Orlena said.

“Supper.”

“I have beans soaking.”

“For tomorrow, then.” Dorbett opened the oven. “Mind your elbow.”

Orlena moved out of the way of the hot dish. It was a pear pie, its rim dark and crumbling. She watched Dorbett carry it to the table.

“You used to burn those.”

“I used to cook them over a fire beside the road.”

“You burnt one in my oven.”

“Once. Sit down.”

But Orlena remained standing until Brisken called her name. He had taken off his boots beneath the bench and set a bowl opposite him.

“Come here. I can't reach the bread.”

She carried it over, sat to cut it, and someone put stew in front of her. Then Lutrel was called back to the door by a young carter. He looked at the laden tables and started to explain that he had been told there were meals here even if—

“There are,” Lutrel said. “Come in. Find a space.”

When she got back, Orlena was eating the stew. Across the room the spice seller's daughter was watching her. Orlena nodded to her with her mouth full.

Dorbett brought the pie to their end of the table. She cut Orlena a corner with more crust than fruit, the portion Lutrel had always seen her grandmother keep for herself when no one was looking. Orlena broke off a piece. Flakes fell down her apron.

“You remembered,” she said.

Dorbett began cutting the next portion. “I like the middle. We never fought over that.”

Brisken leaned across to ask what they had fought over. Dorbett began with the cards; Orlena interrupted to say it had started long before that, with a mule and a sack of plums. Lutrel had never heard about the plums. She pulled her stool closer, and her grandmother, still talking, reached for the pie dish and took another piece of crust.

stories.title: The Red Dot
stories.prompt: They laughed when you pulled out a simple laser pointer. Their expression changed when the 15 foot tall cat made of shadows emerged from behind you and brandished its obsidian claws.
stories.body:
# The Red Dot

Harcott had put a price tag on the handlebars. That annoyed Jovie almost as much as the theft.

"It's worth more than that," she said.

He looked up from polishing the headlamp. "There's room to negotiate."

"It's my motorcycle."

"Then you'll be familiar with its condition."

Her bike stood halfway down the warehouse's broad central aisle, between a marble fireplace and a counter crowded with clocks. Beyond it, eighteen-foot loading doors opened onto an empty yard. Harcott pulled the key from the ignition and put it in his waistcoat pocket. It still had her little rubber skull attached. Someone had stolen the bike and the jacket with the keys in it. Harcott hadn't even bothered to change the key ring.

Jovie set her helmet on the nearest table. She had walked home last night carrying it, in boots that rubbed her heels raw. She had imagined walking straight to the bike now and riding out while Harcott protested behind her. She had also imagined punching him. The two assistants coming toward her made both plans less attractive.

The man in the green apron had very large hands. The woman carried a roll of packing tape with its end already folded for the next box.

"We closed ten minutes ago," the woman said.

Jovie took the laser pointer out of her pocket.

The man laughed. The woman gave a startled snort, and Harcott, who had been watching Jovie's other hand, relaxed enough to smile.

"What are you going to do," he said, "mark the damage?"

She clicked the button and put the red dot on the concrete beside his shoe.

Behind her, the shadow that had squeezed through the open front doorway began to rise.

It came up shoulder first, a black slope lifting from the floor, then a second shoulder and a head with ears like steep roofs. Jovie stood very still as darkness uncurled past her elbow. The cat took one pace into the aisle. Fifteen feet tall on four paws, it stood beneath the high warehouse rafters without acquiring a single highlight on its body.
