This was copper, much polished on the inside and green at the joints. Barnaby wore it on the cover of the second volume, although in the pictured incident he had been keeping it in a pocket because of the cold.

"The Crown of Command," Fulvia said, with renewed pleasure.

"Also the Voice of the Mountain and the Siege Chorus."

"That makes ten entries accounted for." She copied the names. "What does it do, precisely?"

"Carries your voice. You feed it a little power and it carries whatever you say. Through stone, if necessary. I used it to make the people in the fort think there were more of us."

"How many were there?"

"Me. I stood in different places."

She turned the circlet over. "May I try it?"

He ought to have said he would demonstrate it himself. But she was holding it above her hair, and he had spent enough time disappointing her.

"Touch the inner rim with your fingertips. The smallest thread of power. You'll feel it warm."

Fulvia set the circlet on her head, holding it by the outside.

"Will I sound like you?"

"You'll sound like yourself. Speak softly."

She touched the inner rim, and the copper brightened beneath her fingers. Drawing herself up, she glanced at the open book and whispered, "Lay down your spears."

Her whisper came out of the ceiling, the wall behind Barnaby, and the stairs. In the corridor somebody dropped a box of paper clips.

"Take it off," Barnaby said.

"Oh, I'm sorry!"

The apology filled the office. Beyond the partition a chair scraped violently backwards. Fulvia snatched off the circlet, cutting her supply of power, and silence returned with a small metallic ringing in Barnaby's ears.

She held the copper band in both hands. Her hair stood up through the middle.

The person gathering paper clips said, quite clearly, "Again?"

Barnaby looked at her.

"The man who assesses musical instruments works here on Tuesdays," she said. She set the circlet down and brushed at her hair. "You did say softly."

"I did. It's louder since I cracked that joint."

"You could have mentioned that."

He could. He had forgotten the crack, and now hoped she would discover some useful depreciation in it. Instead she wrote six crowns beside the circlet.

"For that?"

"It works through walls."

"It has lost all delicacy."

"You called it the Siege Chorus."

There was no beneficial reply to this. He pushed the circlet across the table and reached into the tin.

The warming cup came wrapped in a pair of his socks. He hadn't polished it: he used it every morning, and it was already annoying enough to have his morning cup detained in a tax office. The Grail of Embers, Winter's Defeat, and the Beggar's Comfort proved to be one squat vessel with a chipped yellow rim.

Fulvia's books showed it in gold.

"It is yellow," Barnaby pointed out, before she could speak.

She put a fingertip against the side. "Cold."

"Empty. Give me a moment."

He fetched tea from the office urn, returned with the cup, and warmed it with his hands around the base, pressing his own power into the clay. It would retain that small charge for half an hour. It couldn't replenish itself; when he forgot, he drank cold tea like anybody else.

Fulvia tested it again. "Three crowns."

"Three? It's a cup."

"It's a cup that heats itself from a charge."

"I do the work."

She waited with her pen above the paper. Barnaby took a sip. He had warmed it more than he intended, and could not pursue his objection until his tongue recovered.

The lifting buckle was the Titan's Favor and the Giant's Hand. Together with its original braided strap, it had once enabled him to carry two injured people in succession up a broken stair. He put the cloak and circlet back in the trolley to give it some weight, then hooked the strap around the handle and supplied the buckle with power through his palm. The trolley became easy to lift but retained all its bulk. Bringing it round, he knocked a corner against the table and scattered the empty cards.

Fulvia retrieved them while he lowered it. Four crowns.

"Can't you allow something for the noise?" he asked.

"From hitting my table? No."

The spectacles had three names too: Eyes of the Deep, Lanternless Sight, and Scholar's Salvation. One lens was held in with wire, the other with a dreadful hard paste he had never managed to remove. By feeding the frames a little of his power he could read in the dark, although he had to tilt his head to keep the two halves of each line aligned. Fulvia tested them under her desk, directing her own power through the frames, and emerged with a gray smudge on her sleeve.

"I can only read one side clearly."

"Tilt your head."

She went back under. He heard a soft bump. This time she emerged rubbing her scalp, with the spectacles in her other hand.

Two crowns. He felt rather protective of them at that price. They had helped him read a warning scratched inside a door he had been about to shut. For years afterwards he had kept a wooden wedge in his boot, ordinary wood, replaced whenever it broke. He was relieved he hadn't put that in a book.

The last thing in the tin was a metal disk in a paper sleeve. Fulvia read the nineteenth card: Key of Return.

"That was your publisher's title," she said. "You call it an exit token in the chapter."

"The publisher owned the headings."

He slid it onto the table. There was no route left in it, only marks and a closing stamp. He had turned it over often enough to make its edges smooth.

"Queen Street," he said, before she asked.

It came back to him with unnecessary sharpness: the white seam in the abandoned tunnel, black rain falling upwards around it, his own breath catching because he was safely through and could at last afford to be frightened. The Exit Witness had taken the disk from his hand and closed the returned token. Barnaby had watched until it was done. Whatever the place beyond that crossing was, he had wanted no unfinished way back to it.

Fulvia tilted the disk toward the window. "Can it open anything now?"

"No. The living seam marked it. The Witness closed it after I returned. It only ever held that route, and the route's finished."

She put it back in its sleeve. "No precious metal. No remaining function. Nil."

He reached for it, then stopped to let her attach its numbered label. It was faintly insulting to have the thing appraised as worthless, but he was not about to appeal.

By then the light had moved off the long table. Fulvia had seven cards in front of her and a chain of pencil marks running through both books. Barnaby's tea had gone cold. Somewhere in the corridor a clock began to strike, and he looked up so quickly she said, "Four. We close at five."

"Have we finished?"

"The inventory isn't signed. I need the places of acquisition."

He looked at the form. Each object had a space about the length of his thumb.

"How much detail?"

"Enough to identify the place, if you know it."

"We called them the Realms. That didn't mean we knew where we were."

"Then write what you do know. There's an additional sheet."

He had spent two books making the doors he had entered sound like destinations. Now he had to distinguish what he remembered from what the chapter headings implied. A copper circlet bought from a woman beside a stair. The stair had been black; the sky above it had moved in strips. Was that enough? Fulvia said to put it down. The cup acquired in exchange for a blanket. The sword bought before his first crossing. The cloak taken as his agreed share of an expedition's finds, from a place he knew only as the third door; maker unknown. The buckle and spectacles purchased from other Runners who had not told him where they'd got them. Queen Street for the token. Dates approximate, where he could remember any.

"The cup wasn't a gift from a king?" Fulvia asked.

"He said he was a king. He wanted my blanket."

She checked the passage, lips moving. "You gave him your last protection against the killing frost."

"Yes."

"But you had the cloak."

"It let the wind through. I'd torn it."

He waited for another annotation. She made none. Instead she turned forward to a small drawing of the cup beside his boots.

"I don't think it's yellow in this one either," she said.

He bent over the additional sheet. At least she was pursuing the illustrator now.

It took the rest of the hour to fit nineteen names onto seven descriptions. Fulvia rejected his first signature because it crossed the box reserved for her stamp. He used the ordinary small one that he signed letters with. He declared that he had listed all retained artifacts, including those of no assessable value, and she passed the whole inventory back for him to check.

The sword was nine crowns. Cloak two, circlet six, cup three, buckle four, spectacles two, token nothing. Twenty-six in total. Fulvia canceled the preliminary bill, entered the corrected assessment, and turned it so he could see both figures.

Barnaby opened the chair envelope.

Sixty-four would remain. The wool chair had the same reclining mechanism; he had checked, before the velvet had distracted him. Four crowns for delivery, the man had said. He could have the chair tomorrow if he went straight to the shop.

He counted out twenty-six. Fulvia counted it again, stamped the bill PAID, and gave him his receipt with the inventory. He looked at the stamp, let out a breath through his nose, and folded the papers into his pocket. While she entered the payment in her ledger, he drank his cold tea and packed everything away. The sword went back into its sheath; he would carry it under his arm.

Only then did she push the first volume toward him.

"Would you sign it?"

He took up the pen with considerable relief. There was generous blank space on the flyleaf, untroubled by boxes. "To Fulvia?"

"Yes, please."

He began, *To Fulvia, who knows the cost of adventure.*

She read it upside down. "I don't want the tax in it."

His pen hung over the paper. He had meant it generously. It was a perfectly good inscription.

"What would you like?"

"The date. And your name. I like the book as it is."

He put a neat line through the dedication, added the date and a handsome signature, and handed it back. Fulvia examined the page, then shut the book over her thumb, smiling. He suspected she preferred having the crossed-out sentence there.

At the door he paused. "On my copy of the inventory, under occupation. You've written retired."

"That's what you told me."

"Retired adventurer. There's room."

She took the paper, added the word, and returned it. Barnaby checked the addition before lowering the trolley carefully over the first stair. He had a chair to buy, and the shops would soon be closing.

stories.title: The Unoffered Hand
stories.prompt: Every autumn, the kingdom’s falcons choose one person they will obey for life. This year, the fiercest bird in the royal mews ignores the princess, the generals, and every master falconer—and lands willingly on the glove of a servant girl who has never touched a hawk before.
stories.body:
# The Unoffered Hand

Sovelda had her hand inside the princess's spare glove when the falcon came down.

She was supposed to be polishing it. The leather had gold leaves worked into its cuff, and she could get the blacking out of their edges more easily with her fingers filling the glove. That was true. It was also true that she had been holding her arm sideways to see how the long tassel swung.

Across the court, the princess stood beneath the autumn garlands with her other glove raised. Cresset had turned his back on her. He had done the same to three generals, who now stood together pretending to discuss a horse, and to every master falconer in the royal mews. One of the masters had tried crouching. Cresset had watched him get down, then watched him get up again.

Now the bird was on Sovelda's fist.

His weight struck through her elbow. She staggered against the table, knocking over the blacking, and held her arm out because there was nowhere else to put it. A barred tail spread across her apron. Above it rose a spotted white breast, a brown head, two bright eyes which, from this close, seemed impossibly large.

Sovelda had never touched a hawk. She had not wanted to. The mews boys carried scars on their knuckles and ate with the cheerfulness of people who had forgotten how they got them.

“Don't move,” somebody said.

She could not tell whether it was meant for her or the bird.

The princess lowered her arm.

Every autumn, from the first yellow leaf until the last, the kingdom's unbound falcons chose the one person they would obey for the rest of their lives. Most chose young. Cresset had been brought out for four autumns. In that time he had opened a general's cheek, killed a kennel rat through the bars of his weathering cage, and driven every other bird away from the highest perch. Sovelda knew these things because the glove-room windows faced the mews, not because anyone had expected her to need them.

“Take him,” she said as the princess approached.

The princess offered her fist beside Sovelda's. Cresset leaned away. When she brought it closer, he opened his beak.

“Cresset.” The princess's voice was low and familiar. “Come along.”

His attention remained on Sovelda. She wished it wouldn't.

Master Tirren came behind the princess with a short block perch. He was a broad man whose leather apron had gone almost black at the waist. He set the block down, moved the spilled polish away from Cresset's tail, and looked at Sovelda's elbow.

“Straighten your wrist. No, leave the elbow bent. That's it.”

“I haven't fed him anything.”

“I can see that. Ask him to step down.”

“Will he?”

“We shall find out.”

She lowered her fist toward the block. “Down.”

The falcon stepped onto it. Tirren put out a hand to draw a strip of leather clear of the bird's foot. Cresset struck at him so quickly that Sovelda heard the beak close after Tirren's hand was already gone.

“Up again,” Tirren told her.

She offered the glove. Cresset climbed onto it, carefully placing one foot and then the other.

Behind Tirren, someone laughed once in astonishment. People began coming away from the garlands. The generals stopped talking about their horse. Sovelda could see the woman in charge of the glove room hurrying toward them, and opened her mouth to explain the blacking.

“Not now,” the princess said, stepping between them.

For the first time since she had entered service, Sovelda watched someone else be sent away from her.

***

By evening she had a room beside the mews, two clean aprons, and permission to eat before the kitchen servants finished serving the upper hall. She was twenty and had never had a room to herself. There was a peg on the back of the door. She hung her second apron on it, took it down, and hung it up again.

Cresset occupied a perch in the adjoining chamber. She could hear him moving. They had left the door between them open because she had asked whether he might forget her in the night.

Tirren had looked briefly at the ceiling.

“He won't forget you. He may forget where he put a piece of meat. That's different.”

The princess arrived while Sovelda was trying the latch on her window.

She still wore her choosing clothes: cream sleeves embroidered with rust-colored flowers, a dark fitted bodice, an orange sash that had acquired a smear of dirt near the knot. A little spray of purple flowers leaned crookedly out of her brown hair. Sovelda had seen that sash brought down for pressing three times before the ceremony.

“You've got my glove,” the princess said.

It lay on the bed. Sovelda picked it up with both hands.

“I'll finish the cuff. I was going to—”

“Keep it for tonight. They'll have to fit one for you.”

The princess went through to Cresset. Sovelda followed. The bird watched the newcomer with his feathers held close. When the princess stopped an arm's length away, he turned his head and began drawing his beak along a wing feather.

“He's tired,” she said.

Sovelda looked at the handsome curved beak. “How do you know?”

“He always does that after the choosing.”

The princess reached toward him, stopped, and pulled a loose thread from her sleeve instead.

“Did you come every year?” Sovelda asked.

“I live here.”

“I meant to see him.”

“Yes.” She rubbed the thread between her fingers. “I came most mornings.”

Sovelda looked away. She had imagined the princess arriving once each autumn, lifting a magnificent arm, expecting the best bird because she had always had the best things. Most mornings was harder to picture.

“Perhaps he thought I was you. Because of the glove.”

“He didn't.”

The answer came so quickly that Sovelda's face warmed.

Outside, a cart rattled across the stones. Cresset stopped working on his feather and watched the open window until it had passed.

“Tirren has twelve new pairs to settle,” the princess said. “I'll come after breakfast.”

“To take him?”

“To show you what to do.”

Sovelda nodded. She wished the princess would leave before she said something else foolish. At the door, however, the princess paused.

“Does that glove fit?”

“Yes, Highness.”

“It came halfway off when he landed.”

Sovelda's bare fingers closed against her skirt.

“It's too big.”

“Then say so when they measure you.”

***

In the following days Sovelda learned that a falcon could make a room smell quite unlike any room she had cleaned before. She learned where to cut his food, how to weigh it, and how much of a morning could be spent waiting for him to finish something unpleasant. Her left arm ached down to the fingertips. Cresset liked to look out while she walked; when she turned toward a wall, he leaned around her to keep the court in view.

The princess showed her how to hold him clear of her body. She demonstrated with the spare glove on her own wrist, moving slowly enough for Sovelda to copy. Without a bird, her arm looked oddly incomplete.

Tirren fitted Sovelda's new glove himself. It was plain brown leather with a cuff as long as her forearm. She thanked him, then caught herself looking at the gold leaves on the other one.

“You can keep that for ceremonies,” the princess said.

“I wasn't—”

“You were. It's all right.”

It might have been kindness. Sovelda could not decide.

The choosing had not given her the bird's thoughts. When she spoke about tomorrow, he watched her mouth. When she asked whether he wanted more food, he searched her bare hand. But a simple instruction addressed to him reached him even before she had learned the proper call. He would come, step down, wait. Once, frightened when he spread his wings beside her face, she cried for him to stop. He folded them at once and almost lost his balance.

The princess caught Sovelda's wrist before she lowered it.

“Let him settle.”

“He startled me.”

“He was balancing.”

Sovelda tried to hold still. The bird's feet tightened and loosened through the glove.

“He'll do what you ask,” the princess said. “He won't know you asked badly.”

It was useful information. It was also the fourth correction since breakfast.

By the fifth morning, Sovelda could call him from one end of the enclosed exercise hall to the other. He came low over the sand, wings beating hard enough to stir her skirt. At the last moment his feet reached forward and the rest of him rose behind them. She learned to let her arm give a little under the landing. Once she did it without thinking, and laughed aloud.

Cresset tilted his head. The princess stood by the far door with the empty traveling perch.

“I want to see him outside,” Sovelda said.

“Tirren will take you to the high field when he has time.”

“He's been in here all week.”

“So have you.”

Sovelda rubbed a mark on her new cuff. Through the mesh above the doors she could see leaves traveling past, yellow against a clear sky. People had begun to greet her in the passages. The mews boys moved their things off the best bench when she brought Cresset out. Yet every day still seemed to end with somebody explaining how far she was from being able to do anything.

“You could take me,” she said.

“I could.”

“Then why won't you?”

The princess set down the perch. “Because when you want him back, you call before you look where he is.”

“He comes.”

“Yes. He does.”

Sovelda could hear agreement being used to make her stupid. She held out her arm, and Cresset shifted his feet.

“You don't have to keep coming.”

The princess went very still. Sovelda had never told anyone of her rank to go away. For a moment she enjoyed the silence so much that she wished there were someone else in the hall to hear it.

Then the princess picked up the perch.

“Take him into the south orchard after dinner. There's room for a short flight. I'll show you.”

She left before Sovelda could decide whether to thank her.

***

The orchard sloped away from the palace wall. Its lower trees had been cut back years ago, leaving a broad grassy strip between the trunks and the boundary fence. Here the wind moved steadily uphill. Fallen apples lay in the grass, some split open, their flesh already browning.

The princess walked Sovelda to the middle of the clear strip.

“Wait here. Let him get above the trees. When you call, give him room to come in from this side.” She swept her empty glove through the air above the grass. “Stay where he can see you.”

Sovelda unfastened the traveling leash as she had been taught. Cresset leaned forward. His whole body seemed to narrow toward the open sky.

She raised her arm.

He left it with a thrust that lifted her onto her toes.

For a second she saw every barred feather separately. Then he was beyond the apple trees, climbing, turning on one extended wing. The light caught his pale breast. She had carried that weight for five days; she had not understood what it could do without her.

“Look at him,” she said.

The princess was already looking. Her mouth had softened. She took three quick steps down the slope, following him, and for the first time Sovelda saw her without any wish to have her clothes.

Cresset passed over the wall. The palace hid him.

Sovelda lifted her glove.

“Wait,” the princess said. “He'll circle.”

There was nothing above the wall. Sovelda went uphill to see past it. She passed beneath the outer branch of an apple tree; leaves brushed her hair.

“Come back to the grass.”

“I can't see him.”

“Sovelda, come down here.”

She heard her name in the voice that had spent the week telling her what she had done wrong. Behind the wall a brown shape rose, banked, and came over the orchard.

“Cresset! Here!”

He turned toward her.

The princess shouted. Sovelda saw the branch between them and pulled her arm down. Cresset followed the movement, folding himself through the narrowing space. One wing struck wood with a sound she felt in her teeth. He fell into the leaves at her feet.

She crouched, reaching with both hands. His beak snapped at her bare fingers.

“Don't grab him.”

The princess knelt on the other side. Cresset stood low in the grass, one wing hanging. He opened it halfway, closed it, and tried again. A dark drop fell onto an apple leaf.

“Is it broken?” Sovelda asked.

“Get your glove under his feet.”

“Is it?”

“I can't tell yet.”

Sovelda pushed the glove through the grass. Her whole arm shook. Cresset placed one foot on it and stopped. She had to hold the position, bent double, while he gathered himself for the second step.

“Up,” she whispered, then wished she hadn't.

He climbed.

***

Tirren examined the wing while Sovelda held the bird. The princess stood beside them with a lamp, although it was still afternoon. Twice Tirren asked her to move it closer.

The bone was sound. A growing feather had broken near its base; the skin beside it was torn. There would be no flying until the wound had closed and Tirren was satisfied with the wing.

“What did he hit?”

“An apple branch,” Sovelda said.

“Calling him in?”

She nodded.

“Where were you standing?”

“Under it.”

Tirren looked at the princess. She stared at the lamp.

“I told her to move,” she said.

“You took her out.”

“Yes.”

He returned to the wing. Sovelda watched the slow movement of his hands. She had wanted the princess to see Cresset come to her in the open air. The wanting had been so large and pleasant that she had barely noticed the tree.

When Tirren finished, the princess carried the lamp away. Sovelda heard it set down in the next room. Then nothing.

“He didn't fly badly,” Sovelda called.

The princess appeared in the doorway.

“I know.”

“In case anybody asks.”

“I'll tell them.”

Sovelda lowered Cresset to his perch. He stepped down more slowly than usual and turned his injured side toward the wall. She kept her glove beside him until he had settled, then sat on the floor because the stool seemed too far away.

“You were right,” she said.

The princess leaned against the doorframe. “Which part?”

Sovelda looked up sharply. The princess rubbed her forehead with the heel of her hand.

“I'm sorry. I heard how that sounded.”

“About me calling him.”

“Yes.”

There was no relief in saying it. Cresset still held his wing oddly. Sovelda could see the place where his breast feathers moved with each breath.

“I liked making you leave,” she said. “This morning.”

The princess looked toward the empty stool, then sat on it.

“I nearly didn't come back.”

“Why did you?”

“I wanted to see him fly.” She watched the bird. “And I was tired of you looking at me as if I'd stolen your afternoon.”

Sovelda pressed the glove flat between her knees. A spot of blood had dried on the thumb.

“I thought you'd hate me.”

“For this?”

“For him choosing me.”

The princess breathed out through her nose. “I did. For most of that first day.”

Sovelda had been expecting a denial. She studied the princess's slippers, which were muddy around the toes.

“I hadn't done anything.”

“I know. That made it worse.”

The princess bent to work a burr out of her hem. It resisted. She picked at it until one of its hooks broke, then laid the pieces on her palm.

“I used to bring my breakfast down here. He'd watch me eat. If I was late, he'd be at the window.”

“He does that when the meat cart comes.”

The princess looked at her.

“I didn't mean—”

“No. You're probably right.”

For a while neither spoke. From the court came the noise of the other newly chosen birds, their handlers calling, Tirren asking someone to stop waving both arms.

Sovelda turned the glove over. “You can still come.”

“I know I can.”

“I mean I'd like you to.”

The princess let the broken burr fall into the bowl beside the stool. She stayed until the daylight faded from the high window. Cresset put his head beneath his good wing and slept through their silence.

***

The orchard lost its leaves. Sovelda learned the sounds Cresset made while asleep, and which piece of the mews roof he preferred to watch after rain. She stopped offering him the glove every time he looked in her direction. Some afternoons he ignored her for hours. Being chosen did not make this less insulting.

Tirren cleared him for exercise, then for flight. Sovelda went to the high field under the master's eye. She stayed in the open. She waited for the wide approach. When Cresset landed she nearly cried, which would have been difficult to explain to the boys carrying the scales.

The princess came on the third outing, riding a mare with a mane the color of chestnuts. She dismounted and handed her reins to a groom. Sovelda had the gold-leaf glove on; it had been taken in to fit her hand. She had done the stitching herself.

“Ceremonial?” the princess asked.

“I like it.”

The princess bent to inspect the cuff. “You've matched the thread.”

“Of course.”

Below them the bare orchard shone silver in the morning light. Beyond it lay stubble fields, a dark fold of woods, distant hills Sovelda had never had a reason to visit. Cresset stretched one wing, then the other. Both opened fully.

“Where will he go?” she asked.

“Let him show you.”

She sent him up. He climbed above the field, circled once, and struck out toward the ridge. Sovelda turned with him until she was facing into the wind. Her eyes watered. She wiped them on her empty sleeve.

“He's going a long way.”

“He can.”

At the ridge, Cresset tipped. His body became a dark mark descending so quickly that Sovelda lost it against the grass. A moment later he rose again, empty-footed, and she heard herself make a disappointed sound.

Beside her, the princess laughed.

“You wanted him to catch it.”

“I didn't even see what it was.”

“Neither did he, soon enough.”

Cresset turned beyond the ridge. Sovelda walked after him, keeping to the open crest. The princess followed for a little way, then went back for her mare.

Hooves thudded past. The princess leaned forward in the saddle, her orange sash lifting behind her. Sovelda broke into a run. She was too far behind almost immediately; she had known she would be, and ran anyway, the tassel striking her wrist, the bird's shadow crossing the grass ahead of both of them.

The princess reined in at the next rise and twisted round.

“Sovelda!”

She was pointing beyond the hill. Sovelda couldn't see from where she was. She hitched up her skirts and kept coming.

stories.title: A Pet Human
stories.prompt: When you are dragged into the demon world as a live sacrifice, you didn't expect to hear "A pet human! Thanks Mother!"
stories.body:
# A Pet Human

The priest put on my boots before he picked up the knife.

They were good boots. I had spent three wet fairs earning them, and he was stretching the left one with his bunion. I watched him wriggle his foot beneath his robe while two assistants bound me to the altar.

“Those won't fit you,” I said.

“Be still.”

“The heel will rub.”

He raised the knife. Beyond his elbow I could see the temple doors, barred from within. Nobody was coming. My mouth kept moving, but I had run out of things to put in it.

Then the stone wall behind the altar split open.

A blue hand came through, caught the front of my green coat, and dragged me backwards off the stone. Rope snapped. My chin struck my chest. I passed through something cold and tight and landed face-first on a carpet that smelled of singed sugar.

Above me, a child's voice squealed. “A pet human! Thanks Mother!”

I stayed facedown for a moment. After what had just happened, I felt entitled to receive my next piece of information slowly.

“He's rather grubby,” said another voice.

“He's *perfect*.”

I lifted my head. The child was seven feet tall, pink, and wearing a yellow party dress with cherries embroidered around the hem. Ivory ribbons hung from her two small black horns. Her mother stood behind her in a blue silk gown; the tips of her own horns almost brushed a chandelier full of smouldering cones. One long hand still gripped the edges of a dark opening in the hearth. Through it, sideways, I saw my altar and the priest peering into the crack.

“Did it take?” he whispered.

The mother blew into the opening. Its edges folded together beneath her claws, and the priest vanished.

“You didn't tell me,” the child said, jumping hard enough to make the chandelier shed ash. “You said no more things with teeth!”

“I hadn't intended to. It was offered.”

“I have teeth,” I said. “I also have an engagement tomorrow at the fair.”

The child sank to her knees and bent over me. Her golden eyes filled my view.

“Mother. He talks.”

“So I hear.”

“Do it again.”

“Send me home.”

“Oh, he's cross.” She reached for me. “Are you cross?”

“Yes.”

She lifted me beneath the arms. My coat rode up; my trousers followed to a lesser and less welcome extent.

“Put me down. You're hurting.”

She dropped me.

“Less quickly,” I said from the carpet.

“Nimmet,” said her mother, “gently.”

Nimmet lay flat on her stomach beside me, her tail whipping behind her like an angry coachman's lash. “I'm being gentle now.”

“Madam,” I said, sitting up and addressing the mother, “I was seized in my lodging, tied to a stone, and very nearly opened. I don't belong here.”

She looked from me to the hearth.

“He called you a willing offering.”

“Did you hear me willing?”

“There was a great deal of noise.”

“That was me.”

Her lips thinned. She picked a broken strand of rope from my sleeve, examined its knot, and let it fall.

“Very well. I shall return you when he calls again.”

“When?”

“Dusk. He expects a boon.” She regarded the closed hearth with renewed interest. “He shall have my attention.”

Nimmet sat up so fast one ribbon slipped off her horn.

“But he's my birthday human.”

“He says he isn't.”

“He doesn't know it's my birthday.” She turned to me. “It's my birthday.”

I was thirty-seven, shoeless, and still shaking. I congratulated her because my mother had brought me up properly, and because Nimmet's mother had just shown me a mouthful of teeth as long as my thumbs.

“I'm Mavrix,” the mother said. “You may wait in here. Keep away from the east balcony. The moths there take bites.”

“Can't you open that again now?”

She scraped a claw across the hearth. Blue sparks followed its point, but the stone remained stone.

“He must call from his end. Then I can reach through.”

I went over and put my hand against it. Warm, solid, unhelpful. When I turned back, Nimmet had produced a woven basket large enough to sleep a pony.

“You can wait in this.”

***

I am Caff. You may have heard me inviting you to view a serpent with two heads, or a woman who could swallow a sword, or a serpent with one head on days when we had suffered a disappointment. I possess a carrying voice, a serviceable moustache, and enough judgment to know when a paying customer needs encouragement.

Nimmet was not paying. This became my chief difficulty.

“Sit,” she said.

“I am sitting.”

“Good human!”

She dropped a sweet into my lap. It was the size of a fist, glazed white, with a sugared violet on top. I had eaten nothing since the previous night. I took a cautious bite.

Almonds. Real almonds, and soft pear inside.

Nimmet leaned close. “Do you like it?”

I nodded around a second bite.

“Mother! He likes his biscuit!”

Mavrix, seated by the tall window with a dish of black cherries, made an acknowledging motion. I discovered another sugared violet underneath the sweet and ate that too.

“What's your name?” Nimmet asked.

“Caff.”

She considered this. “That's a funny noise.”

“It will do.”

“I was going to call you Buttonkin.”

“Caff.”

“All right.” She opened a box and drew out a green velvet collar with a brass bell. “I can still put buttons on this.”

I had worn a false beard made of combings from a horse. I had stood in a barrel while a supposedly trained goose selected a card from my mouth. My professional dignity was flexible. Nevertheless, I set down the sweet.

“Absolutely not.”

Nimmet put the collar away. “Brush, then.”

The brush had curved iron prongs. Beside it lay a pair of shears. She spread a cloth beneath me and made a small, pleased noise at the sight of my moustache.

I got up. “I bite.”

Her face brightened. “How hard?”

“Extremely hard.”

“Mother, he bites!”

“Then keep your fingers clear.”

Nimmet held out the brush handle. I stared at it. She stared at me. Across the room, Mavrix selected another cherry.

“I'm not going to bite a brush,” I said eventually.

“It won't bite you back.”

I went to the far end of the room. Nimmet followed on hands and knees, which made the pursuit considerably worse. I climbed onto a cushioned chair. She settled beneath it with her chin on her hands.

“I shall require wine,” I announced, “and roast fowl. A whole one. Also new stockings.”

Surely there was some limit to the inconvenience a mother would endure before ordering her child to leave the human alone.

Mavrix put down the cherries.

“Fetch the little cupboard from the dining room, Nimmet.”

Nimmet returned carrying a cupboard taller than I was. She planted it before my chair, opened it, and revealed cold birds, glazed buns, white cheeses, and bottles wrapped in straw. At the bottom stood a pair of boots with curled silver toes.

“Those are decorations,” Mavrix said before I could ask.

The wine tasted of plums. I ate a leg, then the other leg. Nimmet watched every mouthful. When I wiped my fingers, she handed me the cloth she had intended to shave me on.

There is a point at which a gentleman must acknowledge that his strategy is failing.

“Fetch,” Nimmet said, and threw a little red ball across the room.

“No.”

She threw it again after retrieving it herself. “Fetch?”

I took another sip of wine.

“He isn't very clever,” Mavrix observed.

This was unnecessary. I had successfully supported myself by speaking outdoors over bad weather and sometimes over bears. I placed my cup on the cupboard.

“Nimmet. Ball.” I held out my palm.

She brought it over.

“Excellent. Now, stand there.”

I pointed. She went. I raised my hand, palm down, and slowly lowered it. She sat.

“Splendid.” I tossed her a bun.

She caught it in her mouth. The whole bun disappeared with a soft *pock*.

“Again!” she said.

I glanced at Mavrix. The cherry had stopped halfway to her mouth.

“He appears to be teaching you,” she said.

“We're doing tricks together.” Nimmet bounced on the carpet. “Watch.”

She got to her feet before I asked, then sat before I lowered my hand.

“You must wait for the signal,” I told her. “Otherwise it spoils the effect.”

“I knew what you wanted.”

“Yes, but your mother didn't.”

Mavrix ate the cherry very slowly.

***

For a child who could lift furniture, Nimmet was easily distracted. During our first bow she noticed a moth behind the glass and ran to pull faces at it. The moth spread wings like a butcher's apron and pressed its teeth to the pane. I decided I would not attempt a window.

For our second bow, I took away the buns. Our third was excellent.

“What else can we do?” she asked.

“Can you roar?”

“I'm not supposed to in here.”

I looked at Mavrix, who had gone to the adjoining room to change for the evening. The open door showed her blue sleeve and the edge of a mirror.

“A small one.”

Nimmet drew a breath. Her dress puffed out. The sound that followed lifted the hair from my forehead and knocked three cherries from their dish.

“Nimmet.”

“That was little!”

“I heard it.”

Nimmet clamped both hands over her mouth. I was on the floor, clutching the foot of the cupboard. We stayed where we were until Mavrix's sleeve withdrew from the doorway.

“Quite sufficient,” I whispered.

“You fell over.”

“Part of the act.”

“Do that again.”

“Later.” I got up, rubbing my hip. We agreed that opening my fist would mean roar, and practised the signal without the noise. Nimmet mimed a splendid catastrophe. I declined to fall over again.

By then the red light beyond the windows had begun to drain upward, leaving the garden below in darkness. I could see rows of pale flowers shutting themselves inside hard, spiked buds. Somewhere out there, something heavy was ringing a chain against a tree.

My hands began to shake again. I put them in my pockets. The priest had searched these too. He had kept my little purse, my lodging key, and the folded bill announcing tomorrow's entertainment. He'd left the landlady's brass-tagged spare in my bedroom door when they carried me out. The knife had had a nick near its point. I remembered that with extraordinary clarity.

Nimmet nudged my elbow with the collar box.

“You could wear it for the tricks.”

“He'll be there,” I said.

She waited.

“The man who gave me to your mother. When she sends me back, he'll still be there.”

“The offering man?”

I nodded.

“Did he brush you too hard?”

“He was going to kill me.”

She lowered the box.

“Why?”

“He wants something from your mother. And he thought nobody would miss me before he'd finished.”

“I would.”

“You hadn't met me.”

“Well, I would now.”

She said it crossly, as though I had been difficult over something obvious. Then she went to the doorway and called for her mother.

Mavrix emerged wearing a black gown. Nimmet immediately clung to its skirt.

“We have to take Caff home properly. The man there kills humans.”

“I remember what he told me, Nimmet.”

“Then don't put him back in the man's hands.”

“I wasn't proposing to.”

“We can take him. And he can show you our tricks.”

Mavrix looked at me. I thought of asking her to terrify the priest on my behalf. I could have described the knife again. Instead I found myself picturing him in my boots, waiting to be rewarded.

“I would like to recover my property,” I said. “With an escort.”

Nimmet swelled with importance. “Me.”

“You will remain where I can see you,” Mavrix told her. “I must hold the opening. No running.”

“Can we roar?”

“You may ask the human.”

I reached for the collar box.

***

The evening call sounded like someone praying inside a saucepan. Mavrix knelt at the hearth, set her claws against the stone, and breathed out. This time they sank in. She pulled the opening wide, dragging its edges upward until the temple appeared beyond her arms.

The altar stood three paces past the threshold. Behind it waited the priest in a gilt headdress, holding the knife. His two assistants carried empty bowls. A dozen people crowded near the now unbarred doors; I recognized my landlady and the man who sold hot chestnuts by the temple steps.

“Great receiver of our gift,” the priest intoned, “we beseech—”

“Nimmet,” Mavrix said. “Slowly.”

I walked through first. The bell at my neck gave a small, disgraceful jingle. Nimmet followed, holding the far end of its loose green ribbon. The priest's mouth fell open.

I stopped beyond the altar, well to one side of his knife. Nimmet stopped behind me. I could hear Mavrix breathing in the opening.

“Evening,” I said.

The priest looked at the collar, the ribbon, and Nimmet. His shoulders relaxed a little.

“The offering has pleased you?” he asked her.

“Yes. He's called Caff. Watch what he can do.”

This was her cue to hand me the ribbon. She forgot. I held out my hand twice before she noticed, then she put the red ball in it.

I shut my eyes briefly, then gave her back the ball. “The other thing.”

“Oh!”

She passed me the ribbon. I unbuckled the collar and put it in my pocket, then faced my audience. I had addressed bigger crowds, although rarely with such excellent support.

“Ladies and gentlemen, you have been promised a manifestation. Kindly remain for the complete performance.”

The priest stepped towards me. “You will be silent.”

The knife moved. My next words caught somewhere beneath my ribs. I lifted my hand as we had practised, curled the fingers, and opened them sharply.

Nimmet roared.

The priest sat down on the altar steps. One assistant put a bowl over his head. The other held his out in front of him, which seemed optimistic.

I drew a breath. My voice came back cracked, but usable.

“That's the little one.”

Nimmet bent close to my ear. “Was I good?”

“Wonderful. Stay there.”

The priest looked towards the doorway. Mavrix's face filled its upper half.

“You described him as willing,” she said.

“The sacrifice was undertaken with the fullest—”

“Put that down.”

He followed her gaze to the knife and set it carefully on the stone. I stepped forward and slid it out of his reach. My landlady made a small, sharp sound at the back of the crowd.

“He took me out of your upstairs room,” I called to her. “After you gave him the spare key.”

“He said you were ill!”

“I did become unwell.”

The priest tried to stand. Nimmet sat beside him, delighted to be at eye level. He stayed on the step.

“Now,” I said, “my purse, my key, and my boots.”

His hand went inside his robe. “There is no need for threats.”

I hadn't made one. I was prepared to start, but Nimmet had become interested in his headdress. Gold leaves trembled on fine wires around its rim.

“Caff. Look. It wobbles.”

The priest handed over my purse and key. I pointed at his feet. He pulled off the boots; the left resisted. I had warned him.

“Can I have the hat?” Nimmet whispered.

Everyone heard her.

“It is a consecrated vessel of divine—”

“Ask your mother,” I said.

Mavrix glanced at the hat.

“You were expecting a boon,” she told the priest. “You may give my daughter a birthday present and then I shall leave.”

He took it off.

Nimmet carefully lowered it between her horns. The gold leaves quivered. She made them wobble again, giggled, and nearly knocked me over with her tail.

I put my boots on sitting beside the altar. It took longer than I would have liked because my fingers would not quite obey me. My landlady came forward and held one steady. Neither of us said anything until I had fastened the buckle.

“Your room's still yours,” she said.

“It had better be.”

Behind us, the chestnut seller began asking the assistants whose money had paid for the hat.

***

“Come on,” Nimmet said, reaching for my hand.

I pulled it back before she could close her fingers.

“This is where I stay.”

Her mouth turned down. I could have refused a demand. This was harder.

“We didn't do the bow.”

“Nimmet,” Mavrix said from the hearth. “My arms.”

“We practised.”

So we bowed. Nimmet went too low and the headdress tipped over her eyes. I caught it, set it straight, and tightened its band. There was some applause, principally from the chestnut seller, who was enjoying himself.

She caught my sleeve before I stepped away. “I want to see you again.”

“Next birthday,” I said, before I could be sensible.

“That's ages.”

“I'm a busy man.”

“I could come to your fair.”

The priest made a strangled noise. I ignored it.

“If your mother brings you. As a visitor. You mustn't carry me about.”

“What if I ask?”

“You may ask.”

Mavrix shifted her grip. Her claws grated against the edges of the opening.

“Nimmet. Now.”

Nimmet thrust the red ball into my hand and stepped back through. She turned at once, holding her skirt away from her feet.

“Don't lose that. It's my best one.”

“I won't.”

Mavrix drew the opening shut. I caught one last glimpse of the gold leaves nodding between the little black horns. Then there was only an ordinary wall behind an ordinary altar, with a priest sitting rather heavily on its steps.

I walked out past him.

Halfway to my lodging, reaching into my pocket for the key, I discovered that the velvet collar was missing. I stood in the street considering the inconvenience of going back for it. My bed was waiting. My boots fitted. Behind me, from the temple, came an increasingly lively argument about sacred expenses.

I went back.

The priest had picked up the collar and was staring at its brass bell. I took it out of his hands.

“Mine,” I said.

stories.title: The Address of Here
stories.prompt: Centuries after humanity quietly disappeared, the androids they left behind have turned their solar-powered cities into lush gardens of their own, complete with rooftop farms, neighborhood festivals, repair cafés, and endless debates over the proper way to grow tomatoes. When a young gardening android discovers an ancient human postcard that simply reads “Wish you were here,” she decides to find out humans went.
stories.body:
# The Address of Here

Zinnet's tomato had grown through the back of a chair and across the seat, leaving her nowhere to sit. Ovolo wanted her to move the chair for a photograph. Three gardeners from the floor below wanted her to remove the side shoots. Zinnet wanted everyone to look at the tomatoes.

There were twenty-seven, some striped green and yellow, some turning the red of her favorite tiles. The lowest hung beneath the seat. She lifted a leaf to show them.

"That one's touching the wood," said a gardener.

"I know. It has a little square bottom."

Ovolo knelt, tilted his camera, and caught the square bottom against the city beyond: rooftop beans, apricot trees along the elevated walk, the broad black petals of the solar collectors turning above them. He made postcards for the neighborhood festival. His best-selling view omitted the factory where everyone got their spare knees, although the factory had a magnificent wisteria.

"You'll have to put the chair in the harvest exhibition," he said.

"Will you help me carry it?"

"After I've finished these."

He had said that about carrying something at the last festival. She gave him the chair's dimensions anyway.

Downstairs, the repair café had spread into the street. Someone was trying out a repaired accordion while its owner argued that it hadn't sounded like that before. Children with unfinished faceplates sorted screws into cake tins. A planting cabinet recovered from a boarded storeroom stood among the tables, its drawers labeled in human handwriting. Zinnet had offered to clean it for the seed exchange.

In the bottom drawer she found a small tin with a lid that still held fast. Its paper seal broke under her thumb. Inside, beneath a packet of hard brown seeds and a sachet of drying crystals, lay a postcard.

She washed the soil from her hands before lifting it out. The picture had yellowed at the edges, but its dark storage had preserved a garden: a path between low beds, a flowering tree, a pale curved window divided by three unequal ribs. Beyond the window was blank blue sky. A sleeve at one edge suggested someone had stepped out of the photograph too slowly.

On the back, in faded ink, someone had written:

*Wish you were here.*

There was no address, no signature, no stamp. Whoever had put it in the tin had left Zinnet nothing else to go on.

She took it upstairs. Ovolo was still photographing tomatoes.

"Where is this?"

He leaned close enough to shade the card. "Oh, lovely. Is it yours? Can I scan it?"

"After you tell me where it is."

"The white-blossomed tree looks like the ones in the southern terraces. I have a picture somewhere."

She knew those trees from a seed catalogue. They made a dry rattling fruit and needed more room than her roof could offer. She had wanted one for three summers. In the photograph there was space for the branches to spread, space to walk beneath them without turning sideways past a chair.

"Humans went there?"

"Humans were everywhere. Before the ships."

Zinnet had learned about the ships when she was little. Humans left, androids remained, cities changed. There were departure dates in the lessons, arrows crossing star maps. She remembered drawing flowers around the arrows. Until that morning, she had never particularly wanted to follow one.

Now there was this path, wide enough for two people. Someone had stood at one end of it and wanted someone else beside them.

"I'll go and look," she said.

Ovolo glanced toward the exhibition bunting. "You'll miss the festival."

She had never missed one. She had been alive for nine of them.

"You can take the chair."

He began to protest, then looked at the card again. "Send me pictures. Proper ones, with space for lettering."

She let him scan the card, then slid it back into its tin. For once she couldn't tell him what she hoped to bring home.

***

The southern terraces lay two days away by the stopping tram. Zinnet took the tram for one morning, got off to inspect a wall of peaches, and missed the afternoon connection. She walked until evening instead.

She had packed her solar blanket under everything else. At a roadside sun court she unpacked socks for protecting fruit, a hand lens, three seed envelopes, a broad hat that shaded her shoulder panels when she wore it, and the tin. Two travelers watched politely until she tried to unfold the blanket with the empty bag still on it.

"Do you want a hand?" one asked.

She did. By sunset they had exchanged the names of six gardens and one lodging house to avoid because its resident geese had learned to pull charging leads free. Zinnet slept under a fig tree with her luggage repacked, then caught the next tram in the morning.

She reached the terraces the following noon. Their gardeners grew pears flat against warm walls and let nasturtiums trail from the balconies of houses painted pink. Metal leaves along the balcony rails angled little solar cells toward the sun. Even the ugly buildings had something flowering on them.

Zinnet found the white trees beside a long greenhouse. She took out the postcard and walked backward and forward, trying to make the tree trunks align with the window ribs.

An android carrying a basket of pear cuttings stopped to watch.

"The greenhouse used to be curved?" Zinnet asked.

"No. The roof was lower, before we raised it for the figs."

"Could there have been another one? Four hundred years ago?"

The gardener set the basket down. "There could. I don't go back that far. What are you looking at?"

Zinnet showed her. The gardener held the card by its corners, then tipped it to escape the glare.

"We have that tree," she said. "Most cities do. The old nurseries sold it by the thousand."

The three trees, which a moment earlier had seemed so distinct, now looked distressingly repeatable. Zinnet studied the card's branches through her lens. In Ovolo's picture she'd found a white tree and a bit of pale roof. That was all she had compared.

"I came because of the blossoms."

"They're very good this week."

"Yes."

The gardener let her be disappointed. Then she pointed to the ribs. "I've seen one of these windows at the old departure ground. In the hall with the climbing roses. My partner made me look at it while we waited for a lecture."

"A whole window?"

"Just a section. Much bigger than I expected. We argued about whether it would fit in our house."

She gave Zinnet directions and a pear cutting. Zinnet had meant to decline anything she couldn't fit in her bag, but this pear had a red interior. She stayed to learn how they grafted it and spent the rest of the afternoon holding branches for someone who had three different ideas about the best angle of a cut.

That evening she sent Ovolo a picture of blossoms.

*Wrong garden. Lovely trees. Your photograph could have been anywhere.*

He replied with a festival image: her chair on a trolley, two helpers at its handles, Ovolo pointing to the tomato beneath the seat. Someone had tied an honorable-mention ribbon to a chair leg.

*The judges couldn't agree what it was entered for. Did you get a wider shot of the terraces?*

She looked at the message for a while, then sent him the same blossoms, cropped closer.

***

In the morning Ovolo sent a different picture. It was a visitor's photograph from the departure ground, with a reflection of the visitor obscuring half a display. A curved window stood behind the glass. Its three ribs spread from an off-center joint, just as they did on the card.

*I checked properly this time. The caption says Farleaf. A garden ship. Sorry about the terraces.*

Zinnet enlarged the photograph until she could read the small type. The window was a construction spare. The one in her postcard had left with the ship.

She lowered her hand to the bench. A bee inspected the flowers in her gathered dark hair, found them dry, and moved on.

So the next garden wouldn't be it either.

She had imagined coming through a gate, perhaps asking permission, perhaps discovering that the tree had died and been replaced. There had always been a place for her feet in the imagining. Now she tried to picture the whole garden lifting away: its paths, its soil, a person picking up a forgotten tool while the ground receded outside that window.

*Do you still want to go?* Ovolo asked.

She sent, *Yes. I want to know where it landed.*

His answer arrived while she was securing the pear cutting across the top of her bag.

*All right. I've sent you the display address. The card photograph is in their collection too.*

Then, a minute later: *Did I make you spend two days going the wrong way?*

*One day. I spent the other on pears.*

She attached a photograph of the red flesh of a stored fruit, cut open for her at breakfast. He sent back six exclamation marks. It was the first picture she had taken entirely for him.

***

The departure ground's old embarkation hall had a roof shaped like an open fan. Solar flowers filled the apron where passengers had once queued. Beyond them, between low hills, stood an enormous empty assembly cradle, its steel hoops full of swallows.

Zinnet arrived on the fifth afternoon with dust in her gold ankle joints. A fern sale occupied the entrance. She bought nothing, because of the pear, and went directly to the roses.

The spare window was taller than her house. From a distance its ribs had seemed delicate. Close up, they were thick enough to contain a passageway. She put her hand on the glass, then withdrew it when she saw the mark she had left.

Beside it hung a new print of the garden. The tree's white flowers were clear, the sleeve green. The untrimmed image showed a row of overhead lamps that the postcard printer had cropped away.

*Farleaf, forward garden, before departure. Photograph by passenger Agata.*

A second image showed Agata beside the tree, grinning with her eyes almost shut. Someone else must have taken that one. She was young, with a dark fringe that divided above one eyebrow, a broad nose, a small metal hoop through her left ear. She had tied her green overshirt around her waist.

Zinnet looked from the portrait to the empty path. That was who had stood behind the camera. She had probably smelled the blossoms. Zinnet moved closer to inspect the bare strip of soil beside the path, looking for something she had missed while she still thought she could go there.

At the information table a broad-backed android was trying to coax a fern from its pot without breaking the pot.

"Were the cards written by Agata?" Zinnet asked.

"Which cards?"

She showed the tin, the postcard, the message.

"Ah. We sell reproductions of that view." He reached for a thin wooden stick and worked it around the fern's roots. "They sold the originals to visitors before launch. Passengers had them too. I don't know who wrote yours."

"I hoped it was her."

"It might have been."

She put the card beside the portrait on her display. The handwriting gave her no reason to choose Agata over any other person. She kept the two images together anyway.

"Where did the ship go?"

"There's a destination map in the next room. Or the full voyage collection, if you want that."

"The full one."

He showed her a reading alcove, brought the still-potted fern to its shaded sill, and returned to the sale.

At first she chose the general departure record. Ships spread outward on its map in a slow scattering. The surviving manifests covered seventy-three years at this ground alone. Some passengers joined relatives already traveling; some spoke of land, of research, of wanting another sky. One recorded interview featured a human who planned to leave after her dog died. A later list contained her name.

There was no final photograph of everyone, no last human closing a city door. In the records from this region the departures thinned, and the notices advertising return passages eventually stopped. Elsewhere the record grew patchy. Zinnet could see why the lessons had used arrows.

She selected Farleaf.

Its launch was four hundred and twelve years in the past. The destination entry identified the fourth planet of a small star eleven light-years away, with navigational numbers precise enough to draw a point on the map. Beside the outward track was a second line, labeled *arrival transmission*.

Zinnet touched it before reading anything else.

A room opened around her on the alcove screens. A human child passed close to a camera, leaving a smear across its view. Someone wiped it. Beyond a roughly built doorway lay a slope of dark gravel beneath a copper-colored sky.

"Go on," said a voice out of sight.

A woman stepped into view carrying a shallow tray of seedlings. Grey hair, a lined face, a green shirt faded almost yellow. She set the tray down with a small jolt, muttered something at a bent stem, and looked up.

The grin narrowed her eyes.

Zinnet paused the recording. Below the picture the passenger index identified Agata. She brought up the old portrait beside it, then the packet's dated crew list. Both belonged to Farleaf's voyage record; the arrival packet carried the ship's identifier and its new position. Agata had survived the crossing. The woman had the same broad nose, the same uneven division of hair above her eyebrow, and now a face full of creases that moved when she smiled.

Zinnet let her move.

"I'm supposed to give you a tour. We haven't finished the roof over the main house, so I'm showing you this room first. It has a roof."

The unseen person laughed. Agata glanced that way and smiled harder.

"And look, these came up. These are from the little striped ones we used to get at the Saturday market. I didn't think any of that batch would germinate."

She lifted the tray toward the lens. Zinnet leaned forward. Tomatoes, with their first true leaves. One of them was decidedly stretched.

"We planted out twice too early," Agata said. "Don't say anything. We've had all the advice already."

She carried the camera through the doorway. People were putting up a long table outside. A child sat in its middle, holding a dish out of reach of the adults. On the far side of the slope, pale sections of Farleaf's hull sheltered beds covered with netting. Agata's breathing grew louder as she climbed. The camera dipped to her shoes, then swung up toward the hills.

"There. That's what I wanted to show you. The red ridge. You can't see it from the houses, but if you come up just this far..."

She held the view unsteadily. Wind worried the microphone. At last she said, quieter, "I still turn around sometimes to tell you things."

Someone called her to eat. She called back that she was coming, kept filming the ridge for several seconds, and then the recording ended.

***

Zinnet watched it twice more. On the third viewing she noticed a white-flowering tree growing inside a sheltered section of hull. She couldn't tell whether it was the same tree. She wanted it to be, with an intensity she found embarrassing even alone.

Then she opened the dates.

Forty-eight years between departure and landfall. Eleven more before the packet reached the world it had left. The archive had received it three hundred and fifty-three years ago. Other files followed in the voyage collection, fragments of measurements and pictures of later construction, but this was its last complete personal recording. There was no present-day settlement report.

She had found people arriving. For the first time the end of a departure arrow contained a garden, a table, a woman cross about her seedlings. She wanted the next recording, and the next, until the years between that slope and this afternoon were filled. The collection wouldn't give her that.

Outside, the fern sellers were packing up. Zinnet called Ovolo and shared the recording. He answered from her roof, where he had apparently brought the chair back. The tomato vine filled most of his picture.

He watched in silence until the tray of seedlings appeared.

"They're a bit leggy."

"I know."

Agata took them out to the ridge. Ovolo didn't speak again until the file ended.

"She went all that way."

"Forty-eight years."

"Oh."

Zinnet tried to imagine forty-eight festivals. She had kept thinking of Agata as a traveler like herself, packing badly, stopping to look at something. For most of Agata's journey there had been nowhere to get off.

"Do you think anyone still lives there?" Ovolo asked.

"I don't know. The recording is very old."

He moved the camera. For a moment she saw only his fingers; then the city appeared, terraces rising behind terraces, the solar petals black against the late sun. Festival streamers had caught in an almond tree. Somebody below was practicing the accordion again.

"She might have liked this," he said.

Zinnet listened to the clumsy tune beneath the hiss of the connection. "Can you keep it there? I want that picture. With the sound."

"The streamers are a mess."

"Keep them."

He held the view for her. A breeze lifted the paper strips. On the nearest roof a gardener climbed onto a stool to reach a peach, thought better of it, and fetched a taller stool.

Zinnet saved it all.

***

In the morning she went to the ground's communications garden. Among beds of tall grasses, a working radio dish listened to the sky; contemporary astronomers shared its schedule with visitors using the old departure addresses. The booking screen offered her a short outgoing slot that night.

She selected Farleaf's destination. A line of small text placed delivery eleven years ahead. Even an immediate answer could not return until twenty-two years had passed.

There were requests from earlier visitors in the public queue history: pictures, questions, recordings of music. Sending would not make her the first person to wonder. She could add her return address to theirs.

She spent the afternoon assembling her message under a solar flower. Ovolo sent an edited city view with the streamers removed. She used the first one. She added the pear terraces, her chair tomato, and a picture of herself taken by the fern seller: ivory cheeks, amber eyes, gold fingers spread awkwardly around the tin. Her pear cutting protruded behind her head.

She recorded her voice six times. In one version she gave too many details about the tin. In another she sounded as if she expected Agata to be waiting beside a receiver. At last she began with her name and the date, explained where she had found the card, and named the old arrival packet she had watched. She addressed whoever might be living where Farleaf had landed.

"I wanted to visit the garden in the picture," she said. "I've only managed the departure ground so far. I'm attaching some photographs of where I live. The tomatoes are mine."

She stopped, considered, and added, "I'd like to see what you grow now."

At her allotted time she watched the dish turn. Its motors made a low sound that she could feel through the bench. The transmission lasted less than a minute. When it ended, the dish moved on to another observer's star.

Zinnet stayed outside. The tin lay open on her knees, the old card visible in the reading light. She could find the destination's region of sky now, although its star was too faint for her unaided eyes. She magnified it in her vision until a point separated from the dark.

Eleven years. She would be twenty. If the graft took, she could be growing those red pears by then.

She imagined the signal passing through the space ahead of her, carrying the accordion, the streamers, herself with a branch sticking up behind her head. Beyond it was a world she had only seen in old pictures: those gravel slopes, that red ridge, the house without its roof. It would have changed. She tried to make the changes in her mind, found she was only planting familiar trees, and let the ridge stand bare.

For a while she looked at the star. Then she played Agata's recording again, starting where the woman picked up the camera and went outside.

stories.title: The Astral Valkyrie
stories.prompt: The Astral Valkyrie appears only when a civilization is about to die, descending from the stars to choose one soul worthy of carrying its memory into the next age.
stories.body:
# The Astral Valkyrie

I was rehearsing what to say against my country when the stars began to move around her.

There were only seven people left on the palace roof. Below us, in the feast hall, hundreds lay beneath tables or stood watching plaster fall into their hair. The other islands of Theskar had gone under during the previous nineteen nights. Our last ships had burned where they were drawn up on the beach. A bright body hung above the western sea, growing brighter, while lesser fragments struck the dark around it. We had stopped calling it a comet. Names had ceased to help.

I had come upstairs because someone remembered a story: at the death of a people, the Astral Valkyrie descended to choose its witness. I had sung that story myself, once, with a chorus dressed in gold. Now I had a split lip, a stolen court cloak, and a speech intended to make our destruction seem overdue.

That was how I wanted to begin this account, too. You would have been on my side before you knew my name.

She came feet first through the falling fire. Gold wings folded behind her, each feather veined with a light that moved as blood moves beneath thin skin. A broken circle of violet crystal turned above her head. Her hair was indigo, immensely long, and remained lifted after her bare feet touched the roof. Nothing else about her floated. She bent her knees to take her weight. She breathed.

The smallest fragments curved away from her wings. One hit the roof ten paces off and drove a piece of tile through a man's cheek. He dropped without letting go of the woman beside him. The light made the inside of his mouth pink and plain.

Vasketh, who had been head historian before the library fell, approached her with both hands open.

“How many?” he asked.

“One living soul. With the body that holds it.”

“To the mainland?”

“Beyond the years in which your people disappear. I can keep one person alive beside me. I cannot turn that away.” She looked west. “I cannot bring back those who have died.”

The woman on the tiles began to swear at her. The Valkyrie stood listening until the woman ran out of breath, then knelt beside the fallen man. Her wings sheltered his face from the glare. They did nothing to stop the blood.

Of the seven, two went back down the stairs. Another sat against the parapet, laughing softly. Vasketh remained where he was. So did I.

“I know our history,” he said when the Valkyrie rose. “I know the smaller languages. The root crops that survive the red moth. Give me a piece of your time.”

“Your hand,” she said. “Offer me something you remember. I cannot take what you withhold.”

He put his palm against hers. At her gesture I touched her other wrist. Her pulse was quick. Then the roof vanished, though I could still feel the hot grit under my feet.

A child was teaching Vasketh a game played with peach stones. He got the counting wrong; she slapped his enormous, hairy knuckles and started again. A page lay on a desk, the ink beginning to spread because he had sneezed over it. Now an old farmer held up two roots, one sound, one rotten, while Vasketh struggled to get the names right. The memories were ungainly, interrupted by his own questions. He offered a woman reciting the last poem she knew in a language he had arrived too late to learn properly. He offered his shame at asking her to repeat it when she was tired.

I could smell the inside of his library: paste, old leather, the beans someone kept eating over the manuscripts. It was too much life. I tightened my grip on the Valkyrie's wrist.

“And the conquests,” Vasketh said. He was still on the roof with me; the child and the farmer had gone. “I have the testimony of the occupied islands. I copied it before the ministry could burn it.”

“You've read about what they did,” I said. “I watched.”

He looked at me properly for the first time.

“Nacorra.”

I hated hearing my name in the old, pleased rhythm of recognition.

“You know her?” the Valkyrie asked.

“Everyone did.”

I turned her hand over and laid my face against the palm. A performer's gesture. I knew it even then.

“Let me show you whom they killed.”

I offered the execution square, the summer before the sky began to fall. My lover stood on the platform in the brown tunic they had given her. They had cut her hair badly. The left side was shorter; I kept looking at that, as if someone might come with scissors and put it right. She was thirty-eight. She had printed the names of villagers our soldiers had buried in a quarry. The court called this aid to an enemy.

Before the executioner pulled the cloth over her face, she found me. I lifted my hand. She tried to lift hers, forgot the rope for an instant, and smiled at her own mistake.

I stopped there. The Valkyrie's fingers were wet against my cheek.

“She wasn't sorry,” I said. “Whatever else you carry, carry that.”

Vasketh took a breath that rattled. “I have her list. Most of it. The quarry was reopened in the seventeenth year of the old king.”

“I know when.”

“Then you know it was the campaign you sang for.”

He had not let go of the Valkyrie. Neither had I. Beneath my feet, the roof gave a long, low knock.

“Come away from the edge,” the Valkyrie said.

A crack opened through the tiles between Vasketh's shoes. For a moment he stared down at it as if something were written there. I caught his sleeve and pulled him toward the stair. Behind us, the parapet peeled outward. The man who had been laughing went with it. I heard him strike something below and then heard stones, too many to distinguish.

We went down sideways, the Valkyrie drawing her wings so close that their light showed through the seams of her dark bodice. Vasketh held my shoulder. His breath smelled of mint leaves chewed long past sweetness.

“Did you ever read our leaflets?” he asked.

“What leaflets?”

“The ones we gave out at your performances. The prisoners' names. Your audience walked over them.”

I did remember. White scraps under embroidered shoes. I had thought someone should sweep the entrance before the queen arrived.

The feast hall was hotter than the roof. Its great doors stood open to a terrace; beyond them the sea had become a sheet of copper light. Someone called for the Valkyrie to save a child. Someone else cried that she was the thing killing us. She passed between the tables with her wings folded, looking into each face that turned toward her. People reached, but the reachers were not lifted. There was no second refuge hidden inside her light.

At the foot of the stair a man lay across two cushions. The bottom half of one leg was missing, and the cloth packed around it had gone almost black. A woman knelt beside him holding his head up. When he saw me, he tried to sing.

It was the march. Of course it was the fucking march.

He could manage only three notes. I tapped the next two against my thigh before I knew I was doing it. His eyes brightened.

“Don't make him,” the woman said. “He starts coughing.”

“I'm not.” I stopped my hand.

The man tried again, dragging breath through the first phrase. I had written it to be sung by thousands who knew nothing about singing. You could shout it drunk. You could gasp it while marching uphill with your feet rubbed raw. I had been proud of that.

“Just breathe,” I told him.

He nodded, but his lips continued moving. The woman looked past me to the Valkyrie and then back at my face. She said nothing. I moved on before she could ask me for anything.

We moved to the western doors. Vasketh sat on the threshold, one foot outside, one in. “May I have a little shade?” he asked.

The Valkyrie opened a wing over him. Its gold dimmed. He closed his eyes in the sudden coolness, then opened them sharply and caught my sleeve.

I knew this room in lamplight. I knew precisely how far a voice travelled from the musicians' platform before the pillars confused it. Even with wounded people on the floor, my eye found the best place to stand.

“There was more,” I said to the Valkyrie. “Before the executions. Before all this.”

“Show me.”

I offered her my hand. Vasketh reached up from the threshold and held the edge of her wrist. I almost asked him to let us alone.

The hall filled with lamps.

I was twenty-nine, and someone had sewn a thousand thin disks of silver onto my dress. They kept catching in one another whenever I sat, so I had given up sitting. Pepper burned on my tongue. My lover, then a printer's apprentice of thirty-one, had stolen a dish of yellow fruit from the royal table and was feeding it to me one piece at a time. She had begun by bowing after every piece; now she was laughing too hard. Juice shone in the hollow of her wrist.

Around us, dancers struck the floor with their heels. Each set of partners approached and withdrew, turned, stamped, came together with a slap of palms. You could miss one step and recover at the next. You could be terrible and still be included, unless the court dancing master saw you, in which case he would descend with an expression of personal bereavement. My lover imitated him with a stolen napkin tucked under her chin. I nearly choked on the fruit.

The Valkyrie's mouth opened. Her free hand made a small motion at her throat.

“The heat,” she said.

“Pepper.”

“It hurts, but you want another.”

“Yes.”

She swallowed. There was no fruit in her mouth, only my remembered taste. Her eyes had closed. In the present, the roof beams groaned. In the memory, my lover wiped my chin with her thumb, leaving a black trace of printer's ink.

“Stay here a moment,” the Valkyrie said.

She wanted another moment at the feast.

I had prepared to make her watch executions. Now I had given her something she wanted. I could feel it in the pressure of her fingers. When she opened her eyes, they were violet even where ours are white. I had never been looked at with such naked appetite.

I let the dance continue. I gave her my pride as the room applauded me, the weight of silver tugging at my hips, my lover's hands spread wide among all the clapping hands. Beyond the pillars, the side doors opened.

I pulled away.

Smoke returned. Vasketh was staring at me. From somewhere near the broken stair came the faint, unbearable start of my march.

“Why did you stop?” the Valkyrie asked.

“It was a long time ago.”

“It was the victory feast,” Vasketh said. “The night they brought the island captains before the queen.”

“You weren't there.”

“There are accounts.”

“Then offer them.”

I took the Valkyrie's hand again. Vasketh laid his other hand on her arm, and the hall became a page covered in a narrow, impatient script. I saw it as he had seen it. The captains entered barefoot. Chains joined them at the ankles. Someone threw a fruit stone. The account named the singer who led the refrain.

My own name was halfway down the page. The writer had underlined it twice.

I broke contact again. A piece of ceiling fell onto an empty table and split it in two. Vasketh flinched and covered his head, then dropped his hands and looked up at the Valkyrie.

“I can remember that page,” I said. “If she chooses me. I can tell it.”

“You could have told it just now.”

The Valkyrie waited. She did not extend her hand.

Here is where I could put a noble thought. You have followed me through a burning palace; perhaps you would accept that I became someone else in its doorway. But I was looking at Vasketh. He knew the names I did not. He could give the dead their own sentences. I wanted him to fail, and I wanted to live, and the memory I had withheld was still in me, warm and crowded and splendid.

“I liked it,” I said.

Neither answered. I had given them too little.

“That night. When they came in. I liked all of it.”

I took the Valkyrie's hand and reached for Vasketh. He drew his own away from me, then put it against her arm.

The captains entered. I stood on the platform, enjoying the sudden hush. One prisoner was a woman with a broken nose and a strip of bandage sliding over her eye. The queen had ordered them to dance. Their chains allowed half a step. They tried to follow the music and collided; one fell, pulling two others down. Laughter came from the royal table. My musicians looked to me.

I raised my hands and brought in the march.

Every heel in the hall found its beat. Our guests stamped around the prisoners as they struggled up. I changed a word in the refrain, replacing *armies* with *dancers*. Such a little alteration. They loved it. The queen threw a bracelet that landed at my feet, and I wore it home.
