My lover stopped clapping. I had omitted that too. She stood below the platform with the dish in her hands, no longer smiling. Later, she would ask why I had done it. I would say it was a song, that everyone had been drunk, that she had enjoyed the feast well enough until then.

I gave the Valkyrie that conversation as well. I heard myself turn cruel when my excuses failed. I heard the door close after my lover left. We would find our way back to each other, but not that night, and not because I deserved it.

When I let go, the Valkyrie was watching the present hall. Her wing still shaded Vasketh. The man on the cushions had stopped moving his lips.

“I didn't want her to die,” I said.

“I know,” Vasketh said. “That is not the part in doubt.”

Outside, the great light widened. Shadows of the terrace pillars stretched across the floor until they reached the far wall.

The Valkyrie folded her wing. Vasketh shielded his eyes.

“Nacorra,” she said. “Will you come?”

For a moment I could not work out what answer she needed.

“I have given you very little,” I said.

“You stopped where I wanted to stay. Then you made me go on.”

Vasketh struggled to stand. “I can go on. I have spent my life going on. There are eight hundred years behind her little court. There are things nobody knows now except me.”

The Valkyrie turned toward him. “I have heard what you offered.”

“Then hear more.”

“We have to leave.”

He caught her wrist. She allowed the touch. Nothing came through to me; I was no longer holding her. I watched his lips move, watched her face, and knew that he was still trying.

She removed his hand gently. I disliked her for the gentleness, although I was already moving toward her.

“Yes,” I said. “Take me.”

Someone inside the hall called Vasketh's name. An older woman, sitting beneath a table, was trying to get up. He looked between us and her. Then he turned and went to her, striking his knee against the broken table edge in his haste. He swore, steadied himself, continued. He did not look back at me.

The Valkyrie lifted me from the terrace with an arm beneath my knees. Her other hand held the back of my head. Her wings opened and there was breath around us, cool air that smelled faintly of her skin.

Below, the hall filled with light.

The people nearest the doors raised their arms. I saw clothing catch fire. I saw a woman trying to drag a burning blanket from the person beside her, pulling until she fell backward with it. Then the outer wall burst inward and the roof came down. Vasketh was under it. I had last seen him bending toward the woman beneath the table. I cannot tell you whether he had reached her hand.

We rose. The island vanished inside a white circle. Beyond it, the sea lifted in concentric ridges, copper turning to gold, gold to a violet so deep it seemed cool. The fragments high above the impact shone like a necklace pulled apart.

You can see how easily I do it.

I pressed my face against the Valkyrie's neck. Under the dark collar her skin was damp. I waited to hear something over her breathing. There was only a deep pressure in my ears, and then nothing of Theskar at all.

We did not go to another world. Far below us the same land turned through seasons I could no longer count. Her living warmth held me while the sky changed around her. Sometimes I woke with my mouth open on a word. Sometimes she asked for the feast again, and I gave it to her through the entrance of the prisoners, through the quarrel afterward. She never asked me to stop sooner. Whether that was sorrow, duty, or appetite, I do not know.

When she set me down, she said six centuries had passed. I stood on a cold beach with a split lip that had not healed. The sea lay east of me; the islands had been to the west. I had to turn around twice before I understood where she had brought me.

“Are there people?” I asked.

“Beyond the headland.”

“Will you come?”

“Their ending has not come.”

She stepped backward. Her hair lifted and the crystal above her head began to turn. I reached out too late to touch her. When I walked around the headland, I was alone.

The people who found me gave me a cloak, then argued about who was going to feed me. I understood that part long before I understood their words. Their children laughed at my accent for years. Their singers could warm the stones beneath their feet with a held note, yet could do nothing to make me learn their scales. It took nine winters before I could write this without someone sitting beside me. I am older now than my lover was allowed to become.

I have put down what I remember of Vasketh's offerings, including the child's game. I have put down the names from my lover's list that I can still recall. There are gaps. I have left them visible. I cannot ask the dead man what came after a word I almost remember, and I still hate him sometimes for knowing it.

You have my country now, as much of it as these pages can give you. You may close them. You may decide the Valkyrie chose badly. I have imagined you doing both, often enough that I began by trying to prevent it.

But there is a woman here who has read this twice. Yesterday she asked me to sing the march so she could hear where the prisoners entered. I took the first breath. Across six hundred years my chest knew how to fill, my tongue knew where to strike, and for one sickening instant I wanted her to join in.

I sang it anyway. When I reached the changed word, she kept her hands still on the open book.

stories.title: The Seraph of the Infinite Gear
stories.prompt: The Seraph of the Infinite Gear appears only when history is about to repeat itself, descending on wings of ivory feathers and living gold machinery to turn the celestial mechanism that rewinds civilization. This time, as her hand reaches for the final gear, she discovers something impossible someone else has been turn her gears.
stories.body:
# The Seraph of the Infinite Gear

The false dawn caught the undersides of her wings. For a moment every ivory feather was pink, every turning shaft among them the color of hot copper. Below, on a thousand terraces, people lifted mirrors to greet a sun their astronomers had made.

The Seraph descended through her rings. Their gold opened around her, warm as flesh. They had enclosed the country three mornings ago, when its rulers committed themselves to repeating the ignition that had melted their ancestral capital. Beyond the mountains, travelers waited at a bright, impassable edge. Inside it, the descendants of the dead had built a larger instrument.

She had watched them polishing its mirrors. Even knowing what they meant to do, she had admired the patience, the ingenious ladders, the little cloth hoods that kept dust off each facet. They had stitched gilt suns on their children's slippers. They wanted so badly to have made a morning.

Now the trial light was rising. When it whitened, they would open the instrument fully.

At the last ring she spread her hand toward the final gear and stopped.

Someone had moved it.

The gear's rim stood higher than a house. Her palm belonged in a depression on its flank; no other hand had ever fitted there. Yet fresh scratches crossed the gold beneath it, and red dust lay in a tooth that should have been clean. A short bronze bar rested on the platform.

From somewhere inside the ring came singing: a man's voice, carrying an unfinished phrase over the machinery. She waited for its resolution. It began again instead.

She slowed the shafts in her wings until she could hear his breath.

“Come out where I can see you.”

He emerged between two spokes, brushing his sleeve against his mouth. A broad man, grown well into adulthood, with a singer's lifted chest and an embroidered collar that had chafed his neck raw. He had lost a fastening from one shoe. His eyes went first to her face, then to her left wing.

“Could you fold your left wing around me?” he said. “I'm very cold.”

She kept it spread.

“Did you move this?”

“A little.” He looked at the bronze bar. “I couldn't get it past the catch.”

The catch still held. Without her living power, he could only rock the gear through the play between its teeth. No hour below had shifted. She touched the scratched gold, and it slowly filled beneath her fingers.

“Why did you try?”

“I wanted you to come down.”

“The light brings me down.”

“Yes,” he said. “I got impatient.”

He said it with such rueful familiarity that she looked behind her, toward the empty upper rings.

“Who are you?”

“Sovekh. I sing the invocation at the opening of the mirrors. Or I'm meant to. I climbed the ceremonial stair the night before your enclosure shut. I brought food. It's mostly gone.”

The stair ended beneath this platform. Each year singers climbed it to send their voices through the great ring, which amplified them across the country. Usually they went home when the ceremony ended. He had stayed beyond its last step, out of sight of the cradle where she woke when a civilization approached an old catastrophe.

“That phrase,” she said. “You keep leaving it unfinished.”

“The high note is difficult when I'm cold.”

She drew her left wing inward. He moved beneath its shelter without waiting to be asked, then checked himself and looked at her.

She let him stay. Gold veins brightened among the feathers, warming the air. He held his hands near them, palms turned politely away from her skin.

“Try now.”

He sang. The note opened into something larger than she had expected, a sustained rising sound with an almost laughing turn at its height. Down on the terraces people were singing the same invocation, but the machinery blurred their voices together. Here she could hear the little grain in his, the effort at the end.

He coughed and looked annoyed with himself.

“Again,” she said.

“Give me a breath.”

She waited. He took his time, rubbing warmth into his throat, and she watched him with an attention she usually spread across a country. The second attempt was better. She bent her head to hear it, black curls falling against the gold at her shoulder.

“You were going to ask what the words mean,” he said. “The first verse praises the sun. The second asks it to make room.”

She had been going to ask exactly that.

“For the light they're making?”

“For ours, yes. My teacher always left that verse out. He thought it would offend the sun.” Sovekh rubbed his throat. “I put it back after he died. I wouldn't have dared while he could hear me.”

She smiled at him. She had been enjoying the song; now she wanted to know about the man who had decided how it should be sung.

“You liked it better with that verse,” he added.

“I have never heard it without.”

“No. I meant before.”

She unfolded her wing.

The warmed air escaped. He watched the feathers move away from him, and for the first time his ease deserted him completely.

“Before when?”

He rubbed a dark stain near his cuff. Below them, the trial sun deepened from rose to orange.

“We've spoken before. Here.”

She remembered three days of watching. She remembered entering the high cradle at the first enclosed dawn. She did not remember him.

“Show me something besides your account.”

He took her around the hub, keeping well clear of her wings. On the inner face of a spoke, where the gold received no healing warmth from her touch, he had scratched seven groups of marks. Each held three long cuts. Smaller marks crowded the spaces between them. Along the platform stood empty food jars and a blanket polished thin at the shoulder.

“Seven times,” he said. “The mirrors open. You turn the gear. We wait three days. The mirrors open again.”

She pressed two fingers against the spoke. Its buried count rose through her bones: seven completed returns, each to the same dawn. This was the eighth approach to ignition. She had spent twenty-one days here beyond the three she could remember.

The upper rings remained outside the return, keeping their occupants with them. He had climbed beyond its reach before the first enclosed dawn; there would never have been another Sovekh waiting on the ground. Even the jars could only empty once.

Her shoulders ached. Until now she had taken the ache for the weight of descent.

“How do I not remember?”

His gaze flickered toward the root of her left wing.

She turned it forward.

Under the lowest feathers, a wheel no wider than her palm kept her own recollection separate from the country's returning time. Its inward coil held the sequence she had lived since the enclosure. Its outer rim could wind that recollection back, as far as the first enclosed dawn. It kept no spare record of what was unwound. Her body would remain where it was, with its hunger, its wear, its healed places.

One feather beside the rim was bent against its grain. Bronze dust lay in the little drive teeth.

“You touched this.”

He nodded.

She felt the old, deep movement of her machinery become suddenly intolerable. Every part of it was warm and exposed. He had stood inside her folded wing while she listened to him sing.

“While you slept,” he said. “After you returned the country. I turned it to the first dawn. You'd wake in the cradle and watch the three days again.”

“And you hid.”

“Until you came down.”

She reached beneath the bent feather. It hurt to pull it free of the rim. He took a step toward her and she raised her other hand.

“Stay there.”

He stopped.

The small wheel could do what he described. She knew that as she knew how her fingers closed. But the knowledge belonged to an untouched part of her life; she had never chosen to wind herself backward. She needed to feel the difference between what this man claimed and what had happened to her.

She slid the wheel's stop against the next tooth, allowing the smallest possible backward motion. On the platform's dusty gold she wrote with her finger: *I am testing my recollection.* Then she set her left hand flat beside the words.

“Say nothing until I ask you something.”

He nodded again, too quickly.

She lifted her left hand and pointed at his sleeve. “What is that stain?” With her right, she turned the little wheel against the stop.

Her left hand was in the air.

“Apricot syrup,” he said.

She remembered setting her hand down. She remembered telling him to wait. She did not remember pointing, or the question. The wheel rested against its stop; her writing remained below her raised hand.

“You asked about my sleeve,” he said. “I spilled it yesterday.”

She lowered her arm. The absence had no edge she could feel. Between laying her hand on the platform and finding it raised, nothing seemed missing until she looked at what her body had done.

Sovekh began to speak. She could see his mouth moving, but she had let the shafts accelerate, and their noise swallowed him. For several breaths she allowed herself that deafness. Then she quieted them.

“Why?”

“The first time, after you turned the great gear, you asked me to stay.” He swallowed. “You wanted the rest of the song. I sang it badly. I was frightened, and you kept watching my mouth. We talked until the light changed.”

She could imagine it with awful ease: the warm feathers, his breath before a note, the pleasure of being kept waiting for something small.

“What did I say?”

“You wanted to know whether I liked singing for all those people. I said yes. You asked why I'd left them, then, and I told you I'd wanted to see you close.”

He looked at her dark hands, at the gold growing along their tendons.

“You said you could carry me beyond the mountains when you were finished here. There are places where the ground is white even in summer. You were trying to describe them. I thought you meant salt, but you said it was cold. You couldn't understand that I'd never seen snow.”

She had wanted to show someone the high white plains for a very long time.

“Did I take you?”

“No. We stayed here. You said you had to learn why they kept opening the mirrors before you could leave.”

“Then what happened?”

“We had three days.” His face changed as he looked past her. “You tried to sleep standing up because the cradle wasn't made for two. You wouldn't tell me you were tired. I thought you'd gone quiet because I was boring you. Then your knee bent and you nearly took me through the floor.”

He laughed once, involuntarily. She felt the urge to laugh with him and hated having to examine it.

“You slept after that. I sat beside you. When you woke, you didn't want me to come anymore.”

“Did I tell you why?”

“You said you'd offered too quickly.”

That was plausible too. Almost anything was possible in the time she had lost. She could have been tender, thoughtless, delighted, unkind. She wanted her own memory of the offered journey, even if recovering it meant remembering that she had hurt him.

“You'd already told me where I'd sit between your wings,” he said. “I had packed.”

There were crumbs of dried fruit in a fold of his blanket. He stooped and picked one out, rolling it between his finger and thumb while he waited for her to answer.

“Was that why you first turned the little wheel?”

“Yes. After the next return, when you slept. You'd shown it to me. You said it was why you remembered when nobody below could.”

“You knew it would erase what we had said.”

“I thought we could have the good part again.”

He let the crumb fall.

The trial sun brightened. Somewhere below, a bell began the long summons that brought the astronomers to their stations. She had heard that bell on the previous morning, calling people to the final rehearsal. Now its deep note trembled through the platform.

“How many times have I found out?” she asked.

He looked toward the scratched spoke.

“Sovekh.”

“Twice. Before today.”

She moved away from him, toward the final gear. He followed along the outside of the ring, keeping the distance she had required but matching each of her steps.

“The second meeting wasn't the same,” he said. “I knew too much. I kept answering things you hadn't asked. Once I told you about the snow before you did, and you thought I'd been there. I couldn't get back to where we were.”

“When I found out, what did I do?”

“You were angry.”

“What did I do?”

He stopped walking.

“You told me to leave.”

The bronze bar was still where she had first seen it. She saw now that its end was narrow enough to reach through feathers. He had been using the same tool on both gears.

“And you waited until I slept again.”

“You have to sleep after the turning. I knew that by then.”

He made no attempt to soften it. Somehow that was worse than his first evasions. She put her palm against the great gear, and the country pressed upward through her: the terraces, the crowded stairways, the animals restless in their stalls beneath the growing light. Soon all of it would be unbearable to touch.

“I remembered you,” he said. “Every time. You could wake up and look at me as if there'd never been anything. I still had all of it.”

She kept her hand against the gear. His words reached her through its deepening vibration.

“I want those days back,” she said.

“I can tell you.”

“You left out the times I told you to go.”

He opened his mouth, closed it, then began the invocation. Quietly, without the public fullness of his singing voice. The phrase she had heard on her descent, with a small hesitation in a different place.

For a moment she listened. Her anger did not make the sound ugly. That had been part of the pleasure too, perhaps: a man bringing something beautiful into the rings and being pleased when she heard it.

“Stop,” she said.

He stopped in the middle of a breath.

“I won't carry you beyond the mountains. When I have turned the country back, I will take you down.”

He stared at the bronze bar. She bent and lifted it. The tool was nearly weightless in her hand; the trouble he had taken to move the great gear with it must have been considerable.

She folded the left wing across her body. The little wheel continued its steady inward winding, keeping this moment. She laid the bar against the outer drive and broke off the exposed teeth.

Pain went through her shoulder. The wing struck the platform hard enough to knock Sovekh to his knees. He reached toward her, then braced his hand on the floor instead.

Gold welled along the broken rim. She held the living edges together and let them grow into a smooth sheath over the coil. The inward axle turned beneath it. Her memories remained: the song, the raised hand, the things he had admitted. There would be no place for his tool when she slept.

Below, the mirrors opened.

White light climbed the spokes. For an instant it showed Sovekh with every shadow stripped from his face, one hand braced on the platform beside the great gear. Far below him, the first roofs lifted from their houses.

She turned the final gear.

Its teeth took hold through the whole breadth of her wings. The white fire stopped rising. It gathered inward, drawing its torn fringes out of the streets, dragging a shower of roof tiles back through the air. Tiles settled into courses. A falling astronomer rose feetfirst to a balcony. His hands found its rail and released it in reverse order.

The fire narrowed to a trembling thread. It withdrew into the instrument.

She turned farther. Sovekh clung to a spoke while the great rim passed beneath the platform, carrying the enclosed country backward through its hours. Within the boundary the recorded light of evening followed morning. Outside it, the stars continued their slow westward motion. A caravan beyond the mountains stood watching a darkness rush across a country that had just been lit like a coal.

In that darkness a festival rebuilt itself. Wilted garlands rose from carts and fastened fresh against doorways. Men climbed backward down ladders with bunting unrolling above their hands. Supper returned to plates. A woman rose from a bench into the last turn of a dance, her partner's waiting hand closing around hers.

The Seraph bent beneath the weight of it. Gold in her wings burned white. Three nights passed over the enclosed land, each lifting into the day that had preceded it. A field gathered its cut stems. A potter's broken bowl leaped together on a shelf. Across every terrace, the gilt slippers of children shrank back into their paper wrappings.

The first enclosed dawn arrived. The catch fell into place.

She could still remember Sovekh singing.

For a while she could do nothing but stand against the gear. Her ivory dress clung to her back. The feathers nearest the small sealed wheel trembled independently of the others, and she had to wait for them to settle before she could fly.

Sovekh got up. Below him the astronomers were waking to three days of preparation. The same rulers held their offices; the larger instrument stood ready for its final polish. She knew no more than before about what would make them stop. Through the cut of one narrow street she could see the council house, where she had watched messengers come and go. She had never gone down to hear what they were saying.

She would have to sleep. First she would take him down.

At the edge of the platform she lowered one wing to make a seat against her side. He hesitated before climbing into it. He knew where to put his feet. She almost told him to move them, then found that they were correctly placed.

“Where were you meant to sing?”

He pointed toward a terrace below the instrument. “The blue platform.”

They descended over the roofs she had seen torn loose. Morning smoke rose from cooking fires. A woman leaned out to shake a cloth, saw them passing, and let it fall from her hands.

The platform was empty. Its blue boards had not yet acquired the scratches of the festival. The Seraph landed beside it and lowered her wing until Sovekh could step onto the ground.

He kept one hand on a feather.

“The first time,” he said, “you asked whether I knew any songs that weren't for ceremonies.”

She waited. He was looking at his hand. Slowly he lifted it away.

She rose, painfully at first, then caught the air above the terrace. Behind her a voice began, too low for a ceremonial invocation. She heard a woman asking for the return of a borrowed coat; then a change in pitch, the other woman's answer. A foolish little song, full of interruptions. She turned her head to catch another line.

She cleared the first roof. Below, his second voice was arguing about the coat.

stories.title: The Last Color Through
stories.prompt: The black door has no lock—only a river of living colors flowing into its frame. Touch red, and it opens onto a world of fire; blue, an endless ocean; green, a planet-sized forest. Every color is a different pocket dimension.
stories.body:
# The Last Color Through

Nerith had brought six kinds of pick to open the black door. By the time she reached it, she had thought of three people who would pay to watch.

The door stood without a wall in the lowest cut of the abandoned quarry. Evening lay blue in the chisel marks. Down the pale slope came a river too bright to look at directly, branching around stones and rejoining in colors that remained separate even where they crowded together. They flowed into the foot of the frame, climbed its sides, and curled over one another along the lintel. There was no keyhole. No handle, either.

She took out her thinnest pick.

“You'll scratch it,” Bozren said from behind the door.

He came around the frame with his pack on one shoulder. A twist of yellow detached itself from the river and followed his boot, then hurried back to the other colors.

“How long have you been here?”

“Long enough to walk round it.”

“I found the map.”

“So did I.” He unfolded a little square of paper. The same triangular tear, the same grease mark where the quarry road forked. Nerith had paid extra for that grease mark. The seller had called it a bloodstain.

Bozren looked from his map to hers. She turned its face against her leg.

“How much?” he asked.

“I'm going to recover my expenses.”

“That much?”

She put the pick away. Perhaps the colored stuff was a seal. She crouched beside the river and laid two fingers across a red strand. It swelled under her touch, warm and firm as a tongue. A little loop curled around her smallest finger. Then it let go and ran up the frame.

The black slab swung outward into the quarry.

Heat drove them back. Beyond the sill, a plain of flame heaved under a sky of thicker flame. White ridges rose out of it, broke into streamers, and rebuilt themselves farther away. There was nothing beneath the fire that she could see. Even the shadows were dark red flames, leaning against the brightness.

Nerith's first thought was that the jewel merchants would come in carriages.

Her second was that her eyebrows were burning.

She clapped a hand over them and moved sideways. On the far side of the quarry, through a gap between the frame and its open slab, lay an ordinary heap of stone. Straight through the frame lay a world on fire.

Bozren bent to look along the sill. A ribbon of red ran around its inner edge. Across the burning plain something like a herd leapt, each shape pulling itself out of the blaze and falling back before she could count it.

“Did you see those?” she said.

“Yes.”

“They had legs.”

“Some of them.”

She wanted a better look. She also wanted the last of her eyebrows. When a hot gust snapped the little hairs on her wrist, she caught the cool edge of the slab and pushed it shut.

Bozren was grinning at her over the top of his collar.

“A silver piece to look,” she said. “Two if they want the front.”

“You were meant to find buried plate.”

“I can change what I sell.”

But she was already reaching past the red toward blue, and his hand got there first.

The door opened above an ocean. Its sill lay barely a hand's breadth over the moving surface. The air tasted of salt; the heat left her face so suddenly that she shivered. No coast interrupted the horizon. Behind that horizon was more sea, and more beyond it, an entire world with nowhere for a wave to break except another wave.

Then one broke against the frame.

Cold water slapped their boots and spread across the quarry floor. Nerith gasped. Bozren laughed with his mouth wide open and got a mouthful. She enjoyed that until the sea darkened.

A translucent back slid beneath the doorway. Through it she saw branching organs blue as veins in milk glass, and, much farther down, other enormous bodies swimming at different depths. The nearest rolled. A round eye, larger than the door, rose level with them. Its pale lid drew sideways. The water between its lashes held miniature rainbows.

Nerith had once spent nine days getting a thumb-sized blue stone out of a dead queen's shoe. Here was blue wide enough to swallow the hill, looking at her.

She lifted her wet hand. The eye did not blink again. After a while the creature sank, drawing the others after it, and sunlight filled the water it had occupied.

“We'd need a boat,” Bozren said.

She pictured one of the little hired boats on the lake below her town, tipped over in the crease beside that eyelid.

“A larger boat than you're thinking of.”

He touched green on the upright. Nothing happened. The ocean continued lifting toward their feet.

Nerith closed the slab. He touched the same green strand, and this time the door opened into leaves.

A branch lay flush with the sill, broad enough for ten people abreast. Moss made ridges along its bark. Far below, treetops crowded against treetops until the whole green surface curved away under a rim of luminous haze. The forest clothed a planet, and they were looking out from a tree so tall that they could see the roundness of the world beneath it. There were forests upon the limbs of that tree, smaller trees rooted in its crevices, and smaller ones upon those, their crowns spangled with yellow flowers.

The scent made Nerith hungry: split fruit, pepper, the hot resin she used to mend her specimen boxes. A winged thing no longer than her hand flew through the doorway, turned in the quarry's chilly air, and flew straight back.

Bozren followed it.

“You've had your turn,” she said.

He was already on the moss, walking with his arms out. His boots sank and released with a soft tearing sound. He went six paces, turned, and returned through the opening. Green sap strung itself between his sole and the sill.

“There,” he said. “You can come back.”

Nerith stepped through before he could offer advice. The branch moved beneath her, a slow rise she felt first in her knees. Above her, a leaf unfurled. Its edge traveled across the sky for so long that she stopped trying to guess where it would end. She went back into the quarry with her neck aching and her heart running hard.

Bozren had sat down to retie his boots. He was looking past her at a yellow flower on an upper bough.

She knew that look. He had worn it while crawling out of a bear's winter den with a piece of antler. He had thought he was following a rumor about ivory stairs. She'd laughed for half an hour; afterward, when he showed her the scratches, she'd wanted to see the den.

“You always like the biggest thing,” she said.

“I like that one.”

“We haven't even opened half of them.”

He got up reluctantly and moved aside. She shut the door, and for the first time saw how much quarry stone showed through the river.

Red was no longer coming down the slope.

Its last length was winding itself up the frame. She put a finger to it. The slab opened, the heat returned, and the red flowed over the sill into fire. She watched its trailing end slide through. The white ridges flattened, grew transparent, and disappeared.

Through the empty frame stood Bozren's shadow on a heap of broken limestone. The slab remained open at her left.

“Do that again,” he said.

She shut it. On the frame, blue and green flowed past violet, yellow, orange, and a narrow dark color she had no name for. She pressed the place where red had been. Then she touched the red cuff of her coat to it, hard enough to rub quarry dust into the wool.

Bozren said her name.

“I know.” She pulled the cuff away.

Far up the slope, orange had begun contracting. Its tributaries drew inward, leaving dry white stone behind. Nerith took a collecting jar from her pack and tried to scoop a little into it. The color divided around the glass. When she put the jar across its path, the strand climbed out of reach along a stone. It waited there until she moved aside.

“They're leaving,” Bozren said.

She could see that. She didn't see why they had started just as she arrived.

“Then open something.”

He caught orange. Beyond the door lay a terrace of honey-colored pillars, all the same height, all slowly revolving. A dry wind rattled between them. Bozren stood across the sill with one foot on a pillar's broad top and one in the quarry, peering down into the spaces.

The orange strand shortened. It slid along the frame toward his ankle, where its tip curled and uncurled. The terrace grew faint. Bozren leaned farther out, and Nerith caught the back of his belt.

“Look at your ankle.”

He looked at the color, then drew his foot into the quarry. Orange swept through the opening after it. The pillars vanished.

Neither spoke for a moment. Nerith was still holding his belt. He looked over his shoulder at her hand, and she let go.

“It waited for you,” she said.

“I wasn't going to find out how long.”

She looked back up the white slope. She could remember colors there that she could no longer name accurately. The river was thinning everywhere, different strands moving at different speeds. She had been imagining a queue of carriages, a roof against the rain, her own journeys in the hours when nobody was waiting. She had not even thought to hurry.

Bozren closed the slab and reached for green.

“No. Mine now.”

His hand stopped. She touched violet.

The door swung onto a slope of hollow mineral shells. Their curled edges protruded from the sand like the mouths of trumpets, some small enough to fit her jar, others large enough to shelter a house. Violet shadows pooled inside them. Beyond the nearest ridge, pale stems carried drops of moisture which gathered, shone, and fell with extravagant slowness.

The air was cool and breathable. Something hummed deep in the shells. Nerith picked up a pebble and threw it. It traveled much farther than she intended, dwindling to a speck before it struck.

A clear note sounded. Another shell answered, then another, until a chord rolled out across the dunes. The pressure of it fluttered the front of her coat. Where the pebble had landed, one enormous spiral raised itself on little articulated feet.

Nerith laughed. It came out too loud. She had spent her first gold on a bronze bowl she'd heard singing in a temple, only to discover that at home it sounded thin and mean. She'd carried it all the way back and sat there striking it until they made her leave. Now she leaned into the opening, waiting for the next note.

Bozren was opening his pack.

“Listen,” she told him.

“I heard.”

“It moved.”

“I saw.” He pulled his climbing cord free of the bedroll. “I want green again.”

She put her boot on the sill. A violet thread touched its leather toe and pulled away. The nearest shell vibrated against the sand. A drop hung above a delicate stem, falling so slowly she could watch it turn.

Behind her came the click of Bozren's pack buckle.

“What are you doing?”

“Going into the tree.”

“For another look.”

He tightened the strap with both hands. “With my things.”

She took her foot off the sill and shut the door. The chord stopped halfway through a descending note. She could still feel it in her ribs.

“You saw what happened to orange.”

“Yes.”

“You can't leave a rope through. What happens when the opening goes? And you can't stand in it and get anywhere.”

“I'm taking the rope to climb.”

His pack was the one he had carried for as long as she'd known him, the canvas patched with pieces of older packs. A tin cooking cup swung from its side. His provisions would last weeks; she had seen him take that pack into the hills and come back at the other end of a season. Once she'd found him still camped beside a stone beast three weeks after they had sold the jewels from its eyes. At night, he told her, moths came out of its empty sockets. She had stayed one night. It had been worth staying.

“Let me see yellow first,” she said. “You might like it more.”

“I'm not asking you to choose for me.”

“I'm asking you to look.”

He opened his mouth, then shut it as yellow suddenly slid away from her reaching hand. It ran up the frame and into the seam. No one touched it in time.

Bozren said, “Move, Nerith.”

She was standing between him and green. She had not meant to put herself there. Her hands were on the frame, one above the other, gripping the hard black corners where no color passed.

“Wait with me.”

He stopped pulling on his gloves.

“Until when?”

She wanted to say until she was ready. Until she'd seen them all. Until she had worked out how a person chose a place to stay when there were still places they had never seen. In the light from the river his face looked younger than it had when he came round the door, eager and offensively hopeful.

“I don't know,” she said.

“I could miss it.”

Green was still thick enough to lay a palm across. Upstream, though, it was gathering its little branches into itself.

Nerith stepped aside. Bozren touched it, and the forest opened. A rain of pollen drifted past, grains big as barley, yellow dust brushing the sill. On the distant bough, the flower he had watched was loosening another petal.

“I used to climb the ash behind my mother's house,” he said, watching it. “I thought it would get taller while I was up there. If I waited.” He rubbed pollen off his nose. “Stupid.”

She had never heard him say that of himself. “How long did you wait?”

“Till she came out with a ladder.”

He stepped across the sill with his pack. Nerith's chest hurt. She wanted him back where she could pull faces at him when he said something she didn't believe. They had met by chance in more miserable places than she could count. She'd come to rely on the nuisance of him appearing.

Bozren paused with his heel still in the doorway.

“You can come,” he said.

She looked past him. The broad limb rose toward a fork, and there were paths among the little trees growing in its bark: openings where leaves had been pushed aside, distant patches of moving brightness. She could follow him. She could see what he saw and complain about his cooking cup, and it would be a life no one in her town had imagined.

Beyond her shoulder, violet slid softly against stone.

“I want to hear the shells,” she said.

He nodded, once. She crouched to put her jar away. Its glass was unmarked; not even a smear of orange had stayed on it. She wrapped it in its cloth and packed it between the dried figs and her spare shirt.

Green had drawn its whole remaining length down from the quarry slope. It circled the frame once, and its tip reached Bozren's heel.

“Go,” she said. “I'll watch till you're through.”

He took two steps, turned, and lifted his hand. She lifted hers. The green flowed after him, unrolling along the moss. Through the fading opening she saw him turn toward the fork and break into a clumsy run beneath the weight of his pack. She laughed, and wanted to be running there herself, and kept her feet where they were.

Then there was only the quarry behind the frame.

Nerith stood with her hand up a little longer. Evening had reached the bottom of the cut. The wet patch left by the ocean had dried at its edges, and the pollen was sticking to the middle of it.

She could go back down the road. She knew how far it was to supper, knew which of the merchants would listen without interrupting, which would offer her money for the map. There would be pleasure in making them believe her. Someone would ask about Bozren. Someone always did.

Violet was the last color left.

She put on her pack. For a moment the weight steadied her into the familiar business of leaving a place she had searched. Then she shut the empty door and crouched beside the violet strand.

It stopped under her fingers. She felt it gather, a small living firmness. It had somewhere to go.

When the door opened, she stood in the sill and listened. The shells were quiet now. Across the slope, the drop she had watched earlier was gone; another was swelling in its place. She could see little tracks where a spiral had crossed the sand. She looked back once, all the way to the lip of the quarry, then hitched her waterskin higher on her belt.

She stepped out. Her usual stride carried her too high, too far. She hung for a startled moment with both feet off the ground, her pack lifting against its straps. She twisted to look back. Violet slid across the sand below her; the rectangle of quarry light narrowed and went out.

Nerith came down on the side of a shell.

Its note threw a ripple through the sand. Spirals stirred along the ridge, opening their many feet. She tried to recover her balance, stepped onto another curved lip, and rang a second note, deeper than the first. The shell bucked under her boot and sent her tumbling upward. Three dunes away something huge began to rise.

She tucked her knees up and watched where she was going to fall.

stories.title: The First Winter
stories.prompt: The witch who raised you has kept the valley in autumn your entire life. On the morning you decide to leave, she admits why: someone has been searching for you since you were born, and she keep the rest of world in time loop to keep you safe.
stories.body:
# The First Winter

I was two hours down the valley with Besset's frying pan knocking against my leg when she caught up with me.

I had been walking carefully in the dark. She had run. Her blue hat hung down her back on its cord, and strands of hair stuck to her open mouth. For a moment she could only bend over, hands on knees, while I tried to remember the speech I had composed on the way.

"I'm eighteen," I began.

She caught my sleeve and pulled me behind a boulder.

That spoiled the speech. I tried to shake her off. Below us the path wound through birches, pale enough to follow without a lamp. Beyond them lay country I had never walked, where people had birthdays with guests and weather happened without Besset deciding whether it should.

"Look," she said.

A man was coming up the lower path. He carried a crossbow against his shoulder. I had never seen another person in the valley, and I leaned out before I thought about the weapon.

He stopped. His head turned straight toward me.

"Down."

Besset's weight struck my side as the crossbow clacked. A bolt hit the birch behind us hard enough to shake its branches. I landed on my knees among the stones, with her over me and the pan's handle digging into my hip.

She shoved my head lower. There was blood on one of her knuckles.

I could hear the man running. The path doubled back below the rock, and his boots scraped first to our left, then to our right. Besset kept looking up at the rim of the hills.

"Who is he?"

"Stay there."

"Who is he?"

"The man I brought you here to escape."

His footsteps stopped. A stone clicked against another stone. I knew that sound from hunting: someone trying to place a foot quietly after making too much noise.

Besset held out her uninjured hand.

Light reached the highest birch. She closed her fingers, slowly, with an effort that pulled the muscles tight beside her jaw. For an instant my ears filled with a pressure I had felt every morning of my life.

The bolt disappeared from the tree. Its torn bark became smooth. Leaves we had knocked down were hanging overhead again, and the man's next footstep never came.

I waited for it.

Up in the branches a bird gave the same three notes it had given before Besset caught my sleeve.

She sat back on her heels. I could see the path now. There was nobody on it.

"He'll start walking again," she said. "At the broken pass. Where he started yesterday."

My knee stung. I pulled up my trouser leg and found grit in the scrape. Dawn had left that alone.

***

I knew what dawn did to the valley. Apples returned to their branches. Ash became wood. A shirt left half-mended on the table would lose the stitches I had put into it; I slept wearing anything I wanted to keep. Besset had taught me to tuck drawings inside my clothes and carry a gathered basket until sunrise. I had learned those things before I learned to count.

She had told me that she kept the valley in autumn because winters here were cruel.

"The country beyond the pass," I said. "Does it do this too?"

"Yes."

"How far?"

"All of it."

I looked downhill again. I had imagined leaving our morning behind and reaching a place where it was spring. Somewhere there ought to have been people living through all the seasons I had missed.

"There isn't a different day outside," she said. "I bring the whole world back to the same dawn. I carry you and me through it, with what we're wearing or holding. Everything else goes back."

The dent in the frying pan was new. I ran my thumb along it while she spoke.

"He has to come around the mountain," she said. "The short crossing is gone. He walks all day and all night, and dawn catches him two hours short of the cottage. That's why I don't let you hunt below the white stones."

"And I walked down to him."

She nodded. Her eyes moved over my face, my shoulders, my hands. She looked ready to search me for a wound I was concealing.

"What does he want?"

She began to reach for my trouser leg. I moved it away.

"Besset."

"He was dying when you were born. He came to your mother as a healer. Instead he bound his blood to yours."

I covered my scraped knee with my palm.

"He can feel which way you are," she said. "Being older won't fool him. Changing your name won't help. He means to take the years you haven't lived."

"How?"

"He has to kill you. Take your heart while his own is still beating."

I remembered the small correction of his shoulder before he fired. He hadn't shouted for me to stop or asked who I was.

We stayed behind the boulder long after he had gone. Besset picked the grit from my knee with the tip of her knife, and I let her.

***

On the way home she told me about my mother. I had known there was a mother, and that she was dead. Besset had given me those facts years apart, whenever I grew old enough to ask a question that could no longer be put off. This time she told me how.

The footbridge across the pass had been narrow, with room for one person at a time. My mother waited until Besset was across with me before cutting its ropes. The man reached her while she was still cutting. Besset saw him strike her, saw the bridge swing against the cliff with both of them on it. He caught a ledge on the far side. My mother fell.

"It took me until morning to finish the working," Besset said. She had stopped where a low branch crossed the path. "He was climbing out by then. Without what she did, he'd have reached us in minutes."

I ducked under the branch. Besset followed.

"So she's still there."

"Yes."

"Below the bridge."

"Yes."

We walked a little farther.

"Could you bring back the day before?"

"No. I can only return to the dawn I caught. She had already died."

A yellow leaf had lodged in the fold of her blue sleeve. I nearly picked it off. Then I put my hands in my pockets.

At the cottage she washed our cuts. The room was exactly as it had been that morning: three apples on the sill, the same wood ready by the hearth, the stool with a split that never widened. My bed was too short. For two years I had slept with my feet sticking beyond its end.

I set my pack beside the door. Besset saw where I had put it. "You can't go yet."

"I know."

She rubbed the cloth between her palms. I had expected relief, but she kept doing it until I reached across and took it from her.

"Have you ever tried to kill him?"

Her left arm rested crookedly against her ribs. She could use that hand to hold bread while she cut it, but she could not raise it above her shoulder.

"When you were four. I waited for him in the birches. I missed, and he didn't."

"You said you fell."

"I did fall. After."

"And this stayed."

She pulled her sleeve back. The scar puckered across the inside of her elbow. I had seen it hundreds of times while we washed clothes.

"I don't go back any more than you do," she said. "If he kills me, I won't be here to renew the day."

I began to understand what she did every dawn with her eyes closed, while I complained about breakfast or tried to sleep. I also remembered telling her, three days ago, that I wanted to leave.

"When I said I wanted to leave," I said. "You could have told me then."

"I was going to."

"You let me pack."

She looked at the bag beside the door.

For a while we listened to the fire. It settled with a familiar pop, and Besset put out a hand to catch a spark before it reached the blanket on her knee.

"I can shoot," I said.

"Rabbits."

"And deer."

"They don't shoot back."

"I know that now."

She opened her mouth, then turned the burnt spot in the blanket toward the light. I waited. I had learned patience in the woods, though Besset seldom saw any evidence of it at home.

"Let me help," I said.

She kept her head bent.

I put my good knee against hers beneath the table. That made her look at me.

***

By noon the little crossbow was lying between us. Besset had brought it down from the roof beams, where I had always been told to leave it alone. She could hold it steady with its stock against her shoulder and its front resting on something solid. She could no longer draw it back.

I loaded it for her.

Outside, she knelt behind a stump and put a bolt into the centre of a scrap of cloth. Then she stayed there, staring at what she had done, until I went to fetch it.

We chose a stony gully below the boulder where she'd pulled me to safety. I knew it from following wounded deer past the white stones, farther than I was allowed to go. The gully bent sharply at its upper end. A flat shelf overlooked the bend; on the other side, a fallen beech offered Besset cover and a rest for her crossbow. Behind us the path climbed toward home.

I would let him see me at the bend. While he watched my bow, Besset would have a shot from his side.

We went down early to clear the branches that would obstruct her aim. In daylight the place looked smaller than I remembered. The shelf was hardly higher than my head. Above the beech, loose stones reached into a thicket of hazel that met the homeward path.

"Keep that way clear," Besset said, pointing through the hazels. "If he stays under cover, we leave."

"And you turn the day back."

"If we can stay ahead of him until dawn."

I looked at the path between her hiding place and mine.

"No going down to see where he's got to," she added.

She took off her hat and tucked it under the beech.

"What if he's dead?" I asked. "You'd bring him back as well."

Besset's hand stopped on the hat brim.

"Yes."

"Then we have to be sure. And you have to let the morning come."

"I know."

She pressed the hat farther out of sight. This time, when I looked at her, she did not look away.

***

The moon came up in its usual place. I had always hated knowing precisely where it would be. That night I watched it move through the branches and wished it would hurry.

Besset waited beyond the gully, mostly hidden by the beech. Once she lifted a hand to show she was awake. I had no need to signal back; she could see me whenever she wanted.

A long time later, a boot scraped on the path below.

He came slowly through the birches, looking up as though he had heard me breathe. At the mouth of the gully he stopped. The moon showed a narrow face, a grey beard, a dark patch of sweat at his collar. His hand shook when he lowered the crossbow.

I stood on the shelf with my bow drawn.

His eyes went to my feet, then to the empty ground behind me. He touched the inside of his wrist.

"You," he said.

I had thought I could loose as easily as I did at a deer. I had never imagined having to watch a man discover me first.

He raised the crossbow.

I fired. My arrow struck the rock beside his shoulder. He threw himself backward into the birches, and the bolt he shot went whining up the gully. Besset did not fire; the trees had already hidden him from her.

I reached for another arrow. The last one had left my fingers badly. I could feel it happening again before I had even set it to the string.

For several breaths nothing moved. Wood creaked in the birches as he reloaded.

Then leaves rustled on our right. He was climbing around the outside of the gully, toward the hazels and our way home.

Besset picked up her crossbow and stepped past the broken end of the beech, toward our way out.

"Besset, down!"

The second bolt struck before she could lower herself. She dropped out of sight.

I scrambled off the shelf and across the gully. My ankle turned on a stone, and I fell against the beech beside her. There was a bolt through the flesh above her knee. She was making a sound through her teeth, trying to keep it small. Her crossbow lay beside her, almost covered by the blue skirt of her coat.

Above us I could see the man coming through the hazels. He had found the open ground behind our hiding place. His crossbow hung empty from one hand, and he had drawn a knife with the other.

I pulled at Besset's shoulders. She cried out and the sound stopped my hands.

"Run," she said.

He watched us over the beech. Then he put his crossbow down, where he could reach it again, and moved toward the tree's broken end.

"Leave her," he told me.

The bow was still hooked over one wrist. I freed it and reached for an arrow.

"Put it down."

I kept fumbling with the arrow. He put his boot against the wounded leg. Besset's breath caught; she tried to pull away and couldn't.

The arrow fell out of my hand.

"That's it," he said. "Now the bow."

I laid it in the leaves.

Up close he smelled of old sweat and bitter medicine. His breath whistled. He looked at my chest with such concentration that I hunched my shoulders to hide it.

"You'll kill her too," I said.

"Come here and I won't have to."

He kept the pressure on her leg as I moved. I wanted to believe him for the length of time it would take to get beside him. Besset reached for the back of my coat and missed. Beneath her coat I could still see the tip of her crossbow.

I stepped past her toward the man. He caught my coat at the throat, dragged me across the gully, and shoved my back against the rock below the shelf. Besset lay by the beech behind him. His knife touched the cloth over my breastbone.

"Hold still."

His hand was trembling again. I thought of the scar in Besset's elbow, the blood on my knee that hadn't gone away.

I caught his knife wrist with both hands.

He drove me against the rock. Something tore in my shoulder. I tried to keep his arm away from my chest, but his elbow kept bending, steadily, bringing the point toward me. There was hardly room left to breathe.

I stamped at his foot. Missed. He shoved his knee between my legs and I slipped lower against the rock.

Wood scraped behind him. Besset was pulling her crossbow up onto the trunk.

He heard it. His grip on my coat loosened as he began to turn. I let my knees fold and slid down the rock, hauling on his knife arm with both hands. He stumbled forward over me as I struck the ground on my back.

The crossbow cracked. He fell across my legs, Besset's bolt standing in his back. His knife hand hit the earth beside my ear, and I caught it again before I understood that his fingers had opened. I kept holding his wrist.

Besset called to me. I could see her mouth moving. The crossbow had fallen from her hands into the leaves, and she was reaching across the space between us.

I could not make myself let him go.

***

We waited until he had stopped breathing. Then we waited longer.

Besset had to tell me twice how to find the pulse beneath his jaw. I held my fingers there while she watched his chest. There was nothing. When I finally got clear of his body, I was sick against the roots of the beech.

We bound Besset's leg with strips from my spare shirt. My shoulder hurt when I lifted my arm. I could move my fingers, and she kept asking me to do it, as though this one small success might become more convincing with repetition.

We couldn't get her up the path before dawn. There was no need to, but both of us kept looking toward home.

As the sky paled, I dragged his crossbow beyond reach, then his knife. Besset watched. She didn't repeat that he was dead.

I sat beside her. Our coats were wet with dew. Below us the bird began its three notes, and Besset's good hand lifted from her lap.

I caught it.

She looked down at our hands in surprise. For eighteen years her fingers had closed at this hour.

The light reached the birches. She spread her hand against mine and kept it open.

A leaf turned in the air and landed on the man's sleeve. It stayed there.

We watched the sunlight move along the trunk until it reached his face. His mouth had slackened. Nothing took him away.

Besset began to cry. She leaned forward with both hands over her face, and I held her so she wouldn't fall against her wounded leg. I was still angry with her. I wanted her to stop crying, and I wanted her to keep making a sound I could hear.

***

It took us most of that new morning to get home.

The following dawn I woke with the spare shirt under my head. Its missing strips had not returned. Neither had the wood we had burned, or the apples we had eaten. Rain arrived before noon, several hours earlier than I expected.

The valley took weeks to lose its leaves. I had expected the season to change all at once, as if winter had been waiting just behind the morning. Instead the gold thinned from the trees a little each day. Bare twigs appeared. Besset learned to walk with a stick, and I learned which movements made my shoulder hurt.

My pack stayed beside the door.

When I finally lifted it, the first snow was blowing across the upper hills. Besset came with me to the white stones. She wore her blue hat with a scarf tied over it against the wind.

There she stopped. I went a few steps farther before I noticed.

"You can come down," I said.

"I know."

I waited on the path while she negotiated the last uneven stretch. When she reached me, she looked beyond my shoulder toward the birches.

"Will you come back?"

"I think so."

She nodded too quickly.

"I don't know when," I said.

She put her hand against the side of my face. I stood still for it. Then I shifted the pack to spare my shoulder and began walking.

By evening I reached a village. Smoke lay over its roofs, and somebody was calling a dog. I stood outside the inn for a while, listening to more voices than I could separate.

Snow caught in my hair while I hesitated. When I brushed it away it melted against my fingers, much colder than I had expected. I wiped my hand on my coat and went inside.

stories.title: Twelve in the Room
stories.prompt: Twelve assassins surround the woman they were each hired to kill—then realize they were hired by her and tonight she has finally managed to get every last one of them into the same room.
stories.body:
# Twelve in the Room

Hesk raised his pistol because eleven other weapons were already pointing at Osselin, and he didn't want anyone noticing that he had hesitated.

His left hand was empty. The packet was supposed to go there. Collect it from the woman in white; check the seal; kill her before leaving. His phone was recording from his breast pocket. The buyer wanted her alive on the recording, identifying the papers she handed over. Half the money had arrived yesterday; the rest depended on that handover and her death. Other buyers might attend, his instructions said, and might be armed. He had understood that to mean he would have to shoot his way out afterward.

He had not understood that he would know them all.

The woman beside him still held her pistol with a crooked forefinger. A pink scar ran from her ear beneath her chin. On his other side stood the bald man who had driven Alvera to the house where she died. Eight years had put flesh on him. Hesk himself had provided the address, then said yes when Paske called to ask whether they should finish it before the girl could speak to her mother again. Yes, finish it. He remembered the exact words, although he generally permitted himself to remember only the address.

All twelve had been on that call. Alvera had stolen accounts of the killings they had carried out for her mother. Hesk had heard each of these people agree that she couldn't be released.

Osselin stood beneath a hanging worklight, pale hair loose over a white coat. A crate at her feet held brown envelopes. She looked past Hesk toward the arched double doors through which he had entered. There was a clunk behind him, answered by another at the far end of the ballroom, beneath the empty musicians' gallery.

He moved away from the doors. Osselin watched him take his place in the circle.

“There,” she said. “All of you.”

Across the light, Paske grinned at a man in a red tie. The man didn't grin back. He was looking at the long gun beside the double doors, its barrel wavering now between Osselin and the people surrounding her.

“You said a private appointment,” Paske said.

“I told you there would be other buyers.”

“Buyers.” He gave the word to the man in the tie, inviting him to enjoy it. “Right.”

Behind the long gun, a gray-bearded man pushed the double doors. They didn't move. At the opposite entrance, a man who walked with a stiff leg kicked its lower panel. Osselin bent toward the crate.

“Slow,” Hesk said.

She stopped, looking directly at him for the first time. At sixty she had learned nothing about being old. She used to summon him with that look, past better-paid men, and find him something that mattered.

“Your envelope first, then,” she said.

“Don't move,” said the scarred woman. “Tell me who gets the original.”

Osselin straightened. “There are twelve originals.”

Hesk noticed the envelopes' corners. Each had one clipped away, a habit of hers from the days when she handed him work across her kitchen table. He had once asked why. So you can find the opening in the dark, she'd said, amused that he needed telling.

“Who booked you?” he asked the scarred woman.

“Fuck off.”

“Was it half yesterday?”

Her pistol moved a fraction toward him.

“Half yesterday,” Osselin said. “A quarter on receipt of the papers. The balance when you sent proof I was dead. Yours were better terms than his. You insisted.”

The bald man made a small choking noise. Paske's grin had gone.

“For you, Paske, a private guarantee concerning the money you lost last spring. I didn't offer that to anyone else.”

Hesk looked around the ring. Near the service door in the left wall, Vestrin was watching Osselin's coat pockets. Beside her a short woman in green gloves had turned her gun toward Paske. At the far entrance, gold spectacles caught the light as their wearer leaned in to whisper to the man with the stiff leg.

“I hired you,” Osselin said. “Every one of you. Twelve separate commissions to kill me. The people you spoke to were spending my money.”

“Then you've overpaid,” Paske said.

He was still looking around for a laugh when she took her left hand out of her pocket. Her fingers enclosed a black control, her thumb pressed flat along its side. With her other hand she pushed back her coat, showing a small pistol in a holster.

“If this hand opens, the room goes.”

The woman in the riding coat, who had joined the gray beard at the double doors, gave a sharp laugh. She stopped when the man with the long gun pointed beneath the gallery. Some of the decorative panels had been removed. Hesk could see dark packages in the cavities, too new against the old dust. More waited behind a fallen strip of paneling near the service door.

He had looked at her hands and missed the room.

“You can put your guns down,” Osselin said. “Or keep them. It won't make a difference.”

Nobody put a gun down. Vestrin took one step backward.

“Stay there.”

Vestrin stopped with her heel against the service door. “Does that one open?”

“Stay there.”

Osselin stooped, awkwardly protecting her closed hand, and lifted an envelope from the crate. She tossed it toward Hesk. It slid across the parquet and stopped against his shoe. He crouched with his pistol raised. The seal had already been broken.

Inside was the note he had written eight years ago: an address, a description of the back room, the hours Alvera worked. Beneath it lay a photograph of her sitting in a chair with her hands tied. She was twenty-seven in the picture. Hesk had last seen her at twenty-six, putting a pink paper umbrella into Osselin's drink because she knew her mother would hate it. She'd stood back to admire the result before either of them laughed.

He folded the picture against the note. He had been promised the only surviving account of his part in Alvera's death. The promise had finally done what three years of offers on Osselin's life had failed to do. He'd wanted that account in his hand, burning.

“Are there copies?” he asked.

“There are now.”

He looked up at her, then remembered the phone recording against his chest.

The scarred woman bent her knees, as though testing whether she could reach Osselin before anyone else reacted. Hesk straightened quickly. Behind him the gray beard swore at the doors.

“I had to stop you running,” Osselin said. “If I'd taken one of you, the other eleven would have disappeared. Some of you already had. New faces. New friends. I kept paying to find you. Then paying to tempt you.” Her eyes returned to Hesk. “You were the last to say yes.”

He wished she hadn't said it like that, as if she'd been waiting for him to visit.

Paske took out his phone. “Let's find out how much you have left.”

“Enough to pay the balances.”

“I'm offering you mine back. With something on top.”

She shook her head. The movement set her hair against the pistol grip at her hip. Hesk remembered the woman who cut it herself above the kitchen sink, who hated a stranger touching her neck. She used to hand him the scissors to straighten what she couldn't see.

“Osselin,” he said, “look at me.”

She was already looking. He had needed a moment to think of what came next.

“You know what I did for you. Before all that.”

“I know.”

“When you were ill. Who came? Who stayed?”

“You brought the pills and ate my food. Alvera stayed.”

He hadn't known that. She'd never been there when he came. He had imagined the long afternoons afterward, Osselin grateful for the brief relief of his company.

“I never touched her.”

“I read what you wrote.”

He could feel the folded photograph becoming wet in his fist.

“You sent us to get her,” he said.

“To bring her home.”

“She knew what you were. She took the accounts. She wasn't coming home.”

Osselin's lips drew back from her teeth. For a moment he thought she would shout. Instead she looked down at her closed hand, the knuckles white.

“I paid you to take my daughter off a street and tie her up,” she said. “Yes. I did.”

Paske spread his arms. “There we are. We all made mistakes. Put the thing down and we can—”

“It doesn't stop if I put it down.”

He lowered his arms.

Hesk watched her swallowing. She had brought them here, spent what she had, laid out the envelopes. Now there was only her hand to open. Her breathing grew loud enough for him to hear it.

“You don't want to,” he said.

Her eyes came up.

He knew that look too. She disliked anyone noticing she needed help.

“We can sit down,” he said. “Nobody has to do anything just yet.”

“Don't come closer.”

“All right. I'm here.”

“Stay there.”

The service door rattled. Vestrin had turned its handle behind her back. Osselin pulled the pistol from her holster, and every barrel in the circle shifted. Hesk could see the scarred woman's crooked finger whitening on her trigger. Sweat slipped down the side of his neck. He wanted to tell her to take the pressure off it, but he didn't want her attention.

“Let her try it,” Paske said. “She won't get far.”

Osselin kept her pistol on Vestrin. Paske tipped his chin at the man with the gold spectacles. The man shook his head. Paske showed him the phone and spoke too quietly for Hesk to hear. After a moment the man moved away from the far entrance. A shoe squeaked beside Hesk. The man in the red tie had come around the outside of the circle and stopped behind the bald man.

“I can come and sit by you,” Hesk said. “Like before.”

Osselin's gaze flickered toward him.

“Now,” Paske said.

The man in spectacles threw himself at her closed hand. Paske came from the other side. Hesk found himself looking into the scarred woman's barrel as she turned toward them. He fired.

Her lower jaw burst open. She staggered against him, spraying his face, then went down with both hands trying to hold the loose part in place. Her gun struck his shoe. He stepped away, dropping the papers, and saw Osselin shoot Paske in the belly.

Paske hit her hard enough to fold them together. His gun went off beside her leg. She screamed and fell to one knee, still gripping the control. The man in spectacles had stopped short, clutching a wrist that hung wrong, though Hesk hadn't seen who had shot him.

At the double doors, the man with the long gun shouted and swung his weapon toward Hesk's side of the room. The man in the red tie hooked an arm around the bald man's neck and dragged him backward. He fired over the bald man's shoulder. The answering shots knocked them both down. The woman in the riding coat fell against the doors and slid to the floor; the gray beard flattened himself beside her, his mouth wide.

Hesk could no longer hear individual shots. The room had become a continuous pressure inside his skull. He kept his gun pointed at Osselin because he didn't know where else to put it.

Paske crawled away from her on his elbows. Blood poured from the front of his shirt, and something pale and folded worked through the hole below his belt. He tried to stuff it back. Osselin pressed her right wrist against her wounded thigh, pistol dangling from that hand. Her left remained closed.

The scarred woman caught Hesk's trouser leg.

He looked down. She lifted her ruined face toward him. The upper teeth were still where teeth belonged; beneath them her tongue moved in a shape that could no longer make words. She kept trying. He couldn't tell whether she was pointing at the gun by his foot or reaching for his hand.

He pulled his leg free.

Vestrin had found a broken chair beside the service door and was hitting the wood with one of its legs. He could see the blows more clearly than he could hear them. The woman in green gloves stood behind her, waiting. The man with the stiff leg came limping across the floor to join them.

Osselin tried to stand. Her knee buckled. Hesk went toward her without deciding to.

She raised the pistol.

“No.”

He stopped.

Paske was saying something. Hesk caught “doctor,” and then “please.” The man with the gold spectacles had begun to cry, staring at his wrist. His lenses were spotted red.

Osselin got her good foot beneath her. She leaned on the crate, tipping envelopes across the floor, and forced herself upright. Hesk watched the control. Her hand shook so badly he thought she must lose it.

Behind him, the service door cracked.

Vestrin pulled it toward her. The upper hinge tore loose and the bottom caught on the raised parquet. She put her shoulder into the narrow opening and heaved until the wood dragged free. Beyond her, Hesk could see a brick wall scarcely an arm's length inside the passage. The way out turned sharply left around it.

“Come away from there,” Osselin said.

Vestrin looked back at the pistol. “I'm leaving.”

Osselin shot her.

The bullet struck below Vestrin's knee. She dropped into the gap, the door sagging onto her back. The woman in green gloves flinched away. Hesk ran past her and got his shoulder against the wood before it crushed Vestrin forward.

“Up,” he said.

“My leg.”

He had been expecting her to help push. He looked down and saw the blood pumping into her boot. She shoved with her sound foot, scraping her shoulder along the jamb. The passage was right there. Cold air touched his wet face.

“Pull me,” she said.

He put his left hand under her arm. She was heavier than he expected. He lifted until she could shift, then squeezed past her into the passage and tried pulling again. Her boot caught against the threshold.

“Both hands, you cunt.”

His right still held the pistol. He could have put it down. Over her shoulder he saw the limping man shoving the woman in green gloves toward Osselin, trying to put someone between himself and her gun. Osselin was coming away from the crate. She dragged her bad leg, leaving a thick track across the papers.

Vestrin gripped his sleeve. He had his feet now, both feet in the passage. He tucked the pistol against his chest and pulled his arm backward until the cloth began to tear.

“I opened it,” she said.

He wrenched free. She fell sideways across the threshold and the door struck the back of her head. Her hand went on reaching into the passage. He turned the corner.

The brick return was thick enough to crouch behind. Ahead, the passage ran through the abandoned kitchen toward a narrow rectangle of night. He could have kept going. But he would have been on his feet in that passage when Osselin opened her hand.

He lay down behind the brickwork and edged one eye past it. Through the doorway he could see Vestrin's fingers closing on the floor. Beyond them, Osselin stumbled into view.

“Hesk,” she called.

He pulled his face back. A shot broke brick from the corner above him. He lay with his cheek against the grit, tasting the scarred woman's blood on his lips.

“Come back here.”

She hadn't opened her hand. She had left the others to come after him. He could use that time to run farther, perhaps. Vestrin's hand had still been moving when he looked. He could go back for her.

He pushed his pistol past the brick edge. Osselin had reached the doorway. Her hair stuck to her open mouth. He aimed above the white coat and fired.

The light vanished. Brick struck his shoulder, and then he couldn't feel the floor beneath him.

When he could see again, he was lying on his back in the kitchen. Dust fell onto his face. He tried to close his mouth, found it full of something, and dug out a piece of wood with two teeth lodged in it.

His right hand still held the gun. He couldn't make the fingers move. Blood soaked his sleeve and dripped from the end of his little finger. Farther down, a beam pinned his left boot. His leg hurt when he turned, but it turned. He pulled until the boot stayed behind and his foot came out of it.

The passage into the ballroom was gone. He saw brick, a dark break in the ceiling, dust. Nothing in that direction told him who might still be alive. His ears gave him a high, thin sound that didn't change when he shouted.

He crawled toward the rectangle of night. There had been a door there once. He got his good hand around the frame and hauled himself over the sill, dragging the pistol because he couldn't let it go.

Outside, his bare foot left a wet print. Then another. He made it three steps before the leg folded and put him face down on the stones.

He tried to get up, but his injured hand folded under him and drove the gun against his mouth. His other hand was good. He put it flat on the stones and pushed until the arm shook. He couldn't get his knee beneath him. He lay still until he could draw breath, then began shouting that he was alive.

stories.title: No One Like Me
stories.prompt: On the world’s biggest broadcast talent show, singers compete to imitate legendary performers. This year’s contested contestant has reached the final by impersonating everyone from opera stars to rock gods. Tonight, she turns to the cameras, declares, “There’s never been anyone like me!” and begins a song no human throat could sing.
stories.body:
# No One Like Me

Jannik gets a strand of his wig caught between his lips on the high note. He spits it out, pushes the hair behind his ear, and tries again.

I give him the entrance in the original singer's voice, complete with the little gulp before the vowel. The sound fills our dressing-room corridor. A woman carrying a tray of microphones turns to look.

“I wasn't asking,” Jannik says.

“You keep coming in early.”

“I'm warming up.” He takes the wig off. Under it his own hair is wet and flattened, and he looks less like a man capable of holding forty thousand people through an instrumental break. “And you're standing on your dress.”

I lift my heel. A long black fold slides free. The gown has gold inside the pleats, so that walking should make light appear to pour out of me. In the corridor it mostly collects things: tape, a loose sequin, the leg of Jannik's chair. I have practised the turn that releases the skirt more often than any of tonight's songs.

He puts the wig in his lap and resumes his scales at half volume. I bend to brush off the hem. My four throat panels shift against the edge of the collar with a tiny, amplified-sounding tick.

“Still doing that?” he asks.

“Only when I bend.”

“Don't bow till they've turned your microphone off.”

On the wall monitor, I am already bowing. It is the season recap: me in the white sleeves of an opera star, then me with a dead rock singer's low-slung guitar, although I never learned to play it. The clips cut at the moment before applause. I resent this every time.

The soprano was my first vote winner. I had spent eleven days learning the slight unsteadiness in her farewell aria, the way the note seemed to search before it settled. Then the velvet baritone, the stadium shriek, the woman who sounded as if she were confiding something unforgivable to every seat in the house. I loved them all. I loved being able to make somebody lean forward before a phrase because they knew, from the first vowel, whose phrase it would be.

Now the recap is showing the eligibility hearings. HUMAN TALENT? says the caption beneath my face. My face then, as now, is white porcelain divided by fine black seams. Gold shows at the jaw hinges; short black hair leaves my neck visible. I did not arrive disguised.

The show permits any entrant who produces the sound live. It forbids playback and requires imitation of the declared performers. The arguments have filled a season anyway. In the recap, a recording critic calls me a loudspeaker. A former winner leans across the panel table to answer him, but before she can, the recap cuts to another shot of me singing.

Tonight there are only Jannik and me. This is the world's biggest broadcast talent show, and the host has spent the evening reminding us of the countries watching: morning audiences, midnight audiences, people eating in front of me who will never once look toward this hall. I can imagine them so vividly that I have to remind myself I cannot hear them.

Jannik taps his knee for his entrance. I hum the little phrase that has been bothering me all week. Two notes level, then a reach upward, then a fall that stops too soon.

“That one,” he says. “What's the rest of it?”

“What?”

He hums it back, shortening the last note. “You keep doing it. In the lift. Yesterday while they were fixing your earpiece.”

I straighten. “Listen.”

I repeat the phrase, set another voice under it, add a bright upper turn and then a second, lower one moving the other way. Four independent air drives, four reeds, four sets of shaping plates: I can make each chamber sing a different vowel through its own opening.
