All season I have blended them behind my lips to reconstruct one famous throat at a time. Now the panels along my neck open, and four lines crowd the corridor.

The microphone woman looks back again. Jannik waits until I finish.

“I meant the tune,” he says. “What happens after that bit?”

“There's a section where the lower voices cross.”

“All right.” He reaches for his wig.

“You didn't like it?”

“I wanted to hear the rest. You've done the same bit louder.”

I could demonstrate how much louder. Instead I ask, in the opera star's offended speaking voice, whether the young gentleman requires something simpler.

He looks at me without laughing. For a moment I keep the grand lady's mouth arranged on my face. Then the stage runner calls his name, and he gets up.

“Hair,” I say.

He puts the wig on, checks it in the black monitor frame, and goes.

Left alone, I sing the phrase quietly. There are words for it now: *The floor is still warm.* The first words came after a rehearsal, with the cleaners folding away chairs beyond the open door. I had been the last to finish. I could still hear a dance number in the empty space where the band had sat.

There are other lines, scraps tried at home, a whole middle passage I have never got through without decorating it until I forget how it began. I have been calling it unfinished because the ending will not arrive obediently. All my borrowed songs come with endings.

My competition medley is unaccompanied. Six legends, four minutes. I know exactly where the house will recognise each one. I can already hear those first delicious cries of recognition, and the bigger noise after my last note. I want the trophy too: the tall gold spiral waiting beside the stage. I have chosen where I will put it.

Jannik appears on the monitor. His first entrance is late enough to hurt. He lets the band go on without him, head tipped, one hand loose at his side. The audience starts shouting before he opens his mouth.

I know this recording. I know the rough catch he has to make and the moment his knees will give. He gets the catch; the knees look foolish in close-up. Then he turns, tosses the hair from his face and pulls a whole long phrase out of what ought to be the end of his breath. I lean toward the monitor. At the last instant he lets it break, exactly as the singer did, and the people behind him on the screen lift out of their seats.

I clap once before remembering he can't hear me.

The stage runner comes for me during his bow. I follow her, gathering the skirt clear of the chair. Under the noise from the hall, I try my unfinished tune again, taking it past the place where Jannik stopped listening. The low part finds two notes I have not tried beneath the fall. I keep them there as we walk.

At the wing, the runner raises a finger for quiet. My cue is coming. Beyond the curtain, Jannik grins through his borrowed hair. I want that applause for myself. The little tune goes on moving through me after I stop sounding it.

Then my name is announced, and I walk out.

The floor is black enough to hold the lights whole. Gold rails curve around three tiers of spectators; above them, violet points burn in hanging rings. The nearest camera moves backward to take in the opening pleats of my gown. On its small front monitor, I see my own pale hand lifted against the dark.

People call my name. Other people boo. Both sounds rise when I smile.

My medley begins with the opera star. I have only to lower my chin and let that first aged, magnificent note come out. The lights are already arranged for her. But the two low notes from the corridor are waiting, and I suddenly want to hear them in this room more than I want to hear the audience recognise her.

I turn toward the cameras, find the red light on the one carrying my face, and declare, “There’s never been anyone like me!”

It comes out rather too loudly. Somewhere close to the stage a man laughs. I hear him distinctly in the pause before I sing.

*The floor is still warm.*

Five plain words. I put the first two notes where a human voice might put them, low enough for someone sitting in a kitchen to hum along. The small rise arrives on *still*. On *warm*, the tune falls and hangs a step above the note that would let it rest.

There is a shout from the first tier. A guess at whose song this is, perhaps; I can't make out the name.

I keep the vowel of *warm* sounding. My lips close. Beneath the sustained note, a second chamber begins the phrase again, slower, on an open *ah*. The first voice has not drawn breath or faded. Its small throat opening stays gold and wide above my collar while my mouth begins the next line.

*All the chairs are on the tables.*

I move the words quickly over the two slower sounds. The last syllable of *tables* passes through the held note and comes out above it. Three separate vowels, three pitches moving independently, all arriving from the body in the black dress. The nearest camera rises toward my neck. I can see the operator's free hand turn palm-up toward somebody behind the lens.

Now the lowest chamber enters with a soft, repeated *dum*. Its pulse is slower than the words. I fit three pulses across four of the melody's steps, and for a while the beginnings refuse to meet. At the end of the phrase they land together. A few people clap on that landing; when I repeat the pattern, there are more.

My left hand marks the slow pulse. My right wrist turns with the melody. I have never known what to do with my hands in someone else's stillness. Now the movements come from the separate sensations at my neck, each reed making a different small pressure in the plates under my jaw.

I change the held vowel from *ah* to *ee* without moving its pitch. The sound brightens. Above it I sing about shoes carried home by their straps, the heel marks left on the floor, somebody looking under a chair for an earring. The words have been waiting in pieces for days; here I discover how long to leave between them. The low pulse goes on through each space, patient and inviting.

A woman beside the gold rail is nodding in time. She begins to mouth something. I return to *The floor is still warm*, and this time her lips move with the last two words.

I nearly smile hard enough to spoil the shape of them.

The fourth line has been keeping the pulse. I release it into a climb while the main tune descends. One voice crosses another and their colours rub together: the thin edge of the climbing reed against the soft round sound that has waited below. My mouth shapes a new verse above two held vowels while the fourth chamber taps out a rapid pattern of closed syllables, each higher than the last. No human throat could separate those four articulations, keep each alive while the others changed their pitch and pace. I have stopped counting the places where a borrowed voice would need to breathe.

The woman at the rail misses the next entrance. So do the clappers. I have pulled the phrases apart again, let one begin before another finishes, put the same words against themselves at different speeds. *The floor* is already *warm* below while the middle line still lingers over *still*. I take the high voice out above them, bright and almost weightless, turning in a rhythm of its own.

There is a wonderful place coming. I can feel the four parts approaching it, each from a different direction. My neck panels open farther; the collar shifts as their edges press against it. When the lines meet, I squeeze their notes close together, holding the harmony under the moving words. The roughness vibrates against my teeth. It is glorious inside my head.

Out in the room, the refrain has vanished.

I hear it through my stage monitor: a hard shining mass, every part insisting. I can find the melody because I am making it, but even I have to search. The woman at the rail has stopped moving her lips. Behind her a man folds his arms. Somebody gives a long whoop, and I push the upper voice farther in answer.

That makes it worse. The words grind into their neighbours. I have reached the passage I kept spoiling at home, with forty thousand people in front of me and the rest of the world beyond the cameras.

There is room here for the rock singer's rasp. I know the exact bend that would cut through everything. The audience would recognise him, and that would tell me where I was again. I shape the beginning of it against my teeth.

Then I let the high part stop.

The two long vowels underneath continue. I soften one, shift the other down until a clean space opens between them. My mouth returns to the refrain. It is almost embarrassingly bare after the noise. I have to sing it once with nobody clapping.

On the second repetition, I turn the lower held note into a pulse, shortening it so it has an end as well as a beginning, and tuck it beneath the words. The silent fourth voice comes back halfway through the phrase, a quiet descending answer that leaves the upward reach uncovered. I can hear all four now, and where to listen next.

*The floor is still warm.*

Below that, the second voice sings a different line: *Someone has left a light on.* It takes twice as long. The pulse keeps stepping through both, and the high answer circles once above *light*, then falls away while the words finish. The woman at the rail lifts her chin. Several rows behind her, a pair of hands begins clapping too fast and is corrected by the hands beside it.

I let the descending answer grow. It borrows the refrain's first notes, turns them, brings them back against the slower words. The two tunes fit without arriving together. I have been trying to make this part magnificent; I hadn't noticed it could dance.

I take three steps across the stage. Gold flashes through my skirt, and the black floor throws it back. A valve clicks between notes. Usually I work to hide that sound, but here it lands beside the low pulse. I shut it more briskly on the next beat and flick my hand outward with the tiny sound. There is laughter near the front. I make the gesture bigger on the next click, a royal flourish, and get another laugh.

The applause starts while I am still singing. It doesn't take the whole hall. Beyond the people standing at the rail, I can see rows that stay seated, faces turned toward companions. I want them too. I want to add something enormous that will bring them up.

Instead I carry the four lines through one last turn. There is the refrain, there is the light left on, there is the little pulse, there is the answer moving down to meet it. When the meeting comes, I close the lowest chamber. The upper answer changes shape over the place it leaves. Then that voice finishes, and the two remaining lines travel together for the first time.

I let *warm* fall the last step.

The other voice stays above it, very soft. For three beats I hold the interval, feeling its easy vibration along both sides of my jaw. Then I stop them together.

The silence is short and ragged. Someone shouts for the rock singer. Someone else shouts my name. The clapping gathers around both and becomes loud enough that I can feel it in the plates of my face.

I bow before remembering the microphone. My neck clicks into the applause.

When I straighten, the host is crossing the floor toward me, pressing one finger against her earpiece. On the monitor above the far seats, my name still sits beneath the six performers I was supposed to imitate.

“Sereva,” she says, “was that an original composition?”

“Yes.”

She waits, perhaps because there ought to be more. I look out at the gold rails. The woman who caught the refrain is still standing.

“Under the final's imitation rule, that performance cannot be scored,” the host says. She gives the words time to reach the hall. “Your final entry is disqualified.”

I nod. I knew the rule before I stepped out, but I have been so full of the song that the word arrives as a fresh disappointment.

There are boos now whose owners I cannot sort. The host turns toward the other wing and announces Jannik as the winner. He walks out slowly, then faster when the trophy is lifted for him. I clap with the audience. Gold confetti catches in the black hair of his wig; he tips his head back, laughing, and the cameras move to him.

The spiral trophy fits his hands badly. I had imagined holding it higher.

During the break before his winner's encore, we stand in the wing while the band resets. He has taken the wig off again. Confetti is stuck to his damp forehead. A runner goes to find somewhere to put the trophy until the final photographs.

“Your last phrase was beautiful,” I say.

“Thanks.” He picks a gold square from his eyebrow. “You could have warned me.”

“I didn't decide till I went on.”

“You'd been working on it.”

“Yes. I didn't know I was going to sing it here.” I look at the trophy as the runner carries it away. “You won, though.”

“I know I won.” He presses his lips together, then says it again, quieter. “I know I won. I'd like to enjoy that for a minute.”

I stop trying to give him a reason to be pleased. On the monitor, they are replaying his final note. He watches himself until the clip ends.

“You lost me in the middle,” he says then. “I couldn't hear the words.”

“Neither could I.”

He gives a short laugh. “Well, you kept going.” He sings the refrain under his breath. On the fall he goes straight to the low note, leaving out my suspended step.

“That's not how it goes.”

“I like it down there.” He tries it again, more slowly, finding his own way through the reach on *still*. “That bit's been stuck in my head since the lift.”

The runner calls him. He makes a face at the abandoned wig, leaves it on the chair, and goes out for his encore. He can choose any song now. He chooses the old dance number from his first audition, the one whose chorus the audition audience sang back at him.

I stand just inside the curtain. He sings the first verse faithfully, looking into the lights. Then, where the band drops out before the chorus, he puts my five words into the space.

The falling note is still wrong. He gives it a rough edge I never intended, and takes a breath in a place where I would have kept two lines going underneath. I open my mouth to supply them, quietly, for myself. But he has already moved on. His next phrase catches the end of mine and carries it into the old song. I close my mouth.

Somebody near the rail sings my words back at him. He grins and raises a hand to hold the band off. I can see that he is going to try it again. I lean farther past the curtain, wanting him to give me back the missing step, wanting to hear what else he might do.

stories.title: Still Taking Runaways
stories.prompt: You promised your childhood teddy bear you’d run away and join the circus together. Twenty years later, you’re the ringmaster, the magic of circus has brough him to life and he handles the tickets, but neither of you is prepared for the little girl who arrives carrying a wooden dragon and asks whether you’re still taking runaways.
stories.body:
# Still Taking Runaways

Idrella had one foot on the ticket wagon's step when her skirt stopped her. A loop of gold braid had caught on a nail. She pulled, remembered what the costume woman had said about pulling, and stood with her knee bent while Rumbit finished serving a customer.

“Two for tonight. Keep them dry. The red end is yours.” He pushed the tickets across the sill with both paws. “No, you've got the whole roll. Just those two.”

The customer detached his tickets and departed. Rumbit looked down from the box that raised him to window height.

“Stuck again?”

“Temporarily detained.”

He came out with the ticket scissors. She took them away before he could cut anything and eased the braid off the nail herself. Between performances, with the lamps unlit and a man asleep beneath the drum wagon, it took some effort to remain the mistress of marvels.

“Are you still taking runaways?”

The girl stood on the other side of the wagon step, so close that the wooden dragon in her arms could have bitten Idrella's knee. It was longer than Rumbit, nose to tail, with green paint rubbed away from its back and wings folded along its sides. One yellow glass eye looked up at the ringmaster. The other was pointed at the ticket scissors.

Idrella put the scissors behind her.

“We certainly are.” Her voice came out with the fullness she used to announce the first act. “You have found exactly the right circus.”

The girl relaxed her grip on the dragon's neck. Beneath one arm she had a bundle tied in a dishcloth. A stocking protruded from its knot.

“Both of us?”

“Both of you.”

Rumbit climbed down from the wagon and came to look. His waistcoat was crooked, exposing the patch Idrella had sewn over his chest when she was twelve. He bent to examine a wing.

“Does that open?”

“Carefully,” said the girl. “His name's Matchstick.”

“Mine's Rumbit. Have you got a saddle?”

“He doesn't need one. I hold his horns.”

“Excellent.”

Idrella cleared her throat. Neither of them looked at her.

“And your name?”

“Velzie. I can turn a cartwheel, but not with him, so you'd have to let me put him down.”

Idrella knelt, spreading her burgundy skirt on the sawdust. Close up, Velzie's face was sticky near the mouth. She had come from somewhere with jam. That proved very little; Idrella had once packed a whole pot for an escape and forgotten a spoon.

“You don't have to perform for us. Are you hungry?”

“No.”

“Is somebody looking for you?”

Velzie considered this with more attention than Idrella liked.

“Not yet.”

“Who will be?”

“Mother. If I'm late.”

Behind Idrella, Rumbit opened the dragon's left wing. Three thin panels of wood spread on little pegs. He whistled.

“Late for what?” Idrella asked.

“Supper. But I shan't be there.” Velzie lifted her chin. “We're leaving.”

There it was: the chin, the bundle, the certainty that a striped tent meant a place entirely outside the world. Idrella had been eight when she told her teddy bear they would run away and join the circus together. She had promised it into his flattened ear, beneath bedclothes hot with her own breath. Twenty years ago. She could still find the place on that ear with her thumb.

“Well,” she said, softer now. “You can stay here while we work out what you need.”

“I'll need a cape. And does he get big all at once?”

Rumbit stopped admiring the wing.

“Who does?”

“Matchstick. When you make him alive.”

Velzie looked from one of them to the other. Idrella recognized the moment an audience discovered that the hat was empty.

“I saw your bear yesterday,” the girl said. “He was eating an apple. My brother said there was a person inside, but nobody's that small, and I saw him swallow.”

Rumbit put a paw over his stomach, evidently pleased that someone had paid attention.

“Very good apple.”

“So you can do it.”

“I don't know how,” Idrella said.

Velzie's eyes went to the great tent, then back to the woman in the gold-trimmed coat. Idrella wished she had answered the first question less splendidly.

“But you did him.”

“The performers did. I was only helping with the horses then.”

She had finally left home at sixteen, with permission obtained through so much argument that she generally omitted it from the story. Rumbit came in her bag. By the end of that first season, the tumblers' living magic followed their hands in threads of light; the singer could hold a note warm in her palm. One wet evening they had passed the bedraggled bear among them, making him bow, giving him their small, impossible gifts. Heat remained in him after their hands withdrew. Then he sneezed on the singer.

Idrella had barely slept for three nights, waking him whenever he stopped moving. On the fourth, he told her to leave him alone. She had been much happier after that.

“He woke up,” she told Velzie. “We were astonished too. We tried with a cloth rabbit afterward, and it stayed a cloth rabbit.”

“I bit it,” Rumbit said. “Nothing.”

“The biting wasn't part of the attempt.”

“I was checking.”

Velzie lowered Matchstick until his claws hung against her skirt. “Could you try anyway?”

Idrella glanced toward the tent. The performers were eating or asleep. Calling them together, setting the dragon in the ring, watching this child's face while nothing happened: no. Yet the little pegs had been mended with such care. Somebody had shaved one replacement to fit, and wrapped thread around the end to hold it.

“May I?” Rumbit asked.

Velzie passed him over. The bear sat on the wagon step with Matchstick across his knees, his paws hardly reaching around the dragon's middle.

“Where have you come from?” Idrella asked her.

“Past the green gate. The house with the pear tree.”

“In town?”

“It's only a little way. But my brother won't find us if we go with you tonight.”

“Has he hurt you?”

“He took Matchstick and held him where I couldn't reach.” She spoke fast now. “He said I was too old to carry him, and then he said I could ride him to the circus if he was a real dragon, and he made Mother laugh.”

Idrella kept her face still. Rumbit rubbed a paw along the wooden back.

“Mother told him to give him back,” Velzie added. “But she laughed first.”

“That was unkind.”

“I'm going to fly over the house. When he sees, he'll have to say he was wrong.”

There was a cape in this plan, and a flight, and a particular person required to stand below and feel sorry. Idrella could supply half a dozen capes. The rest was receding rapidly beyond her abilities.

“I can't promise you that.”

“You said you took runaways.”

“Yes. I should have asked more questions before I started welcoming you.”

Rumbit made a small sound. Matchstick's tail had curled around his ankle.

Idrella stopped.

A thin gold light spread from beneath the bear's paw, following the grain through the dragon's ribs. Rumbit held him closer in surprise, and the light brightened where wood touched the warm patch on his chest. Beneath the sound of the bear's breathing came a second, rasping breath.

“Oh,” said Rumbit.

Matchstick opened his jaw. He worked it sideways, spat a flake of old sawdust onto Rumbit's waistcoat, and blinked both glass eyes.

Velzie dropped her bundle.

“Matchstick?”

The dragon turned his head toward her. His nostrils were only two drilled holes, but Idrella saw them widen. He sniffed the girl's fingers, licked one, and made a noise like a drawer that needed wax.

Rumbit had gone very quiet. Idrella put two fingers on his shoulder.

“Are you all right?”

“I think so. He's warm.” He loosened his hold. “I didn't know I could do that.”

The glow had faded. Matchstick stood on the bear's knees, dragging a claw along the ticket wagon as he stretched. His wings unfolded farther than the pegs ought to have allowed. Still wood, still the size of a large loaf, with a cracked green ridge along his spine. Alive. Idrella pressed her fingers harder into Rumbit's shoulder and felt him press back.

Velzie laughed, a breathless gulp of a laugh that made Idrella want to take off her hat and throw it. Instead she picked up the fallen dishcloth bundle.

“Hello,” Velzie said, bending almost nose to nose with him. “It's me. Look what we did!”

He licked her sticky cheek. She squealed and hugged him, then put him on the ground and stepped back expectantly.

Nothing happened to his size.

“Perhaps it takes a minute,” she said.

Matchstick investigated a discarded ticket. He bit off the corner, chewed, and spat it out. He walked beneath Idrella's skirt, bumped his head on her boot and backed out with an indignant creak. Then he looked toward the road.

“Perhaps this is how big he is,” Idrella said.

Velzie crouched beside him. “You can do bigger, can't you?”

He stretched his neck and scratched beneath his jaw with one hind foot.

Rumbit hopped down from the step. He fitted one leg on either side of the dragon's back and left his feet on the ground.

“Plenty of room for me.”

“Rumbit, get off him.”

“I'm hardly putting any weight on.”

“He has only just learned to stand.”

Matchstick took a step. Rumbit shuffled with him, delighted. The dragon extended both wings, caught the air once, and rose high enough that the bear's feet left the sawdust.

“There!” Rumbit cried.

Idrella reached for him. Matchstick beat his wings again; the bear grabbed both horns, and they lurched over her hand. One wing struck the wagon, sending them crookedly toward the gap between two tents.

“Put your feet down!” she shouted.

He was already too high. His toes bicycled above her head.

The drummer woke as they passed him. Idrella thrust Velzie's bundle into his lap.

“Watch the tickets.”

“Where are you—”

“After the bear!”

Velzie was running ahead of her. Idrella gathered her skirts in both fists, caught up, and steered the girl around a stack of benches. Above them, Matchstick climbed laboriously past the striped canvas. Rumbit's ears streamed backward. For three absurd seconds Idrella envied him so fiercely she could hardly breathe.

Then the dragon dropped a yard.

“Rumbit!”

“Still here!”

She could see that. She needed him to be somewhere else.

Matchstick recovered, bobbed through the gap beside the cook wagon, and headed down the town road. The crowd from the matinee had gone; only a woman carrying a basket stood between the circus and the first houses. The woman ducked. Rumbit waved to her, then clutched the horn again as they tilted.

“Bring him back!” Velzie called. “We're meant to go away!”

They were going away. Idrella had no breath to point this out. Her boots were built for making an entrance down a short flight of steps, and a curl had shaken loose across her eyes. She spat it out of her mouth.

At the first bend, Matchstick turned late. His wingtip scraped the hedge. Rumbit yelped, and Idrella lunged beneath him, arms out. The dragon's tail slapped her hat sideways; she had a glimpse of the bear's pale soles before another clumsy wingbeat carried him out of reach.

“Catch me on the next one!” he called.

“I can't reach! Tell him to land!”

“I've told him!”

The road forked beyond a low spreading tree. Matchstick flew under its branches and disappeared to the left.

Idrella stopped long enough to shove her hat straight. Velzie had stopped too. Her face was blotched, and without the dragon or the bundle she looked much smaller.

“Where?” Idrella said.

“That's our lane.”

A triumphant cry came from behind the hedge, followed by Rumbit shouting, “Not there! Not in those!”

Velzie took Idrella's hand and dragged her through an open gate. They crossed a patch of cabbages, went through a second gate, and emerged among shirts hanging on a line. Rumbit dangled beneath the dragon, his head stuck in a white sleeve and one leg still hooked over Matchstick's back.

Idrella let go of the girl, lifted the shirt with one hand and caught Rumbit's free hind paw with the other. Matchstick's wings beat the hanging sleeves around her head.

“Let go of him,” she said.

“I can't get my foot—”

The dragon tugged forward. Idrella released Rumbit's paw before she could pull him apart. The shirt slipped off his head and slapped her in the face. By the time she fought clear, bear and dragon were departing over the garden wall.

“Velzie!”

“This way. There's a door.”

The girl knew which latch lifted and which gate had to be kicked. Idrella followed her through, and they came out into a narrow yard beneath a pear tree. There was the green gate beyond it. Through the tree's lower branches, Matchstick was approaching an open kitchen window at a determined slant.

“Mother!” Velzie yelled. “Move the things!”

A woman looked up from the table inside. She had time to snatch a jug away before Matchstick came through the window, hit the sill with his back feet and skidded across the table. Rumbit continued without him. A bowl jumped, a white cloud rose, and the bear vanished inside it.

Idrella reached the window. Flour hung on the air. On the far side of the table, Rumbit's head emerged from the bowl. He sneezed, gripped the rim and stood up.

“Excellent,” he said faintly.

Velzie ran into the kitchen through the yard door. Her mother caught her by both shoulders.

“Are you hurt?”

“No. Matchstick's alive.”

“I can see. Where have you been?”

“The circus.”

Her mother's hands remained on her shoulders. Velzie looked at the floor, and then, with evident effort, up again.

“I went to run away. But he came back.”

Idrella took off her hat and hooked it over her wrist. She was leaning through a stranger's kitchen window, red-faced, with half a laundry peg caught in her curls. Inside, her bear was trying to climb out of the flour without leaving any footprints. She ought to explain. For once she let the girl finish.

“I wanted to fly over the house. So he'd see. My brother.”

“On that?” Her mother looked at the little dragon.

“I thought he'd get bigger.”

The woman shut her eyes for a moment. Then she drew Velzie against her apron and held her there. The girl stayed, though her cheek acquired a broad streak of flour.

Matchstick stepped around the flour bowl, testing the table with his claws. He stretched his neck toward a blue dish and squeaked.

“What's he doing?” Velzie asked into the apron.

The dragon opened and shut his mouth. His jaw clicked twice.

“Butter,” he said.

Nobody moved. He reached farther.

“Please butter.”

Velzie pulled free and lifted the lid off the blue dish. Matchstick bit into the yellow corner beneath. He closed his eyes as he chewed.

“He sits here when Mother bakes,” she said. “I always put him here.”

Idrella looked down the lane they had run, then back at the small wooden creature eating butter on his familiar table. Rumbit had climbed out of the bowl and was sitting with his legs spread, breathing hard. She went around to the door.

“I'm sorry about your kitchen,” she said when she came in.

“Is that one yours?” The woman pointed at Rumbit.

“We came together.”

Rumbit held his paws up to Idrella. She lifted him into the crook of her arm, her thumb finding the worn place on his ear. His heart was hammering beneath the patch. She had never felt it go so fast.

“I couldn't get off,” he whispered.

“I know.”

“I wanted to at the tree.”

She rubbed flour from his nose with her thumb. “I was trying.”

He pushed his face against her coat, leaving a dusty oval on the burgundy. She kept her hand over his back until his breathing slowed. Velzie was telling her mother about the light beneath his paws. Idrella listened to her get it right: who had held whom, what had happened first, how nobody had known.

Then Rumbit lifted his head.

“You should have seen the tents from up there,” he said.

Idrella laughed. It shook him in her arm, and he put a paw against her chin to steady himself.

“Oh, Rumbit.”

“I could see right into the cook's wagon.”

“You'd better tell me the whole thing.”

“I shall. I had a very good view until the shirts.”

Velzie drew up a chair, blocking Idrella's path to the door. “I saw that bit.”

Rumbit glanced at her, then at Idrella. The ringmaster set her hat on the table and sat down with him on her knee.

“You went in headfirst,” Velzie began.

“I was trying to duck.”

“You ducked into it.”

“Well, it was coming at me.” He considered the girl for a moment. “Was it a very large shirt?”

Velzie held her hands apart. Rumbit took one paw off Idrella's sleeve and nudged the nearer hand a little farther out.

stories.title: The Place We Keep
stories.prompt: Your father wears a body of iron. Your sister lives in the river. Your mother prefers being a cat. You’re the only one who still looks like the your baby photographs. Every year, you meet at the ruins of your childhood home to watch the eclipse—until your sister arrives with a child and you ask your parents to explain what being human means.
stories.body:
# The Place We Keep

Father had put Mother where I usually sat.

She lay along the broad stone windowsill, one hind foot extended into the ruin, her black belly turned to the sun. Father stood beside her humming through his iron chest. A loose plate gave the tune an accompaniment it had never needed.

"There's room," Father said.

"She'll put her feet on the photographs," I said.

Mother opened an eye. "Then don't put them under my feet."

I set my basket in the grass. She moved before I could ask again, stepping onto Father's forearm and climbing to his shoulder. The iron had been warming all the way down the hill. She settled with her chin between two rivets, and he lifted his other hand to embrace me.

I knew where to put my cheek now, against the smooth plate below his neck. The first year I had caught my hair in a joint. Inside that casing, the little living body his illness had left him worked the iron with a magic he had taken months to learn. I could feel the faint irregular beat through the plate. He smelled of metal and the peppermint he liked in his drinking mixture.

"You look well," he said.

I had acquired two lines beside my mouth since the last eclipse. Father had acquired a new elbow.

Our valley lay beneath the same crossing of the moon each year. We had watched it from this window when there was a kitchen behind us, and from the sill after the roof fell. The house had survived all our departures before it began to come apart. Now grass grew where we had eaten, and the far wall ended in a staircase of exposed stones. Through the opening where the back door had been, the bank sloped to the river.

I opened the basket: bread, pears, Mother's fish and Father's little pot of custard. Under them lay the packet of photographs and, under that, the baby blanket I had been knitting since Selvi told me she and her partner were expecting.

Mother smelled the fish. "You remembered."

"Every year," I said.

"Yes, but I don't know that till you arrive," Mother said.

I gave her a strip. She took it from my fingers without catching them with her teeth.

Father wanted to see the photographs before his hands got sticky. I handed him the one of me at six months, sitting on a bed with a pear in my lap. My hair stood up in a pale tuft. It still did that if I went to sleep with it damp. I was the only one of us whose baby picture remained much use for identification.

"Look at that face," Father said. "Still you."

I leaned against his arm to look with him, although I knew every scratch in the print.

"Are you coming down?" Selvi called.

She had risen in the shallows below the house. Sunlight passed through her shoulders onto the stones behind her. I could see a small fish dart past the place where, on a woman standing on land, her hip would have been. She could raise herself from the river, but not leave it; there were no legs folded out of sight, waiting to walk home.

Across one clear arm lay a clear child.

I had been imagining how Selvi would keep a woollen shawl dry. I had imagined a wet-haired baby with our family's narrow chin, and worried that the river would be too cold. Here was the chin, absurdly, but I could see the pebbles through it.

"Oh," I said.

"Come and see her," Selvi said. "I can't hold her up here for long."

I took the basket down the bank, the blanket under my arm. Father followed, his steps heavy enough to dislodge little showers of earth. Mother rode him halfway, then sprang onto a flat rock at the edge. We had eaten here every year since Selvi's change; she couldn't hear a word from the windowsill when the river was running high.

"This is Ibby," Selvi said. "Your aunt has brought you something you can't use. Say thank you anyway."

The baby's face contracted. Her cry was small and sharp, without the watery bubbling I had expected. Selvi shifted her upright, and a tiny hand struck her mother's chin. Where their bodies touched they remained separate: I could follow the curve of Ibby's cheek against Selvi's breast.

"Can I?" I put out my hands.

"In the water," Selvi said. "Let her lie across them."

I left my shoes on the gravel, knelt in the shallows and slid my hands under Ibby. She was warm, with a weight that yielded and gathered itself again. Her head rolled sideways, following Mother's tail. I couldn't tell where her fingers ended. She curled them into a small fist, then let it loosen into trailing shapes.

"Four months?" I asked.

"On the ninth," Selvi said.

"Was she like this when she was born?"

Selvi watched my hands. "Yes."

"I thought perhaps you had changed her," I said.

"No," Selvi said.

I wished I could scratch my nose. Both hands were occupied and Selvi's attention had become uncomfortable.

"I didn't know," I said.

"Well. You do now," Selvi said.

Ibby opened her mouth. I could see, far inside her, something pale working in its own time. She bent towards the touch of my thumb on her cheek, then complained when it offered nothing to eat.

"She's hungry again." Selvi took her back. A cloudy brightness gathered at her breast as the child settled against it. "I thought we'd make it through the introductions."

Mother crouched close to watch. "How are you sleeping?"

"Badly," Selvi said. "He takes her when it's light, but then I lie there listening for them. Last night I woke him up to tell him she was asleep."

"I used to do that," Father said.

Mother looked up at him.

"With our first," he added.

Selvi laughed, then winced as Ibby's hand tightened. "Ow. Don't pull. There's plenty."

I laid the blanket on the dry rock behind Mother. It was yellow, with a border of white leaves. I had unravelled that border twice to make it right.

Selvi leaned to see. "Oh, you did the leaves after all. It's lovely."

"What was it like?" I asked. "Carrying her."

"Heavy," Selvi said. "I couldn't hold myself up this high for the last month. I had to speak to people with just my face out. And I wanted eggs all the time. Cooked eggs. Getting them was a nuisance."

"I could have brought eggs."

"You could have visited," Selvi said, without looking at me.

Every week I had meant to visit once the border was finished. Selvi had been eight miles away.

Father bent to look at Ibby, who abandoned feeding to examine the dark opening of his mouth.

"Our chin," Father said happily.

I looked from his fixed iron face to Mother's whiskers, then down at my own knees, whitening under the water.

"What does being human mean?" I asked them. "If she has our chin, does that make her human? Or if she doesn't? What do you mean when you say it?"

Father straightened. "She's your sister's child. Of course she's human."

"Her father was born in the river," Selvi said.

"And a very decent fellow," Father said.

"I know he's decent," Selvi said. "I live with him."

Father adjusted the photograph, which he still held between two iron fingers. He had carried my baby face all the way to the bank.

"I'm human," he said. "This doesn't alter that."

He tapped his chest, gently because Mother disliked the sound.

"You remember being a man," I said. "She won't."

"I am a man," Father said. "I don't spend all day remembering it."

That stopped me. He eased himself down beside the blanket. Small movements still took preparation, but he had learned to sit without asking anyone to steady him.

"When I was ill, I wanted to get out of bed," Father said. "That was mostly what I thought about. I wanted to come here. I wanted another pear, though they couldn't promise me pears. I wasn't deciding to become some new thing. I was scared I'd die before the work was finished."

Father looked down at the photograph. "You wouldn't let me have that one. Kept both fists round it, even when you fell asleep."

"That was another day," Mother said. "I took that picture. You were away with your brother all that week."

"I remember the pear," Father said.

"We had a tree full of them," Mother said. "You remember one of the others."

Father brought the print close to the dark apertures of his eyes. "Is that the old blue cover?"

"Yes," Mother said.

"Then perhaps," Father said.

I knew the picture was brown and cream, yet I had always been able to see that blue. Mother must have told me about the cover before. I couldn't remember her telling me, only the colour itself.

Selvi had lowered herself until the river touched Ibby's back. The baby resumed eating. Mother jumped onto the blanket and began pressing it flat with her paws.

"And you?" I asked Mother.

"What?"

"Are you human?" I asked.

"I'm a cat," Mother said.

"But under that."

Mother stopped kneading. "There isn't a woman tucked under my fur."

"I mean the part that thinks."

"That part's enjoying the blanket too," Mother said.

I pulled my cold feet from the water and sat on a patch of gravel. "You could be a woman this minute."

"Yes. I was one on Tuesday," Mother said. "We played cards. I lost rather a lot."

"Then why aren't you one now?" I asked.

Mother looked at me for a moment, ears forward. "Did you want me to be?"

I wanted to say no. I wanted the question to remain a reasonable question about what things were, without having to admit how carefully I had laid out the old photographs that morning, or how often I dreamt that I came in through the back door and found everyone where they belonged.

"Sometimes," I said. "It's easier to hug you."

Mother stepped onto my leg. Her claws went through my skirt and she withdrew them when I flinched. I stroked her between the ears, in the place she liked; it was a small contact and I had asked for a large one.

"I don't want to change today," Mother said.

Father reached for his custard. I got it for him, unscrewed the lid and handed it over. His drinking tube slipped out below his chin. We could all hear him finishing the pot.

Up the bank, the jagged wall had begun to throw oddly narrow shadows. I took our eclipse lenses from the basket and set out the rest of the food. The photographs came out too. I wasn't ready to put them away.

On top was my ninth birthday, with the kitchen full of paper birds. Mother stood behind a cake. Father had caught her laughing, her eyes closed, one floury hand against her waist. Selvi and I wore strings of birds over our dresses. I had made them from the thin paper used between prints.

"That was a good day," I said.

Mother leaned to see. "You two ate the sugar beaks off every bird on that cake."

"They were falling off," Selvi said.

"Into your mouths," Mother said.

Selvi grinned at Ibby. "We were very helpful children."

I remembered the sweetness, hard at first, softening between my teeth, and the damp string that kept brushing my lips. We had danced round the table until we tore our paper garlands on the chair backs.

"I thought you'd make those birds forever," I told Mother.

"They took an age," Mother said. "I was still putting the wings on when you got up. I couldn't get the icing off my fingers for days."

"You loved doing it."

"I loved you having them," Mother said.

It was close enough to agreement that I tried to leave it there. "Look how happy you are."

Mother withdrew her head from beneath my hand. "Your father had just sat on the spare cake. That's what I'm laughing at. I had a toothache. I'd been awake since before dawn and I wanted everyone to go home."

"They hadn't even had the cake yet," Father said.

"I know," Mother said. "I had to wait."

I looked back at the face in the photograph. It was so entirely the face I remembered that the other morning, the one with the toothache, felt like something being done to it.

"Was any of it how I remember?" I asked.

Mother's tail moved across my knee. "Which bit?"

"Being here. Us. You make it sound as if you couldn't wait to get away."

Selvi lifted Ibby higher. "Could someone move the fish? She keeps trying to reach it."

I moved the parcel. My face was hot. The little interruption had left me sitting with what I'd said, while everyone else had something useful to look at.

"I stayed here eight years after you left," Mother said. "You used to tell me to get a smaller place."

"I don't mean the house," I said.

"Then I don't know what you mean," Mother said.

There was hurt in her voice now. I had heard it when I was a child and broken things, and later when I said I was too busy to come home. I put the birthday picture face down on the blanket.

"I've kept all these," I said. "Sometimes I think I'm the only one who wants them."

Father turned his photograph towards me. "You haven't let me have this one."

"You never asked," I said.

"I did," Father said. "Last year. You said they should stay together."

I remembered. I had even looked into the cost of copies, then forgotten. Father held the print against his thigh, taking care not to bend it.

"Ibby won't remember any of that," Selvi said. "She'll know him like this."

"I know," I said. "That's what I'm trying to ask about. Whether she's still—"

I stopped. Selvi was watching me now.

"Still what?" Selvi asked. "She's only just got here."

Ibby thrust a hand towards the fish. Selvi caught it and kissed the place where her wrist briefly narrowed.

"I don't mind questions," Selvi said. "Ask how I had her. Ask about her father. But I'm not going to spend her first visit guessing what she'll call herself when she's grown. I haven't even told you she can laugh."

Mother leaned forward. "Can she?"

"For him," Selvi said. "Apparently I'm not funny."

Selvi made a noise against Ibby's cheek. The baby turned her head with an expression of absorbed suspicion. My sister tried again, less confidently. Father chuckled, and Ibby stared at the opening in his face.

"That," Selvi said. "That's what she's been doing to me for weeks."

I laughed before I could help it. Selvi glanced up. She was smiling, and I was glad she had looked at me in time to see.

I put the other photographs back in their paper sleeve. Father kept the one of me. The birthday remained face down.

"What did you like?" I asked Mother.

Mother looked towards the sun. "When?"

"When we were little."

She settled against my stomach, making me lean back to give her room.

"Taking you out before anyone else was up," Mother said. "You were both quieter outside. Selvi collected things. You made me name them."

"You knew all the names."

"I made some up," Mother said. "You wouldn't accept that I didn't know."

"I still have a stone you called a sleeping tooth," I said.

"Well, there you are," Mother said.

I put my hand around her warm, narrow ribs. She breathed under it, watching something small move in the grass. I had never known she invented names; I had been proud of how much she knew.

"Was it being a mother you got tired of?" I asked.

"I got tired of being needed from the moment I opened my eyes," Mother said. "I liked you very much when you could find your own socks. I like you now."

She paused, then rubbed her cheek on my wrist. "And I like going under hedges. I thought I'd do it for a week when I first learned. Then there kept being things I wanted to do the next day."

"You didn't tell us," I said.

"I tried," Mother said. "You asked when I was coming back."

I had. Even after she'd moved to the little house beside Father's rooms, where I could visit either of them whenever I liked, I had asked.

"I want to know about the hedges," I said, although part of me still wanted to know when she was coming back.

Mother's ears swivelled. She seemed about to answer, but Father said, "Nearly time," and we reached for our lenses. Mother let me hook hers over her ears.

The remaining sun was a thin crooked thread. Colour drained from the grass; the river kept its brightness longer than the stones. I had seen this every year of my life and still felt a brief, childish resistance, as if this time it might go too far.

The last light went. We lowered the lenses. All along the opposite bank the trees stood black beneath a sky that had become much larger. Above our broken house the sun was a dark circle with a white, unruly edge.

Ibby cried.

"Yes," Selvi told her. "It does that."

She held the child close. Father kept watching the sky. Mother climbed onto my shoulder to see past his head, and her whiskers touched my ear. For the few minutes we had come for, nobody spoke.

Then a brightness broke from one side. We raised the lenses again. Birdsong began in the trees, uncertain at first, and Mother grew heavy against my neck.

I lifted her back onto my lap. My skirt was wet, my legs cold. There was bread left, and a whole pear, and we had no reason to go yet.

"After the birthday," I said to Mother. "Did you get to lie down?"

Mother blinked at me.

"When everyone had gone home," I said. "What did you do?"

"Your father took you upstairs," Mother said. "I went out."

"With the toothache?" I asked.

"It had eased by then," Mother said. "There was dancing in the field behind the orchard. I could hear it through the window."

Father shook his head. "You came back with a blister the size of an egg."

"I wore the wrong shoes," Mother said. "I'd forgotten how to be out for a whole evening."

"Were you good at it?" I asked. "Dancing?"

"Better than your father," Mother said.

"I was good enough to marry," Father said.

"I didn't marry your feet," Mother said. "Anyway, there was a drummer. When they stopped to rest, he asked me. Lovely face, no idea what he was doing. He wanted to lead."

Selvi brought Ibby near the rock. The baby was trying to get hold of the reflected light beneath Father's hand. I turned the birthday photograph over again.

"What happened?" I asked Mother.

"I had to teach him," Mother said. "There was this little sideways step, and he kept trying to cross his feet. I'll show you."

She stood up on my knees to show us.

stories.title: A Seat for the Sun
stories.prompt: Sun Goddess Nika was lounging on a cloud when a child’s homemade rocket punched through it, carrying a handwritten invitation: “Please come to my birthday.”
stories.body:
# A Seat for the Sun

Behind her sunglasses, the afternoon shone a pleasant pink through Nika's closed eyelids. She lay along the cloud with one bare foot tucked beneath her other knee, letting the warmth reach the ends of her hair. Below, a dog barked itself hoarse at something which declined to be barked away. Farther off, bells announced the hour. She had no intention of counting them.

Something hissed under her shoulder.

The cloud burst. A pointed red object shot between her arm and her waist, snagged in a lilac ruffle, and hung there, ticking. Through the ragged hole it had made she could see a garden, very small and very green.

Nika sat up. She drew the object out of her dress and held it at arm's length until it finished smoking.

It was a rocket. Its body was a cardboard tube, its fins cut from something that had once advertised biscuits. One fin was bent, and the red paper round its nose had puckered beneath a prodigious quantity of paste. A folded sheet, fastened to the tube with string, bore a yellow circle with twenty-seven rays. Nika counted those, then untied the string and opened the sheet.

“Please come to my birthday.”

Underneath, in smaller writing: *Tebbit. I am eight today.*

There was a drawing of a house, a tree, and a table covered in little dots. An arrow pointed to a rectangle beneath the tree. *This is your chair.* A second arrow pointed to a crooked stick figure. *This is me.* The figure had eight fingers on one hand.

She turned the paper over. No petition for a longer summer. Not even a request to bless the cake.

Nika bent over the hole in her cloud. Directly beneath her lay a tree with bunting tangled in its upper branches, beside a long, dotted tablecloth. The dog was barking at a string of paper flowers. Seven children were running round the table, and one, wearing a yellow paper crown, kept stopping to look up.

She put on her gold sandals, shook the damp from her white hair, and went down with the rocket.

Her feet touched the grass beside the tree. The barking stopped. A woman carrying a jug stood so still that juice spilled over her fingers.

For a moment Nika had the full pleasure of an arrival. Sunlight gathered round her shoulders and glinted along her bracelets; the round lenses of her sunglasses caught the garden in green, violet, and brilliant blue. The woman set down the jug and raised a hand to her forehead in the noon salute.

“Lady Nika.”

On the kitchen windowsill, below a painted likeness of herself, stood a little bowl of honey. Nika inclined her head to the woman. Then the crowned child appeared in front of her, breathing hard.

“You got it! Where did you find it? Is the fin broken?”

He took the rocket in both hands and inspected the bent piece of biscuit box.

“It found me,” Nika said. “Rather abruptly.”

“Did it hurt?” He looked up at her properly for the first time.

“Only my dress.”

He bent to inspect her ruffles, but another child shoved between them to see the rocket. The others crowded close, all talking. Tebbit held it above their heads.

“It went right up! I told you!”

The tallest girl reached easily over him and prodded the damaged fin.

“You can paste that,” she said.

“I know. Don't bend it.”

His mother wiped her wet hand on her apron. “We weren't expecting— Tebbit said he'd invited you, but I thought—”

“I did invite her,” Tebbit said. “She's here.”

“Yes. Get another plate, please.”

He passed Nika the rocket and ran indoors. The tall girl followed, announcing that she knew where the good plates were. Nika's hostess looked from the goddess to the little chair beneath the tree. A sun had been drawn on its back in yellow chalk, with a mouth nearly as wide as the seat.

“I can bring you something more comfortable.”

“That one was promised to me.”

“He scrubbed it himself,” the woman said, and went to fetch a cloth for the juice.

Nika leaned the rocket against the tree and lowered herself to a pleasant floating height above the chair. The garden smelled of crushed grass and sweet pastry. Across the table was a cake with eight candles, purple icing flowers, and a yellow sugar border. Someone had attempted a rocket in icing on its top. The red nose leaned to one side.

Tebbit returned with a plate clutched to his chest. His cousin came behind him carrying three, which she set down with considerable ceremony.

“Can you make it all gold?” the smallest girl asked Nika, pointing at the tree.

Nika tipped her sunglasses down her nose. “Watch the leaves.”

She drew the light between them into long golden threads. Every moving leaf pulled a thread sideways, so that the tree seemed to be shaking out a thousand tiny streamers. The children stood beneath it with open hands. Nika let the threads loosen into bright rings, spinning each one down round a wrist or an ankle. A boy tried to catch his ring in his mouth. The tall cousin jumped through hers before it reached the ground.

Nika laughed, and spread the light wider. The bunting shone. Gold edged every plate.

“Lady Nika,” Tebbit's mother said, “the icing.”

A purple flower was sliding down the cake.

Nika closed her fingers. The rings vanished; the tree became a tree again. She drew in her radiance until the garden settled to ordinary afternoon light, then slipped her glasses up into her hair.

“Will that do?”

The woman nudged the flower back with a knife. “Thank you. Tebbit, leave it. You'll make a hole.”

He took his finger away from the icing.

“Can we do the chairs now?”

His mother looked at the sky as if some further guest might be descending with an appetite. Then she said they could.

Six chairs were already waiting back to back on the lawn. Tebbit dragged Nika's over to join them, then retrieved the rocket from beneath the tree. While his mother fetched a concertina, the children spread themselves round the chairs, leaving Nika a gap.

“Am I to play?” she asked.

“If you want.” Tebbit was straightening the fin with his thumbnail. “You go round till the music stops. Then you sit down. Whoever hasn't got a chair is out.”

“And what happens when I win?”

He went to the table, laid the rocket down, and brought a chocolate sun from behind the jug. Wrapped in gold foil, it was as broad as his palm, with fat pointed rays all round it.

Nika took a closer look. The foil had been pressed into a smiling face. This was a much better likeness than the one on the kitchen sill.

“That's the prize,” Tebbit said. His cousin reached for it, and he twisted away. “You have to win it.”

“I'm looking.”

“You look with your eyes.”

His mother took the chocolate and stood it against the jug. “Come on, everybody. Eight people, seven chairs.”

Nika counted. The deficiency was deliberate, then. She placed herself behind Tebbit, who tugged his crown straight.

“No pushing,” he told the smallest girl. “And you have to keep going. You can't just wait by a chair.”

His mother pulled the concertina open.

Nika had expected something ceremonial, perhaps a procession ending in a change of seats. Instead, the children marched round the chairs at an astonishing pace. She followed, lifting her hem above the grass. The tune skipped and doubled back; the smallest girl kept taking two steps to everybody else's one. Tebbit swung his arms. His cousin watched the concertina.

Nika began to see the attraction. Each chair offered itself and slipped away, and the little golden sun watched from the table. She quickened her pace. There would be a seat directly to her left in three steps, and another two beyond that. If the music stopped now—

It stopped.

Nika folded herself gracefully above the chair with the sun on it, arranging her ruffles with a flick of her wrist. She had secured it well before Tebbit dropped into the one opposite.

Then the smallest girl darted beneath her arm and scrambled onto the seat.

Nika rose to avoid a collision. All seven children were sitting. The smallest girl looked up at her from under a fringe full of grass seeds.

“I was here,” Nika said.

“You weren't sitting.”

“I was sitting over the seat.”

Tebbit leaned round a chair back. “Your bottom has to be on it.”

Nika looked down at the little girl, whose bottom was unquestionably on it.

“That was not mentioned.”

The little girl bounced on the seat.

Tebbit's mother set the concertina on her knee. “I'm afraid you're out, Lady Nika.”

The goddess lowered her feet to the grass. “Might this be counted as a demonstration?”

“We can play another game later.” The woman stood. “Everybody up. We need to take one chair away.”

The children sprang up. Tebbit's mother carried the chalk sun back to the table and placed it beside Nika.

Nika sat on it. Properly. Her knees came up inconveniently high, and she had to gather her ruffles into her lap. The chair was warm where the little girl had been. She moved one sandal to stop a short leg from rocking.

Tebbit came over while his mother counted the remaining chairs.

“You can watch.”

“I had intended to eat the chocolate.”

“I want it too.” He glanced at his cousin, then hurried back into place.

The music started again. From her low seat Nika had an excellent view of the shoes. The smallest girl's buckles flashed; Tebbit's cousin wore soft slippers that hardly left the ground. She stayed very close to the chairs. Nika watched her slip into one as the others were still bending their knees.

The smallest girl came out next. She accepted an apricot tart, sat beside Nika, and immediately asked whether the goddess could make the bright rings again.

“After the game,” Nika said. Someone was going to have to get ahead of that cousin.

More chairs came to the table. A boy complained that the music was too quick. Another protested when it grew slower. One child forgot the game altogether and danced away across the grass; his empty-handed return caused a dispute that Tebbit settled by pointing repeatedly at the occupied seats. Between rounds he lifted the chocolate to check that it was still there, and his mother put it back.

With five chairs taken away, only Tebbit, his cousin, and a boy with red bootlaces remained. The last two chairs stood back to back in the middle of a patch of flattened grass.

Nika leaned forward. Tebbit was doing very well. He had stopped swinging his arms, and his crown had slipped down over one eyebrow. His cousin waited for him to pass, then tucked herself close behind him. The boy with red laces kept to the outside.

The tune came round again. Tebbit peered at his mother. The cousin peered at a chair.

Silence. A scrape. The boy dropped sideways onto one seat and the cousin landed on the other. Tebbit stopped in front of her knees with his hands held out.

“I was going there!”

“I got here.”

He looked at the boy, who planted both boots on the ground.

“But it's my birthday.”

His mother shook her head. “One person comes out each time, Tebbit.”

“I nearly sat down.”

“Come and sit here. We're doing the last round.”

She put a chair beside Nika's and waited. Tebbit kicked a loose leaf off his shoe. Then he trudged over, sat, and pulled his crown up with both hands.

Nika shifted her elbow to give him room.

The two remaining players disputed which way round to walk. Tebbit stared at the patch of grass between his shoes. Nika could have offered him an account of her own treatment, but he had been present for it, and he was picking a hole in the paper at his temple.

“Your cousin is very quick,” she said at last.

“She plays at everybody's parties.”

“Ah.”

“She won a whole bag of figs at my other cousin's.”

Nika watched the girl test the last chair, sitting and standing twice. Such preparation seemed excessive. She wished she had thought of it.

Tebbit reached behind him for the rocket. “Did it leave a big hole?”

Nika held her hands apart.

He sat straighter. “That big?”

“The cloud tore. Your rocket went through the place I had chosen for my shoulder.”

“Could you see through it?”

“I could see this garden.”

He looked up. Her cloud had drifted beyond the roof, and the gap had softened into a notch along its edge.

“I made that,” he said.

“You did.”

“She said it wouldn't get past the tree.” He nodded at his cousin. “The first one didn't.”

Nika followed his gaze. Something red was wedged in the topmost fork, above the bunting.

“Is that also an invitation?”

“Yes. The same one. Except I had to write it again.” He examined the fin, then pressed it gently flat against his knee. “I wasn't eight when I did that one. It was yesterday.”

His mother called for quiet. The last round had begun.

The cousin and the boy circled the single chair. The boy tried walking sideways. The cousin copied him. His foot caught a chair leg, he stumbled, recovered, and flashed an alarmed look towards the concertina. Nika held her breath. Tebbit gripped the rocket in both hands.

The music stopped with the cousin almost past the seat. She sat backwards, twisted, and caught the backrest. The boy's hands landed on her shoulders.

“Won!” she shouted.

The other children swarmed over. Tebbit stayed beside Nika as his mother presented the chocolate. The cousin peeled back a corner of gold, took one deliberate bite from a ray, and carried the rest to her plate.

“She'll eat all of it,” Tebbit said.

Nika had been thinking much the same thing.

“Cake!” his mother called.

Tebbit was on his feet before she had finished. He took his place behind the candles and beckoned urgently to Nika until she brought her chair round to the crowded side of the table. Everybody sang, badly and with great volume. Nika knew none of the words. She joined on the last note, and several children turned to hear it continue long after they had run out of breath.

Tebbit bent towards the candles.

“Wait!” his mother said. “Your crown.”

He pulled it off and blew. Seven flames went out. He attacked the eighth from closer range, puffing his cheeks, and the children cheered when it surrendered.

Nika applauded with the rest. She was hungry now. The little sunlit rings had taken some concentration, and the musical chairs had taken considerably more.

“Which bit?” Tebbit asked her while his mother cut.

“The flower that fell down.”

He leaned over the cake. “I want the rocket.”

His mother lifted the crooked icing rocket onto his slice. Nika received the purple flower and a thick slab of cake, with a fork much too small for it. She ate the flower first. It tasted of vanilla and a great deal of sugar.

The smallest girl held up her wrist across the table. Nika wound a thin ring of light round it, keeping it pale enough to leave the icing alone. The girl turned her hand this way and that, admiring it, while Nika took another forkful of cake. When the girl reached for a tart, Nika let the ring unwind.

Tebbit put his plate on his knees, set the real rocket between them, and picked icing off its paper nose where he had touched it with a sticky thumb.

“I would do better if we played again,” Nika said.

“Me too.” He glanced at the cousin's plate. Half the chocolate sun remained. “There isn't another prize, though.”

“I should still like to see your cousin lose.”

He looked at her, then back at the cousin, who was telling the boy with red laces exactly where he had gone wrong.

“We could do the music,” he said.

Nika considered the empty chairs. “And decide when it stops?”

“Yes.” His voice grew louder. “Mum! Can we do the music for another game?”

His mother was collecting discarded candle stubs. “Can you play a concertina?”

“She can sing.”

She looked at Nika, who took another mouthful of cake and nodded.

“Finish eating first.”

They finished quickly. Tebbit got icing on both cuffs. Nika found crumbs in a fold of her dress and tipped them onto her plate. Around them the other children were already deserting the table, called away from their slices by the news of a second game.

Five chairs went back to the grass. Nika helped carry them. The tall cousin tucked the rest of her chocolate beneath an overturned saucer and inspected the arrangement. Then she took her place among the six players.

Tebbit dragged his chair beside the chalk sun.

“When I squeeze your wrist, stop singing.”

“We must wait until she is between two chairs,” Nika said quietly.

“I know.”

Nika rested her wrist in his hand and sang a brisk tune without words. The children set off. Tebbit followed his cousin with his whole head, waiting. She passed a chair. His fingers tightened. Nika stopped.

The cousin sat almost before the note was gone. Four other children found seats, and the boy with red laces stood looking at an empty patch of grass.

“I can see you squeezing,” the cousin told Tebbit.

He snatched his hand away. Nika looked from her wrist to the cousin's pleased face. While the players got up and the boy carried a chair out, she stood, picked up the little chalk sun, and set it down facing the cake table. Tebbit watched her sit with her back to the players.

“But you won't see when to stop.”

Nika reached round and turned his chair to face the table beside hers. “Neither of us will.”

He sat down slowly. His hand found her wrist again, out of sight in her lap.

Nika began the tune. Behind them, shoes scuffed the grass. She could hear the smallest girl's hurried steps and somebody laughing, but the cousin's soft slippers made no useful sound at all. Perhaps she was passing a chair now. Perhaps she was very far from one. Nika resisted the urge to look over her shoulder and sang a little louder.

Tebbit's fingers twitched against her wrist. She glanced at him. He was staring fiercely at the cake crumbs.

More feet shuffled past. Nika felt the hand tighten decisively and cut the note short.

Feet thudded; a chair scraped. Then the cousin cried, “Oh!”

Nika and Tebbit twisted round together. Every chair was full, and the cousin was still standing. Tebbit flung both hands into the air, and Nika sprang up so abruptly that the little sun chair tipped over behind her.

stories.title: Where the Eagle Lands
stories.prompt: Years after Yavren walked away from the valley rather than become its resurrected Queen, she returns with the man she loves having finally mastered the vast Eagle Shadow sleeping inside her—not to reclaim a throne, but to raise ruined cities, unite the kingdoms that once hunted her, and prove that the most powerful thing she inherited was the choice to build what her former life wanted to destroy.
stories.body:
# Where the Eagle Lands

The family had brought their door. It lay on a handcart between two bundles of bedding, its lower panels scratched white by a dog that had been dead for seven years.

“Second arch on the left,” the woman told Yavren. “We lived behind it. My father made that door. I kept thinking we'd come back.”

Beyond her, Esvay lay open to the spring sky. Grass grew along the fallen streets. The western arcade had come down in the wars after Yavren left the valley, and through its scattered columns she could see the hills where three armies had once hunted her. Nothing moved there now except sheep.

Yavren asked the family to join the others on the slope. Then she walked out among the stones.

Her shadow opened.

It passed beneath the broken arcade, climbed the hillside, and rose behind her in the shape of an eagle so immense that its head stood above the clouds. Along each outspread wing, separate feathers narrowed to points finer than needles. Yavren felt them as clearly as her own fingertips. She slid them beneath the fallen masonry, taking the weight of columns, lintels, the long curved fragments of the market dome. Earth sifted from a thousand rising surfaces. In the sudden shade the sheep began to bleat.

She lifted an entire street into the air.

For a little while Esvay hung in pieces, sunlight passing through the spaces where houses would be. Yavren turned the stones slowly, bringing their sound faces together along the foundations the masons had marked. Replacements for the missing blocks stood newly cut beside the old. These, too, she lifted. The Eagle's pinions spread through the suspended street until every arch had its curve, every column its capital. Then she lowered them.

The sound went through her soles: one long, deep settling.

She withdrew her power. The great wings thinned into daylight, leaving stone to bear stone. Where there had been a field of wreckage stood a roofless street.

For nine years she had carried the memory of another Esvay: banners, painted balconies, a reception where the Eagle Queen had been offered poisoned wine. With it came the remembered desire to break the city down to bedrock. That desire had once felt as intimate as thirst. It was still hers to remember. So were the eyries she had saved, the valley she had spared, and the eastern road she and Pelka had taken while a throne waited empty behind them.

Someone on the slope was crying. The woman with the door was already coming down.

Irdas met Yavren by the rebuilt arcade. He had a loaf under one arm and was trying to shake grit from his dark curls without dropping it. The sight pleased her more than the applause beginning behind him. Six years together, and he still behaved as though hair could be persuaded.

“You've got it all down your neck,” she said.

“Then help me. You're standing there enjoying it.”

She put her fingers inside his collar and brushed out the dust. He leaned into her hand. At thirty-six he had acquired a little silver above his ears; at thirty-three she had begun privately counting it, as though noticing each strand would slow the others.

He kissed her palm before she took it away. Then they ate under the first standing arch while the family fitted their old door into its new opening.

By midsummer there were roofs over four hundred households. The Eagle raised streets in a morning; the carpenters, glaziers, and people deciding where to put their beds took longer. Yavren slept deeply after the great lifts and woke hungry enough to annoy anyone sharing a dish with her. The bakers learned her days. Children learned that when she spread the Eagle over the city, their shadows vanished beneath it, and invented a game in which the smallest child could catch everybody.

Esvay acquired competing dye shops, a school in a former countinghouse, and a bride who refused to shorten her procession when it met a cartload of cabbage. For twenty minutes neither could turn. Yavren, watching from an upper window, laughed until the bride looked up and recognized her; then she hid, delighted and ashamed.

Pelka arrived the following week and found her in the same room, listening to a man explain why his warehouse should be raised before his neighbor's.

“I can wait,” her foster sister said, from the door. “I waited an hour downstairs.”

Yavren ended the audience too abruptly. The man left affronted; Pelka remained in the doorway with her dusty pack.

“They said tomorrow,” Pelka said. “As though I'd come to sell you something.”

“They don't know you.”

“I'm not doing that again. Come and see me for once.”

It stung because Pelka had been back in the valley two years while Yavren and Irdas traveled. Her sister had asked her home three times. Each visit had become possible after some other journey.

“Stay with us,” Yavren said. “There isn't a proper bed yet. We'll find one.”

Pelka looked at her a moment, then let the pack slide off her shoulder.

Over supper she told them the high eyries had fledged eleven young. She had brought the news in person because Yavren never asked enough in letters. She also brought a petition from the valley families: at the western border, returning settlers were having their carts searched and their sons detained for old military debts.

Irdas stopped cutting the cheese. Two of his players were being held at that same border.

“You have players?” Yavren asked.

“Three so far. You met the woman with the red boots.”

Yavren remembered a singer at supper, and Irdas showing her the ruined hall below their rooms. He had been talking about that hall since their arrival. Yavren had liked listening: a man in love with a place spoke about it much as he spoke about a person.

The next morning a royal messenger arrived. The western queen claimed the newly valuable properties of Esvay and expected rent. Before he left, a southern envoy presented the king's older claim. Both carried plans to establish a garrison. Beyond the hill passes, Tolrath's scattered people were asking when Yavren would come to them.

She wrote to all three rulers, including the hill regent. She described the families arriving in Esvay from every kingdom, the empty workshops they would fill, and the trouble already waiting at the borders. She invited the rulers to come after harvest with their councils, prepared to settle the claims together. Pelka added the valley petition. Irdas enclosed the names of the players detained.

That evening Yavren found him marking the theatre floor in charcoal.

She stood in the doorway while he paced away from a semicircle of benches. The hall had once been a nobleman's winter garden; its glass was gone, but its stone vault carried a voice beautifully. Irdas spoke two lines from a play she knew, turned, and spoke them again toward the far wall. The second time she could hear the tiredness in the old father's voice. She had watched him be that father in village squares, on tavern tables, in a field where the audience kept chasing flies. Here, his quietness reached her.

“That's good,” she said.

He grinned. “Come stand here.”

She did. He walked to the doorway and said her name, softly, and she heard him as though his mouth were against her ear.

“I want to open in spring,” he said.

“We'll be in Tolrath.”

“You'll be in Tolrath. I thought I'd stay through winter.”

She looked down at the charcoal near her boot. “You said you wanted to try the hall.”

“I do. With a company. With more than the three people we've found.”

“For how long?”

“Years, if it works.”

The word made the room feel suddenly crowded. All those future winters, already occupied.

“I asked you to come back with me,” she said.

“I came.” He glanced at the benches. “I like it here.”

She had imagined his delight as something they would take away together. They had done that everywhere: a room, a season, a favorite cook, another departure. There had always been somewhere neither of them had seen.

“You engaged people without telling me.”

“I told you about the singer. And the brothers coming after harvest.” He rubbed his blackened fingers on his trousers. “I didn't ask you to stay. I should have asked that.”

“Then ask.”

He came back across the hall. “Live here with me.”

She could have lifted the entire vault more easily than she could answer. Above them waited the two rooms where they slept with their clothes still in traveling chests. She pictured those chests closed while petitions accumulated outside a door everybody knew.

“I don't know how long Tolrath will take.”

“I'm asking where you'll come back to.”

“And when they need another city? And another?”

“You might go.” He sounded tired now, in his own voice. “I might have a rehearsal.”

It was the first time she had understood that she could leave and he could remain, each wanting something the other could not carry.

They went upstairs without settling it. In bed she reached for him, then stopped, uncertain whether touch would seem an answer. He found her hand beneath the blanket and held it against his chest.

“I still want this,” he said.

“So do I.”

In the morning he began writing invitations to actors. She rode north to look at Tolrath, and returned eleven days later with drawings of its shattered terraces. They argued twice more that summer, less carefully the second time. She hated his assumption that she would eventually stay; he hated waiting to discover whether they would live together again. She promised to return for the spring opening. He asked her to mean a particular day. They chose one.

The rulers' replies followed her between the cities. Each offered her guards; each warned against accepting the others' protection. She declined all three. Instead she sent back the names of their own displaced subjects who had volunteered to speak in Esvay. By harvest, each ruler had agreed to hear them.

When the rulers came to Esvay, autumn washing hung across the street where their escorts wanted to assemble. The woman whose father had made her door told a soldier to go around. Yavren watched him obey. Nine years earlier she had hidden from men wearing his colors in a hollow under tree roots.

The city had elected twelve residents to speak beside the crowns. They met in Irdas's unfinished theatre, where there was no raised seat yet and everyone had to step over the same roll of canvas. Councilors occupied the back benches, arguing quietly among themselves whenever a ruler offered something they disliked.

By the third afternoon the southern king had agreed to free the detained travelers if the western queen did likewise. The queen would surrender her rents in Esvay only for a share of the city's future customs. The hill regent wanted that share divided three ways. He also wanted troops from both larger kingdoms withdrawn from the passes.

“So either one can march through after the other leaves?” the western queen asked. “No.”

“Then neither comes back without our agreement,” said the regent.

The southern king pushed aside a dish of apple cores. “Whose agreement?”

The argument widened. A common assembly, the regent proposed, with the crowns and the towns both represented. It would decide the borders and authorize defense. No king would be free to begin a border war on his own. The western queen called that surrender. One of Esvay's elected speakers, a cooper who had lost two sons to different armies, said yes, it was, and asked whether she had come prepared to make any.

Yavren watched the queen's face. Her seal had stood at the bottom of the warrant for Yavren's capture. She was older now, the jaw thinner, but the memory of the folded paper remained terribly sharp.

“My villages are emptying,” the queen said at last. “They're coming here. I am being asked to give up the means of bringing them back.”
