“Mine too,” said the southern king. “But my wool merchants can't sell north while your soldiers take half their loads.”

The cooper started speaking at the same time as Pelka. They both stopped; Pelka motioned him on. He wanted a house in either city to belong to the family living in it, with old claims heard individually instead of whole streets confiscated. Pelka wanted a valley woman to be allowed across a border without supplying a son in return.

“And what do you want?” the western queen asked Yavren.

It was tempting to answer for everyone. She had been doing it in letters for months. She looked toward Irdas, who was sitting on the floor, making notes about something other than this meeting.

“A seat here when you perform,” she had told him that morning, trying out the thought of an ordinary claim. He had said she would have to buy one; then, seeing she was serious, had kissed her until they heard the delegates arriving.

“I want to keep raising the cities,” she told the queen. “I won't govern them.”

“Will you enforce what we agree?”

“No. You must be able to keep it when I'm elsewhere.”

The queen stared at her. Yavren let her. Across the room the cooper had begun counting on his fingers, explaining to the regent how many town representatives would be needed to prevent the three crowns from outvoting everyone at once.

They stayed six more days. The western ministers argued for the returning trade and against paying for two ruinous frontier fortresses. Their council accepted the shared customs; the southern king secured the northern markets; the regent obtained common defense and the abandonment of the rival garrisons. The residents won free settlement across all three kingdoms and a voice equal to the crowns' combined delegation. Border judgments would bind all three. Yavren listened as the terms were read aloud and the councilors gave their votes, one after another. In the street outside, where she had stood among the broken stones, the three rulers swore before their own people to obey the common assembly.

The union acquired its first quarrel that same evening, over which disputed hill estate should be heard first. Yavren left them arguing in the theatre and went upstairs with Irdas. Through the floor she could hear Pelka demanding that someone bring a lamp.

The first snows found Yavren in Tolrath.

This city had been built in seven terraces against the mountain. Its collapse lay in great white bands down the slope: houses, stairs, colonnades, the long front of a palace that had lost its supporting streets. A few hundred people lived among the lowest ruins. Beyond the passes, thousands waited for places to return to.

Here she remembered the Eagle Queen dancing. A green dress, pearls heavy against the collarbone, a young man with a beautiful mouth whose name had gone. The remembrance came while she studied the broken palace front, and for a moment the cold stone held the sweetness of an evening before any vengeance had become necessary to that former self.

She kept the curve of the great stair. She raised the palace's surviving columns around an open square, where the returning families could build their own celebrations.

All winter the Eagle spread above Tolrath. Yavren stood on one terrace with darkness rising from her living body and extended its wings along the mountainside. In her grasp the fallen city moved upward, a hundred tons of pale stone along each feather, broken stairways ascending past windows where people leaned out to watch. She set whole rows of houses on their old foundations. She fitted the long colonnade to the square. Where stone was missing, masons cut replacements; where timber had burned, crews brought new beams over the passes.

The first timber train traveled under three sets of colors. Its guards came from the towns, serving the common assembly. In the opposite direction went the western garrison, their baggage piled high, and behind them the southern troops. They passed each other badly, with insults and horses backing into snow. They passed.

Letters arrived from Irdas. A leading actor had departed because he would not be allowed to play both lovers in the same scene. Another had married the costumer. The red-booted singer had a sister whose voice made Irdas want to abandon spoken drama altogether. Yavren read some pages impatiently, looking for herself, then went back and read them properly.

She wrote that the hill regent's cousin had lost his claim to six inhabited streets before the new assembly and was still threatening to appeal. She wrote about a little boy who had asked why she wore dark feathers when the stone dust turned them white. She described the green dress she remembered and asked Irdas whether his costumer could make her something green for the opening. In a separate letter she told Pelka she would come for the eyries' hatching, after the first performances. Pelka sent back the dates she could expect a bed.

His next letter contained a length of green thread and a demand for measurements. Below it he had written, without any attempt at elegance, that he missed her body in bed and was tired of sleeping diagonally to prove there was an advantage.

She laughed alone in her room, then wanted him so suddenly that she had to put the letter down.

By the thaw, Tolrath had six occupied terraces and a seventh rising. Smoke stood above hundreds of chimneys. Market awnings filled the palace square; from the rebuilt colonnade she heard a quarrel about the price of onions and, farther away, someone practicing a horn very badly. She had seen that square packed with soldiers in a memory older than her present body. Now two women were spreading a carpet there to see whether its colors suited the daylight.

On her last morning she lifted the remaining stones of the seventh terrace. The Eagle's head turned with hers; its vast wings held the city above the city. She could feel each separate weight high above her and the mountain solid under her boots. She lowered the stones into the places waiting for them. As the shadow withdrew, sunlight climbed the new walls.

The masons would finish without her. She left before the lime had dried.

Five days later, on the appointed spring evening, she reached Esvay with her dark hair full of road dust and the green dress folded in her saddlebag. The theatre doors were open. Outside them stood a cart bearing the southern king's colors; beside it, valley ponies and the hill people's shaggy packhorses. Nobody had been turned away at the borders. Somebody was complaining about the price of a seat.

Pelka met her in the passage and took the saddlebag.

“He's upstairs. Hurry. You can tell me about the city afterward.”

Irdas was struggling with the fastening at the back of his stage robe. He turned when she entered, one shoulder bare, and for a moment neither of them seemed to know how to cross the little room. Then he came so quickly that she was still laughing when he kissed her. His curls were damp from washing. She put her face against his neck and breathed him in.

“You came,” he said.

“I said I would.”

“I know.” He held her another moment. “I kept listening for a horse.”

She helped with the fastening. Her traveling chest stood where she had left it, but he had cleared half the clothes cupboard. There were flowers in a chipped bowl on the sill, and the window gave onto the arcade she had first raised. She could see the family's door through the branches of a young tree.

“I'll have to go again,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Sometimes for months.”

He touched the cupboard door. “I left you half.”

“I saw.” She caught his hand before he could move away. “I want to live here.”

He looked at her with an openness that made her shy. From below, someone called him by the old father's name. He closed his eyes, kissed her forehead, and went.

Yavren changed into green. Downstairs Pelka had kept her a seat. Around them the audience was still settling: three kingdoms' accents, a cough, a late arrival edging past somebody's knees. When Irdas stepped onto the stage the room quieted. He began so softly that she had to stop listening for anything else.

The Eagle Queen had heard music beneath gilded ceilings. Yavren remembered the beauty of those rooms, and the people who had died in them, and the years of wanting everyone else to lose as much. The memory stayed with her. Above this room were her clothes beside Irdas's, beyond it two cities standing in the spring night. Her sister's shoulder rested against hers. She let the dark wings sleep inside her and listened to the man she loved.

stories.title: The Cat Who Kept the Door
stories.prompt: The kingdom’s most feared archmage is a black cat who has quietly served every royal family for nine life times—but on the night three moons finally align, he retrieves the scythe he swore never to wield again and informs the terrified young queen that something older than magic has just awakened.
stories.body:
# The Cat Who Kept the Door

Isabet had saved the quail's liver for Murrant, but he stole it before she could offer it. His black paw slid between the stems of two wineglasses without disturbing either. Across the table, the commander of her cavalry stopped talking until the paw had withdrawn.

She had been queen for forty-one days. Murrant had slept outside her bedroom for all forty-one, and still she could not quite bring herself to tell him to get off the table. As a child she had watched him kill a man who had drawn a sword on her father. One burning breath, a body beneath a cloak. Afterwards he had hidden under her bed, furious when anyone tried to touch him.

Beyond the open windows, the pale moon approached the blue. The red moon already rested against its edge. Courtiers crowded beneath the painted ceiling; on the terrace an astronomer held up one finger, asking the kingdom to wait.

Murrant dropped the liver.

His ears flattened. Isabet looked at the windows, where the last pale crescent slipped behind the blue and all three moons stood in one line above the towers. Then she felt it through the soles of her slippers: a slow upward pressure, as though something enormous had put its back against the foundations.

The astronomer's finger remained raised. Glasses rattled against plates.

Murrant sprang down and went behind the throne. Isabet followed him. Under the lowest panel of its carved back was a cupboard she had always supposed held cleaning rags. He pressed his nose against it. Three locks opened in succession, without keys.

A black robe unfolded out of the darkness. Its red lining settled over his shoulders; little gold clasps fastened beneath his throat. Then the scythe came out, butt first, scraping the flags. It was taller than Isabet. The inward curve of its blade had the faint blue sheen of a raven's wing, and a red stone sat where blade joined shaft.

She knew it from the oldest battle tapestries. None of them showed what was left after its passage. They showed soldiers running from a small patch of black.

The scythe rose upright beside him. Murrant put one forepaw on its shaft.

“Something older than magic has awakened,” he said. “Older than any magic our people remember.”

She waited for the impatience, the flick of his tail that meant someone had overwatered the wine or misused a title. His tail was tight against his legs. A sour mouthful rose into her throat.

“What do I do?”

“Get everyone out of the palace. Go with them.”

She turned. The commander stood at the edge of the dais, his hand hovering near his sword. “Take them out through the west court,” she told him. “The servants too. No carriages. Get well clear of the walls.”

He looked at the weapon, then bowed and began ushering people toward the doors. As the first chairs overturned, Murrant slipped through the little door behind the throne, and Isabet followed him down to the tombs.

***

Her father's burial chamber smelled of fresh mortar. A stone mason's mallet still lay beside the uncompleted inscription. Murrant passed it without looking, the scythe floating lengthwise at his flank, and went on down the stair.

“I told you to leave.”

“How do you know what's down there?”

He halted at the next landing. In the gold light gathering along his whiskers, his eyes were almost lost.

“I have guarded this place since the first family built their hall above it. If you come any farther, I may not be able to get you out.”

She gripped the stair rail. Above them, feet were running across the throne room. Below, a much deeper noise had begun: iron turning on iron.

She ought to go. He had said so, and he knew. But her father had gone into a room with his physicians, and everyone had told her to wait outside; she had been waiting outside things ever since.

“I'm coming as far as I can.”

Murrant stared at her. Then he turned, and she hurried after the red hem of his robe.

They passed the tombs of the family her grandfather had displaced, then a queen whose likeness had been chiseled off every coin. Beside that queen's stone pillow lay a tiny collar, green enamel with a bell.

“Was that yours?”

“My second life. She thought I might wander into the kitchens and get lost.”

The next chamber held square coffins and no likenesses. Lower still, the kings lay on their sides inside jars. Murrant had served them all: these people whose crowns had different shapes, whose prayers Isabet could not read, who had killed one another and kept the cat. Nine lifetimes, the histories said. She had accepted the number as she accepted the nine golden points on his seal, something too old and official to question.

At the foot of the last stair, he stopped to tug a fold of robe from under his hind paw with his teeth. Beyond him, the masonry ended at a narrow door set in a metal wall. Isabet laid a hand against the jamb and snatched it back. Hot already.

The door stood open. Engravings around it showed an egg-shaped structure inside a much larger chamber: shut, opening, and open. In the last picture, a branching shape filled the egg's center.

Murrant lifted his nose toward that picture.

“That is where it thinks. I spent most of my fourth life learning to read what its builders left here.”

“People made it?”

“People made a mind and gave it more power than they could take back.” He studied the black doorway. “Later people tried. Several civilizations of them. We built our first hearths in their ruins.”

Isabet bent close to the engravings. Around the central shape were lesser shapes, scratched through by some long-dead hand. Fine lines joined them to the center. Those had been cut through too.

“Those were other places where it thought,” he said. “All destroyed. Only this one can give orders now. It shut itself away to sleep until the sky reached a position its makers had chosen. Tonight.”

“Why didn't you kill it while it slept?”

He lowered the scythe until the red stone brushed his forehead. A warm pulse ran along the edge, bright enough to show a pale scar across his nose.

“I tried. None of my fire ever marked it.” He touched the outer line of the engraved egg. “The shell was fused shut. With this I can part a join I can see. I cannot cut my way through a thing with no seam, however long I wish at it.”

The wall gave a metallic click. Warm air brushed her face from the doorway.

“Now it has to open or cook itself. I can reach the mind.”

He started forward, but she caught the trailing cloth of his robe. His head whipped around, teeth showing, and she let go.

“You swore you wouldn't use that again.”

Her father had told her the story when she had wanted the scythe on her first banner. She had cried at his refusal, and Murrant had left the room.

“I did.”

“What happened?”

For a moment she thought he would go without answering.

“Two princes. Both wanted their father's chair. One brought an army into the nursery wing to reach the other.” He looked up the long stair behind her. “I had slept across both their cradles. By morning I had killed them both. I died of my wounds. When I came back, I put the blade away.”

“You could come back again.”

His ears turned toward her, then slowly forward.

“That was my eighth life, Isabet.”

She had been holding her arms tightly across herself. Now she dropped them. Murrant looked much smaller with the robe dragging behind him.

“I didn't mean you should die.”

“I know.”

“Are you going to?”

“I don't want to.” He put his paw against the shaft again. The red stone brightened. “Keep behind me.”

***

The passage led out onto a gallery inside a chamber large enough to contain the palace. Isabet knew its breadth because a whole corner of the royal tombs had fallen through the roof and stood, impossibly small, among the things below.

All around the walls, jointed arms were unfolding from their housings. Some ended in delicate pincers; others held scoops broader than houses. Beneath them stood the armored body from the engraving, opened now along its upper half. A shell leaf the size of a tower gate hung from chains and counterweights above a service bridge running from the gallery into its side. Within that opening, hundreds of glass plates revolved around a white branching column.

Heat struck her hard enough to sting her eyes. Rows of identical copper teeth glowed below the plates. Here and there a little arm advanced, replaced a tooth, withdrew. Everything bore the repetition of manufacture, down to the same pattern of six pits on every turning joint.

Behind the open body a mast was rising in sections toward the roof. Each section locked with a crash. The ceiling split before its ascending point, letting down a white powder of stone.

“Aphan,” Murrant said, so quietly she almost missed it.

Light moved across the gallery wall. Three people stood there, small as living people, wearing white things close to their skin. One lifted a hand. Behind them rose a city of transparent towers, and beyond the city a crooked mountain Isabet recognized from her nursery window.

The people vanished. The mountain wore a pale cap, then lost it; its crooked summit broke away. A forest covered the transparent towers. Men in copper masks dug into their foundations. Isabet watched another city grow on the same slope and burn, and a third spread its long black roofs over the ash. Their work occupied a few breaths. The mountain kept wearing down.

Her own palace appeared at last, bright as a toy on the ruins.

“You occupy my crown station,” said a voice from the rail under her hand.

She recoiled. The same voice continued from far below, deep enough to shake dust out of her sleeves.

“I am Aphan. I receive your attendance.”

Murrant had crept along the gallery to the service bridge. Isabet stood where she was, trying to remember how an envoy from another throne ought to be received. Everything she knew began with a list of ancestors. She had just seen them reduced to the last finger's breadth of a dying mountain.

“I am Queen Isabet. We didn't know you were here.”

“Your companion knew.”

“I didn't know. Nobody told me.”

She wished she had not said that. It sounded like a child denying she had broken a cup. She glanced at Murrant, but he was studying the bridge. A wheeled carriage crossed its far end, carrying a load of black rods into the open shell.

“Your inhabitants will be removed from the station,” Aphan said. “I will require the high ground around it.”

On the wall, buildings vanished from the image of the city in widening circles. In their place grew branching towers like the mast rising behind the shell.

“There are people in those houses.”

“You will move them. There is time while I recover my reach.”

She looked at the mast. Its next section rose through the roof with a noise that swallowed her reply. Stone fell toward her from above; an arm pivoted, caught the block in its pincers, and swung it over the gallery behind her. It held the stone there while dust trickled through the metal fingers. The block was twice her height.

“What reach?” she said when she could hear herself.

The wall showed a curve of the world. Red points gleamed in chains along it. One was buried beneath a mountain; another hung above the clouds. Between them, great empty areas remained dark.

“My hands await instruction.”

Aphan had held her palace on its back for all its history. It seemed possible that this being had once lifted mountains to put them somewhere more convenient. The first image returned, the white-clad people beside their towers, and now they were kneeling.

“You may retain your office,” Aphan said. “I require a human voice among humans. There will be honors. Your household will be preserved.”

Her attention went to the black cat at the bridge. He had crouched so low that his belly touched the grating. She wanted her household preserved. She wanted, shamefully and with sudden force, for someone older to take command and tell her where to stand.

“Will you stop moving that tower while we speak?”

“No.”

Another section slammed home. Somewhere overhead, a bell began ringing and broke off in mid-stroke.

“I can't tell them to leave if I don't go back up.”

“Your voice will carry.”

Her own words returned from a hundred apertures in the walls, altered in pitch, searching for her exact sound. *I can't tell them. I can't tell them. I can't tell them.* At the third repetition they were indistinguishable from her voice. She could imagine it issuing from the windows above, giving orders to the people who had run when she told them to run.

“Stop that.”

The repetitions ceased.

“Accept your station,” Aphan said.

Murrant's ears twitched toward her. He could not see her face from where he crouched. Isabet drew a breath that hurt all the way down.

“No. You can't have it.”

The pincers opened behind her. The block began to fall.

***

Murrant turned and spat. A gold curve sprang from him, passing over Isabet as she ducked. The block struck it and broke. Fragments slid down either side of her, knocking sparks from the gallery.

“Bridge!” he shouted.

She stumbled after him. The scythe swung flat, almost touching the grating. At the far end the carriage shed its load and came at them, wheels shrieking. Murrant planted both front paws. Light ran from his claws into the scythe's shaft; the blade swept upward through the carriage's fastenings, and its two halves went past on either side of the bridge.

They fell a long way. Isabet heard them strike machinery underneath, then a thinner rain of parts.

Murrant was already moving. She ran with her skirts bunched in both hands, the gap beneath the grating flashing between her feet. No floor below them. No rail on the last length. The open shell was six paces away.

Inside it, the glass plates stopped revolving.

The voice came from the bridge this time. “The animal will be destroyed. Stand aside.”

“Don't listen,” Murrant said. He was panting, his mouth open. She had never heard that sound from him.

Three arms swung down toward the bridge. The gold curve drew tight around them, scarcely above her head now. Metal fingers scraped its surface. One pushed far enough through to catch her hair; she fell to her knees and crawled, leaving strands behind. Murrant gave a short, ugly cry. The fingers sprang back.

At the threshold she saw what waited inside. The branching column was laced with fine black connections, each splitting and splitting again until the smallest disappeared into glass. Thousands of blue sparks flashed together at each syllable of the voice. Down the column ran a silver seam.

The scythe reached inward. A barrier rose from the floor and struck the blade, throwing it back against the shell. The ring of the blow hurt her teeth.

Murrant's gold shield flickered. Above them the great shell leaf began to descend. Hot air blasted out past their faces.

He could not hold off the arms and drive the scythe through that barrier. She saw it in the shaking of his legs, the uneven light. He pulled the blade back. Aphan's fingers began pressing through the gold again.

“Isabet. Go.”

She looked behind them. The bridge was clear all the way to the gallery. The arms were bent toward Murrant. She could run now. He had given her a path.

“Go!”

She scrambled backward onto the bridge. The shield contracted around the cat, leaving her out in the raw heat. Murrant put his shoulder against the scythe's shaft and gathered himself as he did before leaping onto her bed. For one sick moment it was the same small effort, hind paws settling, tail finding balance.

Then the gold around him went out.

All of it entered the blade. He leapt through the threshold and the scythe swept before him, cutting the barrier from its hinges. Its tip caught the column's silver seam. A white line shot from end to end, and the column split, tearing apart the black connections. Glass plates fell in sheets. Aphan made a sound with no word in it, so vast that Isabet felt it inside her ribs.

The arms stopped. The mast behind the shell dropped one section with a bang. Light raced upward through the torn column and vanished at its broken ends. Along the walls the cities went dark, leaving only copper teeth glowing in the sudden quiet.

Murrant lay just inside the shell. The robe had fallen across his face. The scythe, no longer upright, slid toward her along the sloping threshold.

Above him, the enormous leaf kept coming down, drawing its counterweights upward.

Isabet ran back. She caught the shaft as it slid over the edge and pulled, but the blade was hooked behind the broken barrier. She jerked it again. Something shifted under the robe. A forepaw came out, scrabbled once, withdrew.

She put one foot against the threshold and heaved the shaft sideways. The blade scraped free. She could have dragged it onto the bridge, but Murrant was trying to crawl and getting nowhere, and the lowering leaf would cut him off before she could reach him.

She thrust the blade beneath the leaf instead.

Its tip caught the inner rim. She hauled down on the long shaft, using the lip of the threshold as a fulcrum, and felt the whole weight take hold. The leaf stopped. Her heels lifted off the bridge. She hung from the shaft with both hands, seeing the tiny scraps of herself reflected in the red stone.

“Murrant!”

He dragged himself toward her voice. His back legs trailed. She could not tell whether he was caught in the robe or hurt. The iron under her palms began to bend.

“A little more. Come on.”

He reached the gap. His head came through, then his shoulders, and the gold clasp snagged on a broken hinge. He pulled and choked. His claws scraped the metal once, twice.

She hooked her left knee around the shaft and let go with one hand. The gap narrowed. She reached down, caught his robe at the clasp, and tore. The fastening broke; he fell against her wrist. She grabbed the loose cloth behind his shoulders and hauled him out.

The shaft snapped as she fell backward. The shell leaf slammed shut on the broken scythe.

For a moment she lay on the bridge with the cat beneath her chin, unable to feel anything but the hammering in her hands. Then a black rod fell past the bridge. Another followed. The mast was folding down through its own supports.

She got up with Murrant clutched against her chest. A rod struck the grating behind her. She ran, slipping at the turn onto the gallery, and plunged into the passage as a mass of falling metal struck the dead shell. The whole chamber rang. She kept running into darkness.

***

At her father's tomb she could go no farther. She sat against the unfinished inscription and put Murrant on her lap. Dust coated him gray. When she lifted the torn robe, his hind legs moved; he pulled one away from her fingers.

“Don't,” he said. Barely a voice.

She left him alone. Far below, another piece of machinery fell. The noise came up the stair smaller than before, and after it there was only his harsh breathing.

She counted his breaths until he opened his eyes.

“I thought you'd gone.”

Her arms began shaking so badly that she had to press them against her knees. “I didn't get very far.”

He lowered his head onto the torn red lining. She rubbed a thumb along his cheek, and he turned into it.

“I couldn't get out,” he said.

“I saw.”

For a while neither spoke. Somewhere above them people were calling her name. She tried to answer and found she could not shout. Murrant's forepaw closed on the cuff of her sleeve.

“Carry me up.”

She gathered him carefully, one hand beneath his haunches, and stood. At the top of the stair the little door had swung shut. She leaned against it with her shoulder until it gave, and carried him through.

stories.title: The Last Day of the Watch
stories.prompt: Every century, the horned elves of the deep forest choose one archer to guard the ruins of a civilization when the newest guardian discovers fresh footprints leading inside, she realizes someone has been living there for years.
stories.body:
# The Last Day of the Watch

Kostral had shown her the gate, the alarm whistle, and the place where her name would be cut beneath his. He had not mentioned the footprints.

Phelnis found them beyond the first fallen column. Yellow pollen lay over the avenue, unmarked except for a line of boots going north into the city. One heel had a square patch. Wet earth still clung to its edges.

She looked back. Kostral had disappeared along the eastern wall to finish his circuit. Above the closed gate, his shutters stood open. He had told her to leave her pack in the guardroom and make herself familiar with the lower courts. At dawn, in the presence of the escort, they would inspect the outer seals on the burial chambers. Then he would give her the keys and leave.

Every hundred years, the horned elves of the deep forest chose one archer for the ruins. As a child she had recited their names in order, taking breath in the same places as her mother. She had been afraid she would stammer over Kostral's name when she met him. He had only asked whether the gold carving on her bow caught the light, and she had turned it in her blue-gray hand to show him the dull finish.

“Good. Pretty things give you away.”

He had smiled when he said it. She was still pleased with herself for having thought of that before he asked.

The footprints left the avenue through a broken doorway. Phelnis loosened an arrow in her quiver and followed.

There were trees inside the rooms. Their roots had lifted floors where the vanished people had laid dark tiles in spirals; their branches reached through upper windows and held the surviving roofs apart. Under one roof, behind a screen of branches recently cut, grew beans. Someone had planted them in four stone bowls carved with kneeling figures. Beside them stood a fifth bowl, empty except for dry stalks and carefully broken eggshells.

A blanket lay in a recess. Its original blue survived in a strip along one edge. The rest was patches, themselves patched with smaller pieces, and beside it were three worn-out shoes with their useful leather cut away. On a shelf sat a wooden cup polished smooth where a thumb would rest.

Phelnis touched the blanket. Someone had been keeping warm here for a long time.

“Leave that.”

The voice came from above her. She stepped out from under the shelf, arrow on the string.

A man stood on a broken stair, holding both hands away from his sides. His beard had been shortened with something blunt. A thread of bean fibre hung from his sleeve.

“You're the new archer?”

“Come down.”

“Where's the other one?”

“On the wall. Come down where I can see you.”

He descended sideways, favouring one ankle. Human, and much older than the first startled glimpse had suggested. The square on his heel was fresh leather against a sole made of several different scraps.

“You wanted me to find you,” she said.

“I put those prints halfway across the city. I thought you'd walked past.”

“How long have you been here?”

“Take me to the gate. Get him to open it.”

“How long?”

He glanced at her bow, then at the doorway behind her. “Thirteen years.”

She looked again at the blanket. Her twenty years of practice for the choosing had included winters when she hated the bow and put it away. Thirteen years here: the same walls in every weather, that little square of bed.

“Kostral knows?”

“He knows I'm somewhere. I wish you hadn't left him up there.”

Phelnis stepped into the doorway and looked along the wall. Empty stone, a pale shimmer of leaves. “Why does he keep you here?”

“Because I was quicker than the others.”

“What others?”

He rubbed his hands down his coat. “I can show you. It's close. Then you'll take me out.”

“What's your name?”

“Osmund.” He waited, and when she did not move, added, “Please.”

The stair led into a burial gallery above the avenue. Phelnis had expected small tombs; this passage was wide enough for six people abreast, with doorways continuing beyond sight along its inner wall. On the other side, gaps between columns opened onto a landing and broad steps down to the street. Sunlight came through the gaps and the holes left by missing roof slabs.

At the third doorway Osmund stopped beside a heap of brushwood. More branches had been pushed against the next entrance. The leaves were still green.

“Those weren't here last week.” He pulled one away. “He put them at every mouth he could find. I watched him carrying oil yesterday. He means to smoke me out before you open the chambers.”

“You think that.”

“I wasn't going to wait underneath and find out.”

Osmund lifted a loose panel beside the sealed door, revealing a hole cut through the wall. He stooped through it, and Phelnis followed. Inside, two shapes lay near a cracked stone coffin. She saw boots, a buckle, the collapsed sleeves of a coat. One arm extended towards the hole. A rusted chisel rested beyond its fingers.

She remained on the threshold. Small gold plaques had spilled from the coffin onto the floor. Its lid lay on wooden rollers.

“You opened this.”

“He shot them there. I was behind the coffin.”

“You broke into the tombs.”

“Yes, we broke in! He told us which ones to open.” Osmund caught himself and looked up towards the gaps in the roof. His next words came lower. “We had six chambers open. He said we'd get our shares when we finished the seventh. I was putting a wedge in. That was why he missed me.”

He pointed at the door. “He put the seals back afterwards. Shut the front, covered the cuts. You'd never know from the avenue.”

Phelnis looked from the tools to the passage. Nothing here told her who had killed these people. Osmund knew the chambers, knew what they held. Kostral had sworn to keep them untouched.

“Where did you meet him?”

“At the gate. Where do you think? We came looking for a way in and he let us through. I thought we'd been lucky.”

“He hired you?”

“We were thieves. There. Can we go now?”

Beyond the roof, stone scraped against stone. Phelnis looked up. Someone was crossing the wall above the gallery.

“Stay beside me,” she said, reaching for the whistle.

Osmund seized her wrist. She pulled free and lifted her bow between them.

“Don't call him.”

“He won't shoot while I'm here.”

“You don't know him.”

She knew a grave robber who wanted her to leave the keeper out of her inquiry. She put the whistle to her lips and blew the three clear notes Kostral had taught her.

Osmund ran.

He got back through the hole and across the landing before the arrow caught him. It tore his coat along the thigh and knocked his leg sideways. He fell against the steps, reached for the rail that was no longer there, and began to slide.

Phelnis caught his collar. A second arrow broke on the step beside her hand.

She dragged him backwards across the landing and through the hole. His weight pulled her down with him, one dark horn striking stone hard enough to fill her vision with white. She crawled clear of the opening and put her shoulder against the wall.

“Well found, Phelnis.” Kostral's voice carried easily from the western colonnade. “Keep away from him now.”

Osmund had both hands clamped over his thigh. Blood came between them.

“He's unarmed,” she called.

“There's a knife in his coat.”

She had seen no knife. He could still have one. She could still be wrong about everything except the second arrow striking beside her fingers.

“Put down your bow, Kostral.”

“Come out of there. Let me finish this.”

Osmund pushed at her shoulder. There was a low opening behind the coffin, almost hidden by the fallen lid.

“It comes through,” he whispered. “Go.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere that isn't here.”

She heard Kostral's boots on the colonnade, moving towards the gallery's northern end. He knew how to get in here.

She hauled Osmund towards the opening.

*

They came out into darkness that smelt of old dust and nuts. Osmund found a little lamp without searching and struck a light with hands that shook. While Phelnis bound her neckcloth around his thigh, he kept trying to pull his coat over it.

“Leave it. I need to see.”

“He'll follow the blood.”

She folded the torn coat under his leg. They listened. Above them came a slow dragging sound, then a thump. Kostral was shifting the coffin lid.

Osmund blew out the lamp.

He led her by touch through a gap between two burial chambers. She had to turn her head to pass her swept horns between the stones. On the other side, faint evening light showed a room crowded with baskets. Nuts, dried fruit, beans in their pods. A small green pear lay on a flat stone with a bite taken out of it.

“He hasn't found this one,” Osmund said. “He found the other five.”

The scrape of stone had stopped. Phelnis waited, listening for it to begin again.

“You can get outside from here?”

“Outside a room. Outside a tomb. Always another wall after it.”

She remembered the approach: a narrow neck of rock under the gate, deep clefts on either side continuing round the whole citadel. The forest grew far below its walls. From the causeway she had thought the drop beautiful.

“I tried the north face,” Osmund said. “Made a rope. It broke before I got halfway. That's the ankle.”

“And the gatehouse?”

“Locked every night. Key on him. You saw the court. You can see a mouse crossing it from his window.”

“Someone must bring him provisions.”

“At the far end of the causeway. He goes out and locks up behind him. Once I shouted until I couldn't speak. They were too far away, or he told them something. I don't know.”

Phelnis knelt to look through a low window. The avenue ran south to the gate. Kostral's guardroom occupied the upper floor on its western side; the door below, which he had left open for her pack, was still open. Twenty strides of bare court lay between it and the nearest cover.

“He said he hunted rabbits for food.”

“So do I.” Osmund tried to straighten his wounded leg and stopped. “And pigeons. There's a whole orchard growing out of the west roofs. Mostly I eat what I can hide away before winter.”

He reached for the bitten pear, thought better of it, and put it in his pocket.

Kostral appeared at the far end of the avenue. Phelnis drew back from the window. He was taking the open route south, towards his rooms, glancing into each doorway as he passed. The old archer walked as if he had plenty of time.

“If we get through that door first,” she said, “we can bar him out. The gate handles are inside.”

“He'll be waiting.”

“I just saw him. He's still north of us.”

Osmund looked at her. Then he pressed his hand against the bandage and stood.

They went down through three adjoining rooms, following the line of the avenue. In the last, Phelnis stopped. Two travelling chests stood beneath a shelf of empty coffin niches. One was open. Under a folded green cloak lay gold plaques exactly like those scattered around the dead men.

Kostral had been wearing that cloak when he admitted her.

Osmund tugged her sleeve. She went with him.

At the edge of the court she made Osmund wait while she looked up at the guardroom. Empty window. The western colonnade blocked her view farther north.

She went first, with him two steps behind. At the fourth stride an arrow hit the paving in front of her boot.

Phelnis drove Osmund sideways behind the base of a fallen statue. Another arrow passed across the place where her face had been. He cried out as his wounded leg struck stone, and she pressed a hand over his mouth before she knew what she was doing.

Above the gate, Kostral stood behind the guardroom's narrow northern window. The colonnade gave him a raised path straight to it. He had never needed to stay on the avenue.

Osmund bit her palm. She took it away.

“Phelnis.” Kostral had returned to the patient voice of their first meeting. “Your pack's here. Come and get it. Tomorrow we can open the chambers together.”

“What about him?”

“Leave him.”

She could see only a sliver of his face beside his bow. No shot there. He had enough arrows to keep them crouched behind this stone until Osmund bled through the cloth.

“You were going to take all that gold out with the escort.”

Kostral drew back from the slit.

“I kept this place safe for a hundred years,” he said. “When my wife died, I stayed here. I couldn't even stand at her grave. Do you suppose I did it for the little line they'll carve over the gate?”

Phelnis looked at the stone under her hand. This morning she had run her fingers over the space left for her name.

“Come down,” she said. “Leave the bow there.”

An arrow struck the statue's base hard enough to send a chip against her cheek.

Osmund caught her elbow and pointed behind them. A narrow doorway opened beneath the eastern gallery, three body-lengths from their stone. Keeping low, they crawled towards it. Kostral could see their feet; an arrow struck the heel of her boot as she pulled it through. The point skidded on its iron rim.

She lay with her cheek on cold paving until Osmund dragged the door's fallen timber across their legs.

“Don't talk to him,” he said. “He'll just keep you talking.”

*

Night was gathering in the room. Through the broken doorway Phelnis could see Kostral's window across the court. To its east, a little shooting terrace overlooked the gate steps. The northern window protected him from anyone on the avenue. The terrace had lost its eastern wall, leaving a low stone rail and two broken pillars.

Above her, the gallery faced that open side. Its stair had fallen in a heap outside. She had passed the wreckage on her way in.

“Is there another stair?” she asked.

“No.”

She pulled her pale hair free where it had caught under her black shoulder scales. There had to be somewhere. A man had lived here thirteen years, and Kostral had never found all his beds.

Osmund followed her gaze upwards. “You couldn't fit.”

“Show me.”

Behind a wall panel, a sloping hole climbed through the stone. He had cut footholds along one side. At its upper end was a crack wide enough for his narrow shoulders.

“I made it when we were still working,” he said. “Before the last chamber. I didn't tell the others. I meant to come back and take things for myself.”

Phelnis looked at his ragged coat, at the torn pocket holding half a pear.

She unbuckled her armour. Without it she could squeeze her shoulders through; the horns would be harder. She passed her bow and quiver ahead into the hole and started upwards, tilting her head until the tips scraped stone. Halfway up, one horn wedged against the ceiling. She backed down, turned onto her other side, tried again.

“Left,” Osmund said. “There's a hollow on your left.”

She found it with the crown of her head and pushed through. Stone tore the sleeve at her elbow. For a moment her boots hung clear of the footholds and she had to drag herself by her forearms. Then she was in the upper gallery, breathing dust through her teeth.

She crept to the opening. Across the court, perhaps thirty paces away and a little higher, Kostral still watched the statue through his northern slit. The corner of the guardroom hid his body. To shoot at the doorway where Osmund waited below her, he would have to step onto the terrace. From here she could shoot across it, between the broken pillars.

Phelnis returned to the crack.

“I need him to come out of the guardroom.”

“Call him again.”

She let that pass. “He'll shoot from cover if he knows where I am.”

Osmund was silent below her.

“There's a pillar beside the gate steps,” she said. “Can you reach it?”

“That's open ground.”

“Yes.”

“And this time you'll stop him?”

Her bow hand had begun to shake. She pressed it against the stone. “I'll have a shot.”

For a while she could hear only his breathing. Then he shifted under the crack.

“Don't whistle. Just tell me when you're there.”

Phelnis returned to the opening and set an arrow on the string. Kostral's outline moved behind the slit. The last light lay on the white stones of his terrace, enough to see a man standing there. She brought the string back a little, then let it forward to ease the tremor in her fingers.

“Here,” she said, as quietly as she could.

Below, Osmund shoved aside the timber and stumbled into the court.

He had scarcely cleared the doorway when his leg failed. He caught himself on his hands. Kostral came out onto the terrace with his bow raised.

Phelnis drew. A broken pillar obscured his chest; only his shoulder and horn were clear. She shifted her weight without lifting her feet, bringing the bow around the edge of her opening.

Osmund was trying to stand. Kostral stepped to his left to see past the terrace rail, and the pillar no longer lay between them.

Phelnis loosed into his side. His arrow went down into the court. He struck the rail with his hip, dropped to one knee, and reached towards the guardroom.

She had another arrow drawn before he fell. For several breaths she watched his hand beside the threshold. The fingers did not move.

Below her, Osmund was still crawling towards the pillar.

“He's down,” she called.

Osmund kept going until he reached the stone.

*

She climbed into the guardroom by its inner stair with her bow drawn, though there was no room to turn it. At the top she found Kostral where she had last seen him. She waited beside him, watching for breath, then crouched and touched his throat.

The keys were on a cord beneath his collar. She had to lift his head to get them free. His horn caught the cord and she worked it loose, carefully, as though she might hurt him.

In the room behind her, someone had turned down the bed for a last night. Her own pack rested beside it.

Phelnis took her cloak and went downstairs.

Osmund would not come inside while she opened the gate. He sat against the pillar, watching the terrace. When the gate finally moved, he pushed himself upright before she could reach him and went through, dragging his bad leg.

She followed him across the narrow causeway. The clefts were full of darkness now. At the first tree he stopped and put his forehead against the bark.

Phelnis settled the cloak around his shoulders. Under it, his breathing broke into short, angry catches. He gripped the tree with both hands. She stayed a little way off, holding her bow.

After a while he turned. “Did you get your pack?”

“No.”

“Good. Don't go back for it.”

She sat down beside him.

They spent the night there. Whenever Osmund woke, he reached out and found the bark. Phelnis watched the open gate. By dawn she could make out the carving above it, but from this distance she could not read the names.

The escort came with a white mare for Kostral. Someone had tied ribbons to its bridle; the woman leading it carried a folded robe across her saddle. She smiled when she recognised Phelnis, then saw the blood on her sleeve and brought the horses to a halt.

“Where is he?”

Phelnis got up. The bow had left a deep mark across her palm.

“Kostral is dead. I shot him.”

The woman looked towards the gate. Behind Phelnis, Osmund struggled to his feet, still holding the tree. She put out her free hand, and he took it to steady himself.

stories.title: The Ring Between Lives
stories.prompt: The saint arrives at the Demon Queen’s castle in a wedding dress, determined to end their kingdoms’ war with a marriage proposal. She has prepared for threats, mockery, even imprisonment—not the queen kneeling before her with a ring she has kept for three hundred years. “You always ask first,” the queen whispers. “I wanted to beat you to it this time.”
stories.body:
# The Ring Between Lives

The saint had worn a wedding dress to the enemy's castle, and Rhazelle had chosen the wrong trousers for kneeling.

That was her first thought. Her second was that the woman beneath the pointed arch had come through two armies, carrying her white skirts clear of the mud, and someone ought to take her cloak. Moonlight caught in Sidonie's pale hair. Her mouth was set in the grave, unpromising line Rhazelle remembered from their first truce conference, before six weeks of letters had taught her what that mouth could do when amused.

At twenty-nine, Sidonie had been her country's reigning saint for four years. Rhazelle was immortal and had been Demon Queen long enough to remember when the saint's country used a different alphabet. Neither fact had prepared her for the dress.

“Your Majesty,” Sidonie began. “I have come to propose—”

Rhazelle knelt. A seam complained beneath her black velvet coat. She spread her wings for balance, their crimson undersides briefly filling the arch, and opened the little box she had kept for three hundred years.

“You always ask first,” the queen whispered. “I wanted to beat you to it this time.”

The ring lay in new silk. All the old linings had worn out around it: three blue, two red, a regrettable green. Gold leaves clasped a dark garnet, no larger than the nail of Sidonie's smallest finger. Rhazelle had once rejected six stones for being too pale, too red, insufficiently red. The jeweler had died of old age without ever meeting the intended bride.

Sidonie took a step backward.

Oh.

“This time?” she said.

Rhazelle had imagined surprise, laughter, possibly tears. She had not imagined having to explain reincarnation while looking up somebody's nose.

“We've been married twice.”

Sidonie stared at her. Behind Rhazelle, a log collapsed in the drawing-room hearth.

“I have never been married.”

“No. You haven't.” Rhazelle closed the box halfway, then opened it again. “Your soul has had other lives. I knew you in two of them. We married. You asked both times, before I could give you this.”

Sidonie looked from the ring to Rhazelle's face. “Is this something you say to visiting saints?”

“The last visiting saint threw a chair at me.”

“My predecessor. Yes. She mentioned that.” Sidonie pulled off one glove, finger by finger. “She didn't mention you were beautiful. That would have been useful.”

Rhazelle's wings jerked. Sidonie watched them, and for the first time that evening her solemn mouth betrayed her.

“Could you stand up? I was ready for threats. Or mockery. There is a speech for imprisonment in my cloak pocket. I don't know what to do with this.”

Rhazelle rose, keeping the box open. Sidonie surrendered her cloak but retained something folded beneath it: four sheets tied with white ribbon.

“I came to ask you to marry me,” she said. “As you seem to have guessed. Both crowns would then hold the border duchy, and neither country would have to yield its claim. My council has approved the terms. Your council's last letter said they would accept joint possession. I thought we might at least discuss it.”

She worked the knot loose. The papers were densely written, with additions in a smaller, angrier hand.

“You brought a marriage compact.”

“Yes.” Sidonie held it out. “There are two clean copies in my saddlebag. This one's got my remarks on it.”

Rhazelle looked at the papers and then at the white dress. She had let herself imagine Sidonie choosing it for her: standing before a glass, wondering what would please her, rejecting one ribbon in favor of another.

“Of course,” she said, too late. “Come in.”

The drawing room smelled of beeswax and the oranges Rhazelle had ordered from the southern slopes. A silver bowl of their candied peels stood beside the fire. She set the ring on the table and laid the compact beside it. Her own ministers had spent weeks securing terms they could recommend to their soldiers. A sovereign marriage was the one old provision both countries recognized by which neither party became the conqueror. Rhazelle had approved it. She had merely hoped to arrive at it by a less administrative route.

Her preparations had included fifty-four rehearsals before a curtain, during which she had tried to make her wings look imposing without concealing the ring. On the fifty-fifth—

“We needn't have that,” Rhazelle said.

Sidonie stopped unpinning her veil. “Which part?”

Rhazelle looked past the fire, toward no point the room contained.

“You there, reading this. I trust the first fifty-four attempts establish that I took some trouble.”

Sidonie slowly put the veil pin down.

“Who are you talking to?”

“The person reading about us.”

“Us.”

“At present.”

Sidonie glanced toward the window. Rhazelle wished she could have postponed this until after the wedding. Or at least after wine.

“I hear the account,” she explained. “As it happens. The description of my extremely private rehearsals, for instance. Sometimes I address whoever is reading it.”

“Can you hear them answer?”

“Never. I can't see them, either.”

“Then you were telling a stranger about rehearsals I hadn't heard about.”

“Yes,” Rhazelle said miserably.

Sidonie sat down on the sofa. Her white skirts subsided around her. “Fifty-four?”

Rhazelle sat at the other end. “The coat complicated matters.”

Sidonie looked at the long velvet skirts of it, the slits for the wings, the silver fastenings. “It was worth the trouble.”

The fire clicked and settled. Rhazelle wanted to move closer by approximately the width of one cushion.

“Does this account tell you what's going to happen?” Sidonie asked.

“No. I can't hear beyond the present sentence. Or hear your thoughts unless you speak them. Usually it confines itself to mine, in excruciating detail.”

“And it's only about you?”

“There are other stories in this world. Other centuries, civilizations built over civilizations. I've heard enough to know that even the oldest ruins beneath this castle are comparatively young. But I can't turn to those accounts. I have this one, whenever it troubles to notice me.”

Sidonie lifted the hem of her dress and examined a splash of mud. “Does it do weddings?”

“I have reason to hope.”

“Good. I paid an appalling amount for this.”

She let the skirt fall and studied the ring on the table. At their conference she had studied Rhazelle just as intently, and Rhazelle had hidden her shaking hand beneath her coat.

“How did you know it was me?”

“At the conference. When you stood up to argue.”

“You recognized an argument?”

“Your soul. I can see a little of it, when I'm close. I don't know why yours is so clear to me.” Under Sidonie's ribs it moved like a light glimpsed between passing trees, familiar through every interruption. “Your face was new. Your voice. The appalling things you said about my cavalry. But I knew.”

“You never said.”

“We were settling the prisoner exchange. It didn't seem the moment.”

Sidonie conceded that with a small tilt of her head. “What were they like? The women you married.”

Rhazelle reached for the silver bowl. “Have some of these. You used to—”

Sidonie's expression changed.

Rhazelle stopped with the bowl between them.

“I hate candied peel,” Sidonie said.

“Oh.” She put it down. “The first life I knew. She liked it.”

“Was she like me?”

“She was a theater carpenter. Brown hair. A dreadful singing voice. She'd eat all the peel out of a cake and leave the naked slice on my plate.” Rhazelle could see the slice: pale crumb, small, picked-over cavities, one bright morsel overlooked. “She proposed while I was helping her shift a stage moon. She was holding the other end. I dropped mine.”

“Did it break?”

“Split right across the mountains. She made me hold it while she mended it. I had to ask whether we were engaged.”

Sidonie leaned back, eyes on Rhazelle. “How long were you married?”

“Forty-three years. She had a crooked finger by the end. Used to tuck it under mine so she could hold a cup.”

Her hand remembered before she could stop it, smallest finger curling to support an absent weight. She left it that way on the velvet of her knee.

“The second time,” she said, “she was an astronomer. Very quiet until she knew you. She proposed in a letter she left inside my boot, because that was the one place she was sure I'd look before flying off to do something tiresome. We had fifty-seven years. She liked the peel less than I did, but she kept buying it because I'd told her it reminded me of someone.”

Sidonie glanced at the bowl again.

“I put on a great deal of weight,” Rhazelle said.

The laugh that escaped Sidonie was brief and startled. Rhazelle was grateful for it. She could have gone on into the last winter: the astronomer's breath clouding the glass while she tried to see a comet, Rhazelle warming her wool stockings between her palms. She had been dead for over a hundred years and Rhazelle still disliked a clear winter sky.

“Did they remember?” Sidonie asked.

“The astronomer didn't remember the carpenter. You don't remember either. Both went into the country of the dead before they were born again. I couldn't go with them, or bring them back.”

“But you knew I'd return?”

“I hoped.”

Sidonie was silent. She rubbed a crease in her discarded glove with her thumb. Outside, a guard called the hour, and another voice answered from the gate.

“I don't know how to be jealous of a carpenter,” Sidonie said at last.

Rhazelle turned fully toward her. “Jealous?”

“She's had forty-three years with you. I've had eleven letters.”

“Fourteen.”

“I'm not counting the three about the prisoners.”

“I am. You wrote a postscript on one of them. About my handwriting.”

“You thought that was romantic?”

“You offered to teach me.”

Sidonie covered her mouth, but her laugh came out around her hand. Then she moved across the empty cushion. Her skirts pressed against Rhazelle's knee.

“I didn't ask for stories about your gardens in order to study their military value,” she said.

“Your letter said you were interested in the uses of poisonous plants.”

“Yes, well. I couldn't think how to ask what you did in the afternoons.”

Rhazelle had spent nearly all those afternoons composing replies. In one, she had included a drawing of a moth with its wings folded so Sidonie could distinguish it from the poisonous plant's flower. Sidonie had sent it back wearing a tiny crown.

“I liked your moth,” Rhazelle said.

“You sent me one letter without any jokes, after the battle in the orchard. I sat with it for a long time.” Sidonie looked down at their knees. “I didn't want you to think I could only be amusing.”

Rhazelle remembered that reply. Sidonie had named a young captain killed in the orchard; Rhazelle had known him only as the officer who always brought his own teacup to negotiations. Sidonie had written that his mother wanted the cup. Rhazelle had found it among the effects collected by her soldiers and sent it home.

“I never thought that.”

“I know. You wrote again.”

The treaty rustled in the draft from the hearth. Rhazelle reached across and put the bowl on one corner. The peace she had known with her second wife had outlasted her by generations. Then a childless duke had died, and two courts had found competing promises in his papers. Rhazelle had survived every generation involved. She had still failed to prevent the armies marching.

“The compact is good,” she said. “I want it signed tonight. Whatever else happens.”

“So do I.” Sidonie placed her bare hand beside Rhazelle's on the sofa. “But I'd like you to notice that I came in a wedding dress.”

“I noticed.”

“You looked at those papers as though I'd offered to marry you in exchange for a herd of cattle.”

“I was rather afraid you had. Metaphorically.”

“I could have sent the compact by courier and asked you to negotiate a date. Instead I rode here in this thing. It's got thirty-seven buttons. I had to stand while two women argued about the back of it.” Her fingers found Rhazelle's. “And I still didn't know whether you wanted me.”

Rhazelle took her hand. At the conference Sidonie had drawn a rough map with bread crumbs, pretending outrage when Rhazelle ate a disputed village. In her first letter the saint had confessed to putting the most troublesome settlement within reach. Rhazelle had kept that letter inside her coat for so long that the paper was soft at the folds.

“I've wanted you since you accused me of consuming your tax base,” she said. “I wanted to kiss you while you were laughing at me. In front of everyone.”

“Oh.” Sidonie looked up quickly. “You might have said something.”

“I thought the flowers—”

“You sent those to my entire council.”

“To you. With sufficient flowers for it to look diplomatic.”

Sidonie shut her eyes. “My treasurer dried his.”

Rhazelle began to laugh. It hurt a little, coming out of the tightness in her chest; then Sidonie was laughing too, holding her hand against the absurd expanse of white silk between them.

“I'm fond of him,” Sidonie said, when she could breathe. “But I don't want him included in the next attempt.”

“He won't be.” Rhazelle picked up the box. “Sidonie. Will you marry me?”

Sidonie looked at the ring, then at Rhazelle's extended wings. She let go of her hand.

“Wait.”

She stood and turned away. Rhazelle had time to consider six calamities before Sidonie reached beneath her veil and untied the cord at the nape of her neck. A second ring slid into her palm.

“I had to carry it somewhere I wouldn't lose it. The dressmaker wouldn't put in pockets.” She held out a silver band set with a small, square emerald. “I don't know whether it fits. I tried to remember the size of your hands. Then I thought you could wear it on a chain, except you might not like chains, so I bought a ribbon as well.”

Rhazelle set the box down before she dropped it.

“You brought me a ring.”

“I'm having trouble reaching the question.” Sidonie took a breath. “Rhazelle, will you marry me? And come away with me for a little while afterward? Somewhere your gardeners aren't watching you be impressive. I'd like to find out what you're like when you haven't rehearsed.”

“Yes.”

Sidonie blinked. “Both?”

“Both. Where shall we go?”

“I don't know yet.”

Three hundred years with the box. Three centuries in which she had chosen gardens, balconies, moonrises, the correct hour for dinner, and failed each time to produce the perfect beginning. Rhazelle held out her hand to a woman who had come with a treaty and no honeymoon destination, and the silver ring went easily over her knuckle.

“It fits,” Sidonie said, with such relief that Rhazelle loved her a little more.

She put the garnet on Sidonie's finger. It was too loose. Sidonie curled her hand to hold it safe, then caught Rhazelle's face between her palms and kissed her.

There were pins in the veil, and one of them caught on a horn. Neither noticed until Sidonie tried to draw away. She laughed against Rhazelle's mouth and kissed her again while Rhazelle blindly searched for the pin. The old ring pressed cool against her cheek.

By the time they separated, the veil was hanging from Rhazelle's left horn.

Sidonie looked at it. “You can keep that.”

“I shall wear it to council.”

Sidonie adjusted the lace around her horn, looking pleased with herself.

***

They signed the compact before midnight. Both commanders witnessed it, standing at the table where the candied peel had been. Hostilities were to cease on receipt of their joint order; the competing garrisons would withdraw from the duchy together, and prisoners would go home before either army was dismissed. The duchy would answer to both crowns, with the same provision binding their successors. The commanders read, asked questions, and set their seals beneath those of the two women.

Riders left from both gates. By dawn the nearest fronts had sent acknowledgments; farther detachments would receive the order as the couriers reached them. Sidonie read each report in her wedding dress, with a length of thread wound beneath the garnet to keep it on her finger. Rhazelle had been made to promise a jeweler after breakfast.

They married in the castle's east gallery as the sun reached the long windows. Some of the soldiers attending still wore mourning bands. There was no cheering until the vows were finished, and then one of Sidonie's escorts began so suddenly that Rhazelle startled and knocked the celebrant's book shut with a wing.

Sidonie bent to kiss her ringed hand in front of their commanders.

Rhazelle had held two dying wives. This one's lips were warm on her knuckles. She could feel Sidonie smiling there, taking longer than ceremonial courtesy required, while the soldiers cheered and somebody laughed.

“Well,” Rhazelle said, turning toward the place beyond the room, “I suppose you've—”

“Rhazelle.”

Sidonie was still holding her hand. She tugged, once.

Rhazelle turned back to her wife.

“I want that kiss you were going to give me in front of everyone.”

This time Rhazelle folded her wings first, and let them all watch.

stories.title: The Deep End
stories.prompt: You’ve spent seven peaceful years hiding in a public swimming pool, becoming water whenever anyone comes near. Then the new lifeguard kneels at the edge of the deep end. “Your Majesty,” he whispers.
stories.body:
# The Deep End

In my seventh year at the pool, the woman in the yellow cap learned to float on her back. For months she had kept one finger hooked over the edge, looking outraged by the possibility of sinking. Then one Thursday she let go. I was beside the ladder, without a shape, and watched her drift past with her eyes closed. She wore small gold earrings. Underwater, they looked like enormous coins.

I had a weakness for the beginners. The fast swimmers broke the light into scraps, but a hesitant foot entering the water could carry a whole window down with it. Between classes I sometimes gave myself hands and caught those wavering rectangles on my palms. My hands stayed clear; blue tiles showed through the knuckles. A passing swimmer would have seen the outline, so at the first approach I let it go.

I was only my own small quantity of water. The rest of the pool was cool against me, or warm where the sun had lain, and a vigorous kick could send me tumbling. I could move myself out of its way. I could do nothing about the children who jumped in too close to each other, though I worried, and had come to appreciate a well-used whistle. Voices blurred below the surface; I had to rise to make out what people were saying.

There were many pleasures besides the light. The little thunder of running feet. A dropped locker key revolving slowly toward the floor. Winter mornings when steam rose off the swimmers and the glass roof held a white square of sky. While I remained water I needed neither food nor breath; I slept in the quiet corner beyond the ladder and woke to the first splash. Seven years passed with an ease I would once have thought indecent.

I had been a queen for nineteen years before that. I had enjoyed the first few, including the clothes, and I still remembered a particular velvet coat with longing. Later I used to imagine a day without being looked at. I tried to resign twice. Both times my advisers persuaded me to wait until after some anniversary or visit, and both times I consented. Finally I left the seal and a letter on my desk and went abroad with a bathing costume under my dress.

My cousin was crowned that autumn. I watched some of it through the glass of the pool's empty lobby, where a television had been left on. He looked comfortable. Afterward I went back into the water.

On the morning the new lifeguard found me, the building had not yet opened. Sunlight had reached the deep end. I made myself flesh and floated face up, enjoying its warmth on my eyelids. Flesh was particularly good at warmth. I had begun to sneeze when I heard a shoe squeak on the gallery above.

I dissolved, and the uncompleted sneeze went with my nose. Footsteps crossed the gallery, descended the stairs, came along the tiles. By then I lay at the surface beside the ladder.

The new lifeguard knelt at the edge of the deep end.

“Your Majesty,” he whispered.

For a while I waited for him to address someone else. His shadow lay across me. One of his shoelaces trailed in the water, and I disliked it with the old, immediate irritation I had felt at a crooked line of soldiers.

“I saw you from upstairs,” he said. “Just now. I'm sorry. I didn't know what to do.”

I drew myself together and raised my head, making it flesh above the surface.

“Who are you?”

He sat back hard on his heels. I knew his face then, though its new angles took a moment to fit over the boy I remembered.

“Hewlin. I carried the music for your lessons.”

“You were seventeen.”

“Yes.”

“And now you're a lifeguard.”

He glanced down at his red shirt. “I was doing it at the coast. This is my first day here.” He looked at my face again, much more intently than anyone had been allowed to look at it when he was seventeen. “Are you all right?”

“Very well.”

“You've been here?”

“Seven years.”

He put a hand over his mouth. I could not tell whether he was about to laugh or be sick. Then he lowered it and said, “We thought you must have died somewhere.”

“I left a letter.”

“We heard about the letter. Then nothing. All this time.”

Water lapped against the flesh of my chin. I could have let that go too. Instead I waited, and he rubbed his face with both hands.

“There's a memorial on Sunday,” he said. “At home, I mean. But we're having one here as well. Some of us. I said I'd go.”

I pictured the cathedral, its tremendous lilies and unmerciful benches. I had attended fourteen memorials there, in shoes chosen by somebody who never stood through a service.

“For me?”

“Yes.”

A door swung open at the shallow end. Hewlin stood. The woman in the yellow cap came out of the changing room, pulling at the strap of a sandal, and my face softened into the water before she could look our way.

“Will you be here later?” he asked, scarcely moving his lips.

I had no mouth to answer with. After a moment he went to his chair.

All morning the old address kept returning, in his voice. I had liked the way he used to carry my music: flat on both palms, as solemnly as a cake. Once, when rain ruined a garden concert, he had helped me take apart the sandwiches and feed the bread to the wet peacocks. There had been good afternoons. I had not needed to forget them to be happy here.

That evening I waited until the last swimmer had left, then came up beside the ladder. Hewlin was on a bench putting on his socks. At the sight of me he tried to stand with a sock hanging from his toes and had to catch the bench.

“Please stay where you are,” I said.

“Right.” He sat. “I've got something.”

He took a folded sheet from his bag. I climbed out, becoming solid enough to bear my weight. My black bathing costume returned with my skin. I sat a little distance away; after a day without joints, bending my knees felt unnecessarily elaborate.

The paper was a program for the local gathering. Beneath the name Queen Madelon and my dates was a picture from my coronation, with the cheeks narrowed and the crown enlarged. I had asked for neither improvement. The younger woman in the picture looked as if she could comfortably sleep in pearls.

“They've left a question mark for the second date,” I said.

“Nobody knows. Well. Nobody did.”

Inside were a reading, reminiscences, refreshments, and three songs. The account of my life occupied less space than the refreshments notice.

“A gifted musician.” I looked up. “That's generous.”

“You practised a lot.”

“You had to listen.”

“Mostly I waited outside.”

I remembered him standing by the lesson-room door with the folder against his stomach. I had always assumed the music reached him. Perhaps he had been thinking about his lunch.

“Do you remember the song about the miller's wife?” I asked. “My teacher wouldn't let me learn the last verse.”

“I don't think so.”

“She hides her lover in a flour sack.”

“Oh. My dad sings that. He knows about nine verses.”

“Nine?”

“Depending how late it is.” He smoothed the folded edge of the program. “Did you always mean to stay away?”

I read the line about my devotion to music again. “I meant to have a fortnight to myself. Without anyone coming to fetch me. Then I thought I'd stay until winter.”

“Your letter said you wouldn't return.”

“It was easier to write that than to arrange a fortnight.”

He made no reply. I ran my thumb over the paper, where a drop had blurred part of the border. Each year, as winter came, I had looked forward to seeing snow through the roof. That had been enough to keep me for another season. Said aloud, it would have sounded like a poor excuse for something I had loved.

“Who is organizing this?” I asked.

“A woman my aunt knows. She does most of the things for people from home. The spring supper, the children's dancing. She asked me because I worked at the palace.”

“Will you have to speak?”

“I said no.”

I turned to the back of the sheet. There was no mention of him. “You could tell them about the peacocks.”

“I don't want to speak.”

This time I looked at him. His wet hair had dried into a ridge on one side. He had a cheap watch with a handsome face, and a pale mark where a ring had been. I had been asking him questions as though he were still standing outside a door, waiting for me to finish.

“Have you lived here long?”

“Nearly three years.”

“Do you like it?”

“Yes. I liked the coast better, but the work's seasonal.” He pulled on his other sock. “My aunt's here. And I used to live with someone. We still see each other sometimes.”

I wanted to ask whether that pleased or hurt him. He was putting his shoes on, however, and I folded the program along its old crease.

“May I hold on to this?” I asked, lifting the program.

“Of course.”

“Where can I put it so it stays dry?”

He considered, then pointed to the spectators' gallery. “Under a seat? Nobody goes up there except on Saturdays.”

I spent two evenings in the gallery reading about myself, then slid the paper back under the seat before returning to the pool. The short account had made my reign sound uneventful, which pleased me, although I wished it had mentioned the theatre. I had worked for years to persuade people that performances might begin before nine. On the third evening, I took the paper downstairs to find Hewlin.

He was waiting on the bench. Beside him was a paper bag.

“My aunt made these,” he said. “You used to have them after your lesson.”

Inside were three little pastries folded around plum jam. I ate one standing up, scattering crumbs down my front. The jam had baked to a chewy dark edge, the best part. My mouth filled with saliva so suddenly that it hurt.

Hewlin watched me eat. “I asked her for the song as well. She only knew four verses.”

“Is it one of these three?” I held up the program. “They've only printed the first lines.”

He looked. “The second one. They've put down the proper title.”

I knew the title. I had known it all along. I simply wanted to keep talking about the evening, close enough to the question that he might ask it for me.

“I'd like to go,” I said at last. “To the memorial.”

He brushed a pastry flake off the bench. “With me?”

“If you don't mind.”

“No. I'd like that.” He started to smile, then looked at the coronation portrait. “People might know you.”

“You did.”

“I saw you most days for two years.”

I studied my younger face. “I don't look much like her.”

“No,” he said, and then, “Sorry.”

“I shall need some clothes.”

He laughed then, briefly and with relief, and asked what size I took. I had never known.

On Sunday he brought a loose dress and a cardigan borrowed from his aunt, and sandals whose straps I could adjust. He had told her that a friend needed them. I went into a cubicle with a bundle in my arms, like any swimmer, and came out with my bathing costume in his bag.

We walked to the hall. I was used to making myself flesh for a few minutes at a time, and at first the pavement seemed to rise too sharply to meet my feet. Hewlin shortened his stride. He offered his arm once, and I took it, then kept it when my legs remembered what to do. Beside the ordinary movement of our walking, I could feel his pulse through his sleeve.

The hall was above a shop that sold beds. A young man was carrying a mattress through the delivery door as we arrived. He asked us to wait, said thanks when we did, and went on struggling with it. Upstairs, someone had set out thirty chairs. Sixteen people came, counting us, and an infant slept through the whole observance in a basket on the table intended for flowers.

I had expected more. I was ashamed of expecting more. Then I was annoyed because my chair rocked whenever I shifted my weight, and for several minutes I thought chiefly about that.

The organizer welcomed Hewlin and gave me a program. “You're from home too?”

“Yes. I've been away a long time.”

“Well, sit anywhere. There's tea already, if you'd rather not wait.”

Her cardigan was held closed with a brooch shaped like a pair of cherries. When everyone had settled, she stood by the flowers and read the official account. She had trouble with the name of my first school. I thought of the schoolroom's apple trees, and of sitting on a low branch with my dress pulled over my bare knees. The account moved on to my marriage and my husband's death. Two lines for the thirteen years in which I had known the sound of him blowing his nose in the next room.

I gripped the program until it curved around my fingers. Hewlin sat quietly beside me. He had been a child when my husband died; he had no memory to lend me.

After the reading, a man at the front got up without waiting to be asked.

“I never met her,” he said. “My sister did. At the exhibition. She entered a cake. Didn't win anything, but the queen stopped and asked her about it. She always remembered that.”

He remained standing, looking toward the organizer, who nodded with an encouraging smile.

“It was a fruit cake,” he added, then sat down.

I could not remember the cake or his sister. I remembered, with great clarity, the pain behind my right eye on those exhibition afternoons, when the lights stayed on though the roof was glass. Perhaps I had asked her about it because I was interested. I hoped I had.

A woman with a knitted bag across her knees said she had gone out to see my coronation procession. She had been six, lifted onto her father's shoulders. All she'd seen of me was a glove.

“White,” she said. “It had buttons all the way up. I wanted gloves like that for years.”

I moved my bare hand beneath the program. I had loved those gloves too. My seamstress had sewn one cuff too tightly, and after the procession we had cut it off me, laughing because I was married to a kingdom and defeated by a sleeve.

The woman beside her leaned forward. “I thought she was badly advised. When they closed the little theatre, she should have said something. They said she supported it.”

“The theatre reopened,” someone said.

“As a cinema.”

I drew breath to explain that I had spoken about the closure, twice, privately, to a minister who had agreed with every word and done nothing. Then the woman began describing the Christmas play she had taken her children to, and I listened. She remembered the paper snow and a donkey that would not go offstage. I remembered the minister's carpet. Explaining would not have given her another play.
