A child in contact with the Entity could find the sleep of someone they knew. They could take no piece of its mind safely; whatever they carried had to be remade from their own thoughts.

The boy's brother had returned a rude drawing. The Entity still remembered the boy's laughter as he reproduced it.

It had asked many children since then. Did they know Garnet? A girl of thirteen, with a gap where a tooth had never come? It had given them a description of someone who no longer existed in that form.

“How do I go?” Cleo asked.

“Think of finding her.”

Cleo put a finger into one nostril and considered. Beside the house, a landing appeared, with an umbrella dripping on its tiles. There was a brown door with a lock higher than Cleo could reach.

“That's the old lock,” she said. “She doesn't use it.”

The Entity could feel Cleo's remembering, but nothing beyond the door. When she stepped through, the child would be in a part of sleep it could not enter. If she woke, the route would vanish.

“Tell her I kept the house she turned inside out,” it said.

Cleo knocked, waited, and went in.

The landing remained. The door shut. The Entity could no longer feel her attention on it.

Stone bore down between its folds. A thread of mineral water cooled along its underside. It examined the closed door, though there was no lock on this side to examine, no wood it could press against with its living body. It was waiting inside Cleo's dream, in a house she had not wanted, beside a whale she had.

When she came back she was wearing enormous bedroom slippers.

“She says what's in the cupboard?”

“The sea.”

“Oh. I said towels. She was cleaning a bathroom, so I thought she meant that sort of cupboard.”

The Entity opened the cupboard. A little tide ran across the floorboards and retreated, carrying a strand of weed.

Cleo crouched beside it. “Can we go in?”

“Tell her it's the sea. She made it salt. Ask why she never came back.”

Cleo looked from the water to the door. “Then can we go in?”

“Yes.”

She left one slipper beside the cupboard. For a while the Entity watched water darken the cloth toe. It wanted to send the smell of salt after her, and the exact sound of Garnet's laugh when she first stepped out of the hat. But those were its memories. They would reach Garnet with its weight behind them. It held them back.

Cleo returned without the other slipper.

“She says she did come back. She tried for ages, but you wouldn't open up.” She sat on the floor and dipped her feet into the sea. “Did you not like her anymore?”

The Entity began to show her.

It gave her Garnet's mind narrowing beyond its reach; the nights of approaching, drawing away, approaching again; the houses held ready afterward. They crowded around Cleo, small at first, then packed so closely that the whale became all roofs and chimneys. The same unentered room appeared in every window. Beneath it lay the waiting, as much a part of the Entity as the body inside the stone.

Cleo stood. The sea ran off her feet.

“I can't tell her all that.”

There were more houses. The Entity had not understood until now how many nights she thought it had turned her away.

“Stop. I don't know what you want me to say.”

It stopped. The houses hung around her. Between two roofs the whale's tongue lay creased like an abandoned carpet.

“Make them go away.”

It took the extra houses away.

Cleo sat again, this time on the dry side of the cupboard. “She said other things. I forgot because you did that.”

The Entity waited while she picked a thread from the slipper's toe.

“She drove buses,” Cleo said at last. “For years and years. She said to tell you about the bit where you turn around. At the end of the road. There was a house there that she always thought you'd like. I don't know why. She didn't say.”

Buses. Garnet had once made a bus whose top floor belonged to a different bus. The Entity had kept that, too. But somewhere she had held an actual wheel, stopped beside actual houses, and thought about showing one to it.

“What else?”

“I can't remember.” Cleo pulled the thread until it snapped. “I don't want to keep going backward and forward.”

It wanted to ask about every day Garnet had lived. It wanted the house at the turning place. It wanted to know if she still preferred eggs with handles. The questions arrived together, as its thoughts always did; choosing one felt like letting the others sink out of reach.

“Tell her I stopped because I was hurting her.”

Cleo looked at the places where the houses had been.

“Like that?”

“Worse. She couldn't make it into houses anymore.”

“Will it do that to me?”

“It could, when you're older. I'll have to leave your sleep alone.”

Cleo was quiet. Then she said, “I'm going home tomorrow anyway.”

“Yes.”

She tried to put the wet slipper on. Its heel folded under her foot, and she kicked it into the cupboard.

“What do you want her to do?”

The Entity turned toward the room it had kept ready for sixty years. Garnet had been trying to turn its floor into something she could swim through. It remembered her standing ankle-deep in blue tiles, furious that the rest would not change.

It could send Cleo with instructions for finishing that move. It could ask whether Garnet remembered. But it wanted something it had never seen before: Garnet at the wheel of her bus, looking out at a house that might have pleased it.

“Ask her to make me a new house.”

“Then we're doing the whale.”

“Yes.”

“And I'm allowed in the cupboard.”

The Entity tipped it gently onto its back. The sea rose to fill the opening, with room for Cleo to sit on the edge and dangle both legs when she returned. She inspected it, then went to the brown door.

It took her longer this time. Once, the remembered landing flickered. The Entity drew itself away from the edges of Cleo's mind, afraid that its eagerness had become pressure again. The quarry, the cottages, the sleeping child's small body remained where they were. The landing steadied.

Cleo returned carrying a toy bus she was still putting together.

“She made this. It's the one she used to drive, except I couldn't remember all the seats. She says put yourself in it.”

The bus had a silver bell. Cleo rang it three times before setting it down. As it grew, the Entity recognized the kind of vehicle children had shown it in their dreams. This one had a tear in the driver's seat and a red cloth tied around the steering column.

“What did she say when you told her why I stopped?”

Cleo laid her hand on the bell but did not ring it.

“She didn't say anything for a bit. Then she asked if I was all right. I said I was. Then she started making the bus.” Cleo pressed the bell once. “She told me about the egg, too. You made a handle so she could drink it.”

“Lift it. I thought it would be hot.”

“Well, she drank it.”

The Entity let that stand. Inside the bus, the driver's seat warmed beneath its attention. It had no single shape to put there. It made a weight in the cushion, a place from which it might look out.

Around the bus Cleo built a room. Its ceiling rested on the roof, and the walls touched the windows. When she was finished, no door remained in either bus or room.

“You're in a garage,” she said. “She says you've got to get the bus out. One change.”

The Entity considered turning the garage inside out. Garnet would expect that. It tried instead to imagine her driving a room.

It put wheels under the garage.

Cleo laughed as the whole room rolled down the whale's tongue and out between its teeth. The bus went along inside it, and the walls stayed pressed to the windows.

“But it's still in there.”

“Tell her I took the garage.”

“She'll say you haven't got out.”

“Tell her anyway.”

Cleo ran to the landing. The Entity waited in the driver's seat, holding the room still. Through the windscreen it could see only plaster, close enough to touch. Yet it found itself arranging the weight in the cushion, trying a little to one side and then the other, as though Garnet might notice how it sat.

When Cleo returned, she was leading the whale. She folded one wall of the garage down, then climbed onto its head. It pressed its enormous face against the bus window, which softened and let the face through.

“She says you can take the garage, but you have to take the passengers.”

“Is the whale hers?”

“Mine. She said I could.”

The whale was wedged from cheek to cheek in the bus. There was no space to enlarge the seat without enlarging the garage as well. The Entity began to measure what would fit, then heard Cleo say that Garnet was waiting for its next move.

It changed the passenger seats into a sea.

The whale slid in. Its tail hit the bell, and Cleo whooped as cold water closed over the windows. The Entity held its place at the wheel. Beyond the plaster there would have to be a road; it asked Cleo to find out which way Garnet wanted to go.

stories.title: The Lights Beyond
stories.prompt: 500 years ago the horde was defeated and pushed beyond the Great Wall. You are the first human scouts to explore beyond the wall since the war. You see a city covered in lights and metal birds soaring through the night sky.
stories.body:
# The Lights Beyond

The northern gate caught on its own threshold. Dunley put his shoulder to it, and Haskett slipped through sideways with the brass edge scraping her pack. Behind them the victory bells began.

Five hundred years ago, the horde had been defeated and driven through this pass. Since then, human scouts had watched from the Great Wall and gone no farther. Haskett and her brother were the first to step out into the north. The anniversary commission, which had taken three councils and most of the summer to approve, allowed them six days.

“Noon on the sixth,” she reminded him.

“I heard the captain.”

“You were looking at his boots.”

“He had yours on.”

Haskett had put in three requests for new boots. She looked down at the twine binding the toe of her left one, then up at the gatehouse window. The captain was still there. Dunley waved at him with terrible friendliness.

The gate shut. They stood on an old military road, between saplings rooted in its paving. Haskett waited until she could hear something besides bells: water under stones, a bird, the small creak of Dunley's shoulder strap.

He reached across and tightened hers. “There. It'll stop knocking.”

They had been scouting together for eleven years, mostly along the southern slopes, where smugglers and lost sheep supplied the work. Haskett could walk all day without turning to see whether he followed. Next winter they meant to leave the service and buy an inn with a leaning stable and a pear tree growing through the back fence. Six hundred crowns lay in their barracks strongbox, three hundred apiece. Forty more would meet the asking price.

“I thought of a name,” Dunley said as they started climbing.

“For the inn?”

“The Captain's Boots.”

“You can paint the sign.”

She laughed, and the road bent enough to hide the Wall.

It crossed the first ridge by noon. Beyond lay another ridge, higher, with a blue seam of snow in its shade. The road descended into alder scrub, lost a bridge, and resumed on the opposite bank. They camped under a fallen slab and ate cold barley. Human law had kept this road shut for five centuries; scree and winter had done the rest. Along the Wall's flanks the mountains rose into glaciers. Even their oldest maps showed no other pass.

They spent the second day finding a way through the saddle above the vanished bridge. Near dusk the wind changed. Salt reached Haskett first, so unexpected that she stopped and licked her upper lip. Then came a sound too steady for thunder.

She caught Dunley's wrist. Together they crouched below the crest.

The coast lay on the other side.

A city filled the basin between the mountain and the sea, and it was covered in lights. They ran along streets, climbed buildings, outlined a bridge in two bright sweeps. Whole faces of tall houses shone. Beyond them a hundred white streaks trembled on the harbor water. Haskett searched for the smoke such burning must make. There was some above the eastern roofs, but nowhere near enough.

Something crossed the moon.

It had rigid wings, a thin body, a red light beneath one wingtip. As it banked toward the sea, the city flashed silver across its underside. Metal. Another followed, lower, with a row of little windows. The noise came after it: a deep, working drone that pressed against her ribs through the rock.

Dunley had his hand on her sleeve. She had never known his fingers so still.

The second bird passed over the water. It settled, throwing two long fans of spray, and its windows drifted toward a line of piers.

“There are people in it,” he said.

She had seen a pale shape at a window. A face, perhaps. She wanted it to come back so she could be certain.

He took out their map. The northern sheet showed an army's encampments, wells, and a river that their descent had proved misplaced. Beyond the last ridge someone had drawn three waves for the sea. The city would not fit between them.

Haskett watched a light move across the harbor bridge. Many lights. They flowed in opposite directions without colliding, halted together, moved again. Farther inland, a square went dark, then bright with a green brilliance that stained the low cloud. She could make out no fire there at all.

“We need to see it from lower down,” she said.

Dunley put the map away so quickly he tore it on a buckle.

The path into the basin became a lane between orchards, then a smooth black road still warm from the day. Wires hung above it on poles. A wheeled box came humming toward them without horses, windows lit, somebody standing inside with one hand raised to the ceiling. Haskett dragged Dunley off the verge. It passed smelling of hot metal.

He rose from the ditch with grass on his chin. “I was moving.”

“Move sooner.”

After that they watched from behind a wall until they understood which side the boxes used.

At the first houses, a woman was shaking a cloth out of an upper window. Her face was broad, the lower jaw thrust forward. Two pale tusks caught the light. Haskett knew the shape from the carved enemy beneath the victory arch, though the carving had no hanging washing and no little child trying to squeeze past it to look out.

The woman saw them. Her hands stopped. She called into the room, and another face appeared beside hers.

Haskett loosened the strap that held her bow against her pack. Then she let it lie. There were people at the next corner, people behind her, people stepping from a lit doorway. If this became a fight, she would have chosen its place very badly.

A man carrying two loaves gave them a wide berth. An older woman stared directly at Dunley's mouth. He pressed his lips together, which made her lean closer. Somewhere a child laughed. They continued toward the waterfront with their hands hanging empty.

Light poured through shop glass onto their muddy knees. In one window, six small suns burned inside transparent globes; Haskett could get close enough to see there was no wick. Beside them stood a chair with one broken leg and a notice in writing she could not read. She found herself looking from the light to the chair, wanting to know what a person who could make one would do about the other.

At a crossing, a bell rang overhead. The crowd waited. Dunley waited too, watching a little red figure on a pole, and when it turned white everyone moved. On the far side he looked back at her with an expression she knew from difficult fords: pleased to have understood the footing.

Then something wonderful was wasted on a dog. A shopkeeper set a little caged wheel in his doorway and pressed a white disk on its base. The blades blurred, lifting the dog's ears in a draft. It got up and lay in the rainwater gutter instead. Dunley laughed aloud. The shopkeeper glanced at him, followed his gaze, and gave the animal a weary little shove with his shoe.

They reached the water by following the sound of another landing.

The bird came in low over their heads. Haskett flinched at its size, but it was smaller than the one they had seen from the ridge: a shining hull beneath high wings, with an engine and whirling blades above the roof. It struck the harbor, skipped, and drew a crease through the reflected windows. As it approached a floating dock the blades slowed into sight.

A man climbed out at the front and caught a rope tossed from shore. Two passengers emerged behind him, a young couple in good coats. The woman had to sit on the dock for a moment. Her companion crouched beside her, laughing, until she pushed his face away and laughed herself.

Dunley went all the way to the dock's gate.

There was a board there with a painted view of the harbor. A little winged hull followed an arrow around an island and back to the same pier. Below it, two seats had been set beneath an awning, beside the moored aircraft. Haskett had seen carriage owners arrange seats like that outside an inn. Waiting customers could occupy them while the carriage was away.

The pilot approached, saying something and holding up two fingers. He wore an oil-marked jacket. A silver cap covered the end of one tusk.

Then he saw their faces properly. His fingers folded. He stepped back through the gate and pulled it halfway shut, looking from Dunley's mouth to Haskett's bow.

She took the bow off slowly, gripping its middle, and set it on the paving. Dunley did the same. The pilot pointed at their belts. They unbuckled those too, laying the sheathed knives beside the bows, then moved back three paces.

The pilot said something over his shoulder. The couple stopped on their way up the dock and looked. The young man put a hand across his companion's arm; she moved it away so that she could see better. Neither approached.

Dunley lifted one hand, palm out. “We don't understand you.”

The pilot stared a little longer. Then he came out of the gate. He touched his own chest, carefully clear of his jacket pockets.

“Pirvek.”

They gave their names. He made Haskett repeat hers, trying the middle sound twice before abandoning it. When Dunley pointed at the painted city, Pirvek said, “Roskell,” and turned to indicate the buildings rising behind them. Haskett repeated it. The word brought no answer out of anything she had been taught.

Pirvek pointed south, over the black ridges. Haskett nodded. She drew the Wall in the dust with a finger: towers, gate, two tiny figures coming through. He crouched to look. His fingertip stopped beside the figures; then he looked up at the two of them, and for a while nobody tried to explain anything more.

Finally Dunley pointed at the aircraft.

Pirvek stood, glanced at the waiting couple, and said something that made the young woman laugh again. He opened the gate. With a pointed look at their weapons on the ground, he beckoned them only as far as the awning.

Up close, the bird had scratches. A plate near its tail had been replaced with duller metal, and a dark streak ran from under the engine. Dunley bent toward a joint in the wing. Pirvek caught his wrist before he touched a thin projecting tube, then demonstrated with an outstretched hand where he could put his weight.

“He thinks I'm going to break it,” Dunley said.

“You nearly broke your map.”

Pirvek opened a side hatch. There were two seats abreast behind his own, with belts across the cushions. He showed how a buckle closed, pulled hard on the strap, and opened it again. When Dunley reached for the buckle himself, Pirvek let him try. Dunley got it wrong. The pilot waited while he worked it out.

Only then did Pirvek point from them to the seats. He traced the arrow on the board: dock, island, dock. Two fingers again, followed by an extended palm.

Haskett produced a crown from the four she carried for traveling expenses. The six hundred for the inn were far away and safe. Pirvek turned the silver coin over, rubbed his thumb across the stamped tower, and set it on the board's narrow ledge. He tapped it and held up two fingers again.

“Two,” she said. She put a second crown beside the first.

He nodded and left both on the board's narrow ledge. Then he pointed at the bows and knives, unlocked a long cupboard beneath the awning, and opened it for her inspection. Empty except for rope. He held up its key.

Dunley was already looking back toward the hatch.

“We have enough to report,” Haskett told him.

“We've barely been here an hour.”

“We saw the whole city from the ridge.”

He gave her a look so openly disbelieving that she wanted to take the words back. She hadn't seen the dog from the ridge. She hadn't seen anything properly.

“We don't know what happens once we're in there,” she said.

“I know.”

“He shuts the door. He takes us wherever he pleases.”

Dunley looked at Pirvek, who had begun checking the rope that held the craft to the dock. “Yes.”

“Then why are you standing there waiting for me to say it's sensible?”

“I'm waiting for you to decide if you want to come.”

She heard the difference. So he would go by himself. Pirvek might refuse a single passenger; she caught herself hoping he would.

A larger aircraft rumbled above the harbor mouth. Dunley followed it until it disappeared behind a warehouse. Haskett had seen him watch distant roads like that, but always with a destination in common.

“You're still coming home,” she said.

“Of course I am. We said the sixth day.”

“I mean afterward.”

He looked down at the two crowns on the ledge. “Don't give the innkeeper a deposit.”

There it was, in a form that she could do nothing with except hear it.

“You chose that place,” she said.

“I know.”

“You measured the kitchen. You said we'd get two tables in if we moved the stove.”

“I wanted it.”

“This morning you wanted it.”

“This morning I hadn't seen any of this.”

Pirvek came back and held up the belts again. Haskett shook her head, not at him, and he shut the hatch. Dunley started forward. The pilot pointed toward the coins, leaving them where they were, and stood back with folded arms.

“You don't know whether they'd let you live here,” Haskett said quietly. “You can't ask for a bed.”

“I don't know if I want to live here. I want to find out how that thing works. I want to see where the big ones go.” He rubbed his forehead. “I can't spend my three hundred yet.”

She looked past him to the city. The green light they had seen from above was a great glass sign on a roof, going through its colors even though scarcely anyone on the street looked up. It could be doing anything. Advertising fish. Giving orders. Announcing the hour. She had crossed two mountains to stand beneath it and remained unable to tell.

“The inn may be sold.”

“Yes.”

She could have borne another joke more easily.

Pirvek took one coin from the ledge and held it out. He pointed at Haskett, then the shore; at Dunley, then the aircraft. Even he had understood that much.

Haskett left the coin in his hand. She walked back to fetch her weapons.

Dunley made no attempt to follow. That hurt too, although she could hardly have wanted him to chase her across the paving. She picked up both bows, gathered the belts, and returned to the cupboard.

When she had put everything inside, she held out her hand for the key.

Pirvek gave it to her. She tucked it beneath her shirt, tapped the crown he held, and pointed at the second seat. He put both coins in his pocket and opened the hatch.

“I want the side with the city,” she told Dunley.

He looked toward the painted circuit to work it out. She was glad he took the trouble.

Pirvek put them in the rear seats, Haskett on the left, Dunley on the right, and checked the belts himself. He pressed Dunley's pack beneath the seat until it stayed, then did the same with hers. His own seat was in front of them, beyond a low partition full of little round dials. He pointed out a handle above their hatch, making them each touch it before he closed the door. Through the window Haskett watched him cast off, push the hull away from the dock, and climb through his forward hatch.

The engine started with a cough that shook the teeth in Haskett's head.

Pirvek pulled his belt tight. Light appeared inside the dials. He moved a lever, and the dock began to slide backward past her window. Water slapped the hull with a familiar, reassuring sound. For fifty paces they were only in an unusually noisy boat.

Then Pirvek opened the engine.

The noise became too much to hear through. Haskett felt it in the soles of her feet, in her jaw, in the fastening across her belly. Spray burst against the window. They struck the water again and again, each blow harder as they gathered speed. The island ahead had rocks along its edge. She had seen those rocks on the board, and now they were coming much too fast.

Beside her, Dunley gripped the front of his seat. His mouth was open. Had he thought they would float gently away?

The next blow did not come.

Water dropped beneath the window. She saw their pale wake continuing by itself, two trails unraveling into the black harbor, while the roofs along the shore sank down and showed her their chimneys. A gull flung itself sideways below them. The wing held steady over her head, impossibly thin to be doing so much.

She put both palms against the glass.

They climbed past the warehouse that had hidden the larger craft. Beyond it lay another dock, four more winged boats, men moving crates beneath lamps. Farther along the coast, a chain of lights curved north until the land ended in darkness. Behind the city the mountains rose much higher than they flew. She could no longer pick out the saddle they had crossed.

Pirvek turned, saw her at the window, and grinned around his tusks. Then he faced forward and brought them round the island.

Roskell tilted. Streets stood almost upright beyond the wing, their intersections bright as open furnaces; there was the bridge, and the green sign, and a rectangle of grass where figures ran beneath tall white lamps after something too small to see. At the edge of that dazzling field, a row of houses had dark gardens. Somebody there had gone to bed while this was possible above them.

She tried to find the dog. The notion was so absurd that she began to laugh, and found she had been crying a little, without noticing when she started.

Dunley touched her arm. He pointed through his own window at a second aircraft passing farther out to sea. Its lit windows floated level with them. Haskett could see people, certainly people this time, seated inside. One raised an arm. She waved back with her whole hand, although the stranger might have been reaching for a bag.

The turn brought the city straight ahead. Pirvek eased the lever and lowered their nose. Haskett wanted him to wait. They had paid two crowns; she would have given him the other two for another circuit, if only he could have heard her.

The harbor spread wider beneath them. She understood the landing only when the first slap of water came up through her seat. Then there were three more, a rush of spray, and they were a boat again, settling heavily into each small wave.

At the dock she had difficulty standing. Dunley climbed out and sat down exactly where the young woman had sat. He tried to speak, but his throat produced only a rasp. Haskett joined him, their feet hanging above the water, while Pirvek made fast the ropes.

When he came to let them out, she gave him back the cupboard key. He fetched their weapons, careful to offer the knives hilt first. Dunley bowed. Pirvek bowed too, uncertainly, and on straightening knocked the silver tip of his tusk against Dunley's forehead. They both recoiled. Haskett laughed so hard she had to hold the gatepost.

Pirvek laughed too, rubbing the silver cap, and raised a hand as they started back through the city.

They slept above the orchards and left at sunrise. On the return journey, they measured the road more carefully and marked where its broken bridges could be forded. Dunley found a way around the worst scree. Haskett sketched the harbor circuit in the margin of their map, then tried again on the back, giving it more room.

They reached the Wall on the fifth morning. In the barracks, before either had washed, she opened their strongbox and divided the savings into two bags. Dunley watched from his bunk.

“I'm keeping mine here for now,” he said.

She set his bag back inside. “Keep your own key.”

The captain sent for them while she was still undoing the twine around her boot. He had unrolled a fresh map across his table and left a large blank space above the Wall.

Haskett began with the road. She described the ridges, the salt wind, the lights. When she reached the flying boats, the captain put down his pen.

“You saw them leave the water?”

“We were inside one,” she said.

He looked at Dunley, who nodded. Haskett tried to explain the speed and the blows against the hull, but Dunley interrupted because she had left out the moment when they stopped.

“I was getting to that.”

She pulled her chair beside her brother's so that the captain could see how they had sat, and they tried again.

stories.body:
# Sakura-Hearted

A small ringed planet was in the coat cupboard, occupying the hook I used for my jacket.

I stood in our doorway with the anniversary flowers. The planet turned slowly, its cardboard rings almost brushing my chin. Beyond it, somebody had draped a sheet across the entrance to the sitting room.

“Celestine?”

“Just a moment, darling.”

Her voice came from behind the sheet. There was a click, followed by a noise like a teaspoon striking a cup, and then my wife appeared with something pink in her hand.

She took one look at the cupboard. “Oh. That's where you went.”

The thing in her hand was a raygun, sakura pink, with a little silver muzzle and a dial beneath her thumb. It rested easily in one white-gloved hand. She aimed at a disc underneath the planet; a thread of pink light connected them, and the planet backed out of my way. With a small, careful turn of her wrist she guided it along the ceiling toward the kitchen.

“That's new,” I said.

“Yes.” She let go of the trigger. The planet stayed overhead. “Hello.”

She came close enough to kiss me, then stayed there for a second kiss while I tried to put my free arm around her without crushing the flowers. She smelled faintly of the orange soap we kept by the workshop sink.

“You're early,” she said against my cheek.

“I left early.”

“For me?”

“Entirely for you. I nearly left these on the tram in the hurry.”

I held out the flowers. She brought them to her face, paper crackling against the white circle of her belt buckle. For a moment all I could see above them was her brown hair pinned up behind a white headband. Then she lowered them, smiling.

“I love that you always choose the untidy ones.”

“They looked cheerful.”

“They are.” She passed me the raygun so she could loosen the paper. “Will you hang up your coat? Dinner can wait, but I can't.”

I hung up my coat. I also looked at her. She wore a pink dress with a white front panel and a high collar, shaped like the clothes in old advertisements for holidays on the moon. Her white opera gloves reached her elbows; the broad white cinch belt drew in the dress, and below its short hem her white go-go boots rose to her knees. She had several dresses in that hopeful old style. This one was new, with a little circular opening at the throat that made me want to put my mouth there.

She caught me looking and ran a gloved finger down the front of the skirt.

“I finished it yesterday.”

“The whole thing?”

“The dress. The boots I bought.”

I leaned in to kiss her just above the collar. She tilted her head to make room.

“Happy anniversary,” I said.

“Happy anniversary, sweetheart.”

Behind her, the planet gently bumped the kitchen doorframe.

She took back the raygun, tipped the planet to clear the doorway, and lowered it onto the kitchen counter.

“I tested that path without the rings,” she said. She glanced back at me. “You'd think I'd remember. I only put them on this afternoon.”

She laid the flowers beside it and took my hand.

***

Celestine pulled the sheet aside. Beyond it stood the moon ride.

For a few seconds I had no words at all. The pointed nose, the cloudy bubble windscreen, the two red seats: I knew every one of them. A blue comet curled along its side, worn almost to silver beneath the boarding step. On the left seat, a repair ran diagonally across the upholstery. I had caught a trouser button on that seam ten years ago.

I put my hand on it.

“You found it.”

Celestine stood beside me with the folded sheet over her arm.

“The amusement hall sold its equipment. I saw a photograph in the listings.”

“But that was months ago.”

“Yes.”

I looked at her. She pressed her lips together, containing a smile, and nodded.

For months I had accepted that the closed-off end of her workshop contained a drying cabinet. We shared the apartment, and I knew the sounds of her work: the whir of a lathe, the little descending note she hummed while looking for a tool. Apparently I did not know the sounds of a moon ride being rebuilt in sections.

“You said there were trays drying in there.”

“There were. I put the small parts on trays.”

I laughed, and she leaned against my arm, pleased with herself.

The machine sat on a broad rubber mat between our round window and the bookcase. Its motor housing had been polished; a power lead ran neatly along the skirting board. Above it hung a pale paper moon and several smaller planets, each with a receiver disc tucked underneath. Our orange egg chair had moved into the far corner. The dining table was set for two, though I could barely see it past a green globe.

“Does it still do the voice?” I asked.

“Oh, yes.”

“And the terrible landing?”

“A gentler version. I replaced the worn cam.”

I crouched to look through a grille. Inside, everything was clean brass and neat wiring. As I stood, I noticed the chrome bands around her little raygun. Rings like those, no bigger than shirt buttons, had been scattered across her bench that morning.

I pointed to them. “Were these the rings on your bench?”

She followed my finger. “The gun? Yes. The old emitter wouldn't fit. It wasted most of its energy keeping the field steady, so I made it send a sequence of smaller pulses instead. The receivers smooth them out.”

She turned the pink body in her palm. A charge needle rested just short of full.

“How much can it lift?”

“Three kilos on one disc. Less if I want it moving for long. It reaches about as far as our kitchen.”

I put a hand on the ride's nose. “So this is beyond it.”

“Very much.” She tapped the motor housing with her boot. “We stay on the floor.”

I was thirty-eight, she was thirty-six, and it had been eight years since we had promised to grow old together. I had expected flowers, dinner, and a long evening with her feet in my lap. Instead I was looking for the coin slot on a machine I remembered being embarrassingly excited to board at twenty-eight.

Celestine lifted a saucer from the table. It held a heap of old square coins.

“I've been saving these too.”

***

Getting in required a preliminary discussion about whose knee went where.

The seats had been designed for two adults who were better at sitting upright than we were. I climbed in first and promptly discovered that the steering wheel left room for my legs only if I kept both feet together. Celestine stepped onto the running board, one gloved hand on my shoulder, and settled beside me. The skirt of her dress fanned across the red vinyl. I could feel the edge of her belt against my elbow.

“Comfortable?” she asked.

“Extremely.”

She looked down at my knees.

“Mostly,” I said.

She laid her hand over mine and squeezed it. Then she turned the raygun's dial to a little clock symbol.

“That lets the coin timer start the scenery,” she said. “Ready?”

I nodded, and she put a coin in the slot.

A bell rang. Somewhere under us a relay clacked, and the room lights dimmed. The nose rose a little; the ride began to turn slowly on its base. We were still a few inches above the rug, but the familiar forward tilt sent an absurd little thrill through my stomach.

“WELCOME, TRAVELLERS,” said the old recording. “THE MOON AWAITS!”

“Oh, that's him.”

“I thought you'd like to hear him again.”

“You've even kept the crackle.”

“I tried cleaning the sound. It didn't seem right.”

The receiver discs flashed, and the suspended models started along their programmed paths. A blue planet drifted across the window. Pinpoints of light shone through its painted shell onto her glove.

“You're going to miss something,” she said.

“What?”

“On your left.”

I turned too late. Whatever it was had passed behind my seat, and there was now a large green sphere where my view of the bookcase ought to have been.

“Was that the moon?”

“No. The moon comes last.”

“Last time I didn't see it either.”

“Last time you were trying to get your sleeve out of my drink.”

I remembered fizzy orange soaking into my cuff. I also remembered explaining that I never normally spilled things, while attempting to retrieve a straw from under her boot.

“You put the cup in the seat.”

“There wasn't a holder.”

“I'd offered to hold it.”

“You were holding the other one.” She began to laugh. “And trying to steer.”

“The wheel turned. I felt that implied a responsibility.”

Her laughter came in quiet breaths against my shoulder. The ride dipped and I put an arm around her, which was much easier now than it had been ten years earlier, even in the cramped seat. Back then I'd asked whether she was having a good time every few minutes. She had always said yes. I had needed at least six confirmations before beginning to believe her.

“PREPARE FOR THE WONDERS OF THE LUNAR SURFACE!”

She raised her head. “Oh, look, here it—”

The mechanism clicked off. The nose settled and the room lights brightened. A small moon coasted to a stop beside the window, showing us its plain back.

We sat still.

“How long was that?” I asked.

“Ninety seconds.”

“It can't have been.”

“It was ninety seconds then, too.”

I looked at the coin saucer on the table, well beyond my reach.

“May we go again?”

Her smile spread slowly. “As often as you like.”

***

We climbed out to fetch more coins and look at what we'd missed. Celestine used the raygun to turn the nearest globe. It was a small planet whose surface had been divided into eight irregular colored regions. Beside a silver lake stood a green tent, scarcely taller than my thumbnail.

I bent closer.

“The tent leaked on the other side.”

“I know. I put the good side facing out.”

There were two boots standing upside down on twigs outside it. Behind the tent, beneath an overhang of painted rock, was a tiny red enamel pan.

“You made the pan.”

“It took three tries to get the handle right.”

I wanted to touch it, but my fingertip was nearly as large as the whole campsite. She brought the planet lower and steadied it with her free hand so I could examine it.

On our second anniversary we'd gone camping in a valley advertised as sheltered. The wind had flattened the tent before we'd finished arguing amiably about which way its door should face. We had eaten hot peaches from that pan beneath a rock ledge while our socks dried on our knees. Celestine had fallen asleep with her head in my lap. I remembered being unwilling to move even when my foot went numb.

She had painted the lake the color it had been after the rain. That was what undid me: the green just beneath the silver.

I bent to kiss the top of her head. Then I kissed her temple, and she set the planet hovering so she could turn toward me.

“Good?” she asked softly.

“Yes. Very good.”

I held her for a while. The raygun rested cool against my back in her hand.

When I let her go, she straightened my collar, though I hadn't noticed anything wrong with it.

“There's one place for each year,” she said. “I couldn't fit the whole hotel on the yellow part, so it has just our balcony.”

“Our enormous balcony.”

“The chair is half over the edge.”

I found it. The chair had three blue legs and one bare silver one, exactly as I remembered. A towel hung from its back, folded into a miniature band of white.

I asked how she had done the towel. It was a sliver of fabric stiffened over a bent wire, she told me, and then she turned the globe toward the next region. I caught her hand. I wanted the long version: the first failed pan, the bad shade of green, the evenings she had sat beneath her work lamp thinking about a wet holiday I had loved.

She grew pink when I said so.

“I liked making it,” she told me. “Sometimes I had to stop because I wanted to come and tell you what I'd remembered.”

“You could have.”

“And spoil it?”

“Possibly worth it. You could have told me about the tent without mentioning the planet.”

“I did. You were brushing your teeth. You said you wanted peaches.”

“I did want peaches.”

“I bought some for tonight.”

She took my hand and led me around the nose of the ride to the kitchen. The ringed planet blocked the cupboard where we kept the glasses. She considered it, then put the raygun down and moved it by hand.

“There's a button for all of them to return to their stands,” she said. “But then you'd see the rest.”

“We could drink straight from the bottle.”

She glanced at me over her shoulder. “You may. I'd like a glass.”

We found two, poured something cold and sparkling, and stood close enough that I had to raise my elbow for her to open a drawer. She found a pair of scissors and trimmed the flowers. I filled their vase.

“May I put these in?” she asked.

“In the ride?”

“In the sky.”

She took a spare receiver disc from beside the sink and clipped it beneath the vase. When she squeezed the trigger, the vase rose from the counter, water trembling against the glass. The flowers followed her wrist across the room. She set their path above the little table beside the orange chair, well away from our turning seats.

“Will they stay up?”

“For twenty minutes. Then the disc will lower them. There needs to be something beneath it.”

She moved a book off the table to leave room for the vase.

My flowers hovered in the lamplight, untidier than ever. Beyond our round window, evening traffic slid between the towers, the airliners turning on their landing lights. I kept looking back at the tiny campsite.

Celestine watched me looking around.

“I was going to do it in order,” she admitted. “I had a list.”

“Have I muddled it?”

“A little.” She slipped her fingers into mine. “I like seeing which bits you find.”

***

For the second ride I brought the saucer of coins within reach and put our glasses firmly on the table.

Celestine checked the gun's charge, brought the models back to their starting positions, and returned the dial to the clock symbol. She sat down beside me. This time I made room for her arm before we began.

The bell rang. The recording welcomed us again. Our sitting room darkened, and the blue planet shone above the bookcase.

“There,” she said. “Look now.”

On my left, behind a crescent of white cloud, was a tiny model of our first kitchen. The table had been made too large for the room, just as the real table had been. Our old kettle stood on it. Two little cups, yellow and blue, hung from hooks over the sink.

I turned to her. She was already watching me, and her expression made me forget what I had been about to say. I leaned in.

A green planet passed between our faces.

I kissed painted cardboard.

For an instant I stayed where I was, nose against a mountain. From the other side came a small strangled sound. I sat back to let the planet pass, and Celestine folded against my shoulder, laughing.

“I thought I'd left enough room,” she said.

“Apparently my approach was unanticipated.”

“I planned it while sitting here alone.”

She lifted the raygun and diverted the planet over the back of our seats. Then she put her free hand on my cheek and kissed me properly. Her thumb was soft at the corner of my mouth; the machine carried us slowly around toward the window.

I heard the lunar announcement begin somewhere behind my ear. I did not turn to look.

When the ride stopped, Celestine stayed close, her hand now resting on my chest.

“I wanted that on the first ride,” she said.

“A planet in the face?”

“No.” She rubbed her cheek against mine. “A kiss. Before we got out.”

“You kissed me at the tram stop.”

“I got tired of waiting.”

I drew back enough to see her. “I thought you were being polite all evening.”

“Even when I asked you to come and sit beside me?”

“You said there was room.”

“There was room.”

She looked down at our knees pressed together and began laughing again. I remembered the younger version of myself squeezing into that seat as though any accidental contact would have to be explained in writing. There had been orange fizz all over my sleeve and this lovely quiet woman beside me, and she'd said there was room.

“I was trying very hard,” I said.

“I know, darling.” She smoothed the front of my shirt. “I liked you so much.”

“And then you asked me out again.”

“You were already saying goodnight. I was afraid you'd go home and think I hadn't enjoyed it.”

I remembered that too: her holding the tram door with one elbow to ask whether I was free the next evening, and my nodding from the platform because, after several hours of unnecessary talking, I had briefly lost the ability.

I kissed her forehead.

“What would you like this time?”

“Your arm around me. And another go.”

***

She reset the scenery with a touch of the dial, turned it back to the clock symbol, and set the raygun in the little tray beside her seat. I reached for another coin.

“We still haven't seen the front of the moon,” I said.

“We might.”

“Is there something on it?”

“Yes.”

She tucked herself against me, carefully at first, shifting until her shoulder fitted beneath my arm. I could smell the flowers as they passed above the little table. Her belt buckle caught the light, a brief white circle against the pink of her dress.

“Will you tell me?”

“Later.” She took my hand and drew it a little farther around her. “This is nice.”

I dropped the coin into the slot. The bell sounded; the nose lifted. She rested her head on my shoulder, and I bent mine to touch her hair.

The blue planet passed. So did the little kitchen, and the campsite with its upside-down boots. She shifted her hand into mine and settled still closer as the ride turned us toward the window. The paper moon came into view, softly lit, travelling across the dark glass. I saw the beginning of something painted on its face, and then Celestine raised her mouth to mine.

stories.title: The Door in the Ivy
stories.prompt: The queen has retaken her capital, but she cannot bring herself to enter the palace. Resting against the ivy-covered wall where she escaped as a child, she hears the same servant’s door creak open—and the familiar voice of the woman she thought she had left to die.
stories.body:
# The Door in the Ivy

A point of Clarimond's crown caught in the ivy when she leaned her head back. She left it caught. The brick held the afternoon's warmth, and she could stand against it without anyone seeing how much of her weight it bore.

At the front of the palace, her officers were waiting. She had reached the lowest step, heard someone call for the doors to be opened, and discovered that she could go no farther. She had told her captain she needed a moment. Then she had walked around the building, past the rose beds, until the marble gave way to old brick and the path narrowed between the wall and a hedge.

The capital was hers. She had heard its governor surrender it. Her own soldiers held the gates; the palace guard had laid down their weapons; bells were sounding from streets she had last seen seventeen years ago. She had imagined those bells so often that she ought to have known how they would sound. Too loud, it turned out. All of them together, and no room between the blows.

Here the hedge muffled them. She set her sword's point in a gap between the paving stones and closed both hands over the pommel. Dust had settled in the dark red folds below her armor. There was a tear at her knee she could not remember making.

The little door stood three paces to her left. Someone had painted it green. As a child she had known it brown, with the wood worn pale around the latch.

She had not meant to come here.

The hinge scraped. It always began low and rose to a squeal just before the door cleared the stone.

“Clarimond?”

She turned too quickly. The ivy pulled at her crown, and for a moment she could see nothing but leaves.

“Oh, wait. You're caught.”

That was the voice. Its impatience was the same, the impatience of someone undoing a knot she had been told about too late. A woman came out of the doorway and reached up, then stopped with her hand in the air.

She had gray hair above her ears. Her cheeks were heavier, her mouth smaller than Clarimond remembered. She wore a blue dress and a brown shawl, and one foot was set at an angle to the other. The raised hand trembled.

Clarimond let go of the sword with one hand and tore the crown free. A sprig of ivy came with it. She pushed her hand through the circlet and let it hang over her wrist.

“Belda?”

The woman's face crumpled. Clarimond had never seen that happen to a face while it was smiling.

“Yes,” Belda said. “Yes, it's me.”

Clarimond took a step and the sword skidded. Belda caught her elbow; Clarimond caught the sleeve of Belda's dress. They stood bent toward each other, held apart by steel and the blade slanting between their feet.

The sleeve was warm. There were little burrs of wool at the cuff. Clarimond rubbed one beneath her thumb until Belda put her other hand over hers.

“I didn't know whether they'd let me see you. I came as soon as they said the fighting was over. The cook knew me. Not the old cook, her girl. She was in the kitchens when I was here.” Belda was speaking quickly, watching Clarimond's face. “One of your men said you'd gone round the side. I thought of this bit of wall. I thought you might.”

“You were here.”

“Today? Only since the bells.”

“All this time.”

“In the city, yes. Mostly.”

Clarimond was still holding the sleeve. Belda looked at it, and at her, and began to cry in earnest.

“You've grown so tall.”

It was such a foolish thing to say that Clarimond made a sound almost like a laugh. She was twenty-six. Of course she had grown. But Belda had once marked her height against the nursery doorframe with the blunt end of a needle, a secret mark because the steward disliked scratches, and now she was measuring her with her eyes.

“I thought you were dead,” Clarimond said.

“I thought you might be, too.”

The sword was dragging at Clarimond's hand. She eased it away from their feet and leaned it against the brick. When she turned back, Belda was drawing a handkerchief from her sleeve. It was yellow, edged in an ambitious, uneven lace.

Belda wiped her face, then offered it. Clarimond had not known she needed it until she pressed it beneath her eyes. For some time neither of them spoke.

Beyond the hedge a man called for another man. A cart rattled over loose stones. Belda went to the door and pulled it onto its hook so it would stay open. She favored her left leg, putting a hand to the jamb as she came back.

“Your leg,” Clarimond said.

“It mended. Badly, but it mended.”

“Under the cupboard. You couldn't get it out.”

She saw the cupboard before she finished saying it: its white dishes broken across the passage, Belda on the floor with one leg trapped beneath it. The men on the other stair. Someone striking at a lock. She had been nine, small enough to squeeze past the fallen door of the cupboard when Belda pushed her toward the way out.

“Two of the kitchen men found me,” Belda said. “After the soldiers had gone upstairs. They lifted it enough. I don't remember much of that. They took me to the scullery first, then to my sister's in a washing cart.” She drew the shawl tighter under her arms. “It sounds funny now, a washing cart. It wasn't funny at the time. Every stone in the road.”

“I could have fetched someone.”

“I kept listening for someone.”

Clarimond looked along the path toward the lane. It had been empty when she ran into it. At its foot, her father's groom had pulled her through a gate into a stable yard. She remembered fighting him because he put his hand over her mouth. By dawn they were on a fishing boat, and for weeks afterward the people around her had been people who could answer nothing about the palace.

“I told them where you were,” she said. “When we were away. I told everyone.”

Belda nodded. Her gaze had dropped to the handkerchief twisting in Clarimond's hands.

“I didn't dare let people know I'd worked in the nursery. They were still taking people away. My sister said I must keep quiet, and I did. When I could walk again, I went to work with her.”

“But later. When you heard—”

“When they first said in the market that you were alive and raising an army, last autumn, I wrote. Twice. I sent one letter with a grain merchant, and one through the men collecting money for your army.”

“I never had them.”

“No. Well. There was a war on.” Belda tried to smile. “I put things in them you'd remember. I thought they might need proof.”

“What things?”

“That you hated the blue shoes because they pinched, and hid them in the cold stove. Your mother had half the household looking.”

Clarimond pressed the handkerchief hard against her nose. She had forgotten the shoes. Both of them had been found when the fire was laid the next morning, one scorched black along the side. Her mother had tried to look stern while Belda explained.

“She laughed,” Clarimond said.

“She did. It made the steward very cross.”

Her mother's face was suddenly there, as Clarimond had seen it, before anyone had told her about the hurried burial in the palace garden. She had to shut her eyes to keep it. Belda stayed beside her, breathing noisily through a blocked nose.

When Clarimond opened her eyes, Belda was smiling at her feet.

“I expect those fit better.”

“No,” Clarimond said. “These pinch too.”

Belda laughed, surprised by it, and Clarimond laughed with her. It hurt the dry skin of her lips. She wanted Belda to keep looking at her that way, wanted to do something else that would produce the same delighted disbelief. She slipped the crown off her wrist and tugged the ivy out of it.

“This isn't comfortable either.”

“I did wonder.” Belda leaned closer to look. “Is that the little crown your mother wore?”

“My aunt's. She kept it with her when she fled. She had it altered for me.”

“Ah. I never knew your aunt well.”

There were whole portions of Clarimond's life Belda would not know. The realization came pleasantly at first. She could tell her about the house abroad and the old mare she had been given, the people who had taken her in, even the things she had done badly. There would be time.

Belda touched the uneven lace on the handkerchief.

“You can keep that, if you like. My daughter made it when she was learning. I've got a drawer full.”

“Your daughter?”

“My husband's girl. She was seven when we married. Twenty-one now. She does much better work these days; she'd be mortified if she knew which one I'd brought.” Belda held up a corner with a badly joined loop, plainly pleased. “She wanted to come with me, but I said I ought to come first. I didn't know how you'd be.”

“You married.”

“Fourteen years ago. He repairs clocks. You wouldn't have known him. He's always lived in the north of the city.”

Fourteen years. Clarimond had been twelve, living beneath another name, sleeping with her shoes on when it rained because rain reminded her of footsteps in the gravel. Belda had been getting married. There had been a dress and people in a room; perhaps she had laughed like this. Clarimond could not quite put them together, the Belda at her wedding and the one who had lain under the cupboard throughout all those years.

“Is he kind to you?”

“Yes,” Belda said, and then, with a small amused frown, “Of course he is. I wouldn't have had him otherwise.”

“I should like to meet him.”

“He'd like that. He'll say he wouldn't know what to say to a queen, but he will. You'll hear about his clocks.”

Clarimond looked past Belda into the service passage. The walls had been whitewashed. A pail stood beneath a tap that had not been there before.

“We can find rooms for all of you. Somewhere with a separate entrance, if he'd prefer that for his work. You could have the rooms above the south garden. Do you remember? The ones with the painted birds.”

Belda lowered the corner of the handkerchief.

“They're lovely rooms.”

“You could choose others. I don't know what's been done to them.” Clarimond spoke more quickly. “There's no need to decide today. You could come whenever you're ready. I'd like you near me.”

“Oh, love.”

Clarimond knew before Belda said anything else. She straightened.

“I'd only be finding the stairs difficult,” Belda said. “And we've got our house. We've only just got it the way we like.”

“On the ground floor, then. There must be—”

“I don't want to live here again.”

Belda said it louder than she had said anything. She glanced down the path, then back at Clarimond.

“I came to see you. I didn't think you'd ask me that.”

Heat spread from the rim of Clarimond's collar to her face. The offer was a good one. She had meant it kindly. Belda would never have to worry about money or growing old. But she had been arranging a clockmaker's workshop in a room she had not entered since she was nine, and she did not even know his name.

“Forgive me. Of course you must do as you wish.”

Belda's hand moved toward her and stopped. “Don't sound like that.”

“Like what?”

“As though I've come about a position and you won't be taking me on.”

Clarimond opened her mouth, then looked away. There was dirt beneath the hook that held the door. Even that little hook was familiar. Belda had shown her how to lift the door slightly so it would catch.

“You were always here,” she said. “In the mornings.”

“I know.”

“When I saw you, I thought—”

She stopped. Belda rubbed at a wet patch on her cheek with the heel of her hand. Clarimond gave the handkerchief back.

They stood quietly until Belda said, “I'd like you near me too. I don't know how we do that now. But I do.”

The bells had stopped. In their absence Clarimond heard sparrows moving in the hedge, a rustle followed by an indignant scuffle. It was a sound she had heard often outside the nursery windows. She had been allowed to put crumbs on the sill provided she swept them away before lessons.

“You called me,” she said.

Belda waited.

“When I was running. You told me to run, and then you called me back.”

For a long time Belda looked at her. Her mouth was slightly open.

“I heard you,” Clarimond said. “I always heard you. I pretended sometimes that I hadn't, but I did.”

She had meant to turn. At first she had meant to, and then the lane had been there and the turn at the bottom, and she had wanted to be around it where they could not see her. Where no one could catch her. She could remember wanting it more than she could remember loving anyone.

“I kept going.”

Belda pressed the handkerchief flat between her palms. She looked toward the passage and away again.

“I'd hoped you didn't hear that.”

“Did you think I would come back?”

“For that moment, I did.”

Clarimond had to breathe through her mouth. There it was, said aloud by the person she had abandoned, and she had no account of herself to offer. She had carried a sword across a battlefield that morning. At nine she had run because she was afraid, and all the years between could not make that a different act.

“I thought they were coming down the stairs,” Belda said. “I couldn't move. I didn't want to be there on my own.” She folded the handkerchief, missed the edge, and tried again. “I'd just told you to go. I knew you'd only get caught with me if you stayed. But I called anyway.”

The woman beside Clarimond was younger than her aunt. Even now, she was younger. That afternoon she had been thirty-four. Clarimond had never reckoned it before; Belda had simply been grown, as tall and certain as the doors.

“You were frightened.”

“Yes.” Belda's voice had gone thin. “Very.”

Clarimond put her crown on the paving beside the sword. When she stood, she reached for Belda's hand. The first fingers she found were stiff around the folded cloth; she waited until they loosened.

“I'm sorry I left you there.”

“I'm sorry I called.”

They held hands. Clarimond could feel the pulse in her own fingers, or in Belda's; she could not tell. Belda kept her eyes on their hands. After a while she drew a breath that caught, and Clarimond moved closer, wanting to put her arms around her, unsure whether Belda could bear it.

“May I?” she asked, lifting her free hand.

Belda pulled her in before she could finish the movement. A metal edge pressed into Clarimond's ribs. Belda's cheek rested against the leather at Clarimond's shoulder; they shifted, and Clarimond bent her head until it rested above Belda's ear. The gray hair was soft and smelled faintly of smoke from a cooking fire.

Belda was crying again. Clarimond held her while her own face grew wet. Once Belda drew back to breathe, then came close again, and Clarimond was grateful beyond speech for that second, deliberate return.

When they finally let go, the light had moved lower on the bricks. Clarimond's captain appeared at the bend in the path and halted. She raised a hand to show she had seen him, and he withdrew.

“They're waiting for you,” Belda said.

“They can wait a little.”

“There's something I wanted to ask.” Belda was winding the handkerchief around one finger. “In those years away. Was it all dreadful?”

Clarimond began with the safe house, how well guarded it had been, but Belda made a small impatient movement.

“I mean, were you ever happy? You don't have to tell me you were. I just want to know.”

She thought of the things people asked about exile: who had sheltered her, who had paid, when she had begun preparing to return. She had answers for all of those.

“I learned to swim,” she said at last. “There was a millpond. My aunt disapproved of it.”

Belda looked up.

“The miller's daughters taught me. My aunt wouldn't let me take a good shift into the pond, so I cut holes in one.”

“You didn't.”

“I wasn't allowed back for a week. I hid the scissors, as though that helped.” Clarimond remembered the cold water taking her breath, the miller's elder daughter holding her beneath the arms and growing exasperated because she would not kick. “I was quite happy there. In the summers. I got better at swimming, and we'd take bread and cheese and stay until we were hungry again.”

Belda listened as she described the pond: the shallows clouded with mud, the rope hung from a willow, the green smell of their shifts drying on the bank. She had not spoken about it for years. Midway through explaining how the youngest girl refused to enter the water unless everyone turned away, she remembered her name and was startled into saying it would be good to write to her.

“Do,” Belda said. “She'll be wondering about you.”

“She will.”

Clarimond smiled, and Belda touched the side of her face with the backs of her fingers.

“There you are,” she said softly.

Clarimond leaned into the touch. Then she stooped for the sword and crown. Her knee resisted; she had to turn a little to reach them. Belda watched without trying to help.

“When I come to your house,” Clarimond said, “will you tell me about your wedding?”

“If you want to hear it.”

“I do. What you wore. Whether you were nervous.”

“Terribly. I'd had a tooth out the day before. All I could think about was whether my face looked swollen.” Belda laughed under her breath. “There's a likeness my husband had done a few years later. You can see what he looked like before he lost his hair.”

“I'd like that.”

Belda stayed while Clarimond settled the crown among the loosened pins in her dark hair. They kissed each other's cheeks, missing slightly on the second side, and held hands once more before Belda turned down the path toward the gate.

Clarimond watched until she passed the captain. Belda said something to him, gesturing back, and he bowed with a gravity that made her look flustered. Then she was beyond the hedge.

The service passage smelled of damp stone. Clarimond stood outside it with the sword at her side. From farther along it came the clatter of someone setting down a pail.

She lifted the hem of her red skirt over the sill and went in.

stories.title: A Little More Room
stories.prompt: The girl next door, happens to be a really sweet, kind, shy cyborg, always blushing and always in mod dresses, long gloves, cinch belts, and go-go boots. She looks like she walked out of a 1990s anime, carries a small railgun and can't think evil or dirty thoughts because of cognitive filters.
stories.body:
# A Little More Room

When the woman next door knocked, I turned my record down before I opened the door, so the first thing I said to her was an apology for a complaint she had not made.

"Sorry. These walls are basically paper."

"They are composite board," she said. "But they do pass a great deal of sound."

She stood with both hands clasped at the buckle of a white cinch belt. Her dress was turquoise, short and square at the shoulders, with orange circles marching down one side. White gloves covered her arms past the elbow. White go-go boots came almost to her knees. Her black hair swept outward in two sharp wings, and her eyes had the huge dark irises and emphatic lashes of someone who had stepped out of a 1990s anime without adjusting herself to our badly lit hallway.

She was also blushing so hard that the pink reached the fine silver seams in front of her ears.

On her belt, secured in a black molded holster, she carried a railgun about the size of a large flashlight. A blue lock tab crossed the trigger guard. The charge window was dark. Small did not make it decorative.

I lowered my voice as well as the music. "I can move the speakers. Or use headphones. I didn't realize anyone had moved into four-twelve."

"Yesterday," she said. Her blush deepened, which I would not have thought physically possible. "I wasn't asking you to stop. I wanted to know what record that is."

Behind me, a bass guitar worried the same bright phrase over and over at a volume now suitable for a dentist's waiting room.

"Oh." I looked back as if the sleeve might rescue me. "A blue-label reissue. Lots of brass, no restraint."

"Is that the title?"

"No. Sorry. The title is *Satellites for Beginners*."

She repeated it carefully. Her voice was soft, but not frail. There was a faint second note beneath it, a resonant mechanical hum that vanished when she stopped speaking. "Do you like it?"

I had owned the record for nine years and had played it twice. "Very much."

"May I borrow it when you're finished?"

This was how I met Suzette, who was twenty-eight, two years younger than I was, and who had no complaint about the music. I gave her the record before side one ended.

For the rest of the evening I listened through the wall as the brass section migrated into her apartment. The walls were composite board, after all. She played the second side first.

Three days later, she brought it back.

This time her dress was lemon yellow with a row of black squares at the hem. The gloves were black, the broad belt yellow, the boots white again. The same compact railgun rode at her hip. So did the blush. I had begun to understand that the blush was weather, not necessarily news.

"No scratches," she said, presenting the sleeve in both hands. Something clicked delicately beneath the fabric at her knuckles. The gloves hid the mechanical joints but not their movement. "I held it by the edges."

"I trusted you."

Pink rose all the way to her temples.

Or perhaps I had not begun to understand anything.

She had tucked a second record behind mine, in a green paper sleeve softened at the corners. "You said you liked bass. This one has a good bass part in the second track. I think. It makes the glasses in my cupboard walk toward one another."

"That's a recognized critical standard."

She glanced at the record, then at me. "Is it?"

"It should be."

Her smile arrived slowly. It did not reduce the blush. "Will you tell me if you like it?"

I put it on while she was still in the hall. The first track was smooth electronic pop, full of glassy notes and a singer who sounded as if he had never spilled anything in his life. I opened the door again before it finished.

"This one seems like you," I said.

Suzette had made it two doors away. Her boots stopped. "Why?"

There were too many possible answers, and several would have made me sound like I had assembled her from the dress outward. "It's neat. Cheerful."

She listened for four bars. "I don't like this track."

"Oh."

"It's too neat." She tucked a black-gloved finger beneath the strap of her holster and settled its weight more comfortably. "The second track drops things."

Then she went home, leaving me with the useful discovery that sweetness did not oblige her to approve of my guesses.

The second track dropped a drum kit down a flight of stairs and recovered beautifully. I liked it much better.

Our third hallway conversation happened on Friday. Suzette wore a black-and-white dress divided into big offset rectangles, a red cinch belt, red gloves, and white boots. Her wardrobe changed every time I saw her without ever changing its mind. The railgun remained part of it, clipped securely at her right hip. So did the blush, present before either of us spoke.

"Did you like the second track?" she asked.

"Enough to worry your cupboards."

"Good." She nodded once, visibly gathering herself. "Tomorrow evening I'm going to play some records. Would you like to come over?"

"Sure. I can bring a few."

"You may. I was also going to move the little table so there would be room for dancing."

"I have felt pads," I said at once. "For the table legs. They keep the floor from getting scratched."

The hope in her face did not disappear. It became harder to read. "That is useful."

"Seven?"

"Seven."

She went inside. I spent Friday night choosing records as if I had been asked to keep a failing radio station on the air.

At seven the next evening, I arrived with a milk crate against my hip and a packet of furniture pads balanced on top. Suzette opened her door in a cherry-red mod dress with a narrow white panel from collar to hem. Her gloves and boots were white; her belt was red patent leather. The blush was already there, vivid against her brown skin.

"You brought many," she said, looking down at the crate.

"I panicked."

"About music?"

"That's the safest category of panic."

She considered this, then stepped aside. "Come in."

Her sitting room had the same dimensions as mine and none of the same surrender. My sofa, shelves, and square coffee table had divided my room into narrow shipping lanes. Suzette owned a low blue settee, one oval rug, a lacquered table no wider than a dinner plate, and a record player on a long cabinet. There was room to cross the floor without turning sideways.

Beside the door, she pressed two fingers to a recessed wall box. Its lid opened. She released the railgun from her belt, checked the dark charge window, and set the weapon into a fitted cradle. The lid shut with a firm double click.

"Range day?" I asked.

"Thursday."

"It's Saturday."

"Yes." She looked at me, waiting.

There was no invitation to turn her habit into a biography. I set down the crate. "Where's the dangerous table?"

She pointed to the small lacquered circle. We put a felt pad under each of its three legs and moved it beside the settee. Suzette could have lifted it alone. When I took most of the weight anyway, she let go and allowed me my moment of unnecessary usefulness.

"There," I said. "Maximum floor."

"Better," she said.

She chose the first record. It began with handclaps, a cheerful organ, and a woman singing about rain in a voice that suggested rain had personally apologized. Suzette stood in the cleared space, rocking from one white boot to the other. Her gloved fingers traced small shapes at her sides. The motion was so private and pleased that I looked away, afraid attention itself might interrupt it.

I crouched by my crate and began sorting.

"This next one has a better pressing than the copy I lent you," I said. "And this one is strange, but in a disciplined way. The percussionist used kitchen pans. Supposedly."

"Do you want to hear it?"

"I thought you might."

"Later, perhaps."

I made a second stack. Selecting music gave my hands a job and placed me at the edge of the room, where I was most comfortable. Suzette kept moving. The silver articulations in her ankles made tiny adjustments above the stiff shafts of her boots. She knew the beat but did not submit to it; sometimes she caught it, sometimes she let it pass and turned under the next one.

A dull bang came through the ceiling.

I glanced up. "If they keep doing that, we can put on my worst record and aim the speakers upward. Ruin their evening in self-defense."

Suzette stopped moving.

It was not offended stillness. Her eyes shifted slightly, as though searching a shelf where nothing had been filed.

"That would not defend us," she said.

"No. It was a joke. Petty revenge."

"Yes, I recognized the structure after you said revenge." She rubbed one thumb across the palm of the opposite glove. "I couldn't supply the wish inside it."

I rose from the records. "I don't follow."

"My cognitive filters prevent malicious intent from forming. I can understand that noise might annoy us, and that more noise might annoy them. I can't want to hurt or punish them." Her voice quieted. "The filter closes that route before it becomes a thought I can hold."

"You can't think anything bad?"

"I can think your tidy record is bad."

"Right. Fair."

"I can be angry. I can dislike things. I can refuse things." She gave the stacks beside me a concerned glance. "I may refuse several of those."

"Please do."

"The old description says I can't think evil thoughts or dirty thoughts. By dirty, it means sexual thoughts. Not mud." She managed the sentence in one careful run, then went crimson from cheekbones to ear seams.

I kept my eyes on hers. "Okay."

"They are thoughts I don't have. The filters don't stop me from saying the words."

"Okay," I said again. It seemed more respectful than turning her explanation into a question period. "And I'm done with revenge jokes."

"You didn't know."

"Now I do."

The singer on the record reached the chorus for the third time. Suzette's blush had not faded. It occurred to me how often I had treated it like a caption under her face, translating every word into an emotion she had not named.

"Does that always mean you're embarrassed?" I asked, tapping my own cheek.

"No. I always blush." Her shoulders lowered a fraction. "Sometimes embarrassment contributes. Sometimes temperature. Sometimes speaking. Often I don't know."

"So I've been reading unreliable instruments."

"Very unreliable."

She crossed to the turntable and lifted the needle before the last chorus finished. From my crate she selected the tidy electronic record I had said seemed like her. She held it up between both white gloves.

"Not this one," she said.

"Not this one."

She put on the green-sleeved record instead and skipped straight to the second track. The first drum hit came in sideways. The bass followed half a breath late, heavy enough to stir the fine hairs on my wrists.

Suzette stepped back into the open floor.

I began lining the discarded sleeves along the cabinet so none would be bent.

She danced through the first verse alone. Her style had no stable theory. She swung both arms in a clean arc, lost the rhythm during a turn, found a different rhythm, and smiled at that one as if it had waved to her across a station. Once, she tried a sharp little kick. The weight of her boot carried farther than she expected, and she hopped backward to keep her balance. The settee caught her behind the knees.

She laughed. It came out with that low mechanical harmony under it, warm and slightly astonished.

"The table move was wise," I said.

"Yes." She looked at me. "Are you going to dance?"

"I'm handling the records."

"They are not moving."

"Preventive handling."

Suzette's hands went still at her sides. Her face was bright red, but the color could not answer for her.

"Robin," she said, barely louder than the music. "I have records."

"Better ones than mine, apparently."

She glanced down, and I heard the request hidden inside my line: tell me my records weren't a nuisance; tell me I wasn't. She left it unanswered.

"I wanted another dancer," she said.

The bass knocked gently through the floor. A paper sleeve slid from my tidy line and flopped flat.

"I don't dance," I said.

"You move when music plays. I've seen you through your doorway."

I remembered leaning over my speakers with one shoulder jumping, unaware of an audience. "That was equipment adjustment."

"It was during the handclaps."

"Coincidence."

Suzette did not laugh. She waited, growing quieter rather than retreating. "Do you mean no?"

I could have said yes. I could have packed the records, left with everybody's dignity mostly unopened, and spent the next month being agreeable in the hallway. The exit was close enough that I could see the wall box holding her railgun and the neat white toes of the boots she had planted on the rug.

"I mean I'll look ridiculous," I said.

"I look ridiculous sometimes."

"You look like animation directors planned you six months in advance."

She looked down at her dress. "They didn't."

"I know. I mean—" My hand made an unhelpful circle. "You look deliberate. I move like I'm trying to get out of a coat."

"I wasn't asking you to look good." She paused, then tried again, more plainly. "Please don't leave. I want you to dance badly with me."

"All right," I said.

I took off my shoes so I could not damage her boots or feet. This left me in gray socks on a blue rug, which did nothing for my dignity and helped with everything else.

Suzette held out one white-gloved hand. I took it. Her palm was warm. Under the fabric, the segmented fingers adjusted around mine one joint at a time, careful without being delicate.

"Where does the other hand go?" I asked.

"I don't know. I wasn't planning that kind."

"Good."

We stood side by side instead. She showed me the movement she had been trying: two steps left, one back, arms up on the offbeat. Her explanation and her feet disagreed about which direction was left. I followed the feet. On the second attempt I moved too far and struck the lacquered table with my hip. It spun once on its felt pads and stopped.

"A little more room," Suzette said.

We pushed it all the way against the wall.

The first song ended while we were still arranging ourselves. Suzette hurried to the cabinet, white boots thumping, then stopped with one hand above the record.

"What next?" she asked.

My mouth filled with qualifications. I swallowed them. "The blue one. *Satellites for Beginners*. Side two."

"That is the side I played first."

"I know. It sounded better through the wall."

She smiled and found the record in my crate. A quick bass line sprang from the speakers, loose beneath the brass, and I recognized the phrase that had migrated into her apartment on the night we met.

"This one," I said. "I like the bass after the second handclap."
