Suzette returned to the rug and offered me her hand again. Her cheeks were still pink. They might have meant heat, or speaking, or the fact that we were both adults alone in her apartment. They might have meant nothing I could name. She had told me what she wanted, which was better information.

"Then show me where it is," she said.

We missed the first handclap because I was counting too hard. We caught the second. When the bass came in, Suzette's white boots landed on either side of my socks, my hand found her gloved one, and the record kept turning while we tried the step again.

stories.title: The Vacant Throne
stories.prompt: Fifteen years ago, the human king and the demon queen fought a legendary battle that resulted in the king's death. The throne remained vacant until a half-demon child appeared bearing the royal sword.
stories.body:
# The Vacant Throne

Before dawn, the Seatkeeper found a dead moth in the hollow of the throne.

It had battered itself pale against the high windows and fallen between the seat and the carved back, where no servant had dared reach beneath the mourning cloth. She pinched it by one powdery wing and carried it down the seven steps. The throne had been vacant for fifteen years. Dust might touch it. Sunlight might. No living hand had.

At the foot of the dais waited the crown and the succession skin. Her seal lay beside them in a cedar box. By sunset the red wax would hold either a new sovereign's mark above her bounded regency, or her mark alone above the closing line of the caretaker compact. She had spent half her life preventing that second impression from looking like hunger.

The silence had begun at moonset. Black cords bound the court's sleeves, and until the sun dropped behind the western wall, no human voice could take part in the anniversary. The custom was older than her brother's death, meant to deny boasting to victory and excuses to defeat. In fifteen observances it had become chiefly a way to survive remembering him.

The First Captain stood below the open doors with his sword belted and his command staff under one arm. His hands had already rearranged the palace. Two fingers sent guards to the gallery. A flattened palm closed the river gate. A turn of his fist thickened the line before the throne room. He wore no mourning cord.

The Seatkeeper looked through the doors at the crowded antechamber. Three rival houses had arrived before midnight, each carrying enough cousins to become a future. Their banners hung furled by law, bright fringes showing beneath their black covers. At sunset the compact expired. If she did not take the crown, someone would try to take the room.

She closed the cedar box and began the coronation route backward.

Her brother had once walked it from gate to throne through thrown petals and ringing bronze. She had followed six paces behind, watching a loose thread tremble on his shoulder. Now she passed from the throne room into the memorial court, where his stone likeness lay with both hands empty; through the long gallery of ancestral faces; across the rain court; and down toward the outer gate. At each threshold she tested the seal and counted the guards. The Captain followed, correcting her counts with small movements of his staff.

The sky had paled enough to show the gate towers when the wicket opened from outside. The gatekeeper stumbled backward. A child came through after him.

They were perhaps fourteen, perhaps younger beneath the dirt. A hood covered most of their head, but two blunt horn tips had worn holes in the cloth. Dust made a mask of their face except where sweat had cut tracks from the temples. Their coat was demon work, scaled at one shoulder with overlapping red leather, and human work at the other, patched in square stitches by someone impatient. A round iron signet hung against their chest.

The royal sword hung at their hip.

It was too long for them. The scabbard struck every third paving stone, and their hand stayed locked around the belt to keep its weight from dragging the buckle loose. The blue enamel of the pommel had been burned brown on one side. Below it, just visible through a split in the grip, ran a wire repair no court copyist had ever recorded.

The Captain's staff came level. Spears crossed behind the child.

They stopped. Their gaze moved from the spearheads to the walls, to the wicket still open at their back, and then to the Seatkeeper. Their eyes were dark red around human-gray irises. Not flame. Not omen. Merely eyes narrowed against a dawn they had been awake too long to meet.

The Captain opened one hand for the sword.

The child's fist tightened on the belt. With the other hand they covered the signet at their chest. Their shoulders rose, ready for a blow or flight, though the scabbard had already trapped itself between their ankles.

The Seatkeeper stepped under the Captain's staff.

Up close, the sword was worse than any replica would have dared. The scabbard bore white scratches beneath newer travel stains. A crescent of the guard had melted. One side of the grip had been rebound in black cord, but the old repair remained: a double strand of copper passed through three holes in the sharkskin, crossed once, and knotted under the king's forefinger.

She had made that repair at sixteen, furious with her brother for breaking the grip against a pear tree. She had used wire stripped from their mother's ruined astrolabe and hidden the knot because her work was ugly. Her brother had liked the roughness beneath his finger. On the morning of his last campaign he had rubbed it while she fastened his cloak.

The sword did nothing now. It gave off no heat. It leaned with all its ordinary weight against a hungry child's hip.

The Seatkeeper raised both empty hands. Then she took one step back and turned toward the palace. After a moment, the child followed. The Captain lowered his staff, but he did not dismiss the spears.

* * *

On a coronation morning, the long gallery displayed bowls of saffron, salt, coins, and winter fruit, each an old promise made visible. No one had thought to remove them for a succession expected to begin at sunset. The child reached the first bowl, seized a plum, and bit through its bitter skin.

Purple juice ran over their knuckles. A court usher flinched as if a treaty had been torn. The child saw him, looked at the row of untouched bowls, and chose a second plum. This one disappeared into their coat.

The Seatkeeper almost smiled. The impulse hurt more cleanly than grief had in years.

She led them beneath the painted kings. The Captain kept to the child's sword side. Behind him came the keeper of seals, two judges, six guards, and the boldest members of the waiting houses. The procession swelled whenever a side door opened. It was already turning the child's hunger into pageantry.

At the portrait of the late king, the child stopped.

The painter had given him a broad, painless face and a hand resting lightly on the sword. Nothing in it resembled the man who had climbed wet roofs, hoarded quince paste, or laughed with his whole spine. Nothing resembled the body returned from the battlefield either. The child studied the painted hand. Their own thumb began to scrape across the first knuckle of the forefinger.

Her brother had worn that patch of skin smooth whenever he waited for someone else to decide.

The Seatkeeper reached before she meant to. The child recoiled so sharply that the sword struck the wall. Guards caught their hilts. The Captain's staff snapped upright.

No metal cleared leather. In the held breath afterward, the Seatkeeper lowered her hand. She had intended to turn the child's wrist toward the light, to find proof in bone and habit. What she had shown instead was how quickly kinship could become inspection.

The child rubbed the bumped scabbard with their sleeve. They would not look at her.

She turned to remove the line of people behind them. It took time. The rival houses mistook the first sweep of her hand for an invitation forward. The judges mistook the second for a demand that they surround the child. One guard backed into a saffron bowl and stood in yellow dust while the child watched with exhausted, unwilling amusement. At last the Seatkeeper pointed every unnecessary witness toward the side doors and waited until obedience became less embarrassing than refusal.

The gallery emptied to the child, the Captain, the keeper of seals, and one judge from each rival house. The spears remained at the far end.

The Captain's jaw worked beneath the scar that divided it. Yet when the child resumed walking, he moved half a pace farther away from the sword.

At the rain court, sunlight found the signet on the child's chest. The Seatkeeper knew its shape from old border documents and the broken standards carried home after the battle: an iron disk wider than two fingers, its face divided by a deep diagonal groove, one half polished, the other stippled. The demon queen's seal had authorized granaries, marriages, troop roads, and executions long before human songs reduced her to horns above a field of fire. This signet was battered at its edge and dark with the grease of constant handling. It might have been stolen. So might the sword. Together they proved possession, not birth, and possession proved no purpose at all.

The child shifted the disk under their coat when they noticed her attention.

The Seatkeeper turned her eyes away first.

* * *

The memorial court had been built around an accusation.

Her brother's stone figure lay at its center, his empty hands lifted upon his breast. Above him, a wall mosaic showed the last battle as the survivors preferred it: the human king in white mail; the demon queen enormous beneath a red sky; their blades meeting in a burst of gold. Along the floor, a black stone band represented the burned field. Visitors placed human mourning tokens on the raised bier and cast enemy tokens into a bronze ash basin at its foot.

The child entered and became still. The Captain indicated the sword rest on the bier. The keeper of seals uncovered the ash basin. Every trained gesture in the room offered the same bargain. One inheritance could be honored. The other could be discarded.

The child looked at the Seatkeeper.

She had meant to give reassurance. Instead she glanced at the sword rest, too quick and too plainly. The child's mouth hardened.

They unbuckled the royal sword. The Captain leaned forward. The child carried it past the bier and laid it on the black floor band beneath the place where the two mosaic blades met. Then they took off the demon signet.

For an instant the Seatkeeper expected iron to strike bronze. The child set the signet beside the sword.

They knelt on the battle line, not on the king's white marble and not on the red field assigned to the queen. Their head bowed until the horn tips touched the scabbard. One hand closed around the signet; the other held the ugly copper knot in the grip. The pose had no place in court ritual. It was unbalanced and uncomfortable. After a few breaths, the child's knees slid on the polished stone, and they caught themselves with an elbow.

No one moved to help.

The Seatkeeper saw then what the court had required of them: not evidence, but amputation. It had made her brother easier to mourn by leaving no space beside him for the child who had survived him. It had made an enemy eternal so no one need wonder what had passed between king and queen before the killing blow, or why the sword had crossed the border in her keeping.

She did not know whether the demon queen lived. She did not know whether the queen had sent the child as heir, hostage, weapon, or burden. The child's bent head answered none of it. Grief was not testimony, but it was still grief.

The Seatkeeper lifted the bronze ash basin and carried it to the wall. Its feet shrieked faintly across the stone. She set it beneath an old rain stain, far from both child and bier. Then she sat on the black band, not beside the child but near enough that they could choose the distance.

Around the court, certainty broke unevenly. The keeper of seals lowered his eyes. One judge knelt on the white marble; another remained standing. The Captain watched the passage behind them, counting bodies and exits because that was the shape fear took in him.

The child raised their head. Their cheeks were dry. After considering the Seatkeeper for several long breaths, they took the hidden plum from their coat and rolled it across the black stone. It stopped against the hem of her robe. The Seatkeeper set it between them. She did not eat it. Neither did the child.

* * *

At the throne-room doors, the First Captain barred the way.

Sunlight had reached the upper windows. Less than an hour remained before it touched the western wall, and the antechamber beyond the Captain had filled again. The rival houses stood in ordered blocks. Their covered banners were now upright. The silence had sharpened every shuffle, buckle, and drawn breath.

The Captain planted his command staff across the threshold. He pointed to the royal sword, then to the hands of the waiting guards.

The child stared at him. Sweat had pasted their hair to their temples beneath the torn hood. The sword belt was slipping again. For one ugly moment the Seatkeeper feared they would draw. Not because the sword had willed it, or blood demanded it, but because tired children made terrible choices when adults arranged the room to leave only terrible choices.

The child turned around, walked back into the memorial court, unfastened the belt, and placed sword and scabbard in the center of the open floor. Then they returned empty-handed. The weapon lay beyond their reach and beyond the Captain's threshold. It belonged to no one's custody but the witnesses'.

The Captain kept his staff raised. The Seatkeeper removed the audience again.

This time there was no confusion in her gesture. She pointed to the outer gallery, then to each house in turn. Silk shifted. Faces flushed. One by one the blocks broke apart and withdrew until only the three judges, the keeper of seals, and six palace guards remained. The Captain tightened his grip. She pointed the guards out as well.

His eyes found hers. Fifteen years of service stood between them: riots contained, borders held, assassination letters burned, nights when his soldiers had been the only thing between caretaker and crown. She knew what he protected. A command without a monarch became a private army by increments, each defensible on the day. He knew what she had permitted. A vacant throne had let them both call possession duty.

The Captain looked past her to the child. They had begun picking dried plum skin from beneath one thumbnail.

His staff lowered a finger's breadth. The child noticed. They straightened and attempted the soldiers' closed-fist salute. They used the wrong hand, struck their collarbone too hard, and winced. It might have been mockery. It might have been effort. The Captain's face passed through offense, surprise, and something close to shame.

He stepped aside before anyone had sworn loyalty. The child crossed the threshold.

* * *

The vacant throne made them look smaller.

It made everyone smaller; that was part of its design. The blackwood back rose twice a person's height, carved with human victories until no bare grain showed. The child approached only as far as the first step. Their attention fixed on the side passage through which they had entered. The route back to the sword remained open.

From gate to throne, the Seatkeeper had weighed the claim. The private repair and battle damage made the blade more than a court copy. The signet matched the queen's old impressions down to its chipped rim. The child's age, mixed features, and unconscious family habit made theft alone a poorer answer than inheritance. Any piece might deceive; together they met the old law's threshold for a minor claimant under witnessed regency. They revealed nothing about the queen's purpose, and promised nothing about the ruler the child might become.

The Seatkeeper laid the succession skin on the low table. Its old marks were simple: a sovereign's chosen figure in the upper circle, a regent's seal inside a boundary below, military submission at the foot. No mark could prove parentage. No wax could make a good ruler. The instrument could only record what living people had risked in one another's sight.

She opened the cedar box. Her seal showed a key laid across an empty chair. For fifteen years it had granted her power to preserve the estate, collect revenue, appoint judges, and command defense without occupying the throne. At sunset the outer ring would become void. A minor sovereign could renew her service only inside a smaller ring, ending at majority and forbidding her to alter the succession, begin a war, or dispose of the royal household. Those limits were cut into the bronze rim as notches any witness could count.

She warmed the wax. Before the child touched stylus or crown, she pressed her seal into the bounded circle.

The impression came out crooked. One side of the chair vanished into red. Good. Let it be plain that she had bound herself before she knew whether they would choose her.

She placed the stylus beside the upper circle and retreated from the table. Then she took the crown from its cushion and set it on the lowest throne step, leaving both the side passage and the main doors clear.

The child could walk out. The Captain's staff no longer blocked the way. Their sword waited in the memorial court. Whatever the queen intended, whatever the kingdom desired, the space around the succession table held no hand but theirs. The light climbed the western wall.

The child approached the skin. They examined the Seatkeeper's impression, tracing the boundary notches without touching the wax. Their hand went to the demon signet, still hanging at their chest. The keeper of seals offered a shallow dish for it. They ignored him.

With the signet clenched in the left hand, they took the stylus in the right. The first stroke tore the prepared surface. The second wandered. They frowned, scraped a patch smooth with the stylus handle, and began again. This time they made a small figure of three joined angles, cramped but unmistakably deliberate. Then they put the stylus down.

No fire passed through the room. The sword remained on the memorial floor. The mark was valid because the child had made it freely before witnesses, and because the adults present would now be answerable for honoring it.

The First Captain came to the table. His command staff ended in an iron cap worn bright by his palm. Once impressed beneath a sovereign's mark, it submitted the palace garrison and dissolved every emergency authority he had accumulated during the vacancy. He held it above the wax long enough for the sun to touch the final row of carvings.

Then he pressed down.

The keeper of seals folded the skin. The three judges set their plain witness marks along the seam. The caretaker compact ended inside the same breath as the regency began.

The Captain went to one knee. The judges followed, one readily, one stiffly, one after looking toward the empty gallery. The Seatkeeper knelt last. She did not bow to the sword, the signet, or the mingled blood courtiers would soon make into a story. She bowed to a tired child who had been given room to refuse and had chosen an obligation no child should have needed to carry alone.

On the western wall, the last light withdrew.

Somewhere beyond the palace, bells began to strike the end of silence. The child flinched at the first blow. The crown waited on the step, too large and much too clean.

They picked it up, turned it over, and set it on the throne's broad arm. Then they sat on the lowest step with the iron signet safe in both hands.

No one mistook the seat for vacancy.

* * *

Night found the new sovereign in the family wing.

The Seatkeeper had opened her brother's chamber. Its bed had been remade every seventh day for fifteen years, its shutters oiled, its winter robes aired and returned to cedar chests. The child stood in the doorway, took in the vast bed and the preserved boots beneath it, and backed away.

They chose the little map room across the corridor instead.

It had a narrow couch, shelves crowded with rolled borders, and a window seat deep enough to sleep in. The Seatkeeper sent the servants away before they could transform it into another shrine. She brought water, a basin, bread, and the royal sword herself.

The child had removed the torn hood. Their horn tips curved back close to the skull, one ridged, one chipped. They watched as she laid the sword on the window seat within easy reach. For the first time that day, their hand did not close around it at once.

The Seatkeeper placed the plum from the memorial court beside the bread. She indicated the bell pull, the water, the inner bolt. Then she stopped. Practical gestures multiplied when affection lacked permission. She could fill the room with provisions and still make it a cell.

She moved to the door and left it open.

Behind her, wood scraped softly over stone.

The child had hooked one foot around a low stool. They dragged it from beneath the map table, shoved it across the rug, and left it beside the window seat. Not close enough to touch. Near enough that two people could look through the same pane.

Their gaze met hers and darted away. One hand rested on the demon queen's signet. The other, empty, held the stool steady.

The Seatkeeper came back into the room.

She sat where the child had put her, while the sword lay quiet between them and the door remained open.

stories.title: The Gods Are Afraid of Grandma
stories.prompt: You always wondered how you grandma can be so old and fit, despite all her unhealthy habits. Turns out, the gods are so afraid of her that they did everything they could to keep her alive on Earth.
stories.body:
# The Gods Are Afraid of Grandma

Grandma Valka was halfway down the drainpipe when I arrived.

She had one slipper braced on the porch roof, one bare foot feeling for the iron trellis, and a cigarette tucked into the corner of her mouth. Rain silvered her white hair against her scalp. At a hundred and eight, she had the build of a bundled umbrella and the grip strength of a dockworker.

I dropped my overnight bag in the flower bed.

“Don’t yell,” she said. “You’ll make me fall.”

“You are making you fall.”

“Then don't help.”

The gutter had clogged with leaves. She had climbed out the bedroom window because, according to her, ladders were dangerous in the rain. By the time I got under her, swearing and holding both arms up, she was already testing the trellis with her heel.

The rusty bracket tore out of the brick.

For one long second she hung above me, surprisingly quiet. Then a delivery van struck the pothole at the curb. Its back door flew open. A roll of carpet underlay bounced out, hit our hedge, unfolded across the path, and made a thick gray landing pad exactly where Valka came down.

She landed on her backside, took the cigarette from her mouth, and regarded the underlay.

“People throw away good things,” she said.

The van kept going.

I blamed the driver, the road, the weather, and my grandmother, in that order. There was plenty of blame to go around and no reason yet to assign any of it to the divine.

Inside, I made her change out of her wet clothes. She made me eat three potato pancakes fried in lard, with sour cream and a ridge of salt that glittered like frost. She had already eaten four. A bottle of plum brandy stood by her elbow. Her ashtray stood by the bottle.

Our family had spent decades trying to improve Valka. We brought nicotine patches, low-sodium soup, sensible shoes, railings, pill organizers, and articles printed in type large enough to imply a threat. She accepted everything with gratitude. The patches stopped drawers from rattling. The soup went to a neighbor’s dog. She hung onions from the railings and stored sewing needles in the pill organizer.

Then she outlived the neighbor and the dog.

“One cigarette after dinner,” I said.

“Certainly.”

“That one counts.”

“Then I’ll smoke it slowly.”

She dealt cards across the oilcloth. We played gin while rain ticked the kitchen window. Valka won the first hand, the second, and the third, although during the third she paused with two fingers pressed to her neck.

“What?” I said.

“Bad card.”

Her face had gone the gray-yellow of old newspaper. I reached across the table. Under my fingertips, the pulse at her wrist stumbled, vanished, returned once, and vanished again.

From the pantry came a muffled voice.

“Oh, for pity’s sake. Not on my shift.”

Something struck the shelves. A jar broke. Valka’s heart gave a hard, offended thump beneath my fingers and resumed its beat.

She pulled her wrist away. “You’re peeking at my cards.”

I opened the pantry. A crock of pickles rocked on its base. Cloudy brine spread between the tiles. Nobody was there.

“Mouse,” Valka said behind me.

“The mouse swore.”

“You would too, living on what you buy.”

I wanted to call an ambulance. She wanted to finish the hand. We compromised by arguing for twenty minutes and finishing the hand. She beat me with three queens, went upstairs, and fell asleep before I had finished checking that her breathing sounded like her ordinary breathing: raspy, uneven, and stubbornly present.

I stayed in the chair beside her bed until midnight. Rain hissed against the window. On the sill, her forgotten cigarette smoldered in a saucer.

I had just reached for it when a single cold drop squeezed through the closed window, fat as a grape, and struck the ember dead.

There were limits to coincidence. I had found mine.

Downstairs, the loose porch step was no longer loose. Fresh nails shone in wood that had been soft with rot that afternoon. A man in a reflective vest knelt over it, tapping one nail with a little brass hammer.

“Road maintenance,” he said without looking up.

“On her porch?”

“Approach infrastructure.”

“At twelve fifteen?”

He glanced at a wrist on which no watch appeared. “Time-and-a-half.”

Rain ran off his shoulders but did not darken the vest. The pothole at the curb was gone. In its place the asphalt rose in a smooth black patch, warm enough to steam.

“Was that your van?” I asked.

“What van?”

“The one that dropped a mattress under my falling grandmother.”

“Underlay,” he said. “A mattress would have bounced her into the roses.”

He shut his eyes.

“Road maintenance,” he repeated, less hopefully.

I took his hammer. He let me, which frightened me more than if he had turned it into lightning.

“Inside.”

“I have no authority inside.”

“You’re going to discover some.”

I herded him through the kitchen with the hammer raised. He stopped at the pantry threshold as if he had hit glass. From behind the door came furious whispering.

“She caught him,” said one voice.

“Of course she caught him,” said another. “He wore the vest.”

“People trust the vest.”

“People trust roads. They merely tolerate you.”

I opened the door.

The pantry was four feet deep and currently held two more people, neither of whom had been there when I searched it. A broad woman in an apron crouched beside the broken pickle jar, pinching shards out of the brine. A narrow person in a yellow raincoat sat on the flour bin and swung one spotless boot.

The apron woman pointed at the man. “He has muck on my floor.”

“It’s your floor?” I said.

“For the relevant purposes.”

The person in yellow looked me over. “You’re the grandchild who hides the cigarettes.”

“Which grandchild?”

“The anxious one.”

“That does not narrow it down.”

“This is why I said we should recruit the tall niece.”

“She lives two counties away,” said the road man.

“Rain travels.”

“Not usefully.”

The apron woman slapped both palms on her knees. A blue flame leaked between her fingers and vanished. “Enough. She’ll wake.”

“Who are you?” I asked.

They looked at one another, each waiting for someone of lower rank to answer.

The road man finally cleared his throat. “We are powers of longstanding local recognition.”

“Gods,” said the weather god.

“Some of us preserve ceremonial precision.”

“Some of us fill potholes.”

“That is an exercise of authority.”

The apron woman shoved a cloth into his hands. “Exercise it on the brine.”

They were gods. I believed them immediately, not because of the fire or the dry raincoat but because they had the same bad teamwork as the committee at my apartment building, combined with the vanity of people who expected statues.

The hearth god had held authority in Valka’s house since the first stove fire burned there. The road god governed the lane, its ditches, its crossroads, and—as he insisted twice—the lawful approach to the gate. The weather god had the valley’s rain and wind, although not temperature, which belonged to a cousin no one liked.

“People still worship you?” I asked.

The road god drew himself up. “They touch their dashboards and beg to arrive. They curse my bends and thank my bridges.”

“They check my face before they leave the house,” said the weather god.

The hearth god wrung pickle brine into the sink. “They bring families to my table. That will do.”

Their power, authority, and scraps of worship sounded less like a golden age than a collection of jobs nobody had managed to abolish.

“You fixed her heart.”

The hearth god's mouth tightened.

“You dropped the underlay,” I said to the road god. “And you put out the cigarette.”

The weather god looked pleased. “One drop. Very neat.”

“Why?”

All three answered at once.

“Civic duty.”

“She’s beloved.”

“Deferred contractual exposure.”

Silence followed. The road god stared at his knees.

“Explain the last one.”

“No.”

“Then I wake Valka.”

The effect was extraordinary. The weather god slid off the flour bin. The hearth god blocked the door. The road god, still holding the wet cloth, whispered, “There is no need for escalation.”

So I had them.

I brought the card deck from the kitchen and set it on an upturned crate. “Start talking.”

Their story emerged badly.

Forty-six years earlier, when Valka was sixty-two, her heart had stopped for seven minutes on the floor of a bus depot. At the threshold before the underlying afterlife—a place the gods described variously as a cardroom, a tollhouse, and “nothing you are equipped to picture”—she found the three of them playing cards.

They had not caused her death. They agreed on that loudly. They had, however, attempted to delay her passage.

“Why?” I asked.

“There was a jurisdictional uncertainty,” said the road god.

“He owed her,” said the hearth god.

“We all owed her,” said the weather god. “Small things. Then larger things. She notices.”

As a girl, Valka had left bread at the hearth when everyone else had forgotten. She had cleared roadside shrines during a flood and spent three nights insulting the rain until it moved off the wheat. None of those acts had been offered as a bargain, but gods accumulated obligations the way old houses accumulated jars: untidily and beyond counting.

They tried to settle with a game.

“You cheated,” I said.

“The rules permit cooperative play,” said the road god.

“He dealt from the bottom,” said the weather god.

“You marked the queen.”

“Because you kept forgetting which suit was dominant.”

“You changed it four times.”

“Valka caught you,” I said.

The hearth god smiled despite herself. “Before the second trick.”

Valka had taken over the deal and changed the stakes. If she won, their old debts remained due, and when she returned she could name the forfeits. Before she could do so, paramedics restarted her heart. The game, accepted freely and interrupted before collection, remained binding.

“What can she ask for?”

The pantry filled with evasions.

Not everything. Nothing universal. No power beyond their domains. No command that erased another person’s choice. They could not drag her back from the dead, give her endless life, or bar her from the afterlife. But within their authority, they could owe service, yield privileges, surrender worship, perhaps even lose the offices that made them gods.

“Perhaps?” I said.

“We did not let her finish stating the stakes,” the weather god said.

“The paramedics did that.”

“You kicked over the table.”

“The floor shifted.”

“It was a floor.”

The road god pressed the wet cloth to his face.

They had spent forty-six years postponing Valka’s return. The hearth god nudged circulation when her heart misfired at home. The road god diverted vehicles, tightened steps, and once moved a runaway wheelbarrow uphill. The weather god broke heat waves over her roof and sent rain after sparks.

They could only work within their domains. They could only correct what they caught. Their efforts cost them: a washed-out culvert left waiting while the road god softened Valka’s fall; a whole afternoon’s rain held in a cramped cloud while the weather god cooled her fever; six kitchen fires burning too hot elsewhere while the hearth god coaxed strength through one old heart.

And still Valka had arthritis, a smoker’s cough, blood vessels the hearth god called “an insult,” and a liver that prompted all three to cross themselves in different directions. The lard still clogged. The smoke still scarred. Age still narrowed the spaces between emergencies.

“We are not making her healthy,” said the hearth god. “We are catching plates before they hit the floor.”

“Not all plates,” the weather god said.

Nobody spoke for a moment.

Upstairs, Valka coughed in her sleep. I had heard that cough all my life. Now I heard the gaps between the gods’ shifts.

“Protect her better,” I said.

The road god lowered the cloth. “We have just described—”

“I’ll keep your secret. I’ll get the family to stop nagging her, stop asking why the woman who salts bacon keeps passing her medical checks. In return, one of you watches her at all times.”

The weather god laughed once, then saw my face. “Oh. You mean it.”

“No gaps. No missed heartbeats. No falls.”

“We can't.” The hearth god's voice was quiet now. “She is alive. Alive is not the same as sealed.”

“Then make it the same.”

“That is not a thing.”

“You’re gods.”

They flinched as if I had called them frauds.

“Within domain,” said the road god.

“At cost,” said the hearth god.

The weather god picked at a strip of yellow rubber on one cuff. “And until.”

The word emptied me. My prepared threats, my lists, all the sensible instructions I had carried into the house—nothing in them could get purchase on until.

I shuffled the deck because my hands needed a job. One card clicked against another. “Where’s the marked queen?”

No one answered.

I searched the deck. Three queens. The fourth had always been missing from Valka’s cards; as a child, I had accused her of losing it. She told me incomplete decks taught adaptability.

“She kept it,” I said.

The gods began searching the kitchen with such frightened incompetence that I almost enjoyed myself. The road god opened the refrigerator four times. The weather god looked under the same chair twice. The hearth god stood very still, eyes moving toward the bread box, away from it, then back.

Inside the bread box, beneath a dish towel and two stale rolls, sat an old tobacco tin. In the tin lay the queen of hearts. A brown thumbprint marked her throat. One corner had been singed, one warped by water, and one was gritty with something that might have been road dust.

All three gods recoiled.

“So this is what you’re afraid of.” I held the card by its clean edge. “I could burn it.”

The hearth god grabbed my wrist. Her palm was fever-hot. “No.”

“Or I could give it back to her.”

The weather god said a word that rattled every window in the house.

Above us, a floorboard creaked.

Valka came into the kitchen in her nightdress and wool socks, carrying the iron fireplace poker. She looked at the gods, at my captured wrist, and at the queen between my fingers.

“You,” she said.

The road god attempted a bow. The pantry shelf caught him behind the head.

“You.” Valka pointed the poker at the hearth god, who released me. Then at the weather god. “And you still owe me three dry Thursdays.”

“Those were conditional,” said the weather god.

“Sit.”

They sat.

Valka took the queen from me, rubbed the marked throat with her thumb, and placed it face down on the table. Her hands trembled. I had not noticed that before. Or I had noticed and filed it under things to correct.

“How long have you known?” I asked.

“Long enough.”

“They’ve been keeping you alive.”

“They have been interfering.”

“You nearly fell off the roof.”

“I came down.”

“On a carpet.”

“Underlay.” The road god sounded offended.

I turned on him. “Do not help.”

Valka leaned the poker against her chair. “You came to watch me.”

“You climbed out a window.”

“Before you came.”

“That is not better.” My voice sped up. “You smoke, you eat whatever you want, you don’t sleep, you go on the roof, and apparently the only reason you haven’t died six hundred times is that three incompetent gods are terrified you’ll take their jobs.”

“Offices,” the road god said.

“I will put you in the pantry.”

He was already mostly in the pantry, but he moved his chair backward.

Valka waited until I ran out of breath. Waiting was one of her cruelties. She could leave silence on the table until you filled it with the thing you had meant to hide.

“I can’t keep doing this,” I said.

“Then don’t.”

“I can’t not do it either.”

She looked at me. The gods looked anywhere else.

The words came badly, as they always had. “I know you’re going to. I know. But when the phone rings, every time, I think—”

That was as far as I got.

Valka’s hand closed over mine, card and all. Her skin was thin and hot. The blue veins stood up under it. Nothing divine smoothed them away.

“You want me not to leave you,” she said.

I nodded.

“I cannot promise that.”

The gods found the table fascinating.

“I can promise no roof in the rain,” she said. “Not because it is your rule. Because I frightened you.”

“You frighten them more.”

“They have better reasons.”

The hearth god made a small, unwilling sound that might have been agreement.

“And the cigarettes?” I asked.

Valka considered this outrageous addition. “Not in bed.”

“You already agreed to that.”

“Then we have made excellent progress.”

I laughed. It came out wet and embarrassing. Valka squeezed my hand once and let go before either of us could make a ceremony of it.

The queen remained between us.

I could have torn it. I could have hidden it and kept my bargain over everyone’s head. For one ugly moment, I wanted to. The card was leverage over weather, fire, roads, perhaps death’s very doorstep. It was the best pill organizer our family had ever found.

But it was not mine.

I slid the queen across the oilcloth to Valka.

The hearth god shut her eyes. The road god muttered what sounded like a prayer to himself. The weather god reached for the brandy, thought better of it, then reached again.

Valka tucked the queen into the deck. Her knuckles worked slowly. She shuffled once, badly, and pushed the cards toward me.

“Your hands,” I said.

“Are a hundred and eight years old. Deal.”

I dealt five cards to each of us. The gods crowded close, damp, ash-smudged, and unable to relax. Valka lifted her hand, took one look at their faces, and smiled.

“We were in the middle of a game,” she said.

“The previous table is no longer available,” said the road god.

“This one is mine.” She nodded to the empty chair beside her, and this time the invitation was for me. “Stay.”

I put my phone face down. Rain worried the roof, the stove flame burned blue, and every road beyond the windows ran somewhere I could not follow. I pulled my chair in anyway.

stories.title: The First People
stories.prompt: The age of starlight brought with it the advent of life, later evolving to intelligent civilization. The cosmos would give birth to many. Most were peaceful, one was not. Facing an enemy of universal proportions, the stars turned to the oldest among them. The first people. Humanity!
stories.body:
# The First People

Rain had got into the census of the living.

Heshi lay half out of her courier shell with one hand clamped over the spindle at her breast. Water ticked against its cracked face. Each tick disturbed the lights inside: routes, vessels, shelters, the last confirmed populations of worlds that had stopped answering. She dragged the spindle under her coat and tasted blood behind her teeth.

Above her, the road she had fallen from closed to a white scratch in the clouds. It should have gone dark. Instead it pulsed once, faint and regular.

The pursuer had kept her wake.

She pushed herself upright. The shell had furrowed a strip of black shingle and struck a stone wall hard enough to turn one wing inside out. Beyond the wall stood a low house with rain running down its windows. No towers. No guard vessels. No assembly of the legendary elders who had laid paths between stars before Heshi's kind had learned to shape glass.

Only a lamp came bobbing around the wall.

The person carrying it wore a yellow rain coat over loose sleeping clothes. Human, if the old descriptions had not become ceremonial nonsense: two arms, blunt face, bare head gone silver at the sides. He stopped when the lamp found her.

His mouth moved. Heshi's translator, wet and failing, said, “Does your body dispute covering?”

She drew herself straight despite the pain along her ribs. “To the first hearth, from the darkened houses of the later sky, I bring the count of those still breathing.”

The translator told him, “Old mud property. Dependent animals remain in inventory.”

The human stared at her. “Right,” it rendered. “We'll try that indoors.”

He approached slowly and held out a silver sheet. Heshi recoiled. He stopped at once, opened it around his own shoulders, then pointed from the sheet to her and raised his brows.

Not a restraint. Warmth.

She took it. He turned immediately to her wreck, crouched beside the split hull, and reached for the emergency core.

“Do not touch that.”

This time the translator produced a burst of static followed by, “Hands are forbidden.”

“Excellent. A clear sentence.” He pulled the core's cable free.

Heshi lunged, slipped on the stones, and caught herself against the wall. The pale pulse above the clouds quickened.

The human pointed up. “Your ship was shouting where it landed.” He pointed to the dead cable. “Now it isn't.”

She looked from the core to the sky. The pulse slowed again, searching.

He dragged a tarpaulin over the shining half of the shell, using stones to hold it down. What had looked like desecration became concealment, performed with the irritated economy of someone covering a leaking woodpile.

“Martin,” he said, touching his chest.

The translator offered *harbor*, *male offspring*, and then the sound itself.

“Heshi.”

“Ash?”

“Heshi.”

“Heshi.” He got close enough. He pointed toward the house. “Unless you'd rather explain the war in the rain.”

She understood only *war* and followed.

The first house of humanity had three rooms, a stove that smelled of scorched leaves, and a bucket under a ceiling drip. Martin moved the bucket two finger-widths before he did anything else. Heshi had crossed the occupied road under fire. She had watched three escort vessels flower soundlessly in vacuum. The oldest living people in the cosmos had given the leak its own towel.

Martin sat her near the stove, put a dry cloth beside the census spindle without touching it, and worked at a panel in the wall. Its glass filled with symbols too old and simple to be mistaken: the basal route marks from which every younger script had grown.

Heshi stood so abruptly that the room tipped.

“You know the road.”

“I know that you arrived through a system we're not supposed to have heard from in a very long time.” He spoke slowly, watching the translator struggle. “I am a listener. Civilian. Night rotation.”

“Bring those who decide war.”

The machine said, “Deliver owners of violence.”

Martin's expression closed. “We don't have owners.”

“Commanders. Elders. The authority of your people.”

“I can call people. I can't summon humanity to the kitchen.”

She struck the spindle with two fingers. Nineteen lights flared, then seven more, dimmer. “Your children are being extinguished.”

“Not children,” Martin said.

The refusal shocked her more than the room had. Every plea carried the old kinship. First hearth, later houses. First voice, answering voices. The words were why she had kept moving after there was no one left to order her onward.

Martin looked at the translator's text and rubbed both hands over his face. “No. I mean, they aren't ours to own. Start again. Less ceremony.”

“Ceremony preserves precision.”

The translator said, “Incense keeps knives sharp.”

Martin glanced at the stove. “Apparently not tonight.”

He touched the wall panel. Somewhere below the house, something answered with a note so low Heshi felt it through the chair. Lines of human script moved across the glass. The translator caught fragments.

ORIGIN SIGNAL UNCERTAIN.

FOREIGN CORE ISOLATE.

KEEP WITNESS PRESENT.

“They are listening,” Martin said.

“Who?”

“More people than fit in my kitchen.”

He was joking. Heshi could tell because the translator marked the sentence as a probable apology, which was how it handled most human humor. She could not tell what he was apologizing for.

The spindle gave a warning tremor. She put it on the table and unlocked the cracked face. A field of points spread across the ceiling, jittering whenever rain struck the roof. Martin reached for a lamp, then understood and turned every light off.

Darkness made the room large enough.

Heshi touched the oldest route in the census. A thread ran from the point above the table to six others, then branched until the ceiling shone. She closed her fist. A third of the branches vanished.

“The road is taken,” she said. “They enter at one living world and leave at the next. They offer peace. They take routing. Then no message leaves except theirs.”

Until the pursuer, a dispute on the road had meant late cargo, offended envoys, sometimes a duel held well away from the controls. No people had tried to own arrival itself.

Martin watched the absent lights. “How many?”

“Worlds?”

“People.”

There was no ceremonial answer for a count that changed while one spoke it. Heshi showed him the spindle. Most of its records carried margins wider than the numbers.

He fetched a shallow box from under the panel and spilled its contents across the table: ceramic counters, coils of wire, little weights. Listening tools, perhaps. Or the remains of several household repairs. Heshi placed one counter beneath each confirmed refuge. Martin marked lost routes with wire. When she could not make the translator understand an occupied junction, she seized his wrist, moved his finger down the branch, and closed it over the route. He nodded and bound that section in black wire.

They built the war between them without another successful sentence.

At last Martin pointed to the pale scratch pulsing beyond the window. He set one black-bound counter at its end, then tapped the table.

“Coming here?”

Heshi nodded.

He pointed to the spindle, then to Earth.

“Why bring this here?”

“The road begins here.”

He made a small, impatient motion. Obviously. Why else would his wall know the root marks?

“No,” Heshi said. She pushed aside the younger routes and found the deep date layers. The spindle stuttered over intervals too large for its display. She drew the first line alone from Earth into an empty part of the table. No answering worlds. She added another line. Still none. Another. Around them she placed bare counters for seas not yet alive, stone worlds, clouds that had not yet learned the chemistry of breath.

Only much later did she set down the counter for her home.

Martin stopped moving.

The wall panel had begun checking her dates against records below the house. Human symbols multiplied. She could not read the detail, but she knew the shape of agreement: error narrowing, measures locking, separate clocks finding the same past. The wall reached farther back than the road, into the oldest living strata of Earth. Their date settled beneath every cradle in the census.

Earth had begun living first. Humanity had called into silence because, then, there had truly been no one to answer.

“We listened,” Martin said. “There was nobody.”

Heshi touched the young counter that stood for her world.

“Not yet,” he said.

The first people had not emerged from a crowded sky and conquered it. They had opened their eyes to no one. While Heshi's oceans were still warm poison under a young sun, humans had sent machines outward. They had built empty stations around stars where no mind existed to use them. The road had waited through ages for travelers not yet born.

Her teachers had called that part devotion because the alternative was absurd.

Martin stared at the dates with no triumph at all. “Somebody kept the receivers on.”

Heshi swept the later lights back into the sky. “Then take back your road.”

The translator rendered it perfectly.

Martin sat down. For the first time that night, he looked old.

“We can't take it back,” he said. “We can burn it.”

He opened a red cover beneath the wall panel. There were two empty sockets inside, one shaped for a human hand and one for incoming route data. Heshi understood before his explanation survived the translator. A root failure sent through the oldest layer would run outward faster than any vessel. It would force whatever it could from transit and destroy the rest of the fast lattice behind it. No branch selection. No rebuilding from the captured stations. No road for the enemy.

No road for anyone.

“Close it,” Heshi said.

“This closes all of it.” Martin pointed to the counters, one by one. A refuge whose atmosphere scrubbers came by road. A vessel between stars. A habitat supplied from a system with no habitable world. The translator lost his qualifiers, so he wrote numbers in the condensation on the window. Transit loads. Food intervals. Days by road becoming months by the fastest human craft, months becoming years.

Heshi watched him make the cost too plain to turn into legend.

“I did not come to ask this.”

“What did you come to ask?”

“For the first people to lead.”

“Lead what? The road goes everywhere they do.”

She had no answer. She had imagined fleets older than her species, weapons reserved by wise hands, perhaps a command spoken in the first language that would make the road obey. She had brought humanity a child's version of age: age without ruin, without forgotten techniques, without arguments conducted beyond a kitchen wall.

The pale scratch in the clouds became a steady line.

Every light in the room came on.

The voice from the wall was smooth, free of static, translated before it finished speaking.

“First cradle, you are being invited to remain outside a containable dispute among younger civilizations. Release the courier and abstain from damage to common transit. Your safety, autonomy, and continued access will be guaranteed.”

Heshi's throat membrane tightened. The pursuer's voice always sounded reasonable. It had learned to make terror fluent.

“They found the house,” she said.

“I gathered that.” Martin looked at the red cover. “They also speak our language better than you do.”

“They took our translators.”

The voice continued. “The courier carries corrupted traffic data and cannot calculate the consequences of the action she proposes. You may preserve your people, or condemn peaceful worlds to isolation and death. There is no third responsible choice.”

Martin gave a brief, breathless laugh. “Blackmail with a service guarantee.”

The translator said, “A kettle repaired by threat.”

Heshi struck the table. Counters jumped. “My home used kettles while they entered it.”

Martin's smile vanished. “I'm sorry.”

The apology was direct enough that even the translator left it alone.

“Give me to them,” she said. “Keep the census closed. They may pass Earth.”

“They may.”

“Your people live.”

“And they keep every door.” He touched the wire leading from Earth, not looking at her. “Giving them you doesn't make them forget the addresses.”

Below the house, the low note changed. The wall filled with terse fragments, appearing and vanishing too fast for Heshi's translator.

HOSTILE UNIVERSAL ROUTING: CONFIRMED.

ROOT ACTION: CONDITIONAL.

NO SAFE CLEARANCE WINDOW.

LIVE TRAFFIC CENSUS REQUIRED.

Martin read them twice. “Earth will burn the roots if we can reduce the transit loss.”

Heshi covered the spindle with both hands.

The census was not merely traffic. Hidden inside its uncertain counts were the last receptive stations beyond occupied systems, shelters whose transmitters stayed silent, vessels drifting dark beside the road. Connecting it to the root would let Earth see them. It would also let the pursuer see the connection before the burn reached every branch.

“Your machine asks me to expose the living.”

“Yes.”

“If I refuse, you burn without them.”

Martin looked at the counters rather than at her. “Or we don't burn.”

The perfect voice returned. “Close the foreign device. The courier's surrender remains acceptable. Every death after this offer will result from your refusal.”

Heshi's hand moved toward the spindle latch.

Martin did not stop her. “I need the census,” he said. His humor was gone now, and without it his voice seemed less competent, not more. “I don't have a clean way to ask for it.”

She waited for persuasion. He only stood beside the red cover while rain worked at the house and the pursuer's line thickened in the clouds.

All the authority Heshi had left came from people who might already be dead. They had trusted her with the count because a count could make loss harder to disguise. They had not authorized her to reveal the shelters. They had not authorized her to let the enemy inherit every route between them, either.

She put the spindle into the empty socket.

Its lights went white. Across the ceiling, hidden points appeared one after another.

The pursuer's line flared.

“They see it,” Heshi said.

“So do we.” Martin pressed his palm into the human socket.

The room asked a question in both their languages. Heshi's version lost the word that distinguished consent from command.

Martin pulled his hand away. “No. It has to be clear.” He pointed to her, then to the connected spindle. “Do you choose to hold this open?”

The line beyond the window widened until the clouds shone from within.

“I choose it.”

“That translated.”

He set his hand back into the root.

The census poured itself through the house. Heshi saw transit burdens race along the ceiling: cargo, passenger clusters, vessels under concealment, the dim intermittent marks of damaged craft. Earth answered not with a speech but with changing intervals. Hold. Release. Hold.

The root intended to burn outward in one wave. Heshi caught Martin's sleeve and dragged the black wire on the table into a curve. Her damaged census was late along the occupied branches; a single wave would reach three passenger clusters before their emergency ejection marks arrived.

“Wrong order,” she said.

“Show me.”

She could not. The translator gave him *funeral before door*. She tore the wires from the table, laid the shortest branch over the longest, and moved his finger from Earth outward in staggered steps. Then she made three quick fists, throwing imaginary vessels clear.

Martin watched once. “A rolling burn.”

He sent the shape into the wall. The answer came back with a delay long enough to feel like refusal.

SEQUENCE POSSIBLE.

LAST BRANCH MARGIN UNKNOWN.

The pursuer opened the road above them.

For one instant Heshi saw a black geometry behind the clouds, too large to be sky. The spindle bucked in its socket. Several hidden points went red.

“Now,” Martin said.

“The outer vessels—”

“Now, Heshi?”

She checked the damaged intervals. There was no honest answer, only a narrowing range with lives on both sides of it. Wait and the pursuer would enter intact. Burn and one passenger cluster might still be inside the last branch.

The polished voice said, “You have mistaken uncertainty for permission.”

Heshi thought of the escorts disappearing behind her, each one buying another uncertain interval. She thought of her home counter, small and late on humanity's table.

“Now,” she said.

Martin closed his hand.

Nothing exploded. The stove continued to tick. Rain whispered against the glass.

On the ceiling, the first route folded.

Its travelers spilled from the census in a scatter of emergency marks. Some resolved into nearby systems. Two vanished. Before Heshi could count them, the next route folded, and the next. The burn ran not like fire but like a door closing through a house too large for sound. Signals broke in the middle of words.

“—outside, three hulls, one—”

“Pressure holding. We require—”

“Do not send through the—”

Then those branches were dark.

The pursuer drove forward. Its black geometry emerged from the cloud line as the road collapsed behind it. For a terrible breath it had crossed whole, a weapon at the first cradle with no fleet standing before it.

Then the route under it died.

The geometry lurched. Light stripped from its edges. It did not fall; something from Earth caught it beyond the rain, slow human craft moving into place on instruments Martin could see and Heshi could not. The wall gave only fragments.

ONE HOSTILE VESSEL PRESENT.

REINFORCEMENT PATH ABSENT.

CONTAINMENT ATTEMPT IN PROGRESS.

No one in the kitchen cheered.

The last outer branch remained lit. Heshi's passenger cluster crawled toward its ejection margin while the pursuer's broadcast fractured around it.

“—avoidable deaths—your primitive action—final opportunity—”

One vessel cleared. Four. Eleven.

The branch folded.

For a moment the census showed nothing at all. Then six emergency marks returned, scattered far from their intended systems. Three more came back damaged. The rest did not.

Heshi tried to ask how many had been lost. Her voice made no sound.

Martin removed his hand from the socket. The skin of his palm was blistered in the root's pattern. He wrapped it in the same silver sheet she had refused outside and waited beside her while the spindle searched.

The road was silent.

Not the old silence humanity had heard before anyone else existed. This silence had people on both sides of it.

The dead root released what it had caught as it closed. Messages came out of order and without the road's clean translation. A shelter reported that something had ejected above it. A vessel transmitted only breathing and a repeating pressure value. One occupied system said the enemy ships already there had not vanished. Another signal consisted of a hand-drawn star pattern so distorted Heshi had to turn her head before she recognized the request for medical aid.

Her home did not answer.

Martin's wall produced a final cluster of human fragments as the dark outside thinned toward gray.

HOSTILE VESSEL HELD BEYOND ATMOSPHERE.

NO UNIVERSAL ROUTE ACCESS DETECTED.

LOCAL CONFLICTS UNRESOLVED.

SLOW-AID LAUNCHES AUTHORIZED.

Martin read the last line aloud. His voice shook on *authorized*.

Somewhere beyond the wet windows, engines began as a vibration in the table. Heshi had expected the oldest people to answer with an ancient power no one else possessed. Instead, they had destroyed it. What remained sounded heavy, mechanical, embarrassingly slow.

The census recovered enough to mark three clusters within reach of the first craft. One contained survivors from Heshi's route, but not her home. Another had breathable reserves for perhaps forty days. The human craft would need thirty-six if nothing failed.

Martin came to stand beside her. “We can send the first one where your count says.”

It was not a command, and he did not make the choice easier by pretending otherwise.

Heshi touched the mark with forty days of air.

“There,” she said.

Martin relayed it.

Beyond the seawall, a blunt human craft rose into the washed-out morning. It climbed under its own engines, slowly enough that Heshi could follow it through the window. There was no road beneath it and no promise it would arrive in time.

It kept climbing.

stories.title: The Second Wearing
stories.prompt: You are a piece of sentient jewellery. After too long packed in a box, you've just been inherited.
stories.body:
# The Second Wearing

There is no darkness in a box. Darkness is something the sighted have described to me, usually while fastening me for an evening in which they expect to be admired. A box has pressure.

Velvet presses my enamel face. My chain lies in three cold turns across my back. The lid gives a constant, faint answer to the rise of my setting, and the answer does not change when I address it. I cannot speak through velvet. I cannot tug the chain. I cannot make the box resent its hinges on my behalf.

Warmth comes and goes. Sometimes pressure rolls from one edge of me to the other amid a long juddering, then settles with my chain rearranged. Sometimes fingers handle me through cloth, firm and brisk, and new velvet replaces old. No skin. No mind opening at my touch. The silver around my enamel develops first a peppering roughness, then a drag I cannot polish away. I count changes until counting becomes a form of boasting and abandon it.

I tell myself Pavia is making a point.

Pavia had a talent for making points last longer than comfort required.

The great disruption begins with a blow beneath me. Weight piles against one side of the box, releases, piles again. Long runs of sliding pressure end in short collisions. The temperature falls, rises, then holds at the stale mildness of an occupied room. Vibrations multiply around me: loads set down, drawers shunted, footsteps approaching and retreating. I can distinguish activity from silence. I cannot distinguish an hour from a week.

Pressure lifts from my face.

Air reaches the tarnished edge of my silver. My chain tightens above me and draws me out, but the chain is only chain. Whatever hand holds it might be Pavia's, or a thief's, or the final careless hand before a furnace. I hang without balance, blind to my own display.

Then my back meets living warmth.

A pulse strikes through me.

It is quick, uneven, glorious. A body shifts beneath my weight; breath lifts me and lets me fall. Bone carries the tiny thunder of a swallow. Contact opens the inward path that is mine alone, and after so long without a mind to receive me I rush into it without courtesy.

*Pavia? At last. Your handling has become appalling.*

The pulse kicks. Fingers hook under me and wrench me away.

Warmth vanishes. Balance vanishes. The living mind closes so completely that my next words have nowhere to be.

Tension travels in an arc through the chain; I collide with something hard and come to rest on a surface that answers the impact with a flat vibration. Larger tremors follow. Perhaps the person is pacing. Perhaps something else has been dropped. I know only that I am not being worn and that the pulse was not Pavia's. It had the wrong cadence. Too much hurry, too little warning.

A bare fingertip touches my rim.

The path opens, narrow but sufficient.

*Yes,* I say at once. *That was me.*

The finger leaves.

It returns.

*If you are testing for persistence, I persist.*

Gone.

Again.

*You are making an unnecessarily suspenseful experiment.*

The touch breaks. A length of uncertain cold follows. Then the chain draws taut and supporting pressure falls away. No contact travels through the links. Whoever holds me understands at least that much.

My back meets skin again, deliberately this time. Fingers pin me just below a collarbone. Pulse, breath, balance—and a voice, carried inward through bone before the air could have mattered.

“Can you hear me?”

*Now I can.*

“Why now?”

*You are wearing me.*

“I'm holding you against me.”

*A provisional wearing, then.*

“Don't be difficult.”

*I have been in a box beyond the useful reach of calendars. Difficulty is among my fresher pleasures.*

Her pulse slows by one beat and then resumes its haste. I decide this means I have amused her.

“Who is Pavia?”

The question shears the pleasure from contact.

*Who are you?*

“Odelia Strake.”

The surname arrives through her sternum with a low roughness that speech in air never had. Pavia's voice used to travel through me the same way: not heard at a distance but built in pressure, teeth, throat, and bone.

“And you?”

*Lustre.*

“Of course.”

*Pavia Strake wore me.*

“She was my aunt.”

*Was?*

Odelia's fingers tighten. “She died in February.”

I wait for some concealed piece of me to answer with Pavia's death: a break, a fading, a final stored word. Nothing does. I have only Odelia's warmth and the coarse patch of tarnish along my edge.

*How long?*

“Since February?”

*Since she put me away.*

“Thirty-one years, according to the label.”

The number has no shape I can trust. It is too large for warmth and cold, too neat for the shocks of travel, too obscene for the patient argument I have been conducting with Pavia.

*Labels are not always accurate.*

“This one had dates.”

*Pavia could have returned before then.*

“Did she?”

*Not in contact.*

Odelia draws me a fraction away. The inward path thins and snaps. For one blank interval I hang by the chain. When she lets me touch her again, her pulse has quickened.

“Are you Pavia?”

*Certainly not.*

“Do you have her memories?”

*I have my memories. Some involve her.*

“Can you read mine?”

*No.*

“See?”

*No.*

“Make me do things?”

*I can make recommendations of exceptional quality.*

“That's a no.”

*It is a tragically qualified no.*

“Can you stop talking?”

I begin to explain that after thirty-one years a demand for silence borders on decorative cruelty, but her thumb shifts under my rim.

“Stop.”

I stop.

Her pulse continues. A breath enters, holds, leaves. Another follows. Contact remains open, and I occupy it without speaking. The exercise is vulgar but clear.

“All right,” she says. “Start.”

*You might have led with your relationship to Pavia.*

“You might not have shouted her name inside my head.”

*I did not shout.*

“You sounded like you lived behind my teeth.”

*I do not choose the architecture of reception.*

“That's exactly how she used to argue.”

The likeness pleases me before I understand it should not. I take Odelia's continued contact for attention; I cannot feel her attention except as body. That asymmetry has always encouraged me to overestimate my insight.

*I knew Pavia intimately,* I say. *I rested over her pulse for years. I heard what she said when no one stood close enough to hear, accompanied her beyond rooms you likely never entered, and knew every change of breath before she admitted—*

“What did she do the last thirty-one years?”

*I was not worn.*

“Then don't sell me ‘intimately.’”

*The years before a person makes a regrettable decision do not become worthless merely because later years occur.*

“You don't get to grade which of her years mattered.”

Odelia's words shorten when her pulse rises. Pavia's lengthened. I had mistaken this one difference for impatience; now I suspect it is control.

*I can tell you about her,* I say, with less flourish.

“That's why you're still against my skin.”

The admission warms me more thoroughly than the body itself.

*Then fasten the clasp. Your grip is unnecessary.*

“I don't like jewellery at my throat.”

*I am a pendant. The chain is incidental.*

“The chain is currently sawing at my neck.”

She shifts it. My weight slides across skin and lifts away. The path breaks.

I do not know what expression she makes in that silence. I do not know whether the chain has caught, whether she considers dropping me, whether my insistence has ruined the only chance I possess. I can feel the chain's small metallic adjustments, none of them mine. Tension settles into a closed loop.

Skin returns.

“Useful fact,” Odelia says. “You can't hear me when I hold you off.”

*A mean use of accurate observation.*

“Why did she stop wearing you?”

*Taste can fail without warning.*

“Try again.”

*We disagreed.*

“About?”

*Standards.*

“Whose?”

*Mine, principally.*

Odelia holds still. I mistake stillness for victory and continue.

*Pavia chose an inferior ornament for an evening. Cheap metal, red glass, an absurd multiplicity of dangling parts. She called it festive, which is what people say when they mean that craftsmanship should be excused.*

The pulse beneath me changes so sharply I lose my next sentence.

“The cherries.”

*You know them?*

“I bought them for her at a winter fair. I was eleven.”

There are moments when thirty-one years become suddenly credible.

*I was not informed that a child's involvement altered the standards of metalwork.*

“She wore them to my recital.”

*She told me only that the occasion required something cheerful.*

“She was sparing your feelings.”

*She described the clasp as unreliable.*

“It was. What did you do?”

*I objected.*

“How?”

*Precisely.*

Odelia lifts me off her skin again. Contact goes.

When it returns, she says, “Sequence. Not your review of the jewellery.”

Fear sharpens every phrase available to me and makes all of them sound like clauses in a losing contract.

*She held me where you are holding me. She said she would wear the cherries. I said I would not be treated as a second choice. She said it was one evening. I said one evening revealed a hierarchy. She told me not everything was an appraisal.*

“That sounds like her.”

*I told her that if she valued scrap above me, she could put me away until she was prepared to wear me properly.*

Odelia takes one shallow breath. “And?”

*She said, ‘All right, then.’*

For the first time, Odelia laughs. It begins as a held tremor, three beats trapped under me, then escapes through her nose with no elegance at all. The sound strikes a seam in my memory so exactly that for one foolish instant I prepare to address Pavia.

I do not.

“Oh,” Odelia says. “She did exactly what you asked.”

*I did not ask for three decades.*

“Did you give her a duration?”

*It was implicit that she would reconsider.*

“To you.”

*To anyone with proportion.*

“She moved five times after that night. I helped carry this box out of two apartments. The velvet in it isn't thirty-one years old.”

I press into the only defense left to me. *Preservation is not wearing.*

“No. It isn't. She relined it herself. Those crooked corners are hers.”

*You cannot know she meant to return.*

“Neither can you.”

The answer is blunt enough to leave no purchase. Odelia's thumb rubs once across the roughened silver, then stops.

“The label on the box says, ‘For Odelia, if wanted.’”

Hope makes me careless. *Then Pavia intended you as my next wearer.*

“She gave me a box. My throat wasn't in the will.”

*That is an excessively literal distinction.*

“It's my throat.”

I hurry, because the chain has begun to shift. *Naturally. I merely mean that inheritance carries reasonable expectations. Care, continuity, some respect for the evident purpose of the object—*

“You're not an object when that helps you, and you are when that helps you.”

*Language is being asked to cover unusual ground.*

“No. You're dodging.”

Her fingers find the clasp.

*Pavia discarded me.*

“Pavia kept you.”

*In a box.*

“After you told her to.”

*She could have touched me. Once. She could have answered.*

“Maybe. Maybe she was angry. Maybe she respected what you said. Maybe she forgot for years at a time and then felt guilty and changed the velvet. I don't know.”

Neither do I. I know the hard little *all right* that came through Pavia's bones. I know cloth closed around me afterward, so no last plea reached her. I know journeys, relinings, temperatures, tarnish. I have made motive from pressure because motive was warmer.

“Did she promise to come back?” Odelia asks.

*No.*

“Did you ask her not to leave you?”

The chain slackens as Odelia bows her head or lowers her hand; I can feel the alteration, not its cause.

*No.*

“What did you want her to understand?”

There is an answer about worth. I have polished it for longer than Odelia has been alive.

*That I could be hurt.*

Odelia's pulse stumbles once.

“You could've said that.”

*I thought I had said something finer.*

“You said something else.”

The clasp opens.

*Wait. There are distinctions between intent and—*

She removes me.

The world contracts to cooling silver, a chain settling beside me, a hard surface below. Vibrations cross it and fade. I cannot know whether Odelia sits one reach away or leaves the apartment. I cannot know whether the lid waits above me.

I compose explanations. I reduce them. I discard them. With no mind open, even the best phrase is only a private pressure that never moves metal.

Something warm touches my rim.

The narrow path opens through a fingertip.

*I am sorry I hid the part where I ordered the box,* I say.

The fingertip remains. I cannot hear Odelia's answer through it. I resist the urge to improve the apology until it stops being one.

Touch leaves.

Cold spreads again. A short age or a long minute passes.

Then the chain lifts. Odelia sets me against her skin again, beginning the third wearing. Her pulse is steadier now, though one finger holds my lower edge away from the tenderest place at her throat.

“That was better,” she says.

*I had time to edit.*

“Of course you did.”

*Odelia, you inherited the pendant. You did not inherit an assigned collarbone.*

“Right.”

*I would still like to be considered for the position.*

Her breath catches. Not grief this time, I decide. Amusement.

“Here's what I'm deciding today,” she says. “I can leave the box open. I can keep you somewhere I can choose to touch you. I can find someone who actually likes wearing jewellery. Or I can close the lid. None of those is a forever promise.”

The old answer—*wear me*—arrives bright and imperious. Behind it is the word I could not offer Pavia because it seemed too small for me.

*Please do not close the lid.*

“All right.”

The ease of it is almost insulting.

“Why me?” Odelia asks.

*Because you are Pavia's—*

Her finger begins to lift me.

*No. Because you came back after you knew enough to leave.*

She lets me settle.

“Don't turn one decent decision into destiny.”

*I will try to keep destiny within the dimensions of the box.*

“And don't call me Pavia again.”

*Your pulse is quite different.*

“That is a strange apology.”

*It is an observation. I am learning their proper use.*

Odelia adjusts the chain, then releases it. The clasp holds. My full weight rests against her. She has chosen the contact; still, I wait.

“One wearing,” she says. “Until the timer. Here in the empty room. I'm not parading you anywhere.”

*How long?*

“Seven minutes.”

*Seven minutes is an appraisal.*

“Six.”

*Seven has dignity.*

“Do you want it?”

*Yes.*

Small taps travel through Odelia's frame while the chain gives brief changes of tension. When her hand returns to the pendant, its tendons are quick under my edge.

“I have one question,” she says. “What exactly did Pavia say about the cherries?”

I search my own memory, not hers. Pavia's pulse had been brisk with lateness. The cherries were already somewhere outside my reach. Cloth waited beneath me.

*She said, ‘Odelia will look for them.’*

For three beats Odelia holds her breath. Then the same graceless laugh escapes through her nose.

“I did,” she says.

*I know that now.*

“She kept them. One hook broke. She wore them twice more anyway.”

This is an injury to taste and a gift of information. For once I recognize that they can coexist.

*Did she still laugh like that?*

“Until breathing got hard. Even then, sometimes.” Odelia shifts her weight. “She grew terrible tomatoes. Accused everyone else of cheating at cards. Stopped answering calls during treatment and then complained nobody called.”

*Was she alone?*

“Sometimes. Not all the time.”

Her pulse accelerates while her voice becomes flatter. I do not tell her what it means. I have been wrong about stillness, laughter, years, boxes, and the future obligations of a niece. I cannot smooth this rhythm or reach into the thoughts above it. I remain where she put me and listen to what her body carries when her words stop.

After a while Odelia says, “You don't get all thirty-one years tonight.”

*No.*

“Good.”

Then she walks.

The first step swings me a fraction outward; the next seats me against her again. Balance rolls through her from heel to forefoot. Her left side leads each turn. One restless finger catches the chain, releases it, catches it again. Motion returns in layered measures—pulse under breath, breath under stride, stride lifting my weight through the room. Pleasure goes through me so suddenly that speech would only cheapen it.

Odelia is not Pavia with years missing. Pavia settled her weight into her heels and paused before changing direction. Odelia turns sharply, doubles back, stops without warning. I knock once against the small hard ridge below her collarbone.

“Sorry,” she says.

*I have survived an appraisal.*

“Barely.”

She walks again.

When the timer shudders through her hand and ribs, every argument I have rehearsed since the box crowds the inward path. One more minute. Tomorrow. A longer chain. A promise. I hold them where they cannot become her burden.

“Time,” Odelia says.

*Thank you.*

“Don't make it ceremonial.”

*That was inconveniently sincere.*

Her fingers reach for the clasp.

“Tomorrow isn't decided,” she says.

*I understand.*

“Do you?”

*Not fully. I can leave it undecided.*

“That's enough.”

Contact lifts. Pulse, balance, breath, and bone-borne voice vanish together.

Odelia sets me on something hard and cool. No velvet presses my face. No lid answers my raised setting. After a moment, the surface takes a nearby weight with a faint settling tremor, and warmth reaches one edge of my silver.

A fingertip rests on the enamel. The inward path opens. I could fill it.

I wait.

Pressure comes twice—tap, tap—then lifts away.

Room-cool moves over me from every side, and the hard surface carries Odelia's small, irregular shifts beside me.

stories.title: Only Eighteen
stories.prompt: The job of an elf caretaker is hard when the kids aren’t elves. Saying goodbye to those little things after “only” 18 years is so hard.
stories.body:
# Only Eighteen

The first thing Romy did in Ceveth's care was spit milk down the inside of her collar. Denzil, who had been asleep throughout the journey, woke at his sister's satisfied belch and began to scream.

“Yes,” Ceveth told him. “You shall have some too. There is sufficient for everyone, including my underclothes.”

The woman who had brought them laughed, then looked relieved that she had been allowed to. She put the second basket on the floor of the nursery. Beside it she left a bag of clothes which smelled of dried lavender and a little notebook recording what the twins ate. They were six weeks old.

Ceveth had worked in children's households for almost two centuries. The home had hired its first elf caretaker for her experience, her patience, and her willingness to sleep in a room that shared a wall with the nursery. These were her first human babies. She had read about their development before accepting the post; she knew when to expect teeth, speech, the astonishing business of walking. There were tables. She liked a table.

Eighteen years of care, perhaps longer if they needed it. She had owned her indoor shoes for forty-three.
