By midnight she had learned that Romy liked a firm hand beneath her bottom and Denzil required his head at precisely the wrong angle for Ceveth's wrist. By morning she had forgotten which basket she had put the notebook in. There were no tables concerning the sour patch between her shoulder blades, or how to scratch it with a baby occupying each arm.

She rested her cheek against Romy's head. The scalp was hot, with an unexpectedly peppery smell. Denzil stopped crying to listen to something she could not hear.

“Oh, good,” she whispered.

He began again.

For several months she wanted, above all else, to put them down.

***

At five they wanted the story of the hedgehog who stole a bell. Ceveth knew it from a country where she had lived long before coming to the home, and the children liked her to tell it because she could make the bell sound inside her closed mouth.

“Now, the tower in which the bell hung,” she began, “had been built by three brothers, although the eldest—”

“Hedgehog,” said Romy.

“We are coming to him.”

“He's already at the tower.”

“There are things you must know about the tower.”

Denzil, who had his toes tucked into the gap between Ceveth and the arm of the chair, raised a hand. He had recently learned this at lessons and sometimes stood in the privy doorway with his hand up until someone noticed him.

“Yes?”

“I need to know why he wants a bell.”

“To wake the moon.”

“You said for his mum.”

“Did I?”

“His mum was deaf.”

That version did sound familiar. Ceveth had learned the story a hundred and sixty years ago from a woman who changed it according to how much mending she had left. She attempted an explanation of this, but Romy began ringing an imaginary bell and Denzil pushed her foot off his knee. By the time the fight was settled, both twins insisted that the hedgehog had already stolen it. They only wanted the sound.

Ceveth obliged. Romy pressed her ear against Ceveth's chest and laughed at the vibration.

“Again. But enormous.”

Their feet were filthy. Someone had wiped a nose on her skirt. She rang the enormous bell until she was short of breath, and Denzil asked whether they might skip the hedgehog tomorrow.

At nine, Romy made a play of the story in the yard. She cast Denzil as the tower and tied a bucket to his belt. He resigned before the first performance. Ceveth, who had been promised a seat in the audience, spent the afternoon standing with the bucket at her waist while Romy crawled between her feet.

She had sewn little silver leaves along the cuffs of their festival coats that spring. The work took evenings, and she enjoyed the quiet precision of it after the children's noise. In autumn Denzil put his coat on and could no longer straighten his arms. Romy's still fitted, but she wanted her leaves removed. She had decided she disliked silver.

Ceveth unpicked them. It was tedious, and Romy kept asking whether she was cross.

“I am concentrating.”

“Your ears go back when you're cross.”

“They do not.”

Romy crept behind the chair to check. Ceveth turned and snapped her teeth at her, and the child fled shrieking with delight. At supper she asked if the leaves might be sewn onto her stockings instead.

At fourteen Denzil was taller than Ceveth. She made him hold out an arm so she could let down a sleeve and found a burn on the soft inside of his wrist. He had been helping in the home's kitchen after lessons.

“Why didn't you tell me?”

“It's nothing.”

“It was not nothing when it happened.”

“Well, you weren't there when it happened.”

She fetched ointment; he said the cook had already seen to it. Ceveth found she was annoyed with the cook, a sensible woman whom she had liked perfectly well at breakfast.

That night Denzil came to her room with a ridiculous question about the tower. Hadn't the three brothers been giants? Romy was sleeping in the room next door, and he glanced that way before asking.

“Two were,” Ceveth said. “The third had married into the family.”

“Then he wasn't a brother.”

“Sit down. I will explain it.”

He sat on the rug. She took a long time over the explanation, but he did not interrupt her.

***

Four summers later, Ceveth stood holding three pairs of socks outside a closed bedroom door.

“Denzil?”

“Yes.”

“I have your socks.”

“Put them down somewhere.”

“They ought to go in the bag before you fasten it.”

The door opened. He had cut himself shaving under the chin. Her own face had hardly changed while his had acquired, in quick succession, freckles, spots, whiskers. Ceveth reached toward the bead of blood; he rubbed it away before she could speak.

“Thank you,” he said, taking the socks. Then he shut the door, carefully, against her next sentence.

They were catching the noon coach. They had chosen the same day so they could travel together as far as the river crossing. Romy would continue south to join a troupe she had spent the spring pestering. There would be a bunk in a wagon, canvas to scrub, costumes to mend, and, if she proved useful, small parts to play. Denzil's apprenticeship was at a bakery in the town on the other road. Ceveth had gone with him to see the attic room above the ovens, and had eaten a bun so good it had made her briefly resentful.

Both had turned eighteen in the wet week at the beginning of the month. Ceveth had made a cake. Romy had made another because she did not trust Ceveth to use enough sugar. They had eaten both, and Denzil had been sick behind the shed.

They did not have to leave. Their beds were theirs until they chose otherwise. Ceveth had told them so in winter, when leaving had been a thing which might happen after a number of other things. She had written Denzil's first letter to the bakery herself because he had spent three days on a salutation. She had helped Romy work out what the troupe's offered wages would actually buy.

Now Romy's bag was in the passage, standing on a pair of boots. It had been there since dawn.

“What if the coach is early?” Romy called from downstairs.

“It has never been early.”

“It could start.”

Ceveth went down and found her peering through the front window, wearing her new green coat despite the heat. The lining was striped yellow and blue. It was a great deal of coat, and Romy had been showing people the lining for a fortnight.

“You will roast,” Ceveth said.

“I'm taking it off on the coach. I want to arrive in it.”

“Then you would be better to carry it now.”

Romy made a small, strangled noise. She turned, snapped her coat open, and stood displaying herself among the muddy boots and walking sticks.

“Look at it.”

Ceveth looked. The green set off Romy's brown face, and the turned-back cuffs showed how prettily the sleeves fitted. She had put her hair up, badly. All the pins were on one side.

“You look splendid.”

“Thank you.” Romy closed the coat. “That's what I was doing.”

Ceveth wanted to fetch another hairpin. She clasped her own hands instead.

In the kitchen the younger children were being coaxed out to the garden by another caretaker. The twins had endured their farewell at breakfast: sticky kisses, an argument about who could now have Denzil's seat, a small boy crying because he believed the coach would take their beds as well. Ceveth had asked for the rest of the day free. There was no work she could honestly claim to be needed for.

She took the travelling food from the cupboard. Denzil came down with his bag half shut and Romy immediately said, “You've forgotten your brush.”

“I haven't.”

“It's on the washstand.”

“That's yours.”

“Mine has red thread round it.”

“So does mine. You tied it on both.”

“Why would I do that?”

He looked at her. Romy made a face and went upstairs.

Ceveth wrapped the bread more tightly. The cloth had already been folded; she was putting different creases in it. Denzil sat at the table and reached for a plum from the fruit bowl, rolling it beneath his hand.

“Is something troubling you?”

“No.”

“The baker will meet you at the stop.”

“I know.”

“You mustn't worry about finding the house.”

“I'm not.”

The kitchen clock ticked. Ceveth could hear Romy opening drawers overhead, though she had been certain the brush was on the washstand.

“There is another coach on Thursday,” Ceveth said.

Denzil stopped rolling the plum.

“If you felt you wanted a few more days. I could write. You are only eighteen.”

Romy had come back to the kitchen doorway. She was holding two brushes.

“We're eighteen,” she said. “You were there.”

“I was speaking to your brother.”

“He wants to go.”

“Leave it,” Denzil said.

“You do. You've been talking about that bakery since—”

“I said leave it.”

His voice was loud enough to startle them all. Romy set his brush beside him and took hers into the passage. Denzil slid it into his bag without looking at her. Ceveth heard her pull the straps of her bag tight.

Denzil rubbed the plum against his trousers. “Now she'll be like that.”

“She is excited.”

“I am too.” He bit into the plum, which was not ripe enough, and grimaced. “I just feel a bit sick.”

Ceveth had a hundred things for that. She could offer cool water, bread, a damp cloth. They rose readily to her tongue.

“Do you want Thursday?” she asked.

He chewed for a long time. “No. I'll be worse on Thursday.”

She set the parcel of food beside his bag and went into the passage.

Romy was undoing one strap and redoing it, gaining nothing.

“I said only eighteen because it seems very quick to me,” Ceveth said.

“It wasn't quick. I had to go to lessons every day.”

“Yes.”

“And I had to be seventeen for ages. They wouldn't take me last year. I told you.”

“I remember.”

Romy pulled too hard and trapped the edge of her finger under the buckle. She sucked it furiously.

Ceveth remembered much less than she wanted to. There were winters she could not separate, birthday meals at which she could not place the guests. Yet she could remember a particular afternoon when Romy had laughed milk out of her nose, down to the wet crescents on her upper lip. Somewhere around that afternoon Ceveth had felt she was beginning to get the hang of them.

“I would like you to stay,” she said. “That is making me tiresome.”

Romy let go of her finger. “Well.”

“I am sorry.”

“You can come and watch. When they let me do something.”

“I would like that.”

“Not in ten years.”

“Before ten years.”

“Ceveth.”

She had, in fact, put off visiting an old friend for eleven years because the journey involved an inconvenient ferry. “Send me the date. I will come for that date.”

Romy nodded. Then she turned around. “Can you do the back? It's coming out.”

Ceveth removed two pins, held them between her lips, and caught the slipping weight of hair. Romy had cut a section of it herself the previous autumn, denying it even while loose clippings clung to her collar. The shorter strands escaped Ceveth's fingers now. She smoothed them in with the rest as well as she could.

“Don't pull it tight.”

Ceveth loosened her hold.

***

The road lay in white sunlight beyond the shade of the home, and a fly followed Denzil's food parcel with infuriating persistence. Romy walked ahead of them, swinging her free arm. Once she turned to make sure they were watching, and opened her coat again.

“Yes,” Denzil called. “It's got an inside.”

She stuck her tongue out. Ceveth laughed; it came so easily that the morning loosened for a moment. She wanted to go on walking. They could follow this road through the fields, eat their bread under a tree, come back by the narrow path behind the laundry. Denzil would complain about his shoes. Romy would get bored and take a shortcut which wasn't one.

At the stop they still had twenty minutes. Romy put her bag beside the milestone and stood in the road to look for the coach.

“Off the road, little one,” Ceveth said.

Romy glanced back. Ceveth raised her hands in surrender. Romy moved as far as the verge.

Denzil sat on the low wall. His boots were broad and new, his trouser cuffs a little too short. She had made them the right length. She knew she had. He brushed grit off a space beside him, and she sat down.

“Does she know about the window?” he asked.

“Who?”

“The baker. That I like it open.”

“I don't believe I mentioned it.”

“Good.” He picked at a loose thread on his bag. “I can tell her.”

Beside the milestone, Romy had found a white stone and was trying to balance it on the toe of her boot. She dropped it, picked it up, dropped it again.

“If I don't like it,” Denzil said, “the bakery. I don't mean the window.”

Ceveth waited.

“Could I come back for a bit? If it turns out I can't—if it isn't what I thought?”

“Of course.”

“Even if it's quite soon?”

She pictured him back at the kitchen table before the month was out. He must not see how much she liked that.

“Whenever it is.”

He nodded and scraped at the thread again. Then he leaned sideways, his shoulder bumping hers. She put an arm around him. It did not reach as far as it used to. His hair smelled of the harsh soap he had insisted on buying, and beneath it, faintly, of his warm scalp.

“Your ears are going back,” he said.

“They are not.”

“I can see one.”

“It is a very bright day.”

He put his head against hers and stayed there. Romy stopped trying to balance the stone.

Then the coach came, early after all, and there was too much to do.

The driver wanted their bags. Romy had the tickets but could not find the pocket she had put them in. A woman leaning out of the coach window asked whether this was the stop for the mill. Denzil dropped the food; Ceveth caught it against her knee and said something she hoped the woman had not heard.

“Not till the next village,” Romy told the woman. “Ceveth, which pocket did I show you?”

“The one inside.”

“They're all inside.”

She found them while Denzil was saying goodbye. He put both arms around Ceveth and lifted her an inch off the ground, whether by accident or intention she could not tell.

“Mind your back,” she said into his shirt.

“It's a very old elf. Heavy with years.”

“That is a dreadful joke.”

“I know.” He set her down. “I know.”

She kissed his cheek, and he made no attempt to wipe it away. The driver was strapping Romy's bag to the luggage rack. Denzil went to watch and offer advice which was not wanted.

Romy stood in front of Ceveth, tickets crumpled in her hand.

“Well, then,” she said brightly.

Ceveth opened her arms. Romy stepped into them with the haste of someone hoping to get a thing over with; then her whole weight changed. Her face pressed into Ceveth's neck.

“Oh,” she said, muffled and angry.

Ceveth held her. One of the pins dug into her cheek. She would have stood there until nightfall with that pin digging into her cheek, but Romy pulled away, blinking.

“I'm getting on.”

“Yes.”

“Don't look like that.”

“I don't know what I'm looking like.”

Romy wiped her nose with the back of her wrist. “Neither do I.”

They laughed badly. Ceveth touched the green sleeve, then let it go.

The twins climbed aboard and found a window, quarrelling briefly over which of them should sit beside it. Romy won, but she shifted forward to let Denzil lean past her. The driver called to the horses. The coach shuddered.

“Do the bell,” Denzil said suddenly.

Romy turned on him. “What?”

“Just do it.”

Ceveth closed her mouth and made the deep, ridiculous sound. It shook her lips. Denzil tried to answer it and produced a thin nasal hum. Romy covered her face, laughing. The woman going to the mill leaned away from them.

The wheels began to roll. Romy uncovered her face and waved with both hands.

Ceveth waved back. She walked three steps with the coach, then stopped before she had to run. Denzil called something she did not catch. She cupped a hand to her ear, but he was already too far away, and Romy was laughing at whatever it had been.

They were still leaning out when the coach reached the bend. The green sleeve disappeared last.

Ceveth went back to the wall and sat in the space Denzil had cleared for her. Dust settled on her shoes. She was still wearing the smile she had wanted Romy to see when the first sob bent her over.

stories.title: A Note of Spite
stories.prompt: Defense spells applied like perfume. "My dear, you smell divine tonight. Is that a new protective enchantment you're wearing?"
stories.body:
# A Note of Spite

Lavinia had put on too much protection. Halfway up Clorinda's stairs, in the heat from the candles on the landing, the neroli opened so violently that the gentleman behind her stopped to sneeze.

She moved aside to let him pass. A spark leaped from a wick toward her sleeve; she breathed out, felt the familiar cool tightening over her skin, and watched it die an inch from the lace. At least the blend worked. She had paid enough for it, though the perfumer had insisted the price was mostly for the flowers.

At the top of the stairs, three women were comparing wrists. One had worn a rain defense with so much moss in it that she smelled faintly flooded. Another was trying to tuck a handkerchief under a bracelet before its fresh anointing reached her pale cuff. Lavinia passed them with her hands well away from her own gown. She had chosen cream, a color which depended on other people's good behavior.

Clorinda stood at the drawing-room door in a green dress Lavinia had never seen. Her bosom was sprinkled with little seed pearls. In the warm hollow above them, something delicious was flowering.

“My dear, you smell divine tonight. Is that a new protective enchantment you're wearing?”

“Very new.” Clorinda offered her wrist.

Lavinia bent to it. Pear first, the firm flesh just under the skin; then violet, deep and powdery. She turned the wrist slightly, finding the warmth beneath.

“You've finally abandoned that dreadful almond.”

“You gave me the almond.”

“I was younger.”

“It was at midsummer.” Clorinda pressed her cheek to Lavinia's, laughing. Her skin was hot. “I'm so glad you're here. Look at my dress.”

Lavinia stepped back. The dress was good, which ought not to have surprised her. Clorinda generally dressed as if she expected to be called upon to carry something; tonight her sleeves ended at the elbow and the skirt swept clear of her shoes in front, showing green silk stockings. She had chosen the stockings herself, apparently. She revolved to display a row of small covered buttons.

“You can't possibly do those up alone,” Lavinia said.

“I didn't.”

“How promising.”

“My maid. Don't be tiresome. There's wine in the next room.”

Fifty suited Clorinda. She had told everyone she was fifty, written it on the invitations, and ordered a cake large enough to make concealment absurd. Lavinia, who was fifty-two and said so only when asked, had spent some pleasant afternoons threatening to arrange all fifty candles around a looking glass. Clorinda had threatened to invite a gentleman who read his own translations aloud. Neither threat had been carried out. The unoccupied corner by the piano was plainly waiting for them.

Lavinia took a glass and drifted back to the doorway. She liked watching Clorinda receive people. Nobody was allowed to get away with touching her fingers and murmuring; she drew them in, demanded to see a recovered ankle, remembered a marriage, sometimes the wrong marriage. Lavinia had been rescuing her from such mistakes for thirty years.

A woman in blue approached with a husband whose whiskers grew almost into his eyes. Clorinda held out both hands.

“How very delighted I am that you could—”

Lavinia pinched a fold of air between her finger and thumb, breathed a tiny working into it, and flicked.

The trick ought to have lifted *come* into a canary's squeak. It was a little trick, their oldest: one syllable, nothing sore or lasting. Clorinda had once used it on Lavinia's very sincere thanks to a committee. Both of them had been asked to leave.

“—come,” Clorinda finished, in her usual substantial voice.

A sharp green smell cut through the pear, like the snap of a leaf stem. Lavinia's fingers tingled. The working came apart against Clorinda's throat.

The woman in blue sniffed appreciatively. Clorinda glanced at Lavinia, then turned to her guests.

“I was just admiring it,” Lavinia said. “Such an unusual finish.”

“Is that the violet?” the woman asked.

“No,” said Clorinda. “It's something else.”

“Does it keep mosquitoes off? We couldn't sit out at all last week.”

“Only interference with the voice.”

Lavinia looked down at her wine. A throat defense. She had seen them sold for public speakers, though never in such a pretty fragrance. Usually they smelled of burnt fennel and the conviction that somebody else ought to stop talking.

“I wish I'd had it when my sister visited,” the woman said.

“It wouldn't stop your sister,” Clorinda said. “Only a hex on your own voice.”

The woman was disappointed. Her husband had found a dish of olives and did not appear to have heard any of it. Clorinda steered them toward the wine, leaving Lavinia by the door with her unused laugh.

So that was tonight's game. Clorinda had made arrangements. Lavinia lifted her glass to her, but Clorinda had turned away.

There were more chairs than usual in the drawing room. Several stood in rows facing the piano, and a low vase had been removed from its lid. Lavinia went to examine the little card propped on the music stand. Clorinda's large handwriting announced a piano piece, *a song*, and supper. Beside the middle item, in smaller letters, she had added her own name.

Lavinia found her fastening a brooch on an elderly guest whose hands were unsteady.

“I see we're to have music.”

“We are.” Clorinda squinted at the catch. “There. Will it do?”

“Too high,” the guest said.

Clorinda unfastened it again.

“And a song,” Lavinia said.

“Yes.”

“Which one? Am I to guess?”

“The soldier and the little dog.”

Lavinia laughed. They had learned it as girls, along with other songs their teacher had considered insufficiently elevated. A soldier serenaded his sweetheart beneath her window, boasted of all the things he dared, and was defeated by the smallest animal in the house. Clorinda had always given the soldier an enormous chest and no neck.

“Oh, we must do the march first. Do you remember? When we came in backward?”

“I'm only singing.”

“I could carry a sword. That poker would do.”

“There.” Clorinda stood back from the brooch. “Better?”

The elderly guest inspected herself in a small mirror and said it would have to be. As she moved away, Clorinda rubbed the dent the catch had made in her thumb.

“You'd miss the piano coming in,” she told Lavinia. “And I've practised it without a march.”

“You've practised?”

“Of course.”

Lavinia glanced at the card again. The name had been added in the same ink, with the same pen, but cramped into a space too small for it. She had imagined Clorinda writing the programme that afternoon, laughing at her own impulse. Apparently there had been rehearsals.

“With whom?”

“The gentleman who's playing. He's in the other room somewhere. A brown coat.”

“That does narrow it.”

“He has one eye.”

“Considerably.”

Clorinda did not laugh. She was looking down into her bag.

“Have you lost something?”

“My scent. No, here it is. Come through a moment. I want the glass.”

Lavinia followed her into the small room off the hall where guests left their wraps. Clorinda had put out cotton and little bowls of unscented oil for lifting away defenses that had spoiled on the journey. One shawl smelled powerfully of thunderstorms. Someone had left an open bottle beside it, and Clorinda corked that before attending to herself.

Her own bottle was narrow, with a violet glass foot. She touched the stopper beneath each ear, then to the hollow of her throat. With two fingers laid over her pulse, she drew a slow breath, supplying the force that the fresh oil would hold close to her skin. Pear filled the room. Without her, it would have been expensive oil in a bottle; on her, breathing and warm, it had just undone Lavinia's neatest little hex.

“How long does it last?” Lavinia asked.

“A few hours. Less if it's hot.”

“It's very hot.”

“That's why I'm doing it again.” Clorinda frowned at a glistening spot above the pearls. “Too much there?”

Lavinia held out her hand for the stopper. Clorinda gave it to her automatically. For a moment it was like their old preparations, the crowded glass, the whispered estimates of who might come, Clorinda unable to decide on earrings until Lavinia threatened to go without her. She used the flat edge of the stopper to lift the excess oil away before it could run into the dress.

“There. You'll stain yourself otherwise.”

“Thank you.”

“You've gone to a great deal of trouble to prevent one squeak.”

Clorinda looked at her in the mirror.

“Yes.”

“I might have chosen something else.”

“I hoped you wouldn't.”

Lavinia replaced the stopper. Somewhere outside, a guest launched into a story she had heard from him twice that month. She could have made a remark about that, and Clorinda would have laughed; she could practically feel the little doorway opening between them. But Clorinda was straightening her pearls.

“You know,” Lavinia said, “if you're worried about the singing, we can make it funny from the beginning. A helmet, perhaps. I could find a saucepan.”

“It is funny.”

“Yes, but deliberately. I mean the entrance. Let them know what they're getting.”

“They're getting a song.”

“Of course. But you've never liked that part in the second verse. There's no need to stand there and wrestle with it while everyone watches. We could come in with the saucepan and—”

“I don't want the saucepan.”

“You haven't seen it yet.”

Clorinda put the bottle in her bag.

“It might be a very good saucepan,” Lavinia added.

“I heard you.”

Lavinia turned toward the door. Across the hall, a footman was trying to find room on an already crowded tray for an abandoned glass. She waited until he had gone past.

“I wasn't proposing to spoil it.”

“Then don't.”

“I was proposing to help.”

Clorinda pulled a chair out from the wall and sat, carefully spreading the green skirt. Under its edge her foot began moving, heel planted, toe lifting and falling. Lavinia could hear a little tune in the rhythm. She had never particularly liked being the only person standing.

“How long have you been preparing this?”

“Since the spring.”

“The spring.”

“Not constantly. On Thursdays, mostly.”

“All those Thursdays.” Lavinia sat on a stool beside the washstand. “I thought you'd given it up. We both gave it up.”

“I gave up the lessons.”

Lavinia remembered why. There had been a recital, and Clorinda had lost her place. Lavinia, seated beside her to turn the pages, had sung the missing passage in the voice of their teacher. It had been very good. The girls in the back row had howled, and Clorinda had laughed so much that they never finished. They had gone home arm in arm, still doing the voice.

“You didn't tell me you still sang.”

“You know I sing. You complain if I do it in a carriage.”

“Everyone complains about that. You're very loud in a carriage.”

“Well.”

“It isn't the same as this.”

“No.” Clorinda smoothed one of the folds of her skirt, then spoiled it with her thumb. “I wanted to do this.”

From the drawing room came three testing notes on the piano. Clorinda's foot stopped.

Lavinia imagined her standing there, round-cheeked and eager, reaching for the upper note. The whiskered husband would go on chewing. Someone would look down into a glass. There would be a little silence where people decided how warmly to applaud. Lavinia knew exactly how to break that silence. She always had.

“I don't see why you didn't simply ask me to leave your voice alone.”

Clorinda opened her mouth, closed it, and rubbed a finger along her eyebrow.

“I didn't want to argue about it before my birthday as well.”

Lavinia's own perfume suddenly felt heavy. There was too much of it under her chin, and the little room was too warm.

“Well, I can go, if you'd prefer.”

“No. I wouldn't.”

“You appear to have made all the arrangements.”

“It's my house.” Clorinda looked exasperated, then almost immediately tired. “Oh, don't go. Please. I wanted you here. I wanted you to hear it.”

She reached across and caught Lavinia's fingers. The gesture was awkward from the chair, and Lavinia had to lean forward or let her hand be pulled off her lap.

“The whole thing,” Clorinda said. “I've done all this practising. Even the stupid bit with the dog.”

“That's the best bit.”

“I know. But I can't start there.”

There were voices in the hall. Clorinda released her and stood to let two arriving guests lay down their wraps. She took one woman's hand in both of hers and exclaimed over a ring. The pear fragrance went with her into the doorway, leaving behind a little violet and the sharper smell clinging to the storm-scented shawl. Lavinia sat for a moment longer on the stool.

When she returned to the drawing room, the pianist was already playing. He was an old man in a brown coat, as described, with a black patch over one eye. Lavinia chose a chair near the front because it was empty and because choosing the back now would look like something. She put her bag on her knees and listened to the piece. It was longer than she expected. Several times it seemed about to end and thought better of it.

Clorinda sat against the wall with her hands clasped. Once she saw Lavinia and lifted her fingers, just off her lap. Lavinia nodded.

Then the piano piece really did end. There was applause, and Clorinda rose. Her skirt caught on the chair leg. She bent to free it, showing a stretch of green silk above her shoe, and Lavinia felt the person beside her turn for a comment.

There was an excellent one available about mounting a defense against furniture. Lavinia had only to murmur it. Nothing in Clorinda's bottle could stop her.

But Clorinda had straightened. She was looking at the pianist, who was moving the music on the stand. Lavinia was trying to remember whether they used to begin after four bars or eight; by the time she remembered, her neighbor had turned away.

“A little slower,” Clorinda told the pianist.

He nodded and played the opening. She drew breath. Pear and violet reached Lavinia over the heads of the first row.

The first note was too small for the breath that had preceded it. Clorinda tried again on the next one, louder, and sang the soldier's arrival at his sweetheart's gate with her eyes fixed somewhere above the listeners. Her lower voice was pleasant. Lavinia had forgotten that. There was warmth in it, and a roughness near the bottom which made the soldier sound as though he had been travelling without much comfort.

He had crossed mountains and fought robbers. He had other accomplishments Lavinia missed because she was watching Clorinda's hands. They had been pinned to her sides; now one lifted, palm up, making an uncertain mountain.

In the second verse the tune climbed. Here came the part Lavinia had offered to conceal beneath a saucepan. Clorinda looked at the pianist. He looked back. She took the phrase lower than Lavinia remembered, letting the piano carry the high notes over her. It was a different arrangement. Of course it was. They had had all those Thursdays.

The woman beside Lavinia shifted her feet. Behind them a glass clicked against another. Clorinda's voice shook on a held note, and Lavinia discovered that she had tightened every muscle in her own throat, as if that might steady somebody else's. She swallowed. She had missed the next line.

The soldier was at the gate now, calling on his sweetheart to admit him. Clorinda looked down at an imaginary latch, put her hand on it, and stopped.

The piano gave two quick, high notes.

Clorinda peered downward. Her chin went back into her neck. The splendid chest she had inflated during the first verse began to subside.

Lavinia knew what came next. She had known it for thirty years. But she did not know that Clorinda would try to step around the invisible little dog, find it occupying that part of the floor too, and retreat half a step into the tail of her own gown. The grand voice went thin with indignation. She demanded the removal of the animal. A second pair of notes answered her.

Then the soldier, who had faced lions and blades and tumbling rocks, attempted a friendly whistle. Almost no sound emerged.

Lavinia laughed. It broke out of her at an ugly volume. Clorinda glanced at her, and for an instant Lavinia thought she had spoiled it after all. But Clorinda held the look, drew herself up for another attempt, and produced an even smaller whistle.

The woman beside Lavinia laughed too. Someone farther back asked what had happened. Clorinda continued, pressing herself against the piano as her soldier begged to be admitted by another gate. The last line arrived in a rush; she nearly overtook the accompaniment and had to wait, visibly, for the final chord.

She bowed before it had quite finished.

People applauded. Some warmly, some because the song was over. The whiskered gentleman was clapping with the slow, conscientious air of somebody who had been elsewhere for most of it. Clorinda thanked the pianist, then bent to say something to him which Lavinia couldn't hear. He laughed and shook his head.

Chairs scraped back. The door opened on the smell of supper, and the room began to rearrange itself around the possibility of food. Lavinia stayed seated. Clorinda came toward her, stopped to accept a compliment, and then came on, pink to the ears.

“Well?” she said.

Lavinia looked up at her. The pear had softened. Violet lingered about the warm green silk, and there was no bitter leaf in it now.

“That whistle.”

“I nearly couldn't do it.”

“Do it again.”

Clorinda glanced toward the departing guests. Then she raised her magnificent soldier's chest and tried, unsuccessfully, to summon a dog no larger than her shoe.

Lavinia covered her mouth. It was worse from this close. Clorinda began laughing too, losing the face she was trying to make, and caught hold of Lavinia's shoulder.

“They'll think that was you,” she said.

“I should like the credit.”

“Well, you can't have it.” Clorinda gave her shoulder a small, possessive squeeze. “I practised.”

stories.title: An Ordinary Education
stories.prompt: "Wait why do you visit a normal school instead of a magic school? I thought demi-humans were inherently magical." "Naturally born ones, yes." "Naturally born..." "I was created in a lab, by a bunch of amoral scientists determined to play god, if that's what you are asking."
stories.body:
# An Ordinary Education

The headphones in the language classroom were supposed to go over your head. Delsie had worn hers under her chin, with the cups pushed up behind her jaw, while a recorded man repeatedly asked directions to a swimming pool. Her rabbit ears had heard him perfectly well. The cups were mostly there to satisfy the teacher.

At lunch, Bettina put two fingers under her own chin and said, “Like this?”

“Higher. You have to look as though your tooth hurts.”

Bettina tried it. Delsie laughed with a mouthful of sandwich and got bread on her sleeve. It was the first time she had laughed at school without first checking whether somebody was laughing at her.

“Wait why do you visit a normal school instead of a magic school? I thought demi-humans were inherently magical.”

“Naturally born ones, yes.”

“Naturally born...”

“I was created in a lab, by a bunch of amoral scientists determined to play god, if that's what you are asking.”

Delsie took another bite. This was when people generally apologized or became very interested in something behind her. She had practiced the sentence until she could say it without having to choose any of its words.

Bettina kept her fingers under her chin. Then she lowered them.

“Oh. That's horrible.”

“Yes.”

“Are they still there?”

“At the lab? It's closed. Two of them are in prison.”

“Good.” Bettina pulled the lid off her yogurt, saw the watery bit, and put it back on. “Sorry. I thought you just didn't get in. My cousin didn't get in and he won't talk about it.”

“I wouldn't get in. I haven't got any magic.”

“None at all?”

Delsie shook her head. The movement sent one gray ear brushing against the strap of her bag. There was a pale scar inside the other, mostly hidden by fur. Bettina glanced at the ear and then at the yogurt again.

“Do you want this? I hate it when it does that.”

“You can stir it.”

“I know. Do you want it?”

Delsie took it. The yogurt was peach, with little cubes of something that could just about have been fruit. They ate without talking for a while. Around them, chairs scraped and pupils shouted across distances they could have walked in four seconds.

“Do you skate?” Bettina asked.

Delsie had no sentence prepared for this.

“Yes.”

“Come on Friday, then. Roller rink. Six o'clock. I was going with my cousin but he's doing some stupid thing with his boyfriend.”

“All right.”

“Have you got your own?”

“Not anymore.”

The first lie had been very small. The second gave it a past.

Bettina took out her phone and slid it across the table so Delsie could put in her number. The case had a raised pink strawberry on it, and the strawberry had lost every one of its painted seeds.

***

By Thursday, Delsie knew that Bettina hated peach yogurt but liked actual peaches, lost one particular silver ring so often that finding it had stopped making her happy, and wanted to cut her own fringe despite a previous attempt for which there was photographic evidence.

Bettina knew that Delsie lived with a guardian above a pharmacy, took two buses to school, and was bad at chemistry. The chemistry had come as a disappointment.

“But you were made by scientists.”

“They didn't let me mark the tests.”

“No, I just thought you'd have picked it up.”

Delsie turned over her exercise book. Seven out of twenty was too low to leave facing upward. Bettina, who had got nine, let her copy a corrected diagram until the teacher came past. Then she covered it with her elbow, trapping Delsie's pencil.

They drew increasingly ugly versions of each other in the back of Delsie's notebook. Bettina gave Delsie ears so long they went off the top of the page. Delsie drew Bettina's proposed fringe as a single square tooth. Bettina wanted the drawing photographed to send to her sister, but only after she had added a much better nose. On Thursday she sent Delsie a song with a message saying it was terrible. Delsie listened to it nine times before bed.

Delsie learned things about Friday without asking questions that would reveal anything. When Bettina mentioned the rental counter, she said, “Are the skates still awful?” and found out that you had to leave your shoes there. When Bettina complained about the price of drinks, Delsie learned how much money to bring. She learned that the floor was wood, that the music was loud, and that you went around in the same direction as everybody else.

At home she watched skating videos with the sound low. Her guardian knocked, brought in the laundry, and told her she could have a lift home on Friday if she called before nine.

“Unless you want the bus,” she added.

Delsie did not want the bus. She wanted a lift that nobody saw her get into. She negotiated a meeting point outside the supermarket, then spent twenty minutes practicing bent knees and a confident expression on her bedroom carpet.

She had been out of the laboratory for two years and at this school for four days. Adults still sometimes spoke about how well she was settling. She hated the pleased surprise with which they said it, even when they were kind. Bettina had invited her somewhere without consulting anybody or asking whether she would find it too much. Delsie wanted to keep the invitation exactly as it was.

On Friday she packed thick socks and wore the green T-shirt she had bought herself. She left the house so early that she had to walk twice around the block before going into the rink.

***

Bettina was already there, sitting on a bench in the carpeted area beside the floor. Her own skates were white, with red wheels and one black lace. Delsie had seen them in photographs. In person they looked terribly professional.

“You're early,” Bettina said.

“So are you.”

“Yes, but I meant to be. Have you got the money? You pay over there.”

The boy at the counter asked Delsie's shoe size, gave her brown skates, and took her trainers. It felt wrong to watch them disappear onto a shelf without her. She tied the skates tightly and stood up.

On carpet, they were heavy shoes. Heavy shoes were manageable.

Bettina took her elbow while they crossed to the entrance in the barrier. “Watch the little step.”

Delsie watched the little step. Beyond it, the polished floor reflected strips of violet light. People moved together in a broad, counterclockwise river: small children flapping, teenagers in twos and threes, a white-haired man who hardly seemed to move his feet. A boy with curled horns coasted past with tiny green lights hopping between his fingertips. An attendant pointed at a sign, and the boy closed his fist around them.

Bettina rolled onto the wood. Delsie put one foot after her. The foot left.

She grabbed the barrier and brought the foot back underneath her by force. Her other skate tried going in the opposite direction. Bettina turned, skating backward for a few feet, and laughed.

“Oh, don't. You'll make me fall.”

Delsie laughed too, loudly, as though the whole thing had been intentional.

Then Bettina kept going.

Delsie stayed by the entrance, both hands gripping the rounded wooden rail. Somebody behind her said excuse me. She shuffled sideways, helped along by the barrier, and got out of the opening.

Bettina returned after a circuit. “Are you coming?”

“These are different from the ones I had.”

“Are they too loose?”

“No. The wheels.”

Bettina looked down. “They're normal wheels.”

“I can see that.”

“Have you only done inlines?”

The videos had explained what those were. “It's been ages.”

“Oh, right. Here.”

Bettina offered her forearm. Delsie left her right hand on the rail and took the arm with her left. The skates rolled forward six inches, quite smoothly, and for those six inches she could see herself doing this all evening: green shirt, gray ears, somebody to talk to, her body taking her where she wanted.

Then Bettina turned toward her and Delsie's left foot veered outward.

“Whoa. Knees,” Bettina said.

“I know about the knees.”

“Then bend them.”

“They're bent.”

“More. Like you're sitting down.” Bettina dropped into a squat and rose again, all while moving. “See?”

Delsie had seen. Seeing was not the problem.

They traveled the length of the barrier with Delsie's right hand dragging along it. Bettina pointed out the drinks counter, the toilets, and three girls from the year above who were gathered near the middle of the floor. One wore an enormous blue skirt that swayed around her knees. Bettina waved. The girl in the skirt waved back.

“That's who I told you about. With the video?”

Delsie did not remember a video.

“The one doing the thing with her feet. I showed you yesterday.”

“You showed me lots of things.”

“Well, that was one of them.”

They reached the bend. Delsie stopped.

“You can't just stop,” Bettina said, stopping beside her. “You've got to turn.”

“I am turning.”

“You're looking at the turn.”

A little girl went past pushing a low wheeled frame. Her father followed, carrying a coat and a bag and a second, smaller coat. The girl had a sparkling purple helmet. Delsie studied the floor until they were gone.

“Do you want one of those?” Bettina asked.

“No.”

“They're not just for little kids.”

“I said no.”

“All right. Don't pull my sleeve, though. You're stretching it.”

Delsie loosened her grip. Bettina's sleeve slid through her fingers and she grabbed it again.

They got around the bend. Delsie let go of the rail for perhaps a second, perhaps less. Bettina said, “Good!” so loudly that the white-haired man looked toward them.

“Don't do that.”

“What?”

“Announce it.”

“I only said good.”

“Yes. I heard.”

Bettina pressed her lips together. For a little while she said nothing, and Delsie could hear the wheels against the wood and a singer insisting that tonight was the night. She wished it would be whatever night he wanted so he could stop asking.

Near the far corner, the girls in the middle began trying a sideways step together. The girl in the blue skirt beckoned to Bettina.

“In a minute!” Bettina called.

Delsie moved her right hand farther down the rail. Her palm was hot. There was a place on the wood where the varnish had worn through, and she could feel every ridge.

“You're doing the walking thing again,” Bettina said. “Try pushing. Just a little.”

Delsie pushed. Her legs separated, her stomach dropped, and she clutched Bettina hard enough to pull them both toward the wall.

“Okay. Again, but smaller.”

A bell had hung above Delsie's bed in the laboratory. For three nights one spring, they had kept waking her and telling her to make it ring without touching it. She remembered the brass rim, the dent on one side, the man saying again while he ate something from a paper bag. She had cried because she was tired. On the fourth morning he had written uncooperative on her chart.

Bettina was waiting beside her in a stretched yellow sleeve. She was sixteen. She didn't know about the bell.

“I don't want you telling me every single thing I'm doing.”

“I'm trying to help.”

“Well, don't.”

“Fine.”

Bettina freed her arm. Delsie caught the rail with both hands.

“Go and do the foot thing,” Delsie said.

Bettina looked over her shoulder. “Are you going to come off, or—”

“I can manage.”

“You're cross whatever I do.”

“I'm not cross.”

Bettina gave her a look that would have annoyed Delsie even if it hadn't been deserved. Then she went.

Delsie had expected another question. Perhaps one last, irritating offer. Instead Bettina was already halfway to the middle, lifting her arms to join the others, and Delsie was left with the exact amount of help she had requested.

She hated the blue skirt.

***

The music changed. Delsie made herself go forward as far as a pale patch on the rail. Then to a screw head. Then to where a person had carved half a rude word before either stopping or running out of talent.

She wanted to leave. She wanted Bettina to look over and see her skating brilliantly. She wanted her trainers back, and she wanted the brown skates to belong to her so she could take them home and learn in private for six months and return to this particular Friday.

A child rounded the curve too widely and brushed her arm. “Sorry!” he called, already gone.

She had worried that everybody would stare. Almost nobody had time. They needed the space immediately ahead of them, the next turn, their friend's hand. When she looked toward the middle, Bettina was concentrating on the older girl's feet.

They did the step slowly: one foot across, one behind. Bettina copied. The three older girls turned. Bettina turned the other way and ended up facing their backs. She hurried around them, laughing with her mouth open too far. The girl in blue demonstrated again.

Delsie watched with great satisfaction.

Then Bettina got the first part right. She glanced toward the barrier, apparently to see whether Delsie had noticed, and Delsie looked down too late.

Bettina raised a hand. Delsie did not raise hers.

For another half circuit she argued with Bettina in her head. She explained that some people had not spent their childhoods being driven to birthday parties. Bettina said something ignorant, and Delsie answered it perfectly. By the time she reached the entrance again, she had made herself so unhappy that she almost missed the gap.

She shuffled through onto the carpet. Her legs stopped trying to escape. There was the bench, there were the shelves with her shoes, and there was a clock showing that they had been here for thirty-eight minutes.

She sat down.

Her phone offered a way out. She could say she was ill. Her guardian would come early, buy something unnecessary in the supermarket while she waited, and take her home. There would be the room where she already knew how to do everything, because she had arranged it that way.

Delsie opened their messages, then closed them. Across the floor Bettina was trying the step again. She was still getting it wrong. She kept trying it beside people who could see.

Delsie took one skate off. A red seam marked her ankle above the sock. The skate looked quite small on the bench beside her. She lifted it, loosened the laces, and put it back on, leaving more room at the top.

She was tying the second one when Bettina came through the barrier.

“Have you finished?”

“No.”

Bettina sat at the far end of the bench. She bent to pick a twist of fluff from beside one wheel, then stopped and looked at Delsie instead.

“I can't do that stupid step.”

“I saw.”

“You could've waved.”

Delsie tugged the ends of her lace unevenly. One loop was long enough to go under a wheel. She undid it.

“I thought you didn't need me for anything.”

Bettina frowned. “It was a wave.”

“I know.”

The music came through the open entrance less loudly here. Somebody dropped coins beside the drinks machine and swore. Bettina ran a finger under the tongue of her skate.

“I've never been,” Delsie said.

“What?”

“Skating. Ever.”

Bettina looked at her brown boots, then at her face. “Why did you say you had?”

“I don't know.”

She knew, but not in a way she could get out without making it sound worse. She wound the lace around her finger.

“You could have said,” Bettina said. “I wouldn't have just gone off at the start.”

“Yes. You'd have been all...” Delsie made a small, helpless gesture.

“All what?”

“Careful.”

Bettina pulled a face. “I was careful. You nearly took my arm off.”

Delsie looked at the stretched sleeve. There was a faint gray smudge where her hand had been.

“Sorry.”

“It's fine. It'll wash.”

“No, for being horrible.”

“Oh.” Bettina picked at a loose thread. “You were a bit.”

Delsie waited. No explanation of how understandable it was arrived. Bettina's hair had come partly out of its clip and was stuck to her forehead.

“I still want to do it,” Delsie said. “But I don't want that purple baby thing.”

“The frames are yellow. The helmet was purple.”

“Whatever.”

“And I'm not holding you the entire time.”

“All right.”

“I mean it. My shoulder hurts.”

Delsie nodded. Bettina rubbed the shoulder, and Delsie felt an unpleasant pinch of guilt. She had not meant to hurt her.

“Can you just come around once?” she asked.

Bettina considered. “Slowly?”

“Obviously slowly.”

“You don't have to say obviously. I know now.”

Delsie finished tying her skate. This time both loops were short enough.

***

Bettina went through the entrance first and waited out of the traffic. Delsie followed with her hand on the rail. The floor was no less slippery. The song Bettina had sent her began, and Delsie resented how much of it she had to spend looking at her own feet.

“Look where you're going,” Bettina said.

Delsie looked up at her.

“Not at me. Over there.”

There was nothing to look at over there except a long stretch of floor. Delsie looked anyway. She moved one foot, then the other, and for a little distance the wheels carried her without doing anything unexpected.

Bettina skated beside her with both hands clasped behind her back. After a while she began singing the chorus.

“Those aren't the words,” Delsie said.

“Yes, they are.”

“No. It's 'stay awake.'”

“That's what I said.”

“You said 'steak away.'”

Bettina sang it again, much louder and deliberately wrong. Delsie snorted. Her skate wobbled, and she steadied herself against the rail without seizing Bettina. Neither of them mentioned it.

At the bend she offered her left hand, palm upward. Bettina took it. They rounded the corner, inconveniently slow, and Delsie's left skate caught Bettina's right. For one suspended instant both girls stood there with their feet touching, trying to decide which of them should move.

“Wait,” Delsie said.

Bettina moved.

They folded down against the barrier, Bettina landing on one knee, Delsie on her bottom. It hurt, but not enough to stop her hearing Bettina make an extraordinary honking noise. She had never heard anyone laugh like that at school.

“Your foot,” Delsie said, with all the dignity she could retain from the floor, “was in my foot's way.”

“My foot was there first.”

“It was beside me and then it was under me.”

“Because you brought yours over!”

Delsie tried to demonstrate with the offending skate. Bettina shoved it away, still laughing, then caught Delsie's hand before she could slide any farther. Delsie held on and began her explanation again, louder this time, because Bettina was plainly not listening.

stories.title: Where It Hurts
stories.prompt: A knight became very famous among adventurers for wielding a sword that inflicts "emotional wounds." Today, you saw someone get struck by that sword.
stories.body:
# Where It Hurts

Dovran gave me his hat and asked whether, if the knight struck him, I would tell people he had been protecting me.

“From what?”

“Think of something. I'm about to be busy.”

He took the hat back, pulled out its feather, and gave it to me again. He had bought the feather that morning. Already its preservation required two people.

I laughed. In the inside pocket of my coat was a ticket for the evening coach, bought before he woke. My pack was waiting at the booking yard. I had paid for a winter room inland, with a window that shut and no gap between the bed and the wall, and I had not told him any of this. We had been travelling together for four years. I wanted one more pleasant afternoon with him.

At the hiring fair there were people who had survived things no sensible person would approach, and nearly all of them had come to watch Sir Frascot. His sword was famous wherever adventurers drank. I had heard of a captain who, struck by it, had wept into his own helmet; of a highway robber who had apologized to a horse; of a swordswoman who had carried on fighting and won. That last account was always disputed by somebody who hadn't been there.

The wounds were emotional. Everyone knew that much. No severed fingers, no wound fever, no holding your insides in with your coat. We found this very funny at night, around fires, while picking ticks out of ourselves.

Frascot was taking challengers in a roped square between the horse pens and the tables where expedition leaders sat with their lists. First touch won. The fair paid a silver piece to anyone who touched him; so far its money was safe. An enterprising man outside the square sold wooden copies of the famous sword. Frascot's actual weapon was rather plain, and the copies all had jewels.

Dovran had watched two bouts decided by surrender before a blow landed. He had disliked the second surrender in particular.

“At least let him try,” he'd whispered to me. “You've put on all those buckles.”

“You go, then.”

“Shall I?”

I had meant it. I liked watching him fight. He wasn't elegant, but he was quick, and when frightened he made a furious little whistling sound through his teeth which he refused to believe in afterward. He'd be delighted if he won a silver. If he lost, I'd buy him a drink and we could add some outrageous circumstances to the account.

Now he ducked under the rope, tucked the feather inside his shirt, and drew his own sword.

Frascot looked tired and hot. He had removed his helmet, leaving a damp band across his brow. His padded sleeves were patched at both elbows.

“You understand what I'm using?” he asked.

“Unless you've brought the wrong one.”

Somebody laughed. Dovran glanced toward me, pleased.

“You may feel badly hurt without any cut,” Frascot said. “Bad enough to stop you. It can last for days. If you want an ordinary bout, I'll use a practice blade.”

“No, this one.”

“You can withdraw at any time.”

Dovran saluted him. His face had settled into its fighting look, loose mouth and narrowed eyes. I knew that face better than the one he made when somebody drew his portrait on a tavern wall.

Frascot laid his bare thumb against the guard. A pale gleam passed from his hand into the narrow grooves along the steel. It brightened when he tightened his grip. Then he raised the blade and waited.

Dovran tried a cut toward the shoulder, drew it back, and came in low. Frascot stepped to his left. Their swords met near the guards with a clack; Frascot turned his wrist, let Dovran's edge slide past, and tapped him under the ribs with the flat.

It was a small sound. I could hear the horse dealer behind me still counting out a price.

Dovran hopped backward, grinning. His coat was whole.

“Well,” he said. “That's a—”

He looked at me. I was laughing because of the hop, which had been absurdly nimble for a man with his reach, and because we had all been holding our breath for nothing. A few others laughed too. One man clapped.

Dovran's mouth stayed open. He drew a breath to finish whatever he'd been about to say, then turned his head toward the clapping man. His sword drooped until its point caught in the dirt.

“Dovran?” I said.

He tried to lift the point. It dragged a small furrow.

Frascot stepped back and took his thumb off the guard. The grooves went dull.

“Bout's over.”

“I know,” Dovran said, too loudly. “I know it is.”

The laughter died unevenly. Those who couldn't see over the people in front were asking what had happened. Dovran stood looking among us, from one face to another, and I ducked under the rope with his hat in my hand.

“Come on,” I said. “You nearly had him.”

“Don't do that.”

His voice was ordinary enough to make me stop. Up close I could see that the muscles beside his mouth were trembling. He kept trying to press them still with his lips.

“What is it?” I asked Frascot.

“Let him tell you.”

Dovran swallowed. Somebody beyond the rope said they couldn't see any blood.

“I feel,” he said, and stopped. He looked at the place where the sword had touched his coat. “As if you all want me to go away.”

“We don't.”

“Yes, thank you, I gathered it was the sword.” He took his hat from me and pushed it onto his head without putting the feather back. “Can you stop it?”

Frascot shook his head.

“Hit the other side, perhaps?” Dovran said. He gave a short, ugly laugh. “No? Thought not.”

“It usually eases over a few days. Keep company tonight. Don't travel alone.”

“How many days?” I asked.

“I can't promise you a number.”

He wiped his palm on his breeches, then used that hand to steady the scabbard while he sheathed the sword. There was no glow now. He tied it down with a leather thong, and the next challenger, already loosening his cloak, protested.

“I'm done,” Frascot told him.

Dovran was trying to sheath his own sword and missing. I held the scabbard still for him. He let me, though he wouldn't look at me.

“You call this better than cutting someone?” I said.

“Better than killing him.”

“Nobody needed killing.”

Frascot looked past me at the man selling the wooden swords. “No.”

I wanted more from him than that. Dovran caught my sleeve.

“Can we just get out?”

We went through the rope. People made room, which was what I wanted, until I saw Dovran's face when they did it.

Beyond the horse pens I put an arm around his shoulders. We often walked that way after a good evening, mostly because one of us would be trying to steer the other toward another tavern. He hunched under my arm. I took it away.

“Sorry.”

“It's hot.”

It was hot. His collar had left a red line across his neck. He pulled at it, found the feather, and looked surprised to be holding it.

“Worth keeping safe,” I said.

He didn't answer. I wished I had let the feather go unnoticed.

At the edge of the fair, a woman frying cakes asked whether we wanted the last two. Dovran shook his head. She put them into a bag for somebody else, and he stopped walking.

“What?” I asked.

“Nothing.”

We stood while the woman took her money and started scraping the pan.

“I said no,” he told me, very quietly. “I know I said no. I'm not confused about it.”

“I can buy you something else.”

“I don't want a cake.”

He walked on. I hurried after him, then slowed because I could hear myself hurrying. Everything I did seemed to come at the wrong speed.

“Do you want to lie down?”

“No.”

“A drink?”

“Not yet.”

“We could sit somewhere.”

“You could stop asking me things for a moment.”

So we walked without speaking. He kept the feather in his hand. In four years I'd seen him feverish, frightened, furious over a cheated purse, and so homesick that he'd tried to make his mother's dumplings in a helmet. I'd eaten those dumplings. I had mentioned them at every opportunity afterward. I couldn't think of a single thing to say about them now that wouldn't be asking him to laugh for me.

We came to the street that led back to our lodging. Dovran turned into it. I went another three steps toward the coach yard before I stopped.

“This way,” he said.

“There's a bench under the awning over there.”

“There's a bed in the room.”

“You said you didn't want to lie down.”

He stared at me. Then he looked at the yard, where a porter was rolling a barrel up a pair of planks. A coach stood in the shade with both doors open. It wasn't mine; I had checked the painted destination without meaning to.

Dovran watched me check it.

“What are you doing?”

I put my hand inside my coat. It would have been easy to leave it there and tell him we should go back to the room. I could miss the coach. There was one every morning.

I brought out the ticket.

He leaned forward to read it, his face close enough that I saw the dust caught in the wet corner of one eye.

“When?”

“This evening.”

“That's now.”

“Not quite.”

He stood back. I folded the ticket along its existing crease.

“I'm going inland for the winter,” I said. “I've found a room. Well, it's been found for me. I've paid the first month. It's not far from the coach stop.”

“You've paid?”

“Yes.”

“When did you do all this?”

“The room was arranged last week. The ticket this morning.”

He rubbed the feather between his hands. Small barbs broke loose and stuck to his damp palms.

“Your pack?”

“Here already.”

“Ah.”

There was a bench under the awning, as I had said, but he didn't go to it. He leaned against a post in the yard entrance. I stood beside him, in everybody's way, and waited for him to ask about the room. It had a stove. I'd spent a surprising amount of time thinking about the stove.

“This morning,” he said. “Before we went out?”

“Yes.”

“You sent me to buy the feather.”

“You wanted the feather.”

“You said the stall would close.”

I had. He'd been dithering over its price. I'd wanted ten minutes alone to take my pack down.

He pushed himself off the post, then leaned back again.

“I'd have bought it anyway,” he said. “You didn't have to do that.”

A cart was coming through. We moved a few steps into the yard together, by habit, his hand going to my elbow before he pulled it back. The driver thanked us. Dovran studied the cart's rear wheel until it had passed.

“I wanted to tell you properly,” I said.

“When?”

I had already answered that question, but not the one he meant. After lunch had become after the fair. I had imagined him helping to put my pack on the coach, grumbling about the fare, shouting something indecent after me to amuse the other passengers.

“Before I went.”

He nodded several times. I hated that more than if he'd shouted.

“You mustn't think this is because—”

“I heard you. You bought it this morning.”

“I meant because of you.”

“Oh. Well. That's a relief.”

“I'm trying to tell you. I can't do another winter on the road.”

“Then you could have said.”

“I've been saying I'm tired for months.”

“So have I. It makes people offer you chairs.”

He was looking at me properly now. I could have laughed at that, on another afternoon. Even now, I wanted to.

“After the flooded mine,” I said, “I told you I wanted to stop.”

“We did stop.”

“For two days.”

“You wanted to leave that inn. You said you could hear things chewing inside the mattress.”

“There were things chewing inside the mattress.”

“I know. I heard them too.”

We looked at each other, and he laughed once. I started laughing as well. Then he put a hand over his eyes.

I couldn't tell whether I'd made it worse. I waited until he took the hand away.

“I don't want another inn,” I said. “I want that room. I want to take my boots off and know I won't have to put them on in the dark because something's coming. At the last job, when you woke me for the watch, I couldn't get out of my blankets. I pretended I hadn't heard you.”

“I thought you were ill.”

“I wasn't ill.”

He looked down at my boots. They were the pair he'd helped me bargain for in the spring. One lace had a join in it where I'd broken it pulling too hard.

“All right,” he said.

“But I don't know if it's just the winter.”

He kept looking at the boots.

“I don't want to promise I'll come back in the spring,” I said. “I was going to tell you winter, but I don't know.”

“I heard you.”

By the stable door, a boy was whistling. Dovran tried to brush the fragments of feather off his hands, then gave up and wiped them on his coat.

“I'd have tried to talk you out of it,” he said. “If you'd told me.”

“Yes.”

“I might still.”

“Please don't.”

He breathed through his mouth for a while. When he spoke, his voice was thick.

“I bought that map yesterday. You looked at it with me.”

“I know.”

“You said the ferry would be cheaper downstream.”

“It would.”

He made an impatient movement, and I stopped.

We had sat with the map between us while he drew little boats in the margins. One of them had capsized under the weight of my luggage. I'd drawn him beneath it, being eaten by a fish. That was after I'd sent the money for the room.

“I liked sitting there,” I said. “With you.”

“So did I. I was planning a journey.”

I put the ticket away. It had begun to soften where I was holding it.

“Do you need some of the money back?” he asked.

“What?”

“For the map. Your half.”

“No. Of course not.”

“Good. Because I've drawn all over it.”

He tried to smile and couldn't. I reached for his sleeve, then let my hand drop before touching him.

“This would be easier if he hadn't hit you,” I said.

“Yes, probably. What do you want me to do about that?”

“Nothing. I didn't mean—”

“I know there's something wrong with me.” He stopped, rubbing his face. “Wrong happening. Whatever. I know that boy doesn't hate me. He's never seen me before. I know you don't hate me either.”

The boy had stopped whistling. I wished he would start again.

“I don't,” I said.

“I said I know.”

I let him stand without trying to touch him. After a while he took off the hat, looked inside it, and put it back on. The damaged feather was still in his other hand.

“I wouldn't have done it,” he said. “The bout. If I'd known you were leaving today.”

“I'm sorry.”

“We could've gone somewhere. Not stood about watching other people fight.”

“There's still time.”

He turned toward the yard. The porter had finished with the barrel and was carrying bags out of the booking office. My pack was among them, recognizable by the strip of red blanket Dovran had sewn around a failing strap. He'd charged me for the thread, then spent twice the amount buying me a drink to celebrate the repair.

“No,” he said. “I'm going back.”

“To the room?”

“Yes.”

“Frascot said you shouldn't be alone.”

“I'll sit downstairs. There are people there.”

I wanted to ask whether he'd tell them what had happened. I wanted him to tell it well, with the hop and the feather and his suggestion of a second blow, and leave my part in the afternoon out of it. I looked away from him.

“Could you stay until the coach comes?” I asked.

“No.”

He pushed the feather into the band of his hat. Half its barbs were missing. It leaned sideways, and for a moment I thought he'd make one last joke about it. He saw me looking and took the hat off again.

“Was it all right, though?” I said. “Us. Travelling.”

His face crumpled. He turned it away quickly, but I'd seen.

“Don't ask me that now.”

“Sorry.”

He nodded without looking at me and walked out of the yard. I followed him as far as the entrance, then stopped. He was still carrying the hat when he reached the corner. He turned into the street toward our lodging without looking back.

The porter wanted to know which pack was mine. I showed him, and he set it on one end of the bench under the awning.

I sat down. There was dust on the knees of my trousers from ducking under the rope. I brushed one knee clean and left the other. Across the yard, the stable boy began whistling again, lost the tune halfway through, and started over.

I kept looking at the entrance. I wanted Dovran to come back, although I hadn't found anything better to say to him. A driver came out of the office and I stood, but he was only fetching a coat he'd left on the bench. I moved my pack so he could reach it, then sat down again.

stories.title: Late for Dinner
stories.prompt: One of the neat things about being married to one of the most feared generals in the kingdom, is that she will show up with her legion and eviscerate your foes, if your battle is making you late for dinner.
stories.body:
# Late for Dinner

The first warning that dinner would be late was a man in enemy colors stepping out of the ditch and saying, with surprising courtesy, “Please stop the mule.”

The carter hauled the reins. The mule, who had no opinion about border wars but strong opinions about men appearing from ditches, stopped somewhat later. By then the wagon had slewed across Plover’s Cut, the crock of cream had tipped into the onions, and three spears had risen from the thorn scrub on the western bank.

Rellan looked back. More soldiers had closed the road behind him. Ahead, where the sunken track climbed toward the barley fields and Juniper House, a mounted pair waited beneath a dun-colored banner.

His household guard reached for his sword.

“Don’t,” Rellan said.

The guard did.

Everything after that happened with the graceless speed of a cupboard collapsing. A crossbow snapped. The bolt struck the wagon rail rather than the guard, but the mule lunged, the carter lost the reins, and the left wheel climbed the chalk bank. Rellan caught one glorious glimpse of the pears he had spent half the morning choosing as they rose around him like green stars.

Then the wagon overturned.

He landed among sacks of flour and something sharp enough to be either a buckle or the expensive cheese. The guard struck the road hard and lay with one leg pinned beneath the wagon shaft. The carter rolled free, swearing after her mule as it tore north through the startled soldiers, trailing half a harness and all hope of arriving home with dignity.

Steel rang twice. Somebody cried out. Then a different voice, furious and frightened, shouted, “Alive, you fools. He is worth nothing dead.”

The fighting stopped.

Rellan lay in the white dust and considered that sentence. His left ear rang. Rosemary crushed beneath his palm made the air smell clean and domestic, which felt insulting.

A narrow man in a battered officer’s coat came down the road. Blood darkened one sleeve, though he did not seem to notice it. The silver braid at his collar had been cut away in places, perhaps sold, perhaps used for bandages. He glanced at the guard, the carter, the broken wagon, and finally Rellan’s iron wedding ring, engraved with the broken spear that marked Nerava’s dispatches.

“Rellan of Juniper House?”

Rellan pushed himself upright. “At present, Rellan of the ditch.”

The officer stared at him. His soldiers did not. They watched the banks, the mouths of the road, the evening sky. Their boots were caked with two colors of mud, and several wore cloaks with the badges ripped off. Not an ambushing force, then. A force that had run until it found a hole and mistaken that for safety.

“Captain Cadren,” the man said. “You will come with me.”

The guard strained against the shaft. Rellan heard the breath whistle between his teeth.

“I will not,” Rellan said. “But if your people lift this wagon, we can discuss the matter while my guard keeps his leg.”

Cadren’s mouth tightened. He had prepared himself for terror or defiance. An objection about furniture did not fit anywhere useful.

“You are in no position to bargain.”

“That is a man under a wagon, Captain. It is not a bargain.”

For a moment Cadren seemed likely to refuse merely because Rellan had made agreement difficult. Then one of the enemy soldiers said, “Sir, the south watch saw riders.”

Cadren looked toward the hidden southern mouth. “How many?”

“Couldn’t tell.”

“Then why are you telling me?”

The soldier had no answer. Cadren rubbed dust across his forehead and ordered four soldiers forward.

They raised the wagon enough for the carter to drag the guard clear. Rellan crawled after him and tore a strip from his dinner linen to bind the swelling leg. The cloth had been white when he packed it. Now cream, onion skins, and road dust had made a map of it. He hung the remaining linen from the wagon shaft.

Cadren waited until the knot was tied.

“General Nerava is encamped three miles east of here,” he said.

“Four and a half.”

“You will write to her. My company requires unhindered passage to the western road, with our arms and wounded. Once we are clear, you will be released.”

Rellan sat back on his heels. “No.”

Several spear points shifted closer.

Cadren looked almost relieved. This, at least, was a kind of answer he understood. “You mistake your circumstances.”

“You mistake my marriage. I cannot order Nerava to move a legion.”

“You can ask your wife to spare your life.”

“I can ask. She can say no.”

The carter made a small sound that might have been a laugh if she had not immediately pretended to cough.

Cadren’s face reddened. “Write.”

“My paper is under the wagon. My ink is in the cream. And the messenger you send will be taken by the first patrol outside this cut.” Rellan looked at the sun balanced above the bank. “You would do better to leave now. I am expected home for dinner.”

Silence spread outward from Cadren. Even the guard opened his eyes.

“Dinner,” Cadren repeated.

“My wife has been away for five months.”

“My company has been without bread for two days.”

“Then we are both having poor afternoons.”

That was the wrong thing to say. Rellan knew it before Cadren’s expression changed, but knowing a mistake at once did not make it less made.

Cadren ordered the ring tightened.

His soldiers dragged a splintered handcart from the ditch across the southward track and built a rough breastwork of baskets, wheels, and Rellan’s winter kindling. The household party was left inside a narrowing oval around the overturned wagon. The enemy did not rush them. Cadren wanted Rellan standing and recognizable, and every one of his exhausted soldiers knew it.

Rellan wanted, with increasing pettiness, his pears back.

He had planned this evening too carefully. Nerava had eaten campaign food for five months: hard biscuit, salt meat, whatever could survive both a saddlebag and an officer’s conscience. He had promised no officers, no petitions, no maps on the table. Just roast onions with thyme, soft cheese, pears warmed in honey, and the two of them in a room where nobody called her General.

For once, nobody was meant to obtain anything by saying his wife’s name.

Now Captain Cadren had built a fort out of dinner.

The bank behind the wagon was steep but not impossible. Rellan waited until Cadren had gone to berate the south watch, then pushed through the thorn scrub on hands and knees. Chalk crumbled beneath his boots. He made six feet, caught hold of a root, and discovered too late that it belonged to a dead thistle.

He slid back into the road in a shower of dirt and landed on a basket of onions.

An enemy soldier laughed. Another joined him before remembering he was under orders. Cadren turned. The laughter stopped badly, one man choking on the last of it.

“Again,” Cadren said to Rellan, “and I bind you.”

“You could have said the bank was loose.”

“This is not hospitality.”

“No. At Juniper House we warn people about the footing.”

The guard caught Rellan’s sleeve before he could continue. Pain had blanched his face. “Sir. Perhaps less talking.”

It was sound advice. Rellan ignored it for another quarter hour.

He tried offering the enemy food, which Cadren took for an insult until one of his own soldiers snatched a dirt-coated onion and ate it raw. That broke something. Hungry people came forward from both ends of the ring. The carter cursed them for thieves, then began throwing bruised pears hard enough that they had to catch them. For a little while the battle reduced itself to complaints about rot, stones in the bread, and who had taken the cheese.

Rellan watched the light creep up the eastern bank. The cut would fall into shadow before the fields above it. Nerava would reach Juniper House at sunset. She would find the table laid, the kitchen hot, and his chair empty.

She would wait perhaps three minutes before asking where he was.

Perhaps two.

At the last crossroads, his guard had offered to ride ahead when smoke first showed above the western road. Pride had kept Rellan from sending him. He had wanted to solve one ordinary delay without summoning the kingdom’s most feared general like a household remedy for mud. Now, listening to Cadren repeat the same orders to soldiers who had begun pretending not to hear, Rellan’s worry shifted.

It was no longer that Nerava might fail to come.

It was that she would.

Cadren returned to find him sitting on the wagon bed beside the wounded guard.

“I will give you quarter,” Rellan said.

Cadren stopped. “You.”

“Yes, unfortunately. Lay down your weapons before my wife arrives. I will stand before her and the crown’s officers and say you surrendered to me. Your wounded will be treated. No one here will take revenge.”

“You have just explained that you command nothing.”

“I command my word.”

“Can your word open the western road?”

“No.”

“Can it keep my soldiers out of prison?”

“I don’t know.”

Cadren gave a short, ugly laugh. “Then you offer a prettier cage.”

His company had crossed the border expecting an easy march behind two larger columns. The larger columns had broken. Cadren said this in pieces, as if each piece had been forced from him by the inconvenience of Rellan not understanding. Farms had shut their gates. Bridges had been burned behind them. Three men sent to bargain at a village had not returned.

“My soldiers know what waits if they put down steel,” he said. “Your people call your wife the Ash General.”

Rellan had heard the name. Nerava disliked it. Not because it frightened anyone, but because the battle that earned it had been fought in spring rain and there had been very little ash.

“My people call her a dozen foolish things. She keeps terms.”

“Because her husband says so?”

“Because she does.” Rellan stood. The movement made the world tilt briefly; he caught the wagon rail. “But she also knows this ground. If she comes, she will take the heights before you see a boot. She will close both mouths. She will leave you nowhere to retreat and nothing useful to threaten except me. And when she sees you threatening me, Captain, your afternoon will become worse.”

Cadren glanced upward despite himself.

Above the western bank, a flock of plovers burst from the barley. They wheeled once, flashing pale undersides, and fled east.

Nobody spoke.

Far beyond the cut, a horn sounded one low note.

The enemy soldiers knew an army horn. They did not know that one. Rellan did. He had heard it outside six towns, from balconies and muddy fields, each time before Nerava came home only long enough to leave again.
