Cadren seized Rellan by the front of his coat. “Tell her you are alive.”

“She cannot hear me.”

“Then climb the bank.”

“Your archer nearly killed me when I was standing beside a wagon. I am not showing Nerava a ring of armed people and letting her guess which ones have discipline.”

The horn sounded again, farther north than before.

Cadren released him and began shouting. Half his company rushed to the south barricade. The other half rushed north. A horse screamed from somewhere above, then came sliding riderless down the chalk, its reins cut and its eyes white. Men scattered. One fell. Another lost his shield and crawled after it until Cadren kicked it back to him.

Dust rose beyond both banks.

Then soldiers appeared along the western rim.

They did not cheer. They did not wave weapons or announce who they were. One moment the ridge held thorns and yellow grass; the next it held a line of dark shields, each overlapping the next. Bowstrings drew together with a soft, enormous creak.

On the eastern rim, mounted troops rose against the pale sky. At the north mouth, legionaries advanced behind rectangular shields. The southward track vanished behind another rank. Cadren’s company, which had spent an hour making Rellan’s world smaller, discovered that theirs had shrunk to the width of Plover’s Cut.

The first flight of arrows struck the road beyond Cadren’s outer ring. Dirt jumped in a perfect line. His soldiers recoiled from it into one another.

The second flight did not warn.

Rellan pulled the carter down behind the wagon. Arrows hammered shields, split spear shafts, and drove men from the banks. At the northern barricade, Cadren’s soldiers charged because standing still had become worse. They met the legion with a crash that shook kindling from the cart. Figures pressed, stumbled, disappeared behind shields. A man rolled into the ditch clutching his arm. Another lay very still beneath the dun banner.

The legion kept coming.

This was what fear of Nerava misunderstood. People imagined fury because fury made comforting sense. Fury wasted itself. Nerava’s battles moved with the dreadful economy of a hand clearing a table: this removed, that contained, the necessary space made empty.

Rellan saw her at last on the eastern bank.

She sat a gray horse without a plume or bright armor. Five months had sharpened her face and put new silver at one temple. While officers shouted around her, she looked down into the cut until she found the overturned wagon.

Until she found him.

Everything in her went quiet.

Cadren saw it too. He dragged Rellan upright and set a sword beneath his jaw.

The pressure was light. Cadren’s hand was shaking.

“General!” he shouted. His voice cracked on the second syllable. “Western passage, or your husband dies.”

Nerava raised two fingers.

The legion stopped so quickly that the sudden absence of impact seemed louder than the fighting. Shields remained locked. Bows stayed drawn. Somewhere in the cut, a wounded man begged somebody he could not see for water.

Nerava looked at Cadren. “No passage.”

“I will kill him.”

“Then you will still have no passage.”

Cadren’s fingers clenched in Rellan’s coat. Around them, his soldiers had begun lowering their weapons without permission. One man flung down his spear and shouted, “I take the quarter!” A sword followed. Then another. The legion’s ranks did not open, and the bows above remained drawn.

Cadren shouted, “Hold!”

No one did.

Rellan saw his stained dinner linen hanging from the wagon shaft. He reached for it.

Cadren jerked him back. The blade nicked skin this time, a bright small sting. Nerava’s bow line adjusted. Rellan knew that movement too. It meant the next decision would be very fast and would not belong to Cadren.

“Captain,” Rellan said. His mouth had gone dry. “Let me raise the cloth.”

“She’ll loose.”

“She might. You have not given her much to work with.”

Cadren stared at the ranks closing both ends of the cut. His command had come apart one dropped weapon at a time. He wanted a road. He wanted not to beg. He wanted the last hour to have meant something.

Rellan wanted to go home.

“It is quarter,” Rellan said. “Not victory. Not freedom. Living through the evening. Take it.”

Cadren’s sword lowered half an inch.

Rellan pulled free, snatched the linen, and climbed onto the overturned wagon. The wounded guard swore at him. The carter told him to get down. Someone on the bank shouted his name as if volume could make him less exposed.

He raised the dirty cloth.

Nerava’s gaze moved from it to his face. “Is that yours?”

“Yes.”

“Terms?”

“They put down weapons. They live. Treat the wounded. Hold them for the crown if you must, but no revenge here.” Rellan heard himself beginning to rush and forced the rest out plainly. “I gave my word.”

Cadren said behind him, “He promised protection.”

“I promised you would live,” Rellan snapped. “You kept arguing about the road.”

Cadren’s formal rage cracked. Beneath it was plain embarrassment, arriving late and unwelcome.

Nerava watched Rellan. Not the cloth. Not Cadren’s sword. Him.

“Do you stand by it?” she asked.

“I do.”

She lowered her hand.

“Quarter stands,” she said.

The words moved through the legion faster than a horn call. Bows eased. Shield ranks opened narrow lanes. Officers repeated the terms. Cadren’s soldiers dropped what remained in their hands and stumbled toward custody.

Cadren stayed where he was.

Rellan climbed down from the wagon. His knees nearly folded when his boots touched the road. He held the stained linen out to the captain.

“You wanted my marriage,” he said. “There it is.”

Cadren looked past him at General Nerava, who had dismounted and was coming down into the cut. Then he looked at the linen. He took it as though it weighed more than his sword.

The sword fell from his other hand.

Nerava passed Cadren without a glance. She stopped before Rellan and touched one finger to the cut beneath his jaw.

“You’re bleeding.”

“A very little.”

“You are standing on one foot.”

Rellan looked down. This was true. “The other has an onion in the boot.”

Her eyes closed. For one dangerous instant he thought she might either embrace him or demand an accounting before he could breathe. Instead she took his face between both hands and pressed her forehead to his.

Around them, the feared legion stripped weapons from prisoners, carried the injured to level ground, and cut panicked horses free of tangled harness. Nobody looked at their general.

“You brought the legion,” Rellan said.

“I was with the legion.”

“All of it?”

“The rear cohorts are at Juniper House.”

“That is not better.”

Her thumbs moved once against his cheeks. “You were late.”

“I noticed.”

“There was smoke on the western road. Your wagon had not passed the east post. A patrol found the mule.”

Behind Rellan, the carter cried, “You found him?”

Nerava turned her head. “He is eating barley in my command tent.”

“That animal has no respect for rank.”

“So I gathered.”

The carter went to help with the guard, satisfied that her mule had survived and aware that the man beside her still needed help.

Rellan looked at Cadren’s company kneeling in small, exhausted groups. “Thank you for stopping.”

Nerava’s attention came back to him. “You asked me to.”

“I was not certain that would be enough.”

“Neither was I.” She glanced toward the still figure beneath the dun banner, then to the legion surgeons already moving among both uniforms. When she spoke again, her voice was lower. “It had to be.”

She assigned Cadren’s prisoners to three separate watches, ordered every wounded person treated before questioning, and refused an officer who tried to arrange the legion along the road for her departure. There would be no victory display at Plover’s Cut. The living had enough to carry out.

By the time Rellan and Nerava reached Juniper House, night had settled over the barley. Campfires covered the eastern fields in orderly rows. Soldiers had watered their horses in the orchard trough, stacked shields beside the kitchen garden, and left a respectful empty circle around the house itself.

Inside, the dining room candles had burned down by half. The roast onions were black at the edges. The cheese was somewhere under a wagon. Of twelve pears, four had returned in a legion supply cart, and only one had escaped bruising.

Nerava unbuckled her sword belt at the door. For a moment she looked around for somewhere proper to set it. Rellan pointed to the peg beneath his market cloak.

She hung it there.

They sat at the kitchen table instead of the dining table. Rellan could not bear the sight of all the unused plates. Nerava ate cold bread, one roasted onion, and two damaged pears with the concentration she gave any meal after campaign. Without the officer’s coat and sword, she seemed at once more familiar and more tired. The silver at her temple was not dust. He wanted to ask when it had appeared. He wanted to complain about the cheese.

For a while they listened to each other eat.

Then Nerava said, “Did you know I would come?”

Rellan turned the one perfect pear in his hands. “I knew you would notice.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“Yes.” He looked at her. “I knew.”

“Did you want me to?”

The honest answer had changed during the afternoon. “By the second horn.”

Nerava leaned back. Something in her shoulders loosened—not much, but enough that he could see how tightly she had held herself since the cut.

“I wanted one evening,” he said, “when nobody used me to reach you.”

“Cadren did.”

“He tried.”

“And you offered him quarter.”

“He was afraid of you.”

“He had cause.”

“I know.” Rellan set the pear on his plate. “Sometimes I hate how much cause everyone has.”

She did not defend herself. Her hand stayed beside his on the table, and she waited.

Rellan picked at the split in the tabletop. “Cadren thought I was a gate he could put a knife against.”

“You are not a gate.”

“I know that. You know that. It was a crowded afternoon for slower learners.”

Her mouth twitched.

“I did not send for you,” he said, “because I did not want to need the Ash General every time a road went wrong.”

“Good. I dislike that name.”

“You dislike all your names.”

“Not all of them.” She reached across the table and turned his wedding ring once around his finger. “Next time the road goes wrong, send for Nerava.”

He covered her hand with his. “There will not be a next time.”

Outside, three thousand soldiers answered the first-watch horn with one vast shift of armor and canvas.

They both listened.

“There had better not,” Nerava said.

Rellan glanced toward the window. It was only a moment. When he looked back, the unbruised pear was gone from his plate.

Nerava bit into it without shame.

Rellan began, at last, to laugh.

stories.title: Not About That
stories.prompt: “J-Just because I have to turn into a girl to use my magical powers doesn’t mean I’m trans! Being a magical girl isn’t about that!”
stories.body:
# Not About That

Lowen discovered the first problem with stealing a magical focus when his feet stopped fitting the roof.

He had known about the rest. The label tied to the copper clasp had been blunt enough: LIFT-STEP, SINGLE FIGURE, FEMININE, GROUND COMPLETELY BEFORE RELEASE. The clasp had lain for years in the family practice box between a cracked rain-calling comb and six spools of ribbon that only worked for their aunt. It had no mind with which to want him, no mouth with which to call him anything. Sarena had explained that part until he could repeat it while half asleep. A focus shaped what a living person supplied.

Lowen had supplied his power deliberately. Three breaths, both thumbs against the blue glass inset, and yes.

Then the roof seemed to drop six inches.

His sneakers drew tight, flashed white, and became soft boots fitted to feet a little shorter than his own. Dark tights smoothed up unfamiliar legs. A blue pleated overskirt snapped around his hips beneath a short copper-buttoned coat, all of it as neat as if somebody had ironed lightning. His balance went wandering and came home somewhere lower. His hair, usually an argument with gravity, slid in a heavy black rope between his shoulder blades.

Lowen grabbed the chimney cap before the new weight of it pulled his head back. His hand was narrower. His voice, when he said, “Oh,” came out bright and unmistakably a girl’s.

That was not the problem.

The problem was that the body felt wonderful in motion.

He pushed away from the chimney, wobbled once, and stepped where there was nothing. A pane of blue light rang beneath his boot. The next step lifted him above the clotheslines. On the third, wind poured cold along his tights and under the copper coat, and the whole block opened below him: tar roofs, green water tanks, laundry courtyards, tram wires, a bakery chimney smoking sugar into the late-afternoon air.

The sky was busy. It was always busy. Two magical girls in red delivery capes skimmed west with insulated supper boxes hanging between them. A little practice circle on the school roof burst into applause when one of its members managed a somersault, then into jeers when she came out backward and dropped her wand. High above, a woman in yellow oilskins towed a string of rain clouds toward the vegetable district. Somebody trailing pink sparks had written WAIT FOR ME across half a city block.

Lowen laughed. The sound startled him, and then the startling made him laugh harder.

The chalk circle Sarena had drawn for tomorrow waited beside the water tank. She had promised him a supervised trial after school, provided he did not touch anything alone, improvise, show off, or listen to their cousin about “unlocking his instincts.” At fifteen, Lowen was old enough to know that “three out of four” would not impress her. He had obeyed three anyway. Mostly.

He stepped higher. Each blue pane appeared only after he committed his weight, which was alarming for exactly one attempt. After that it was the best thing anybody had ever invented. His new center of balance turned a clumsy hop into a clean, buoyant sweep. He could feel the focus answering through the clasp at his chest, taking the lift he gave it and laying the next foothold into the air.

Across the alley, a coral-clad girl banked around an aerial and kicked both heels together. Her path flared into a gorgeous hook.

Lowen could do that.

He could not, in fact, do that.

His heels struck. The blue pane tipped nearly vertical. He shot past Sarena’s chalk circle, past the water tank, and straight over the parapet with enough speed to make every rooftop in the city wheel sideways.

He flung out a foot. Light cracked under it and redirected him upward instead of back. The laundry courtyard fell away. His stomach stayed behind.

“No, no, no—”

A gray shape rose over the opposite wing of the building. Sarena had one arm through a paper grocery sack and three silver wind-knots streaming from the other. Her transformed coat was longer than his, slit for movement, with faded red lining that flashed when she turned. She saw Lowen, saw the stolen clasp, and dropped the sack.

Oranges rained into the courtyard.

Sarena snapped two fingers. A wind-knot unreeled beneath Lowen, caught him behind the knees, and flipped him onto a laundry canopy. He landed in somebody’s sheets. The metal frame groaned, sprang him up again, and returned him to open air wearing a damp pillowcase like a veil.

Sarena caught the back of his coat.

For three breathless seconds they hung beside the fifth-floor balconies: Sarena braced on two trembling wind-knots, Lowen bicycling his shorter legs, the pillowcase over both their heads.

From an open kitchen window, the fifth-floor auntie shouted, “Sarena, why is your brother in my clean wash?”

“Research,” Sarena shouted back.

Lowen yanked the pillowcase free. “You dropped the oranges.”

“I’m going to drop you.”

“You won’t.”

“Today has been surprising.”

She hauled him onto the opposite roof and let go only after both his boots touched tar. Blue light pooled under his soles. Instead of draining away, it pushed him into an undignified half crouch.

Sarena stared at the clasp pinned beneath his chin.

Lowen tried to tuck his long hair behind one ear. The wind put it back in his mouth.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

“Technically it is tomorrow somewhere.”

“Not even cousin-level reasoning. That was pantry-moth reasoning.” She pointed at his feet. “Don’t bounce.”

He immediately bounced.

Sarena caught his sleeve before he floated over a vent. “How much lift did you stack?”

“I took maybe nine steps.”

“Lowen.”

“Fourteen? The last one was complicated.”

“You cannot revert until you put it back into a controlled landing.”

“I read the label.”

“Did you read it while hurtling past the place I told you to land?”

He looked across the courtyard at the chalk circle, small and reproachful beside their water tank. “I was coming around.”

Sarena bent to inspect one of his boots, then his knees and wrists. She did not ask permission in words; she held out her hands and waited for his nod before touching. That was how she did injury checks with everybody, even people she had just pulled out of chimneys. Lowen resented the courtesy more than grabbing would have deserved.

“Nothing twisted?” she asked.

“No.”

“Head clear?”

“Clear enough to notice you’re crushing a tomato.”

One of the fallen groceries had landed behind her heel. Sarena moved her boot. Red pulp clung to the sole.

“That,” she said, “was for dinner.”

Lowen smiled despite himself. The unfamiliar cheeks shaped it differently, narrower at the chin. Sarena’s gaze caught on his face, moved to the blue panes still guttering beneath his boots, then returned.

“You like being—”

The fear had been waiting inside the delight, thin as a trip wire. It pulled tight before she finished.

“J-Just because I have to turn into a girl to use my magical powers doesn’t mean I’m trans! Being a magical girl isn’t about that!”

His voice carried beautifully. It crossed the courtyard, struck brick, and came back smaller.

Sarena’s hand dropped from his wrist.

For a moment the only sound between them was a delivery cape flapping overhead.

“I was going to say flying,” she said.

Lowen’s face burned. “Well, you looked—”

“I looked at you.”

“You know what I mean.”

“No.” Sarena wiped tomato from her boot on the roof gravel. Her movements had gone careful and plain. “I don’t think I do.”

“I’m just saying you shouldn’t assume.”

“I didn’t.”

“You were about to.”

“Apparently you can air-step and hear the future.”

She tugged one silver knot loose from her wrist. The wind holding it went slack. Lowen watched the strand fade and told himself she was only conserving magic. She gathered the surviving groceries without offering him a hand.

“Where are you going?” he asked.

“To put these inside.”

“I’m still stuck.”

“Then stay on the roof.”

“I can ground it myself.”

Sarena glanced at him, and there it was: not a diagnosis, not secret knowledge. Anger. Worse, the kind she did not trust him to handle without turning it into another argument.

“Of course you can,” she said. “You’ve been doing excellent research.”

She disappeared into the stairwell.

Lowen lasted until the door banged shut before trying to cross the courtyard.

The sensible method would have been to wait. The humiliating method would have been to call Sarena back, apologize, and admit that the thought of anyone enjoying this body on his behalf scared him more than the five-story drop. The available method was to study the coral girl, who had circled back and was now hovering above a florist’s roof while arguing with her friend about whose turn it was to carry a bucket.

She bent one knee, swept her arms, and descended in a spiral.

Lowen bent one knee.

From the stairwell doorway, Sarena said, “Her power is ribbons.”

He startled. His boot hit a blue pane at the wrong angle. He pinwheeled off the roof.

Sarena swore and dove after him.

This descent was slower, if no more dignified. Lowen slapped footholds into the air whenever he neared a balcony, which kept him from hitting brick and also kept him from going down. He bounced from the fourth-floor laundry rail to a striped awning, from the awning to a blue pane, and from the pane into Sarena’s shoulder. She shoved him away, missed her own wind-knot, and both of them landed in a balcony planter.

The planter belonged to no magical tradition. It responded to their arrival by breaking.

Soil poured through the railing. Lowen and Sarena clung to it while a rain of basil struck the courtyard below.

“That was basil,” Lowen said.

Sarena’s mouth twitched.

“Do not laugh.”

That finished her. She made one strangled sound, then buried her face against her sleeve.

“I almost died.”

“You almost got seasoned.”

Lowen started laughing too. His grip loosened. A leftover pulse of lift peeled him off the balcony and sent him drifting backward.

Sarena’s laughter stopped. “Lowen. Left foot down. Flat.”

He heard instruction as command, the change in her tone as proof she had decided what he was, and he kicked left harder than he needed to. The pane flashed. Instead of lowering him toward the courtyard, it shot him across it.

He crashed through three lines of laundry and emerged in a white shirt, two aprons, and a pair of enormous bloomers. The fifth-floor auntie leaned from her window with a wooden spoon.

“Boy,” she called, “if you stretch those, you buy them.”

“Sorry!”

He tore free and struck another foothold. Behind him, Sarena said, “Lowen, stop making steps.”

“Then I fall.”

“You float. That focus wants to spend the lift. Let it.”

“You said left foot.”

“I made a bad call.”

He glanced back. Sarena hung three yards away, one boot planted on a wind-knot that shook under her. Dirt streaked her cheek. Her transformed coat had ripped at the elbow, and one of the groceries bulged from its pocket as if she had hidden a turnip there during battle.

“You never say that,” Lowen said.

“You never listen long enough.”

He pulled the white shirt off his head. “You laughed.”

“Also bad.”

The apology arrived without polish and without asking anything from him. That made it harder to refuse.

Lowen held still.

The stored lift carried him upward by inches, gentler now. Sarena drifted beside him without touching. Across the open side of the courtyard, the city shone in fragments between buildings. Magical girls crossed every strip of sky: one seated sideways on a crescent of green glass, one pumping a broom like a scooter, four holding hands around a wobbling globe of rain. None of them looked over. A boy in a girl’s body hanging among laundry was not the strangest part of anyone’s afternoon.

The blue light around Lowen’s boots thinned.

“There,” Sarena said. “You feel the sag?”

“No.”

“Your right hip dropped.”

“Maybe this body has a lower right hip.”

“It doesn’t.”

“How would you know?”

Sarena’s face closed again.

The words left the same silence as his outburst. Sarena had told him what his hip was doing, and he had dragged her transness into the answer as if it were an accusation. Once could have been panic. Twice was something uglier.

Below, the courtyard chalk marks waited where Sarena had practiced landings with him in sneakers all summer. Heel, bend, hold. She had drawn ridiculous little faces beside his worst attempts and a crown over the one good one. She had spent three weeks talking their mother into letting him try a focus at all. Lowen knew that. He had known it when he opened the practice box early.

“I’m going down,” he said.

“Good.”

“Alone.”

“Less good.”

He let himself sink. Sarena followed at a distance.

At the third floor, a warm gust rolled through the courtyard carrying sugar smoke from the bakery chimney. Lowen’s long hair lifted before the rest of him. He liked the tug at his scalp. He liked the coat tails fluttering around his legs and the easy, buoyant alignment of this body. Liking it did not feel like a verdict until he imagined saying it aloud.

The gust slid under the remaining lift and carried him past the courtyard circle. He reached for a foothold by reflex.

“Don’t,” Sarena said.

He made one anyway.

The pane caught the wind like a sail.

Lowen rose through the courtyard faster than Sarena could follow. Balconies blurred by. He cleared the roofline, hit the colder current above it, and kept going. The building shrank beneath him. His next foothold appeared faint as breath on glass.

“Lowen!”

Sarena came over the parapet with only one wind-knot left. She stretched it until the silver line shivered. She could reach him or brace a landing, not both.

The city had changed color while they argued. Windows burned amber. Streetlamps pricked on below. The girls who had filled the afternoon sky were heading home in twos and threes, their trails crossing violet dusk. Lowen saw no one near enough to reach him before his last pane failed.

Sarena held up her remaining wind-knot. With her other hand she pointed at the copper belt fastened over Lowen’s coat.

He understood. The knot could turn his fall, but not carry him. Sarena would have to anchor it, and he would have to take it.

Lowen shook his head. The silver strand was the only thing under her boot.

Sarena bared her teeth at him. Then she stepped off it.

She dropped past the parapet, let the knot unspool just long enough to turn her toward the roof, and landed beside the water tank. Her knees buckled. Before Lowen could decide whether that was part of the plan, she wrapped the strand once around the tank’s iron leg and threw its loop back into the air.

It rose toward him and stopped a foot short.

The final blue pane bent under Lowen’s boots. Sarena waited below, one palm pressed to the tank, her hair loose in the wind. She was offering exactly what she had, not an answer to anything else.

“Sarena!”

She looked up.

“I said it like being you was awful.”

Her hand tightened on the silver line. “You did.”

“I’m sorry.”

She did not forgive him. She snapped her wrist, and the loop jumped another six inches.

Lowen stepped off the pane to meet it.

For one plunging second he had neither light nor line. Then he caught the loop in both hands. His long hair tangled around his wrists. He dragged the knot over his head and worked it beneath the copper belt, trusting the magical coat to hold where his grip might not.

The blue pane shattered above him.

Falling was nothing like flying. His stomach climbed into his throat; the wind packed his overskirt with cold. The knot went taut at his waist and swung him toward the building in a wide, ugly arc. On the roof Sarena slid a yard across the tar before her shoulder struck the water tank. She held on.

Lowen kept his hands off the magic. The chalk circle rushed up beneath him. He turned his hips the way Sarena had shown him all summer, found the roof with both soles, and let his knees fold.

His heels held for one beat. Then his momentum pitched him sideways and rolled him out of the circle in a storm of hair and blue pleats.

Light washed over the chalk. The roof gave a deep satisfied thump, and all the stored lift vanished.

Lowen lay on his back, abruptly and wonderfully heavy. The silver knot loosened from his belt. Several feet away, Sarena sat against the water tank with one hand clamped over her torn elbow.

Neither of them spoke until their breathing slowed.

“I did like it,” Lowen said.

“You laughed for half an hour.”

“Seventeen minutes.”

Sarena gave him a look but did not finish his thought for him.

“I wasn’t scared of being you,” he said. The sentence came apart after that. “I mean, I was scared, but not of— It sounded like—”

“Lowen.”

He stopped.

Sarena looked at the dusk instead of him. “Don’t make me the thing you have to not be.”

There was no clever answer hiding behind his teeth. “Okay.”

“And don’t steal my practice box.”

“Our practice box.”

“See, this is why apologies take you all evening.”

Lowen sat up. His long hair had wound itself through the wind-knot and around two copper buttons. Sarena came over and crouched in front of him. She worked the silver strand loose without yanking, though the set of her mouth warned him not to mistake care for pardon.

When the knot was free, Lowen put his thumb on the blue glass. Then he stopped.

“Do you have your phone?” he asked.

Sarena narrowed her eyes. “Why?”

He nearly said it did not mean anything. That would have been the same mistake in a fresh coat.

“I want a picture,” he said. “Of me like this.”

Sarena studied him, the long hair and the blue pleats and the face he had enjoyed wearing. “For you?”

“Yes.”

She drew her phone from an inside pocket and held it upright. Lowen stood in the chalk circle. He tried arranging the overskirt, then his hair, then both at once. Every position looked like somebody else’s idea of a magical girl.

Sarena’s phone clicked while his hair was still caught in his mouth.

“Not that one.”

Sarena took the battered turnip from her coat pocket and aimed it at him like a wand.

Lowen laughed. Her phone clicked.

“I’m still mad,” she said.

“I know.”

He pressed the blue glass and deliberately let go.

The copper coat loosened into his old sweatshirt. The pleats snapped back into jeans. His feet lengthened inside battered sneakers; his balance climbed; his hair sprang short and stubborn around his ears. Lowen missed the wind along its vanished length immediately.

The focus came loose in his palm. He handed it to Sarena, and she put it away without promising him anything.

“Do you believe me?” he asked.

“You’re my brother.” She looked down at her phone. “You’re also blurry.”

Lowen leaned over her shoulder. In the photograph, his long hair crossed his mouth, his copper coat shone in the last daylight, and one hand was still trying to rescue the crooked overskirt. The ridiculous turnip floated at the edge of the frame. He was laughing too hard to pose.

“Send me that one,” he said.

Sarena did. She kept the terrible first one too.

stories.title: The Bride Who Came Back
stories.prompt: Each winter, the frozen kingdom sends one bride south to keep the fire kingdom from invading. This year, the woman they sent returns alone—while the southern capital burns behind her
stories.body:
# The Bride Who Came Back

Ylva knew her sister by the way she lost every seventh step.

The figure on the causeway was still too far away for a face, no more than a black stroke moving north across the lake. Behind her, beyond the southern mouth of the pass, Cyrak burned. Smoke climbed over the mountains in a wall, turning the afternoon dark, and every gust showed a red seam at its roots.

But six steps came evenly. The seventh dragged.

“It’s Marzena,” Ylva said.

No one on the watchtower answered. Below them, the gate horns had already sounded three times: stranger approaching, southern fire, bar all doors. Soldiers heaved the last oak crosspiece into place. Frost sifted from its iron brackets.

Queen Tirza stood at the parapet with one gloved hand around the stone lip. “We cannot know that yet.”

“She broke her left ankle on the fish stairs when she was twelve. She still cheats that foot when she’s tired.”

“Many people limp.”

“Not at seven.”

Ylva counted again. Six, drag. Six, drag. The woman’s dress was the black of wet coal, though no cloth should have shone at that distance. Orange points ran over it and went dark. Her head was bare. Wind worried loose strands from the knot of her hair.

At first snow, twenty-three days ago, Marzena had gone south in a hood of white fox and a gown made from Iskal’s winter glass. She had walked between two files of Orravan soldiers without looking back. One bride each winter, and the fire kingdom kept its army below the pass. That was the treaty. In school, Ylva had been made to copy it until the words felt as natural as weather: one bride, one winter, one border at peace.

Brides did not return. They lived in the warm courts of Cyrak, Iskal was told, honored and secluded by southern custom. When Ylva had asked why none came north even to be buried, her tutor had struck a line through the question and made her copy the treaty again.

The figure stumbled. One hand struck the ice. A circle of water opened beneath her palm.

Ylva ran for the stair.

“Stop.” Tirza’s voice carried the clean edge it had in council. “Until we know what she carries, the gate remains barred.”

Ylva turned. Her mother’s face had gone pale except where the southern light laid copper along one cheek.

“She carries your daughter.”

“She may be followed.”

Ylva pointed into the pass. Nothing moved there but smoke.

“Smoke can hide an army,” Tirza said.

“Then keep the gate shut. I’m going out.”

She did not wait to hear whether this was forbidden. At twenty-four, Ylva had outgrown the fear that her mother could stop her feet. She had not outgrown the wish that Tirza would try for the right reasons.

In the lower guardroom she took a coil of lake rope, an ice hook, a wool cloak, and the short iron knife used to cut frozen harness. The captain at the postern looked past her toward the stair, hoping for a different order.

“Tie the rope to me,” Ylva said.

“Her Majesty said the gate stays shut.”

“This is not the gate.”

“Princess—”

“If I fall through, pull.”

That, at least, was an instruction he understood.

The postern opened just wide enough to put her outside. Cold took the wet from Ylva’s eyes and stiffened it on her lashes. The causeway was not a bridge but a winter road laid across the narrowest part of the lake, black ice thick enough for wagons and polished by a hundred years of bride processions. Today it groaned under one woman.

Ylva went quickly until she felt the rope tighten at her waist. Then she shortened her steps. Marzena had stopped on the southern half of the causeway, bent forward with her hands on her knees. Steam came off her shoulders.

“Marza.” The childhood shortening slipped out before Ylva could stop it.

Marzena lifted her head.

The south had changed her in less than a month. Soot filled the hollows beside her nose and lay in the fine cracks of her lips. One eyebrow had burned away at the end. The black gown fitted her too closely, not sewn but hardened around her ribs in overlapping scales. Hair-thin cords ran from its collar into the skin below her ears. Other cords trailed from the skirt, drawing bright scratches across the ice.

Her eyes were the same. Grey, irritated, and at that moment fixed on the cloak under Ylva’s arm.

“Don’t,” Marzena said.

The word ended in a cough. She held up a hand when Ylva moved closer.

“The wool will catch.”

“You’re freezing.”

“I’m not.”

Around her boots, meltwater widened by a finger’s breadth.

Ylva stopped an arm’s length away. She had imagined this welcome in the time it took to descend the tower: an embrace, Marzena’s face against her shoulder, some proof that twenty-three days could be undone by holding tightly enough. Instead there was heat between them and a dress that made a faint ticking sound as it cooled.

Ylva bent two fingers into her palm, the sign they had used under the supper table to mean *Mother is watching*.

Marzena looked toward the parapet. Tirza was a small white shape above the closed gate. Then Marzena made the answering sign with the wrong hand.

It meant *save me the last pear*.

“You’ve forgotten,” Ylva said, and almost laughed.

“No.” Marzena’s mouth shifted. “You always did.”

The laugh came out of Ylva anyway, one ugly breath in the freezing air. It hurt more than crying would have.

From the gate Tirza called, “State your name and purpose.”

Marzena closed her eyes.

Ylva shouted back, “You know her name.”

“The gate requires an answer.”

“The gate is wood.”

“Ylva,” Marzena said. “Later.”

Her voice had the old shape of command, but not the strength. She took two steps north. On the second, a cord at her hem caught in a shallow crack. The gown pulled hard against her neck.

Ylva reached for it. Marzena slapped her hand away.

“Hot.”

“I had gathered that.”

“No. Hot enough to open your fingers.”

Ylva packed snow around the cord until its orange veins dimmed, scored it with the harness knife, and struck the cut with the handle. The glass snapped. Its loose end whipped across the ice and hissed into a puddle.

Marzena drew a full breath for the first time.

“How many?” Ylva asked.

“Four more behind. One at the collar.”

“And if we leave them?”

“The road goes into the lake.”

Practical answers. Marzena had always given them when the other kind cost too much.

Ylva moved behind her and began on the next cord. “Did you burn Cyrak?”

Marzena’s shoulders tightened. “Yes.”

The knife skidded. Ylva caught it before it spun away.

“That isn’t the whole answer.”

“It is the part you asked for.”

Marzena started walking again.

They went north a few steps at a time. Ylva cooled and cut each trailing cord while the rope dragged after her over the ice. At the gate, people were gathering despite the horns: soldiers along the wall, servants in the arrow slits, the bridal glassmakers in their silver masks. No one cheered. Cyrak’s fire painted all their faces alike.

When the third cord broke, something slipped from inside Marzena’s sleeve. She tried to catch it, missed, and swore.

Ylva picked it up. It was a strip of copper as long as her hand, blackened at one end and punched with rows of tiny marks. The seal of Iskal appeared at the start of every row. At the end of every row but the newest, a square had been driven through the metal.

“What is this?”

Marzena kept her eyes on the ice. “Their tally.”

“Of what?”

“Us.”

The wind pushed smoke over the sun. For a moment the whole lake went blue-black, and the marks in the copper seemed to multiply.

“How many are alive?” Ylva asked.

“The newest one.”

Ylva looked up. “You.”

Marzena nodded.

From the parapet, Tirza called, “What has she given you?”

Ylva could not make her voice work. Marzena answered instead.

“The marriage record.”

“We have the marriage record.”

“You have the arrivals.” Marzena coughed into her wrist. “This is the rest.”

The queen’s white figure did not move.

Ylva closed her hand around the copper. “Tell me.”

Marzena looked south. Fire showed in brief pieces when the smoke moved: a roofline, a tower, a running brightness that might have been a whole street.

“The gown is a bridle for their heat channels,” she said. “They fix the cords into the Crown Hearth. A living body inside Iskal glass keeps the winter fire from running wild. When the next bride arrives, they renew the binding.”

“Renew.”

“They take everything left in the old one.”

Ylva understood the punched squares. She wished she did not.

“The letters,” she said. Each bride sent three: safe arrival, gratitude for southern hospitality, assurances of health. Marzena’s first had praised oranges, although she hated them. Her second had used Ylva’s full title. There had been no third.

“Written with three readers behind me.”

At the gate, Tirza said, “You signed them.”

Marzena turned so quickly that the cords at her neck flashed. “I hate oranges.” The effort broke her voice.

Wind swallowed whatever Tirza said next.

Ylva put the copper inside her coat. “How did you get free?”

“I pulled the hearth hook out.”

“And the fire?”

“Went back through everything joined to it. Palace furnaces first. Then the bathhouses. The kiln street.”

Ylva saw, unwillingly, rooms she had never visited filling with flame. “You knew?”

“I knew it would go back.”

“How far?”

“No.” Marzena’s answer came sharp, before Ylva had finished. “They never told me how far. They told me enough to keep me still.”

“Did you warn anyone?”

“The women in the dressing room. The kitchen stairs. People on the east road when I ran.”

“Did they get out?”

Marzena stared at her.

“I don’t know, Ylva.”

The fourth cord took two blows from the knife handle. The fifth had worn a groove of water behind it; Ylva scored it twice before it snapped and sank, spitting, into the lake.

There it was: no innocent account waiting under the damaged one. Marzena had learned what her freedom would cost and had torn loose anyway. Ylva wanted to ask whether children had been in kiln street, whether the fire had reached the river quarter, whether Orravan soldiers were marching north because they had nothing left to guard. She wanted numbers that would make love simple.

The ice gave a deep, splitting knock.

Water ran across Ylva’s boot. They had reached the old pressure ridge at the center of the causeway. Heat pooled around Marzena’s feet, filling white cracks and turning them transparent.

“Move,” Ylva said.

“The collar first.”

Ylva went behind her. The final cord was thicker than the rest and vanished beneath the high collar, then emerged between Marzena’s shoulder blades as a glass loop bright enough to throw red through the skin around it. Ylva swallowed.

“I can’t get the knife under without cutting you.”

“Then go back.”

“Very useful.”

“I mean it.” Marzena’s breath snagged. “The loop spills all at once. Take the tally and go.”

Ylva crouched to pack snow against the collar. It vanished into steam.

“Was I next?” she asked.

Marzena said nothing.

“My measurements were taken again yesterday. Mother said it was caution.”

“Your name was first on the list they sent with me.”

The truth landed with less surprise than shame. Ylva had known. Somewhere underneath her outrage, underneath every hour she had spent at the watchtower, she had known why the glassmakers kept coming to her room.

“Is that why you came back?”

“Get off the ice.”

“Is it?”

Marzena rounded on her. The collar flared, and she flinched but did not turn away. “You were next. I wanted my own bed. I did not want to die in a room called Second Warmth. Choose whichever reason makes you move.”

“I took your bed.”

For one astonished second, Marzena looked offended. “Already?”

“You had six rooms in Cyrak.”

“I had one room with no latch.”

“You can have it back.”

“I don’t want your pity-sheets.”

The laugh hurt Marzena. It folded her at the waist, coughing, one hand pressed uselessly to her ribs. Ylva caught her forearm. This time Marzena did not pull away.

“You crossed the pass to insult my bedding,” Ylva said. “You don’t get to send me back now.”

“I crossed the pass because south had nothing that was mine.”

It was the closest Marzena had come to asking. Ylva tightened her grip.

Behind them, wood boomed. The postern had opened.

Queen Tirza came onto the causeway alone.

She had left her white mantle behind. A second rope circled her waist, its far end looped around the postern hinge; she had tied it herself rather than let a guard follow. Her boots were thin court leather. On the first slick patch, her arms flew out and one hard, ordinary curse crossed the lake.

Marzena made a sound that might have become another laugh in a kinder hour.

“Go back,” she called.

Tirza kept coming.

“Your Majesty,” Ylva said, because titles returned when intimacy hurt. “The ice is failing.”

“I can see that.” Tirza’s breath came fast. “If the cord is removed, what happens?”

“Heat,” Marzena said.

“How much?”

“They neglected my instruction.”

Tirza reached them. Up close, she looked older than she had on the tower. Meltwater darkened both knees of her gown where she had fallen.

“Where may I hold you?” she asked.

Marzena glanced at her, startled. “Left arm. Not the cloth.”

Tirza took her arm above Ylva’s hand. Marzena stood between them, rigid as the glass around her.

“I knew the treaty forbade return,” Tirza said.

Marzena looked toward the gate.

“I did not know it killed you.”

“You didn’t ask.”

“No.”

The lake shifted under their feet. Tirza’s grip slipped and closed again.

Ylva heard herself shout, “Why not?”

For once, her mother had no council answer ready. Her mouth opened, closed. She looked past them at the southern road as if an answer might still be coming up it.

“Because then I might have had to say no.”

No one forgave her. The wind went on dragging smoke north.

Ylva pushed the knife under the collar loop. Marzena jerked.

“Wait,” Tirza said.

“There isn’t time.”

“I was not speaking to you.” Tirza shifted her hand, not tighter but steadier. “Marzena. Now?”

Marzena shut her eyes. After a moment, she nodded.

Ylva cut.

The loop sprang apart with a noise like a plate breaking. White heat struck the ice. Water leapt around their boots, and the causeway dropped half a hand beneath them. Tirza went down. Marzena fell against her. Ylva’s rope snapped taut and threw her backward, but she kept hold of the knife.

For several breaths the severed cord burned beneath the water, orange, red, then a dull cherry glow. It did not reach for them. It did not follow. It spent what remained and went black.

Tirza struggled to one knee with Marzena’s weight across her shoulder.

“Was the fire an accident?” she asked.

“No,” Marzena said.

“Are you asking me to pardon you?”

“No.”

“What are you asking?”

Marzena’s answer was so quiet Ylva nearly missed it. “Open the gate.”

Tirza looked at the black water spreading over the road, at Ylva, and then at the daughter she had sent south. She raised her free hand.

The crosspieces began to move.

They reached the gate as the last one lifted. Soldiers stood back from Marzena’s smoking dress. No one knew whether to bow. Tirza stepped across the threshold first, then turned and waited.

Marzena stopped outside.

“Am I under arrest?” she asked.

The queen opened her mouth. Ylva watched her reach for law, condition, title—any clean thing that might stand between them.

“No,” Tirza said.

“Then what am I?”

Tirza had no answer. Instead she stepped aside, leaving the whole width of the doorway clear.

After a moment, Marzena crossed it.

Inside the guardroom, the healers peeled the dead glass from the gown with bowls of snow and blunt iron. They worked behind a screen, and Marzena refused sleeping draught until every cord lay cooling in a bucket. The captain brought news in scraps: no southern troops at the pass, no messenger, no way to see beyond the smoke. By morning, any of those things might change.

Tirza listened, then pointed to the copper tally in Ylva’s hand. “Lock that in my private chest.”

Marzena’s head came up.

The queen stopped. “No. Keep it.”

Ylva put it back inside her coat.

“And the procession?” the captain asked. Everyone in the room knew he meant Ylva’s.

Tirza looked at Marzena, wrapped now in three grey blankets, her face slack with exhaustion.

“No bride leaves Iskal,” she said. “Not tonight. Not at dawn.”

It was not a plan for the army Orrava might send. It was not justice for whoever had failed to outrun the fire. It was one door held shut.

They took Marzena to the room that had once been hers. Ylva had, in fact, moved into it on the ninth day after the procession, though she had kept Marzena’s cracked blue cup on the sill and her collection of bent hairpins in the drawer. She began to apologize for this. Marzena was asleep before Ylva reached the apology.

Tirza stayed at the threshold, wet and soot-marked from holding her daughter. Without the white mantle she seemed uncertain where to put her hands.

Ylva sat on the edge of the bed. “Are you coming in?”

“If she permits it.”

Marzena did not open her eyes. “Shut the door,” she whispered. “You’re letting the cold in.”

Tirza obeyed. Then she sat on the floor beside the bed, boots still wet, while Marzena slept before any of them could ask her for another thing.

stories.title: The Dress They Brought Her
stories.prompt: A woman with dark messy hair, dull grey eyes, skin covered in tattoos, and piercings all over her body sits in a cell. She drags on a cig she bummed off a guard. A man in a suit enters and hands her a sparkly pink dress and wand. "The other magical girls are dead, you are the last one."
stories.body:
# The Dress They Brought Her

The guard had crushed the cigarette's filter when he slipped it through the meal hatch, but he had given her more than half. She sat on the edge of the cell's bolted bed and made it last. One drag, a wait while the ember considered going out, another drag. The ventilation pulled the smoke toward the door and then changed its mind.

In the steel mirror above the sink, her dark hair looked as if somebody had searched it and found nothing. It had been messy before the cell and was messier now. Her eyes were the same dull grey under every light. Her skin was covered in tattoos chosen over years: the black leaves climbing her left hand, the blue match on one finger, the bird with three crooked wings along her ribs, the old bright shapes crowding both arms. Piercings caught the ceiling glare at her brow, nose, lip, ears, and in glints all over her body. Some were metal, some clear prison retainers, all noted on the intake map as circles and numbers.

She had bummed the cigarette off the guard by looking at his breast pocket, then at him, until he sighed through his nose. Neither of them had spoiled the arrangement with words.

Footsteps came down the range. The guard appeared first, his shoulders held differently. Behind him walked a man in a charcoal suit that had been brushed clean except at the cuffs, where pale dust remained in the weave. He carried a flat white case. No prison insignia. No tie pin. A black credential rested against his shirt with its face turned inward.

The door opened. The suited man entered her cell as if entering a room he had reserved.

He set the case on her bed, released two silver catches, and lifted out a sparkly pink dress. The skirt had enough layers to stand up by itself. Tiny hard stars had been sewn along the hem. Beneath it lay a pink wand with a silver handle and a five-pointed head, the sort of object that ought to have been either priceless or sold beside birthday candles.

He put the dress into her arms. Then he placed the wand across it, physically careful, like a medic settling a splint.

"The other magical girls are dead, you are the last one."

The guard watched the cigarette. The suited man watched her face.

She drew in smoke until the paper warmed her fingers. Then she let it out over the glitter.

Nothing in the dress stirred. Nothing in the wand answered. The star at its tip was molded around a seam; one point bore a shallow scrape. She rolled the handle against her palm. No hidden weight shifted. No warmth entered her skin. The dress smelled of new plastic, sealed cloth, and the faint burnt odor that had got into everything since the western sky went white.

The suited man took a tablet from inside his jacket. Its first card showed a plain numeral above a thin grey line.

`era-local ultrahuman count: 1`

Below that were two empty fields.

`IDENTITY: UNAVAILABLE`

`LOCATION: UNAVAILABLE`

He touched the screen. A separate card slid over the count: a packet number, an amber recovery seal, and her booking portrait. In the photograph her hair had been wet from the intake shower. Her expression had been the one she saved for cameras owned by other people.

The man drew his finger from the count of one to her face.

She looked at the join between the cards. A narrow dark line remained there. The number knew no name. The packet claimed it did.

He opened the packet.

Most of its pages were thumbnails with heat-blackened edges. Pink crests. Dense columns of old print. A uniform diagram had lost everything except one white glove and the curve of a skirt. Another page displayed a row of little crown shapes, each crossed through in red. Whatever the packet had once known, fire and water had eaten the useful parts first.

At its end sat a clean white human outline stippled with marks.

Her marks.

The bird at her ribs had been reduced to three dots and a code. The leaves on her hand were a shaded patch. Rings and bars became numbered circles. Beside the outline appeared her booking portrait and the number `P-80417`.

The suited man enlarged the match result. Green brackets settled around the tattoos visible above her prison shirt. A percentage climbed. It was high enough to make his shoulders loosen.

She pinched the dress fabric between finger and thumb. The outer layer rasped. One star snagged against the blue match tattoo. She freed it without haste.

Another gesture brought up a transfer route. Cell. Intake. Exterior recovery gate. Vehicle court. The last two boxes lay beyond the prison hold. An authorization mark was already green; there was no request for her consent and no place for a signature. The unit had not come to ask whether she was somebody. It had come to collect the somebody its records had made.

For a moment she saw only the exterior gate.

The battle had broken half the cameras on the wall and pulled staff into twelve-hour shifts. Beyond the vehicle court were roads with dark traffic lights, abandoned checkpoints, houses standing open after evacuation. Recovery custody would still be custody. The man would still be watching. But it was movement, and movement sometimes developed gaps.

She could put on the dress. She could let their mistake carry her past concrete and wire. Later, if later arrived, she could become difficult in a place with windows.

The wand remained dead in her hand. The tablet's green brackets held the ink on her skin as though strangers had put it there for this purpose.

She dragged the packet thumbnails sideways with one fingernail.

The man allowed it. He mistook examination for recognition.

At the left edge of the body map, nearly cropped away, was a black-and-white measuring strip. She knew the thickness of those bars. She had stood against them barefoot while an intake camera flashed. In one corner was the triangular shadow of a property-bag seal. The paper was not some secret portrait rescued from a magical archive. It was the first sheet of her prison booking.

She tapped `P-80417`, then tapped the same number on the band around her wrist.

The man nodded too quickly. Of course the number matched. That was his proof.

She swiped upward. A source strip appeared: five burned packet pages scanned at the evacuation station, a thin black rectangle labelled unreadable, then the body map one minute later. The strip grouped all seven pages beneath the recovery seal. At the far end, almost hidden by the portrait card, a property-bag icon waited behind a lock.

She touched the icon.

The tablet asked for internal property verification.

She pointed down the range, toward intake.

The guard's gaze moved from her finger to the bundle in her lap. The suited man tapped the transfer route. A new green check appeared beside personal effects. He thought she wanted her belongings before she left.

Good enough.

The guard held out his palm for the cigarette. She took one last drag, pressed the ember dead against the steel lip of the sink, and gave him the butt. He wrapped it in a scrap of foil from his pocket. His eyes rested on the wand, then on her. The favor between them had become something he might have to explain.

They took her out without normal waist restraints. The suited man's credential had changed the rules faster than anything she had ever said could have done. She carried the dress folded over one arm, badly, its stiff pink skirt knocking against her thigh. The wand lay along her forearm. Glitter collected on her prison shirt.

The man walked half a pace ahead. At every security door he presented the tablet before the guard could reach his own badge. Cellblock grey gave way to the sour cream paint of intake. Emergency cables ran along the floor under black rubber mats. Through a wired window at the final turn, she could see a slice of outdoor evening and the high lamps of the vehicle court.

She slowed at the window.

The suited man looked back. He showed her the route again, tapped the green exterior box, then pointed ahead. Certainty had made him generous with the future.

She shifted the dress higher and followed.

The property counter stood behind mesh and thick glass. Nobody occupied the chair on the other side. The night system worked by itself: a shallow pass-through drawer, a receipt scanner, and a belt that brought sealed bags from the caged shelves. To the right, the recovery transfer reader made a doorway of blue light. Beyond it, an exterior gate waited open by the width of a hand.

The guard scanned her wrist. Somewhere behind the wall, machinery clacked into motion. A clear bag slid down the belt and struck the drawer.

`P-80417` showed through the plastic.

Inside were the metal pieces intake had made her exchange for clear retainers, a black cord, three coins, a comb missing two teeth, and the clothes she had arrived in. A folded carbon receipt sat in a sleeve on the outside of the bag. Her thumbprint smudged one corner purple. Across its top, half hidden by the fold, ran `NEW BOOKING — PROPERTY P-80417` and the same minute shown beneath the packet's final page.

The blue transfer reader brightened.

The suited man put his palm toward it. The tablet displayed the next step: live identity anchor. Once she crossed that light, a fresh scan of the body that matched the intake map would replace the packet's damaged proof. The system would stop depending on a bad page boundary. It would have her, now, confirming itself.

Outside air touched the wet corner of her eye through the narrow-open gate. It smelled of hot pavement and rain that had not yet fallen.

She set the dress on the counter.

The man took that for readiness. He lifted the wand from her arm and offered it back point-first toward the blue doorway.

She took it by the silver handle but turned away from the light. She jerked the carbon receipt from its sleeve and shoved the property drawer closed, hard enough to make the guard's hand jump.

The counter flashed a warning. She flattened the receipt beneath its red beam. Purple thumbprint. New-booking header. `P-80417`.

Her custody record filled the display. The booking portrait appeared beside the body map, but this time the header was plain: prison intake, property opened, property sealed. No crown shapes. No pink crest. No survivor claim.

Before either man moved, she hooked the star of the wand through the strap on the suited man's tablet. She pulled its lower edge across the counter and under the red beam.

The guard drove her forearm down against the laminate. Pain struck from wrist to elbow. The wand clattered onto the counter. The suited man caught his tablet with both hands.

The scanner had already read the packet code.

Both records appeared side by side. Between them, `P-80417` burned red.

The counter disliked an outside file claiming an internal property number. It opened the raw sequence without being asked. The display simplified what the recovery tablet had dressed in seals and green brackets.

Five burned pages.

One black, unreadable separator.

One prison body map.

The times beneath them differed by sixty-three seconds. Above the body map, the counter restored a clipped line from its own copy:

`NEW BOOKING — PROPERTY P-80417`

Below the black rectangle, the recovery system had supplied its conclusion:

`PREVIOUS PACKET CONTINUES`

The suited man stopped pulling on the tablet.

She kept her cheek near the counter where the guard's hold had put it. From there the answer was almost offensively clear. Charred pink paper ended. Her white intake sheet began. The missing separator had let one file swallow the next, and the first thing it swallowed was her body.

The guard looked to the suited man.

The suited man raised one hand. The pressure left her arm.

He enlarged the raw sequence, not the match percentage. His eyes moved once from the sixty-three-second gap to the restored booking line, then to the carbon receipt still under her fingers. He photographed the three together with the tablet's rear lens. He did it again after moving the dress so its glitter did not cover the number.

The blue transfer reader pulsed. Its light divided the floor at her toes. Past it, the exterior gate opened another hand's width with a hydraulic sigh.

The route remained authorized. No alarm had cancelled it. The suited man had not yet touched the hold control. If she stepped forward, the live reader would take the tattoos, the piercings, the dull grey eyes, every measurement the prison had made, and fasten them to the burned packet. It would also take her through the exterior gate.

He looked from the evidence to her. Doubt had entered his face, but so had urgency. Somewhere inside his system there was still one anonymous danger, and he had arrived prepared to leave with a person.

She could give him one.

The night beyond the gate was close enough to smell.

She stepped backward.

The reader's light fell away from her body. She gathered the dress with both hands, trapping the wand in its pink folds, and pushed the bundle against the suited man's chest. He had to take it or let it fall. He took it.

Then she scanned the carbon receipt again, alone.

Her prison record returned. `P-80417`. Custody unchanged. External identity blank.

She turned the suited man's tablet screen-up on the counter but kept its code beyond the beam. With one finger she drew a boundary in the source strip: burned page, burned page, burned page, burned page, burned page; unreadable separator; new booking. She stopped at the black rectangle.

The man watched the sequence. After a long moment, he moved the boundary to the same place on his own screen.

The body map slid out of the recovery packet. Her portrait went with it. The packet collapsed to five damaged pages and an amber field where a person had been.

`IDENTITY: UNASSIGNED`

He opened the grey count card beneath it.

`era-local ultrahuman count: 1`

The number did not flicker. No face appeared. No map opened. Whatever the count counted, it had never needed her record and offered no direction toward anyone else.

The suited man saved the raw scan. He touched the hold control on the transfer route.

The exterior gate closed.

He tucked the wand fully inside the dress so that only one silver point showed, then carried the pink bundle under his arm. It looked less like a relic that way and more like something returned to the wrong shop. At the corridor door he paused. His gaze dropped to the red mark rising along her forearm where the guard had pinned it. Then he turned his credential outward for the first time and used it to cancel his own extraction.

The guard resealed her property bag. He returned the carbon receipt to it, keeping her number with her things. When the belt had carried the bag back into the cage, he gestured toward the cellblock.

She went with him.

At her cell, he opened the door and waited until she was inside. Before closing it, he took the foil from his pocket. The crushed half cigarette had gone out but had not broken. He held it between two fingers, coaxed the ember back with his lighter, and set it on the steel sink lip.

The lock engaged. The suited man's footsteps receded with the faint rasp of stiff pink fabric.

She sat on the bolted bed. Glitter remained in the black leaves on her hand. She picked it out piece by piece, then reached for the cigarette. The smoke went toward the door, reversed, and spread thin against the ceiling.

stories.title: The Seventh Night
stories.prompt: An adult elven adventurer has spent years hiding an infuriating curse: if she goes too long without taking a lover, the magic begins stealing her youth and beauty, rapidly aging her until she gives in and the clock resets.
stories.body:
# The Seventh Night

By the time Galten laid the broadside beside the gravy, Thalenna had already dismantled half a roast bird with the precision of a field surgeon and the innocent expression of a woman who had never been naked in a dungeon in her life.

The private dining room had been left to the two of them. Candles warmed the dark timber and the gold fittings of Thalenna's green-black armor. Her cloak, a deep green better suited to dramatic arrivals than supper, hung from the back of her chair. Long golden-blonde hair fell over one shoulder, carefully freed from every buckle and hinge, and the little red jewel at her brow burned above eyes as green as bottle glass. Poise had required preparation. So had the hair.

Across the table, Galten tapped the broadside with one blunt fingernail.

"You said there were three lies."

"Three material lies." Thalenna cut another slice. "Demonic blood. Helpless thralls. Stolen youth. The rest is merely vulgar arrangement."

"It says the orgy began at midnight."

"That is not material."

"It began before midnight."

"That is not the useful correction."

She set down her knife. On the broadside, an inked elf with horns, breasts of ambitious geometry, and six yards of hair beckoned three kneeling swordsmen toward a dungeon bed large enough for a duke. The title promised the true account of the *Demon-Blooded Delver of the Seventh Night*. Below it, smaller type suggested she had drained the youth from her victims and applied it to her own face.

The engraving had given Galten a moustache. He was a grown human man, quite capable of growing one, and had chosen not to. This was its least plausible claim.

"You agreed to discuss what we tell people," she said.

"I agreed to dinner."

"The dinner is for discussing what we tell people."

He looked at the platters: roast bird, buttered roots, onions glazed dark with wine, a loaf still warm beneath its cloth, and a quince tart waiting under a silver cover. "Then you ordered too much food for two sentences."

"There will be more than two."

"I was afraid of that."

Thalenna folded the broadside so the horned caricature vanished. "We returned from an extended expedition in compromised condition. Malicious observers invented a sexual spectacle. We deny the invention, decline particulars, and preserve the dignity of all four adults involved."

"Four adults who weren't involved?"

"Four adults whose involvement is no one's business."

His jokes had been coming half a heartbeat too quickly since he sat down. Galten joked when a wound was small enough to expose and large enough to resent. Thalenna had learned this over two years, several contracts, and a love life whose map required colored pins.

She reached for her wine. "The broadside is wrong where it matters."

"Then say what happened."

"You were there."

"I want to hear which version of me was."

The bird cooled between them.

Thalenna disliked a battlefield on which stillness counted as an attack. "The seventh day underground, I became ill."

"You told us it was tomb dust."

"We were in a tomb. There was dust."

"Your hair went grey between breakfast and noon."

"Ash adheres to hair."

"By noon you looked eighty years older and were pretending not to notice."

Her pointed ears heated. She hated that he could still see it. "I had hoped to disclose the relevant facts after we escaped."

"You couldn't straighten your fingers by supper."

"I couldn't get the damned gauntlet off."

Galten leaned down, brought up a gauntlet, and placed it beside the folded broadside.

It was hers: dark green-black leather, narrow in the wrist, worked with a gold leaf at the cuff. She had spent two days claiming it had been lost in a flooded gallery.

"Traitor," she told the gauntlet.

"It was in my pack. Under your left boot."

"My left boot was also lost."

"No. I wore it out."

"I had wondered why you limped."

"You asked if I'd developed a seductive gait."

Against her will, the corner of her mouth moved. She hid it in her wine.

Galten tore bread instead of eating it. "Tell it properly."

Properly was not a condition Thalenna associated with that night. Still, he had brought back her gauntlet. He had also brought the broadside instead of showing it to anyone whose laughter would travel.

"Six days is usually safe," she said. "After that, if I haven't had sex, I start to age. You saw how quickly."

"Would it have kept going?"

"Decades in hours. Until I had sex. Then I'm my own age again, with every cut and bruise I had before. Just as tired. No improvement in my disposition."

"Nothing improves your disposition."

"Several people have tried."

His bread suffered a second, more thoughtful tearing. "No other way?"

She had spent years testing answers: fasting, feasting, potions, prayer, counterspells, solo efforts, and two expensive healers who had disagreed on everything except their fee. Galten had known about the curse for two nights. He still asked as though she might have overlooked something.

For years she had hidden the result behind short contracts, invented family obligations, and a romantic calendar complicated enough to require colored ink. Ordinary travel could be managed. An extended crawl swallowed dates, privacy, and the comforting fiction that heroes controlled their own schedules. Stone did not care who was expecting her home on the sixth night.

"No cure," she said. "No substitute. And no demon, whatever that thing says." She nodded at the broadside. "I can't make anyone want me. I still have to ask."

Galten's gaze lifted from the bread. His expression had lost its joke.

She gave the onions a look usually reserved for mutinous scouts. "So I called the three of you together."

The archer had grown children. The ward-scribe was a widower old enough to have gone grey honestly. Thalenna had still rehearsed the announcement as though she expected them to faint.

"You told us while wearing one stocking on your arm."

"I couldn't bend far enough to get it on my foot. My hand was cold."

"You called us to a tactical conference."

"There was a tactical difficulty."

"You stood behind a hanging bedroll and announced that the situation required carnal cooperation."

"I was attempting not to alarm anyone."

"The bedroll fell down halfway through *carnal*."

"Galten."

"Properly," he reminded her.

She carved a root vegetable into four increasingly small pieces. "I explained badly. You laughed. I considered killing you. Then I asked if you wanted to. You all said yes."

"Because we already wanted to."

"I was there for that part."

"You keep leaving it out."

The knife stopped. Galten met her eyes, then looked down first and put bread into his mouth as if he could chew the admission back into harmlessness.

Thalenna resumed cutting. "We barred the door. What happened next is staying off the record."

"At last," he said around the bread, "an accurate sentence."

"When we were dressed again—"

He coughed.

"What?"

"A generous use of *dressed*."

There lay the treacherous heart of the story. The middle, which the broadside had inflated into a perfumed siege, had gone as middles went: intimate, ridiculous in places, and nobody else's. The aftermath had required leadership. The aftermath had not received it.

"I was dressed," Thalenna said.

"You had one boot, my shirt, and your cloak fastened backward."

"A cloak is reversible."

"Not when the clasp is between your shoulder blades. You told the archer it was a court fashion."

"She had been staring."

"Your backside was showing."

"Then she was rude to stare."

Galten laughed into his cup. This time the sound came late enough to be real.

Thalenna speared an onion. "It all came back so quickly. I'd fastened the mail while I was still shrivelled. Then my hair grew back and caught in the links at the collar."

"We had to oil you."

"You oiled the mail."

They had possessed one cup of clean water, two cloths of uncertain history, and a thumb-sized cake of soap for four recently unclothed adults in a crypt. Galten remembered the arithmetic with vindictive clarity. Thalenna maintained that her hair required half the water because it represented half the cleaning surface. He maintained that dungeon dust could not possibly have reached the back of her knee in the quantity alleged.

"Dungeon dust travels," she said.

"With purpose."

"Unlike some people, who spent ten minutes polishing a belt that was not theirs."

"It looked like mine."

"Yours does not have silver stars."

"The light was poor."

"You put saddle dressing on it."

"You used the massage oil on your sword."

"The sword slid out beautifully."

Galten choked on wine. Thalenna ate her onion with serene attention until he recovered.

"That," he said hoarsely, "was deliberate."

"I don't know what you mean."

She did. Victory restored her appetite.

"The inventory took nearly an hour," Thalenna said, returning the conversation to defensible ground. "Four belts became five because someone counted the baldric. We found three left boots before locating a right. Your shirt had a tear shaped like a small country. The ward-scribe found my brow jewel in a folded map, and the archer found a stocking in the ration bag. But why was there a spoon buckled into your sword harness?"

"You blamed structural collapse for the spoon," Galten said.

"The tomb was unstable."

"The spoon was secured with two buckles."

"I did not say it collapsed quickly."

By the time their account reached the privacy rope, Galten had eaten half his roast without noticing. Before the private choice, the rope had supported two bedrolls as a screen. Afterward, Thalenna explained, four adults who had recently displayed nearly everything to one another discovered an urgent need to change clothes separately. They retied the rope, added a blanket, and produced a knot of such moral seriousness that no blade wished to approach it.

Then they needed the rope to cross the broken stair.

"You cut it," Thalenna said.

"You ordered me to."

"I suggested decisive action."

"You said, 'Cut the damned thing before I age another year.'"

"The shortened rope wouldn't span the gap," she continued, "so we tied belts to it. Two belonged to the wrong people. One held. One surrendered. The third had never been a belt at all, but the ward-scribe's instrument strap."

"His measuring frame rang all the way down the steps," Galten said. "You tried to count the bounces."

"I was estimating the depth."

"You reached thirty and said the tomb was being theatrical."

"It was."

Thalenna buttered bread. "No one was injured."

"My dignity was injured."

"Your dignity was wearing my boot."

"Only because you had mine."

She glanced beneath the table, where both her present boots sat properly paired. "It was dark."

"You walked three miles before admitting the heel was loose."

"I know. The reset doesn't heal blisters."

"It also doesn't heal bites."

"That mark came from falling masonry."

"Masonry with excellent teeth."

She pointed the bread knife at him. "The act remains off the record."

"The aftermath has tooth marks."

"Many dungeons do."

For a moment neither managed to eat. Thalenna pressed her lips together. Galten stared at his plate with both shoulders shaking. When he made the mistake of looking up, her restraint broke. Her laugh came out inelegant and too loud for the small room. It loosened something under her breastbone that armor had nothing to do with.

The broadside lay folded between them. Its hidden ink waited.

Galten wiped his eyes. "You forgot the watch."

"We did not forget the watch."

"Then who had it?"

"The archer."

"She was repairing your cloak."

"The ward-scribe, then."

"He was looking for his belt."

"You."

"I was getting your hair out of the mail."

"I was clearly occupied."

Their laughter thinned as they reconstructed the missing watch over cooling plates. There had been no watch for forty minutes. Nothing had attacked them. Something had eaten the honey from the ration bag with delicate, scraping bites, leaving the spoon and taking the last clean cloth. Four celebrated delvers had then accused one another of licking the jar.

"It could have been the archer," Thalenna said.

"She said it wasn't."

"So did I. You believed her."

There it was: her own jealousy, springing a trap intended for his. Galten's eyebrows rose.

Thalenna took refuge in the roast. "The point is that by dawn, no one had slept, our equipment was distributed according to chance, and we left looking less like heroes than survivors of a wardrobe explosion. That is the truth behind the rumor."

"Not all of it."

"You keep saying that."

He unfolded the broadside. The horned elf returned, smiling with supernatural confidence. "I know this is rubbish. I know we all wanted to be there."

"Then what are we arguing about?"

"Would you have asked me without the curse?"

Thalenna had an answer about shortened expeditions ready. She looked at him and let it go. Galten put both hands flat on the table, then seemed to dislike the display and picked up his knife. He sawed at meat already cut small enough.

"I don't want to be another bit of equipment," he said.

Thalenna looked at the gauntlet between them. Her gauntlet, carried in his pack. Her missing boot, worn out because he had put it on in the dark and kept moving when the dungeon demanded movement. For two years, she had treated gratitude as a dangerous opening through which other words might get in.

"You weren't," she said.

"Then why do you keep editing me out?"

"I am editing everyone out."

"Even here?"

"My reputation is not an ornament. It gets us contracts. It gets doors opened before things behind them finish eating people. The songs call me the Golden Thorn, not the Elf Who Requires Scheduled Company."

"The second one scans badly."

"And if this version spreads, every victory becomes seduction. Every refusal becomes proof of enchantment. Every person I share a room with becomes a victim, and every person I actually choose becomes a fool."

Galten stopped cutting. That, at last, had reached him. Not perfectly; he still had to swallow before he answered.

"I don't want it spread," he said. "I brought you the sheet. I'm not taking your truth outside this room."

"You also brought a prosecution."

He laid the sheet aside and looked down at the scraps of meat on his plate. "I did. I'm sorry."

Thalenna loosened her grip on her knife. "I don't mind wanting someone. Having to ask before my hands stop working is rather different."

"And I've made you explain it all again." He put his knife down. "I'll stop."

She could have ended there. He had agreed on the important thing: no public correction, no public testimony, no feeding the rumor a second course. The curse would remain private. The broadside would have only mismatched gear and tired witnesses to chew on until a fresher scandal arrived.

But the quince tart waited between them, and Galten had not touched it. He loved quince. Thalenna hated it. Ordering it had seemed much less compromising when it was under a lid.

She removed the silver cover.

Galten looked at the tart, then at her. "Bribery?"

"Final course."

"Same thing in better pastry."

She cut the tart. The crust resisted, cracked, and sent a fan of crumbs over the open broadside. Galten brushed them away.

"You have asked why there were four of us," she said.

"I have thought it loudly."

"One would have reset the curse."

His face did something small and ugly before he could stop it. "The ward-scribe, then. Very efficient."

"He spent a quarter hour trying to unlace a boot that belonged to the archer. Efficiency was not our governing principle."

"I thought you might have asked her anyway."

"I might have."

Galten shut his mouth. Thalenna waited until he looked at her instead of his plate.

Thalenna gave him the larger slice. "I asked all three because I wanted all three. I'd have preferred to say so with my boots on and a little less urgency."

"And me?"

"You were among the three."

"A stirring distinction."

She ate a spiteful forkful of quince and regretted it at once. The fruit was perfumed wool. Across from her, Galten waited badly, his shoulders held too square, his fork untouched. She could remember asking him. Explaining why was proving worse.

"I asked you first," she said.

"Because you knew I'd say yes."
