"No." Her fork clicked against the plate. "Because you were the one I was afraid would say no."

Galten's attention dropped to the table between them, to her bare hand beside the gauntlet. He drew a breath, but said nothing.

Thalenna could feel the ceremony trying to rebuild itself around her. She did not let it.

"It has been two nights since the reset," she said.

He looked up.

"I didn't need to invite you tonight. I wanted dinner with you."

He smiled, but did not rescue himself with a joke. Instead he reached across the table and turned her hand palm-up. His fingers rested in hers, warm and ordinary, carrying no magic at all.

"I was jealous of the archer," he said.

"I know."

"Not the ward-scribe."

"That is extremely rude to him."

"I'll apologize if he ever finds his belt."

Thalenna folded her fingers around his. With her other hand she pushed the broadside beneath the empty silver cover. The agenda had ended. The candles had shortened; the tart remained; neither of them moved to leave.

"Eat," she said. "I ordered the revolting thing for you."

Galten took his hand back only long enough to pick up his fork. "Properly," he said, and stayed.

stories.title: The Queen After Ten Thousand Years
stories.prompt: 10 thousand years after the last pharaoh was entombed, the some of kings and queens of ancient Egypt awaken but exactly as they promised, cloned from ancient DNA a product of generics —  the great queen rebuild her lost kingdom into a vast technological super-empire spanning most of the world.
stories.body:
# The Queen After Ten Thousand Years

The first thing Merneith knew was that the gold was wiring.

It climbed the black wall in bright, branching channels, entered the spread feathers of a solar falcon, and vanished beneath the stone couch where she lay. Turquoise coolant ticked through glass capillaries under her palms. Everything had been made to resemble a tomb by people who did not believe in tombs.

She sat up too quickly. The room tipped. A woman caught her by the wrist, laughed once, and let go when Merneith stiffened.

“Good,” the woman said. “You dislike being handled. They will be disappointed.”

Merneith knew six languages, three systems of orbital mechanics, the chemistry of the coolant, and the probable century of her own death. She remembered lessons delivered across the accelerated years of her body's growth: diagrams, rehearsals, arguments with patient tutors. She remembered no husband, no son, no First Dynasty court. The life pieced together from seals, tomb goods, and later scholarship was a house whose foundation plan she had studied from outside.

According to every instrument, she was a clone made from ancient DNA: surviving sequence where the fragments allowed, modeled genes where decay had erased them. No instrument could call her the woman who had died.

The woman beside her wore gray laboratory cloth. Her shaved head made the long planes of her face severe. She looked familiar because Merneith had been taught the surviving statues.

“Hatshepsut,” Merneith said.

“That is what they hope.”

Beyond the glass wall, geneticists and custodians watched without pretending not to. One held a ceremonial collar on a cushion. Another held a museum contract.

Merneith looked down at herself. Adult hands. Fine scars where growth monitors had entered the skin. Black hair, still damp, falling almost to her waist. “How long?”

“Since the last pharaoh was put under stone? Ten thousand years, give or take the arguments. Since they pulled your viable sequences out of a tooth and began filling the gaps? Nineteen.”

“I am nineteen?”

“Your bones disagree. Your opinions will have to catch up.”

Merneith swung her feet to the floor. The technicians had warmed the stone, an unnecessary kindness she resented because it worked.

“Did you wake with memories?” she asked.

Hatshepsut shook her head.

“Did any of them?”

“No.”

Merneith pressed two fingers to her brow, absurdly searching for a seam. Nothing opened. She had expected nothing else. She had been taught the limits until she could recite them under sedation: genes could rebuild a body within tolerances, not retrieve a vanished mind; resemblance was not recollection; the missing portions of a genome were estimates, not revelation. Still, a person might be reasonable and disappointed at once.

On the wall, a translation of an ancient burial promise glowed above the observers: the name enduring, the body renewed, the ruler joining eternity. The laboratory had used it in every funding appeal.

“They call it the Return of the Sovereigns,” Hatshepsut said. “Until one of us complains. Then they call it the Heritage Genome Initiative.”

“Which did you choose?”

“Hatshepsut. For now. It opens doors, and I like the shape of it.” She folded her arms. “They cannot give it to you. That part is yours.”

The glass door opened. A custodian entered with the collar and a smile disciplined by months of rehearsal.

“Your Majesty,” he began, in reconstructed court Egyptian.

His vowels were dreadful. Merneith knew that because her tutors disagreed about them.

She glanced at the contract. Six years of appearances in the Giza Renewal Vault, supervised interviews, approved clothing, no political endorsements. Beyond the custodian, the observation gallery held the silhouettes of donors who had purchased the privilege of seeing history blink.

“Show me the Nile,” she said.

The custodian faltered. “The orientation sequence—”

“A map will orient me.”

The wall abandoned the funeral promise. A river appeared, narrowed by drought works and studded with the lights of quarrelling city republics. There was no Egypt on the political layer. The name survived only on archaeological zones, commodity brands, and the laboratory beneath her feet.

Merneith touched the nearest light. It opened into water prices, ration hours, power losses, a municipal appeal unanswered for eleven months. The figures were new to her and instantly intolerable.

“How long has it been divided?” she asked.

“Which time?” said the custodian.

Hatshepsut snorted. Merneith looked at her, and the other queen tried unsuccessfully to make her face innocent.

“I choose Merneith,” she said. “Let the historians keep their question marks. The name is mine.” She lifted the ceremonial collar from its cushion and placed it around her own neck. It was too heavy and one clasp pinched. “Now show me who owns the pumps.”

* * *

Her second throne had wheels.

It rolled along the half-built audience hall in Alexandria on a magnetic track while welders worked above the petitioners. Black composite columns rose around old blocks of limestone too damaged for any museum to want. Gold conductors ran openly along their sides. At the far end, the wings of a solar falcon spread thirty meters across the wall, each feather a heat exchanger feeding the district grid.

Merneith had ordered a fixed throne. Hatshepsut had put it on the track so construction crews could move her out of the way.

“Symbolism should be useful,” Hatshepsut said when challenged.

“It symbolizes that my chief builder is insolent.”

“And mobile.”

Four years after the Vault, the river cities had not so much bowed as discovered that Merneith's power contracts used the same junctions as her water contracts, and both improved when councils stopped charging one another at every boundary. She had bought failing solar fields, repaired desalination mouths, and linked them to a single Nile spine. Cities joined because the lights stayed on. They stayed because neighboring cities had joined first.

This was not the return she had been promised. It was better. A dead queen could only be admired. A living one could make herself difficult to remove.

She dismissed three tariff petitions and opened the route survey for the southern conductor. A straight gold line crossed the map.

Hatshepsut reached over her shoulder and bent it east with two fingers.

“Put it back,” Merneith said.

“There are houses there.”

“The survey says scrubland.”

“The survey is nine years old. I went.”

“You went?” Merneith disliked how childish the question sounded.

Hatshepsut enlarged the ground image. Courtyards clustered under patchwork shade. A child had drawn blue fish on a cistern. The new line curled around them and cost an additional eleven days.

“Straight lines are excellent for dead kings,” Hatshepsut said. “Nothing moves into them.”

The petitioners heard. One covered a smile with both hands.

Merneith restored the curved route. “Twelve days,” she said, because yielding eleven would look affectionate.

“Cruel woman.”

“You may spend the extra day apologizing to the survey office.”

Hatshepsut leaned against the throne, close enough that their shoulders touched. She had taken to growing her hair and cutting it again whenever sculptors settled on a likeness. She accepted no title longer than her name. Merneith had offered her First Royal Builder, Co-Sovereign of the Two Banks, Beloved of the Renewed Sun. Hatshepsut had asked whether any came with better boots.

Their arguments became part of the court's machinery. Merneith pushed until Hatshepsut showed her what would break. Hatshepsut repaired what Merneith refused to abandon. Between them, the Nile spine reached the sea.

At night the solar falcon shone over Alexandria, each feather carrying more current than the Giza Vault had consumed in a year. People began stamping Merneith's profile on batteries without permission. She sued the first manufacturer, licensed the second, and bought the third.

When the last river council signed the union charter, Merneith removed the wheels from her throne.

Hatshepsut kept them in her workshop.

* * *

Ramesses woke in the twelfth year of the New Egyptian Empire and spent his first public morning arguing about furniture.

“Equal height,” he told the attendants. “The historical record is unambiguous.”

“It is not,” Hatshepsut said.

“My building program alone—”

“You have not built anything. You have been awake for eight days.”

He turned to Merneith. He had the broad face reconstructed from the mummy and the immense confidence reconstructed from everything else. “Great Queen, I speak of precedence.”

“You speak of six centimeters.”

“Six visible centimeters.”

Merneith let the attendants raise his chair. They had gathered beneath the completed falcon in Alexandria, where warm light moved through its gold veins and turquoise fluid carried heat toward the night farms. Beyond the palace, aircraft lifted silently from the harbor. Above them, the first Egyptian mirrors were opening in orbit.

A petitioner waited inside the throne map, transmitted from a drought-struck coast beyond the western desert. Wind tore at his robe. Behind him, a salt storm had turned noon brown.

“We need nine rainfall towers,” he said. “Your physicians too, if the fever crosses the camps. We are not asking for soldiers, flags, or a queen.”

“He asks for weather,” Hatshepsut murmured as Ramesses drew breath.

“Weather has always been strategic ground,” he said.

The petitioner squinted at the three of them. “Is that one new?”

Ramesses sat straighter on his elevated chair.

Merneith concealed her pleasure. “The towers require orbital mirrors. The mirrors require defended ground stations. I will not place Egyptian crews beyond Egyptian law.”

“Then sell us the machines.”

“You cannot maintain them yet.”

“Teach us.”

That was the dangerous answer. Merneith admired him for finding it.

She offered a twelve-year compact: shared courts for the stations, local command beneath an Egyptian shield, physicians without charge, engineers paid by both governments. At the sixth year, a vote. At the twelfth, another. She made the words sound temporary and the power sound immediate.

“And if we vote you out?” the petitioner asked.

Merneith looked at the brown sky behind him. “Then you will know how to keep what we build.”

Hatshepsut looked at her. Not disbelief. Worse: measurement.

The compact passed. Then three more did. Ramesses took command of the shield fleet after making Merneith repeat before the court that he served as a king in alliance, not as a general in obedience. She repeated it. He heard what he needed and became magnificent in battle.

There were battles. The old states did not vanish because Egypt had better pumps. One bomb opened the western spine and left eight million people counting the hours in their cisterns. Ramesses broke the blockade without burning the cities behind it, though he complained that restraint made poor relief sculpture. Merneith used the victory to bind eleven governments into a water league. Hatshepsut used it to force redundant channels into every later design.

At the compact's twelfth year, the coast voted to leave.

The throne map put the result in Merneith's palm. Fifty-two percent. The ground stations now protected three neighboring territories, two of which had joined the empire, and the rainfall towers fed reservoirs across every border. Withdrawal would darken the shield for thirteen minutes and leave the eastern basins dry by the next summer unless Egypt built a separate lattice.

Merneith postponed the vote's effect until that lattice existed.

“There is always another lattice,” Hatshepsut said in the empty hall.

“There are people beneath it.”

“Yes. That is why it works.”

Ramesses paced between their thrones. “They accepted protection. They used our blood to defend it.”

“It was mostly machines,” Hatshepsut said.

“I am speaking as the Usermaatre Setepenre, Sovereign of—” He stopped, jaw working. Humiliation made him reach for titles as if one might contain the sentence he had lost. “They cannot spit us out when the wells fill.”

“That,” Hatshepsut said, no humor left in her, “is not better.”

Merneith approved the postponement. She also funded the separate lattice at triple speed and forbade Ramesses to occupy the coast. None of them called this consent. None of them found a clean way to keep the shield up without making departure expensive.

The coast left nineteen months late. Its neighboring territories did not.

* * *

At twenty years, Merneith's throne faced east.

At thirty-two, it faced the entire Earth.

The map changed faster than the regalia. Gold entered the northern ice cities by treaty, the eastern island belts after a cyclone season, the inland federations behind Ramesses' shield ships. Turquoise marked water and medicine. By forty years the colors touched across three oceans, and the New Egyptian Empire governed more human beings than all the states beyond it together.

Merneith crossed it in ceremonial aircraft whose wings echoed the falcon at Alexandria. She opened genomic clinics where children stopped inheriting the poisons of ruined soil. She watched autonomous foundries raise black towers from desert glass. In one mountain city, people threw apricots instead of flowers and stained her gold mantle orange. In another, they turned their backs because an accession governor had taken grain for a launch rail. She removed the governor and kept the rail.

The other sovereigns awakened one by one. A young king accepted his ancient name, served six months, and left to repair fishing craft under the number from his birth room. A queen whose face existed on ten thousand banners refused to look at any of them; Merneith gave her a house where the walls held no screens. Two rulers joined Ramesses. One became a composer. None remembered Egypt.

Merneith made their freedom a law and their faces a pageant. The contradiction bothered Hatshepsut more each year.

“You let them go,” she said once, “and then project their empty chairs behind you.”

“The chairs are historical.”

“The emptiness is current.”

Merneith's hair remained black long after the first silver appeared, thanks to an indulgence so minor she refused to be ashamed of it. Her hands would not cooperate with the same vanity. Veins rose beneath the skin. The imperial rings had to be widened twice. In audiences, she learned to keep one hand open over the map so its tremor became command.

Fewer people entered the room unfiltered. Petitions arrived cut to ninety seconds, then forty. Governors learned that one weeping child survived compression better than a thousand figures. Merneith knew this and still remembered the children.

Hatshepsut alone walked in without being announced. She brought broken components, unflattering reports, fruit with bruises. Sometimes she sat on the lowest step of the throne and read while Merneith ruled most of the world. Sometimes she disappeared for a year to build something too ordinary for court notice.

Merneith never asked her to stay.

* * *

Sixty years after Merneith opened her eyes, the last great accession unfolded above the Giza Renewal Vault.

The equatorial republics had signed at dawn. Their votes gave Egypt an unbroken planetary energy exchange and put nearly four people in five beneath the double crown. Celebrations filled the approaches to the pyramids, but deep underground the Vault remained cool and nearly silent. The old viewing gallery had been removed. In its place stood three thrones beneath the winged falcon: Merneith's at the center, Hatshepsut's and Ramesses' one step lower.

Merneith had ordered the tableau for the noon transmission. One timeless royal house. Ancient promise, modern dominion. The words had tested well in seventeen languages.

Ramesses inspected his chair. Age had thickened him and softened none of his sensitivities. “One step.”

“It is a shallow step,” Merneith said.

“It is photographed from below.”

“Everything is photographed from below when I commission it.”

He almost smiled. Then he saw Hatshepsut had not dressed for the transmission.

She wore gray work cloth like the day of Merneith's waking. Her hair was cropped close again. On the center throne lay the museum contract Merneith had refused, its old surface crazed with age.

“Where did you find that?” Merneith asked.

“The wheels were in the same cupboard.”

“What do you want?”

“To leave before noon.”

Ramesses looked from one woman to the other. “Leave the room?”

“The court.”

“Today?” His offense was almost tender. “We have just acquired the world.”

“Most of it,” Hatshepsut said. “Do try to leave someone unconquered. It gives the maps texture.”

“Hatshepsut,” Merneith said.

The joke died. Hatshepsut slid the contract toward her.

“They grew us, dressed us, and arranged us in this room so strangers could see the dead agree with them. You walked out. I helped you walk out.”

“You helped me build.”

“I did. I chose it. Then I chose it again. That does not make every next choice yours.”

Ramesses touched the back of his throne as if steadying it. “You carry office. There are oaths.”

“My office expires in nine days. She wants me to renew it on camera.”

Merneith had prepared concessions: a five-year term instead of life, independent budget, veto over new accessions. Each one sounded smaller in the Vault.

“You could have told me before the chairs were installed,” she said.

“I have told you for thirty years. You hear engineering beautifully.”

Merneith turned to the falcon. Its glass channels carried the same turquoise pulse she had seen on waking, though every pump behind them had been replaced. Above its bronze head, a dark mirror reflected the three rulers without flattering any of them.

The transmission director signaled from the doorway: six minutes.

“If you leave now,” Merneith said, “they will make it a repudiation.”

“It is a refusal.”

“They will not preserve the distinction.”

“You own most of the transmitters.”

There it was, the old abrasive confidence that Merneith could fix any material difficulty, and beneath it the request Hatshepsut would not make: do not make me escape you.

Merneith wanted her face on the right of the throne. Not because the republics required it; their signatures were already sealed. Not because the empire would fracture; it had learned to survive worse things than honesty. She wanted one witness from the impossible morning who could look at all this and call it a return. Ramesses believed because belief enlarged him. The crowds believed at a useful distance. Hatshepsut knew exactly what had been absent from Merneith's first breath.

“Say it once,” Merneith said. Her public voice had entered the room without permission. “Say you recognize what I have restored.”

Hatshepsut's mouth tightened. “I recognize you.”

It was not enough. It was the only answer Merneith trusted.

The director raised five fingers.

Merneith removed Hatshepsut's nameplate from the right-hand throne. The magnetic catch resisted, then released with a hard little snap. She handed it across.

“Your transport?” she asked.

“Waiting.”

“Of course it is.”

Hatshepsut put the nameplate into the pocket of her work coat. For the first time that morning, she looked uncertain. She reached toward Merneith's hand, changed her mind, and touched two fingers to the old contract instead.

Then she left by the same door through which the custodians had once entered with a collar.

Ramesses watched her go. “What shall I tell the court?”

“That Hatshepsut has resigned.”

“They will ask whether she remains Hatshepsut.”

Merneith looked at him until he glanced away.

The noon transmission showed two sovereigns beneath the falcon. Hatshepsut's empty throne remained outside the frame. Merneith accepted the equatorial republics into the New Egyptian Empire. Orbital mirrors flashed in sequence over most of the Earth; deserts lit under solar wings; water moved through continental arteries whose first crooked segment still bent around a cluster of houses south of the river. In the square above, millions spoke her chosen name.

Afterward she returned alone to the Vault. The floor carried the warmth of machines through her thin soles. Someone had removed Hatshepsut's throne. Merneith sat in the central chair and let her old hands lie where they pleased.

Ramesses appeared at the door without attendants, crown, or visible grievance. He stood there long enough to lose the sentence he had prepared.

“Great Queen,” he said at last. “May I have a private audience?”

The remaining chair was still one step lower and several meters away. Merneith released its floor catch, took the gilded arm in both hands, and dragged it up the shallow rise until it stood beside hers.

stories.title: The Way Around
stories.prompt: A young relic hunter enters a forbidden desert labyrinth to prove she deserves a place among the great explorers, relying on an uncanny talent for making shots everyone else calls impossible—bouncing arrows off stone, threading gaps she cannot see, striking targets around corners. But when her small expedition uncovers something vast and ancient beneath the desert, her gift begins escalating beyond reason, until distance, walls, dimensions, and eventually reality itself seem to become nothing more than obstacles her arrows can find a way around.
stories.body:
# The Way Around

At the mouth of the Azhra Labyrinth, Ivara aimed away from the door.

The bow nearly spanned the sandstone slot. Its upper limb scraped a sunlit wall; its lower tip hovered beside Tressa's boot. Ivara set her shoulder against the opposite rock, weathered green cloak bunched over a dust-brown leather coat, and drew until the string pressed a line into her bracer.

Mazin flattened himself around the water skins. “If it comes back at us, I want it recorded that I objected.”

“If it comes back,” Ivara said, “duck.”

Tressa had already opened her ledger. “I will not record that as a safety plan.”

Ivara smiled without looking at either of them. A shelf of stone hid the old entrance latch. The arrow had no clear road to it, only a pale patch on the left wall, a dark chip high on the right, and the narrow breathing slit above the door. She could feel the shot anyway: not as a line, exactly, but as three small certainties waiting for one another.

She released.

The blunt head struck the pale patch, skipped upward with a sound like a snapped cup, kissed the dark chip, and vanished through the slit. A heartbeat later, iron clacked behind the sealed door. Sand poured from its seams. The stone sank into the ground.

Mazin peered after the arrow. “Now ask it to open again from this side.”

“That was opening.” Ivara slid through before the sinking slab could reconsider.

Tressa lingered long enough to touch both impact marks. Brown hair had escaped Ivara's braid and stuck to her damp cheek; she pushed it back while waiting for the verdict.

Tressa wrote. Her pencil made a dry, stingy noise.

“Well?” Ivara asked.

“Two observed deflections. One concealed impact.”

“You could write impossible.”

“I could also draw you taller.” Tressa stepped into the dark. “Neither would improve the evidence.”

The door opened on stairs too steep for comfort and too clean for a ruin. Their lamps found treads, a wall, and then nothing. Above, the afternoon remained a hard blue strip between the cliffs. Below, Azhra swallowed light as if the desert had been built over a well.

Ivara retrieved her arrow from the latch and led them down.

The warning pillar outside had called the labyrinth forbidden in three surviving scripts. Tressa had copied all three. Mazin had read the row of older expedition marks cut beside it and asked why people who wanted to be great explorers so often began by ignoring dead ones.

Ivara had not answered. Tressa's signed account could carry a find past tavern disbelief and into the expedition halls, where the wall maps held names she had known since childhood. Those names crossed white wastes, drowned archives, cities under roots. None belonged to a hunter hired to fetch other people's relics from places already measured.

She needed one place the maps had failed to contain.

The stairs ended at a sandstone shutter. Its release lay beyond a gap no wider than two fingers, around a bend in the wall. Ivara knelt, laid her cheek to the stone, and listened while Mazin tapped the far side with a knife pommel.

“Again,” she said.

He tapped.

She sent a narrow arrow through the gap. It scraped once out of sight, struck something with a bright metallic note, and the shutter folded downward in four slabs.

Beyond it, rings filled the earth.

They were not wheels. Some stood on edge, some lay flat, some entered the walls and continued on the other side. The nearest was broad enough for a wagon road. The farthest rose through the lamplight until its curve disappeared, suggesting a circle large enough to cup a city. Each ring was built of close-fitted blocks scored with shallow channels. Dust lay everywhere except inside those channels.

Mazin lifted his lamp. “You wanted something that wouldn't fit in the ledger.”

Tressa turned a page. “I brought more paper.”

Ivara laughed, and the rings gave the sound back from places too distant to see.

They followed a ledge between them. The route curled downward, passing square windows that looked only onto stone. At the third window, a slab sealed the ledge from wall to wall. Somewhere beyond it, a loose chain ticked in a draft.

Tressa put a hand on Ivara's quiver. “We have enough. The size, the construction, the entrance mechanisms. We leave, bring a lawful party, and return.”

“With whose claim?”

“Ours, if we stop making it easy to deny.”

“A door and some circles are a rumor with measurements.” Ivara eased Tressa's hand away. “The chain is a latch.”

“You cannot see the chain.”

“You came because I don't need to.”

Tressa's face closed in the particular way that meant Ivara had struck what she aimed at and should have aimed elsewhere.

She nocked the recovered narrow shaft. The expected route bent left off the ledge, glanced from the window's inner edge, and entered the hidden space behind the slab. She held the ticking chain in mind. Its sway. Its height. The small oval link her arrow would catch.

At full draw, another route appeared.

It used no surfaces. It cut through the slab's thickness: the fact of the arrow here and the chain there, with the troublesome stone made unimportant.

Ivara released before the feeling could vanish.

The arrow flew left. There should have been a scrape, then a ricochet. Instead came a heavy knock from directly behind the slab. The concealed chain snapped taut. The whole barrier lifted.

Her arrow lay on the other side.

There was no slit. No hole. Fine red powder coated the head, but the wall stood whole.

The nearest ring answered with a pulse too low to be sound. Dust jumped from its channels. The pulse passed into the next ring, then the next, descending and rising through the dark until Azhra seemed to take one immense stone breath.

Tressa shut her ledger. “Now we go.”

Ivara stared at the arrow. The impossible route remained in her mind, faint as an afterimage. It led through the wall, though it had already been used.

“Ivara.”

“You saw it.”

“Yes.” Tressa's voice had lost its dry edge. “That is why we go.”

They turned back. The ledge carried them around one curve, then another, and brought them to a chamber none of them had passed before.

It stood beyond a waist-high opening, near enough to touch and entirely enclosed. Pale sand covered its floor. A stone peg protruded from the far wall beneath a carved relief of nested rings. Cold air breathed from the opening, although no opening existed on the chamber's side.

Mazin took the chalk from Tressa and marked the ledge. “One look. Then we follow our mark out.”

“That chamber is inside the ring,” Ivara said.

“Wonderful. It can stay there.”

The stone peg held a dark metal loop. A small relic. Portable proof. Ivara pictured an arrow curving through the enclosed chamber and clipping it free.

Tressa saw her reach for the quiver. “Don't.”

“One shot.”

“That is what the last one was.”

Ivara loosed.

The arrow crossed the opening, entered bare stone, and emerged inside the chamber without breaking either surface. It struck the peg. The loop rang loose onto the sand.

For one bright instant, Ivara felt the clean snap of every locked door in her life coming open. No wall. No angle too sharp. The arrow had found a way because she had asked it to.

Then the path stayed open.

An arrow-thin line joined the ledge to the sealed chamber. Cold air hissed along it. The line widened to a black seam, and pale sand began spilling through—not down, but sideways, spraying past Ivara's boots into the dark.

All around them, the rings moved.

Mazin caught Ivara by the back of her cloak as the ledge tipped. Tressa fell to one knee, clutching her ledger. A wall dropped between the three of them. It missed Ivara's hand by less than a finger and came down across Mazin's rope.

When the stone stopped, Ivara and Tressa stood together on one side.

Mazin's lamp shone from a square window twenty paces away, though his muffled swearing came through the wall at Ivara's shoulder.

“Are you hurt?” Tressa shouted.

“Only in my judgment.” His voice arrived again, much fainter, from somewhere below. “And I have one skin of water. You have the other two.”

Ivara put both palms to the partition. The old way to judge distance—echo, grain, the minute change of air against her face—broke into several answers. Mazin was an arm's length away. He was twenty paces away. He was below them, above them, and standing in the cold chamber with sand flowing past his knees.

She snatched her hand back.

Tressa reopened the ledger. “Describe what you see.”

“A wall.”

“Mazin.”

“Several walls. One has teeth.”

Ivara paced to the window. Mazin's lamp vanished before she reached it. In its place, for half a second, she saw a slice of night sky freckled with unfamiliar stars. Then stone covered it.

“The chalk mark is gone,” Tressa said.

“The ledge moved.”

“After your shot.”

“I noticed.”

“Did you? You looked pleased.”

Ivara rounded on her. “Would you prefer I couldn't do it?”

“At present, very much.”

The wall pulsed. A trickle of sand rose from the floor and crawled into a channel overhead.

Mazin knocked three times from inside the stone.

“I would prefer,” he called, “that you save the quarrel until I can enjoy it properly.”

Tressa drew a line across the page. “Tell me about the teeth.”

His answers came in pieces, sometimes through the wall, sometimes from the floor. A row of triangular blocks. A dark loop beside the fourth, or perhaps the fifth. The floor sloped toward him unless the water was lying. He could reach the loop but not pull it; the block above it shifted whenever he put weight on the rope.

“How large is the loop?” Tressa asked.

“Thumb-sized.”

“Whose thumb?”

“Not Ivara's. She has absurd little thumbs.”

“They fit an arrow nock,” Ivara said.

“Everything comes back to arrows with you.”

Tressa's pencil paused. “Can you put the rope through it?”

After some scraping and a bitten-off curse, the trapped length of rope jerked beneath the fallen wall. Mazin tugged twice. The second tug came from the square window, now visible high above them.

Tressa drew what he had described, then turned the ledger sideways. Her neat diagram made no sense. She rubbed out half of it with her thumb.

“Stop making it a room,” Ivara said.

“It is a room.”

“Not from here.” She crouched over the trapped rope. Its fibers tightened at an angle the floor denied. “Give me the part that matters.”

Tressa's mouth tightened. Her pencil shook, but it kept moving. Then she tore a strip from the margin of her precious ledger and folded it twice. “The loop is here. The shifting block bears here. If Mazin pulls, the bottom edge lifts.” She held the folded paper against the wall, not as a map but as an angle. “You need to strike behind the loop, upward.”

“I said the fourth tooth,” Mazin called.

“You said perhaps the fifth.”

“It became the fourth when I counted again.”

Ivara closed her eyes. She felt Tressa's paper angle against the back of her fingers. Mazin tugged once, then twice. The rope's strain gave her a direction no corridor could be trusted to provide.

She fired at the floor.

The arrow vanished point-first into sandstone. Mazin yelped. A hard crack followed, then the clatter of a released block. The partition rose one handspan.

Mazin came through it sideways, shoulder first, clutching the water skin. Gravity changed its mind halfway. He struck the floor beside them in an explosion of chalk dust and dignity.

“Fourth,” he gasped.

Then every route opened.

Cold air poured from the sealed chamber. Hot wind rushed from a corridor that showed blue noon at its end. The slice of starry sky spread across a wall like spilled ink. Sand fell up, down, and across. One of Tressa's water skins sailed into the noon corridor and vanished; the other struck a rising block and split, its stream crawling up the wall. An arrow Ivara had lost minutes ago flashed through three rings at once, each copy casting the same crooked shadow, before all of them vanished.

Tressa hauled Mazin upright. “Can we leave now?”

Ivara looked for the stairs and could not remember what *up* felt like.

“I don't know where they are,” she said.

It was the first admission that silenced both of them.

The rings shuddered again. Their ledge cracked. Beyond the fracture, every available passage curved toward the same dark opening.

Mazin wiped chalk from his beard. “Then I vote for the hole not pretending to be daylight.”

They went inward.

* * *

The central hollow had no proper floor. A bridge of fitted blocks crossed its middle, curving beneath their feet and above their heads until the distinction failed. Rings crowded the dark in all directions. Their channels glimmered only when an old arrow route passed through them, a brief polishing of stone by something that had no business touching it.

The oil windows on both lamps showed almost empty. It had been afternoon at the entrance. Whatever the routes had done to distance, ordinary hours had carried on without them.

On the bridge's central plinth, the nested-ring relief appeared again. Tressa set her lamp close. No writing surrounded it, only grooves: circles within circles, each cut open at one point. All the openings connected by a single wandering line. At the relief's upper edge, the line ended against an uncarved wedge.

“A shut-stone,” Tressa said. “The outer closure, perhaps.”

“Perhaps is doing heroic work,” Mazin said.

Ivara traced the grooves without touching them. Every route she had fired still pressed at the edge of her awareness. They crossed, shared pieces, and reached for fresh ways around one another. The relief's blank wedge was the only place none entered.

The lattice had not chosen a thing. It had taken the aim she supplied and made more road than the shot required. Each arrow had left it another answer. Now those answers were tangling the place apart.

A section of bridge disappeared. It did not break; it was simply gone. Through the gap lay a white chamber where dust hung motionless in the air. Mazin jerked back before his foot crossed into it.

“Can you hit the wedge?” Tressa asked.

Ivara set an arrow to the string and aimed at the relief. The target felt dead beneath her attention. A picture of a closure was not a closure.

She lowered the bow. Four arrows remained. Only one had the narrow hardened head that had survived the stone.

“It isn't here,” she said. “This is showing the outside.”

Mazin looked around at the inward-curving dark. “Excellent. We'll step outside.”

The cold route widened with a boom. The lamp flames bent toward three different drafts. Somewhere, far off or immediately behind them, stone began to fall.

Tressa flipped backward through her ledger. “The entrance faced northwest. The first stair descended roughly east, then the large ring carried us south—”

“No.” Ivara's own sense of those directions turned over like a sick stomach. “Don't give me a route.”

“You need a target.”

“I need the stone itself.”

Tressa pressed her lips together and flipped another page, still trying to arrange observations that would not hold still. Mazin, meanwhile, was staring at the relief's blank wedge.

“There was a dark cap near the entrance,” he said. “Outside. I put the water against it while you two admired the warning.”

Tressa frowned. “A capstone?”

“A hot rock.”

“Shape?”

“Rock-shaped.”

The plinth lurched. Ivara caught Tressa's ledger before it slid into the white chamber. A loose page crossed the boundary and stopped, hanging flat in the air a pace below and impossibly far away.

“Mazin,” Ivara said. “Put your hand how it lay.”

He planted his broad palm against the plinth, fingers slanting down. “Like this. It was hotter here. Gritty at the edge, smooth in the middle. There was a little groove under my second finger.”

Tressa caught his wrist. “Crescent groove.” She found the first page of her entrance sketch. “I drew its shadow. The exposed stone tilted eleven degrees from the doorway face.”

“Eleven?” Mazin said. “It tilted a bit.”

“Your bit is not reproducible.”

“Neither is eleven degrees while we're falling through the world.”

“Stop.” Ivara had already lost the picture by trying to decide which of them was right. Around her, the routes hummed through stone, eager without wanting, multiplying without thought. “One at a time.”

They looked at her.

She swallowed. Her mouth tasted of old dust. “Tell me what I didn't see.”

Tressa started with the doorway because that was where her certainty lived: the capstone's upper edge, the thin shadow it had cast, the relation between its crescent groove and the warning pillar. Halfway through, Mazin interrupted to say the groove was chipped on the left. Tressa snapped that the shadow proved the chip was on the right.

“From inside or outside?” Ivara asked.

Tressa stopped. Looked at her sketch. Turned the ledger around.

“His left,” she said.

Mazin gave a short, frightened laugh. “A historic day.”

Then he described the stone by touch: sun-hot center, coarse rim, one pocket that held cooler sand. He could not explain the smell until Ivara offered words—baked clay, lamp soot, rain—and he rejected all of them.

“Like the first hot day after you store a blanket all winter,” he said at last.

It made no sense. It was exactly what she needed.

Tressa held two fingers at the capstone's slant. Mazin set his palm beneath them. The ledger gave the wedge a relation to the buried rings. His skin gave it heat and grain. Neither knew the stone whole. Ivara let their incompatible pieces remain incompatible and held them together anyway.

The target arrived.

Not north. Not above. Not a distance. A sun-warmed shut-stone on the exterior of the vast thing enclosing them, chipped on Mazin's left, crossed by Tressa's crescent shadow. A place Ivara had stood beside and failed to notice because she had been looking at the door.

She nocked the hardened arrow.

The bow resisted as though the string had been tied around all the rings of Azhra. Her shoulders shook. The routes crowded her mind: through wall, under bridge, across cold chamber, into the false noon, along the strip of stars. Every one ended inside.

She did not choose among them.

She held the outer stone and drew.

Tressa's fingers stayed angled in the corner of her sight. Mazin's palm stayed braced below. Neither spoke. The bridge dropped a fraction beneath them.

Ivara released.

The arrow did not fly across the hollow. Its head departed first, then the shaft followed into a point in the air too small to contain it. The fletching twisted once and was gone.

For a breath, nothing happened.

Then an impact struck from beyond every wall.

It came up through Ivara's boots and down through her teeth. The nested channels flared with rushing dust. One by one, the wrong spaces pinched shut: the white chamber folding to a line, the noon corridor going dark, the stars snapping to a single point. Cold sand splashed to the bridge and fell in one ordinary direction.

The rings stopped.

Weight returned so hard Ivara dropped to both knees.

Across the hollow, blocks ground aside. Behind them lay a steep stair packed with sand and open at the top to a thread of predawn gray.

Mazin stared at it. “That had better be the real sky.”

Tressa closed her ledger around the loose pages. “If it isn't, don't tell me yet.”

They climbed.

No route shortened the stair. Sand collapsed under their boots. Mazin's remaining water skin had split at the neck, and they shared what was left in three mean swallows. Tressa had to be pushed through the half-sunken entrance; Ivara lost a glove digging Mazin free when the last tread gave way. By the time they crawled beyond the warning pillar, dawn had bleached the desert and all three of them were too tired for greatness.

For several minutes they lay in the cooling sand.

Then Tressa sat up and opened the ledger.

“I am not writing that the arrow went around reality,” she said.

Mazin had draped a sweat-dark cloth over his face. “Write that reality was unhelpful.”

“I can substantiate walls, discontinuous chambers, conflicting orientations, and one appalling use of my margin.”

Ivara rolled onto an elbow. The labyrinth entrance was stone again. The dark cap beside it bore a fresh, pale chip across its crescent groove.

“Write the impact,” she said.

“I did not see it.”

“You felt it.”

“Feeling is not location.” Tressa looked toward the chipped cap, then down at her first sketch. “Mazin saw the stone. I fixed its angle. You did whatever that was.”

“And carried the water,” Mazin said from under the cloth. “Until architecture attacked it.”

Tressa tapped her pencil against the page. “The finding needs a primary name.”

Yesterday, Ivara would have answered before the pencil finished rising.

Something hissed overhead.

All three looked up too late. An arrow dropped out of empty morning, struck the sand between them, and buried itself to the fletching. The hardened head was gray with dust from the outer capstone. A thin crescent of dark stone had lodged behind one barb.

Ivara's hand moved toward it, then stopped.

Tressa went still. Mazin pulled the cloth from his face and stared.

Only when both of them had seen the arrow standing there did Ivara reach for it.

Tressa lowered her pencil to the ledger. Beside the fresh entry, she ruled one line wide enough for three names.

stories.title: The Thousandth Fall
stories.prompt: A monk uncovers The Wrong Way to Use Healing Magic and now, he trains beyond human limitations, using his self-healing abilities to gain absurd strength, unrivaled stamina, and insane speed.
stories.body:
# The Thousandth Fall

Rasden discovered the wrong way to heal himself because Palla would not let him finish doing it properly.

He had missed the turn on the Midsky Cloister stair and gone shoulder-first into the rain trough. Water slapped over the tiles. His left arm hung numb, his ankle had folded somewhere beneath him, and Palla leaned over the rail above with the expression of a woman who had just won something.

“Seven landings,” she called. “You made seven.”

Rasden pushed wet hair out of his eyes with his good hand. “There were eight.”

“The trough isn't a landing.”

“Then why am I on it?”

Laughing hurt his ribs. He pressed two fingers below his breastbone and drew the opening breath of a self-mend.

The working found the last sound shape of him: shoulder seated, ankle straight, ribs without their bright cracks. That was how a mend worked. It held the body's last whole pattern and persuaded blood, bone, and breath to return to it. Warmth packed his shoulder. His ankle pulled straight with a deep, unpleasant click.

All that remained was the closing breath.

Palla vaulted the rail, dropped beside him, and plucked his sandal from the trough. “You owe me three honey cakes.”

“Two.” Rasden rose to take it from her.

He had answered before closing the mend.

The warmth should have faded. Instead it moved with him, quick and curious, down his thighs and into the foot he planted on the tiles. Rasden stopped. The working stopped with him, waiting.

“What?” Palla asked.

“Nothing yet.”

He jumped from the trough to the stair rail, a distance he usually crossed with an undignified scramble. His bare foot struck the narrow stone. His calf tightened, his ankle wobbled, and the open mend flashed through both, not dragging them back to their earlier state but holding the landing he had just survived. When he sprang to the next rail, the motion came cleanly. Easier.

Palla's grin went crooked. “Do that again.”

He did. Then he jumped two rails.

They moved to the laundry roof, where the drop was high enough to make Rasden's stomach float. He opened a fresh mend, stepped off, and landed in the herb bed with both feet under him. Pain flared up his shins. The spell followed it, learned the shape of the impact, and left him standing.

On the second drop, the pain was less. On the third, he barely bent his knees.

Palla pulled a courier's cord from her belt and tied the first knot.

“One,” she said.

Rasden looked up at the bellhouse roof. “That hardly seems worth counting.”

“Good. Impress me.”

He tried the bellhouse next and discovered the first limit by arriving on his back. The mend repaired him, but it repaired him to the last landing he had actually completed. It would not pretend a failure had been a success. It could not invent strength, quickness, or balance. It could only accept what his living body had done and make that achievement the new whole.

So they went higher by honest increments. The right way to use a self-mend was to remain still and let yesterday's body rescue today's. Rasden's way was to leave the working open and give it a better body to remember.

By the end of the afternoon, Palla's cord held twelve knots. By sunset, Rasden had stopped hearing the ground as a warning. It had become an answer coming up to meet him.

Over the next season, they learned that the spell remembered motions, not wishes. A harder fall taught him to fall. It did nothing for his arms until Palla began piling monastery grindstones on a carrying bar and Rasden began lifting them, one more each time, while the mend listened. Running required its own progression: stair, courtyard, ridge road, mountain circuit. Every gain had to be completed alive. Every new effort began just beyond the last one.

They loved it.

At one hundred falls, Rasden stepped from the cloister wall and landed hard enough to crack the paving beneath his heels. Palla inspected the cracks, then deducted two falls because he had used the same paving stone twice.

“The ground doesn't care,” he told her.

“The ground doesn't keep the cord.”

At three hundred, he could drop from the bellhouse, rebound from the courtyard, and clear the outer wall without touching the stair between. At six hundred, he began using the quarry shelves below the cloister. Palla would stand at the top and throw pebbles after him. He always reached the bottom first.

Strength announced itself on the east road after three days of rain. A grain wagon had sunk to its hubs on the uphill turn. Twelve oxen leaned into the traces until their flanks shone, and the wagon did not move the width of a fingernail.

Palla looked from the stalled team to Rasden. “Absolutely not.”

“You brought me here.”

“To help push. In a humble, monk-like manner.”

The drovers unhitched the oxen. Rasden crouched under the wagon's rear beam, found his grip, and opened a mend. Grain filled the bed higher than his head. The iron-rimmed wheels were sunk halfway into black mud.

He lifted.

The first pull tore every muscle across his back. The working swept through the damage, preserving the completed inch. He reset his feet and lifted again. Mud released the wheels with four enormous sucking sounds. The whole laden wagon rose until daylight showed beneath every wheel.

Rasden walked it forty paces uphill and set it on dry road.

No one spoke. Even the oxen watched him.

Palla recovered first. “You tilted it.”

“Did I?”

“Terribly. Grain could've shifted.”

“Take a knot away.”

“Strength isn't falls. I keep standards.”

Stamina took longer to become ridiculous. Rasden ran from one sunrise to the next along the ridge circuit, never letting the mend close. Palla rode beside him to count the laps. She changed horses at noon, changed again at moonrise, and borrowed a fourth before dawn. The fourth horse was blowing foam when the sun returned. Rasden was still taking the uphill turn at the same pace as the first lap.

Palla swayed in the saddle. “If you say ‘again,’ I will push you off a mountain.”

“Would you count it?”

“No.”

He ran another lap while she thought of a worse answer.

For speed, Palla planted a red pennant at a target half a mile across the high meadow. She carried the strongest courier bow and a flight arrow fletched in white so Rasden could not claim he had lost sight of it.

“You leave when I loose,” she said. “Not when I breathe. Not when I blink. When the string speaks.”

“You blink loudly.”

The bow snapped.

Rasden drove one foot into the earth. The meadow flattened into a green roar. Wind crushed his robe against his chest, then lost hold of it. He reached the target, tore free the red pennant, and turned while Palla's arrow was still a white fleck climbing through the blue. It struck the straw butt as he passed the halfway stone on his return.

He stopped beside her with the pennant streaming from his fist.

Palla stared at the target, then at him. “I blinked.”

“Loudly.”

She hit him with the bowstring cap. She was laughing too hard to make it hurt.

The cord filled, and Palla retied its single knots into tens and its tens into hundreds. She miscounted twice, accused Rasden once, found both missing knots in her own work, and refused to apologize. Nine hundred became nine hundred and fifty. They moved their falls to the gorge shelves where cloud shadow passed below their feet.

Fall nine hundred and ninety-nine began on the highest shelf above Midsky Cloister.

“Make this one ugly,” Palla said. She stood far below on the bell terrace, the counting cord wrapped twice around her wrist.

Rasden stepped into open air.

For three long breaths there was only the plunge, robe snapping, mountain turning around him. He struck the terrace in a low crouch. Stone burst outward in a ring. Before the debris landed, he was running uphill. He crossed the cloister stairs, circled the bellhouse, caught the great bronze bell one-handed beneath its rim, and lifted it clear of its timber cradle.

The clapper gave one soft, astonished note.

Rasden set the bell down as gently as a cup. The mend remained open inside him, following fall into sprint into lift as one unbroken effort.

Palla held up the new knot. “Nine hundred and ninety-nine.”

“You're sure?”

“I could untie one.”

He began jogging circles around her. If he came fully to rest, the working would settle around what he had already achieved. He wanted the thousandth fall to complete the same great sentence, from the high shelf to whatever dawn gave them.

Palla walked backward to stay in front of him. “At sunrise, the south face.”

“Too easy.”

“In the dark?”

“Better.”

“Fine. Blindfolded.”

“Now you're trying.”

Rasden completed ten more circles. The bell stood quiet in its cradle, and Palla had begun proposing increasingly foolish blindfolds, when a sound much larger than bronze rolled across the mountains. Rasden turned.

Two ridges away, the western wall of Suncleft Gorge split along a water-dark seam. Spring melt had worked deep into the stone; now a shelf the size of a village square peeled loose under its own weight. It fell in a pale, grinding sheet. The western anchorage of the Pilgrim Span vanished with it.

The bridge was crowded. For one suspended instant Rasden saw the caravan against the sky: bright packs, walking staffs, adults reaching for children. Then the far end dropped. The span folded into the gorge.

Palla shouted his name, but Rasden was already gone.

The road to Suncleft was two steep miles. He crossed it before the first crash finished echoing. Trees hammered past. A mule on the approach threw up its head at the thunder of his feet, and then he was at the eastern anchorage as the last main rope tore through its stone guide.

Rasden caught it.

The rope burned through both palms and hauled him to the lip. Forty yards of timber deck swung down with a caravan tangled across it. He saw the cliff rushing up to meet them and planted one foot.

The stone beneath it shattered. His knee bent, his shoulder opened with a hot internal rip, and the mend flooded every break. Rasden pulled. The bridge stopped a man's height from smashing into the eastern wall.

For a heartbeat it hung from his hands and the one surviving main rope. Then he dragged the whole span upward until its lower decking struck a broad sloping ledge. Timber shrieked. The ledge held. Rasden threw the rope he had caught around its scarred stone horn and pulled until the fibers locked. Between the two eastern ropes and the ledge, the ruined span held.

Palla arrived on a lathered horse, flung herself from the saddle, and skidded to the rim. “Forty-seven!” she gasped.

“People?”

“No, turnips. Yes, people. I think. The bridge moved.”

The ruined span hung almost vertically against the cliff. Pilgrims clung to planks, side netting, and one another. Rasden could have hauled all of it higher, but arms and ankles were threaded through torn ropes. His mend healed only him. One hard jerk would save the bridge and kill the people on it.

He ran down the cliff.

“Blue coat under the second crossbeam!” Palla called. “Can't use her leg.”

Rasden found the woman wedged beneath a rail, broke the rail with two fingers, and lifted her against his chest. A boy had both arms around her waist. Rasden took him too and climbed.

He did not climb as other people climbed. His fingers struck cracks and released. His feet touched stone just long enough to drive him upward. He reached the rim, placed both pilgrims in waiting hands, and turned without letting his heels become still.

“Two,” Palla said.

“You said forty-seven.”

“Then stop chatting.”

Down again.

On the second trip he carried three. On the third, four, two under one arm and two gripping the rope across his back. Each descent lowered him through drifting dust and the creak of failing timber. Each ascent carried more lives against the pull of the gorge. The open mend raced around his ribs, through his shoulders, behind his knees. It repaired what the effort tore, and what he completed became the strength for the next trip.

“Nine!” Palla called.

Rasden ran down.

“Red shawl, left side!”

He crossed the hanging deck.

“Other left. Mine. Sorry!”

He changed direction so sharply a plank spun away beneath him. “Your left is terrible.”

“My left can see!”

The red shawl proved to be tied around a pack. The pilgrim hung three yards lower in a gray cloak, too frightened to call. Rasden gathered him up and was back at the rim before Palla finished swearing at the shawl.

“Ten!”

Trip followed trip. Dust thickened, and the ledge beneath the bridge shed chips into the gorge. Rasden's counting narrowed to grips, bodies, turns: a pair of sisters who would not release each other's hands, a man with a bleeding temple, a baby shoved at him by three different arms. None of them could borrow his healing, so he made his speed gentle, a burst through empty space and a smooth turn when he carried someone, never a stop.

“Thirty-one!”

Palla ran the rim above him, dropping to her belly to see under each fold of the ruined span. Her early calls had carried jokes. Now they came clipped and raw.

“Two beneath you. One lower. Lower!”

Rasden tore open the side net and found them.

Seven more came up through dust and swinging rope.

“Forty!”

He brought up an old man and two young pilgrims bound together by a loop of handrope. His breath still arrived as easily as it had on the first descent. Palla's did not. She was on hands and knees at the edge, hair white with stone dust.

“Quit dancing,” she said as Rasden jogged a tight circle to keep the mend open.

“Nine hundred and ninety-nine is still listening.”

“Show-off. Go.”

He went.

The lower net held only packs twisting in the dust. Rasden swept beneath it once, saw no reaching hands, and ran back as the surviving anchorage cracked.

Palla counted the people behind her. Her lips moved twice. “Forty-three.”

“Four missing.”

She looked over the edge. Her face changed.

Beneath the lowest intact planks hung the bridge cradle, the deep woven basket used to carry small children across the span. Four pale faces looked through its netting. The cradle had twisted under the deck where Rasden could not see it from below.

Palla pointed. “There. Rasden, there!”

The eastern anchorage shelf tore out of the mountain. Rope, timber, and cradle dropped together.

Rasden reached the edge. The thousandth fall had been meant for dawn, with a blindfold and Palla's worst possible counting. Instead there were four children falling into Suncleft Gorge and Palla beside him with the cord clenched in both fists.

“Count this one,” he said.

“Just go!”

He went.

The cradle had a head start. Gravity was fast. Rasden had become faster.

He struck a falling plank with both feet and drove it upward, himself downward. A second crossbeam spun below; he caught it with one hand, swung past, and kicked away. He used the collapsing bridge as a stair built out of instants. Rope snapped by his cheek. The gorge wind tore the breath from his mouth. He passed the broken deck, passed the long end of the main cable, and saw the cradle above him.

Rasden hit the cliff below it running downward.

Three steps matched the cradle's plunge. On the fourth he turned, got both shoulders beneath the bridge's central beam, and caught its full falling weight.

The impact drove him twenty feet down the wall.

He let it. His legs folded a little at a time, bleeding speed from the cradle instead of stopping it all at once. Rock exploded under each foot. The four children bounced in the net but did not strike the beam. Behind them, forty yards of wet rope and timber bucked like a living thing.

Rasden's spine bowed. Something tore from hip to ribs. The open mend blazed through him, restoring not the man who had begun at Midsky, not the man who had lifted the grain wagon, but the man who was still holding a bridge.

He stopped falling. Then he climbed.

Strength turned the full weight upward. Speed found grips before shattered stone could leave them. Stamina, after two miles and trip upon trip along the cliff, kept his heart driving with the same delighted force. The working joined all three because he gave it no pause in which to divide them.

Rasden ran up the face of Suncleft Gorge with the broken Pilgrim Span across his shoulders.

Palla's voice reached him from above, cracked beyond any joke. “Come on. Come on!”

He climbed through the dust. The rim drew near. Hands reached down and snatched the cradle's net, but Rasden did not surrender its weight until all four children rolled onto solid ground. Then he heaved the bridge beam over the edge and landed beside it on both feet.

The thousandth fall ended at the top.

For a moment Suncleft Gorge was silent except for settling stones and Palla trying to breathe.

Then forty-seven survivors began shouting.

Some cried Rasden's name because they had heard Palla screaming it down the cliff. Others simply cheered. The boy from the first trip wrapped both arms around Rasden's leg. One of the children from the cradle looked at the wreckage, looked at Rasden, and demanded, “Again!”

Palla sat down hard and laughed until she coughed.

Rasden took the closing breath. The mend settled through him, warm as sunrise, around a body that had caught a bridge and carried it upward. Nothing diminished. Nothing rolled back.

Palla rose with the counting cord. Her hands shook as she worked a new knot into its end.

“That's ugly,” Rasden said.

“It's a thousand. It gets to be ugly.” She pulled it tight and looped the cord around his wrist. “Also, I called the red shawl correctly.”

“You called a pack.”

“There was a person near it.”

“On the other side.”

Palla lifted her chin toward the forty-seven people alive behind him. “Forty-seven. Right enough.”

Rasden looked at her. Dust striped her face. Her eyes were bright, and there was no fear in them now, only the enormous answer he had wanted from her and never known how to ask for.

Palla glanced away first. “You wanted a proper thousandth.”

“Was that proper?”

“No. It was ridiculous.” Her grin returned, ragged at the edges. “It'll do.”

Beyond the broken span, mountains rose in blue ranks farther than Rasden had ever traveled. Sunlight caught snow on the highest peak.

Palla saw him looking. Of course she did.

“That one,” she said, pointing at the farthest white summit. “Before sunset.”

“What do I win?”

“Fall one thousand and one.”

Rasden bent forward. Behind him the survivors shouted his name. Palla shouted louder, because she was still ahead on volume.

He ran, and Suncleft Gorge gave his first stride back as thunder.

stories.title: The Help Network
stories.prompt: The Magical Girl's Help Network started as just a few magical girls of different parts of the same town exchanging contact information and has somehow grown into an association of magical girls designed to share information and help each other around the globe.
stories.body:
# The Help Network

On the third afternoon after the showcase, Cassia balanced an index card on her knee in the back stairwell at Northbridge Secondary and wrote **BACKUP CONTACTS** across the top.

The phone beside her shoe was warm from messages. It had been quiet during the two mission-free nights they had promised one another—properly quiet, with the compromised relay disconnected and no copied voice telling anyone what to do. Then the other girls around town had begun asking questions.

Not civilian questions. Nobody offered a surname, a school, or a face. A girl who watched the rail yards wanted to know how Mothlight's team had realized their channel was wrong. Someone near the river sent a seven-second voice note consisting of wind, traffic, and, eventually, *Do you have another number if yours goes bad?* A third person typed that she was “asking for later,” then added three question marks when no one replied for eleven minutes.

“We give them ours, they give us theirs,” Cassia said. “That's it.”

Drita took the card from her and crossed out the heading. Her wrist was still taped beneath her sweater cuff. “Backup for what?”

“For anything.”

“Absolutely not for anything.”

Bryn sat one step above them with foam plugs in her ears, though the stairwell was empty except for the radiator knocking in the wall. She opened a fresh note on her phone. “Categories. Transport, observation, relay, first aid—”

“Not first aid,” Drita said. “Somebody will read that as medical.”

“Recovery snacks?” Cassia suggested.

“That's worse.”

She took the card back. Under Drita's new heading, **CONTACTS—ASK BEFORE FORWARDING**, Bryn made four columns: alias, offered help, limits, and permission to pass the contact onward. Cassia added a fifth for when the person was usually awake. Drita drew a hard line through it.

“Time window,” she said. “Not sleep schedule.”

“Right. Obviously. I knew that.”

Cassia had not known it. That was why it felt good to have all three of them there, reducing a huge soft wish into things that could fit on a card.

The first entries were uneven. One girl offered rooftop sightlines but not pursuit. Another would stay on a call after a frightening transformation, but only by text and never past her household's bedtime. Someone else wrote, *can carry heavy / cannot do blood*, then asked that the last part not be forwarded. Cassia put down Mothlight, listening and relay, **any time**.

Drita crossed out **any**.

“I mean it,” Cassia said.

“That's the problem.” Drita replaced it with **evenings, usually**. Then, after a moment, she added **okay to forward** and pushed the card back.

They photographed it against the gray stair tread. Bryn sent the image to four alias-only contacts. One of those contacts asked permission and sent it to two more.

By the time the late bus groaned into the school loop, the card had left their hands.

* * *

The first altered copy came back with a tea ring over Cassia's entry and the word **SOURCE?** squeezed into Bryn's columns.

That addition arrived because a warning about blue sparks in a storm drain had traveled across town as if it applied to every drain, every kind of magic, and perhaps the color blue. By lunch, three people had stayed away from a harmless blue-painted mural. By dinner, the girl who had actually seen the sparks wrote, with some irritation, that the problem had been one leaking charm under one particular grate.

Bryn began tagging messages **SAW IT**, **HEARD IT**, or **GUESSING**. Other people changed the words to versions they liked better. Cassia liked **GUESSING**, because it made uncertainty sound less like failure.

The requests were rarely grand. Someone wanted company on the walk from a bus stop because a false alarm had left her shaking. Cassia stayed in her earbud and described the dog in the apartment window until the girl reached home. Someone asked whether terrible hunger after using magic meant something was wrong. Cassia wrote that it happened to *her* after too many decoys, then passed the question to two girls whose costs were different. A check-in about a closed underpass became gossip about a cape caught in a bicycle wheel. The owner of the cape entered the thread to say the cape had behaved with dignity and the bicycle had not.

Cassia answered through algebra, through the scrape of dinner plates, through her mother calling from the kitchen that the recycling would not develop legs. She learned the little pulse of usefulness: a question, the brief open space before anyone replied, then her own thumbs filling it.

At school, Drita put a carton of juice on Cassia's worksheet.

“I have juice.”

“You have an empty box in your bag.”

“That is a historical juice.”

“Drink this one.”

Cassia peeled the straw from its wrapper. Her phone vibrated twice against the desk. She turned it over without looking, which felt so virtuous that she expected Drita to notice.

Drita did not. “How many last night?”

“Two.”

The phone vibrated again.

“Two that needed me,” Cassia amended. “Some of the rest were just forwarding.”

“Forwarding is the part somebody else can do.”

“I know.” Cassia punctured the foil too hard and got juice on her thumb. “I let them.”

This was almost true. She let people forward messages after she had read them, labeled them, checked where they were going, and watched for the reply. If she closed her eyes, the unseen routes felt like a room full of doors. Somebody ought to stand in the middle and hear which one opened.

After what had happened to their own channel, an unanswered voice had edges. Cassia could still remember the copied calmness telling them to transform. She could remember, more strongly, her own voice asking for one unhurried breath and Bryn waiting for both of them before making the cut. Nobody had been left alone with the command.

So Cassia kept the phone faceup during lunch.

* * *

The card crossed oceans by ordinary means. A girl carried a copy on a family visit and showed it to someone who showed it to someone else. Numbers lengthened with country codes. Photographs came back with handwriting in scripts Cassia could not read and translations pasted crookedly over the columns. One version replaced **limits** with **things I refuse**. Another removed the offered-help column altogether and said to ask what a person needed before proposing a solution.

There were mornings when a girl's after-school message arrived while Cassia brushed her teeth, and nights when the background of a voice note held breakfast dishes. A joke about a monster's manners crossed two translations and returned as *the disaster is wearing polite shoes*. Cassia laughed so hard she had to sit down. The original sender reacted with a baffled face, then asked to have the broken version back.

Help looped through the same hands. The girl from the bus stop later kept a dawn check-in for somebody else. A person who had once asked what to eat after transforming became the bridge for a language Cassia did not speak. She translated *stay warm* as *stay in light*; the requester sent a photograph of one blanket corner, a third person corrected the phrase, and all three reacted with laughing faces. Cassia had introduced none of them.

The name appeared near the middle of the term.

**MAGICAL GIRL'S HELP NETWORK**, said a clean printed card photographed on a striped blanket. Beneath it, in smaller type: **Local contacts choose local practice. Ask before passing private details.**

“The apostrophe is wrong,” Drita said.

“It could be singular possessive,” Bryn said. “A network for a magical girl's help.”

“That is worse.”

Cassia enlarged the photograph. Three translated versions of the name ran along the bottom. “It's kind of sweet.”

“It sounds like one magical girl owns all the help.”

“Maybe she's very generous.”

Nobody they asked admitted to naming it. By then the words were already printed on wallet cards, copied into radio introductions, and handwritten at the top of a page whose last column meant **no photographs, even transformed**. The three of them complained about the apostrophe for a week and used the name every day.

Some request headers now said **FORWARD TO THE ASSOCIATION**, though the messages still traveled person by person.

Bryn tried to make a master list. It lasted four days. Two contacts changed their hours without telling her. A cluster elsewhere replaced individual forwarding permission with permission for each request. A voice relay kept no written list at all. Someone marked Bryn's carefully translated safety note with a question, then a correction, then a joke she did not understand.

“They are forking the document,” she said in the stairwell, staring at five incompatible versions.

“They're using it,” Cassia said.

“Those aren't opposites.”

“Your face thinks they are.”

She sent her a look over the top of her phone. Drita snorted.

Cassia offered to keep the routes instead—not a master list, exactly, only a place where she knew who might know whom. She saved screenshots and remembered time windows. If a message stalled, she nudged it. If two replies crossed, she reconciled them. When someone else answered first, relief came with a small, embarrassing pinch, like arriving at a door with soup and finding the person had already eaten.

She never told Drita or Bryn about the pinch. She told herself it meant she cared.

* * *

Months after the index card left the stairwell, Cassia woke to her phone shivering against the wooden floor beside her bed.

The charging cable worked only when bent beneath a textbook. The phone was at nineteen percent and hot enough to leave a red patch in her palm. On the screen, a request had passed through four relays. Each had removed something before sending it onward.

> A contact tells me transform on camera to prove I am true.
>
> I do not trust this contact.
>
> No name. No place. No system. No proof.
>
> Need someone remain.

Cassia sat up. Her room emerged in pieces: heap of uniform on the chair, glow-in-the-dark stars fading above the window, water glass within reach. She typed before she was fully awake.

> Are they with you? Can you say if you're indoors? Do they know your civilian—

Drita's reply appeared in the trio's side channel.

> Stop.

Then, almost at once:

> Sorry. She said no place.

Cassia deleted the unfinished questions. In the main thread, the requester wrote:

> No body. No call. Do not ask sky.

Someone must have asked for a window photograph before the request reached them. Cassia imagined four strangers trying to help and each making the same frightened grab for certainty.

Bryn came online. Her first message was only **reading**. Her second filled the screen: preserve the original messages, mute the contact if that would not make things worse, do not follow links, consider whether the contact could be copied, consider whether the contact could be real but coerced, consider local emergency services if there was an immediate physical threat—

The requester interrupted her.

> Too many. Slow language.

Bryn's typing indicator vanished.

A relay posted a machine translation of an earlier line: **I am not danger.** Someone asked whether that meant the requester was safe or whether she meant she was not a danger to others. Another person replied to the wrong interpretation. Three dots appeared and disappeared beside the requester's blank icon.

Cassia wanted to gather every loose thread before it tightened around the person at the other end. She wanted one fact she could trust. A voice, a landmark, the shape of a focus token—anything. The want frightened her more when she recognized it.

> We are making this worse, she wrote in the side channel.

Drita answered:

> Yes.

After a pause, she added:

> We can stop.

The main thread stayed silent. Cassia counted one breath without rushing it. Then another. At the third, the requester sent:

> Remain means do not disappear. Not make plan.

Cassia put both feet on the cold floor.

> Here, she wrote.

Drita sent the same word. Bryn sent a single dot.

For five minutes, nobody asked anything.

The requester returned with a corrected translation chosen from two versions offered by someone in her own relay.

> I am not in danger now. I may be if the contact learns more. I will not transform for them.

Cassia began, *We know exactly—* and erased it. They did not.

> Something similar happened to three of us, she wrote. A trusted voice told us to transform. We treated the order as a reason to disconnect. That was our case, not a rule for yours.

Drita added:

> You don't owe this thread proof either.

No answer came for long enough that Cassia's screen dimmed. She touched it awake and saw her own face, faintly reflected over the blank thread.

Then:

> This helps. Less words now.

Bryn reacted to that message instead of replying. In the side channel, she wrote and deleted three different plans. At last she sent:

> Ask what remain should look like?

Drita replied:

> Ask one thing.

Cassia offered choices in the main thread: a dot at agreed intervals, silence with the channel open, or a relay to someone the requester herself selected. The requester chose one dot every five minutes and asked whether a person nearer to her could take over.

Not *find me somebody*. Not *tell me whom to trust*.

> I choose, she wrote. You carry request only. Do not carry reason.

The regional relay said it could send her a private list of people with whom she had already exchanged messages. Cassia would not see the list. Neither would Bryn or Drita. The requester could pick one, or none, and the chosen person would receive only this: **Can you be present now? No call unless asked.**

Bryn typed, *We cannot authenticate—*

Cassia watched the words appear in the side channel.

> She isn't asking us to authenticate her, she wrote. She's asking us to carry what she chose.

Bryn's half-message disappeared.

> Yes, she answered.

At the next five-minute mark, Cassia sent a dot. Five minutes later Drita sent one. Then a person whose waking hours usually overlapped none of theirs took the interval after that. Another helper posted from her lunch break. The dots were not perfectly spaced. Two arrived together; the requester responded with **one only please**, and Cassia put both hands under her thighs to keep from apologizing into the thread.

Her interval came around again. Before she could send, a dot appeared from the regional relay.

> I've got this one, it wrote.

Cassia's thumbs hovered. She had promised to remain. Leaving felt like breaking the promise, even though nobody had asked *her* in particular to make it.

Drita called her privately. Cassia answered without video.

“You're doing the face,” Drita said.

“You can't see my face.”

“I can hear it.” Her voice was rough with sleep. “One interval. We each said one.”

“What if the handoff goes wrong?”

“Then the people in it tell us what they want next.” Drita yawned, swallowed it, and started again. “I mean—we don't decide from here.”

On the main thread, the requester wrote:

> I picked someone. She knows a bad joke I made before. Enough for me.

The outer thread received no introduction, photograph, or transformed proof from the local person. The next part happened in a private channel beyond Cassia's view.

One last message came back by permission.

> I have company I chose. Stop the outer thread.

That was not *safe*. It was not proof. Cassia waited for a second sentence until the screen began to dim again.

None came.

She closed the thread.

* * *

The next version of the card reached Cassia as a photograph while she sat cross-legged on her bedroom rug. It carried the same disputed name and no list of officers. The offered-help columns differed by cluster. So did the hours, the labels for uncertain information, and the way each group ended a request. Along one edge, in several hands, people had added a common instruction: **The requester decides what confirmation travels back.**

Bryn sent a proposed central document to the trio, then withdrew it before Cassia opened it.

> Too many local differences, she wrote.

> Your face okay? Cassia asked.

> No.

Drita sent a laughing reaction, followed by a photograph of their first card. Cassia's **any time** remained visible beneath the line through it.
