No one answered. The scout turned a page. The hedge-worker sent one new light into a lantern and lost another; it guttered above Oruvane's nose. He blew it gently across the room. Brum bounded after it, struck the quartermaster's table, and sent three spools rolling under the settee.

For a moment the library came together. Torvik caught one spool between his boots. Oshara rescued the wine. The scout laughed into her book. Cavren seized Brum by the ruff before he reached the lantern stand, while the hedge-worker hurriedly drew her wandering light back into both hands. Oruvane's eyes brightened.

Dabria restored the table, the lantern, and the wolf. By then the moment had dispersed.

"We need something with rules," she said.

Oruvane's lids descended halfway. "Do we?"

"Tomorrow. Second bell. You choose the game."

"Any game?"

"Within reason."

"There it is," he said. "The little fence around every adventure."

Dabria wrote *Oruvane's recreation* on the back of the evening card. When she glanced up, Cavren had closed his pack. Oshara and Torvik were whispering behind the raised book. The scout read, the quartermaster stitched, and the hedge-worker kept her small suns alive. Everyone was still in the room. Oruvane was in the center of them, his painted wing making a blue night over half the library.

Brum left Dabria and went to lie against the dragon's foreleg.

For the next six days, Oruvane gave them games.

He turned the dining chairs toward the walls and strung retired climbing rope between the pantry and the plates. He hid challenge cards in books no one had opened since the old king's grandfather learned to lie. He moved the handbell to the highest gallery, tied spoons to half the door latches, and declared the sugar jar a besieged fortress. The hedge-worker supplied sparks for one treasure map and singed its north edge; the quartermaster sewed colored markers while complaining that none of the quests respected fabric; the scout found Oruvane's hiding places too quickly and began pretending not to.

Some of it was fun. Torvik cheated with such confidence that Oshara joined the opposing side solely to catch him. Brum dragged an entire rope course into the library and bound Cavren's ankles together. Even Cavren laughed, once, before looking annoyed at having done it. On the fifth night, though, Oshara had a headache and Torvik refused a map Oruvane had spent all afternoon painting. He went upstairs with her. Oruvane hung the map anyway.

Dabria wrote clearer rules. She posted starting times. When a chair cracked under Oruvane's tail, she added limits on moving furniture. The games became smoother and shorter. At second bell people appeared in the library and asked what he had prepared. At third bell they disappeared down corridors that admitted his narrow head and foreclaws but stopped him at the shoulders. Oshara and Torvik closed their door. Cavren took maps to the smaller stove in the east room. The three old campaign hands returned to their separate work. Oruvane remained among the books, surrounded by abandoned clues.

On the seventh night, Dabria woke to cold air moving through her bedchamber and found that her door was gone.

So were its hinges.

The hall had become indecently audible. Water ticked into a basin two floors below. Someone poked a fire. Torvik said, "I have trousers," and Oshara replied with a word she had once reserved for a necromancer.

There were thirteen empty frames between Dabria's room and the library.

Light poured through the library arch. Inside, the missing doors stood upright in a crooked maze around Oruvane. Green, blue, oak, and iron panels leaned against benches and retired spear shafts. Shields hung from their knobs. A hooked pole lay beside coils of rope leading back through the empty frames; he had drawn each freed door toward the library inch by inch. Challenge cards promised treasure, peril, and one "truth too terrible for polite architecture."

The rest of the household was already containing the damage. The scout braced a ladder while pushing a drift of books out of danger with one boot. The quartermaster crawled along the outside of the maze collecting hinge pins in her apron. At the arch, the hedge-worker breathed fresh lights into being one by one and sent them where people called; each floated only while her fingers remained spread. None of the three offered an interpretation. They had survived six years of Dabria's interpretations and knew when to protect the shelves instead.

Brum plunged between two doors and vanished.

"Put them back," Dabria said.

Oruvane raised his head above the maze. A gold chain slipped down his throat with a soft bright sound. "Welcome to the Labyrinth of Lingering Fellowship."

Oshara arrived in a robe over her nightclothes, with Torvik one-booted behind her. Cavren came last. He saw the gap where Brum had disappeared and stopped.

The wolf backed into view, tugging Cavren's packed traveling chest by its handle.

"Brum," Cavren said.

Brum pulled harder. The chest slid out from behind the blue drawing-room door, bumped over a carpet ridge, and sprang open. Winter cloak. Wrapped rations. Whetstone. Road kettle. The shield straps from the library evening lay neatly coiled on top.

Torvik glanced at Cavren, then at Dabria. Whatever joke had offered itself, he let it die.

"East side is clear to the outer corridor," the scout called. "If you want privacy for the murder, use that."

"No murder near the books," said the quartermaster from beneath a door.

Dabria climbed onto a bench. The lovers' oak door, marked by a pale scratch near the latch, blocked the west aisle. Cavren's stood across the hearth beside his chest. Beyond the inner turns, the iron-banded gate to the roof court made a final wall.

Dabria was still furious when the route began arranging itself in her head.

"Oshara, Torvik, take the west route. Cavren, come with me. We clear the small panels and make a path to the roof gate."

"No," Cavren said.

Not loud. Not negotiable.

Oruvane's tail slid between the doors and pulled one brace sideways. Benches groaned; the west route folded shut.

"The labyrinth rejects stale tactics," he said.

"The labyrinth took the privy door," Oshara said. "Its judgment is compromised."

For several minutes they accomplished nothing. Torvik climbed a pantry door and knocked down a copper warming pan. Dabria found a gap and lost it when Oruvane shifted his elbow. The hedge-worker's lights bobbed over the maze in answer to three contradictory requests. Brum crossed wherever he pleased, moving from Cavren to Oruvane to the scout as though the household had no walls at all.

At last Oshara gripped the bottom of the scratched oak door. "Dabria. Lift."

Together they tilted it free. It was heavier than it looked, and the narrow passage forced them sideways, Oshara walking backward while Dabria steered from the latch.

"Left," Dabria said. "No, your left. On three."

Oshara lowered her end to the carpet.

"What?"

"You pinned the first evening card to this door."

"It was nearest the library."

"It was ours."

Behind them, Torvik announced that the warming pan had always been that shape. Oshara did not turn.

"You moved the card," Dabria said. "I thought it had fallen."

"We moved it twice."

"You could have said something."

"I did. You were explaining the colors."

Dabria tightened both hands around the latch. "The card brought everyone down."

"Our door did that. You kept putting things on it. You kept opening it."

"I knock."

"While you open."

The distinction had seemed small in the campaign. A closed door had meant someone might be bleeding or burning evidence behind it. Dabria had learned to cross thresholds quickly and apologize when everyone was alive.

Oshara wiped hair from her mouth with an angry wrist. "Sometimes Torvik and I are busy with each other. Sometimes I am reading and he is making up songs about the plumbing. I want one room where you don't come in because you've lost a whetstone."

"That happened once."

"Twice," Torvik said from beyond the door. "The second time it was my whetstone."

Oshara shut her eyes.

"Sorry," he said. "I thought accuracy might help."

It did not. Dabria could feel her own reply assembling: the door unlatched, the danger over, the whetstone needed. All the reasonable parts of it.

"Where do you want this?" she asked.

Oshara looked at her across the width of the door. "Out of our way. Slowly. There's a nail by your knee."

They carried it to the arch. Dabria set it where the quartermaster directed and did not hang the next light from its knob.

When she returned, Cavren had freed his own door. His left forearm shook under the weight. He shifted his grip before Dabria could mention it.

"Where are you going?" she asked.

He looked toward the open chest. "East road. Escort work until the first snow."

"When?"

"Eight days."

"You were going to leave a note?"

"I was going to tell you."

"When?"

"Not while you had a card in your hand."

A brace cracked near the hearth. The green pantry door lurched. Torvik slipped beneath it; Cavren dropped his end, caught Torvik by the belt, and threw him clear before the panel struck the carpet. The maze answered with a shivering clap of wood.

"North brace," Dabria said. "Cavren, take the weight."

He remained crouched beside Torvik. "No."

"It's slipping."

"I heard you."

"This is not the time."

Cavren stood. His shaking hand closed and opened. "It never is. You promised relief on the final stair."

No one asked which stair.

"The lower breach opened," Dabria said. "I had to send Oshara and Torvik."

"I know."

"Then you know there was no one else."

"I know that too." His voice had shortened until each word seemed put down separately. "You promised. You couldn't come. Both happened. You only tell the part that makes you right."

Dabria had defended that choice to generals, ministers, singers, and herself. Cavren had held the stair. The kingdom had lived. In the songs, this was proof of her judgment.

"You held," she said.

Cavren's mouth tightened. She had reached the wrong thing again.

She saw him after dawn, sitting against the stair wall with his split shield across his knees. She had come with healers, a prince, and half the victorious court. She had asked whether the shield would survive the procession.

"I should have come back alone," she said.

"You didn't."

"No."

"Then stop there."

All her reasons crowded behind her teeth. She swallowed until her jaw hurt.

"All right," she said.

Cavren did not soften. His chest remained open. His east road remained eight days away. But when the brace slipped again, he chose where to put his shoulder, and Dabria took the other side without directing him.

Beyond the last turn of the maze, Oruvane had laid the roof gate flat. Travel bags hung beneath his wings: canvas pouches, two small casks, a rolled blanket, and the brass pan he used to warm sand for his joints. No saddle. No battle harness. Nothing that offered a rider any place upon him.

Predawn silvered the open court beyond.

Oshara saw the bags first. "You're leaving too."

"I am embarking upon a voyage of private magnificence," Oruvane said.

"Where?" Torvik asked.

"Away."

"Poor roads. Worse inns."

Usually Oruvane met Torvik's foolishness with something larger. This time he worried a groove in the flagstone with one claw.

Dabria looked back through the tilted doors. Four human thresholds stood around the one room Oruvane could inhabit easily. Each evening they passed through openings too small for him and called their disappearance privacy.

"Was this meant to stop us leaving?" she asked.

"It was meant to be a quest."

Brum walked to him and sat on one blue foot.

"You took my chest," Cavren said.

"It was packed. Suspiciously."

"You searched my room."

Oruvane's gaze moved to Oshara's door at the arch, then away. "The quest was poorly designed."

"Yes," Oshara said.

Smoke leaked between his teeth. "I wanted to know whether you'd notice one of us gone." His gaze found Dabria. "Without a card."

The question had needed thirteen stolen doors and Cavren's chest before Dabria heard it. She started to ask why Oruvane had not simply told her. Then she remembered dumplings.

"Do you want company?" she asked.

Oruvane considered. "No."

Torvik's expression pinched before he covered it. "Do you want an insulting wave? I have several."

"One. From a distance."

Oshara pointed at the doors. "You are still putting ours back."

"When I return."

"Before you go."

Oruvane sighed smoke over her hair, but bent his neck to the work. The quartermaster brought hinge pins. The hedge-worker held three trembling lights above the frame. Cavren took one edge of the gate; Dabria reached for the other, then stopped.

"Do you want me here?" she asked him.

He adjusted his grip. "Upper pin."

Dabria took the upper pin. Together they hung the gate crooked, and it opened.

They went with Oruvane as far as the roof court. The wind lifted the gold chains at his throat as he stepped to the parapet.

"I may be gone three days," he said. "Or not."

"If it's more than eight, I'll be gone," Cavren said. "East road."

Oruvane turned sharply. "Then I may find you."

"You may."

Dabria could have asked for routes, dates, signals. She could have made departure safe enough to feel like permission. Instead she put both hands in her empty pockets.

"I'll miss you," she said. "Even if the roof leaks. That isn't—" She stopped. "I'll miss you."

Oruvane watched her long enough that she nearly explained. Then his wings opened, painted blue and gold against the whitening sky, and he left without an order to return.

* * *

It took two days to put the hall's doors back. Dabria knocked on Oshara and Torvik's even while carrying the missing hinge, and waited until Torvik opened it a hand's width. Cavren repacked the chest Oruvane had disturbed. When Dabria offered to help, he said no. When she asked whether he wanted company on the east road, he said he had not decided. The final stair stayed between them, neither buried nor crossed.

On the third evening, the library filled without a card.

Not completely and not all at once. The scout came first with her book. The quartermaster brought the cushion she was still mending. The hedge-worker lit only two lanterns and let the fire provide the rest. Oshara and Torvik arrived together, took separate chairs, and gradually failed to remain separate. Cavren sat on his packed chest with Brum at his knee. Dabria read three pages of a history and understood none of them.

The room held clusters, not a formation. People left for wine and returned. The quartermaster went to bed. No one accounted for her.

A shadow crossed the high windows. The roof gate struck stone once, and Oruvane shouldered into the library smelling of rain and some sharp mountain herb crushed beneath his claws. Conversation snagged. Brum rose so quickly that Cavren's book fell from his lap, bounded across the carpet, and pressed his whole white body into the hollow behind Oruvane's foreleg.

No one had posted a watch. No one had prepared a welcome.

"You began without me," Oruvane said.

"Twice," Torvik told him. "It was peaceful. We hated it."

Oruvane lowered himself among the chairs. The scout shifted closer to his wing without losing her page. Oshara moved the wine. Cavren picked up his book, but his packed chest stayed beside him.

Dabria did not ask where Oruvane had gone or whether he would leave again. She lasted almost half a minute.

"Did you find a quest?" she asked.

"No." He settled his chin onto one foreclaw. "I found weather. Tomorrow I may tell you about it."

"Tomorrow?" The old instinct reached for a time.

Oruvane's eye opened.

Dabria stopped. "If you want."

"Perhaps after the dumplings."

There were none. Torvik proposed hunting them anyway. Oshara told him to hunt quietly. Brum rolled onto his side against Oruvane's scales, Cavren's boot resting in his fur. Torvik's proposed dumpling trail crossed the scout's complaint about his shuffling; Oshara asked the hedge-worker about a lamp and answered Cavren by mistake. One conversation broke apart. Another started before it had finished. Dabria let her unread history close in her lap.

Across the fire, Cavren met her eyes. He was still leaving. He was still there.

This time she did not count either fact away.

stories.title: All the Good Things
stories.prompt: Every catfolk carries the instincts of the wild ancestor their bloodline came from, but inside a quiet little restaurant good food, soft music, and an ancient house rule are the only things keeping those instincts from turning dinner into a hunt.
stories.body:
# All the Good Things

Linette had just asked whether she should bring the smoked-pepper char when Ceret heard herself say, “Yes, and the lemon potatoes for Veslina, and Mezzara will want—”

Linette laid three menus on the table, though only one chair was occupied. “You may choose water for people who aren’t here.”

“Veslina always orders the char.”

“Last time she ordered the mullet.”

“Only because the char was sold out.”

“She can tell me when she arrives.” Linette turned the empty glasses upright. Her black tail curved behind her apron, still except at the tip. “I’ll bring the water.”

Ceret folded her hands under the table before she could straighten the menus into a single exact fan. “And three plates?”

“That much I can assume.”

The restaurant’s one small room glowed in layers of amber: candle cups on the tables, shaded lamps along the plaster walls, a copper shine from the open kitchen hatch. The chairs had curved gaps beneath their back rails so tails could hang or curl without being trapped. Ceret had chosen the round table near the guitarist, close enough to hear the brush of fingers on strings but not so close that conversation became work.

Joia sat on a low stool in the corner, tuning quietly. She drew one string down, listened with one russet ear inclined, and adjusted it by a fraction. Around her, the early diners kept their voices low without seeming to mean to.

Since spring, the three friends had managed hurried cups of tea and meetings in pairs, but no supper together. Ceret had missed the interruptions as much as the talk.

Ceret checked the door. Then she checked it again.

Linette set down the water. “Still absent.”

“I was looking at the rain.”

“It remains wet.”

The door opened before Ceret could answer. Mezzara entered first, unfastening her damp green coat as she walked, and Veslina crowded in behind her with a striped shawl over her head and a paper parcel tucked under one arm. Rain had darkened their sleeves and tails. At the sight of them, Ceret stood so quickly that her knee struck the table and made all three empty glasses chime.

“That was almost musical,” Veslina said.

Mezzara kissed Ceret’s cheek, then pressed two cool fingers to the silver-speckled fur at the base of her ear. “You’re early.”

“I’m on time.”

“For us, that’s early.”

Veslina embraced Ceret one-armed, still protecting the parcel. She smelled of rain, citrus soap, and the cold street. “Please tell me there’s food coming.”

“Linette wouldn’t let me order yours.”

“Good.” Veslina dropped into her chair and guided her tawny, dark-ringed tail through the open back. “I changed my mind on the walk.”

Ceret sat more slowly. “About the char?”

“About everything. Then back again about most of it.”

Mezzara hung her coat on the wall peg. The fur along one dark ear was still beaded with rain. “We took the wrong tram.”

“It wasn’t wrong,” Veslina said. “It went past the soap shop.”

“It did not come here.”

“But I needed soap.” Veslina lifted the parcel as evidence. “Now I have two bars.”

“You made us get off six streets away.”

“And now I have soap.”

Linette arrived with a folded cloth for the damp table edge and waited while Veslina moved her parcel. She did not glance at Ceret.

Veslina read the menu from top to bottom, lips moving slightly. “I’ll have the char.”

Ceret looked at Linette, who remained professionally blank.

“With the green olives, not the potatoes,” Veslina added.

“You don’t like olives,” Ceret said.

“I didn’t. Someone has been putting them in rice at home, and apparently I like them when I’m not told in advance.”

“Who is someone?” Ceret asked.

Veslina opened her mouth, but Mezzara spoke over her. “Salt-baked bream for me, please. And the tomato salad.”

Ceret turned. “Not the river trout?”

“I can have trout another day.”

There was no sensible answer to that. Ceret picked up her own menu, which she had already read twice. “Then the herb-roasted bass. We’ll share all three.”

“If you ask before moving food onto my plate,” Mezzara said.

“When have I not asked?”

Mezzara and Veslina looked at each other.

“Recently,” Ceret amended.

Linette took the menus. “I’ll begin with the small gilt fish and fennel. You can practice.”

Once she was gone, the first few minutes broke apart pleasantly. Veslina wanted to know whether Ceret had cut her own fringe; Ceret insisted it had merely dried badly in the rain. Mezzara asked if the loose window above Ceret’s sink had finally been fixed. Ceret asked why Mezzara had a streak of white dust on her sleeve. Veslina unwrapped one of the soaps to let them smell it, then complained that the rose scent was much stronger in the warm room than it had been in the shop.

“You’ve bought a cupboard fragrance,” Mezzara said.

“It smelled like orange peel outside.”

“Outside was mostly tram smoke.”

Ceret pushed the soap farther from her water glass. “Give it to the someone who taught you to eat olives.”

Veslina started folding the paper around it again. “They chose the other one.”

“They?”

“I’ll tell you. I was going to tell you.”

“After the soap?”

Veslina’s ears tipped outward. “The soap was meant to lead there.”

Mezzara reached for the water jug. “You started at the wrong end.”

“Then I’ll begin again after food.”

The small fish arrived on a dark oval plate, their skins crisp and gold, laid over fennel shaved thin enough to turn translucent at the edges. Preserved lemon shone between them. For a while the talk narrowed to ordinary negotiations: which fish had the fewest bones, whether Veslina had taken all the lemon, who wanted the last piece of bread while it was still warm.

“This was our first table,” Ceret said when only tails and bright smears of oil remained on the platter.

Mezzara looked toward the window. “No, the first one was against that wall.”

“It was this table. I remember the candle wobbling every time the kitchen door opened.”

“There wasn’t a candle,” Veslina said. “It was afternoon.”

“It was dark.”

“Because it was raining.”

“It was night,” Ceret said. “We had spent all day moving Mezzara’s boxes, and the bottom came out of the one with the blue bowls.”

“The bottom did not come out. The knot slipped.” Mezzara extracted a neat backbone from the last fish and placed it at the side of her plate. “Also, there were eight bowls.”

“Twelve,” Ceret said.

“Eight bowls and a blanket.”

Veslina pointed her fork at Mezzara. “A wet blanket.”

“Because you set it in the gutter.”

“To catch the bowl I saved.”

“You saved no bowl. Ceret caught the stack against her coat.”

Ceret could see it as soon as Mezzara said it: her younger self kneeling on slick paving stones, a tower of blue ceramic pressed to her ribs, rain dripping off her chin. She had forgotten the weight of the bowls. She had remembered only Veslina laughing and Mezzara saying, with terrible calm, that the blanket would wash.

“We came in because we could smell grilled fish from the street,” Ceret said.

“We came in because you wouldn’t let us carry another box before supper,” Veslina said.

“We came in,” Mezzara said, “because it was open.”

They considered these accounts.

“All of that can be true,” Veslina decided.

“Not the candle,” Mezzara said.

Joia began to play before Ceret could defend it. Her thumb kept a soft, quick pattern on the lower strings while the melody passed above it, light enough that the clink of cutlery stayed part of the room. Ceret watched Veslina’s ears turn toward the corner. Mezzara rested both wrists beside her plate. At another table, a child stopped trying to balance a spoon on one finger.

No one at Ceret’s table spoke until the piece ended. Their applause joined the room’s, brief and warm. Joia nodded without standing and started another tune.

The second tune left longer spaces between its chords. Ceret let her eyes settle on the candle. This one did wobble when Linette passed with a tray, though there was no kitchen draft anymore.

When Joia paused for tea, Linette cleared the first platter and brought the tomato salad. Mezzara caught Ceret looking at the white mark on her sleeve again.

“Plaster,” she said.

“I guessed plaster.”

“You asked why.”

“I assumed you would eventually tell me.”

“I looked at a room this afternoon.”

Ceret expected the rest: a temporary room before another journey, a place to leave two cases while Mezzara worked elsewhere. “For how long?”

Mezzara spooned tomatoes onto her plate. “I hope for years.”

Veslina bit into a strip of bread, apparently unsurprised.

“Here?” Ceret asked.

“Three streets over. Above a cabinetmaker. The room has an east window, and the little alcove is wide enough for a table.”

“I thought you still wanted to go north in the autumn.”

“That was four autumns ago.”

“You said you’d never live where you could hear the same bells every day.”

Mezzara’s mouth bent. “I said I would never live above the bell shop again. The apprentice tested them before breakfast.”

Veslina covered a laugh with her napkin.

“I may have remembered the broader meaning,” Ceret said.

“You made it broader. You do that when a story has an untidy edge.”

Ceret picked up the salad spoon. “Does the alcove get the morning light?”

“Some. The building across the lane takes part of it.”

“Enough for a lemon tree?”

“Perhaps herbs. A lemon tree would have to be very forgiving.”

“And the plaster?”

“I leaned against the wall while the landlord found the key to the cupboard.”

“Is the cupboard good?” Veslina asked.

“We never found out. He had brought the cellar key.”

Veslina nodded gravely. “Promising. A man with many keys suggests many cupboards.”

“Or one cupboard he has never opened,” Mezzara said.

Ceret began to offer the name of another street, another landlord, a sunlit top floor she had once passed on her way to the market. She stopped after, “There’s a building near—”

Mezzara waited.

“What do you want in it?” Ceret asked instead.

The question seemed to please her more than Ceret had expected. Mezzara put down the spoon. “A table I don’t have to clear before I eat. A cupboard that closes. Light enough to sew black thread without carrying the sleeve to the window. Two comfortable chairs.”

“Only two?” Veslina asked.

“Other people can sit on ordinary chairs.”

“I have a green chair you can take.”

“I said comfortable.”

“The green chair has character.”

“The green chair leans toward the door.”

“It encourages visitors not to linger.”

Their main plates arrived before Mezzara could reject it again. Linette carried the fish one at a time: the char with dark pepper and a bowl of glossy olives; the bream under a shell of salt that she opened at the table, sending up a clean thread of steam; the bass surrounded by roasted tomatoes, herbs, and small yellow potatoes. She turned each platter so the serving spoons faced inward.

“The peppers are hotter at this end,” she told Veslina. “And yes, you may all exchange pieces. Ceret has asked properly.”

“Once,” Mezzara said.

“A beginning,” Linette replied, already moving toward another table.

They tasted each fish before returning to anything important. The bream was tender and sweet beneath its salt crust; the char left warmth at the back of Ceret’s tongue. Veslina discovered that she liked the green olives less on their own than she did in rice, and deposited two on Ceret’s plate without asking.

“The someone,” Ceret prompted.

Veslina drank water. “Yes.”

Mezzara, occupied with a fish bone, said, “Try the middle this time.”

Veslina arranged her fork and knife, then rearranged them. “I’ve been seeing someone. No, that sounds recent. We’ve been together for a while. They stay most nights. Nearly every night, except their early mornings are easier from their own rooms, so some weeks it’s four nights, and some—”

“How long?” Ceret asked.

“Since late winter. Properly. Before that, it depends what counts.”

“Who counts?”

“We do. Differently.” Veslina’s tail tip tapped once against the chair leg. “I wanted to ask whether they could come to supper sometime.”

Ceret paused with a piece of bass halfway to her plate.

Veslina went on at once. “Not every time. Not this table, I mean this table is fine, but I don’t mean they belong at every supper because that would make it a different—unless you wanted—”

“Ceret is holding hot fish in the air,” Mezzara said.

Ceret put it down. “I was wondering if they eat fish.”

Veslina blinked. “They eat almost everything. Not fennel.”

“Then the first plate would have been difficult.”

“They could move it aside.”

“What are they like?” Ceret asked.

Veslina’s shoulders lowered. “Patient with kettles. Impatient with hems. They read the last page first, which I object to, although not enough to stop lending them books. They leave tea in every room.”

“That’s what you do,” Mezzara said.

“I leave cups. They leave tea in the cups.”

“A household distinction,” Ceret said.

“You’ll understand when you see the windowsill.” Veslina rubbed her thumb over the edge of her napkin. “I wanted you to meet them. And I wanted this sometimes. Still. I couldn’t find a way to ask for both without making one sound like the apology for the other.”

Ceret had been ready with questions about work, family, how they had met, whether they treated Veslina well. They crowded behind her teeth. She began with the easiest. “Do they know how much you talk during the quiet parts of songs?”

“I do not.”

Mezzara looked toward Joia’s stool. “You whispered through half the last piece.”

“That was before it began.”

“Joia had begun.”

Veslina turned to Ceret. “You see why I need another person on my side.”

“I’d like to meet them,” Ceret said. “Bring them one evening, if they can come.”

Veslina smiled, not broadly, but for long enough that Ceret had time to notice. “All right.”

“And some suppers can still be three,” Ceret added.

“Please.” Veslina picked up her fork again. “That was the part I kept making worse in my head.”

Mezzara passed her the char. “It took you four months to produce that sentence.”

“The sentence took four months. Other things happened meanwhile.”

“The soap, for example.”

“The soap happened today.”

Ceret reached for an olive from Veslina’s plate, and Veslina tapped the back of her hand away with two fingers. “Ask.”

“May I have the olive you don’t want?”

“No. But you may have this one.” Veslina selected another, apparently identical olive, and set it on Ceret’s plate.

Mezzara leaned back while Linette replaced their water. “What about you, Ceret?”

“What about me?”

“We have supplied rooms, keys, poor chairs, soap, and a person who abuses tea. You’ve told us nothing.”

“Nothing has happened.”

“Did they fix the window over your sink?” Mezzara asked.

“Yes. In May.”

“And the damp patch?”

“Dry. Mostly.”

Veslina tucked one foot beneath her chair. “Did you move your bed away from the cold wall?”

Ceret looked at her. “Last month.”

“Does your shoulder hurt less in the morning?”

“A little.”

“And the basil?” Mezzara asked.

“Dead.”

Veslina clicked her tongue.

“It was a weak plant.”

“You said it had survived two winters.”

“Then it was an old, tired plant.”

“What did you put in the pot?”

“Mint. My sister gave me a cutting.”

“The one that tastes like pepper?”

“That was the other mint. This one tastes like mint.”

Mezzara waited while Veslina served herself another potato. “You were going to have supper with your sister on Thursdays.”

“I do. When she isn’t working late. Her youngest has decided soup is an insult, so we eat a lot of bread.”

“And the clarinet downstairs?” Veslina asked.

“Upstairs. The boy knows six notes now.”

“Last time it was four.”

“The fifth was a difficult week.”

They both laughed, and Ceret did too. She had called the months empty because no single event seemed large enough to set in the middle of the table. Yet Mezzara remembered the wall by her bed. Veslina remembered the boy’s four notes.

“I’ve been leaving work early on Tuesdays,” Ceret said. “Not early. On time. I walk home by the long street and buy whatever fruit is cheapest.”

“What was cheapest this week?” Mezzara asked.

“Small red plums. Sour ones.”

“You like those,” Veslina said.

“I’d forgotten.”

Joia returned to her stool. She tightened one string, played a chord, and looked toward the kitchen hatch. Linette lifted a hand to say she had heard. The next set began with a slower tune, low notes opening beneath a plain melody.

At Ceret’s table, forks settled. Veslina wrapped both hands around her glass. Mezzara’s ears inclined toward the music, and the candle traced a narrow line along the dark fur of her cheek. Ceret listened without trying to decide what the tune was about. Joia repeated the melody, changed two notes, and let the last chord fade under the murmur of the room.

During the applause, Linette offered them honey cakes. They agreed to one plate and then, after Linette looked at the cleaned fish, two. Veslina claimed she could eat only half and finished a whole cake before the second song.

Joia played three more pieces. Between them came the sounds the music had made room for: a chair easing over the floor, rain ticking at the window, someone near the kitchen laughing into a napkin. Veslina’s tail curled loosely around one ankle. Ceret’s lay warm against the leg of her chair.

When Joia finally set the guitar aside, the room’s conversations rose by degrees. Mezzara lifted her teacup and frowned into it.

“I never finished telling you about the room,” she said.

“You reached the cupboard,” Ceret said.

“Barely. I didn’t tell you the measurements.”

Veslina leaned closer. “How wide?”

“Five and a half paces, not counting the alcove.”

“Your paces or the landlord’s?” Ceret asked.

“Mine. His were enormous and he kept stepping on the hem of his coat.”

Veslina moved the candle toward the center of the table. “Say this is the window.”

“That is the alcove,” Mezzara said. “The window is the sugar bowl.”

“Then where’s the warm wall?” Ceret asked.

Mezzara shifted the cups aside and laid one hand flat beside Ceret’s plate. “Here. The bed would go along it, and the table would face this way...”

stories.title: Hello, Lover
stories.prompt: A demon appears before your party, exclaiming “Hello lover!” Everyone looks at the bard, but then the cleric speaks up. “Actually, my ex is referring to me.”
stories.body:
# Hello, Lover

The sanctuary door had swollen in the first cold rain of autumn. Emet Sarn put his shoulder to it while Udren lifted the latch, and together they admitted the last two carters from the road. Wet cloaks already covered every peg in the House of Common Shelter. Bedrolls crowded the common room between the plain altar and Bosk's stool by the stove.

“One more hard shove in the morning,” Udren said, “and we will have a door-shaped hole.”

“Then it will never stick again.” Bosk turned his hand drum toward the stove. Its damp hide gave a dismal little plunk. “I believe this is called preventive maintenance.”

Emet had just found space for the carters beside a family with three snoring dogs when a red seam opened across the north wall.

It was too straight for lightning and too bright for fire. Mortar flashed to steam. The seam widened from floor to lintel, showing a tiled room on the other side and a demon striding through it with heat rolling off her work leathers. Brass capped the points of her swept black horns. Her dark red hands were powdered to the wrists with white kiln clay.

She planted one boot on the sanctuary floor and called, “Hello lover!”

Every head in the room turned toward Bosk.

Bosk looked behind his stool, as if another bard might be hiding there.

Emet raised one hand. “Actually, my ex is referring to me.”

The silence held just long enough for one of the dogs to sneeze.

Lacrixa looked Emet up and down. Nine years had added a silver ring through the ridge of her left horn and taken nothing from the level way she could make him feel improperly assembled.

“Good,” she said. “I would hate to have crossed this far and found the wrong bad decision.”

Then the red seam tore sideways.

Udren's shield struck the floor between the crossing and the bedrolls. A gust of kiln heat bent the room's rushlights flat and rolled two sleepers into the shield's broad back. Beyond Lacrixa, figures shouted in the tiled room. Something heavy shattered. Bosk caught his stool with one foot and his drum with both hands.

Emet saw the hinge leaf bolted into the new frame.

It was a hand-long strip of yellow bronze with a split-tailed end, its face darkened by years in a wrapping no one else had known existed. His thumb knew the shallow notch near the lower screw. His knife had made it on a rainy evening in Lacrixa's room, when the two of them had fitted a courtesy hinge because crossing the kiln court after midnight meant waking six households and a flock of vicious white geese.

He had told her he destroyed it.

He had kept it in the stitched lining of his field breviary. Three days ago, at a crowded ford, someone had slit that lining and taken nothing Emet was willing to report missing.

Now his leaf was mounted in a stranger's ironwork.

Lacrixa followed his stare. “That does not look like ash.”

“I didn't mount it.”

“You kept it long enough for someone else to do so.”

Udren leaned her weight into the shield as another hot gust struck. “How many people on your side?”

Lacrixa turned at once. The tiled room behind her had once held a bed, two chests and a table Emet could never make sit level. It now held racks of glazed bowls. Past its open arch lay the kiln court: brick galleries, firing pits, wash troughs, and more than two dozen people trying to move hot ware out of the wind.

“Thirty-one in the court,” Lacrixa said. “Six in this room. All adults, two with bad legs. How many here?”

“Seventeen guests,” Udren said. “And us.” She pointed to the sanctuary's ordinary front door, eight paces behind her. “Bosk, count them out. Emet, tell me what this is.” She angled her shield and started the first group moving.

The crossing stood as a doorway-wide rectangle between the two rooms. The sanctuary lay on Emet's side; Lacrixa's old room and the kiln court lay on hers. Three black iron loops telescoped through its throat: one against the sanctuary jamb, one midway in the red-lit depth, and one flush with the plane where the worlds met.

A courtesy hinge had two keyed leaves. One leaf mounted alone was inert. Bring both living bearers near their leaves, and they supplied the hinge with enough power for a step between familiar doors. The rig around these leaves had no power and no judgment of its own. It could only redirect what Emet and Lacrixa were giving it. Someone had added three borrower loops and stretched a private step into a road.

Breaking either leaf would stop the supply. With people crowding both approaches and the loops forcing the route open in the wrong shape, the plane could slam shut through anyone caught in the throat.

“The loops come off from this jamb inward,” Emet said. “Then we break the leaves when both approaches are clear.”

“We?” Lacrixa asked.

The leaf under its iron clamps warmed at Emet's nearness. Across the plane, the matching leaf shone on the old room's tiled jamb, exactly where they had mounted it. Lacrixa had left hers in plain view. It could have reached nothing by itself.

“Both bearers,” Emet said. “It needs our hands.”

“Of course it does.”

Udren continued moving guests behind her shield toward the front door. Lacrixa snapped instructions over her shoulder, and the kiln court answered with motion: workers banked firing pits, overturned sand bins onto sparks, and carried a limping glaze grinder away from the arch. Bosk settled his drum strap across his chest and gave the rim three clear taps.

“Three loops,” he said. “Seventeen guests. It is comforting when disasters can be counted.”

“You are on twelve,” Udren told him.

“Less comforting. Twelve.” The drum spoke once as a carter ducked through the ordinary door. “Thirteen.”

Emet approached the first loop. Heat pressed against his eyes. On the far side Lacrixa matched him, bracing one clay-white hand against the iron. They had moved kiln shelves together, long ago, and carried sacks of House grain up narrow stairs. His body remembered where she put her weight. That was not the same as knowing her. His body did not care.

“On Bosk's fourth beat,” Emet said. “Lift, quarter-turn toward the court, then down.”

“It will bind on your lower corner.”

“The corner is clear.”

Lacrixa rapped the iron with one knuckle. The note came back flat. “That is the sound of a corner preparing to embarrass a cleric.”

Bosk began the measure. On four, Emet and Lacrixa lifted. The loop moved a finger's breadth and seized exactly where she had said it would. Heat bit through Emet's glove.

Lacrixa swore, shifted her hip, and said, “Blue-bowl turn.”

Emet dropped his right shoulder before the memory arrived. The phrase had been born when they tried to carry a broad blue mixing bowl around the crooked stair in her court: yield the high corner, take the weight low, and do not pause to argue. They had broken the bowl anyway and laughed until the neighbors came to complain.

Their hands made the old adjustment. The loop rolled free.

For half a breath they stood with its weight balanced between them. Lacrixa's grip tightened.

“I did not mean to say that,” she said.

“I know.”

“Then stop looking as if I gave you something.”

Emet looked down at the hot iron.

The crossing bucked. They dropped the loop clear as Udren drove the rim of her shield into the floor. Bosk's drum marked the last sanctuary guest through the front door.

“Seventeen. Udren, they're out.”

The first loop hit the stones and split along a seam. A smell like hot pennies filled the room. With one borrowed route gone, the crossing contracted. The old room sprang into painful focus.

The bed was gone. The uneven table was gone. New racks covered one wall, but a border of green-and-cream tile still ran behind them, including the piece Emet had set upside down and Lacrixa had refused to fix because it annoyed him more each year. Her leaf remained openly screwed above that border. On Emet's side, the first loop's fall had peeled back an iron clamp and exposed a scrap of gray cloth trapped beneath it: the prayer-stitched wrapping from inside his breviary.

Lacrixa saw the cloth.

Light flared orange through the seams of her clenched fingers. She put a hand against the tiled jamb. The glaze beneath her palm crackled into a white web, and three chips spat onto the floor. Bosk struck the opening beat for the middle loop. Lacrixa did not move.

“Hold,” Emet said.

Bosk flattened his hand against the drumhead.

Lacrixa took her palm from the wall. Little glazed scales clung to it. “I left my leaf where everyone in my court could see it. It was dead. I wasn't tearing out good tile because you left.” The air shook above her shoulders. “Pride. Mine. But you told me its twin was ash.”

“I know.”

“Were you about to tell me I kept mine too?”

Emet rubbed his thumb across the iron.

“Of course.” She scraped the glaze from her palm. “Before I put my hand into the middle of this thing, I want the rest. Did the House ever forbid us?”

There was no safe category of answer. He had spent nine years inventing them anyway.

“No,” Emet said. His burned hand slipped on the iron. “The House of Common Shelter never forbade our relationship.”

Lacrixa went still. Behind her, court workers dragged a wheeled rack away from the arch. One wheel screamed on its axle.

“The circuit takes twenty years,” Emet said. “No posting beyond one season. Every first frost, I packed while the people around me banked the hearth. If we had stayed together, you would have had to leave your court again and again, or I would have had to give up the circuit.”

“So you chose.”

“I chose the road.” His breath would not finish. “I said they chose for me.”

The crossing gave a deep metallic groan. Emet's right boot skidded toward it.

Udren came in behind him but did not seize him. She planted her shield edge on the stone at his back.

“Left sole,” she said.

“Stone.”

“Right.”

“Stone.”

“My shield is here if you want it.”

He leaned. Its oak face held firm between his shoulder blades.

Udren's voice stayed low. “Next lift yours?”

“Mine.”

“Then ask for it.”

Emet looked across the red plane. “Lacrixa, will you help me take off the middle loop?”

She wiped her hand once on her apron. “I will help the people in these rooms.”

Bosk lifted his palm from the drum.

The second loop had twisted as the crossing narrowed. Emet could reach its lower arc, but Lacrixa had to step onto the ledge of the old jamb and hook an arm over the upper. They did not use the old shorthand. Bosk gave them a slow six count instead.

On five, the red depth pulled like a river. Bosk's stool went first. His drum followed. The strap snapped across his shoulder, and the drum sailed between Emet's hands, struck the far jamb, and burst its hide with a sound like a door slammed in an empty house.

Bosk stared after it for one beat.

Then his heel hit the sanctuary floor. “Six. Again. One, two—”

His count was smaller without the drum, and more stubborn. Emet and Lacrixa worked the warped loop up by increments. Lacrixa's breath rasped. Emet's burned glove stuck to the iron. Udren held the shield behind him without pushing.

At six, the middle loop cleared its catches. Lacrixa kicked her side away. Emet dragged his down. It struck the first loop, and both went dull.

The crossing shrank to the inner loop. The rectangle was still doorway-wide, but now the whole pull of the leaves ran through a single iron ring flush with the plane between worlds. Emet stood on the sanctuary side with Udren's shield at his back. Lacrixa stood opposite him, her back toward the old room and the court arch. Bosk took Emet's left, stamping the measure into the stones.

“Old room clear!” Lacrixa called.

A stack of bowls toppled from the nearest rack. The crossing caught them in midair and flung glazed shards through the plane. Udren raised her shield over Bosk. Emet ducked, but one shard sliced his bare wrist above the glove.

From the kiln court came a shout. The limping glaze grinder had returned for a leather tool roll lying beside the arch. The floor tiles lifted under him like cards in a gust. He fell, slid through Lacrixa's reach, and struck the inner loop hip-first. One leg crossed into the sanctuary. The other remained in the old room.

The ring screamed.

Lacrixa caught the grinder under both arms. Emet locked his hands around the near arc to keep it from folding across the man's body. Udren set her shield against his back and braced one boot against the altar step.

“Pull him courtward,” Emet said.

“I know where my court is.” Lacrixa hauled. The grinder cried out. His trapped boot had caught beneath the far catch.

Bosk stamped. “One. Two. Three.”

The iron tried to close. Emet's burned palm opened against it.

He held.

Udren grunted behind him. Lacrixa let go with one hand, struck the catch with her fist, and sent a short tongue of flame across its pin. The pin softened. She tore the grinder's boot free, seized him again, and pulled.

Bosk kept the count with his heel. “Four. Five. Six.”

The grinder's knee passed the plane. His ankle followed. Lacrixa dragged him across the old-room tiles until two court workers caught his coat.

She looked down and said, “Both feet clear.”

He held.

The inner loop remained open between them. Lacrixa straightened slowly. Behind her, the grinder was carried out beneath the court arch. The old room stood empty except for broken bowls, her mounted leaf, and the wreck of Bosk's drum.

“Emet,” Udren said. She did not increase the pressure of the shield. “The approach is clear.”

“Wait.” His arms shook. “If I let the ring go, the crossing closes.”

“Yes,” Lacrixa said.

“We can take the leaves out of this rig and mount them properly. Only as a rescue route. Or we could—”

“There is no reunion,” Lacrixa said. “Not now. Not after. Do you understand me?”

He did. His hands did not open.

“The court could catch again,” he said. “You could need shelter. I kept the leaf because I thought—”

“You do not keep me safe by keeping access.”

Emet looked at the gray cloth pinched beneath his leaf. With his free hand, he bent its split tail out over the iron ring while the screws still held the other end to the clamp. Across the plane, Lacrixa wedged the claws of a kiln hammer beneath her own leaf. Bosk's heel struck once, twice.

“Goodbye, Lacrixa,” Emet said.

Her jaw worked once. “Goodbye, Emet.”

On Bosk's third beat, Lacrixa levered her leaf in two against the tiled jamb. Emet drove his palm down on his. The keyed bronze split beneath his blood. Red light ran through both broken leaves and collapsed toward his fingers.

Emet withdrew.

The inner loop fell flat on the sanctuary floor. The rectangle filled with a brief view of the old room: Lacrixa standing amid broken glaze, one hand on the shoulder of the injured grinder. Then there was only the north wall, wet stone, and a cooling iron ring.

For the next hour Emet worked on the sanctuary's injured. Two guests had blistered forearms from the first kiln gust. A carter had struck her head against Udren's shield, and Bosk's snapped strap had left a purple weal across his collarbone. Emet washed grit from eyes, spread burn salve, checked the carter's pupils twice, and wrapped his own palm last.

When everyone could sit without falling over, he gave Udren and Bosk the full account. He told them when he had taken the leaf, what he had told Lacrixa, where he had hidden it, and why he had said nothing after the lining was cut at the ford. Bosk sat on the altar step with the broken end of his drum strap in his lap. Udren wrote each fact in the field ledger.

When Emet finished, she turned the ledger around. She had struck his name from solo threshold watch and from route decisions.

“Until field trust is rebuilt,” she said. “No threshold watch alone. No choosing our routes. Do you accept that?”

“Yes.”

Udren nodded. She unwound the bandage he had tied one-handed, smoothed the twisted pad, and wrapped his palm again without pulling the knot too tight.

Bosk disappeared into the pantry. He returned with a cup of water and sat beside Emet, their shoulders not quite touching.

“I had a song for this,” Bosk said.

“Had?”

“It was in the drum.” He handed Emet the water.

By dawn the rain had passed. Udren propped the ordinary sanctuary door with a chipped hearth brick, and cool morning moved over the sill.

stories.body:
# The Witchknight’s Measure

Rhoswen had two fingers against Demech's wrist when the third bell rang.

The sound meant the pulse-thorn had crossed their lane. She knew that before she looked up. A pale barb quivered in the straw patient behind them, deep enough that its black sap smoked against the stuffing. Rhoswen's iron lay in the mud where she had dropped it.

Under her other hand, the cut on Demech's forearm had closed to a shining pink seam.

"Dead," Instructor Fremda said.

Demech, who was sitting in a puddle and very much alive, glanced over his shoulder. "Which one of us?"

"Both, if the thorn was feeling industrious. Talder, release."

Rhoswen broke contact. The warmth of her pulse-work recoiled into her palm, followed by the familiar empty flutter behind her breastbone. One breath. Two. She had been told to count six before touching prepared iron again. Knowing the rule did not stop her from wanting to snatch up the bar and prove she could still raise a guard.

Fremda crouched beside Demech and inspected the sealed cut. "Clean edges. No heat trapped. Good care."

Then she rose and put a chalk stroke in the failure column.

Around them, eleven other pairs reset the intake lanes. They were healers from village rooms, river barges, noble kitchens, mining camps. A grey-haired bone-setter was digging mud out of his collar. Two young infirmary sisters argued over which of them had missed a signal. All had come through Candlemere Chapterhouse's narrow practical gate: application letters, service records, and the fees or sponsorships required for twenty-four months of training, longer when a gate had to be repeated.

Rhoswen picked up her iron. It was a plain forearm-length bar wrapped in cord, heavy enough to punish a lazy wrist. "He was bleeding."

"He was complaining, too," Fremda said. "Neither is a mortal sign."

"I wasn't complaining," Demech said. "I was reporting with feeling."

Fremda pointed at the lane. "Reset. Talder repeats after supper."

"Clinic duty is after supper."

"Then you repeat after clinic duty."

That was Rhoswen's first morning of witchknight training.

By the eighth morning, the skin beneath her pack straps had rubbed raw. By the twelfth, she could fall in a breastplate without putting out a hand and breaking a wrist. By the twentieth, she had learned that knowing every small bone of the foot did not teach the foot where to stand.

"Your heel's wandering," Demech said.

Rhoswen kept her iron extended across the chalk lane. The captive pulse-thorn rustled behind its wicker screen, seeking the warm beat of the trainees beyond it. Her guard made the bar hum against her palm. "My heel is attached."

"That's not the same as loyal."

He nudged the back of her boot with his own. Demech had spent six years carrying survey chains through upland bogs before training as a field healer. He could settle a load on his hips as if he had been born with pack straps. His descriptions of injuries, however, were criminal.

"Bend the rope behind your knee," he said.

"There is no rope behind my knee."

"The long bit."

"There are several long bits."

The thorn struck the guard. Iron rang. Rhoswen's straight knee took the force, and she skidded across both chalk lines.

Demech caught her pack before she went down. "That bit. Bend it."

At dawn they marched with sandbags. Before noon they drilled stance, blade work, and falls until the breastplates bruised their hips. After the midday meal came triage lanes and switching practice. The same living current in Rhoswen could close tissue or pass through prepared iron to turn the thorn's probing pulse, but it could not do both. To change tasks she had to break contact, let the first working settle, and count six clean breaths. Switch too early and the iron gave a weak, shivering guard. Spend too much on healing and six breaths became ten, then twenty, then a hand too unsteady to hold anything.

At first she counted too fast.

"That was four," Fremda said.

"It was six."

"Again."

"You weren't counting aloud."

"I was watching you breathe."

Again meant that Demech reset the straw patient, Rhoswen checked its painted injuries, and they ran the lane from the first bell. Again meant sweat cooling inside her shirt while the chapterhouse kitchen carried the smell of onion broth across the yard. Again meant being late to equipment duty and rubbing rust from six practice bars after she had cleaned her own.

In the clinic that night, an orchard worker came in with two crushed fingertips. Rhoswen washed the hand, set the small bones, and fed warmth into the purple flesh until the man's nails regained their color. There she was quick, certain, useful. The work used the same current and none of the humiliating iron.

Her hands began to tremble as she tied the last bandage.

She tucked them under the table before Fremda, passing through with a stack of clean cloths, could see.

Fremda set the cloths down. "How many?"

"I don't need iron in here."

"How many breaths until you could?"

Rhoswen hated the question because she knew the answer. She counted while the orchard worker told Demech that a ladder had kicked him. At fourteen, her thumb stopped jumping.

Fremda made no speech. She wrote fourteen on the slate beside Rhoswen's name.

The first autumn stripped leaves from the chapterhouse lindens and leather from the trainees' palms. Winter froze the practice yard into ruts. Candlemere did not shorten the loaded marches. It issued cleats and added time for boot repair.

At the winter gate, Rhoswen and Demech carried forty pounds each up the east track, crossed a ditch, and entered the screened lanes with their breath already ragged. Snowmelt ran beneath the wicker. The pulse-thorn moved where they could not see it.

Demech took the first guard. Rhoswen dragged the weighted patient to the red marker. They exchanged positions on his raised fist: his guard held; she could prepare to take it. She counted six, set her iron, and felt the working catch.

Then a concealed hook sliced Demech's calf.

It was part of the gate, though the blood was real. He slapped his palm over the cut and said, "Surface. Still walking."

Rhoswen saw bright red leaking between his fingers. She saw dirt at the wound edge, the shortening of his step, the small pinch beside his mouth. In the village clinic she would never have left it. She planted the iron point in the snow, caught his ankle, and poured warmth into the torn flesh.

"Rhos. Enough."

The cut closed slowly. She chased the last seep. Demech swore and reached for her abandoned bar just as the first thorn struck.

She broke contact. One, two, three—

"Don't," Demech said.

She grabbed the iron on five. The guard flashed crookedly and died. Pain needled up both arms. For a moment she could not remember which marker was red.

Demech held the lane alone while she knelt in the snow, staring at her shaking fingers. He turned one strike and then another. The third caught the weighted patient's chest. The bell rang.

Afterward, Demech limped into the reconstruction room and dropped his wet glove on the table.

"I said surface."

"You also said rope for a tendon yesterday."

"I know my own blood."

"You couldn't see the cut."

"Neither could you. Not after you put your head down."

Fremda laid three pieces of chalk beside the glove. She did not tell them to be quiet. She waited until they noticed her waiting.

"Talder," she said, "what could he do?"

Rhoswen looked at the floor plan scratched into the tabletop. "Walk. Hold pressure. Guard, if he had to."

"Demech, what could she do after the healing?"

He glanced at Rhoswen's hands. The tremor had stopped, but she had folded them in her lap. "Nothing useful for twenty breaths."

"Seventeen," Rhoswen said.

"Delightful."

Fremda pushed the chalk toward them. "Mark where each of you spent the other."

They rebuilt the failure one decision at a time: the missed signal, the lowered iron, the wound that could have waited, the early switch that bought neither healing nor guard. By the time they finished, the evening lamps had been lit.

Rhoswen's winter score put her into the standard extra quarter. Eleven names were posted with hers. Demech passed the gate, though not highly enough to leave their practice group.

"You can request another partner," she told him.

He was scraping dried mud from his boots with a spoon he had stolen from the dining hall. "I can also request roast duck on rest days."

"I'm serious."

"So is the duck situation. Hold this."

He handed her a boot and went on scraping. She held it.

Spring training began with rain blowing sideways across the yard. Their hand signals, careful indoors, dissolved in it. Rhoswen tapped two fingers to her wrist to mean *capacity falling*; Demech thought she meant *injury here* and dropped his guard to look. He swept one arm low to warn of bad ground; she mistook it for permission to move the patient. The bell rang twice in one run.

Fremda made them stand at opposite ends of the lane while water streamed from their chins.

"Again," she called.

"Which part?" Demech called back.

"The part where neither of you understood anything."

They reduced the signals until no gesture needed fingers or subtlety. A fist held high meant *I hold the guard*. A flat palm meant *wait where you are*. An arm chopped once across the body meant *switch*. For a timed cover, each open-handed strike against the chest promised five safe breaths, where the movement remained visible through rain. Demech disliked losing his low sweep, so Rhoswen made him shout about holes like everyone else.

She learned his kind of work in return. They carried sacks, practice bodies, and eventually each other. Demech shifted her stance by inches, made her settle weight over the back foot, and taught her to rise under a loaded shoulder without wasting her legs in the first ten steps. Rhoswen taught him the difference between blood that looked frightening and blood that stole strength. He continued to call tendons ropes when he wanted to annoy her, which was often.

The extra quarter was not a revelation. It was eighty-three mornings, thirteen split boot seams, and a pale groove worn into the cord of her iron. Rhoswen worked clinic shifts after drills. She mended buckles because damaged gear waited for no one's exhaustion. She failed the ice carry, passed it on the second attempt, then failed the dusk switch by one breath. Some days improvement meant only that Fremda corrected her twice instead of five times.

On the last rain gate, Demech cut his palm. Rhoswen saw the blood, judged the grip still sound, and kept her iron up. He guarded after her switch. They moved the patient together. At the finish his glove was red.

She reached for it as soon as the lane closed.

"Now," Demech said, and gave her the hand.

Fremda moved Rhoswen's name out of the extra-quarter column. She ranked seventh in a group of twelve.

During the second year, the corrections grew farther apart. That did not make the days shorter. Rhoswen walked patrol roads with senior pairs, cleaned iron after wet clearings, restocked clinic drawers, and reported every time her recovery count changed. Once, beside a flooded cart track, she held a guard while another healer reduced a carter's shoulder. The man's shouting made every part of her want to turn. She watched the thorn hedge instead. Once she felt the first flutter of overdraw at five breaths and passed the iron to Demech without pretending she had six. Once he missed a swelling beneath a patient's ear, and she made him examine it again without calling him a fool until after supper.

That summer Demech earned an extra quarter of his own by choosing a fast route through a flooded-ground gate and stranding both bearers knee-deep. He blamed a clump of reeds until the next morning, then redrew the route.

Their pack weights rose. Their times did not always improve. The work became less dramatic as they became better at it.

In their twenty-seventh month, Rhoswen and Demech were assigned the autumn capstone together.

The live clearing lay below the chapterhouse wall, where a pulse-thorn had rooted into an abandoned stone channel. Every autumn group worked a piece of it under supervision. Their task was ordinary: enter behind Fremda's outer guard, reach the channel marker, remove a weighted casualty, and clear the lane. Candidates had rung the withdrawal bell before. Candidates had repeated the capstone the following season. The names of both sorts were posted in the same square hand.

Rain had softened the bank to brown paste. Demech tested it with his heel. "Left side will go."

"Then don't use it," Fremda said.

"I enjoy these advanced lessons."

The first section went cleanly. Fremda held the thorn's outer pulse while Rhoswen and Demech moved inside it. He called the footing; she took the forward guard. Iron beat against her palm in steady, unpleasant blows. At the marker they found the weighted figure half under a root shelf.

Demech crouched to rig the carry strap.

The bank went anyway.

Mud and stone struck Rhoswen's hip. Her knee buckled, but the stance Demech had rebuilt for two years gave backward instead of sideways. She kept the iron between them and the thorn. When she could see again, Demech lay waist-deep in the collapsed channel. A slab pinned his left boot. Blood darkened his trouser leg above it.

Beyond the wicker screens, someone reached for the withdrawal bell.

"Wait," Fremda said. She had both hands locked around her own iron, holding back the outer growth. "Report."

Demech tried to pull free. His face changed. "Can't move the foot. Cut above the knee. Ground's still sliding."

Rhoswen's body had already chosen to go to him. She stopped it. The thorn struck. She bent the rope behind her knee—the absurd phrase arrived in Demech's voice—and let the force run through her stance into the bank.

"Pressure on the cut," she said.

"Already doing it."

"Harder."

"There, you've cured me."

The joke came too quickly. His next breath ended halfway.

Rhoswen looked without lowering the iron. The blood spread steadily but did not leap with his pulse. His skin held its color. He could answer, press the wound, and complain. Treatable. Not first.

The channel wall shifted again. Demech slapped a flat palm toward her: wait. Then he pointed above his trapped boot. "Slab's wedged under the root. Lift me wrong, it rolls inward. Take the dirt on my right."

She obeyed his terrain read. One-handed, still guarding, she kicked and scraped a shelf beside his hip. The thorn battered her iron. The hum climbed into her teeth.

Fremda raised a fist: she held the outer guard. Then she struck an open hand against her chest four times.

Twenty safe breaths of cover.

Rhoswen chopped her forearm once. *Switch.* Fremda's answering fist stayed high.

Rhoswen broke contact with the iron and counted. The thorn recoiled from Fremda's widened guard. One breath: she dropped beside Demech. Two: she cut his trouser cloth open. Three: no spurting vessel, no backward bend in the knee. Four: his boot remained trapped, but his toes moved. Five. Six.

Only then did she put both hands above the cut and send pulse-work into him.

Warmth drove down her arms. Torn tissue drew together under her palms, not cleanly, not completely. Demech hissed and tried to twist away.

"Still," she said.

"Stone's moving."

She felt it through her knees. She stopped healing before the wound closed. Enough to slow the loss. Enough for the carry. She took her hands away.

Fremda had six breaths left.

Rhoswen wanted the iron. She made herself wait. One. Mud slipped under her boot. Two. Demech's head sagged, then lifted. Three. Fremda's shoulders shook. Four. The thorn pressed her guard inward. Five.

On six, Rhoswen closed her hand around prepared iron. The current caught without a stutter. She set her back foot and raised the guard.

Fremda released hers, stumbled once, and pointed to Demech.

"Slab," Rhoswen said.

Demech wiped rain from his eyes. His answer came in pieces. "Don't lift. Dig the heel. Pull me toward you when it drops."

Rhoswen dug while he kept pressure on his leg. Fremda, outside the inner lane now, drove an iron spike into the firm side of the bank and hooked their carry line around it. Demech counted the small movements of the slab. On his third count it settled away from his boot.

Rhoswen hauled him free.

There was no graceful way to shoulder a wet man in armor. He knocked his chin against her helmet and called her something muffled. She got beneath his right arm, settled his weight over her hips as they had practiced with sacks and bodies and each other, and rose without spending her legs at once. The weighted figure stayed under the root shelf. The exercise had ended when the bank fell; now they had a real casualty to extract.

Fremda took the outer line. Rhoswen kept her iron forward in one hand and Demech upright with the other. Step, set, receive the strike. Step, set, breathe. His weight dragged at the repaired seam in her shoulder strap. The wound seeped against her side. It could seep for twelve more steps; his hand still pressed it, and his answers stayed clear. Rhoswen left it alone and kept the guard. Demech was conscious. Demech was helping. Demech was not the only life in the lane.

At the steep patch he lifted two fingers against his chest.

"Two breaths?" she said.

"Two steps. I can give you two."

He pushed. Fremda pulled the line. Rhoswen held the guard, and together they brought Demech across the final marker before the thorn struck again.

The clearing bell rang once.

For several breaths nobody moved. Then Fremda lowered her iron and said, "Lane clear. Healer, you may fuss now."

Demech sagged onto the grass. "She's been saving it up."

Rhoswen knelt and put her hands to his leg.

Demech spent six days in the chapterhouse clinic and another three weeks on light duty. The slab had cracked two bones in his foot. The wound above his knee needed stitching after Rhoswen's field closure was opened and cleaned. None of this made the notice board.

The capstone results did. Three candidates qualified. One had withdrawn and would repeat in spring. Rhoswen's name appeared between two others in the same square hand Fremda used for clinic inventories.

Fremda called her into the equipment room, where rain ticked on the narrow windows and forty iron bars waited for oil.

"Why didn't you heal him when the bank fell?" Fremda asked.

Rhoswen had answered versions of the question for twenty-seven months. This time she did not search for the answer Fremda wanted. "He could hold pressure. You couldn't hold both growths for long. I needed the lane before he needed me."

"And after?"

"I stopped when he could be carried."

Fremda looked at her hands. They were steady. "Good."

She signed the qualification line and passed the page across.

Rhoswen read it twice. There was no commendation attached, no mention of the bank, no new rank beyond the one she had trained for. The form assigned her to an ordinary road rotation with a senior witchknight and gave the date of her first refresher gate.

When she came out, Demech was waiting on a bench with his foot splinted and her healer's bag beside him.

"Well?" he asked.

Rhoswen handed him the form.

He studied it. "Refresher in twelve weeks. They must suspect you've forgotten everything."

"Give me your foot."

"It's attached."

"That isn't the same as loyal."

He laughed, then winced and surrendered the splint for inspection. Rhoswen set her iron within reach, opened the healer's bag, and began.

stories.body:
# The Sky Remembers Us

Seyathi learned the weight of her own arm while she was falling.

It was an ordinary weight. That was the obscenity of it. Her shoulder pulled against its socket; blood ran from her palm to her wrist because the world had remembered which way down was. Around her, the Ithrom Array came apart in black ribs and white-hot bolts. The shattered junction had once joined six immensities. Now not one spark hid in the wreckage. Not one dead circuit dreamed. Grace did not gather beneath Seyathi's skin, or in her name, or in the mouths of anyone who might still have worshipped her.

Faris had made his last account exact.

No more magic.

He fell below her, turning slowly among pieces of the Array. His face appeared, vanished behind a spinning plate, appeared again. Seyathi wanted to strike him. She wanted him to see what he had done. She wanted, with a fury too mortal to sort into its separate hungers, not to die alone beside the person who had betrayed everything in order to end it.

She reached.

Faris saw. For an instant he only watched her hand come through the glare. Then his own arm lifted. Perhaps he meant to take it. Perhaps he meant to apologize, or prevent one last collision, or merely meet the final fact with another human fact. Whatever he meant remained inside him. Their fingertips stayed a hand's breadth apart as the wreck turned between them.

They struck the earth. They died. Nothing rose from them.

But light had already touched their faces and their reaching hands. Light required no spell. It left Ithrom at the oldest speed there was, carrying surfaces, angles, the red of blood, the distance between two sets of fingers. It carried no mind and offered no judgment. It could not forgive Faris, restore Seyathi, or tuck one grain of power beneath the ruins for a luckier age.

It went outward.

Stars were born behind it. Stars failed ahead of it. On the world it had left, mountains wore down, continents shouldered into new shapes, languages filled the air and disappeared from it. The crater of Ithrom sank, rose, split, and weathered into a high black plain. Children played in the hollows where impossible engines had once decided the fate of civilizations. They found no magic there.

The light went farther than the name of light.

At last it met a sky that was not space.

* * *

Keshen woke with someone else's fall burning above her bed.

Her realm had no stars. Its people lived along inward folds, where a ceiling might become a road if two living minds agreed on the turn, and a doorway could bring a beloved room near when the people on both sides welcomed the visit. Every person cast several shadows, one for each direction in which they might willingly be approached. The pale reach overhead was not a roof and not an emptiness. It was the limit beyond which their magic found no living answer.

Now two strangers tumbled across that limit.

Keshen flung herself upright. One of the hanging sleep-cloths wrapped her ankle, and she hit the floor on both palms. The image above her did not react. A dark-haired figure reached down. Another reached up. Wreckage revolved soundlessly between them.

"Don't," said her oldest friend from the next sleeping hollow.

Keshen glanced back. "They're falling."

"They have been falling since before your grandmother's grandmother learned to turn a corner. Look at the light."

"That is not an argument."

"It is if you know anything about light."

Keshen did not, particularly. She knew distance. She knew the small courtesy by which a path asked both its ends before becoming short. She knew how to feel for a living presence through six folded rooms and how to stop at the first recoil. She knew that the sky had never answered anyone.

The falling woman looked directly at her.

Keshen reached.

She gathered the living brightness from her muscles and laid it against the boundary, trying to bring the stranger one arm-length nearer. The force returned at once. Her room lurched. The doorway flattened to a shining line; the next hollow bulged close enough for her friend's startled face to press out of empty air. One of Keshen's three shadows tore loose from her heels and climbed the wall without her.

The falling figures remained where they were.

Keshen released the reach. Distance slammed back. She tasted blood.

Her friend crawled through the restored doorway and took Keshen by the chin, turning her face toward the ordinary light that grew from their living walls. "How many fingers?"

"On which hand?"

"Good. Annoying is good."

Above them, the ancient wreckage turned. But beyond the two falling people, behind layers of darkness the old light had never contained, another face appeared.

Alive. Round-cheeked, wide-eyed, hair whipping in a wind Keshen could not feel.

The stranger stared back.

* * *

"You promised we were only looking," Miraq said.

Dalo kept one hand on the broken pillar and leaned farther over the drop. "We are looking."

"Your knees are past the edge."

"My eyes are attached to them."

"That is worse, Dalo. That makes the whole arrangement worse."

The wind worried at their coats and pushed grit over the black plain. By daylight the footprint of the Ithrom Array was nothing but fused gullies, half-buried arches, and stone that rang dully under a hammer. No one had ever found so much as a warm patch among it. Tonight, however, a brightness hung over the deepest chasm, too broad for a star and too still for a fire in the upper air.

Dalo had dragged Miraq three days from home to see it. She had said there would be a trail. There had not been a trail for the last half-day. She had said the climb was easy. The sole of Miraq's left boot was tied on with Dalo's scarf. She had also said, repeatedly, that the old family tale put the returning light directly above Ithrom's northern edge.

On that point, infuriatingly, she had been right.

Within the brightness, two people fell forever through a storm of metal.

Miraq stopped complaining.

Dalo knew the figures. Not their faces, not truly, but the reach between them. Their grandmother had called it the sky's memory and drawn it in stove ash while winter rattled the shutters: the mortal goddess and the person who ended all magic, falling from the broken place after the six great powers went dark. She had always put the hands closer together than this. A story-teller's mercy.

"Faris," Dalo whispered. "And Seyathi."

"Or two people who look like the story because the story came from this."

"Could you wait one breath before correcting me?"

"I did. You used it to name dead people in the sky."

The image widened. Behind the fall lay something with no proper depth: pale surfaces curving inward, doorways suspended on different planes, living lights moving like slow breath. A woman knelt there with blood beneath her nose. She had one hand raised.

Dalo raised hers.

Nothing happened. The wind did not change. The black stones did not wake. No force gathered in her arm. She was as magicless as every person born since Faris's last words, and the dead earth beneath her was empty all the way down.

The woman beyond the brightness moved her fingers.

Dalo waved.

The woman folded both arms across her chest.

"I think you offended her," Miraq said.

"With a wave?"

"You have more range than you know."

Dalo tried pointing to herself, then to the woman. The stranger touched her own chest and made a shape with both hands, drawing them apart, then together. The air above the crater stretched. For one sickening instant, Dalo saw the stranger's hand near enough to show pale scars across the knuckles, while the woman's face receded to the size of a moon.

Then the whole vision snapped small. On the far side, one of the woman's shadows had climbed away from her body. She staggered after it and caught herself against the living wall.

Dalo's excitement went cold.

"She did that," Miraq said.

"I saw."

"It hurt her."

"I saw."

"You say that in the same voice you use when you're about to touch something."

Dalo lowered her hand. "I am not about to touch the sky."

Miraq looked pointedly at her knees, still over the edge.

She edged back.

Across the impossible distance, the stranger sat with another person beside her. They argued. Dalo could hear no sound, but the second person jabbed a finger at the loose shadow, then at the sky, then mimed lying down with such fierce exaggeration that Miraq barked a laugh.

The seated woman saw him. Her mouth opened. Her shoulders shook.

The loose shadow stopped climbing.

"Well," Dalo said. "Your medical value is established."

"My what?"

"You made her laugh."

"I was laughing at her friend."

"Try explaining that with your hands."

Miraq put both of his in his pockets.

* * *

By the time the first rim of dawn should have appeared, night covered half the world and the strange brightness covered all of its sky.
