“She pulled me clear,” the daughter said. Her voice shook now that nobody was shooting. “She got hit doing it.”

Her father considered Elspeth across the ruined tile. Then he lifted two fingers. His people lowered their guns.

“This settles tonight,” he said. “Not the road your car took.”

“I know.”

He turned to his daughter and began giving slow instructions about the car, the doctor, her brother.

The ward captain stood carefully. Blood from his dead officer had reached the knees of his trousers. “The perimeter will remain while we conduct an orderly disengagement.”

Elspeth held out her hand.

He stared at it.

“Your phone.”

“That is official property.”

“Then use it. Cancel the raid.”

He glanced at the deployment paper, at the dead men belonging to both houses, at the underboss's surviving loyalists facedown by the gallery stairs. His next radio call contained provisional assessments, revised thresholds, and resource concerns. It took him ninety seconds to say the operation was over.

Outside, engines started. One by one, the police vehicles moved away without entering.

The driver pointed at the man who had dropped his gun. He was on his knees, staring at the bodies. “Him?”

Elspeth had to follow her finger twice before she understood.

“He froze,” Elspeth said. “He didn't turn.”

“And tomorrow?”

“He comes back without a gun.”

The driver nodded and gave the man a strip of cloth for somebody else's wound.

Elspeth surveyed what remained. Four active traitors lay dead. Two had surrendered. One had escaped through the kitchen and would keep running until fear or hunger made his next decision. Her runner was still back in her private room, cooling on the blood-soaked boards. The man with the chest wound had stopped breathing during the fight. The lieutenant sagged against the east door, upright only because the metal bar held him.

“Get the wounded into cars,” she said. “Then go back for the runner.”

Men older than her moved. The lieutenant moved first.

stories.title: The Fourth Blood
stories.prompt: You're a sorcerer in the mountains, trying to unlock the secret of immortality thru blood magic. Instead, you're starting to figure out that humans have blood types.
stories.body:
# The Fourth Blood

The healer brought the last case up the mountain six days before the first snow, though I had assured her the snow was three weeks away.

She set it on my bench and kept both hands on the lid. Meltwater darkened the shoulders of her wool coat. Behind her, through the tower’s western slit, clouds had swallowed the high pass where my weather rods stood pointing at a sky they could measure but not persuade.

“Twenty-eight,” she said. “Sealed separately. The marks match the ledger.”

I reached for the case. She did not release it.

“And?”

“And you read the permissions back to me.”

The convergence frame occupied most of the room: four rings of silver wire around an empty stone basin, with a place for each vessel along the outer rim. It looked magnificent. It did nothing. The wire could hold a shape I gave it; the stone could keep a working from spilling; the samples in their glass were only samples. Without my hand on the pulse plate, every costly piece was as magical as a spoon.

I tapped the ledger. “They permit comparison, joining in the final pattern, and retention until the thaw.”

“Some permit all three. Five permit comparison only. Two want what remains returned before the pass closes.”

“Then those two will not be retained.”

“Say the rest.”

The clouds lowered behind her. I had spent nine years approaching this morning: nine years proving that age was an error of repetition, that a living pattern frayed because it renewed itself alone. Braid enough human continuance together, I believed, and no single failure could end the whole. A rope survived the breaking of a fiber. A river did not die when one spring went dry. My own blood-linked trials had held for minutes, then hours, then one full turning of the moon.

The ledger was not the work. The ledger was what people placed between the work and its completion.

“Nothing enters a body,” I said. “Nothing treats an illness. No sample outside its permission. I supply and end the working.”

Only then did she let go.

“Soup’s in the lower pot,” she said. “You look thin.”

“Immortality will correct that.”

“Eat before you test it.”

She hung her coat beside the stove, inspected the salt crock, and told me the mule would make only one more trip if the eastern shelf iced over. I was already fitting the separately sealed vessels into their numbered rests. She had made the marks deliberately dull: squares, bars, dots, no sign of who had been strong, sick, young, old, related, or well fed. The human particulars I considered noise had been removed for me.

Nothing in the first comparison behaved as blood ought to have behaved.

I set my palm to the pulse plate. The frame waited through one beat of my heart and took the second. Pale light moved outward from my hand, not from the glass, and touched two vessels at once. I meant the light to rise into a single steady loop, the smallest proof that separate lives could support one pattern without losing their difference.

The loop held.

I chose a third vessel. The light went out.

Not dimmed. Not weakened. Extinguished back to my palm so quickly that my wrist struck the edge of the bench.

The healer looked up from the ledger. “Stop.”

“A flaw in the channel.”

“Your hand is shaking.”

“Because the return surprised me.” I moved the vessel to another rest and began again. My pulse entered the silver. Two samples held the loop; the third erased it. When I exchanged the third for a fourth, the light returned, steadier than before.

The healer came beside me. “Which permission?”

I read the mark twice before I found it on the page. “Comparison and final joining.”

“Not whatever you decide this has become.”

“It has become a correction.”

“Then correct inside the boundary.”

She had a talent for making a boundary sound less like a wall than a sequence of doors, each requiring its own answer. I resented it because doors delayed me. I obeyed because the case would never have come up the mountain otherwise.

By dark I had repeated the comparison with different rests, different lengths of silver, and a fresh circle drawn on the pulse plate. The frame remained blameless. So did the glass. Every shape began in the beat under my palm and ended when I lifted it. Yet the same pair held, the same third extinguished, and two others I tried divided themselves around that difference.

“Cold,” I said.

The healer was cutting yesterday’s loaf into the soup. “It’s cold in here, yes.”

“The samples. Some crossed the upper bridge after noon.”

“The marks don’t tell you which.”

“You do.”

“Not until you write down what happened before I tell you anything.”

“I know what happened.”

“Write that, then.”

The next morning I learned the extinguishing sample had arrived warm with the others. The morning after that, authorized comparisons divided recent samples and older ones into the same alliances. Hunger did not explain it. Neither did fever, recovery, the high farms, or the damp houses by the river. Each possibility had the decency to fail. The original pattern did not.

By the fourth day I had drawn three columns in my book.

I called them measures of vigor. The healer crossed out the heading.

“You cannot alter my record.”

“Then stop leaving it open while you come down for onions.”

Her rooms below the ridge smelled of steam, ash, and wet wool. Six people waited there for ordinary care. Nobody cared that I had divided human vitality into three elegant orders. They wanted dry boots, a cough quiet enough for sleep, and news of whether flour had come before the bridge washed out.

The healer carried the onions to the pantry. “There are frail people in each of your columns.”

“Frail now.”

“And strong people in each.”

“Strength is not always visible.”

She put one finger on the heading in my book. “Then this word is a guess. Cross it out.”

I followed her between shelves. “If the strongest pattern accepts the others—”

“You haven’t found strongest.”

“The first column sustains the cleanest loop.”

“With itself.”

“Purity often looks like that at first.”

A cup struck a table behind me, hard enough to spill.

The resident from the mill had been sitting near the stove with both boots wrapped in blankets. I had not seen him since the earlier charm. He was thinner. The gray under his eyes made me think of insufficient recovery, an error I nearly offered aloud.

“Don’t call it that,” he said.

“Call what?”

“Mine impure.”

“I don’t know which is yours.”

“You told her I was, after the charm.” He nodded toward the healer. “You said something in me muddied the line.”

I remembered the trial as a page of failed ratios. Three volunteers’ sealed samples had rested in separate arms of a holding frame while I supplied the charm from my own pulse. No blood had passed between anyone. The spell was meant to let one person’s strong rhythm steady another’s fatigue across a few paces. It had instead put the miller on the floor.

“That was an uncontrolled interference,” I said. “This may explain it.”

“Explain this.” He pressed two fingers beneath his ribs. “Everything pulled tight here. Then my mouth tasted like old coins, and the room kept tipping after you stopped. Is that one of your columns?”

“The charm never entered you.”

“I know where it didn’t enter.”

The healer came back carrying a heel of cheese. She did not rescue me. She set it beside his cup and waited.

I heard myself begin again, faster. “A connection need not transfer matter to impose pattern. If the joining tried to reconcile two unlike structures, the rebound would have traveled through the living source—through me—but the linked participant might experience a sympathetic—”

He pulled the blankets off his boots. “No.”

“I am answering you.”

“You’re making a longer question.” He stood, caught the table when the room moved under him, and looked at the healer. “Do I have to leave my sample up there?”

“No,” she said. “You allowed comparisons until the snow. You can withdraw that now.”

He glanced at me once. “Then I withdraw it.”

The loss was immediate and ridiculous. One vessel out of twenty-eight, yet I saw a hole in the design larger than the basin. “If it is the sample that produced the unusual result, removing it destroys the chance to understand what happened to you.”

His hand stayed on the table. “You didn’t understand it when you had it.”

“I understand more now.”

“Then tell me when it’s enough to be useful.”

He left with the cheese in his pocket. The healer watched until the outer door shut.

“Return his vessel,” she said.

“Today?”

“You have a mule going up.”

“It will disrupt the series.”

“Yes.”

There was no pleasure in her answer. That made it harder to fight.

I ate the soup cold that night. Before removing the resident’s vessel from the frame, I copied only the comparisons already permitted and performed. Then I wrapped it, sealed my copy of his withdrawal beside it, and sent it down unopened.

The fourth blood appeared two days later.

The healer had relabeled an authorized subset while I stood outside my own workroom in sleet. She changed every position and kept the key. I protested that concealment punished expertise. She said, “Good. Predict without it.”

I predicted.

The first group held only with itself. The second held in combinations that extinguished the first. The third seemed broad until one pairing exposed a clean refusal. Then there was the fourth: three vessels I had scattered among the other columns because their donors’ ages, diets, and winter health tempted different explanations. Blind, they found one another. Under my pulse, the light took a tight, low arc unlike the other loops. When I lifted my hand, it vanished. The three vessels sat in ordinary glass, dark and silent.

“Again,” I said.

The healer checked the permissions before she moved anything. “One comparison. Then you rest.”

“I’m not tired.”

“Your thumb won’t stop twitching.”

“That is not fatigue.”

“What is it?”

I put my thumb against my palm. “Revision.”

She gave me one comparison. The low arc returned.

The categories in my book stopped being a ladder. I drew them as separate circles, then struck out the circles because they suggested clean borders the evidence had not earned. One vessel still changed its apparent allegiance when compared across days. I could not decide whether it marked a fifth pattern, an error in my own control, or a distinction too fine for the spell. I wrote a question beside it and disliked the look of my handwriting.

Outside, snow covered the weather rods to their elbows.

The convergence remained scheduled for the longest night of the fortnight. I told myself the new groups did not invalidate it. A rope could carry fibers of different strength. A river accepted unlike waters. A chord required different notes. Each analogy arrived polished, obedient, and false in a slightly new way.

The frame had already shown me what difference did under pressure: the pattern did not broaden. It went dark.

Still I set every permitted vessel around the basin on the final evening. Five comparison-only samples stayed locked in the case. The withdrawn sample was gone. The remaining glass stood in its marked rests, each separate, while silver channels led toward the empty center. Activating the frame would not mix a drop, but it would pool every linked pattern inside the working and drive the whole convergence through the only living source in the room.

Me.

That had once seemed like a virtue. I would become the knot that could not be cut because every human line reinforced it. Now the frame offered another possibility: incompatible lines forced together, returning through my pulse and outward along every connection before I could release them.

Snow struck the slit in handfuls. The pass had vanished. Down in the valley, people slept under roofs already carrying winter’s weight. Some had allowed me to compare a sample. Some had allowed a final joining because I had told them it was the last step in a theory I understood.

I placed my hand above the pulse plate.

My heart beat against the silence. It was not the serene clock I had described in nine years of papers. It hurried. It skipped when I held my breath. A small animal in a locked room, throwing itself at the door.

I wanted more time. Not a noble quantity of time, not centuries dedicated to wisdom. I wanted the next morning because the next morning existed and I might not. I wanted enough years to prove I had not wasted the ones behind me. The desire was ugly only in its appetite. It was also mine.

My palm hovered until the skin cooled.

Then I lifted each vessel from the frame and put it back in the case.

The basin remained empty. The silver remained wire. Nothing woke.

Near midnight the healer came through the storm with a lantern and a sack of barley. She found me at the smaller comparison board, not the convergence frame.

“The shelf iced over,” she said. “The mule’s staying below.”

“You walked.”

“Yes.” She stamped snow from one boot, then the other. “Is it done?”

I pointed at the unopened case.

She did not praise me. “What are you doing now?”

“One comparison. The permissions allow it. The labels are still blind to me.”

“Why this one?”

The answer unfurled at once: predictive distinction, independent confirmation, the philosophy of categories as instruments rather than essences. Her face made me stop halfway through the first breath.

“Because I wrote down which pair would fail before you arrived,” I said. “If it fails, the groups explain the old result better than cold or weakness did. If it doesn’t, I write that.”

She took the ledger from her coat. “Whose permission?”

I showed her the two marks.

She checked them slowly. “Do it.”

My pulse entered the board. For a moment the light held between the vessels, and hope rose with it—mean, immediate hope that every distinction would dissolve and return my beautiful design. Then the line folded inward and went dark.

I released the board.

“It failed,” the healer said.

“It predicted.” I had to say the word twice before it came out quietly. “The kinds are stable enough to predict.”

“Kinds of what?”

I looked at the two sealed vessels. Not kinds of courage. Not measures of vigor. Not purity, longevity, or human worth. The spell had never seen a soul. It had only met a recurring difference I had been too ambitious to notice.

“Blood,” I said. “Human blood has types. At least these patterns, among these people. Perhaps more. One result still won’t hold still.”

“And the convergence?”

“Canceled.”

The word hurt more than the failed loop.

In the morning, when the resident returned to help clear the lower path, I gave him an account at the healer’s table. I began with the pattern because beginnings were where I hid.

He listened until I said *interference*.

“What happened to me?” he asked.

The healer had a list of stores open beside her. Lamp oil, two jars. Barley, enough for eight days. She left the pen lying across the page.

I tried once more. “The charm forced unlike blood patterns into one magical rhythm—”

“Mine didn’t go anywhere.”

“No. It stayed sealed. I made the link. My spell forced the rhythm. You felt the harm, and I called your blood impure because that protected my theory.”

He studied the tabletop. “Can you tell me it won’t happen again?”

“That charm won’t happen again.”

“Not what I asked.”

My explanations crowded up, each eager to be chosen. I let them go unanswered.

“No,” I said.

He rubbed the place beneath his ribs, then took his hand away. “Keep the note about what happened. Not my sample. Not my mark beside your four kinds.”

“It was returned.”

“Good.” He looked to the healer. “Is there stew?”

“At noon.”

“Then I’ll clear to the bend and come back.”

That was all he offered. It was enough to change the record.

The healer and I spent the rest of the morning separating permission from possession. Some volunteers had asked for their vessels back; those went into the traveling case. Some allowed their samples to remain through the thaw; those stayed sealed. Each person would be told privately what I had observed and what I had not. My book retained comparisons without turning the marks into names. The plan after winter was small: ask whether the patterns persisted among newly willing volunteers, seek the reason for the wandering result, and count no number of types as final. No treatment. No bodily trial. No claim that one group was safer, stronger, or more human than another.

The healer read the page twice.

“You left out immortality,” she said.

“It is no longer part of this investigation.”

“No. I mean you left out what you’re going to do about it.”

Snowlight filled the room, clean enough to make every stain on the table visible. “I don’t know.”

She closed the ledger. “All right. Bring the lamp oil.”

We went downhill together, carrying the records and the vessels due for return. Above us, the convergence frame waited in a cold room with an empty basin. It would never hold the pooled working I had built it for. I had not unlocked eternity. I had found four recurring patterns and one result that would not settle, and I had learned how quickly a grand design could make people disappear into marks.

The path was narrow under new snow. The healer went first, testing each buried edge with her staff, and told me where to place my feet. I followed with the case held level against my chest. Inside, glass clicked softly with each careful step. Beneath it, my heart kept its frightened, finite pace.

stories.title: The Weight They Never Counted
stories.prompt: You are the weakest, the absolute bottom of the barrel in your Village. After joining a trading caravan the second you turned 18 to escape the constant bullying, the Leader of the Caravan asks you how in all thats holy you are lifting and comfortably carrying 200kg without even breaking a sweat.
stories.body:
# The Weight They Never Counted

The clerk struck the adulthood chime at sunrise.

“Eighteen,” she said, turning your slate from its child side to its adult side. “Your standing is now your own concern.”

You stepped over the whitewashed boundary before the bronze note had faded.

That was how quickly the village let a person go, provided the person left owing nothing. Your bundle had been hidden under the clerk’s bench since dark: two shirts, a blanket, four heel cakes, a twist of salt, and the work token the caravan leader had given you the evening before. The token promised the cheapest position on the road. Board would be deducted. Breakage would be deducted. Wages, what remained of them, would be paid at the market.

Someone behind you laughed. “Careful with that bundle. It may be the first thing heavier than your pride.”

Another voice, less amused, called, “They’ll have you back before supper.”

The clerk had already reached for the next slate. “Ranks are settled at adulthood. Don’t block the line.”

You did not turn. The caravan waited beyond the last houses, eight wagons in the pale dust, their canvas covers damp with dawn. The leader stood beside the rear wagon checking tokens against a wax board. She took yours, pressed her thumbnail into its edge, and pointed toward a shovel lashed beneath the driver’s seat.

“Road hand. Dung, firewood, water, whatever the crew won’t stop to do. You asked for the low rate.”

“Yes. It’s fine.”

“Boots?”

You lifted one foot. The soles had been patched twice.

She looked at them without comment. “Walk near the rear. If a driver calls, answer. If you don’t know, say so before you touch anything.”

The lead teamster snapped two fingers in the air. Harness chains tightened, wheels creaked, and the village began sliding away behind a screen of road dust. You kept waiting for someone to call you back on a rule you had missed. Nobody did.

By noon, the houses were gone.

* * *

The rut looked shallow until the sixth wagon put its left wheels into it. Mud swallowed the rims. The mules leaned, traces humming, while the wheels turned in place and painted themselves brown.

“Hold them,” the teamster called. “No whip. They’ve given all the pull they’ve got.”

The loader ducked under the rear canvas and began naming what had to come off. “Two grain. Tool chest. Both scale blocks. Keep the lamp crate where it is.”

You climbed onto the bed because the other road hand had gone for branches. The scale blocks sat against the tailboard, squat iron shapes with lifting loops, each stamped 100 kg beneath a seal. The loader wrestled a grain sack onto one shoulder.

“Blocks take two each,” he said. “Wait for hands.”

The wheels sank another finger. Somebody shouted for haste. You took one loop in each hand, straightened, and stepped down.

The weight settled through your shoulders and hips, even and quiet. Less awkward than the village water yoke, because the blocks did not slosh. You carried them twenty paces to the firm verge and set them on two flat stones so their seals stayed out of the mud.

When you stood, the caravan leader was looking at your hands.

“How in all that’s holy can you lift and comfortably carry two hundred kilograms without sweating?”

Every nearby sound seemed to make room for the question: the mules blowing, a wheelwright hammering a branch under the rim, the loader’s sack settling against the road.

You checked the blocks. Both marks did say one hundred. Perhaps the seals were false. Perhaps you had moved the wrong things. “They’re balanced.”

“They’re two hundred kilograms.”

“Yes, but only just.”

“Only just what?”

You searched her face for the joke’s direction. “Only just carrying. I couldn’t run with them.”

The loader lowered his sack. “I couldn’t stand up with one.”

“I’m not very strong,” you said. It came out too fast. “At home, I mean. I’m the weakest there.”

The other road hand returned dragging brush. He stopped, saw everybody stopped, and said, “Are we freeing this wheel or holding a funeral?”

The leader’s attention snapped back to the wagon. “Freeing it. Grain to the verge. Crib the right rear before we pull. You”—she pointed at you—“no more blocks until I check the marks.”

The order felt like the beginning of a punishment. You obeyed it with relief.

The seals proved sound. After the wagon came out, the clerk cleaned the blocks and compared them against the cargo papers. Two hundred kilograms, no mistake. For the rest of the afternoon, nobody asked you to lift anything heavier than sticks. That was worse than being laughed at. Laughter told you the rules. Silence kept changing them.

At camp, the leader called you behind the supply wagon. The loader came too, carrying a portable beam scale and three slings.

“Private,” the leader said when the cook craned her head from the fire. “Unless we discover an appetite. Then it becomes your problem.”

“Every appetite becomes my problem,” the cook said. “That’s why none of you die ignorant of it.”

The canvas screened you from the rest of the crew. The leader inspected your palms, asked where old calluses came from, counted your pulse, then made you lift nothing at all until she had looked inside your boots.

“Soles are thin,” she said.

“They’re still usable.”

“That wasn’t my question. Any pain?”

“Not much.”

“That means some.”

“The left heel rubs.”

The loader grunted. “A bad foot drops good cargo. We pad it before testing.”

He cut felt for your heel, then rigged a broad yoke with equal slings. They began with fifty kilograms. You lifted it. The leader watched your knees and breathing, not your face.

“Walk to the ash tree and back.”

You did.

At one hundred, the yoke felt worth noticing. At one hundred sixty, your soles pressed hard enough to read each pebble through the leather. At two hundred, the familiar deep warmth began along your thighs and lower back, the warmth of carrying grain jars from the communal storehouse. You could have gone farther. You did not volunteer that.

“Pulse up, but not much,” the leader said. “Breath even. Any strain?”

“A little, maybe.”

“Where?”

You indicated the yoke edge against your shoulder.

The loader slipped two fingers beneath it. “Harness problem. Not body.”

They added twenty kilograms. Your steps shortened. At twenty more, something pulled behind your right knee, faint as a thread catching on a nail.

“Stop,” you said.

The loader had the sling down before you finished the word.

The leader wrote on her wax board. “Good. What changes it?”

“Uneven sides. Soft ground. Anything that moves inside its container.”

“Distance?”

“I don’t know in road lengths. At home, from the lower fields to the storehouse. Then food.”

“How much food?”

You described two morning bowls, bread in the fields, the noon pot, nuts or fat in the afternoon, and broth salted until a spoon nearly stood in it. The loader stopped coiling the sling.

“That’s for everyone?” he asked.

“Most adults take more. I didn’t earn the full field share.”

The leader made another mark. “What did everyone carry?”

“The usual things. Water jars. Stone baskets. Grain. The others carried more.”

“How much more?”

You gave her the village ranks because there was no safer answer. At the bottom stood your name, though you did not say it. Above it began capacities that would have required teams anywhere else on the road.

The cook pushed through the canvas with a bowl and your four heel cakes in one hand. “These were all you brought?”

“They last if you soak them.”

“For half a day.” She set down a bowl filled to the rim. “Eat. Then another.”

“It can come from my wages.”

“It will come from somebody’s figures. Right now it’s coming from my pot.”

The leader fetched a waterproof packet from her chest. Between route permits and faded toll schedules lay a copied page, the letters crowded and patched by several different hands. She read only fragments aloud: hill populations fitted for sustained freight, dense bones, layered load-bearing tissue, high requirements for food, water, salt, and recovery. The original survey had been found broken. The copy did not say who had changed those people, or when, or whether they had agreed. Two later copyists had argued in the margins over whether the old word meant bred, built, or repaired.

“Does your village teach any of this?” the leader asked.

“We’re told our backs are good because our habits are good.”

The loader snorted.

“And yours?” she asked.

“Mine isn’t. Not there.”

The leader folded the page. “Here, two hundred kilograms moves without four wages. It also tears through our rations and gives us one worker whose safe limits we don’t know. That’s not a miracle. It’s an unpriced risk.”

The words should have disappointed you. Instead, they gave the strange fact edges. Risks could be measured. Prices could be written down.

You scraped the bowl clean. “Could we measure it properly? If it’s not too much delay.”

“At first light,” she said. “Tonight you rest.”

* * *

The test at first light ended with a working number lower than what you could lift.

On level, packed ground, with matched slings and a loader watching, you carried two hundred kilograms for two hundred paces. At two hundred forty, the pull returned behind your knee. When the loader suspended a half-filled water cask at one side, you stopped at eighty. The water struck the barrel wall after each step and dragged your balance after it.

“There,” the loader said. “Half a cask and your stride’s gone. That sling needs a second belly-band.”

The wheelwright, passing with an oiled hub pin, glanced at the yoke. “Put that much in the wrong quarter of a bed and you’ll bow the axle. I’ll leave the whole wagon for you to carry.”

The teamster heard and called from the picket line, “And don’t make the mules match your pace. They get the hill they get.”

The cook handed the leader a tally of meal measures. “This is the number you forgot.”

The leader studied all four contributions. “One hundred eighty for ordinary flat-road assignments. Two hundred only when the loader clears ground and rigging. No catching, no rolling loads, no live animals, no tilted beds. We revise after a week.”

“That sounds generous,” you said.

“It’s cautious.”

“I meant the work.”

“Work isn’t a favor. Neither is pay.” She turned to the clerk. “Price porter rate, additional ration, salt, and boot leather. Show deductions separately.”

The clerk’s mouth tightened at the board. “The rate for four hands assumes four hands can split.”

“Then price one hand and a required spotter.”

“That saves less.”

“Write what it saves, not what you hoped it would save.”

The loader took apart the test sling because the stitching at one corner was wrong. The cook demanded her measuring cup back. You ate a third breakfast portion and fell asleep against a wheel before the harness bells rang.

For the next four days, the caravan taught you all the ways weight could become somebody else’s problem.

The loader taught you to distrust a neat stack. He rapped crates and listened, checked seals for damp, and rejected rope that looked strong but had gone furry between its twists. His instructions came in clipped pairs. “Loop high. Pull low. Again.” When you apologized, he usually answered, “Again.”

The teamster cared less about cargo weight than where it made the animals work. “Hear that breathing?” she asked on a long rise. “That’s the pace. Not the schedule.” She would postpone a wagon to cool a mule, then curse for ten minutes when anyone delayed the same wagon through carelessness.

The wheelwright spoke to wheels as if they were defendants. “You’ve been overloaded right rear,” he told a hub. “Don’t deny it.” To you he said, “A road leans even when your eyes don’t. Check the gap above the springs.”

The clerk let numbers keep their full sharpness. “Gross is not freight. Freight is not chargeable freight. If you sign the wrong one, hunger will not improve the arithmetic.”

You said yes to all of them.

Yes, you could hold the axle while the wheelwright set a pin. Yes, you could move two flour chests after unloading your assigned copper. Yes, you could fetch water before eating. Yes, you could stand in place while the loader fetched a better strap. The tasks were each small compared with what people at home demanded, and every request sounded like another day’s permission to stay.

On the fourth evening, the cook found you beside the water wagon rubbing salt into your gums from the empty twist you had brought from the village.

“You missed the noon pot,” she said.

“There was axle work.”

“The axle did not eat your portion. Somebody else did.”

“That’s all right.”

“Not to my count.” She shoved bread folded around cold beans into your hand. “Tomorrow, answer me when I call. I don’t chase freight.”

The next morning your right knee had stiffened, and the patched heel had opened into a raw crescent. The leader saw the shorter step before you reached the wagons.

“Report.”

“It’s not bad. I can still carry.”

“That is not a report.”

Under her questions, the missed meal, extra lifts, and soreness came out in scraps. Your answers shortened as her wax stylus cut deeper lines.

“Who assigned the extra work?”

“No one exactly.”

“Then who accepted it?”

You looked at the board.

The loader arrived with a sling over one shoulder. “Not loading them today.”

“I could do a lighter—”

“No.” He pointed toward the clerk’s seat. “Copy the third and fourth wagon columns. No lifting.”

The leader changed the roster. It cost the caravan time. The other road hand carried your ordinary share and did not pretend to be pleased about it. At noon he dropped beside you, accepted his second bowl, and said, “If you volunteer me into this again, I’ll hide your boots.”

“Sorry.”

“Eat.”

You did.

* * *

The road on the seventh morning narrowed along a slanted shelf of clay. Rain had passed in the night, leaving the high-side drainage strip sticky while the lower wheel track shone hard and wet. The wheelwright walked ahead prodding the surface with an iron rod.

The fifth wagon’s uphill wheel broke through the crust over a drainage hollow.

The bed tilted. Harness snapped tight. Inside the canvas, something heavy slid and struck the sideboards hard enough to bow them.

“Hold the team!” the teamster shouted.

“Uphill side clear,” the loader called. “Nobody beside the lean.”

You were behind the wagon, clear of the sideboard but close enough to see the uphill end of the rear frame dropping. The wheelwright thrust a crib block beneath it, but the block skated in mud.

“Shoulder here,” he said. “Steady only.”

You set your back beneath the frame and took the corner’s weight. It was not two hundred kilograms; it was a changing fraction of wagon, cargo, and slope. For one breath it pressed cleanly down. Then something rolled inside. The force twisted across your spine.

The loader reached for the rear ties.

“No,” you said.

He stopped.

The old reflex tried to finish the sentence with an apology. Another object shifted against the sideboard.

“Don’t open that. It’s moving into the uphill board.”

The leader came up behind you, her boots sinking at the heels. “How long can you hold?”

“I can’t. Not if it moves again.”

“Then we set it down. Wheelwright?”

“Need two blocks under the rear frame, one broad pad under the buried hub. I can’t place the pad while it’s settling.”

The clerk had abandoned her seat with the manifest hugged beneath her coat. You had copied that wagon’s column the day before: copper coils high at the rear, sacks of meal along the center, lamp crates forward, two half-filled oil casks wrongly returned to the uphill rail after inspection.

“The oil casks are what rolled,” you said. “Rear, uphill side.”

The loader swore once. “They were meant to be wedged.”

“Can we take the copper out through the downhill flap first? It’s high now. Then pass meal sacks downhill for ballast. The casks stay shut until the bed is on blocks.”

The leader looked to the loader.

He was already reaching across the raised side for the cover ties. “That gives me a safe opening.”

“Teamster?”

“I can slack the rear pair. Leaders stay braced.”

“Wheelwright?”

“If steady means steady.”

The leader pointed, assigning hands. The cross-talk collapsed into work calls.

“Copper coming.”

“Hands high.”

“Block seated.”

“Trace slack.”

“Meal downhill.”

Mud squeezed under your boots. Your shoulder trembled, not from the clean downward weight but from small corrections as the crew removed it in pieces. When the second crib block seated, the wheelwright slapped the frame twice.

“Lower.”

You bent slowly. The wagon came to rest on wood instead of your back.

The loader made everyone stand clear while he opened the rear and wedged the oil casks. The teamster walked both mules for cuts. The clerk crossed out a delivery estimate. The leader sent you to the cook for salt broth, then stood over you until you drank it.

Two hours later the wagon was upright. The wheel held. The caravan moved at half pace, and the loader walked beside the repaired corner with one hand on the rail, feeling for every shift.

You walked empty-handed.

* * *

At the market, the clerk laid the proposed contract on an upturned crate. Around you, awnings cracked in the afternoon wind. Porters rolled handcarts between the wagons, shouting ordinary warnings about toes and corners. Nobody knew you had been the weakest person in a village beyond the hills. Nobody asked.

The leader tapped the first figure. “Porter premium, less board. Full crew ration plus the cook’s added measure. Salt issued daily. New boots charged over six pay periods.”

You read the load clause twice. “It says one hundred eighty.”

“That was the tested ordinary limit.”

“On flat ground, yes. Most of the road isn’t flat.”

The clerk looked up. The leader waited.

Your mouth had gone dry. “I think one hundred sixty should be ordinary. If that’s workable. Two hundred on level ground, with the loader checking the sling. Nothing that rolls or shifts. No holding wagons.”

“Emergencies don’t read contracts,” the leader said.

“Then I put it down.”

The sentence was small. It stayed where you set it.

The leader tapped the wax board against her palm. “If putting it down endangers someone?”

“I call it before I lift. If the ground changes, we stop and crib it. If someone orders a catch, I refuse.”

“That costs time.”

“Yes.”

The loader, sorting hooks nearby, said, “Costs fewer knees.”

The clerk drew a line through one hundred eighty. “Recovery?”

You almost said whatever was usual. “Meal calls. I stop for them. One full rest day in seven, and no extra lift added while I’m already under load.”

“Training hours?” the leader asked.

“Half a shift with manifests and load plans. If you still need that.”

“I need the wagon planned before it’s loaded. Apprenticeship rate until you can do one without the wheelwright sending it back.”

“Paper deserves what it gets,” the wheelwright said from beneath a nearby bed.

The leader ignored him. “Six-week trial. We revise limits only after another controlled test. Either side can end at a market stop.”

The clerk added each term in cramped script. The cook came to check that “full ration” meant her measure, not the clerk’s. The other road hand complained that the rest-day roster would have to change. The teamster wanted the route grades copied before dawn. By the time everyone had protected their own work, the contract was ugly with insertions.

You pressed your thumb into the wax.

The next morning, the loader assigned you two sixty-kilogram cloth bales in a matched shoulder rig. A modest load, stable and dry. The clerk handed you the manifest board as well.

“Third wagon,” she said. “Check gross against axle allowance. Mark the steep grade after the noon well.”

The cook pushed a paper twist of salt into your pocket. The teamster called the start. Harness chains tightened down the line.

You checked the sling, checked the figures, and took your place beside the third wagon. When the road began to rise, you were already looking at its angle.

stories.title: His Infernal Majesty Says No
stories.prompt: As a reigning hell lord, no matter how cruel and tough you portray yourself, your darling daughter’s request on her birthdays always turn you into a mushy enforcer. However on her 18th birthday, she wants to go to a human college which you are against
stories.body:
# His Infernal Majesty Says No

At eleven minutes before my daughter's eighteenth birthday audience, I sentenced a tax reeve to thirty years in the tally vaults.

He had brought ledgers, witnesses, and the carcass tag from the last pack beast in his district. Fever had killed the animals. Without them, the ore carts had stopped; without ore, his quarterly payment had fallen short by nine iron bars. His defense was thorough. I disliked thorough defenses. They suggested that circumstance might outrank me.

"The vaults, Majesty?" my chancellor asked. He had perfected the courtier's trick of making a question sound like praise.

"The lowest vault," I said. "Seize his house against the deficit. His family may keep their clothes."

The reeve's wife stood behind the petition rail. Two boys clung to her skirts. She did not beg after that. Fear had taught her the value of conserving breath.

My decree was still being copied when I noticed that the ribbons above the western arch were scarlet.

"Who approved those?"

Six courtiers looked up. The reeve was dragged toward the side door. Everyone else looked at the floor.

My chamberlain swallowed. "The decorating staff believed red would more suitably honor the throne."

"My daughter asked for rose."

"A nuanced distinction, Majesty."

"Then nuance their wages to nothing until the distinction is corrected."

The chamberlain hurried away. Rose was not pink, as I had explained that morning, nor was it the color of fresh flame. It was the color of the paper flowers Nimelza had cut for herself when she was nine, because the royal gardeners had presented her with black lilies that hissed at guests. She had wanted a gentle color. I had dismissed three gardeners and compelled the fourth to breed a thornless variety by supper.

This was how her birthdays worked. Once a year, before the court and under the protection of custom, my daughter asked for something. When she was six, she had asked for a pear cake. I had made pears available in every infernal market by the following week, although three trade ministers resigned and one orchard arrived with its bewildered goats. At twelve she asked for a morning without screaming from the punishment galleries. I relocated the punishments beyond the eastern vents and fined the masons when the first new chamber carried sound. At seventeen she requested that no one bow to her until noon. Two barons forgot to stand upright. I put them in neck braces.

Cruelty requires consistency. So, apparently, did tenderness.

Nimelza entered the audience hall as the last scarlet ribbon came down. She wore no crown, only the smoke-gray dress she had chosen and the soft-soled slippers I had ordered warmed to precisely the temperature of bathwater. Her dark hair was pinned up with one bent silver clasp. I had given her better clasps. She preferred that one because I had fastened it badly on her seventh birthday and she had laughed until her nose ran.

She glanced toward the side door through which the reeve had vanished.

"What did he do?" she asked.

"Failed me."

Her gaze moved to the wife and boys, then back to me. "I see."

She did not say it with approval. Nimelza had become skilled at placing four or five unspoken sentences inside two harmless words.

The servants brought her breakfast tray to the little chair beside my throne: pear slices, hot chocolate, and a roll with the seeds scraped off because she hated how they lodged between her teeth. I inspected the cup before she drank. Lukewarm. I sent the cupbearer to kitchen duty for a month and ordered another.

"I could have drunk that," Nimelza said.

"You should not have to."

"That isn't the same as saying I couldn't."

"It is your birthday. Don't argue over chocolate."

Her mouth tightened at one corner. "May I make my request now?"

The court arranged itself to witness my surrender. Even the reeve's wife looked up. They expected a menagerie, perhaps, or a holiday for kitchen cats. My marshal had prepared contingencies for snow, music, fireworks, a temporary ban on spiders, and the release of any prisoner whose offense Nimelza found tedious.

I leaned back. "Ask."

"I want to attend a human college."

No one moved. A fresh cup of chocolate steamed in the cupbearer's hands.

"No," I said.

Nimelza watched me as if I had mispronounced a common word. "You said I could ask."

"You have asked. I have answered."

"I was admitted."

That landed less like an argument than an opened trapdoor. Around us, courtiers discovered urgent flaws in the rose ribbons.

I rose. "Seal the royal gate. No member of my household crosses without my hand on the seal. Clear the hall."

The reeve's wife tried to speak before the guards removed her. My marshal interpreted clearing the hall as a military evacuation. Within a minute there were only abandoned petitions, a spill of hot chocolate, Nimelza, and me.

She looked at the spill. "You frightened him."

"He frightened himself."

"He was carrying boiling chocolate."

"Then he should have had firmer hands."

She picked up her breakfast roll and tore it in half. It was an old habit from when her hands had been too small to manage one neatly. She ate one half and wrapped the other in a napkin.

"Come with me," she said. "I have documents."

I had expected tears, or at least the advantageous trembling of the lower lip that had obtained an indoor pony on her eighth birthday. Instead she led me to her sitting room and opened a writing desk I had commissioned for her. The false bottom was not my work.

Inside lay human forms, examination results, correspondence, a residence contract, and a letter offering enough scholarship money to insult the royal treasury.

"You applied under my roof."

"Mostly from the west laundry. Your wards interfere less with the signal there."

"My wards kept you alive through six assassination attempts."

"Five. The scorpion pie was meant for you."

"You ate the crust."

"It was good crust."

For a breath we were discussing pastry, and she was ten again, and the solution to danger was to remove every scorpion within a day's flight. Then she slid the admission letter toward me.

She had completed human equivalency examinations under a shortened version of her own name, supplied authenticated records, interviewed twice, and earned a place in an engineering program. She showed me the first-year timetable. Materials, mathematics, design, a laboratory in which students broke beams to learn why they failed.

"We break beams here," I said.

"Here they confess before they break. I want to learn what a structure does when nobody has ordered it to stay standing."

"You can hire human tutors."

"I don't want tutors who know your guards are outside the door. I want bad dining-hall food and a roommate who doesn't care which fork I use. I want to be wrong in a room where nobody gets punished for noticing."

The last sentence had been practiced. I could hear the clean edge on it. She heard it too and looked down at her papers.

I began with the dangers because dangers were countable. Human iron. Human doctors. Infernal rivals who would follow her across. The political value of a royal heir. The ease with which eighteen years of careful survival could end in an unlocked residence window.

She had answers. The room had a lock and only one ground-level window. The campus employed night staff. She had tested common metals against her skin. She had arranged money through a lawful exchange and learned the four-minute walk from the human gate to the residence desk. She had packed medicines, copied her records, and practiced folding her horns under a knitted cap.

"You have not practiced being unguarded," I said.

"No. You never let me."

"Because the first failure could kill you."

"It could."

I had prepared for denial. Agreement left me holding my anger without a handle.

She touched the admission letter. "There is a final confidential check at nine. I have to complete it myself. Then I have to arrive before midnight or they give the room to someone else."

"You arranged a deadline so I could not investigate."

"Yes."

"You used your birthday audience to corner me."

"Yes. I thought you'd care more about breaking the custom in public than about stopping me. I was wrong."

Her fluency had begun to roughen. Good. Anger restored the proper order of things.

"You will withdraw."

"No."

"That was not a request."

"Mine was."

At nine, the confidential check appeared on a flat pane of human glass balanced on two poetry books. The woman on the screen wore a blue sweater and spectacles. Behind her stood a filing cabinet with one drawer that did not quite close. I had crushed rebellions with tidier headquarters.

"Good evening," she said. "Can you hear me?"

"Perfectly," I said.

"I need the applicant to answer."

Nimelza sat at the desk. I stood behind her, which was my right in every room I owned.

The woman verified Nimelza's date of birth, course, funding, residence choice, and intention to enroll. She asked each question plainly and waited through the faint crackle in the connection. When I corrected the amount of Nimelza's available funds, the woman did not look at me.

"Will you be traveling with anyone?" she asked.

"No," Nimelza said.

"Yes," I said.

The woman made a note. "The residence booking is for one student. Guests follow the visitor policy. Security arrangements need approval in advance."

"My guard does not seek approval."

She finally looked up. "Are you the applicant?"

"Do you know to whom you speak?"

"No. Applicant, are you choosing to enroll?"

Nimelza's shoulders lowered by a fraction. "Yes."

"Has anyone required you to accept the offer?"

"No. He's requiring me not to."

The registrar typed. No shock, no moral pronouncement, no admiration. "Do you have an emergency contact?"

"My father."

"Can the college contact him by telephone?"

"Not by telephone. I have a signal mirror, and there is a one-use return token in my luggage."

"Does the residence staff know how to use either?"

Nimelza opened her mouth. Nothing came out.

The registrar waited.

"I wrote instructions," Nimelza said at last. "But they would have to know what I am. If the mirror opens in the residence, it could show the other students. Or let someone on this side see them. I can keep it covered, except if I'm unconscious, then—"

She stopped. Her fingers had pressed white marks into the edge of the desk.

I could have filled the gap with twelve guards, a physician, and a small occupying force. The answers crowded my teeth.

The registrar asked, "Do you have a local contact who understands your medical needs?"

"No. I thought the standard clinic would be enough. I checked everything they list, but they don't list me."

"All right. Standard emergency care is available. Staff may share necessary information if someone's life is at risk. We can't promise more than that. If you enroll, do you understand?"

Nimelza took a breath. "Yes."

"You can update an emergency plan after arrival. You still need to check in at the residence desk before midnight. Bring the identification we discussed. Ordinary luggage only."

"Define ordinary," I said.

"The applicant can email if she has a question."

The screen went dark a minute later. Nimelza remained at the desk, looking at her own reflection.

"You did not solve for incapacity," I said.

"I know."

"You would expose yourself or endanger strangers."

"I know. I thought I had it."

The admission papers trembled when she gathered them. Her grand speech, if she had prepared one, did not survive the first real hole in her plan.

I summoned my advisers.

They came eager to transform affection into an operation. The marshal recommended six guards dressed as students, with another twelve in nearby rented rooms. The chancellor suggested purchasing the residence, then the neighboring buildings, then the college if negotiations became discourteous. My chamberlain proposed replacing Nimelza's assigned roommate with a trained attendant of similar age.

"Replacement by incentive, of course," he said. "Or by a discreet impediment to the original person's arrival."

"No," Nimelza said.

They continued. A private dining hall disguised as a student café. Faculty contracts backed by penalties. A tunnel beneath her laboratory. A compulsory midnight report. The marshal had already drafted a response plan for any human who saw her horns; the chancellor called it a memory-hygiene measure.

With every proposal, I watched Nimelza become quieter. I mistook that silence for concession until she took the folded half-roll from her pocket and set it beside my hand.

"I withdraw my request," she said.

The advisers stopped.

"Nonsense," I said. "I am considering how to grant it."

"You're moving this court into a human building and calling it college. I don't want that."

"You cannot demand protection and then object to its shape."

"I didn't demand protection. I asked to go."

"With an emergency plan that fails the moment you cannot hold a mirror."

Her rehearsed confidence was gone now. "Yes. It fails there. So I'll defer. I'll find a contact who agrees to know. I'll apply again, and I won't wait until my birthday to tell you. But I won't go with people spying on my roommate."

The chamberlain cleared his throat. "The young highness has expressed a prudent willingness to revisit the timetable. We might describe the outcome as a strategically postponed fulfillment."

"Leave," I said.

He bowed too quickly. The marshal and chancellor followed. At the threshold, the marshal looked back for orders regarding covert deployment.

"If you send anyone across tonight," I told him, "I will assign you to the tally vault beneath the reeve."

That he understood.

Nimelza gathered her papers and the half-roll. "The registrar needs an answer. The signal is clearer at the gate."

"You are not crossing."

"I heard you the first time."

She walked out carrying the small case she had packed before asking permission.

I remained in her sitting room. On the desk lay a list in her tight handwriting: socks, notebooks, medicine, cap, soap, spare clasp. Beside *emergency contact*, she had written *father*, then drawn a box around it as if ink could make me usable from another realm.

The royal gate stood at the end of a bare basalt corridor. I had always liked its simplicity. No heraldry, no carved victories: only a doorway filled with pale moving air and, at its center, the black disc of my seal. The disc did not merely prohibit passage. It made prohibition material. That was the kind of magic I trusted.

Nimelza sat on her case before it, the human glass on her knees. The registrar's crooked drawer showed behind a box asking whether the applicant wished to relinquish her place.

"Nine minutes," Nimelza said without looking up.

I put my palm against the seal. It was cold.

She glanced at me then. "You don't have to watch."

"This gate is mine."

"Of course it is."

I could leave the seal where it was. In nine minutes the problem would become next year's problem, and by next year I could strengthen the wards, close the west laundry, acquire the college, or persuade Nimelza that engineering was beneath her. The court would remember that I had said no and made the realms obey.

I turned my hand. The seal resisted because I had ordered it to resist everyone. It split the skin across my palm before recognizing the difference between everyone and me. The black disc came free.

Pale air rushed through the doorway. On the glass, the registrar looked up.

Nimelza stood. "What are you doing?"

"Your identification," I said. "Is it in the outside pocket?"

"Yes."

"That is a foolish place."

"It is the place she told me to put it."

I reached for her case. She pulled it closer. I released the handle.

From my coat I took a plain copper token. It could open one brief route home for its holder. It carried no mark by which I could find her, a defect I had previously considered intolerable.

"Does it report where I am?" she asked.

"No."

"Can anyone follow it?"

"No."

She held out her hand. I set it there.

Footsteps rang at the far end of the corridor. The marshal appeared with four guards despite possessing a strong instinct for self-preservation.

"Stay behind the third arch," I said. "All of you. No disguises, no watchers, no one across."

"Majesty, if the heir is unescorted—"

"Choose your next word with care."

He chose none.

Nimelza tapped the enrollment box. The registrar asked her name, her intention, and whether she understood the emergency limitation. Nimelza answered. Her voice was not steady, but the answers were hers. The registrar told her to bring the screen to the residence desk and wished her a safe trip.

The moving air brightened. Beyond it waited a tiled passage with a humming light, a metal door, and a printed arrow taped crookedly to the wall. No trumpets. No receiving delegation. An ordinary route into a place that had made no arrangements to fear me.

Nimelza put on her knitted cap. One horn made a small peak in the wool.

"It's showing," I said.

"I know. I'll fix it outside."

"Six pairs of socks are insufficient."

"There are shops."

I had not considered shops a serious answer to anything. She bent to lift her case.

"You aren't coming," she said.

It was not quite a question.

"Your residence has a visitor policy."

For an instant, her face folded as it had when she was small and trying not to laugh during an execution notice. Then it settled. She stepped through.

The pale air shivered around her case and closed behind her heels. She hurried down the passage. At its far end, a human hand took her papers and waved her through the metal door with two minutes left. The printed arrow stirred. At midnight, the route narrowed to a blank doorway, and my daughter was gone.

I replaced the seal without closing it to her token. The marshal waited behind the third arch, pale and obedient.

"The court is still assembled," he said.

Of course it was. There were sentences to sign, shortages to punish, and a family without a house waiting somewhere beyond the audience doors. In the hall, Nimelza's rose ribbons hung at last, exactly the shade she had asked for. Her warmed slippers were gone. Her pear cake remained beneath its silver cover.

I sat on the throne. The chair beside it stayed empty.

"Bring the next petition," I said.

stories.title: The Kingdom of Later
stories.prompt: You’re a commoner in a fairytale kingdom just trying to get by. Frustratingly, nothing really ever gets done because ...
stories.body:
# The Kingdom of Later

The first drop struck the boot between my hands just as I drew the closing stitch tight.

It left a dark coin on the new brown leather. I stared at it, needle lifted. A second drop hit the cutting bench, close enough to the rolled hide that I felt the splash on my wrist.

Above me, under the rafters, the crown's roof token chimed for dawn.

The token was a thin square of tin nailed beside the attic ladder. A blue thread ran from its stamped seal, through the keyhole, and out toward whichever royal office had promised to repair my roof. At every dawn bell the date scratched on the tin moved ahead one day. I had watched it do so for three months. Still, habit was quicker than sense.

"They said they would come today," I told the empty shop.

The blue thread brightened. On the token, *today* slid neatly into *tomorrow*.

Water found the edge of my best hide.

I lunged for it. The hide was heavy, half a winter's money wound around a wooden core, and damp had already curled the outer handspan. I dragged it under the worktable, kicked a basin beneath the leak, then dabbed the boot with my apron. The mark lightened but did not vanish. The pair belonged to a miller with wide feet and exacting heels. The miller was coming at dusk. The payment was meant to buy a week's rent, lamp oil, and enough onions and oats to keep me from counting crusts.

Someone rapped twice and opened the door before I answered. The rent collector ducked beneath the lintel, shook rain from a dark wool shoulder, and opened the ledger carried against his chest.

"The week's rent is due at sunset."

"The roof was due before the last three rents."

He found my line with one clean finger. "The tenancy ledger and the repair claim are separate processes."

"The rain has joined them."

His gaze moved to the basin, the hide beneath the table, and the boot in my hand. He did not smile. Collectors were commoners too; this one had soles worn thin at the outside edge. "I can record interior damage for future assessment. Payment remains due now."

Due now. Those two words passed through the kingdom's grace untouched. Kings had never wished their taxes postponed.

I pressed my thumb over the darkened leather. "Come back at sunset."

"I am required to."

He shut the ledger and left me with the rain.

The roof clerk kept morning hours beneath the covered market, where the gutters overflowed in silver ropes and half the petitioners held blue-threaded tokens. I wrapped the miller's boots in oiled cloth, shoved every scrap of leather away from the leak, and carried my token there in my pocket. Its thread paid out through stone and timber without tangling. The fairy's magic lived in it, everyone said. No scissors had ever proved otherwise. A cut end simply shone from both pieces until morning and the promise remained.

The clerk sat behind a high counter with three calendars and no basin. I laid the wet token before him.

"The slate over my stock is open. I need someone on it now."

He turned the token with a quill. "Your claim remains eligible."

"My leather does not."

"Interior goods are assessed after the exterior remedy is complete. An inspector will attend after the next scheduling dawn."

The thread looped once around the quill. The clerk's hand stopped an inch above the calendar, held there as gently and completely as a nail clenched on the wrong side of a sole.

He exhaled through his nose. "As stated. After the next scheduling dawn."

"Send the inspector now."

"Immediate dispatch is not available until the future inspection has established emergency eligibility."

His words grew longer when pressed, each condition sheltering behind the next. I put both hands on the counter. "There is daylight through my roof."

"Then your evidence should be straightforward to verify."

Behind me, someone shifted weight with a grunt. The slater had come in out of the rain carrying a trowel and a coil of narrow ladder rope. Lime dust lived in the creases of his coat. One trouser knee was bound with cloth.

The clerk nodded toward him. "You accepted preliminary observation on this claimant's roof. State the undertaking for the record."

"From the lane," the slater said. "My other roof requires me before noon. This knee gives me one climb if the ladder is kind."

"Your physical limitations can be entered after the observation."

The slater looked at the rain beyond the awning. "I'll point out the damage from the lane. Nothing else."

The clerk wrote it down. Blue light passed from his calendar into the thread at the slater's wrist.

"If temporary mitigation is appropriate," the clerk said, "eligibility will be determined following authorization."

"Don't add to it."

"The sequence requires no additional undertaking at this stage."

The slater tried to lift his trowel. It jerked flat against his thigh, the first useful motion of the promise already held for dawn. He swore once, without ornament. I snatched up my token and led him out before the clerk found another stage.

At my shop, the rain had eased to a fine mist. From the lane we could see where one slate had slipped sideways above the back eave, exposing a black gap no wider than two fingers. Water did not need more. The slater planted his sound leg, leaned back, and squinted.

"I can look from here," he said. "There. Rotten lath under the left corner. Patch can't bear on that."

He raised the trowel to point. It would not rise. The promise held its first useful movement until morning.

"Use your other hand," I said.

"I undertook the observation, not the trowel. The grace is thorough when it gets the chance."

A gust came over the chimneys. The loose slate lifted, slapped once, and skated down the roof.

The slater moved before either of us spoke. He caught it against his coat, staggered under the edge, and thrust it into my arms. It was colder than the rain and heavy enough to bruise.

We both looked at his hands.

"You caught it," I said.

"Didn't say I would."

The trowel still hung at his thigh. The slate rested freely in my arms.

I set the slate on my bench. "Put it beside the basin now. If you choose."

He did. No thread stirred.

I put my hand on the fallen slate and lifted it. Nothing stopped me.

The slater would not climb. His knee was swelling under its binding, and another household had paid him for the one height he could manage. He would not lend me his ladder either; it was his way down. But he measured the gap by eye and told me I needed three sound slates, not one, because the neighboring edges had gone soft. He had two salvaged pieces in his yard and would sell them now. He would stand below my ladder for the price of a heel repair, so long as standing did not grow into a promise of rescue.

The rope-maker in the next row had a short tarred coil already finished. She flexed both hands while I counted coins on her counter. The skin along her thumbs had split and been wrapped in linen.

"I can't make another length today," she said. "No hemp left dry, and I can't close my hands by noon."

"This coil. Its price now."

She named it. The coins I set down had been folded in cloth for the rent collector.

"I need one pull from the lane as well," I said. "When I call down."

Her hands closed carefully around the money. "One pull now, if now comes before I shut my stall. Not a climb. Not a catch."

"Agreed."

I bought the slates with the rest of the rent money and carried everything to the shop. The blue thread from my token followed, bright against the wet gray lane.

In the attic, the leak sounded bigger. Drops struck the basin in quick uneven taps, and a dark tongue spread along the underside of the lath. I laid out what I had: three slates, the tarred rope, a jar of pitch, short nails, my cobbler's hammer, and leather.

Not scraps. Scraps were too small to run uphill past the gap. The underlay had to reach beneath the sound course and extend below the broken one. I unrolled the hide I had saved that morning. The outer turn was water-marked; the next was flawless, thick enough for boot soles. I measured a rectangle with my hand.

My knife would not descend.

Blue light ran along its back.

"The covered remedy has begun," said a voice near my ear.

I turned so sharply I struck my shoulder on a rafter.

The fairy stood on the roof token. She was no taller than the length of my awl, a living woman in a rain-dark coat, with four clear wings folded tight to keep them from the rafters. Blue thread passed through loops at her belt and away in every direction. The seal beneath her feet was only tin. She was the one holding my knife.

"Let it go," I said.

"Do you withdraw the action, the request, or the claim?"

"My roof is open."

"That is a condition. It is not consent to a withdrawal."

The knife waited in my fist. Beneath us, another drop struck leather.

"I want to patch it myself."

"A replacement promise does not release the first one. Your claim includes a guaranteed remedy. Any first action toward that remedy remains postponed while its undertaking is framed for later."

"Then move the undertaking back to now."

"The grace does not permit an official to turn promised labor into immediate compulsion."

"No one is being compelled. No one is here."

The fairy's gaze went to the ladder rope and the bought slate. "You are here. The slater is below. The rope-maker has accepted one present act. I will protect each refusal separately."

She spoke without haste, even while the wet spread over the lath. Promise, protection, withdrawal, consent: each thing had its own edge for her, as clean as pieces cut from a pattern. Mine were all piled together under the word *roof*.

"Can you make the clerk send someone?"

"No."

"Can you decide they've neglected it?"

"No. The grace preserves the right not to begin work merely because a crown or master has made later impossible. It cannot judge whether delay is being abused."

"You can see what it's costing me."

"Yes."

I waited for more. She did not decorate the answer.

"If I withdraw the claim?"

"The knife becomes yours to move. The crown's guarantee ends. No reimbursement for materials, lost stock, labor, or failure. No reinstatement by renaming the same promise."

The miller's good leather lay under my hand. The rent collector would return at sunset. I knew how to keep water out of a boot. A roof had different weight, different wind, and a fall beneath it. The sensible choice was to preserve the guarantee.

A drop struck the cut line I had marked.

"I withdraw the roof claim now," I said.

"Entirely and without a substitute undertaking?"

My mouth had already shaped *I will do it*. I shut it, swallowed, and looked at the knife. "Entirely."

The fairy put one hand on the tin seal. The light came out of the blue thread and gathered beneath her palm. All the lengths running through the attic went slack. They were ordinary dyed fiber for one breath; then they faded, leaving lint on the rafter and a pale groove across my wrist.

The knife dropped through the leather.

Its sound was quiet. That hurt worse than the price.

I cut the underlay, warmed the pitch, and worked it into the rough side with a stiff brush. Below, the slater braced my short household ladder at the back eave. It reached the low roof if I stood on the last safe rung and hauled myself over the edge. He tapped that rung with two fingers.

"No higher from the ladder. Your weight goes to the roof before your foot."

"The rotten lath is left of the gap."

"Wider than you think. Keep your knee on the sound run."

The rope-maker came into the lane, coat buttoned over her bandaged hands. "Where's the pull?"

I tied one end of her rope through the holes I had punched in the leather. The other end went over the roof on a stone wrapped in cloth. She took it loosely.

"Draw it toward the chimney now," I called. "Stop when the knot reaches the gutter."

"One pull," she said.

"One."

The fairy hovered beside the eave. Blue light touched the rope-maker's wrists, not binding, only present.

"She may stop before the knot," the fairy said.

"I heard her," I said.

The rope-maker pulled. The leather slid up the wet slope. Halfway, the knot caught beneath a tile edge and her wrapped hand opened.

"That's my pull."

She let the rope fall and went back to her stall.

I wanted to call after her. Instead I climbed.

Rain began again as I got my chest over the eave. The roof smelled of wet lime and old wood. Slate was not leather. It gave nothing under my palms, then shifted all at once. I kept my right knee where the slater pointed and crawled far enough to free the knot. The gap showed the attic below: basin rim, cutting bench, the pale roll of hide. From up there my livelihood looked small enough to cover with my body.

"Send the underlay beneath the top course," the slater called.

"I need tension or it will buckle."

"Not boot tension. Let the slate carry it."

I fed the pitched leather uphill, using the awl to lift the sound edge. It went crooked. Water ran along the raised side and poured through the gap in a sudden sheet.

Below, the basin clanged over.

I pulled harder. The leather stretched; pitch squeezed from the seam.

"Stop," the slater said. "You're thinning the middle."

"A loose seam drinks water."

"A roof sheds it. Top over bottom. Ease your pull."

My fingers had gone slick. I loosened the rope a handspan and the underlay settled. He passed me one slate at a time from the ladder, never taking the last rung. The first covered the lower gap. The second had to tuck beneath the surviving course, but my cut leather bunched under its corner.

A gust lifted the whole patch.

The slate in my left hand skated. I caught its edge against my forearm. Pain burned to my elbow. Below, the slater gripped the ladder and could do nothing else without trusting his bad knee to it.

"What are you doing?" he shouted.

"I'll reset—"

Blue thread flashed around my hammer hand.

The hammer stopped above the nail.

The fairy hung level with my face, wings thrashing in the wind. She had supplied the grip in that thread; I could feel her living attention holding the first stroke away from tomorrow.

"Withdraw those words," she said.

Rain ran into my eyes. The loose slate sawed at my sleeve.

"No undertaking. I withdraw it." My breath came short now, too small for explanations. "Hammer. Mine. Now."

The thread released.

I struck the nail—not through the slate, which would split, but through the leather tab below it. One hit, then another. My work knew that much: where piercing weakened a surface, where a hidden fastening could take strain. I folded the bunched corner under itself as I would skive a heel seat, thick side downhill, and pinned the fold beneath the slate's weight. The runoff divided around my wrist and went over the lower edge instead of under it.

"Left side," the slater called. "Still high."

I felt under the slate. A nub of old mortar held it up. The awl knocked it free. The slate settled with a flat stone click.

We placed the third piece while the wind worried my coat. The slater's directions shortened to body and work.

"Knee right."

I shifted.

"Hand off that edge."

I moved it before it broke.

"Enough pitch. Nail the tab."

I did.

When I backed down, my legs shook so badly that I sat on the attic floor. The fairy landed on the rafter. The slater climbed only far enough to put his head through the hatch and inspect the underside.

"Basin upright," he said.

I righted it. We waited.

Rain drummed over the roof until speech would have been work. A thin stream appeared along the far rafter and dropped into the basin. The patched lath darkened at one nail, then stopped. Beneath it, the cutting bench stayed dry. So did the boots, the remaining hide, and the shelves of finished shoes.

The slater touched his bound knee. "That corner needs proper lath. Not me today."

"I know."

"Your heel repair is due now."

"Leave the boots."

He did, and limped toward his paid roof.

The fairy lifted from the rafter. Beyond the walls, blue threads shone through the rain, hundreds of them leading toward kitchens, bridges, fields, and chambers I would never see. She chose one and took hold of it. The thread brightened with her departure.

My token remained dull.

By dusk I had dried the miller's boot, worked color into the water mark, and burnished both toes until the stain hid in the grain. I had no lamp oil for work after dark. A strip of good sole leather was gone from the roll. My rent cloth held three copper bits and nothing else.

The miller arrived while rain still whispered in the gutter. He turned the boots over, pressed each welt with a broad thumb, and pointed to the darker patch.

"Wet?"

"Dry now. Put them on."

He sat. The right boot went on easily. The left caught at his heel.

"Pull there," I said, pinching the back seam. "Now stand."

He stood, stamped once, and walked the length of the shop. Above him, one drop fell into the basin. None touched the leather.

He counted the payment onto my bench. Outside, the sunset bell began, and all across the kingdom tomorrow moved one day farther away.

I pushed the coins toward the rent side of the bench and crouched at the miller's ankle.

"Again," I said. "Left foot first."

stories.title: Where Rival Gods Go Quiet
stories.prompt: The head priests of two opposing gods fall in love.
stories.body:
# Where Rival Gods Go Quiet

By the time Levara found Holdfast's command in the salt crust of the stern line, three hundred people were watching her pretend not to read it.

The letters had risen white between her gloved hands, small and hard as fish teeth.

BRING TARN HOME TO ME.

Levara closed her fist. Crystals bit through the worn leather at her palm. Around the launch basin, the people of Holdfast waited beneath dripping awnings while, across a channel no wider than a cart road, Farwake's congregation crowded the open wharf and accepted the rain as an endorsement.

It was the seventh year Levara Quist and Ambel Tarn had made the Brackwater Circuit together. Holdfast required a properly tied mooring before he would still the inner water. Farwake answered only a craft deliberately released toward open sea. At spring tide, where the two powers crossed, either god could roll a skiff if the invocations came out of order. Thus the opposing head priests shared one boat, one route around the reef, and a liturgy neither side trusted the other to perform alone.

Levara was thirty-eight. She had been head priest long enough to recognize an instruction dressed as an invitation.

"Line secure?" called her launch keeper.

"Secure," she answered.

The rain stopped dimpling the basin. Every drop met the water and vanished without a ring. Holdfast had taken the knot.

Across the channel, Ambel stepped into the circuit boat. He wore Farwake's coat of pale sailcloth with the cuffs unfastened, and his dark hair had already plastered itself to his forehead. At forty-one, he ought to have learned that loose things traveled seaward in his god's presence. The wrapped loaf under his arm began inching toward the gunwale before he caught it with one elbow.

Laughter rose from both wharves, affectionate on one side and hostile on the other.

Ambel bowed to Levara. "Your god has made the water very obedient."

It was the customary opening insult, though not the customary wording.

"Your god mistakes drift for freedom," she replied.

The Holdfast wharf stamped its approval. Farwake's people hissed. Ambel's mouth moved at one corner. She knew that movement. It meant he had thought of a better answer too late and would save it for the return.

Levara stepped aboard. The boat sank under her weight, then seemed to think better of rocking. She fixed the home line to the stern cleat and checked the six turns with her thumb. When she reached for the bow line, Ambel said, quietly enough for the rain hoods nearest them not to hear, "Left buckle."

Her sandal strap had worked loose. She fastened it without thanking him.

"Bow away," she called.

The launch keepers shoved them into the still water. Oars carried the boat past the last rows of listeners, past Holdfast's warehouses with their ropes furred white and sound beneath the crust, past the Farwake shrine where no cup was ever left unattended on a sill. Only when the shouted responses had thinned behind them did Ambel open the loaf wrapping.

"If your people stamped any harder," he said, "they could have driven the pilings for the new smokehouse."

"That would constitute labor. They came for theology."

"And to watch us drown."

"Only your side. Mine know Holdfast would return the body."

He looked at her over the loaf. "You rehearsed that."

"For seven years. You finally gave me the opening."
