“That's not a good reason.”

“No.” Teyo looked at his parents. “It wasn't.”

“You wanted release?”

“I wanted to know if I could fly.” He glanced at Corven. “Before the lecture.”

Corven said, “There will be—” and stopped. “Yes. Later.”

“Do you want to go home with them tonight?” I asked.

Teyo drew the bottle closer. “Yes. I want you to check the arm first, and I want food. Then home. Medical care tomorrow. They can be angry after I eat.”

Olya laughed once, badly, and covered her mouth. “May I?”

Teyo considered her open arms. “You can sit here. Don't squeeze my right side.”

She crossed the tape only after I moved it and sat beside him. He leaned against her left shoulder. Corven waited until Teyo crooked two fingers at him. Then he joined them, plain and careful, and offered his hand instead of taking Teyo's.

Pippa pulled me into the hall while Teyo ate toast with honey. “Now they can ask the godparent thing,” she said. “But not because I fed him. He would've got fed anyway.”

“Agreed.”

“And I talk first if it's for me.”

“You ask first. We decide together.”

Back in the flight room, Corven wiped honey from his sleeve while Teyo denied putting it there. The power remained out, but his temperature had begun to rise.

“Explain the offer,” I said. “Exact obligations. No ceremony.”

Corven straightened. “Godparent is the nearest English term, not an exact translation. In our family, adults may make one optional pledge to a household whose child has sheltered theirs. Until Pippa turns sixteen, we would owe her truthful warning of any danger our family causes or brings near her, as much as three nights of emergency shelter, and practical help such as transport, food, or supplies when we can provide it safely.”

“What do you get?” Pippa asked.

“No custody,” he said. “No access to you or your home. No obedience, secrecy, service, or claim. We do not become family unless you use that word. Refusing causes no offense.”

Olya said, “And this is our gratitude to carry. Not yours. Not Teyo's.”

“Can you ask again if I say no?”

“No,” Corven said. “Not unless you invite the question.”

“Why me?”

Olya started with a sentence, lost it, and touched the damp patch over her own knee. “Because you kept noticing what he did. Because when we were foolish at the door, you—”

“I told you about the board,” Pippa said. “That doesn't mean you know me.”

“No.” Olya gave a small nod. “It is what I know tonight. The pledge can stay unmade.”

Pippa and I went to the kitchen alone. She asked whether emergency shelter meant sleeping in the wing coat. I said we could prohibit the coat. She asked if they could take her anywhere. I said not under the offer and not under any agreement I would accept. She asked whether Teyo got to be her friend without the adults' pledge.

“Yes,” I said. “Separately. With the usual rules.”

“Group messages?”

“No hidden messages. No deleting. At first, the family account.”

“That's annoying.”

“It is.”

She ate half a piece of Teyo's toast while she thought. Rainwater crawled down the dark kitchen windows. At last she said, “One year. Then we both have to say yes again. You and me.”

“Either of us can end it sooner.”

“And no surprise visits. They knocked like a horror film.”

“No unsupervised visits or outings.”

“Not even flying ones,” she said, and that decided it.

We returned with the terms written on a page torn from the care log: a one-year trial, renewable only with Pippa's and my joint consent; either of us could end it; no custody, secrecy, surprise visits, unsupervised access, or contact hidden from me. The obligations Corven had named remained theirs. Pippa did not owe thanks, work, or a relationship in return.

Corven read it twice. “This is acceptable.”

“Just say yes,” Teyo said through another piece of toast.

“Yes.”

Olya asked Pippa directly, “Do you want this for one year?”

“I want to try it,” Pippa said. “But you text before you come even if it's raining.”

“Yes.”

Teyo chose his own departure just as carefully. He borrowed dry clothes from the emergency bin, let me fit a sling, and decided he could walk to their car if Corven carried the warmed bottles. Olya asked before touching the front door. I asked before giving Corven a copy of the care log. Pippa and Teyo exchanged contact details as peers on the family account, separate from the pledge, while the battery pad blinked down to seven minutes.

At the threshold, Pippa sent the first test message. Four phones sounded, not quite together.

“The supervised visit can be next Saturday,” I said. “Afternoon, after I speak to your doctor.”

Corven entered it. Olya checked that our number had arrived. Teyo asked Pippa to photograph the corrected board before she threw it away.

Pippa looked at Corven's screen. “You put two sevens in Saturday's date.”

He took his wet glove off and started again.

stories.title: Roads Under Impossible Stars
stories.prompt: Two estranged best friends take a beat-up car into the desert for one last road trip before their lives go separate ways. Late one night, beneath a sky crowded with impossible stars, a meteor burns across the horizon—and the girl who wished things could go back to how they were discovers that, for a few minutes at a time, they can. But every time she rewinds the night, the desert changes: roads lead somewhere different, abandoned buildings appear where there was only sand, and her friend remembers pieces of conversations that technically never happened.
stories.body:
# Roads Under Impossible Stars

The heater blew hot dust at Keely's knees while frost silvered the lower corners of the windshield. Hollis kept one hand at twelve o'clock on the wheel and the other hovering near the temperature controls, as if the hatchback might misbehave out of embarrassment if she watched it closely enough.

"Pick something without handclaps," she said.

Keely scrolled through the old road-trip playlist. "That removes most of the decade."

"Good decade for clapping. Bad decade for water pumps."

The temperature needle had climbed past the white slash Hollis had drawn on the gauge with correction fluid. The heater was helping pull warmth off the engine, which was why they were roasting inside a car that let the desert night in through every door seal. Behind them, two water jugs knocked together beside a folded blanket, a jack that Hollis trusted, and a spare tire she did not.

Keely chose a song with no handclaps. Hollis listened for six seconds, then turned it down until the drums became a pulse under the engine rattle.

The road ran pale through low scrub. Their headlights caught the reflective stakes one at a time and gave each back to the dark. Keely had printed a map because Hollis's phone was out of storage and hers had been searching for service for an hour. The paper was already softened at the folds and striped with three routes in Keely's different-colored pen.

"The overlook road should be after the cattle guard," Keely said.

"Was after it."

"It's still on the county map."

"So is the campground with the toilet on its side."

"That was one time."

"It was on its side the whole time."

The joke reached the place where their old laughter should have met and stopped there. Hollis leaned toward the windshield. Keely folded the map along a line that had begun to tear.

At sixteen they had spent whole drives fighting over music and still arrived laughing. In the last three months, neither had used *best friend* where the other could hear it.

This was their last trip. Keely had used those words when she proposed it, then rushed to explain that she meant last before the move, not last forever. Hollis had said she understood. Since then Keely had built a calendar in her head: calls on Tuesdays, a visit every six weeks, the winter concert they had attended since they were sixteen. There were ways to keep a friendship if both people followed through. She had made a list.

The cattle guard jarred the hatchback hard enough to make the stale cheese crackers jump in the cup holder.

"There," Keely said. A dirt entrance slipped past on the right.

Hollis checked the mirror. "Can't turn here."

"There's room."

"There's a ditch. We'll take the next wide patch and come back."

"If we turn around now, we can be at the overlook by eleven forty-five. Stay twenty minutes, get the picture, then head back before the gauge—"

"I can see the gauge."

Keely opened the crackers. "I know. I'm just saying the timing works."

"You do keep saying that."

The next wide patch was farther than either of them remembered. By the time Hollis swung the car across the empty road, the heater smelled faintly sweet. She shut off the fan.

"We should go back," she said.

Keely heard herself answer too fast. "We came all this way."

"And the car came all this way. That's the part I'm trying not to push."

Above the windshield, the sky had become crowded.

Keely first mistook it for the clean abundance of a place without streetlights. Then she saw that there were too many layers. Bright points hung behind dimmer ones and in front of them, as if distance had folded flat. One cluster repeated itself upside down near the horizon. Thin rivers of stars bent in opposite directions without crossing. Hollis coasted onto the gravel shoulder and stopped.

They got out. The cold found Keely's damp shirt at once. The hatchback ticked and settled behind them.

"That's not weather," Keely said.

Hollis looked up, then at the road, then back up. "No."

A white spark burned across the horizon, then climbed. It should have fallen. Instead it cut uphill through the impossible layers, dragging a green tail that split into three and joined again.

Keely wished backward. Not in words at first. She wanted the cattle guard before they missed the turn, the afternoon before this trip became a test, the month before Hollis found out from somebody else that Keely had applied for the job. She wanted the years when silence inside a car had meant there was nothing they needed to say.

Then the wish narrowed in panic: just go back.

The meteor opened soundlessly, white from end to end.

Keely lurched against her seat belt.

The heater blasted her knees. The song with no handclaps was playing louder. A whole cracker rested on her tongue, dry and square, though she had swallowed it beside the shoulder. Her phone lay on the map and read 11:38.

It had read 11:42 when they got out.

Hollis drove with one hand at twelve o'clock. "Every six weeks," she said.

Keely choked on the cracker.

Hollis glanced over. "What?"

"Why did you say that?"

"I don't know." Hollis rubbed her thumb over the cracked wheel seam. "It was there. Just the words."

Ahead, the dirt entrance appeared after the cattle guard. It had been a single track. Now it forked immediately, one branch climbing toward a ridge that had not been there four minutes ago.

Hollis braked. "Was that a fork?"

Keely looked behind them. Beneath the car, the road was as it had been: two narrow lanes, patched tar, white edge stripe. About one car length back, the stripe hooked into a broad curve they had never driven.

The dashboard clock had been dead since Hollis bought the car. Its display now held one green digit: 4.

Keely reached toward it.

"Don't," Hollis said.

"I wasn't."

The recessed button beside the display was meant to set minutes. Keely could just fit a fingernail into it. She pulled her hand back.

Hollis took the right branch because its washboarding was shallower. Keely marked their bearing on the map and watched the temperature needle. For the first minute, the track ran toward the old overlook. During the second it curved north, though the compass on Keely's phone insisted the original road lay south of them. At the third, their headlights found a field of black stones. There had been pale sand there before.

"Turn around," Keely said.

"When I have room."

The gauge climbed over Hollis's white mark. The track narrowed between stones large enough to split the oil pan. Keely looked at the green 4.

"Wait," Hollis said. "I'm stopping."

Keely pressed the recessed button.

The world pulled sideways through her inner ear.

She was back at the fork with both feet braced against the floor. The heater was on. The temperature needle sat below the white slash. Her phone said 11:38 again, although four minutes of fear remained sharp in her mind. The nausea did too, a slow rotation behind her eyes.

The clock showed 3.

Hollis swallowed. "Don't take it."

"Take what?"

"That's all I've got." Hollis tapped two fingers against her lips. "I heard myself say it, but I didn't hear a voice. No picture. Nothing around it."

The right branch was gone. The left ran straight for thirty yards, then divided around an abandoned service building standing where the black stones had been. Its two pump islands had no pumps. Moonlight shone through the office windows.

"We moved back four minutes," Keely said. "Exactly. The car too. Look at the gauge."

Hollis did. "You pressed that."

"I needed to know if it was the same as before. The first time just happened."

"And now?"

"Three. I think it means three left."

Hollis shifted into neutral but kept her foot on the brake. "You think."

"We know it undid the heat. Fuel too, probably. We can use that. We take a road, check it for four minutes, come back if it's wrong."

"The road changed."

"Which is why we test it."

Hollis looked at her. Not angry, Keely thought. Not yet. This could still be handled if Keely gave her the information in the right order.

"The building gives us shelter if the radiator goes," Keely said. "Maybe a landline, tools, old water tank—"

"No one has put a landline in that place since before this car was born."

But Hollis eased forward. The asphalt ended one hatchback-length beyond the tires, clean as if cut with a blade. Gravel began there and led toward the building.

They made it to the first pump island. Beyond it, the driveway dipped. Hollis stopped and opened her door to look down.

"Stay here," she said.

"I can hold the light."

"Then hold it at the ground."

Keely followed. The beam showed tire tracks running into the dip and ending at a crust of sand. Hollis scraped it with her boot. The crust fell through. A drainage channel yawned underneath, wider than the tires.

"Back up," Hollis said.

The gravel broke under her next step. She caught the door frame. Her shoulder struck it, and the open door slammed into the concrete island with a metal crack. Inside, one of the water jugs toppled. Its cap sheared against the jack, pouring water across the cargo floor.

Keely grabbed Hollis's sleeve. "Are you hurt?"

"No. Let go. I need to see if the hinge—"

"I can undo it."

Hollis went still. "Undo what?"

"The door. The water. Your shoulder. All of it. And then we don't come this way."

"Keely, wait. Let me finish."

Keely pressed the button.

The seat caught her. Vertigo rose harder, cold and immediate, and for a second the windshield seemed to roll while the car stayed still.

The clock showed 2.

The water jug stood capped behind them. Hollis's shoulder was unmarked. The driver's door shut cleanly, without the pale crease left by the concrete.

"Let me finish," Hollis said.

Keely closed her eyes.

"There's another one, isn't there?" Hollis asked.

"One phrase."

"No picture. I don't know what I was finishing." She flexed the shoulder that had never struck anything. "What did you do?"

"The ground gave way. The door got bent. We lost one jug. You hit your shoulder."

"So you pushed it."

"It fixed everything."

The service building was no longer ahead of them. It stood far off to the left, turned sideways, with no road reaching it. The new track curved right. The compass showed west; on the printed map, west was open desert for thirty miles.

Hollis examined the ground through the windshield. The same rectangle of old asphalt held the car. Beyond the hood, at almost exactly its length, the surface became reddish gravel.

"You don't choose the road," she said.

"Not yet."

"That's not what I said."

Keely's stomach rolled again. She took a cracker for the salt and found the packet sealed. Even the tear had been taken back. She opened it along the same crooked seam.

They drove the rightward track at walking speed. Hollis called the surface as it came: packed gravel, loose gravel, shallow rut, stone shelf. Keely watched the clock and tried to repair the rest.

"About the six weeks," she said. "I wasn't making a rule. I meant I could come back more often if that felt—"

"I didn't ask."

"Not this time. Before."

Hollis took her foot off the accelerator. "Before when?"

"Before the first reset. You said visits weren't the same as telling you I applied. I was trying to explain that I didn't tell you because nothing was certain, and you would have spent three months thinking I was already gone."

"Did I say that?"

"You said I don't get to make your waiting easier by leaving you out of it."

The words had survived in Keely complete and exact. She had already tried one answer to them. She could do better now: start with agreement, remove the part about Hollis not answering messages, keep her own voice level.

"You were right," she said. "But I wasn't trying to leave you out. I was trying not to hand you a problem before I knew if it existed."

"You know what I'm going to say?"

"No. I know what you said."

"That isn't better."

The track climbed. Keely could see the useful next version of the exchange as branching roads: if Hollis said she was tired of being managed, Keely could explain the difference between planning and control; if she went quiet, Keely could give her room without letting silence harden. Four minutes was enough to get past the bad opening.

Ahead, a pale strip that looked like pavement descended over a low rise.

"That might join the highway," Keely said.

Hollis stopped before the crest. "It doesn't."

"We can't see from here."

"I can see the outside edge slumping. And there's no uphill cut for a road coming back out."

"We could walk it."

"Engine's hot. I'm not leaving it idling."

"Then shut it off. I'll check."

Hollis set the brake but did not move. "Did we have this argument already?"

"Not this one."

"Did I tell you not to take a road?"

"You don't remember that."

"I have the words."

Keely heard the accusation that might follow and began answering it before Hollis spoke. "I'm not making you repeat yourself. The ground changes. The only advantage we have is that I remember, so I have to compare what happened and—"

"You keep answering things I haven't said."

"Because I'm the only one with all of it."

"You're changing your answers."

"I'm using what I know."

"On me." Hollis took her hand off the gearshift. "Don't push it. Not for this."

Keely's finger was already in the recess. She told herself the road was unsafe, the gauge was high, the four-minute window nearly gone. Hollis had set the brake. Nothing was falling. Nothing was broken.

She pressed anyway.

For one long instant there were two directions of down. Keely clamped a hand over her mouth and tasted metal.

The clock showed 1.

Hollis stared through the windshield. "Not for this."

Keely breathed through her nose.

"That's the piece," Hollis said. "Three words."

The old asphalt beneath them remained. One car length ahead, it ended in a broad fan of stable gravel. Beyond that, a broken ribbon of pavement descended into a dry wash and stopped at a wall of pale dirt. The service building had vanished. Behind them, the track they had just climbed did not exist.

Hollis turned off the engine.

"No more driving until you tell me the rules," she said.

Keely put both hands in her lap. The night continued its slow rotation around her, then steadied.

She told Hollis what she knew and only what she knew. The first return had come with the meteor and her wish. The others happened when she pressed the clock button. Each was four minutes. The number counted down. The car returned to its earlier position with its fuel, heat, contents, and damage restored. So did they, except Keely kept the erased time and the spinning in her head. Hollis kept one piece of speech.

"Words only," Hollis said.

"You said no pictures."

"I'm checking."

"Words only, as far as I can tell."

"And the road?"

"The patch under us stays. Past about a car length, it changes. Every time it's moved farther off the route on the map. The compass tells us where this road points now, but not where the next one will be."

Hollis considered the gravel fan, the wash, the hood. "One push left."

"Yes."

"You don't push it without asking."

Keely started to say that an emergency might not leave time. Hollis was looking at the dashboard, not at her.

"Okay," Keely said.

They inventoried the car. Hollis did the work; Keely wrote it down. A little under half a tank. One full water jug and one three-quarters full. Four foil blankets, a flashlight at sixty percent, six cheese crackers, three fruit candies melted into a single striped brick, one spare hoodie, a weak jack, a doubtful tire. No signal. The radiator reservoir was low enough that Hollis would not restart until the engine cooled.

"Highway should be south," Keely said.

"Map south."

"The compass still says south."

"The compass doesn't say there's a road there."

They walked no farther than the gravel fan. Hollis crouched and pressed both palms to it, then swept the flashlight over the slope. Angular stones, no crust, no dark line of a drop beneath. Safe enough to move the car fully off the broken pavement if they did it now.

"You're dizzy," she said.

"I can steer ten feet."

"I can steer my car. You watch the passenger side and don't wave unless I'm near the edge."

Hollis restarted. Keely got out and held the flashlight low. The hatchback crept onto the gravel, its tires crunching one careful quarter-turn at a time. Keely wanted to guide every inch. She made herself watch the passenger wheel and say only, "Clear," when Hollis asked.

Once the car sat level, Hollis killed the engine again. Heat soaked upward. A wet hiss came from beneath the hood, followed by a white thread of steam. Coolant began to spit from the overflow line and darken the gravel.

The green 1 lit Keely's hand as she reached for the clock.

Four minutes back would fill the reservoir, cool the engine, put them on the intact patch. It would also take away the inventory and Hollis's condition. The road beyond the tires would change again. Keely could return with the right explanation ready. She could ask before touching the button and know which words had failed.

Hollis stood outside by the hood, waiting for Keely to pull the release. She did not say don't.

Keely withdrew her finger.

"It's venting," she said.

"I hear it. Pop the hood, not the cap."

Keely pulled the lever. Hollis raised the hood and set the prop, keeping her face away from the steam. They lined the cold front seats with two foil blankets, kept the other two for themselves, put on both layers they had, and moved the water out of the cargo area. Hollis tore the striped candy brick in half with the jack handle. It broke unevenly; she took the smaller piece.

"At first light," Hollis said, "we check the hose. If it holds, we add water after it's cold and try the gravel back to the highest point. Slowly. If the track is gone, we stay with the car and use the mirror to signal."

"We should climb the ridge first and look for the highway."

"After daylight. Together. Ten minutes out, ten back."

Keely wrote that below the inventory.

The sky remained impossible, dense with overlapping distances. Without the engine, the silence made room for the small sounds of their camp: foil snapping, candy against teeth, coolant ticking onto stone.

Hollis sat sideways in the driver's seat. "Every six weeks."

Keely looked up.

"That one," Hollis said. "What was around it?"

"I said I could visit every six weeks after I moved. You said visits weren't the same as telling you I'd applied."

"Anything else?"

Keely could have given her the whole erased exchange, including Hollis's long silence and the exact place her voice had thinned. "You said I made the schedule before I asked whether you wanted one."

Hollis pulled the foil blanket closer around her shoulders. "Sounds like me."

"It does."

They did not decide on Tuesdays or visits. Hollis took first watch because, she said, Keely looked as if the parked car were still moving. Keely objected once, then climbed into the passenger seat and set her phone alarm for two hours.

"Wake me if the steam gets worse," she said.

"It'll stop when it's cold."

"Then wake me if you get too cold."

Hollis adjusted the flashlight so its beam rested across the gravel and the first broken edge of road. "Two hours. I'll wake you."

Keely put the unopened half of the crackers between them. The dashboard clock held at 1. Outside the windshield, the broken pavement ended at the wash. Hollis listened to the radiator, and Keely waited for the alarm.

stories.title: The Players Above
stories.prompt: "I apreciate your advice, formless voice, but what do you want with me?" "Me and some friends are having a cosmic game. One of us has created a great peril and the rest of us must guide you and your companions to both figure it out and then solve it" "Like in a TTRPG?" "Oh, you have those too?"
stories.body:
# The Players Above

The last die was still turning when Ludek asked which way everyone was going home.

It was the sort of question that ended every game in the mill room. Boots were found under the table. Cups were stacked beside the flour ledger. Reniya, who had spent the evening calculating the odds of imaginary bridges collapsing under imaginary armies, gathered the painted route tiles into their box and said, “I’ll walk with you past the upper press, then take the orchard stair and—”

Something chimed beneath her chair.

A silver filament pushed through the seam between two floorboards. It grew the width of her hand in a blink, following the direction her finger had drawn across the table. Its tip struck a nail, forked around it, and shed a splinter no longer than a barley awn. Reniya picked it up before Veysa could slap her hand away.

Cold bit through her fingertips.

*Do not complete that move,* said a voice with no place in the room.

Reniya dropped the splinter onto the table. The voice stopped. She touched it again with one finger.

“I appreciate your advice, formless voice, but what do you want with me?”

Veysa stared at her. Ludek, halfway into his left boot, remained halfway there.

*Some friends and I are having a cosmic game,* the voice said. It spoke as if each clause had to wait for the previous one to clear a narrow gate. *One of us created a great peril. The rest of us must guide you and your companions to discover it and solve it. That is our turn.*

“Like in a TTRPG?” Reniya asked.

For the first time, the presence in the metal lost its measured pace. *Oh, you have those too?*

Then it was gone. The splinter remained painfully cold.

“What said that?” Veysa asked.

“A player.” Reniya looked at the silver thread between her boots. “Possibly.”

“Whose player?”

“Not ours.”

Ludek pulled on his boot. “Good. I was worried I’d forgotten to pay someone.”

Veysa was already on her knees. She took the lamp from its hook, set its hood low, and ran a thumbnail along the floor seam. She had repaired the mill’s west wall after two wet winters, and she distrusted any crack that arrived with an explanation. “Lift that board.”

“It’s pinned.”

“Yes, Reniya. Mills generally prefer their floors to stay down. Get the short bar.”

They cleared the game pieces and pried up two boards. Beneath them, the old joist carried a metallic root: silver at its narrow tip, dull gray behind, its surface wrinkled like metal poured over twine. The newest length pointed toward the orchard side of the mill. It did not move while they watched.

“You were naming the orchard stair,” Ludek said.

“I hadn’t named where I was going after it.”

“It had enough to start.” He crouched without touching the root. “This afternoon I told the flour porter I was carrying receipts to the vinegar yard. Something jumped under the bins. I thought mouse, nail, old mill.”

Veysa looked toward the bins. “Show me.”

“Show you where I heard it, or tell you where I’m going?”

“The first. Keep the second behind your teeth.”

They found another gray ridge below the bin platform, aimed toward the lane that led to the vinegar yard. A third had buckled the plaster beside the delivery door. Ludek remembered a mill hand announcing a walk to the market scales before supper.

Reniya sorted possibilities because sorting them was better than imagining silver roots reaching the crowded square at dawn. The voice itself had not made the filament grow. Neither had her question. All evening they had declared journeys for their game pieces—to the ash fortress, through a paper swamp, twice to the moon—and the floor had stayed quiet. Those routes had never been theirs.

“We test one fact at a time,” she said.

Veysa’s head came up. “On what?”

“Empty floor. Short distance. No cutting.”

“On my floor, then.”

“Technically the miller’s.”

“Tonight it’s mine.”

Ludek took the lamp to the far wall. “Ask me something.”

Reniya silently decided to carry the route-tile box to the north window. She pictured the few steps, took them, and set the box on the sill. The root did not move.

Reniya understood. “Are you going to the water jug?”

“No.”

Nothing sounded below them.

“I came here by the south lane,” Ludek said. Still nothing. He pointed at the flour bins and announced, with a courier’s plain certainty, “I’m walking from this wall to those bins now.”

The silver tip beneath the lifted boards shot forward. A second filament creaked under the floor along the line Ludek had glanced across the room. It stopped when it reached the bins. Ludek walked there after it, jaw tight.

“Past travel does nothing,” he said. “A question does nothing. Something I mean to do next does.”

Reniya said, “I’m going to the bell tower.” She had no intention of leaving the room. The root did not stir.

Veysa lowered the lamp until its brass rim nearly touched the old growth. “And lies do nothing. We have enough for a working rule.”

The cold in Reniya’s fingers shifted. A new presence fitted itself around the splinter, not entering so much as finding the only open chair.

*Your inquiry is permitted.* The words arrived all at once, clean-edged and impatient.

Reniya nearly asked who it was. One useless question, and perhaps one answer gone. She looked at the root instead. “Exactly what feeds this growth?”

*Audible, sincere intent to travel, originating within half a mile. A remembered journey is excluded. An inquiry is excluded. False declaration is excluded. Guidance without a body is excluded. I may report the condition; I cannot perceive your buried result.*

Reniya repeated it, losing the formal edges as she spoke. “It says a spoken route you truly mean to take feeds it, if you’re within half a mile. Not thoughts, questions, lies, old journeys, or the voices. It can’t see underground.”

“Half a mile from what?” Ludek asked.

The presence did not respond to him. Reniya had expected that; the splinter still made her bones ache with the certainty of being the only open channel.

Veysa took up the short bar. “From the thing we find by following this.”

“Wait,” Reniya said. “We have one answer left from this one.”

“Then don’t spend it asking whether we ought to wait.”

They left the lamp burning over the open floor and followed the cooled root.

It had worked through the stone sill rather than under it, splitting a wedge from one corner. Outside, moonlight turned the lane pale and the root dark. The metal had taken the routes people imagined, not the roads themselves. One branch went under a wall where a walker would have used the gate. Another rose through packed soil on a slant toward the orchard stair, following Reniya’s unfinished intention as far as she had formed it. Behind every silver point lay a gray seam already cooling in the night air.

Ludek walked first. He knew which alleys people named and which they used without naming, where carts had worn diagonal escapes between terraces, where a courier saying *upper road* might mean any of three grades. He held up a hand before each turn instead of calling it.

At the base of the first orchard terrace, the root vanished beneath a retaining wall.

Veysa pressed her ear to the stones. A faint ticking answered from inside. “The face is loaded.”

“Can you tell how far?” Reniya asked.

“I can tell it wasn’t ticking yesterday.” Veysa scraped mortar from a joint with her knife. A hairline crack ran upward between two blocks. “Don’t make me improve an answer I can’t honestly improve.”

The silver root brightened at Reniya’s feet, though none of them had named a route.

“We didn’t say anything,” she said.

Ludek pointed downslope. Two late workers crossed the lane below, talking as they went.

“—taking the east cartway to the tannery,” one called.

Under the terrace, metal groaned. A bright spur punched through the mortar and aimed southeast.

“That’s inside half a mile,” Ludek said. “Market morning will be worse.”

The first produce wagons would arrive before sunrise. Porters would call deliveries. Traders would give directions to half-awake apprentices. Hundreds of sincere routes, spoken within reach.

Veysa wedged the short bar behind the shining spur.

“Don’t cut it,” Reniya said.

“I’m checking whether it’s fixed to the stone.”

“It was made by someone calling this a game.”

“The wall doesn’t care what they call it.” Veysa leaned only enough to feel the resistance, then stopped. “Ask what cutting does.”

Reniya closed her hand around the splinter. “What happens if we break the root before it stops growing?”

*The living maker supplied one finite charge. Severance while charge remains releases new growth toward the last accepted destination. Intervention is not permitted to me. Warning is.*

The presence closed like a door. Its two answers had been spent.

Reniya relayed the words. Ludek looked down the slope, toward the sleeping roofs gathered around the market.

“Last accepted destination,” he said. “Which was the tannery.”

“If that man meant it.”

“He works there.”

Veysa eased out the bar. “Finite is useful. Charged is the word that keeps our hands off it.”

They climbed.

Above the terrace, the root split into old courses. The cooled seams showed its history as plainly as wagon ruts. Reniya began to see a rule in their failures to overlap: a new filament would approach an older gray line, turn aside at the last finger’s breadth, and run beside it or branch away. Twice it had made long detours around its own buried track.

They followed those detours through two orchards, over a dry irrigation lip, and into a weed-choked trench built around the remains of a kiln. The kiln had been taken down years ago; only its circular footing remained, half buried above the catchment that supplied the market cisterns. Moonlight lay on the stone ring. Silver threads entered from every side.

At its center, something under the earth pulsed hard enough to shake dust from the weeds.

The third presence arrived as a fan of spoken possibilities inside the cold: outward, inward, beneath. Reniya formed a question silently and received only more branching. It could not hear her think.

*If the line continues outward, it may branch at the obstruction. If inward, it may surface beside the origin. If beneath—unobserved. Choose the question that removes the most paths.*

Reniya knelt beside one place where the new silver veered from a cooled seam. “Can fresh growth cross a seam it has already laid?”

*Not after that seam cools. A course closed around the origin forces the remaining charge inward. The core then becomes reachable.*

“It says close a route around the center. The growth can’t cross its cooled metal, so the charge knots inward and pushes the core up.”

Veysa walked the ring, counting paces. At the downhill side she thrust the short bar into the weeds and hit stone almost at once. She tried again two steps left, then right. Stone each time.

“Catchment crown,” she said.

Reniya looked from the old kiln footing to the buried wall. “The voice suggested the core might surface.”

“Beside the origin, it said. Or under it, which it cannot see.” Veysa drove the bar once more, gently now. “The catchment crown runs under this side. If we force metal down, it enters the wall. If we dig where your friend is offering branches, we unload the soil holding that wall.”

The presence spread more alternatives: excavation inward, a straight trench outward, removal of obstructing stone. None accounted for a catchment it could not perceive.

Reniya wanted to ask which path had the highest chance. The question formed perfectly. So did Veysa’s answer before she gave it: chance of what, based on whose wall?

“We don’t dig,” Reniya said.

Veysa nodded once.

Ludek had gone around the kiln and was kicking leaves from a shallow stone channel. “Here. The old service course.”

It began beside the kiln’s loading apron, curved along the uphill half of the footing, then descended at each end toward a dry spillway. Kiln carts had once used the course to circle without backing near the catchment edge. A century of silt blocked the spillway mouth.

“It comes back to itself,” Ludek said. “Or did.”

Veysa examined the downhill stones. “Open the spillway and the route can close above the crown. If anything runs loose, the channel carries it away from the wall.”

The voice offered a straight line through the footing, shorter by half.

“No,” Veysa said when Reniya relayed it. “Shorter for the root. Riskier for everyone who drinks tomorrow.”

*That consequence lies outside my observation,* the presence replied, unasked.

“Not an answer,” Reniya told it.

The branching pressure continued.

Ludek put his shoulder to a spillway slab. “Could the two of you settle the nature of answers while lifting?”

They lifted.

Mud sucked at the slab. The channel beneath smelled of wet lime and old apples. They cleared it with the short bar, Veysa’s knife, and their hands, passing stones downslope without saying where they meant to carry them. Reniya marked the intended loop with game tiles from her pocket, bright squares at each turn. Veysa moved three of them when the line came too close to the buried crown. Ludek stood at opposite bends and used gestures to confirm sightlines. They planned in questions, lies, and pointing. The root stayed still except when distant night workers fed it another destination.

By the time the spillway lay open, the silver at the kiln center had thickened to a fist. Dawn had begun to gray the eastern haze.

“We need an honest route,” Reniya said. “One of us could speak the full circuit and walk it.”

“Too long,” Ludek said. “The footing’s already shifting.”

Veysa put her palm to an uphill stone. It clicked against its neighbor. Her speech shortened with it. “Three legs. Joined at the tiles. Each mean your own. Each walk your own. No downhill shortcuts.”

“Does joining three intentions count as one course?” Reniya asked.

“That’s your calculation.”

Reniya looked at the root’s branching history. Separate declarations had made separate filaments, but filaments joined when their imagined courses met. The likelihood was not comfortingly high. It was merely higher than waiting for market bells.

“It should.”

Ludek wiped mud on his coat. “Should like a bridge in one of your games?”

“No. Should like every piece of evidence we have and one gap.”

“Better.” He took the longest section, the outer curve where the route bent out of sight.

They set themselves at the three bright tiles. Reniya’s mouth had gone dry. She could hear the last voice mapping branches through the splinter: if one intent failed, if one line reached a cooled seam too early, if the charge found the wall first.

Veysa struck the footing with the flat of her bar. “Now.”

“I’m going from the loading stone, around the upper kiln curve, to the blue tile,” Ludek called.

The earth opened behind him. Silver root rolled into the cleared course, fast as water down a steep gutter. Ludek ran, no joke left in him, glancing back only at turns. The metal followed the course he had pictured rather than every placement of his boots.

At the blue tile Veysa took over. “I’m going along this sound footing to the spillway head.”

Her line grew broader and slower. She watched the masonry, not the root. Halfway down, one stone dipped.

“Stop there. Reniya, move your mark uphill. Two feet. More. Hold it.”

Reniya shifted the final tile. Veysa adjusted her declared course with the confidence of someone accepting the load herself. The root curved away from the catchment crown.

Reniya began her leg. “I’m going from the spillway head down—”

“Not below,” Ludek shouted. “Not below. The service lip, then the red tile.”

The half-spoken intention pulled a bright needle toward the catchment. Reniya bit off the rest, stepped sideways, and forced herself to picture the actual safe course rather than the destination she feared.

“Along the service lip,” she said, breath clipping each phrase. “Around the outer stone. Back to the loading apron.”

The needle bent. Metal chased her through the opened channel. Heat came off it now, burning the damp from her boot soles. Ahead waited the first cooled seam, gray and unbroken across the place where her route must close.

Too late, she saw that her imagined line met it at an angle instead of joining Ludek’s starting point. Would touching count, or must it overlap? One question remained.

She gripped the splinter. “Must the new growth retrace the first seam to close the course?”

The answer divided around what the voice did not know. *It must meet a cooled boundary that encloses the origin. It cannot cross. Your elevation, wall, and chosen safety are not visible to me.*

Reniya relayed only what they needed. “Meeting closes it. It doesn’t have to retrace.”

The voice began another branching shape and faded before completing it.

Reniya ran the last six paces. Behind her, silver struck gray.

The impact made no grand sound. It made the small, dreadful sound of a spoon cracking a cup. The new root tried to cross the cooled seam, flattened against it, and raced both ways around the circle. Where it met the other new lines, the whole loop tightened.

At the kiln center, earth humped upward.

“Spillway!” Veysa shouted.

They threw themselves clear. A white-hot spur broke from the center and snapped downhill, but the loop turned it sideways into the open channel. It ran ten yards, shedding beads of molten silver, then thinned to wire, to hair, to nothing. The pulsing beneath the kiln stuttered. Once. Twice.

Stopped.

Veysa approached first, testing each stone before trusting it. The closed course had exposed a dark metallic pod among the kiln bricks. It was the size of Reniya’s two fists and folded around itself like a seed. No light moved in its seams.

“Cold?” Reniya asked.

“You’re holding the supernatural splinter.”

“You’re the mason.”

Veysa touched the pod with the back of one muddy finger. Then she laid her palm on it. “Cold.”

Ludek crouched at the spillway and watched the last silver bead dim. “And finite.”

Veysa set her knife in the pod’s exposed seam and tapped the handle with the short bar. The shell parted without resistance. Inside lay a dull grain of metal, no warmer and no more alive than a dropped nail.

Reniya closed her hand around the splinter. Nothing spoke. Whoever had made the peril offered no protest, no explanation, no sign of having watched. The other presences had spent their answers and gone with the charge.

They lifted the grain into the empty route-tile box and carried it to the catchment. Veysa checked the crown stone by stone while Ludek climbed down to the inspection hatch and called back dry measurements. One joint had opened a fingernail’s width. It would need mortar before the first draw. The wall itself held.

Below them, shutters began to knock open around the market.

“Mill floor first?” Reniya asked.

Veysa handed her the short bar. “Catchment joint.”

“Then the mill floor,” Ludek said, climbing out. “Then breakfast.”

Veysa looked at the mud on all three of them. “Bring mortar.”

Ludek sighed and took the heavier end of the tool basket. Reniya tucked the cold box under her arm, and together they started down to the wall.

stories.title: A Very Good Dog
stories.prompt: The ultimate evil guy turns themselves into the pet (Dog) of the hero to break into their home and do bad things but then being a pet is dope, they just chill and no one knows where he went.
stories.body:
# A Very Good Dog

Inside the body of Brightguard’s much-pampered dog Pickle, Maledict discovered at seven-oh-three in the morning that breakfast had rules.

Brightguard, already dressed for patrol from the waist up and wearing old gray running shorts below, set down a bowl of chicken, rice, and something green. She waited. Maledict advanced.

“White foot first, sweetheart.”

He looked down. Pickle’s left forepaw ended in a neat blaze of white fur. His right was brown. Maledict offered the white one as if granting a boon.

Brightguard took it, squeezed once, and touched two fingers to his nose. “There you are.”

Only then did she slide the bowl across the heated tile.

Maledict had spent eleven months designing the exchange device and six weeks studying the security shell around Brightguard’s condominium. He had not allocated a minute to the dog’s table manners. He had certainly not expected the smell of roast chicken to erase, for several alarming seconds, the location of Brightguard’s private response key.

He ate. There was no dignified way to do it, so he did it thoroughly.

Above him, Brightguard drank coffee while scrolling through overnight incident reports on a translucent wrist display. She was sixty-one, with silver threaded through her close-cropped hair. The blue fabric across her shoulders was impact mesh, not a cape, and the bright plates stacked beside her tablet would unfold into the field harness that let her lift a bus without putting the full complaint through either knee.

She glanced down. Maledict had licked the bowl into the pantry.

“You left the peas.”

He froze.

“Since when do you leave peas?”

He ate the peas individually. Brightguard watched the last one disappear, then bent with the careful hip hinge of someone whose lower back had been through three collapsing buildings.

“And no kitchen victory lap.” She rubbed behind his ears. “You feeling off?”

Maledict intended to recoil from his enemy’s touch. Pickle’s ears, traitorous structures, leaned into her fingers. The spot was astonishing.

He could correct course. The response key lived in the home office, keyed to Brightguard’s pulse but transportable when she wore it. Pickle normally fetched her left wrist guard at the emergency tone. Maledict had arranged an emergency. At nine, drones would begin peeling the municipal archive’s roof like the lid from a tin.

Until then, he had only to behave like a dog.

Brightguard opened a cabinet. “Salmon crisp?”

His studies had not covered this either.

He accepted the little pink square cautiously. Salt, smoke, fat. It shattered between his teeth.

Maledict sat without being asked.

“Oh,” Brightguard said. “So we remember that one.”

***

Across the Tri-City Area, on the seventy-first floor of a black glass skyscraper with its own weather instruments, Maledict’s butler removed a bronze letter opener from Maledict’s mouth.

“No, sir.”

Maledict’s human body released it readily and put both hands on the carpet. The body was forty-two, tall, and ordinarily carried with enough menace to make a room rearrange itself. At present it sniffed the butler’s cuff, sneezed, and crawled under a steel console after a stray almond.

The butler closed his eyes for half a second. His employer had described the contingency as *temporary cognitive misalignment*. The brass dial on the exchange console said 00:11 ELAPSED and 13:49 TO RETURN. Its paired silhouettes—one human, one canine—glowed a reassuring green.

Nothing else about the morning was reassuring.

He canceled the nine-thirty intimidation of a zoning commissioner. He redirected three senior operatives from the residential floor. Then he moved the glass coffee table, sealed the interior stairs, and spread a duvet on the carpet where Maledict’s body could lie without bruising adult knees.

“Water,” he said, placing a shallow mixing bowl beside the duvet. “Please take it slowly.”

Pickle-in-Maledict’s-body slapped one hand into the water and looked delighted.

The butler fetched towels.

The instructions lay open on the console, written in Maledict’s compressed technical hand.

EXCHANGE PRESERVES TWO LIVING OCCUPANTS. NO BLEND. NO COPIES. NO DELETIONS.

DEFAULT RETURN: FOURTEEN HOURS.

There were two more lines beneath a black security strip. The butler tried a lamp, a polarized lens, and a document scanner. The strip remained black.

Pickle’s attention shifted to the apartment door. The human body bounced once on the balls of its feet, then glanced back.

“I regret that the terrace is inadequate.” The butler touched the secure lift control. “We will use the service garden.”

Pickle bounced again.

“Yes. Now.”

***

At eight fifty-seven, Brightguard’s alarm gave three rising notes.

Maledict sprang from the heated oval bed in the living room and sprinted for the office. At last, the plan.

“Guard, Pickle.”

He crossed the office threshold. A low electrical hum prickled through his paws, unpleasant but tolerable. Brightguard stopped fastening her field harness.

“Pickle.”

He kept going. The left wrist guard lay in its charging cradle beside the response key, a flat red wafer no larger than a thumbnail.

“You hate this floor.”

Maledict turned. Brightguard stood in the doorway with one silver brow up.

The correct behavior, apparently, was not to enter the room containing the thing he needed. He backed onto the hall runner.

“That’s more like you.” She pointed at the guard. “Can you bring it?”

He had rehearsed this. He trotted to the cradle, ignored the current fizzing through his pads, and took the guard gently between his teeth.

The red wafer sat half an inch away.

One sweep of the tongue—

“Not the key.”

Brightguard’s tone changed less than her posture did. Her knees softened. Her right hand settled near the harness control at her ribs.

Maledict lifted his head with the guard and attempted Pickle’s innocent expression. He had practiced it from surveillance stills. Judging by Brightguard’s face, he had produced an expression associated with tax fraud.

She took the guard, wiped dog saliva from its inner seam, and clipped it on. “Office stays locked today.”

From a wall screen came an aerial view of three drones descending toward the archive. Brightguard swore mildly. Maledict’s chest filled with satisfaction.

“Somebody’s getting predictable.” She tapped her wrist. “City response, this is Brightguard. I’m three minutes out. Keep people off the west roof.”

She crossed to the balcony launch panel, then looked back at him. He sat exactly where she had left him.

Pickle, he recalled too late, brought her shoes.

“No shoes?”

He ran for the entryway, selected a blue sneaker, and returned with it.

Brightguard stared at the shoe. “Those are for walking. You bring the red boots for work.”

Maledict dropped it.

The building shook as the launch doors opened. Wind pressed the fur flat along one side of him. Brightguard hooked her helmet to the harness, its clear visor waking with maps and civic channels.

“Blanket’s on the sofa. I’ll be home for the noon walk.” She hesitated. “Don’t eat the key.”

Then light gathered under her boots, and she shot between the towers.

Maledict waited until the balcony sealed. He raced back to the office. The door rejected paw, nose, voice, and one shoulder-first assault that hurt more than it accomplished.

He found Pickle’s communication mat under the kitchen bench. Six rubber buttons offered OUT, WATER, PLAY, BLANKET, BRIGHTGUARD, and CHEESE in Brightguard’s recorded voice. He pressed OUT, then BRIGHTGUARD, then CHEESE by accident.

A dispenser chimed and released a small golden cube.

He ate it.

After a moment’s reflection, he pressed CHEESE again.

The dispenser said, “All done.”

“Rrrr,” said Maledict.

At nine twenty, the cleaning robot emerged. At nine twenty-one, Maledict remembered that Pickle rode it from room to room on Tuesdays. He climbed aboard for camouflage. The robot warmed its top panel, played quiet jazz, and took him directly past the locked office toward a broad window full of morning sun.

Maledict woke at eleven forty with his chin on the robot’s soft bumper.

***

The service garden occupied the skyscraper’s fifty-sixth floor, a strip of turf between solar fins. Pickle-in-Maledict’s-body refused shoes but consented to socks after the butler rolled each one over a human foot slowly enough to be inspected. The suit was impossible. He found a black tracksuit in the private gym.

“This arrangement is temporary,” he told the head of security through the closed garden door. “Mr. Maledict is unavailable.”

Behind him, Pickle chased a falling leaf, caught it against the glass, and looked for praise.

“Well done, sir.”

Pickle grinned with Maledict’s entire human face. The result was dreadful. The butler nevertheless clapped twice.

At 04:26 ELAPSED, he offered a meal on an unbreakable plate. Pickle rejected toast, eggs, melon, and an expensive mushroom preparation. Chicken disappeared. Peas went next. When the butler placed the salmon garnish down, Pickle made a breathless sound and offered his left hand.

The butler took it. “Thank you.”

Pickle touched his nose to the butler’s fingers.

The gesture was so practiced that the butler looked toward the exchange console.

He had assumed the animal body was a disguise selected for access. He had not considered that the animal might have come from an occupied life.

At four hours and forty-five minutes elapsed, he searched Maledict’s planning files. The target packet included Brightguard’s address, patrol routes, dog-walker cancellations, food orders, and a photograph of a small brown dog with one naturally white forepaw asleep under a lemon-yellow blanket. The animal was labeled ACCESS BODY: PICKLE.

The butler returned to the residential suite. Pickle was sitting at the secured elevator, one human hand resting on the seam.

“Home?” the butler asked.

Pickle looked at him, then at the door.

“Yes,” he said. “I believe so.”

***

Brightguard returned at noon with a smear of drone lubricant on her cheek and no patience left for mysteries.

Maledict met her at the door because the lunch pouch at her belt smelled like beef. Pickle usually spun twice before greeting. Maledict remembered after one turn, attempted another, and collided with the umbrella stand.

Brightguard caught it without looking. “All right. Kitchen.”

She set her helmet on the counter and crouched. Up close, fine fatigue lines webbed the skin around her eyes. “Show me what hurts.”

Nothing hurt. Maledict pressed CHEESE.

“That wasn’t the question.”

He pressed OUT.

“We’re going. First, paws.” She picked up Pickle’s soft walking harness. “Blue or green?”

Maledict selected blue because blue was the color of dominion.

“You’ve refused blue since it pinched you at the lake.”

He removed his paw.

“And you’ve never forgiven the mail carrier, but you let her scratch your ears this morning. You slept through the blender. You went into my office.” Brightguard sat back on her heels. “You know commands you shouldn’t and forget things you love.”

Maledict pressed OUT with emphasis.

Her wrist display pulsed. She read the caller identification, and her face went still.

“This is Brightguard.”

The butler appeared on the kitchen wall screen, framed by dark stone and a slice of cloud. “Madam. I serve the man you know as Maledict. I believe I have your dog.”

Maledict lunged for the wall controls. Brightguard closed one hand around the back of his harness and lifted him onto the counter.

“Show me.”

The image widened. Maledict’s human body crouched beside a lemon-yellow throw the butler had evidently found in a guest room. The moment Pickle saw Brightguard, he scrambled upright. His hands struck the screen. Then he vanished from view and returned carrying one black dress shoe in his teeth.

Brightguard’s breath caught.

“Red boots for work,” she said.

Pickle dropped the shoe, searched frantically offscreen, and brought back a burgundy house slipper.

“Close enough, baby.”

He spun twice.

Brightguard gripped the counter until the composite edge creaked. When she spoke to the butler again, her voice had the clipped steadiness of civic radio traffic. “Is he injured?”

“No. He has eaten, taken water, rested, and used the garden. I’ve barred the stairs. His distress increases at closed exterior doors.”

“He’ll want home. Don’t promise it unless you can deliver.”

“Understood.”

“How long?”

“The device indicates automatic return at nine this evening. Fourteen hours after exchange.” The butler glanced aside. “There are concealed instructions I have not yet opened.”

Maledict found Pickle’s text tablet docked beneath the communication mat. Its large keys were meant for Brightguard’s gloved hands. He pawed laboriously:

THIS IS A DEEPFAKE.

Brightguard looked at the message, then at him.

He added:

I AM PICKLE.

Onscreen, Pickle shoved his borrowed slipper at the camera and whined.

“No,” Brightguard said. “You’re really not.”

Maledict began typing a threat. Brightguard opened the beef pouch.

He lost his place.

The journey to the skyscraper required a ventilated carrier, because Brightguard did not fly with unsecured passengers. Maledict refused to enter until she lined it with Pickle’s lemon-yellow sofa blanket. He then discovered a cooling vent at nose height and spent the flight with his chin on folded fleece, watching the Tri-City Area stream beneath him.

The butler kept Pickle on the residential side of the laboratory door, away from the body that had been taken from him. Brightguard moved back and forth: checking the device with the butler, sitting on the floor with Pickle, bringing Maledict measured snacks so he could not claim starvation and could not eat himself sick. Maledict meant to use those hours to recover command of the situation. The tower supplied warmed towels, a silent brush with flexible rubber teeth, and braised beef whose preparation had once occupied a chef through an entire hostage negotiation.

By eight thirty, he had revised his strategic objectives.

***

At eight fifty-three that evening, four occupants waited in Maledict’s private laboratory: Brightguard in full harness; the butler beside the exchange console; Pickle in Maledict’s body on a padded exercise mat; and Maledict in Pickle’s body beneath the main worktable, finishing a bowl of braised beef.

The two anchor plates stood eight feet apart. One was human-sized. The other held the imprint of four small paws. A line of violet light joined them through the floor. In the console, the exchange’s single braided filament had blackened at both ends; it retained enough charge to complete this one finalization cycle and nothing after it.

“Seven minutes,” the butler said.

Brightguard knelt beside Pickle. The human body was exhausted from being strange. He leaned his forehead into her shoulder while she rubbed between his shoulder blades.

“You’re going home,” she said. “Then the vet, then your own bed.”

Pickle tugged at the padded blue harness Brightguard had put on the dog body across the room. Maledict bared Pickle’s teeth.

“Green tomorrow,” Brightguard said without turning. “I heard you.”

The butler had exposed the hidden writing with heat from the console’s own vent. He read it again. “The automatic return is intact. When the dial reaches fourteen hours, each occupant returns to the body in which the exchange began. No memory or identity transfer beyond that movement.”

Maledict climbed onto the smaller plate. A black rivet nestled beneath the edge of his collar.

Brightguard saw his paw move. “Leave that alone.”

He pressed the rivet three times.

The console struck nine o’clock and went violet.

Pickle jerked against Brightguard. Maledict remained a dog. The dial cleared and printed 01:59:59.

The butler leaned over it. His composure narrowed to a white line around his mouth. “You’ve engaged the occupant hold, sir.”

Maledict went to the text tablet on the floor.

I REJECT REVERSAL.

Brightguard moved between him and Pickle. “You don’t get to reject it for both of you.”

THE BODY SUITS ME.

“That body is Pickle’s.”

I HAVE CONQUERED IT.

Brightguard picked up the tablet before he could continue. “No. Pickle gets Pickle. You can choose what happens to you.” She handed the tablet to the butler. “Find that choice.”

Maledict barked at her. The sound had more outrage than menace. From the mat, Pickle barked back using Maledict’s human lungs—one rough, startling syllable—then hid his face against Brightguard’s side.

The butler traced the concealed lines below the instructions. The violet light had made more text visible.

“The hold suspends return,” he said. “It opens a two-hour finalization window. At expiry, the present exchange becomes fixed.”

Brightguard’s gaze cut to the descending seconds. “Other options.”

“Mutual restoration.” His finger moved. “Or restoration followed by source recast.”

Maledict stopped barking.

The butler read silently for several seconds. “Recast returns both occupants first. It then reshapes only the initiating body—your body, sir—around its restored occupant. The dog’s body and occupant are excluded. The change is irreversible and requires continuous confirmation from you after you are human again.”

Maledict took the tablet.

DOG?

“An available template,” the butler said.

WITH BED?

Brightguard stared at him. “We’re at one hour fifty-eight, and that’s your first question?”

Maledict typed:

SNACKS ALSO.

“Pickle’s bed is Pickle’s. Pickle’s snacks are Pickle’s. Pickle’s home is Pickle’s.” Brightguard unsealed her helmet and set it aside. “If you recast yourself, the butler remains responsible for you and your operation gets dismantled. I’ll supervise temporary containment because I have the space and because he”—she rested a hand on Pickle’s borrowed shoulder—“comes first there. Separate bed. Separate bowls. No office. If Pickle wants you across the room, you go across the room.”

The butler folded his hands behind his back. “I will manage your legal affairs, salaries, surrendered equipment, and restitution. If you remain in Pickle’s body, I notify emergency services now.”

Maledict looked from one to the other. His message came more slowly.

NO TOWER?

“Not unsupervised,” the butler said.

NO MONDAY BRIEFINGS?

“No.”

NO ZONING COMMISSIONER?

“Canceled.”

Maledict sat. Pickle’s tail swept once across the plate before he mastered it.

The laboratory waited. Beyond the glass, three cities burned in the harmless colors of traffic and office lights. Brightguard checked the timer, checked Pickle’s breathing, and said nothing.

At last Maledict pressed DOG.

The console offered a rotating field of canine forms. He nosed past anything resembling Pickle and stopped at a deep-chested black dog with long legs, upright ears, and a small gray patch under the chin. Distinct silhouette, distinct coat, no white forepaw.

“Larger,” Brightguard said. “We’ll need another gate.”

Maledict selected the form.

The butler placed Pickle on the human plate and Maledict on the canine one. “Restoration first. You will wake in your own body, sir. If you remove your hand from the confirmation field, recast stops before alteration begins. Once alteration begins, releasing your hand will not reverse it. Do you understand?”

YES.

“Pickle?” Brightguard held out her palm. Pickle placed Maledict’s left hand into it. She squeezed once and touched two fingers to his nose.

He went still.

The butler activated mutual restoration.

For one breath the violet line rose into a bright wall. Pickle’s dog body folded gently onto the smaller plate. Maledict’s human body straightened on the other, inhaling with his own lungs.

“Brightguard,” he began, his restored voice sonorous with habit, “you stand before the voluntary apotheosis of—”

“Pickle first.”

She had already unclipped the dog harness. Pickle tumbled into her arms, licked her chin, wriggled free, and ran two ecstatic circles around her boots. He offered the white-furred forepaw. Brightguard took it with both hands.

The butler checked the console. “Identity separation stable. Both occupants restored.”

Maledict placed his hand in the confirmation field.

“Thirty seconds,” said the butler. “You may still release.”

Maledict looked at the paperwork waiting on three screens, at his butler, and at the beef bowl beneath the table.

“Will the heated bed be of equivalent quality?”

“It will be appropriate to your size.”

Maledict kept his hand down.

The field closed around his consenting human body. Its light was opaque and brief. When it cleared, a black dog stood on the human plate, long-legged and entirely unlike Pickle. The gray at his chin gave him the grave appearance of a magistrate until he smelled the beef bowl and stepped directly into it.

Pickle retreated behind Brightguard.

“Across the room,” she told Maledict.

He started to object, found himself without a tablet, and went.

***

The veterinarian cleared both dogs at one forty in the morning. Pickle’s original body was unharmed. Maledict’s new one was healthy, microchipped, and increasingly offended by the indignities of a thorough examination. Brightguard carried Pickle home although he was perfectly capable of walking. The butler followed with Maledict on a reinforced lead and two shopping bags from an all-night pet store.

By breakfast, Pickle had slept in his heated oval bed, rejected the blue harness again, and inspected every room. His bowls, blanket, buttons, and place on the sofa remained exactly where they belonged.

Maledict’s new bed waited on the other side of the living room. It was larger, orthopedic, and—after a quiet adjustment by Brightguard—not quite as warm as Pickle’s.

The morning news displayed Maledict’s skyscraper behind a reporter. Authorities had found disabled drones, canceled operations, and records moving toward an independent investigator. Maledict himself remained missing. The butler, exact even at seven in the morning, had issued no comment on his whereabouts.

Brightguard set down two bowls. Pickle approached his and offered the white forepaw before she asked. She squeezed it once and touched his nose.

Maledict shoved in beside him.

Pickle growled.

“Wait,” Brightguard said.

Maledict backed onto the mat. He watched Pickle eat the chicken, rice, greens, and first salmon crisp. His ears followed each crunch.

Brightguard stretched one knee, checked the time on her wrist guard, and let him wait through the whole familiar ritual. Then she set down the second bowl.

Maledict forgot the news, the skyscraper, and breakfast decorum all at once.

stories.title: Nine Lives of Excuses
stories.prompt: you inherit a magic cat that gives advice about life when you complain to it. However, one day it snaps, giving you a long frustrated lecture about how much of a waste you are and that you are the source of your own problems
stories.body:
# Nine Lives of Excuses

At 8:13 on Tuesday morning, Mizzle was sitting on the signature page of my personal guarantee.

This was not sabotage. Mizzle sat on anything that was both rectangular and important, a preference that had survived all ten months since I inherited her. The guarantee had only become important at midnight, when I moved it from beneath a cookbook to the kitchen table. Before that it had been paperwork, which was a different category entirely.

I drank my coffee and discovered it was cold.

"Mizzle, this is disgusting."

She opened one green eye. "You poured today's coffee onto yesterday's and then forgot it beside the sink. Make fresh coffee."

Her eye closed.

That was how her advice worked. A sincere complaint, spoken directly to her, bought one reply. It could be six words or six minutes; the length belonged to Mizzle. Questions got silence. Praise got silence. Fake grievances got the kind of silence that included slow washing between the toes. In the first weeks after she came to me, I had treated the rule like a coin-operated wisdom machine. I complained about sleep, work, whether to buy cheap shelving, and the woman downstairs who practiced scales at seven in the evening. Mizzle advised blackout curtains, sending invoices on time, wall anchors, and growing up.

Mostly, she was useful.

My phone buzzed beneath the sugar bowl.

My sister's message read: FOUR O'CLOCK. If you're in, bring the signed guarantee. If you're out, tell me by noon so I can ask for the back unit. After four they keep the whole $8,400. I won't chase you again.

The message made it sound as if the decision had been sitting around waiting for me. It had, technically, but not in that accusatory way. There had been the first lease packet, and then revised numbers, and then the contractor's estimate, which altered the numbers enough that anyone sensible would have paused. My sister's answer to the estimate had arrived nineteen days earlier. A person could hardly be blamed for wanting the dust to settle around a life-changing decision.

Mizzle shifted. The corner of the guarantee appeared beneath her flank, already creased.

"She's cornered me," I said. "Mizzle, I can't believe my own sister would put me under this kind of pressure."

Mizzle stood.

She was a small gray cat, round through the ribs, with one white paw and a dark stripe down her nose that gave her face the look of a document someone had tried to amend. Her tail expanded to twice its ordinary width. She stepped off the guarantee, leaving four warm dents in the paper, and looked up at me.

"Your sister did not corner you this morning," she said. "You drew the corner, furnished it, lost the key in a bowl, and complained the room was poorly designed.

"You have been waiting to say this happened to you. I have watched you prepare. Six weeks ago you brought home those keys and slid them across the floor for me because you were happy. You said the front room could hold six tables, the ovens would go along the east wall, and your sister's morning buns would pay the rent before the lunch trade even began. You called her at eleven forty-eight at night. You told her you had found the place. You told her not to be afraid of the deposit because there were two of you.

"Then there were two of you when she paid eight thousand four hundred dollars, but only one of you when the landlord asked for signatures.

"I know the order. I slept on the first packet for three days. Each time you lifted me off, you stared at the last page, took a photograph of it, and put it back under the green cookbook. You complained that legal language was meant to trick people. I told you to mark what you did not understand and call the tenant adviser. You marked two paragraphs. You did not call. When your sister found the adviser, you complained that the appointment was too early. It was at ten thirty.

"The contractor's estimate was higher. That was a real problem. Your sister came here with the cinnamon rolls you left uncovered until they hardened, and the two of you cut the plan. She removed the second oven. You kept the painted sign. She asked you to choose between six tables and a longer counter. You said you needed to see both versions. She sent both versions. You opened neither for five days.

"On the sixth day you complained to me that spreadsheets make your eyes swim. I told you to read one line at a time. You spent forty minutes choosing a color for the bakery calendar instead.

"This is what you do. First a thing must be done. Then any person who names the thing becomes your new problem. The client who did not pay you was greedy until you found the invoice in your drafts. The landlord was neglectful while the pipe dripped under the sink, although you had not sent the photograph. The emergency plumber cost too much after you waited until the cabinet floor swelled and the door would not close. Yesterday I yowled through your call because my water dish was empty. You complained that I always need something at the worst time. You asked me what would make me stop. Water made me stop.

"You collect advice so that the choosing will belong to someone else. If the advice works, you were clever to ask. If it fails, you were misled. If you never follow it, you remain a person who might have succeeded under better circumstances. You have asked me whether to sign this guarantee four times without complaining, because you know questions do not compel me. Then you complain about your sister, hoping I will answer the question you are too proud to ask and too frightened to answer.

"You are not cornered. You are the source of the pressure in this room. Your sister's messages became sharper because you ignored the soft ones. The deadline became dangerous because you used the safe days imagining how trapped you would feel on the last one. Her money is at risk because you asked her to risk it and then treated your name as the only expensive part.

"And yes, you are a waste. You waste food, work, sleep, favors, money, and every answer you drag out of me. You waste your sister's competence by turning it into rescue. You waste your own talent by keeping it theoretical, where nobody can reject it. You have spent ten months making me hear the same complaint wearing different trousers, while I depend on you to remember water and food and the box in the laundry cupboard. I cannot leave. I cannot tell you in words that my dish is empty unless you first make my need about your inconvenience. Then you ask why I sound impatient.

"Perhaps you do not want the bakery. Perhaps you only wanted to be the person who was brave enough to propose one. I do not know. You have hidden so thoroughly behind delay that even you may no longer know. But do not stand over a paper you requested and tell me your sister built this morning. If four o'clock costs her more, it will be because you used the safe days without answering and made everyone ask again."

Her mouth closed. The refrigerator hummed. Somewhere in the building, a pipe knocked twice.

I realized I was gripping the handle of my mug hard enough to ache.

"That was vicious," I said.

Mizzle's whiskers angled forward, but a statement was not a complaint. She said nothing.

"The pipe was rotten before I ever moved in, Mizzle. I hate how you turn every bad thing into evidence against me."

"The pipe was rotten," she said. "The soaked cabinet was seven days of you not sending one photograph. I used the examples I have. You selected the one with a rotten pipe and ignored the draft invoice, my empty dish, your sister's six messages, and the paper under my body."

"The invoice got paid."

Silence. Another statement.

"It's unfair that you get to decide when something counts as a real complaint."

Mizzle sat down. "I do not decide. You do. That is why your voice changes when you mean it."

I hated that answer partly because I could hear the change she meant. I tried, "Mizzle, the weather is persecuting me," in a tone of theatrical despair.

She began washing her white paw.

"Should I sign?"

The paw passed over one ear.

"You just spent all that time telling me I caused this, and now you won't even tell me how to fix it."

"Correct," she said. "I will not choose whether you bind yourself to a business."

"Then what was the point of any of that?"

Question. Silence.

I picked up the guarantee. The last page asked for my signature beneath a paragraph stating that I understood what I was undertaking. My sister had placed a yellow tab beside the line. The tab said SIGN, not because she thought I could not identify a signature line but because she had once watched me return an unsigned tax form.

"You act like signing is the honest answer," I said. "But I can't stand the idea of being there at five every morning, smelling fryer oil in my hair, smiling at people who say a five-dollar pastry is too expensive. I don't want to spend the next five years pretending the rush is exciting. I don't want it anymore, and that makes this whole thing impossible."

Mizzle stopped washing.

"Then tell her," she said. "Leave out the five years and the fryer oil if you need to. Tell her you do not want it."

"You don't know what my sister can afford. You don't know why I stopped wanting it. You don't know whether I'll regret it."

"No. I know what I saw and what you told me. I know you wanted the shop when you found it. I know you stopped opening the plans. I know your sister paid because you promised. I do not know her accounts. I do not know whether the shop will succeed. I do not know what you will want next year. I know she does not know what you want today."

"So tell me what to do."

Mizzle looked at me for a long moment, then jumped down. I had given her an order, not a complaint. She walked to the bedroom, pushed her head through the door I had left almost closed, and disappeared.

I flattened the signature page over the rest of the packet. My pen was in the key bowl beneath three dead batteries, a grocery receipt, and the brass ring holding the temporary shop keys.

Ninety minutes passed. I read the guarantee twice, opened the bakery projections, and answered no messages.

Signing would have solved the immediate problem. It would prove Mizzle wrong about me wasting advice. It would prove my sister right to trust me. It would turn the morning into an ugly but useful shove, the kind successful people later thanked someone for.

I wrote the first stroke of my name.

Then I saw what I was doing: letting an angry cat choose, only in reverse.

At 10:26, I tore the signed corner off rather than pretending the mark had been accidental. I printed a new page. At 10:41, I put the guarantee, the two shop keys, and the contractor's revised plan into my canvas bag. I did not send my sister a message saying we needed to talk. I had sent three of those already.

The shop was a forty-minute walk if I cut through the park. I left at 10:47.

Outside, the morning had the chilly brightness of a day that resented coats. Delivery trucks occupied half the curb. At every crossing, I composed explanations in which the estimate had changed, the lease was aggressive, retail was unstable, and my sister had moved too quickly. Every sentence was true enough to be useful. None included the fact that nineteen days ago, while we stood in the empty shop with blue tape marking the counter, I had imagined arriving before dawn and felt not fear but absence. Nothing. No warm leap at the room becoming ours. Only the wish to go home.

I had known then. I had let her order the electrical drawings twelve days ago.

The brass keys knocked against my water bottle all the way there.

My sister was kneeling inside the front window when I arrived. She had a tape measure stretched from the wall to a strip of blue tape on the floor. In the bare room, every sound returned thinner. The previous tenant's sign brackets remained above the window, and flour-colored dust from the ceiling repairs lay in the corners.

She looked at the canvas bag. "Did you sign it?"

"The guarantee puts a lot of exposure on both of us. With the revised build-out, there are concerns that I don't think we've fully—"

"Yes or no?"
