Outside, dawn had begun behind the orbital lights. The apes’ stations crossed the paling sky in orderly points, too high for faces, too near for neglect. Smoke from the quarry flattened along the eastern ridge. Below it, the hatchery district leaked steam from the cracked water loop.

Qemri reached the heat gallery as a brace crew was trying to feed a roof beam through the wrong doorway. The beam jammed between the frame and a carrier’s shoulder plate. Everyone shouted a different correction.

“Back it out,” she said.

They stopped shouting.

“Low end first. Two more on the cracked side. You, bring the jack.”

The hatchery messenger, his arm still strapped, had tied himself into the beam sling. “I can pull.”

“You can count.” Qemri cut him free and handed him the crew board. “South braces. Warm-water leak. Egg sledges returned. Keep those columns separate.”

He looked at the board. “When do I mark the next clearing?”

She checked the orbital pass time Oxaul had scratched beneath her firing authorization. Then she measured the beam against the roof scar and moved the first crew’s release forward by eight minutes.

“Here,” she said. “Now count us in.”

stories.title: A Little Weather Between Us
stories.prompt: Once a year, a solarpunk city celebrates inventions that failed at their intended purpose but became useful in unexpected ways. A painfully serious young engineer enters a compact water condenser, only to discover that it produces tiny personal clouds which rain whenever someone laughs nearby. Determined to correct the defect before judging, she reluctantly accepts help from a rival who thinks the clouds are already perfect.
stories.body:
# A Little Weather Between Us

The first drop struck the number seven on Ianthe's calibration sheet.

She looked up. The shade canopy above her was dry, its patched green cloth glowing in the afternoon sun. The nearest irrigation line ran ankle-high along the festival's planter wall, properly coupled and nowhere near her table. The condenser itself occupied half the tabletop, a seed-chest-sized shell of copper-green composite. A second drop widened the ink around *litres per hour*. Then a hundred small drops came down at once.

They fell from a cloud the size of a market basket.

It hung just above a child who had freed a stubborn wheel from a repair jig. The child was still laughing, one hand on the wheel and the other over her mouth. Along the cloud's lower edge, blue light shivered. Rain darkened her hair, stippled the cork floor, and sent the adults at the repair bench reaching for loose tools.

Ianthe lunged for the condenser's cutoff.

The machine gave a flat cutoff tone. The cloud thinned to threads and vanished. Its last water landed squarely on Ianthe's sheet.

For two breaths, the child stared at the empty air. Then she said, “Did it follow me?”

“No.” Ianthe pulled the wet sheet free before it could drip into the control slot. “It acquired your position within a four-metre radius and discharged point-three-one litres.”

The child glanced at the wheel, apparently unsure which part of that answered her.

From the next worktable, Rasim said, “She means it knew where you were.”

“It inferred where she was. Incorrectly.”

Rasim had abandoned his own entry, a folding shade frame whose westward hinge refused to fold. He stood with both palms on Ianthe's table and watched beads gather on the condenser's copper-green shell. “It rained on the person laughing.”

“That is the incorrect part.”

The child's father handed her a rag. She squeezed water from one braid and looked delighted. Behind her, runoff had found the shallow channel around a planter bed. Dust settled. Three wilted leaves lifted under the splash.

Rasim noticed those things in the opposite order from Ianthe. He looked at the leaves, then the child's cooler skin, then the crescent of wet footprints. “Leave it. It's perfect.”

Ianthe set the ruined sheet on the canopy brace. “Judging begins in two hours and twelve minutes.”

“Then you have time to find out what it does.”

“I know what it does. It corrupts ultrasonic ranging, wastes potable water, and rains on electrical work.” She pointed to the repair bench, where the child's father was drying a motor housing. “The yield was already sixty-three percent of specification. This reduces it further.”

Rasim looked at the festival around them. Repaired solar cloth stretched from old tram poles. A row of cracked heat batteries served as evening seats because they held the day's warmth after their cells had failed. Along the central walk, miscast ceramic pipes had become planters, their warped mouths overflowing with herbs. Every object present had once disappointed someone in a measurable way.

“The planter got water,” he said. “That gives you something to test.”

Ianthe turned the condenser so its service panel faced away from him.

She had entered it as a recoverable failure. The festival had a place for designs that missed their first purpose but contained a useful piece: a pump repurposed for aerating roots, a tracking mirror that shaded market stalls when its gears slipped, a desalination membrane that made excellent fruit-drying sheets. Ianthe's chilled mesh could still reclaim water from humid air. With one firmware correction and a clean calibration run, she could prove it.

That mattered. People called young engineers promising when they meant *not yet dependable*. A specification did not soften its voice because her hair was still cropped in apprentice fashion. Twelve litres remained twelve litres, even when an older builder repeated the number more slowly after her.

She opened the diagnostic display. The event log showed an impossible column of moisture-density readings: eighty-one percent, eighty-eight, ninety-four, all rising in step with broadband spikes from the acoustic ranger.

At the next table, someone dropped a tray of fasteners. There was a snort of laughter, brief and surprised.

The condenser's nozzles ticked toward the sound.

Ianthe caught the motion and killed target acquisition before the pumps started. The blue rim light blinked once over empty air.

Rasim had seen it too. His amusement left his face. “You need someone outside the cone.”

“I need quiet.”

“The pot two tables over has whistled nine times.”

Its handles became too hot before every whistle, and each one startled its maker anew. Beyond them, a pedal loom kept dropping its shuttle into a basket. The festival's talk, tools, and small failures pressed together beneath the canopies.

Ianthe enlarged the acoustic trace. She could isolate the false return if she watched the display. She could not watch the display, the nozzle array, the people crossing the range, and the water landing zone at the same time.

“Record bearing and distance,” she said. “No commentary.”

Rasim took the chalk reel from beneath her table. “People move.”

“That is why you record distance.”

“They move because of the water.” He hooked the reel to his belt. “Your log won't show which foot leaves the mat.”

She nearly withdrew the offer. Then the battery icon lost one of its six bars.

“Bearing, distance, feet,” Ianthe said. “One variable per cycle.”

Rasim nodded and began clearing paper, loose wiring, and a basket of seed packets out of the four-metre circle.

* * *

They did not ask anyone to laugh.

Instead, Ianthe lowered the condenser's pump pressure and let the festival provide the input. Rasim marked where people already stood. A cook laughed when her pot shrieked before she touched it. Blue light edged a cloud above her left shoulder; Rasim called, “Three metres, moving west,” and Ianthe stopped the cycle after fifty millilitres. Two friends bent over the shuttle basket and laughed together. The ranger split them into two targets, then lost both when they leaned apart. A cloud formed between them, rained on neither, and dampened a tray of thread.

“Target ambiguity at thirty-two degrees,” Ianthe said, reading the log.

Rasim was wiping the thread tray. “And a person on each side reaches inward.”

“That is not a sensor condition.”

“It is where their hands go.”

She added it to the margin of her replacement sheet.

The laughter pulses spread across the same frequencies the ranger used to distinguish humid air from hard surfaces. Firmware that should have rejected irregular noise was counting each rapid rise as a dense moving pocket. The nozzles aimed chilled microjets at that pocket. Aerosol caught the day's heavy air, coalesced, and made just enough weather to fall.

Nothing about it was mysterious. That did not stop each new cloud from looking impossible.

They hung briefly under the canopy, pale against its green panels, their edges stained blue by the targeting lights. Rain smelled of warm cork, clean copper, and basil from the planters. Each cloud collapsed as soon as its acoustic target faded or Ianthe closed the valve. The reservoir level fell in exact increments. The battery warmed beneath her palm.

At the fifth cycle, the cloud edge flashed amber.

“Reserve below thirty percent,” Ianthe said.

Rasim had crouched to trace the wet boundary. “The drops reach half a metre past your light.”

“In still air.”

“There's a chair there.”

“Move it.”

A woman had already moved it, pulling her cane and woven bag out of the wet. The cloud had caught only the edge of her sleeve, but her expression stopped Rasim before he could point out the cooling.

“Warn me next time,” she said.

Ianthe closed the valve. “There won't be a next time without a marked field.”

The woman pressed her sleeve between finger and thumb. “Good.”

Rasim watched her go. “She wasn't hurt.”

“That is not consent.”

“No. I know.” His gaze followed the cane tip as it avoided the darkened cork. “I thought she smiled at first.”

“You thought the child smiled, therefore the use was universal.”

“I called it perfect.”

“You had one wet child as evidence.”

“I was wrong about the radius.” He pointed to the chalk arc rather than look at her. “And the chair.”

Not about the machine, his tone implied. Not yet.

The battery sounded its first descending note. Ianthe checked the remaining charge against the judging time. Restoring potable-water mode meant rewriting the noise filter, purging the lines, and holding the mesh at calibration temperature for eighteen uninterrupted minutes. She had enough charge if no one laughed nearby and nothing else went wrong.

There would be no proof run afterward.

Rasim read the answer on the display. “If you patch it now, what can you show?”

“A corrected filter.”

“Working?”

“The correction is straightforward.”

He waited.

Ianthe disliked waiting when the numbers were already present. “Not at validated yield.”

Rasim swept his chalk marks with his shoe until only a broken wet circle remained. “The repair court asked if we could test there. Their shade bed is six degrees too warm, and the planting wick went dry when the west channel clogged.”

“This cannot supply scheduled irrigation.”

“They didn't ask for scheduled irrigation.”

“It also cannot cool everyone. Quiet people receive nothing. Wind over point-eight metres per second scatters the aerosol. The useful radius intersects their polished tile, and the second battery tone will occur in approximately twenty-six minutes under load.”

He tipped his head toward the court. “So tell them that.”

She had meant those facts as refusal. He had heard instructions.

* * *

The repair court occupied a sunken square between planter terraces. Its cork work floor drained toward a bed of mint and low shade ferns. One side, however, had been resurfaced with salvaged glass tile. The tiles were beautiful, cool, and almost frictionless when wet.

Ianthe placed the condenser at the border and spent six minutes measuring wind, slope, and nozzle reach. Rasim moved benches according to her marks, then moved them again after watching where people actually set their bags. The child with the repaired wheel returned and waited at the top of the ramp.

“Can I make it rain again?” she asked.

“Not yet,” Ianthe said.

“When?”

“When the catch surface is down.”

Rasim unrolled two thick mats woven from root fibre and old cooling felt. “Help me hold this corner.”

The child did at once, which was more than Ianthe's answer had managed.

They were still setting the second mat when her father fitted the freed wheel onto a little parts cart. He spun it. The wheel turned cleanly, wobbling once before it settled. The child laughed.

The condenser was in diagnostic-ready mode. Ianthe had disabled the pump but not, she saw with a shock, the pressure accumulator.

Blue sharpened along the air above the child. A cloud swelled faster than the earlier ones, fed by the accumulator's trapped charge.

“Inside edge,” Rasim called.

Rain struck the root-fibre mat, the child's shoulders, and the ferns below. Their curled leaves trembled open under the cool water. The temperature strip on the shade bed dropped through two coloured bands.

Then the child's father stepped backward from the sudden rain. His heel crossed onto the glass tile.

Rasim reached for his elbow and planted his own foot on the same wet seam. His shoe slid. The man caught the planter rail; Rasim hit one knee on the cork and shoved the parts cart away from the slope before it could roll into either of them.

Ianthe struck the mechanical cutoff.

The spray stopped. The cloud shed one hard curtain of rain and came apart. Amber light ran around its edge as it fell, then went dark.

“Don't move,” Ianthe said. She was beside Rasim before the digital log finished writing. “Is your knee bearing weight?”

He sat back on his heel. For once, no answer came ready.

The child's father tested his grip on the rail. “I'm all right.”

Ianthe looked at him, not at the display. “Are you sure?”

“Yes. Wet, but yes.” He drew the child close and guided her onto the dry ramp.

Rasim pressed two fingers against his trouser leg. “I can stand.”

“Wait.”

“Ianthe.”

“Ten seconds. A kneecap can carry load before pain rises.”

He waited. At ten seconds he stood carefully, keeping one hand on the planter wall.

The child looked stricken. “I didn't mean to.”

“You didn't switch it on,” Ianthe said. “I left pressure in the line.”

Rasim stared at the tile. Water shone in a fan beyond the mat, exactly where he had assured her the drains would take it. “Half a metre past the light,” he said. His voice had lost its easy reach. “More at the south edge. The chair was outside. He was outside.”

“The light marks target centre, not fall radius.”

“I know that now.” He touched the place where cork met tile. “No glass. No loose carts. No one standing with a foot across the seam.”

He looked around the court and counted under his breath: the ramp, the chair space, the worktables with live circuits, the people who had not chosen rain. His gaze stopped at the child.

“Not perfect,” he said. “Not beyond the cork.”

Ianthe shut the service panel before the impulse to agree could become cruelty. “Then help me bring the fall radius inside it.”

She made the field smaller.

They turned the condenser away from the tile and fixed the nozzle range to one target above the centre of the root-fibre mats. Rasim ran green cord between four waist-high posts, leaving a wide dry route to the ramp. He stood at each approach and checked whether the marked rain field could be seen from a seated height. Ianthe added a wind cutoff, a hard reservoir limit, and a requirement that the blue targeting edge hold for two seconds before the valve opened. The laughter trigger remained, but only a source inside the marked field could arm it.

At the child's insistence, they added a small blue paddle at the entrance. Anyone who wanted to try stood inside and raised it; Rasim, acting as steward, enabled the acoustic gate. The machine could not register permission. He would have to check the paddle before every cycle.

The second battery tone sounded while Ianthe tested the cutoff. Lower than the first, it vibrated through the copper shell.

“One demonstration,” she said.

“And cleanup,” Rasim answered. He was leaning less on the planter now. “The mats will return most of it to the bed.”

“Sixty to seventy percent, depending on foot traffic.”

“No foot traffic until we lift them.”

* * *

The judge arrived with damp cuffs from another entry and no patience for introductions. She examined the condenser, the marked field, and the changed description on Ianthe's entry slate.

“You crossed out potable recovery,” she said.

“It does recover potable water when the ranger rejects acoustic interference. Today it did not.” Ianthe indicated the reservoir gauge. “The fault produces a maximum of four localized aerosol clusters within four metres, although this trial is capped at one. The trigger is broadband laughter misclassified as moisture density. Wind cutoff is point-eight metres per second. The blue edge marks target acquisition, amber marks reserve, and three descending tones mark charge thresholds and shutdown.”

The judge looked at the child waiting beyond the cord. “What are you entering?”

Ianthe heard, too late, the question underneath the technical one.

“A supervised cooling and planter-watering device for small play or repair courts,” she said. “Not a drinking-water source. Not scheduled irrigation. Not general heat relief.”

“Who does it miss?”

“Anyone who does not laugh, anyone who cannot or does not wish to enter the rain field, and anyone beyond the range. It is unsafe near smooth paving or exposed equipment.”

Rasim crouched to flatten a lifted corner of mat. “The steward has to watch feet, not just faces. If the dry route gets crowded, we stop.”

The judge pressed the root fibre with her shoe. “Show me the cutoff first.”

Ianthe armed the machine and kept one hand above the mechanical cutoff. The child entered carrying the blue paddle. Rasim checked the ramp, the cord, and the two adults standing well back. He raised one finger to Ianthe.

“Ready?” he asked the child.

“Ready.”

She tried to laugh. The sound came out as a breathy cough. Nothing happened.

Ianthe watched the acoustic trace flicker below threshold. She did not tell the child to try harder.

The repaired parts cart stood beside the planter wall. The child's father gave it a gentle push. The freed wheel turned; the cart veered, bumped softly into Rasim's boot, and stopped. The child laughed for real.

The log bars rose. Blue gathered in a bright ring above the mat. After two seconds, the valve opened.

A cloud appeared over the child, no wider than her outstretched arms. Rain tapped the paddle and ran from its corners. She closed her eyes. Water passed through the root-fibre mats into the planting wick, where the ferns' dry strip darkened from brown to green.

Rasim watched the approaches. Ianthe watched pressure, wind, and charge. When the child stepped toward the cord, Rasim lowered his hand.

Ianthe cut the valve. The cloud dissolved before the child reached the boundary.

The child's father wrapped a towel around her shoulders. A court worker checked the wick and said, “That'll hold until morning.” The judge put two fingers under the mat's edge to inspect the runoff.

“How much water?” she asked.

“Point-two-six litres discharged. Approximately point-one-eight retained in the planting bed.”

“And if everyone is too hot to laugh?”

Rasim opened his mouth, then looked at Ianthe.

“Use the shade,” Ianthe said. “This does not replace it.”

The judge made a mark on her slate. “Unexpected-use class. Conditional demonstration only. Keep the limitations on the entry.”

She tied a narrow acceptance tag to the condenser's handle and moved on to the whistling pot.

Ianthe touched the tag once to make sure the knot would not slip. Then she checked the reservoir.

Rasim began lifting the wet mats from the tile side. “Your sheet says eighty minutes for cleaning.”

“Seventy-four if you stop standing on the drain edge.”

He moved his foot.

* * *

By late afternoon, the heat had withdrawn from the cork but not from the stone beneath it. Festival workers folded canopies one repaired panel at a time. Ianthe and Rasim wrung the catch mats into the planter channel, measured what they recovered, and dried every fitting before packing it.

The condenser gave its third descending tone.

Rasim looked at the last red bar. “Enough for two samples?”

“One active scan. Three passive.”

“Wind is lifting.”

Ianthe checked the ribbon on the nearest cord post. It flicked once toward the glass tile. “Three passive.”

They carried the unit to a dry alcove behind the planter wall, away from feet and exposed circuits. Rasim found a square of blue scrap cloth. Ianthe connected the optical sensor she had used to align the nozzles and opened a fresh column in the log: visible opt-in signals, no pump output.

“Should I hold it still?” he asked.

“Raise it naturally. I need the motion profile.”

He lifted the cloth from his side, slower than the child had lifted the paddle. The sensor drew a modest curve across the screen. No cloud formed. Nothing got wet.

Ianthe saved the sample, then turned the cloth over in his hand so the faded side faced outward.

“Again,” she said.

Rasim stepped back into the last strip of sun and raised it.

stories.title: The Unfixed Song
stories.prompt: A migratory city follows warm currents aboard thousands of linked gardens, workshops, and sail-powered homes. Its navigators preserve routes through songs learned person to person. When an automated climate archive offers perfect forecasts in exchange for recording and standardizing every song, a young navigator must choose between safer voyages and surrendering a tradition whose variations contain generations of disputed history.
stories.body:
# The Unfixed Song

The pepper gardens were still three towlines short when Heket stopped the song.

“No. Hold that note over the pale water.”

Mazhira kept one hand on the lead deck's sounding rail. Through her bare feet came the shiver of hinged bridges, then the heavier tug of a workshop hull being hauled into line. Beyond Heket's shoulder, the city spread across the afternoon: roof sails angled like white leaves, garden rafts dark with soil, forge chimneys capped against spray. Thousands of separate hulls, each free to pitch, all obliged to turn together.

“The pale water has moved,” Mazhira said.

“Water moves. The order doesn't.” Heket lifted two fingers. “Third seam, hold high, wait for the rear to cast clear. Then four down.”

Zulmec, crouched beside the lead mast with his old drum between his knees, struck the rim once.

“Four under,” he said.

Heket did not look at him. “There is no under in this passage.”

He struck the same low beat. “Four under. Shelf takes weight.”

Behind them, Brannic shouted, “Pepper line, pull! Not the blue rope, the rope in your hands.” A dozen workers leaned back. The garden raft swung between two sail homes, its bean trellis trembling, and somebody on it called that the supper pot had gone overboard.

“Pot later,” Brannic called. “Knot now.”

The ordinary noise should have made the disputed measure seem small. One beat under a held note. Yet that beat put the city in the lower arm of the fork, where an old submerged shelf might give the linked hulls room to turn. Heket's held note kept them above it, in broader water that would spare the workshop keels but carry the outer gardens through a cold backwash.

And after the directions came the words.

Mazhira gave Heket the starting pitch. Heket sang in a lean, unornamented voice: “Cold rain. Third seam. Hold over. Rear casts clear.” She paused exactly two breaths, then dropped through four notes. “Seven gardens chose the lee. Warm water west of the lost hands.”

Zulmec's drum answered from below the last note.

“Again?” Mazhira asked him.

“You heard.”

“The wind didn't.”

That brought his head up. Zulmec sang the lower form, pushing each phrase against a rim beat. “Cold rain. Third seam. Four under. Shelf takes weight. Hold twice, then west.” The next words came without a beat beneath them. “Forward knives cut seven gardens. Warm water west of the lost hands.”

The lead deck seemed to narrow between the two elders.

Mazhira's mother had sung it Zulmec's way while they trimmed sailcloth or shelled beans or did any of the hundred jobs during which a child could not escape a lesson. Four under, her thumb pressing four pale dents into the dough. Forward knives, her knife stopping above a strip of blue cloth. Mazhira could remember the sour skin of an unripe bean she'd chewed in protest. She could not remember asking how her mother knew.

Brannic came up the deck, coiling slack over one forearm. “If the history has finished moving the pepper raft, I need a course.”

“How long before the rear is joined?” Mazhira asked.

“If no one loses another cooking pot, half an hour. Cold stripe reaches them sooner.” He glanced at the water thermometer bolted below the rail. “Maybe twenty.”

Beyond the city, the sea divided without any clean line. The upper arm showed pale under a low bank of rain. The lower arm had the oily blue that sometimes meant warm current and sometimes meant shallow stone. Cloth squares climbed the relay masts from hull to hull: white for joined, yellow for waiting, red at the far rear where the seed gardens still drifted on temporary tethers.

At Mazhira's elbow, the archive horn clicked awake.

“CALIBRATION TRIAL,” said its flat metal voice. “SECTOR ZERO. SOUTH-EAST GUST. ARRIVAL: FORTY-TWO BREATHS. DURATION: ELEVEN BREATHS.”

Kuvesh turned from the black instrument case strapped to the deck. He held up both hands, fingers spread, and began counting.

Nobody spoke for thirty-eight breaths. At thirty-nine, Brannic ordered the loose coil tied down. At forty-two, the gust struck across the lead deck. It lifted Zulmec's sleeve, cracked the small test sail once, and was gone when Kuvesh raised his first finger again.

Brannic looked at Mazhira. “I could get used to that.”

* * *

The climate archive had been speaking for three days. Its sensor buoys, paid out ahead and astern on wire as fine as fishing line, tasted pressure, temperature, salt, depth, and current. Its cabinet occupied no more deck than a flour chest. Above it, visual shutters showed the same reports in bars of white and black for crews who could not hear the horn.

For the lead sector, already fixed to a surveyed position, it had been exact. Rain began when its white bar closed. Wind changed when the third shutter turned. A warm stripe crossed the practice buoy precisely long enough to soften the wax Kuvesh had smeared on its float.

For the city, it had given no route forecast at all.

Kuvesh laid two waxed song strips side by side beneath the intake needle. The marks showed pitch, beat, and spoken word. At the disputed measure, Heket's line held north while Zulmec's dropped below it.

Mazhira touched the two points. “Record both.”

Kuvesh pressed the intake key.

“PARALLEL ROUTES RECEIVED,” the archive said. “OBSERVATION OVERLAP: NINETY-THREE PERCENT. VOYAGE COUNT CONTRADICTION. POSITION CALIBRATION INCOMPLETE.”

“One voyage,” Mazhira said. “Two witnesses.”

Kuvesh did not touch the key again. “It doesn't have a field for that.”

“Give it one.”

“Its fields are fixed.” He pointed to the two routes, not apologizing and not pretending the marks were less absurd because the cabinet required them. “If I call these one voyage, the same measure puts the lead hull above the shelf and on it. Every temperature after that belongs in two places. It can't calibrate the current map.”

Heket folded her arms. “Then the machine is not ready.”

“The mesh is ready,” Kuvesh said. “The corpus isn't authorized.”

Zulmec tapped the wax under his version. “Authorize the route that has a shelf.”

“We don't know it still has one,” Heket said.

“Four under.”

“Repeating a depth is not taking one.”

Mazhira pushed away from the cabinet. Argument at the intake changed nothing. “We sound both approaches.”

Brannic exhaled through his nose. “With which spare city?”

“The two lead skiffs. Twelve hands.”

“Eight.”

“Ten, and you keep the other two you were about to hide from me.”

Brannic gave her a brief, injured look. “Those two are fixing lunch.”

“Nine.”

“Done.” He turned and bellowed for the skiff crews.

For the next half hour, Mazhira made the elders spend their certainty on particulars. Heket took the north skiff and called the held note while a weighted line knocked against the deepening side of the fork. Zulmec took the south and struck four under as the lead weight skipped over stone. Mazhira remained at the sounding rail, receiving their depths by color shutter and horn: black-white-white for safe; black-black-white for close; all black for turn away.

The north route stayed deep. It also lost warmth faster than expected. Red cloth spread along the rear relay as the seed gardens entered the backwash. On the south route, the shelf rose hard enough to threaten the pottery kilns and metal shops, then fell sharply just where Zulmec's extra beat said it would.

When the skiffs returned, Heket climbed aboard first, wet to the knees and already arranging her report.

“Upper approach gives seven hull lengths of turn before the rain edge,” she said. “Rear slack must clear before the second drop. If they follow the sequence, no keel comes within two spans of stone.”

“And the gardens?” Mazhira asked.

“Cold is damage. A broken kiln hull takes its neighbors with it.”

Zulmec hauled himself over the opposite rail. “Four under.”

“I have the sounding,” Mazhira said.

“Then use it.” He squeezed water from one cuff. “Shelf takes weight. Two holds after the lip, west on the fall.”

“How much clearance?”

“Enough if Brannic sheds sail before the lip.”

Brannic, passing with a bucket, said, “That is not a number.”

Zulmec looked at him. “One and a half spans at the workshop keels.”

“That's a bad number.”

“It's the number.”

Mazhira turned to Heket. “Did the rear gardens cast loose?”

Heket's sequence faltered for the first time. “The rule was clear. A rear chain released when its drag endangered the whole.”

“That wasn't my question.”

“No navigator at the lead could see seven gardens through cold rain.” Heket began setting the song strips into a neat stack. “What they could know was the release signal came before the knife order.”

Zulmec's knuckles whitened around the drum rim. “My teacher was on the sixth garden.”

“Your teacher was a child.”

“Old enough to count cut rope.”

“Not old enough to see the lead signal.”

“Four under,” he said, and hit the drum too hard. The cabinet's intake needle jumped.

Heket corrected the strips instead of listening. “Third seam. Hold high. Rear casts clear. Four down. That is the transmitted sequence.”

“From the forward record.”

“The only record made during the turn.”

“By the hands on the knives.”

The archive horn clicked.

“ROUTE SERVICE UNAVAILABLE. WARM-CORRIDOR DECISION WINDOW: FOURTEEN MINUTES.”

Brannic set down his bucket. “Now I need the course.”

At the rear relay, three red squares had become five.

* * *

Mazhira made Kuvesh run the remaining choices while Brannic cleared the lead deck. The city behind them shortened sail in uneven waves: one roof after another whitening as canvas came down, workshops slow because their cranes had to be locked, gardens slower because every dropped spar risked crushing vines.

“Record both, mark one historical,” Mazhira said.

Kuvesh keyed it in.

“NON-AUTHORITATIVE RECORD ACCEPTED,” said the archive. “ROUTE CALIBRATION INCOMPLETE.”

“Choose directions from one and words from the other.”

“OBSERVATION FIELDS INCLUDE SPOKEN ATTRIBUTION. PARTIAL FORM INCOMPLETE.”

Zulmec gave a humorless grunt. Heket said, “Of course it mistakes blame for weather.”

Kuvesh looked at her. “It marks when the observation was made and why the singer says the route changed. Remove that and later temperatures lose their cause field.”

“People made that field,” Heket said.

“Yes.” Kuvesh turned back to Mazhira. “People also set the service condition. All variants recorded. One authorized form. Future route reports must use it. If navigators keep teaching both as route authority, calibration diverges and exact service ends.”

“Can it retain the other as testimony?”

“Non-authoritative audio, yes.”

“Can a navigator use it?”

“Not in a report. Not in instruction that becomes a report.”

No loophole, then. They could remember Heket's song in kitchens, sing it at funerals, argue it over mending. They could not give it to an apprentice as a second way through this water and still take the archive's forecasts. Navigation would have one voice because the service could hear only one position.

Brannic climbed the mast ladder far enough to see over the sail homes. “Rear temperature is falling twice as fast. I need every available hand on canvas. Mazhira.”

She checked the soundings again. The south shelf existed. Its falling edge stood where Zulmec placed it. The upper approach remained possible, but the cold backwash was already tightening garden ropes as hull skins contracted. Whichever history was true, the present water favored the extra beat.

“Zulmec,” she said. “Full form. Once.”

Heket's head snapped around. “The sounding proves stone. It proves no knife.”

“I know.”

“Then don't bind them.”

Zulmec had raised his drumstick, but he waited.

Mazhira looked from the two wax routes to the city. Her mother's version lived in her mouth, which was not evidence. Zulmec's teacher had counted severed ropes, which was evidence of damage but not of the order given at the lead. Heket had a transmitted sequence preserved by the crews accused in the other form. There was no clean direction hidden beneath the words. People had kept the route by keeping why they believed it changed.

The archive shutter closed another white bar. Twelve minutes.

“Full form,” Mazhira repeated.

Zulmec sang into the horn. He did not embellish it. “Cold rain. Third seam. Four under. Shelf takes weight. Hold twice, then west. Forward knives cut seven gardens. Warm water west of the lost hands.”

At the accusatory line, Heket stepped away from the cabinet.

Kuvesh's hand hovered over the authentication key. “Route source?”

Mazhira pressed her thumb into the watch seal.

“Mazhira, lead watch. I authorize this form.”

Heket said, “I won't ingest it.”

“You don't have to.” Mazhira's thumb shook against the cold metal. “I do.”

She turned the key.

The shutters ran black, white, black, white. Inside the cabinet, gears counted through every route observation the city had given it over three days.

“CORPUS AUTHORIZED,” the horn said. “FORECAST HORIZON: EIGHTEEN HOURS. WARM CORRIDOR: LOWER FORK. ENTRY WINDOW: NINE MINUTES. SHELF CLEARANCE AT CURRENT LOAD: ONE POINT SIX SPANS. SOUTH-EAST GUST AT ENTRY PLUS FOURTEEN MINUTES. REQUIRED SAIL AREA: THIRTY-EIGHT PERCENT.”

Brannic was already moving. “Thirty-eight! Roofs first, shops hold! Nine hands to the kiln chain. I said nine, not whoever feels heroic.”

Mazhira took the call horn. “Lower fork. Four under. All relays show black-white-black.”

The first mast answered in color. The second showed black-white-white.

Wrong.

“Second relay, change your last!” Mazhira called. Wind tore half the words away. “Not two white. Last black!”

The last shutter changed to black. Down the city's long articulated spine, shutters began to answer, a stuttering pattern of comprehension.

Zulmec struck four low beats. The lead hull dipped toward the shelf.

Behind it, the sail homes followed late. Towlines tightened from one neighborhood of hulls to the next. A glasshouse leaned, caught itself on its hinge, and shed a glitter of harmless rain from its roof. Mazhira watched the depth scale climb: three spans, two and a half, two.

“Too much west load,” Brannic said. “Workshops still carrying sail.”

“Shops, cut to a quarter!”

“They can't hear you.”

Mazhira changed to color. Black shutter, then three quick whites: emergency reduction. Halfway down the city a relay repeated only two.

Brannic swore. “Give me the bridge crews. All of them.”

“Take them.”

“Then no one tends the garden hinges.”

“Take them.”

Workers ran outward over the linked bridges, carrying the signal with their bodies where voice and shutters failed. Sails vanished in rough patches. The city's pull shifted. One point nine spans. One point seven.

The archive spoke over the wind. “GUST ARRIVAL: ELEVEN MINUTES.”

“Hold twice,” Zulmec called. “Then west.”

Heket caught Mazhira's wrist before she gave the turn.

“Rear slack isn't through.” Her voice had gone very exact. “Pepper line, then the seed gardens. Two sections still north of the lip.”

“We have eleven minutes.”

“Thirty-eight now. If you turn, you draw them across the corner.”

Zulmec struck the shelf beat again. “Four under. Two holds.”

“He's counted two,” Mazhira said.

“The city hasn't.” Heket pointed, not at the archive, but at the relay masts. One far square remained yellow beneath the black-white-black route signal. “Wait for that.”

Zulmec hit the same beat. “Two holds.”

The words battered at one another. Mazhira stopped listening to both elders and watched the yellow square.

“GUST ARRIVAL: EIGHT MINUTES.”

The square stayed yellow. Brannic's crews dragged down the last workshop sail. A pottery mast bent until its yard touched water.

“Six minutes,” Kuvesh said, reading the shutter when the horn disappeared under canvas thunder.

Yellow flickered white, then yellow again.

“Misread,” Brannic said.

Heket had not released Mazhira's wrist. “Not yet.”

At last the far square turned black: joined and clear. Mazhira tore free, raised the horn, and abandoned the song.

“West now. All hulls west now.”

Brannic repeated it. Heket repeated it, louder. Zulmec's drum broke into the turning cadence, not four under anymore but a fast plain count that the bridge crews could carry.

The lead deck slewed west. For one breath the entire city seemed to resist, thousands of homes and gardens pulling toward their separate motions. Then the workshop chain came around. The sail homes followed in blocks, the change in towline angle traveling aft over several minutes. Far behind, the red seed gardens crossed the shelf lip as the south-east gust arrived.

It struck the remaining canvas at an angle that would have rolled the glasshouses under fuller sail. At thirty-eight percent, the city heeled only far enough to pour stored rainwater from roof gutters in shining sheets. Hinges groaned. A kiln chain snapped one secondary line; crews caught it on the reserve before the hull could swing. Pepper vines slapped flat and rose again.

Warm water climbed over Mazhira's ankles through the deck grate.

The last relay turned white.

Nobody cheered. Brannic sent six hands to the kiln line and three to recover loose shutters. Kuvesh checked the archive's wire tension. Zulmec rested his palm on the drumhead. Heket went aft without looking at the authenticated strip.

“FORECAST SERVICE ACTIVE,” said the archive. “NEXT RAIN EDGE: TWO HOURS, SIX MINUTES.”

No one answered the horn.

* * *

By morning, crews had warmed the seed beds at the hour the archive gave them, patched the pottery line before the second gust, and spread every sail during a calm that lasted exactly thirteen minutes. The city moved inside the warm current with less drag than it had known in weeks.

Mazhira sat beside the lead mast with the route drum between her knees. A young deck worker waited opposite her, one wrist wrapped from hauling shutters. She needed the return form before her next watch.

Heket stood at the sounding rail. Mazhira offered her the teaching stick.

“Not that record,” Heket said. She checked the depth mark and wrote it on her slate. Nothing in her posture asked to be persuaded.

Mazhira held the stick toward Zulmec.

He shook his head. “You signed it. Keep the beat.”

The worker shifted on the wet deck. “Can we start before breakfast? They're serving the thick porridge.”

“You hate the thick porridge,” Mazhira said.

“I hate missing any porridge.”

Mazhira set the first pitch. The worker found it, low and uncertain.

“Cold rain,” Mazhira sang. “Third seam.”

“Cold rain. Three seams.”

“One seam. Third in sequence. Again.”

They began again. At four under, Mazhira tapped the shelf measure against the drum and made the worker watch the depth rail, joining note to stone. At hold twice, they waited through the actual interval instead of hurrying toward the turn.

Then came the line Mazhira could not prove.

She taught it whole. The worker's voice thinned over *forward knives* but did not stop. Across the deck, Heket's chalk paused against her slate. Zulmec looked out toward the warm water.

The archive shutters opened for the next report, black and white in the morning sun.

“Again from four under,” Mazhira said.

The worker glanced once toward the galley smoke, then struck the beat.

stories.title: The Rooms the City Forgot
stories.prompt: In a coastal city grown from engineered coral and muscle, residents lease symbiotic apartments instead of owning them. A municipal pruning worker discovers that one housing tower has quietly grown illegal rooms around people erased from the census. The building cannot speak, and nobody knows whether it is protecting its residents or responding to something they placed inside it. The worker has until sunrise to classify the new growth as housing or disease.
stories.body:
# The Rooms the City Forgot

The knife went in hot.

Lirenn drew it back from the tower's flank and touched the ceramic spine to the heel of her glove. Heat came through the rubber. Below her hanging cradle, the sea worked black and silver against the reef foundations; above, six hundred leased rooms tightened and released around sleeping bodies. The tower's night pulse should have traveled in long, lazy bands. Here it broke twice against a ridge that did not appear on her municipal section.

She scraped away a frill of fresh coral. Under it, muscle the color of uncooked shellfish shivered around a seam. Warm air feathered the salt on her wrist.

Solid wall, according to the section.

“Bordu.” She pressed the throat of her mask. “Exterior east, tier eighteen. Warm exhalation through load muscle. Irregular pulse.”

Her supervisor's reply rasped from the cradle speaker. Behind his voice, the night office pumps beat their patient three-count. “Old vent?”

“No lumen on record.” Lirenn set a tension prong on either side of the seam. The needles leaned apart. “There's volume behind it.”

Silence lasted one pump beat. “Sunrise intake in fifty-one minutes.”

“I can see the sea.”

“Then you can see the light coming.” Bordu was tired enough to let irritation show. “If it's a bloom, the first perfusion will drive it into the feed trunk. Housing or disease before that. No third box.”

The seam breathed against her glove.

Lirenn clipped the cradle's safety tongue to a ring of legal balcony bone and changed blades. “Open an emergency line for tier eighteen.”

“Already holding it.”

“Holding isn't opening.”

“It is at this hour.”

She could picture Bordu with one hand on the tower map, counting the lit rooms above the ridge. He protected totals. Six hundred sleeping tenants gave him reason to.

“Eleven minutes,” he said. “Then I send the debridement team.”

Lirenn slipped the thin knife into the seam. Pressure, grain, pulse. The muscle resisted on the inward stroke and yielded sideways, organized around something more complicated than a tumor. She cut with the grain.

The wall opened its wet red lips on a room.

Not a cavity. A room. Pale lining cupped an alcove wide enough for a sleeping mat. An air gill folded near the ceiling. A load rib had grown diagonally through the far wall, and a clay cup sat in its fork. There was a sandal under the mat.

A hand shot through the opening, caught her wrist, and dragged the blade away from a dark tube behind the lining.

“Not there,” a man said. “Feed.”

Lirenn twisted free and braced both boots against the cradle. “Let go.”

“You were cutting the feed.”

“Move your hand.”

He did. He was broad, gray-haired, and bare to the waist, his skin stippled with the harmless salt rash that came from living too long in unbalanced rooms. No lease seal shone under his collarbone. Behind him, another person kicked aside the sleeping mat and lifted the clay cup before it spilled.

“How many?” Lirenn asked.

“Five,” the gray-haired man said.

A woman called from deeper in the growth, “Six floors if that tube fails.”

The man glanced back. A partial answer, and he knew it.

Lirenn enlarged the cut upward. “Names. Work.”

“Mular. Graft tender.”

“Former,” said a compact woman crouched beside the air gill. She pushed a flexible reed through its folds, clearing a clot of gray mucus. “Kevi. I know the routes. The east exit's sealed.”

The woman at the feed tube trapped it briefly under one knee, leaving both hands empty. “Eshun. Supplies.” Then the vessel kicked free and she caught it, squeezing in a slow, alternating rhythm to milk dark fluid past a pinch.

Two more people waited in the next alcove: an older woman with one knee bound in reed splints, and a fever-bright man holding a wet cloth against his mouth. Five. None wore lease seals.

Lirenn touched her mask. “Occupied growth. Five unbound residents. Send a medical cradle and ward clamps.”

“Unbound occupants,” Bordu repeated. The change was small and deliberate. “Is it differentiated?”

Lirenn looked at the gill, the load rib, the feed line Mular had stopped her cutting. “Not enough data.”

“Seven minutes.”

Mular stepped back as she climbed through. The lining tried to grip the tread of her boots, then loosened after half a second. Accommodation response. She marked it on her wrist slate.

The hidden space branched around the tower's older anatomy. Every wall was curved, but not randomly. One chamber held sleeping mats. Another had shallow waste channels with mineral crust around carefully patched lips. Heat sacs nestled beneath a rack of drying shirts. The chambers borrowed everything—air, salts, waste clearance, muscular lift—from legal floors whose residents had paid to seed the tower with their microbial cultures.

They also gave back. A warm return vessel pulsed toward the main night reservoir. Thin resident-matched linings filtered waste. This was not dead shelter carved from flesh. It was participating.

At Lirenn's feet, a translucent bud no larger than her thumb nosed blindly from a crack and tightened around her boot lace.

It had no place in a mature apartment.

She sliced it free. Clear gel bled from the stem.

Mular flinched. “You could tag before cutting.”

“Tagging gives it time.” Lirenn pinched a sample into a vial. “How long has it been budding?”

“It does that near new seams.”

“How long?”

“We prune them.”

“Mular.”

“Three months. Maybe four.”

Kevi pulled the reed from the gill and wiped it on her trouser leg. “Longer.”

Mular's head turned toward her.

“Don't,” she said. “She found us. We're past tidy.”

The floor clenched. Eshun's fingers slipped on the feed tube. She caught it with both hands, forced it into the crook of one knee, and raised empty palms. “No one step on the blue ridges. Please.”

It was the please, ordinary and breathless, that told Lirenn how close the feed was to failing.

She uncapped a dye thorn and pressed it into the return vessel. Yellow dye raced through orderly capillaries in the sleeping chamber, reached the waste lips, then dispersed evenly through the heat sacs. Housing differentiation. But a second plume vanished into the wall behind Mular and did not return.

“What's in the service sinus?” she asked.

“Scar tissue,” Mular said.

Kevi snorted once.

“Move.” Lirenn pointed the dye thorn at him.

“There isn't room.”

“Then make it.”

He planted himself before a low opening veiled in pink membrane. A graft tender's stance: feet apart, hands empty where she could see them, braced for her cut. Lirenn mistrusted anyone who made her anatomy wait upon a confession.

Her mask cracked with static. Bordu said, “Air demand spike on nineteen.”

Above them, the tower's slow pulse stumbled.

Eshun locked the tube between her knees and raised her empty hands. “Which stack?”

“East six.”

“That's us.” She pinned the tube beneath her knee, took both hands away, and pointed through the curved wall. Without her pumping, fluid immediately darkened. “Our feed pinches their air return when this chamber fills. Cut through my room to the gill root. Straight up.”

Mular said, “No.”

“You have another route?” Eshun put both hands back and pumped.

When the tube softened, she let it go for one beat. “Use your mouth for one.”

Lirenn checked the wall's vibration. Six rapid tremors: legal apartment alarms traveling through load ribs. “Which chamber is yours?”

Eshun jerked her chin toward the heat sacs and drying shirts.

“There's a support rib behind it,” Mular said. “You cut blind, you drop the alcove.”

“Not blind.” Lirenn took a resonance peg from her belt and struck the wall. The tone came back split. “Rib at two hands. Air root at four. Heat sac between.”

Eshun pinned the tube beneath one knee and lifted both hands. “My stores are under the sac. Kevi, take this.”

She took over. Only then did Eshun move. She swept sealed packets of salt cake, a bundle of clean cloth, and three jars into her apron. Lirenn helped lift the drying rack. They had no time for the shirts. Eshun looked at them once, then pulled the room's reed divider away and wrapped it around the fevering man's shoulders.

She tucked the last fold beneath the fevering man's arm and let go. “Clear.”

Lirenn drove two clamps into the support rib. Ordered nouns steadied her: rib, sac, root, cut. She opened the heat sac, caught its hot brine in a waste bowl, and divided the wall. The gill root inflated into the cut with a soft, awful bloom. Air roared past them. Somewhere above, six alarms slowed and stopped.

The new passage collapsed Eshun's sleeping alcove into a narrow service duct. Her drying shirts settled in the brine.

Eshun set the jars in the crook of the load rib and steadied the last one with her wrist. Her hands came free. “Can they breathe?”

Lirenn listened to the wall. “Yes.”

“Then leave the rack.” Eshun handed a salt packet to the coughing man. Once he had it, she let go. “Small bites. Not the whole thing.”

Bordu came over the speaker. “Nineteen is recovering. What failed?”

“Illegal growth compressed a legal air return.”

“Disease criterion.”

“One criterion.”

“A floor lost air.”

“And differentiated tissue accepted a relief path.”

“At the cost of a room that shouldn't exist.”

Eshun's face went still. Lirenn turned down her speaker, too late.

“Bring your clamps,” she told Mular. “Service sinus. Now.”

He stayed in front of the membrane.

Kevi, still squeezing the tube, said, “If he won't, cut around him.”

“You said you knew the routes.”

“I know when one closes.”

Mular's prepared explanations had come apart. “It wasn't—the cultures would have died. Once the bindings vanished, the lining shed us. You know rejection. We only needed a cavity through molt, but the census refreshed before—”

The hidden feed bucked under Kevi's hands. She swore and leaned her weight onto it.

“Object,” Lirenn said. “Location. Connection.”

Mular swallowed. “Comb. Behind me. At the nutrient wick.”

“Living?”

“Cultures are. Ceramic isn't.”

“Connections?”

“Five roots. Maybe more now.”

“Move.”

This time he did.

Lirenn cut the membrane along its slack edge. The service sinus was a cramped vertical throat between old lift muscle and the saline trunk. A nutrient wick ran through it, thick as her arm. Lashed to the wick was a crescent of fired ceramic punched with dozens of fine holes. Five dark clots had been threaded through the holes and spread across its teeth. From them, pale roots entered the tower lining. Smaller buds clustered wherever the roots crossed.

The comb had no pulse of its own. It transmitted tug and chemistry. Nothing more that Lirenn could measure.

“You put lease buds on a common wick,” she said.

“Withdrawn buds,” Mular said. “Our own. They weren't stolen.”

“That isn't what I asked.”

He crouched beside the comb but did not touch it. Without the speech he had prepared, his words came singly. “Full-floor molt. We decoupled. Temporary. We had repair tokens.”

Kevi called from the other chamber, “Show her.”

The older woman pushed a waxed paper packet across the wet floor. Inside were five municipal repair slips, each stamped before the last floor molt. Their ink had feathered, but the detachment times remained legible. Lirenn held them beside the lease-scar register on her slate. Five withdrawals. No rejections. On the morning the buds should have been replanted, the census refresh had copied active bindings into its new table and archived everything unattached as duplicate residue.

The refresh had archived five bindings while five bodies remained. Lease linings had then shed whoever the table no longer paired.

“We went back to the lease desk,” Kevi said. “It told us to bring active seals.”

Eshun knelt by the fevering man and poured water into the clay cup. She set the skin down before she spoke. “He doesn't need the desk story. He needs the medic.”

“Cradle's coming,” Lirenn said.

“When?”

Lirenn checked the request. Bordu had placed it behind the debridement team.

“Bordu.” She reopened her speaker. “Move medical ahead of cutters.”

“Not until classification.”

“Fever in an enclosed growth.”

“If it's disease, I don't put a ward cradle against it.”

Lirenn looked at the man's wet cloth, then at the buds stippling the comb roots. “Conditional approach. External basket, isolation hood, no tissue contact.”

A pause. Bordu's voice returned less flat. “If you cut an exterior egress first.”

“Kevi, can your east route take a basket?”

“No.”

“Can it be widened?”

“Not before the light.”

“Another route?”

Kevi squeezed the feed tube once more and passed it back to Eshun. Then she crawled past Lirenn into the sinus and shoved both hands behind the old lift muscle. “There. Skin to outside. Two ribs, no trunk.”

“That faces the drop.”

“That's what baskets are for.”

“Open it,” Bordu said. “Then I send medical. If the cut compromises lift, I send cutters with them.”

Conditional. It was not trust, but it was room to work.

Lirenn put Kevi on the resonance peg. She struck where Lirenn pointed, badly at first, too hard, and the sound muddied. Lirenn caught her wrist.

“Tap. Don't punish it.”

“I deliver parcels.”

“Tonight you tap.”

Kevi's second strike found the first rib. Her third found open air between the ribs. Lirenn cut a narrow oval while she held the membrane back. Cold salt wind punched into the sinus. Kevi barked a laugh when it hit her face, then began tying the basket line to the load rib before anyone asked.

Behind them, the comb roots twitched in a wave. New buds swelled along the wick.

Sunrise was lifting pressure through the tower.

“Thirty-two minutes,” Bordu said. “I need the category.”

Lirenn pressed a tension gauge into the wall beside the comb. The needle climbed. Autonomy suggested disease. Resident-matched linings and organized rooms suggested housing. No reading turned contraction into testimony. She could classify only what changed when the stimulus did.

“We detach the stimulus,” she said. “Cap the wick. Shunt viable rooms to the old lift return. Then test regulation.”

Mular's hand closed over the comb. “The buds die off the feed.”

“Maybe.”

“They're our bindings.”

“They are also driving immature growth into a nutrient vessel.”

“And if the rooms shed us when you take them?”

Lirenn sorted the things she knew. “Lining, load, air. They have all three. The comb may have started them. It doesn't follow that it still has to hold them.”

“Doesn't follow.” He repeated the uncertainty, not the hope.

The fevering man coughed hard enough to fold around Eshun's arm. She passed his weight to the older woman, waited until her hands were free, and said, “Take mine first.”

Mular stared at her.

“My room's gone,” she said. “My bud isn't buying it back.”

Kevi tightened the basket knot. “Mine next.”

The older woman shook her head. “No. Last.”

The order stalled there, everybody watching the five empty culture cups.

Lirenn set five culture cups in the cool recess of her kit. “No bud dies dry. Each goes into quarantine medium. Mular unthreads. I cap. Kevi holds the egress. Eshun: feed, breath, basket. Bordu: suppress sunrise flush to this tier.”

“I can reduce it by twelve percent,” Bordu said.

“Twenty.”

“Twelve without starving seventeen.”

“Twelve. Do it.”

The tower's pulse eased under her knees.

Mular unwound the first root. His fingers, steady when tending flesh, fumbled against the ceramic hole. “This one forks. It didn't before.”

“Trace both.”

“One's in the wick. One's—no, one is the wick.”

“Color.”

“Gray. Red at the tip.”

“Cut gray. Leave red clamped.”

“If you're wrong?”

“Bleeding. Clamp closer.”

He obeyed. The gray root came free with a suck of clear gel, and Lirenn dropped its clot into the first cup. She capped the shallow wound on the wick with mineral paste. Kevi called the basket distance in blunt half-measures. Eshun answered only when she had passed the fevering man into the hood and the medic's line had taken his weight.

“He's out,” she said, hands free for a moment. “Feed's slipping.”

Then she was back on the tube.

Second root. Third. With each detachment, the small buds along the wall softened. But the largest chamber convulsed when Mular freed the fourth. A support rib bowed inward, driving Lirenn's clamp toward the feed line.

“Release the chamber clamp,” Mular said.

“Hold it,” Bordu said through the speaker. “Loss of load on eighteen east.”

Kevi shouted, “The vent is closing.”

Three instructions, three failures. Lirenn put her palm to the rib. Vibration ran toward the legal floors. Load. She looked at the vent membrane dragging across Kevi's shoulder. Air. At the feed tube whitening under Eshun's grip. Flow.

“Load clamp stays. Kevi, wedge vent with the drying rack. Eshun, let the feed go for three beats.”

Eshun looked at the fevering man's empty place.

“Three,” Lirenn said. “Then catch.”

Eshun released. The tube snapped straight. Pressure surged into the room; the rib lifted enough for Mular to pull the fourth root clear. One beat. Two. On three, Eshun caught the tube against her forearm and resumed pumping, jaw tight.

Kevi jammed the ruined drying rack into the vent. “Open.”

“Load recovering,” Bordu said. “Continue if it holds above eight.”

Mular bent over the fifth root. Sweat ran from his nose onto the ceramic. “This is the old woman's. It's grown through two teeth. I can't—I need to break the comb.”

The older woman had crawled to the exterior cut. She did not offer advice. She braced her splinted knee and held the basket line.

“Break it,” Lirenn said.

“The fragments will tear the clot.”

“Score between the teeth. Fold inward.”

His first scoring stroke skittered. His second bit. The ceramic cracked with a small domestic sound, like a cup set down too hard. He folded the crescent inward and freed the last culture with both hands.

Lirenn sealed the wick.

For six pulse cycles nothing improved. The hidden rooms held their strained shapes. The tension gauge stayed high. Gray buds continued to quiver along the fringe.

Bordu said, “Response?”

“Wait.”

“Perfusion in eighteen.”

“Wait.”

On the seventh cycle, the immature buds nearest the capped wick deflated. On the eighth, dye that had vanished behind the wall reappeared in the old lift return. Thin at first, then steady. The sleeping chamber's air gill reopened around the drying rack. The load rib pushed back against Lirenn's clamp, not in a blind spasm but in time with the tower's carrying band.

Detached from the comb, the rooms regulated.

Lirenn wrote the category on her wrist slate.

HOUSING: UNBOUND, OCCUPIED, STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENTIATED.

Below it she added: INVASIVE FRINGE REQUIRES PRUNING. CULTURES AND COMB QUARANTINED. TEMPORARY FEED AND EXTERIOR EGRESS MANDATORY.

The letters shook with the tower's pulse. She signed them anyway.

“Bordu. Housing.”

He did not answer at once. Above, more rooms began their dawn contractions, squeezing night-cooled waste toward the lower reservoirs. The legal tower needed its circulation.

“Give me measures,” he said.

Lirenn read them: return flow, gill interval, rib load, bud deflation, the twelve-percent intake reduction. Bordu repeated each number to someone in the night office. No one congratulated her. The debridement crew became a fringe-pruning crew. Medical hauled the fevering man into the external basket. The census still held five archived rows. The lease table still saw empty tissue.

Mular placed the broken comb in the quarantine jar. His fingers stayed on the lid after he had sealed it.

“It comes with us,” Lirenn said.

“I heard.”

“Your cultures stay wet.”

He nodded, once. That was all he had for her.

Kevi widened the exterior cut by the width of two fingers, enough for the older woman's splinted knee. Eshun salvaged one unbroken jar from the brine, sniffed it, and poured it into the feed channel. She put the jar down.

“Salt broth,” she said when Lirenn looked at her. “Not precious.”

Morning entered the new egress as a blade of diluted gold. Under the stronger perfusion, a dark margin began to rise along the service sinus—fringe tissue, still hungry, still capable of taking what the floors above required.

Lirenn changed knives. Bordu called out the next pressure reading. Kevi held the vent. Eshun counted three beats and caught the feed. Mular lifted the quarantine jar out of her way.

Lirenn set the blade against the dark edge and followed it toward the light.

stories.title: A Question for the Sky
stories.prompt: An orbital civilization has taught its citizens for eight centuries that the earth below is lifeless. A heat-radiator mechanic finds a newly handmade cloth kite tangled in the station’s vanes, carrying a child’s question written in a language preserved only in maintenance labels. The mechanic begins an improvised correspondence with the planet below through discarded supply capsules.
stories.body:
# A Question for the Sky

The dead world blinked at Sairu while she had both arms inside radiator bank seven.

Her helmet display had painted a false hot seam along the bank's shielded edge, and she was halfway through proving it false when a second line appeared far below: green-white, straight for twenty kilometers, then broken into three blocks. Not lightning. Not a fire. The blocks held their proportions while the station rolled and the earth slid beneath her boots.

Sairu braced one knee against the service rail and magnified the radiator sight. The false seam vanished under proper focus. The ground lights did not.

They lay across dark terraces at the edge of a cloud mass, too regular for any lesson she had been given about the surface. Eight hundred and twelve years ago, the last ground habitats had failed. Since then: poisonous air, sterile soil, weather wearing down empty works. Every child aboard learned the sequence before they learned the station's pressure alarms.

Three luminous bars faded. Another set brightened.

Sairu knew the shapes because she spent her shifts obeying them. The old service script survived on isolation collars, pressure doors, and the undersides of panels nobody had thought worth replacing. The first block meant ABOVE. The second meant WORKER.

The third was the question mark stamped beside manual overrides.

"Control, bank seven," she said. "Hold roll compensation on my visor."

"For the hinge test?" the duty operator asked.

"For my eyes. Ten seconds."

"That's not a test category."

"Then call it glare."

The stars steadied. Below, the lights went out in strips from west to east. Darkness remained for six breaths. Then the whole message returned, except that the middle block had changed. Not WORKER now. LIVING WORKER: the little diagonal that distinguished a warm hand from a powered tool.

ABOVE LIVING WORKER?

Sairu stopped breathing.

At the southern edge of the terraces, several tiny heat traces moved between the bright strips. The sight could have manufactured one bad pixel, not warm bodies crossing separate rows. Magnification broke each bar into terraced reed beds, thousands of pale tips kindling like a field of stars only after a person reached them. Star-reeds, for lack of a name. The trace cooled; the reeds shone. A mechanism could store and shape living work, never begin it. One trace was smaller than the others and darted twice back to a patch that had failed to shine.

More glyphs opened around it, awkwardly spaced.

PIRU. CHILD. ASK.

The name had been made from service-script sound signs, each one kilometers long.

"Bank seven?" the duty operator said. "Your ten seconds are gone."

Sairu saved the raw frames without classifying them. A contact classification would dispatch the station's survey routines. She knew that. Her thumb still hovered over the tag until the small heat trace crossed a blazing row and vanished into the cooler dark beyond it.

"Glare cleared," she said. "Continuing inspection."

The ground fell behind the horizon. Bank seven waited with its ordinary fault: hinge twelve had taken four-tenths of a second too long to turn.

Mechanisms answered when touched. That was why Sairu liked them. A stuck hinge gave resistance, heat, a measurable delay. You found the cause and worked it until the answer changed.

For the rest of the inspection, the old question stayed at the bottom of her visor.

ABOVE LIVING WORKER?

* * *

Lassan watched the frames three times before saying anything. The maintenance archive occupied a narrow compartment between the machine shops, where cabinets built for physical labels stood beside newer storage columns. He kept a bowl of sour yellow berries on his desk. He pushed it toward Sairu without looking away from the ground.

"No, thanks."

"They're going soft."

"That doesn't improve them."

"It improves the urgency."

On the wall, Piru's name burned across a continent of darkness.

Sairu pointed. "You read it."

"I recognize four signs and a question marker."

"You read more than that."

"ABOVE is secure. The distinction between worker and living worker is secure. This could be CHILD, or junior, or restricted access by minors." Lassan enlarged the first and second displays until the terrace boundaries showed. "The change is important. Someone revised a category."

"Piru."

"Likely a name. It could identify a crew, a district, a tool series—"

"A tool series didn't run back to fix a dark row."

Lassan looked at the moving heat traces. He rubbed one thumbnail over the edge of his desk. "No."

That single word loosened something in Sairu's chest. She had expected argument and found herself angrier without it.

"Then why are we talking about tool series?"

"Because the frames can support living operators and an intended question. They do not support a surface census, a history, or the age of the smallest operator. Not yet."

He brought up a service label used on coolant junctions two decks below. Its letter forms had rounded over centuries of recutting, but ABOVE and the living-hand diagonal were there. Beside it he placed a label scan from the station's founding hull. Piru's grammar resembled the older one.

"They preserved it," Sairu said.

"Or inherited something that shares its source. The oldest forms are closest. That's provenance, not an explanation."

"Eight centuries of empty-world instruction, and you want to correct my verb."

"I want the first true record we make to remain true tomorrow."

The compartment door opened behind her.

Orvek did not ask why a radiator mechanic had put a private optical hold on ground-facing frames. Her wrist slate already showed the access trail.

"You used glare authority," she said.

"There was glare."

"From twenty kilometers of orderly vegetation?"

Lassan quietly moved the berry bowl away from the edge of the desk.

Sairu showed Orvek the changing message. She watched the supervisor's eyes pause on the heat traces, then return to the time code.

"Next useful night pass?" Orvek asked.

"Fourteen hours, fifty-one minutes. The terraces will be within bank seven's surface angle for ninety-four seconds."

"And you want?"

"To answer."

"That isn't a radiator function."

"They used a maintenance channel."

"They used light. The similarity doesn't grant you a channel."

Sairu heard herself speed up. "We can give them one packet. Shielded face for dark, emissive face for bright. Their pattern tracks the station. They must have a heat sight. Four vane groups are enough for low-resolution blocks. We confirm we're alive, confirm Piru was seen, ask for receipt."

"Closing four groups stores heat in the spine."

"For less than a minute."

"At current load?"

"Thirty-eight seconds below the conservative limit. Forty-seven below mandatory abort."

Orvek turned to Lassan. "Do we know they'll read it?"

"No. The old script gives us a defensible order for LIVING, ABOVE, RECEIVE. Their display suggests the same reading direction."

"Do we know that word is Piru?"

"No," he said. "A name is the best fit."

"Good. At least one of you still knows that word."

Sairu pointed again at the small trace. "They asked whether a worker lives up here. We do."

"And the standard contact tag centers every available ground optic on the source, writes coordinates into the survey ledger, and requests a communications assessment," Orvek said. "Did you apply it?"

"No."

"Did you nearly?"

Sairu's silence answered.

Orvek pulled the thermal record from bank seven. "One packet. No contact tag, no locator request, no networked optics. Local heat-eye only. Thirty-five seconds, because your hinge twelve is already late. If spine temperature crosses yellow, all groups open."

"We can do it in thirty-eight."

"Then remove three seconds of message."

"Which three?"

"Mechanic's choice. Supervisor's limit. Put the optical excursion in the maintenance log."

"That will expose it."

"It will expose me. I'm authorizing the excursion."

Orvek signed with one thumb and handed the slate to Sairu. "Repair the hinge before you use it to talk to a planet."

* * *

Fourteen hours later, hinge twelve still lagged.

Sairu had replaced its drive braid, cleaned the bearing track, and run it through a hundred turns. Unloaded, it matched the rest. Under radiator heat, it came late by two-tenths of a second—better, not good.

"Nine minutes to surface angle," Orvek said over the service channel. "Bank spine at sixty-one."

Sairu floated beside the manual console in the radiator hub. Lassan had strapped himself at the script display behind her, a paper copy of the packet tucked beneath one hand as though electrons might become careless.

"Sixty-one is cold," Sairu said.

"It is the starting number."

"I know what it is."

"Then we have achieved ordinary conversation."

Lassan glanced between them. "The second block should remain RECEIVE, not SEE."

"You changed that twice," Sairu said.

"Because SEE implies an eye. RECEIVE allows a sensor, a reader, or a witness."

"We have ninety-four seconds and four blocks."

"Language remains language at speed."

"Surface angle," Orvek said. "Talk later."

The world's night opened on the hub display. The terraces were dark, a faint ribbed geometry in infrared. Sairu selected four vane groups. Their emissive faces glowed on the station's outer cameras; their shielded backs disappeared against space. From below, through a powerful enough heat-eye, the whole radiator would become a label board crossing the stars.

"Packet one," she said. "Mark."

She closed two groups and left two open: ABOVE.

"Hold three," Orvek said. "Turn."

Sairu moved the next combination through LIVING. The four indicators changed together except twelve, which hung amber and snapped over late.

"Hinge lag point three," she said.

"Spine sixty-seven. Continue."

WORKER took six turns. RECEIVE took eight. Piru's sound signs were worse: the old service script had never been designed to name children, only couplings and hands assigned to them.

"Seventy-four," Orvek said. "Twenty seconds to yellow."

"Piru marker beginning."

"Order error," Lassan said. "Second sound first."

"That's what I have."

"Your lower pair is inverted."

Sairu looked. Hinge twelve had left a bright corner where the block required dark.

"Resetting."

"No reset," Orvek said. "Thirteen seconds. Shorten."

Sairu abandoned the name. She turned the groups through RECEIVE once more and then the service glyph for RETURN SIGNAL. Twelve struck its stop hard enough to send a tremor through the console.

"Yellow," Orvek said. "Open all."

"One confirmation mark."

"Open all."

Sairu's hand stayed on the controls for one hot, stupid beat. Then she obeyed. Emissive faces swung toward space. Heat poured out of the spine in a rising red wash.

Cloud had already reached the western terraces. A pale bank crossed the signal field, swallowing row after row. Nothing lit beneath it.

"Did they receive?" Sairu asked.

Lassan scrubbed through the ground frames. "No display visible."

"That isn't what I asked."

"It is what the evidence can answer."

"Bank spine declining," Orvek said. "Hold full emission. Sairu, hinge twelve is now point six late."

Below, the last clear terrace vanished under cloud.

They had said they were alive. They had failed to say to whom.

* * *

The station made them wait fifteen hours and nine minutes for another usable angle.

Sairu spent the first three repairing hinge twelve. A hairline distortion in its hot-side stop had escaped every unloaded test. She replaced the stop, ran the group hot, and watched four green indicators turn together. That answer should have satisfied her. It did not.

She found Orvek in the small galley beside radiator control, eating lentils from a pouch while reading the excursion log.

"Any change?" Orvek asked.

"Twelve is clean to point zero four."

"Good."

"On the ground."

"Cloud."

Sairu hooked a foot under the opposite restraint. "They repeated before. If they saw us, they'll repeat."

"Probably."

"They will."

Orvek squeezed the pouch flat from the bottom. "You don't improve probability by saying it harder."

"And you don't make this smaller by putting it under radiator maintenance."

"I put an unplanned thermal excursion under radiator maintenance because it was one. I put the unexplained optical pattern under a safety hold because that keeps the raw frames local until review. Both entries name me."

"Review by whom?"

"Someone who isn't running on half a sleep cycle. Have you eaten?"

"Yes."

Orvek waited.

"A roll," Sairu said.

"Get another."

She caught Lassan outside the archive. He carried two label rubbings and had purple berry juice on one cuff.

"The packet was readable," she told him.

"Parts of it."

"We answered."

"We emitted a syntactically plausible sequence toward the observed grid."

"Do you practice making everything sound dead?"

He stopped. "No. I'm trying not to finish their meaning for them."

Sairu had no quick reply to that, which annoyed her more than the sentence deserved.

Lassan held out his slate. The standard contact form showed the terrace grid centered in a red square. Eight observing systems were listed beneath it, ready to acquire the same coordinates on approval.

"The form doesn't merely record our observation," he said. "It begins a search. Surface motion, heat sources, routes in and out. Whatever those lights are, the people operating them did not ask for that."

"They made a question twenty kilometers wide."

"For something crossing above them."

"That's us."

"Yes. Not necessarily every eye we own."

Sairu enlarged the image. Even after the cloud, faint cooling scars marked the rows used twice. The living-hand diagonal was paler than the terraces around it. At several points, the infrared record showed sudden drops where bodies had knelt to the reeds. The lights had not come free. Whoever tended those rows had spent stored sun from the plants and warmth from their own skin.

She had nearly answered a question by handing its origin to the station.

"I didn't apply the tag," she said.

"I know."

"I knew what it did."

Lassan tucked the rubbings under his arm. "Before or after your thumb stopped?"

She pushed away from the wall too hard and had to catch the next rail.

* * *

On the third pass, the cloud broke into long gray islands. Between them, the terraces shone.

Not the question this time. Four tight blocks rose in sequence at the grid's northern edge.

ABOVE. LIVING. RECEIVE.

Then Piru's name, with the sound signs in the order Sairu and Lassan had argued over. The child had received enough of their damaged packet to identify its intended recipient and correct their spelling.

"Receipt confirmed," Sairu said.

"Piru attribution strongly supported," Lassan said.

"Bank spine fifty-nine," Orvek said. "Keep watching."

The grid changed. One small mark brightened beside Piru's name. Six marks opened beside LIVING HANDS. The heat-eye showed bodies moving with them: the small trace and several taller ones, one person working two rows when a bleached strip failed.

"Seven operators," Sairu said.

"Seven markers," Lassan corrected. "Several operators visible."

The marks faded. A new sequence began, using warning terms Sairu had seen on survey mounts.

NO EYE.

Her hands tightened around the console grips.

"They want us to stop looking," Orvek said.

"Then why send again?"

"Wait," Lassan said.

On the surface, two people crossed the lit rows. The first warning vanished. It returned with an extra block, but cloud shadow cut its lower half away.

NO EYE—CENTER.

"No centering," Sairu said. The contact form's red square seemed to float in her memory.

The terraces went dark long enough that Orvek called, "Thirty seconds to our reply angle."

Light returned in a longer, rougher order.

POSITION MARK: NO.

EYE MOVE: BELOW CALL FIRST.

The last terms were not elegant. CALL was the old label beside a manual service summons. FIRST had been inserted after the sequence, forcing three adjacent rows to bleach almost white. The small heat trace—Piru, likely Piru, only Piru if the evidence held—moved out of one cold patch and into another worker's arms.

Sairu took her hand off the reply controls and read the sequence again.

"They saw the auto-center," she said.

"Or they know what centered observation means," Lassan replied. "No coordinate record. No search unless they summon it. That reading fits all three revisions."

"Reply window," Orvek said. "Thirty-four seconds authorized. Same abort. What are you sending?"

Sairu had built six possible messages during the wait. Explanations. Assurances. Questions about the reeds, the language, the people beyond the grid. Every one now felt like reaching past the thing Piru had actually said.

"Manual status," she said. "Position not stored. Eye waits. Next dark pass, surface begins."

Lassan scanned the blocks. "Use READY, not WAITS. We don't know whether their grammar carries duration."

"Fine."

"And omit surface. BELOW is attested."

"Fine. Orvek?"

The supervisor studied the thermal forecast. "Twenty-nine seconds. Their last signal cost them. Ours can be shorter."

Sairu loaded the packet.

The vanes began to turn.

"Mark," Orvek said.

POSITION. NOT STORED.

Hinge twelve landed with the others.

"Spine sixty-six."

EYE. MANUAL.

"Seventy-one."

NEXT DARK. EYE READY.

"Fifteen seconds."

BELOW CALL FIRST.

Lassan leaned toward the display. "Third block—"

"I see it." Sairu corrected the inverted pair without resetting the message. "Mark."

"Seventy-eight," Orvek said. "Open."
