"Every time they put my face on a screen, you come here afterward," they say. "You tell me what they said. Then you wait."

"I don't wait."

They shut off the water.

"I'm not here so you can tell me they still love me," you say. "I don't want their house. I don't want the crest if wearing it means standing beside them while they call you—"

"Don't make me the reason."

"You're not listening."

Auden puts the toothbrush beside the sink. "Then why is there a bag in your car?"

Your injured hand pulses inside the towel. With the other, you reach into your coat and take out a square of black ceramic no larger than a shirt button.

The anger leaves Auden's face before any other expression replaces it.

"Where did you get that?"

"My impact buffer. From the bridge."

They know the suit pieces better than you do. Rampart used to check every latch before a family deployment because Palisade believed inspection looked nervous on camera. The ceramic square records six seconds on either side of a disabling impact: suit loads, collar audio, the family's shared structural model, whatever the forward lens can see. Your suit shed it into the lining when the first carriage struck Auden's field.

Auden wipes their hands on their coat, leaving two wet marks. "The board said your buffer was corrupted."

"The file entered into evidence was. This is the local original. I found it in my suit lining six months ago, and I should have brought it then, but Father said reopening the finding might make things worse for you. I thought if the board used it to—"

You place it beside the detergent.

Auden stares at the little square. Dryer eight knocks twice.

"Six months," they say.

"I didn't believe him. Not exactly. I was afraid he might be right."

Auden picks up the grease-stained trousers and carries them to washer eleven. They feed the fabric through the round door without checking the pockets. That frightens you; they always check twice. Quarters strike the metal slot one by one.

"I brought it now," you say. "I can put it out during the broadcast. The whole buffer—the structural model, the audio, everything. They can't call you a failure after people see—"

Auden slams the washer door. "No."

"You haven't watched this copy. It shows all the carriage loads, every route, the timing. It proves there wasn't another way."

The dozing customer lifts his head. Auden waits until he turns toward the television again.

"How much afterward?" Auden asks.

"Six seconds."

"Does it show me beside him?"

You nod.

The clip ends with Auden on their knees beside Shearpoint. You have never played that part with sound.

"I can cut that. I wasn't going to use it."

"You said the whole buffer."

"I meant the whole proof. Tell me where to stop it."

Auden puts one palm against the washer door. "Nothing goes out because you're angry at Mother."

"I'm angry because she lied. That doesn't make the file less true."

"Nothing goes out yet."

The washer drum lurches once and stops. A red imbalance light begins to blink. Auden presses start. The motor complains, turns half a revolution, and gives up.

"You left the buckle fastened," you say.

"I know."

"It catches the fabric on one side. You taught me that."

"Not now, Mica."

You open the washer. With one working hand, you struggle to free the wet trousers from themselves. Auden watches you fight the weight for three seconds, swears under their breath, and steps in. Together you unhook the buckle, shake out both legs, and arrange them around the drum.

When the machine turns smoothly, Auden sits on the molded chair between washers ten and eleven. They hold out their palm.

"Let me see it before I decide."

You have an adapter in the detergent box. The ceramic square clicks into it, and your phone fills with numbers too small for the screen. You enlarge the field diagram and set the phone on Auden's knee.

The first image is the inside of the lead carriage tipped toward the river. Rain needles through a broken window. Your own breath rasps close to the collar microphone.

Auden drags the playhead to the fourth structural pulse.

Time remaining: 1.76 seconds.

The train drops eleven centimeters. The suit marks each carriage in red. Beneath them, Auden's support field flares from eighty-nine percent load to ninety-seven.

Through the window, the surviving rail glints. Shearpoint is a narrow figure at its far end, one palm laid flat on the steel. His first three pulses have split the braces below him. The fourth is gathering under his hand.

The phone speaker gives you Auden's voice, raw with strain. "Take your hand off the rail."

Shearpoint looks toward the hanging carriage. Toward you. He drives his shoulder down.

The field diagram changes. Auden can release the train and strike across open air. Four red boxes fall. They can turn the new pulse into either edge of the support field. Two cars roll out of the bowl. They can delay. The broken brace reaches terminal shear before the next full heartbeat.

One route stays green: back through the rail carrying the pulse, to its source.

You remember the next part without the screen. Auden's hands closing. The tremendous stillness when the carriage stops dropping. Shearpoint flung from the rail, not bloodied in your view, only suddenly loose. The sound Auden makes when they understand he will not rise.

Auden stops the clip before the return travels.

"Again," they say.

You play it again.

On the third viewing, they point to the transfer log in the corner. Two devices opened the full upload at three fourteen the next morning. The damaged file did not enter evidence until four hours later. One device belongs to Crownfire. One belongs to Palisade.

"They opened the full file," you say. "They saw the loads and every estimate. They heard you warn him, and four hours later the board got the damaged copy."

Auden rubs a thumb against the phone's cracked edge. "Do you remember what you said to me in the ambulance?"

You remember asking whether the two of you had killed him. You were drugged, shivering, your shoulder strapped flat. Auden answered, *No. I did.*

"You wouldn't let me take any of it," you say. "Not even the part where I froze until you told me what to do. And now they get to put all of it on you, and I keep coming here as if hearing me say that changes where you have to wake up. It doesn't pay the rent. It doesn't give you the hearing back. It doesn't—"

They glance at the dryer clock. Eleven minutes. Their thumb stays against the crack in the phone case.

"I hear you, Mica."

You open a blank statement on the phone. Your first sentence is: *Auden had no choice.*

They cross it out with one hard stroke of your finger.

"No."

"There was no other move. You just watched it three times."

"Then write that. And write what I did." Auden taps the blank line. "I sent the force back. I knew where it would go. If you leave that out, don't use the recording."

So you start again.

You write only what your collar lens and your own eyes establish: the eleven-centimeter drop; the 1.76 seconds; the support load; the warning; Shearpoint's hand staying on the rail; the one route that did not drop a carriage. You write that Auden sent the force back. You write that Shearpoint died because of it.

When you type *saved everyone*, Auden deletes the word *everyone*.

"The passengers," they say.

You write *the passengers, including me*.

Auden allows three seconds of video. No impact. No body. No ambulance. Their warning and the field diagram end on the final green route. They keep the transfer record showing your parents opened the data. They make you turn off comments on the original file even though copies will sprout them everywhere else.

Under the eyewitness statement, you type Mica Serrin.

At the bottom of the release form, they type Auden Serrin.

You watch the surname appear. "You still use it on everything?"

"Work insists on paychecks matching bank accounts. Very old-fashioned."

"You could change it."

"I could change my boots. These pinch too."

"Auden."

They look down at the form. The cursor blinks after the last letter.

"The week they threw me out, you left six messages," they say. "My phone still sorted us together under Serrin. I left it that way."

"You never called back."

"I listened."

You almost tell them you are leaving the family anyway. The packed bag waits in your car, one boot holding its zipper open.

Instead you ask, "If I say this tonight, will you release the clip?"

"If you say your part. Not mine."

"What does that mean?"

"Don't call me innocent. Don't say I had no hand in it. Tell them where you were and what you saw."

"And after?"

Auden rises when dryer eight buzzes. "After, you're going to a doctor about that wrist."

They open the door. Warm work clothes spill against them, the loose buckle silent at last.

***

At six that evening, your mother fastens the family crest over your heart because your right hand cannot manage the clasp.

She smooths the fabric around it. "You look tired."

"I was doing laundry."

"Tonight you can sleep at home."

The packed bag is no longer in your car. You put everything back before dawn. If your parents send you away tonight, they will have to do it while you are standing there.

On set, Palisade takes your uninjured hand. Crownfire takes the one bound in a proper brace. To the audience, it will look like unity. The memorial wall behind you is paired to your suit relay for the rescue footage scheduled later in the program.

The host reads the prepared question about the bridge memorial and whether the Serrin family has found peace. Your father answers first. He speaks of standards. Your mother speaks of sorrow. Then the host asks whether Auden might ever deserve the crest again.

"A hero who kills because they fail to imagine another way has failed twice," Crownfire says. "Auden remains our child. Their choice remains a disgrace."

The control room gives you the cue to agree.

"You watched the buffer," you say.

Your father's grip closes around your fingers. "Mica."

"Both of you opened it at three fourteen the morning after the bridge."

Your mother's eyes flick toward the producer off camera. Her smile stays where it is. "Grief can make memory feel certain—"

"Mine isn't the only record."

You touch the relay pad inside your braced wrist. Somewhere across the city, Auden has the release page open. You cannot make them press it. If they decide not to, you will speak without the clip.

The studio wall behind you changes from the memorial seal to the three seconds Auden chose.

Rain. A listing carriage. Red load marks. Auden's warning. Shearpoint lowering his shoulder. One green route and 1.76 seconds.

The image freezes before anyone dies.

"I was in that carriage," you say. "The train had dropped eleven centimeters, and Auden was carrying ninety-seven percent of its load. Shearpoint began another pulse after they warned him. No path remained that spared him without dropping at least one car. Auden sent the pulse back to keep the cars up. Shearpoint died, and I am alive because they did it."

Palisade says, very softly, "Stop now and you can come home."

The host hears him. So does the collar microphone.

Your mother reaches for the crest. You cover it, and pain shoots through your wrist despite the brace.

"You may believe Auden should carry that death," you say. "They do. But you knew what happened when you called them a failure. You knew when you called them a disgrace. I won't repeat either word for you."

The red light on the main camera dies.

One side camera stays live long enough to show your father unfasten the crest. He does not tear it away. He presses the clasp, lifts the joined flame and shield from your uniform, and sets it face down on the table.

"Then you do not represent us," he says.

Your mother lets go of your hand.

By the time a studio guard returns your coat, the clip is everywhere. So are claims that it is forged, incomplete, stolen, proof of murder, proof of sacrifice. One message asks how a real hero spends 1.76 seconds. Another lists the train's passenger count as if Shearpoint can be subtracted without remainder.

Nothing on your screen resembles acquittal. Auden does not answer your first call.

Then a photograph arrives: washer eleven, red imbalance light blinking above its stopped drum. Under it, two words.

*Your fault.*

You go back to the laundromat in the uniform with two small holes over your heart. Three camera crews follow your car. You leave them on the pavement and walk inside where Auden is kneeling in front of the washer with one wet trouser leg over their shoulder.

They look at the bare place on your uniform where the crest used to sit. Their hand closes on the wet cloth. Then they point at the washer.

"Same trousers?" you ask.

"Same buckle."

"You fastened it again."

"I was reading your messages."

"That is still not my fault."

The cameras can see through the front glass. Auden sees them seeing, then points at the other side of the drum.

"Take that leg," they say.

You set your coat on the folding table and crouch beside them. With your good hand, you reach into the cold water.

stories.title: Friends of the Night
stories.prompt: While your predecessors were busy hunting the beasts that hid in the shadows, you decided to befriend them. And when war came to your lands, your enemies found their armies shrinking in the night.
stories.body:
# Friends of the Night

At sunset I set two river eels on the flat stone and backed away twelve paces.

Crooktail watched from under the hazels. I knew it by the right angle in its tail and the pale seam along one forepaw, though neither mark showed until it chose to move. Shadow beasts were not made of darkness. They had ribs, burrs in their fur, mud between their broad toes. Crooktail even sneezed when the hazels flowered. But its coat held so little light that my eye kept losing the edges of it, and when it lowered its head the ground seemed to open a mouth.

For six years, this had been our measure. I brought eels or a hare's liver. I struck the stone once with a hazel switch. Sometimes Crooktail ate while I sat nearby. Sometimes it left me to the flies. Once it had followed me almost to the lower gate, pausing whenever I turned, and for a month afterward I had called that proof of friendship. Then I learned that a slaughterhouse cart had dripped blood along the same road.

That evening it did not look at the eels. Its ears had turned toward the western rim.

Drums came over the ridge, softened by distance but too regular for thunder. One by one, points of fire appeared above the barley fields. They multiplied down the road until the rim of Shalegate looked stitched with red thread.

Crooktail withdrew under the hazels. The brush gave one dry shiver, then nothing.

“Tavik!” Torma called from the fort wall. “Inside. Now.”

By the time I reached the gate, the western host had begun pouring into the valley: pikes first, then wagons and horse, all taking their places with the dull competence of people who expected to sleep on conquered ground. Torma stood above the arch in a boiled-leather coat, counting standards. Beside her, Denek was unhooding the east beacon.

“Leave that covered,” I said.

Denek did not turn. “A dark wall is an invitation.”

“A high flame will throw every sentry's shadow across the beast runs.”

Torma leaned over the parapet. “How far?”

“On level ground? Thirty paces, perhaps more. It depends on the flame and where they're moving.”

“Can you keep them off the wall?”

“No.”

She waited. Torma had a way of leaving silence open until a weak answer walked into it and died. I gave her no second answer.

“Light the beacons,” she said. “Double water beside each. Tavik, mark every run you know. Denek, keep the lower ward off them.”

The old keeper struck flint. “That was always the rule.”

Pitch caught with a greasy cough. Light vaulted over the inner roofs, and our shadows sprang westward along the wall.

The first man shrank before the enemy finished pitching its command tent.

He was an east-wall sentry carrying a bundle of quarrels. One moment his boots thudded above me; the next came a small metal clatter, no louder than a dropped cup. I found him hanging from the drain groove in the wall walk, his fingers hooked over its edge. He, his coat, his sword and the bundle on his back had all dwindled together. I could have covered his body with both hands.

“Don't pull,” he gasped as I reached for him. “The buckle's caught.”

That was our first good fact: the change had not hurt him, and fear had not taken his sense. I freed the buckle with my knife and lowered him into my cap.

Below the wall, Crooktail stood on the bare run with its jaw closed around the sentry's long black shadow. There was no tearing, no blood. The shadow narrowed between its teeth like cloth drawn through a ring. Then Crooktail released it and vanished under the thorn fence.

A shout rose from the enemy's near pickets. Another followed, farther south. Torches moved, stooped, scattered. By midnight our scouts had brought in five diminished soldiers they had found struggling through grass that reached their shoulders.

One of Torma's spearmen looked down at the captives. “What do we do with these?”

“Get a bread tray,” I said.

“I meant after.” His boot shifted closer.

Torma caught the back of his belt and hauled him one step away. “After, you obey the law. Bread tray.”

The captives were cold, furious, and too frightened to sit still. We put the east-wall sentry with them because he refused to be carried alone. Under shielded lamps, which cast no useful reach for a beast's jaws, I checked each of them. Armor rivets, scabbards, bootlaces: all reduced in proportion. A picket's dropped torch had remained full-sized where it fell.

“How do you undo it?” Torma asked.

“The shepherd boy who shrank three winters ago recovered beyond the north ledge.”

“That boy was delirious.” Denek folded his arms. “He told us a moon spoke to him.”

“The moon did not return his height. Distance did.”

“You hope.”

“I observed.”

Torma pointed to the friendly sentry in my cap. “Take him to the ledge. If he grows, come back before dawn. If he doesn't, keep going.”

The north path stayed behind the fort and climbed out of the beasts' feeding range. Denek came with me, a spear in one hand and the tiny sentry's bundle in the other. He repeated the old rules as we walked: flame high and close, stone underfoot, no reaching into brush. I knew them. I had learned them from him before I learned how many beasts his drives had killed.

At the third boundary cairn, the cap jerked in my hands. I set it down just in time. The sentry unfolded out of it, first the size of a child, then of a man crouching naked in the cold, except that his clothes and gear were growing with him. His sword knocked over two stones. Denek jumped back and leveled the spear.

The sentry lay panting on the path. “Can I stand now?”

“Try your left foot first,” Denek said.

He could stand. He was hungry and shaking, but whole.

On the way down, Denek carried the cap.

At noon, Torma met the invaders under a white shield hung from a pike. She took me because I knew the beasts, and Denek because he knew when I mistook a wish for a fact.

Marshal Drost arrived with six guards and a clerk. He wore bronze scales over blue wool. The guards wore no open flame, and all of them watched the grass. Behind them, soldiers were raising siege frames while carpenters measured our gate.

“Six pickets are missing,” Drost said. His voice still had ceremony in it. “You will return them and remove the affliction.”

“Five are inside,” Torma said. “The sixth ran west after he changed. We did not catch him.”

Drost looked at me. “You are the keeper.”

“I keep people from crossing the runs. I don't keep the beasts.”

“Then you have failed at the smaller task.”

“You brought twelve hundred open flames into their range.”

His clerk glanced down at the tablet before him. Drost did not. “One thousand eight hundred and forty-two. Your wall has perhaps four hundred fit defenders.”

“Four hundred and six,” Torma said. “All behind stone.”

I crouched and drew the valley in the dust: fort, barley fields, western road, outer ridge. “Put out the fires. Withdraw on this road. Beyond the ridge, your people recover.”

“You have tested that?”

“One man, northward.”

“Your man.”

“The beasts caught him under our beacon. They don't know your colors.”

For the first time, Drost looked toward the wall instead of through us. Then he wiped out my road with the toe of his boot.

“Nets at every fire,” he told the clerk. “Two handlers to each. Widen the fire lines by dusk.”

“Longer shadows give them more to reach,” I said.

“And more light gives my handlers something to see.”

Torma lifted the white shield from the pike. “Your five soldiers will be set outside the south gate at sundown. That is the last courtesy you get in my fields.”

We walked back without speaking until the gate shut behind us.

Denek stopped under the arch. “He is doing what we did.”

“You used hounds and hooked poles.”

“We used beacons first.” He rubbed his thumb along the old spear shaft. “Beacon nights pulled the beasts toward the outer houses. Shadows crossed beds, cradles, doorways. People ran small into winter rain. We killed the beasts because we could not move the wall.”

I had heard the death counts. I had dressed them in my own explanation: frightened keepers, ignorant hunters, an easy cruelty inherited as custom. “You told me they came into the houses.”

“They did. After our light laid a road to them.”

“And you kept lighting it.”

“There were raiders then too.” Denek looked up at the blazing east beacon. “Darkness never promised to spare us, Tavik.”

Neither had Crooktail. That was the part I had made soft in my mind.

When I took Denek's post, I shuttered the house lamps, moved slaughter scraps away from the lanes, and cut new runs toward the stream. The drives ended. No resident had shrunk in six years. I had called that friendship because I needed a word better than truce and warmer than successful drainage.

The second night showed me the limit of all three words.

Drost's bonfires made noon-colored islands across the valley. Each soldier standing near them cast a black road forty or fifty paces long. Nets lay open beside the flames. At first the handlers laughed when small shapes flickered at the edges. Then the shapes crossed between fires, and men began dropping below the line of shields.

A pike company collapsed unevenly as shadows passed over the south run. One soldier dropped to knee height; another dwindled until the grass hid him. Their clothes and weapons changed with them, but the ladders they held did not. Timber crashed. Horses reared above riders suddenly too small to manage reins. Orders broke apart into names and warnings.

From the wall I counted seven beasts. Then ten. Then I found the crook in one tail.

Crooktail had entered a net beside the largest fire. The handlers dragged the corners tight and pinned them with hooked stakes. Crooktail rolled, silent, while flame lit the pale seam of its paw. Every struggle wound the mesh closer around its throat.

“Open the lower gate,” I told Torma.

“No.” She was moving archers away from the long beacon shadows as she answered. “That camp is folding without us.”

“The beasts are trapped between their fires and ours. Douse the wall. Give them dark to leave through.”

“If I douse it, I lose the barley approach.”

Another ladder fell in the camp. Someone screamed for water; someone else screamed not to bring a torch.

Denek joined us at the parapet. “No dark gate during siege,” he said. “Keep the flame high. Keep stone under your feet.”

“Can you reach that net?” Torma asked him.

He watched the fire, the ditch and the folds of ground between. His lips moved once, repeating distances. “By the old drive path. Two men, no lamp.”

“Take Tavik.” She turned to the beacon crews. “Hood the east. Then the south. Lower gate opens one body wide, and it shuts behind them.”

The wall went dark in sections. Each vanished beacon erased a row of roofs, then joined the space between fort and field into one deep black. Wind carried sparks from Drost's camp, but the beasts now had somewhere the long fire-shadows did not reach.

Denek and I slipped out.

He led without hesitation. “My shoulder,” he whispered. “Stay level with it.”

“I can see the ditch.”

“Good. Don't step in it.”

The old drive path bent through thorn gaps I had never noticed because Denek's hunters had cut them to funnel fleeing beasts. Twice he put a hand against my chest and stopped me before a shadow swept across us. Once a diminished soldier blundered into my shin and clung there.

“Road west,” I whispered, turning him by the shoulders. “No fire.”

He stumbled away without answering.

At the largest bonfire, the world became glare and hard edges. Crooktail's net was fixed to four stakes. One handler had shrunk inside his own loop of rope; the other had fled. Denek crawled behind a supply chest, reached the first anchor and sawed through it with his belt knife.

I smothered a fallen torch under my coat. The shadow attached to Denek's hand vanished an instant before a beast snapped at it.

“That's one,” he said. His voice was steady, but he cut the next rope too fast and nicked his thumb.

The net loosened. Crooktail twisted, baring teeth no darker than ordinary teeth. Mesh still cinched its hindquarters to the last two anchors.

Boots approached from the fire side. At first I expected a child. Then I saw the bronze scales, each one reduced to the size of my thumbnail.

Drost stood no higher than my shoulder. Two guards flanked him, one scarcely reaching his waist. Rank had not left his face, but ceremony had.

“Three hundred eleven changed,” he said. “Forty-eight cannot clear the wagon ruts. Seventeen are missing. How long?”

“Until they cross the western ridge.”

“How long until more change?”

A shadow beast worried at a darkness stretched from the far fire. A soldier beside it dropped below the height of the supply chest.

“As long as you make those shadows,” I said.

Drost looked at the net. “This one leads them?”

“No.”

“You feed it.”

“It comes when it chooses.”

“Then why are you here?”

The final rope creaked as Crooktail strained. Denek shifted his knife into a stabbing grip, not toward the beast. Drost noticed.

“Because I know this one,” I said. “Cut that anchor, put out every fire, and I can mark your road. Torma can keep our bows on the wall. Those are the pieces I have.”

“No guarantee?”

“The boundary restored our sentry. I won't promise what the beasts do between here and it.”

Drost's smaller guard raised his spear. “Marshal, we can take them.”

“You can reach his knee,” Drost said. “Lower it.”

He drew a short bronze knife, stepped onto the loose edge of the net and cut the last anchor himself. Denek severed the remaining cord. Crooktail came free in a rush. It struck my shoulder, knocked me into the ash and crossed the firelight without looking back. The other beasts followed its movement only because open ground had appeared ahead of it, a scattering of black bodies choosing the same dark.

Drost watched them go. “Take me to your captain.”

Torma would not open the gate for him. She spoke through the waist-high wicket while Drost stood outside with Denek and me. A shielded lamp inside gave her enough light to see our faces and threw no shadow past the threshold.

“Engines stay,” she said. “Pikes stacked in the west field. Every open flame out. Your first file moves before the next dusk is gone.”

“I have three hundred eleven diminished and seventeen uncounted.”

“Find them by daylight.”

“I need two wagons for those who cannot keep pace.”

“Take wagons. Not towers, rams or throwers.”

“My host does not leave its sidearms.”

Torma considered that. “Sidearms stay sheathed until you're past the ridge. One drawn blade, we close the road.”

Drost's jaw tightened. “Your archers could cut us apart at the boundary.”

“They could cut you apart now.”

“Not before my full-sized ranks reach your gate.”

“Then we're both still counting.” Torma bent to hear a report from someone behind her, answered it, then returned. “You get one daylight. No fire tonight, no fire tomorrow. Departure at dusk.”

Drost did his own counting in silence. Supply intervals, walking speed, the time needed to lower the siege lines without flame: I could see the numbers replacing anger because numbers were ground he trusted.

“At dusk,” he said.

The third day passed under a pale sky. Drost's soldiers dismantled nothing they could not carry. They left the siege engines standing like stripped trees and stacked pikes in the barley. Torma's archers watched from the dark wall. Some asked why we did not fire while the enemy was broken below us.

“Because I said hold,” she answered each time. No speech. No appeal to mercy. The order was enough, and she kept giving it.

Denek and I marked the western road with a waist-high rope. Where it forked near the burned hazels, we closed the wrong branch with carts. Drost sorted his diminished soldiers by pace. Those unable to cross wagon ruts rode in blanket-lined grain beds, guarded from wheels, boots and horses. No one laughed. At that scale, a dropped buckle was weight enough to break a foot.

Near sundown, Denek found a collapsed den beside the south fire line. He knelt, put his ear to the earth, and began clearing the entrance with his hands.

“We have to finish the rope,” I said.

“The rope is visible.”

“Not after dark.”

He pulled out another fistful of scorched soil. “Then stop talking.”

I dug beside him until we uncovered a narrow breathing space. Nothing came through it. We went back to the road.

The host began moving when the last rim of sun left the ridge. Their fires stayed cold. Shielded lamps hung inside three wagons, enough for officers to read tally boards but not enough to lay a shadow across the fields. Everyone else followed the rope by touch.

Darkness took away the shape of the army. I heard it instead: boots scuffing, harness rings, wheels easing into ruts, Drost's officers calling intervals. The smallest files made almost no sound. Torma's defenders heard them too. Bows creaked on the wall whenever a horse shied or a cart struck stone, and each time Torma said, “Hold.”

At the burned hazels, one soldier struck flint beside a tangled wheel trace. Three people shouted at once. Drost reached him first and knocked the tinder into mud.

“Use your hands,” he said. “Lift on three.”

There was no threat in it, only the next necessary thing. Six soldiers lifted; the wheel came free. The file moved.

I walked beside the rope until the land rose toward the western boundary. Denek stayed at the fork, repeating the same directions to anyone who lost the line: right hand on rope, carts to the left, ten paces before the cairns. He had spent half his life teaching frightened people how to move through beast country. The purpose had changed. The rules had not.

Restoration began beyond the first cairn. A larger diminished soldier carrying a child-sized comrade cried out as both bodies grew against each other; they had crossed too close together. After that, Drost widened the intervals. Men and women emerged from the dark at mismatched heights, staggered as boots and limbs returned to them, then moved on before the next file arrived. Armor expanded with low clicks of settling plates. Swords stayed sheathed.

Drost crossed near the end. At the boundary he grew from my shoulder height to his full stature in three unsteady steps. He braced one hand on the cairn until the dizziness passed.

“Seventeen?” I asked.

“Fifteen found. Two absent.” His eyes remained on the moving files. “One thousand eight hundred and forty alive at last count.”

“Keep them beyond bow range.”

He gave a tired, irritated motion that might have been agreement or dismissal. It was enough. He went after his army.

By dawn, the last wagon had crossed the ridge. Torma's people collected the abandoned pikes and posted watches around the engines. Drost's host continued west, and its rear guard did not turn before the road bent out of sight.

The valley smelled of wet ash. Three dens had burned. At the south run, Denek found tracks entering the breathing hole we had cleared, though none came out while we watched. One beast was still missing. Crooktail's tracks crossed the fort road twice and ended at the stream.

Torma put the carpenters on the gate and went to argue about grain stores. Denek returned to the collapsed den with a shovel. I carried a new flat stone to the feeding hollow and settled it into the scorched earth.

Near midday, Crooktail appeared beyond the hazels. A band of fur had been rubbed raw around its hindquarters. It watched me tap the stone level with the butt of my knife.

Denek glanced over from the den. “Left edge is high.”

“I know.”

“Then fix it.”

I wedged a chip beneath the right edge. When I looked up, Crooktail had crossed our old twelve-pace measure. It stopped on the near side of the stone, close enough that I could see ash caught in its whiskers.

I set down the eels. Crooktail did not retreat, so neither did I.

stories.title: The Throne Neither of Us Wanted
stories.prompt: You and your older sibling were very anxious if confused when a prophecy was made that one of you would kill your kind father for a throne neither of you particularly wanted. Even stranger, father was entirely unbothered.
stories.body:
# The Throne Neither of Us Wanted

My father was cutting the burned edge from his toast when the rite keeper told us that one of his children would kill him.

The rite keeper had warmed the shallow forecasting dish between her palms until the winter water in it steamed. When she lifted her hands, black grains climbed through the water and fixed themselves against the silver bottom. The dish was only silver. The grains were only grains once her living heat left them. But the pattern they made had not failed in the three hundred years our household had kept records.

My sister read the words first. Her chair struck the tiles behind her.

I read them after.

Before the next turning of the year, one blood-heir will kill the seated king for his throne.

“Does *for* describe motive,” my sister asked, “or result?”

The rite keeper looked tired already. She was accustomed to births, treaties, harvests, ships. Not breakfast with a possible murder between the jam and the butter.

“The pattern does not distinguish.”

“And ‘kill’?”

“The king will die by an heir’s act.”

“Which act?”

“It does not say.”

My sister leaned over the dish as if another clause might be hiding under the rim. She always questioned a disaster until it broke into tasks. At twelve, when I fell through the icehouse roof, she had asked the surgeon which bone, how far, how long, while I screamed at her to stop talking. Later I learned that she had been holding my coat shut around the break.

At breakfast, all I heard was calculation.

“You got to those questions quickly,” I said.

She glanced at me. “Should I have waited?”

Our father slid the charred strip to the edge of his plate. His knife trembled once against the china. Then he reached for the marmalade.

“Father?” I said.

“Mm?”

“Did you hear her?”

“Every word.” He opened the jar, inspected the surface, and pushed it toward my sister. “This is the bitter one. You prefer it.”

She did not take it. “The forecast says one of us will kill you.”

“Yes.”

“For a throne neither of us has asked for.”

“That does make it inconvenient.”

He did not smile. That kept the remark from being a joke, though I wanted it to be one. He spread a careful square of marmalade across the part of his toast that remained.

I could feel my pulse in my gums. “Which of us do you think it is?”

The knife stopped.

“I will not answer that.”

My sister pulled her chair upright. “Because you don’t know?”

“Because the question would do damage whichever name I gave.” He set down the knife. “Your tea is going bitter too.”

This time I heard the tremor in the cup when he lifted it.


The rite keeper let us follow her to the records room because my sister invoked an heir’s right of inspection and I refused to be left alone with our father’s calm.

The room occupied the cold side of the palace, where the windows were narrow and the cabinets smelled of wax, dust, and damp wool. My sister went straight to the succession shelves.

“If we both leave,” I said, “there’s no heir present to act.”

“The line includes blood-heirs abroad.”

“Then we renounce.”

“Renunciation is an act concerning the throne.” She pulled down a ledger. “We don’t know whether it satisfies the forecast.”

“We break the throne.”

The rite keeper was sorting old forecast copies into two stacks. “You may break a chair. You would not break the act already forecast.”

“It is not a chair.”

“It is not a mind either,” she said. “It cannot want you seated. Neither can this morning’s pattern.”

My sister opened the ledger on the nearest table. “Has anyone defeated a reading?”

“People have delayed one. They have misunderstood one. They have committed ugly acts trying to avoid one. Every completed line matched the record in the end.”

“So it compels us.”

“No.” The rite keeper put a finger on the silver dish. The grains had fallen flat now, an illegible grit. “It reports an act. It does not make an heir perform one.”

My sister’s eyes narrowed, not in disbelief but in concentration. She copied the wording onto a scrap, leaving space between every important noun.

“Couldn’t you be frightened like an ordinary person?” I asked.

“I am frightened.”

“You’re making columns.”

“Those are not opposites.”

She turned the ledger toward herself. Tucked beneath its cover was a folded packet in her handwriting. I caught the heading before she covered it with her wrist: *Emergency instruments on death of the sovereign.*

The room went still around me.

“You’ve been here before.”

“I’ve read the current forms.”

“You prepared them.”

“Some of them.”

“Before the prophecy.”

She closed the ledger. “Father has taken medicine four times a day since midsummer. He cancelled the southern circuit. Last week he had the council brought to his room because he could not manage the stairs.”

“He said the old injury was troublesome.”

“Yes.” Her answer was too quick. “And if it became more than troublesome, I wanted us to have options.”

Us. She used that word when she had chosen something for both of us.

I pulled the packet free. There were draft regencies, limits on emergency taxation, a notice preserving my place at the physicians’ college, and a letter to the western survey asking that my sister’s spring commission be held for one year if succession delayed her departure.

I tapped that letter. “Generous of you to postpone your escape.”

“Give me those.”

“You drafted my life after Father, and you were going to mention it when?”

“When there was something to mention.”

“A murdered king might qualify.”

The rite keeper quietly took the silver dish to the far cabinet. My sister reached for the packet, but I held it away.

“If it’s me,” she said, each word clipped clean, “the council will try to keep you here as the next heir. If it’s you, they will try to call your training undignified. I was closing both arguments.”

“You cannot close every argument before the rest of us know we’re in one.”

“Apparently I cannot close this one at all.”

The door opened. One of our father’s attendants stood there with a covered cup.

“The king’s medicine,” she said. “He asked for both of you.”

It was an ordinary sentence. The cup rattled against its saucer in her hands.


We found him in his private room, halfway between the window and the bed.

He was standing only because one hand gripped the curtain cord and the other braced against a table. The physician knelt beside an open case, laying out bottles. Father’s breakfast composure had come apart with his clothes: his collar hung loose, sweat darkened his undershirt, and every breath stopped before it was finished.

My sister dropped the packet. Papers skated under the bed.

“Don’t lift him under the arms,” the physician said. “Support his back. Both of you.”

We obeyed. My sister took most of his weight because she always did; I shoved pillows behind him and knocked one of the medicine bottles over. The physician caught it before it rolled off the table.

“Blue cup,” she said.

The attendant passed it to me.

“Two mouthfuls. Slowly.”

Father drank because I held it to his lips. A thin line escaped into his beard. I wiped it with my sleeve, angry at the medicine, the beard, the hand that had begun to shake in mine.

When his breathing eased, the physician checked his pulse again.

“Tell them,” Father said.

She looked at him. “All of it?”

“There seems little profit in fractions now.”

My sister had gone very quiet.

The physician pulled the chair close to the bed but remained standing. “The scaffold accident last year crushed the king’s chest. The injury was fatal.”

I waited for a second sentence to make the first one sensible.

“He came home,” I said.

“Yes.”

“He recovered.”

“No.”

My father closed his eyes.

The physician continued in the same measured tone she used when telling a patient that a fever had broken or a finger could not be saved. “The coronation working suspended the consequence of the injury while he remained the seated ruler. It gave his body an interval. It did not repair what happened.”

The throne. Not a mind, the rite keeper had said. Not a chooser. A worked mass of black stone beneath a canopy, waiting in a room we visited twice a year for ceremonies we disliked.

“How long?” my sister asked.

“No case in the medical archive passed eighteen months. His pain and weakness have accelerated for six weeks. After this morning, I cannot promise him even another full day of the interval.”

My sister began at once. “Can the working be renewed? Can another living practitioner supply it? Can he resign without transfer? What if the office is divided, or placed in trust, or—”

“No,” the physician said.

The word stopped her.

“A direct heir must freely accept the office,” the physician went on. “The heir sits, takes the ruler’s hand, and speaks acceptance. The support ends when the office passes. What follows is the original injury.”

Kill the seated king for his throne.

I looked at Father. “You knew what the prophecy meant.”

“I suspected.”

“At breakfast, you knew.”

“Yes.”

“And you passed the marmalade.”

His face tightened, whether from pain or shame I could not tell. “It needed passing.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No. It is what I did while I failed to answer.”

My sister stooped to gather her papers. She sorted them on the carpet: regency, tax limits, college, survey. Her hands moved faster than they needed to.

“Why did you hide this?” she asked.

Father looked toward the physician.

“Not her decision,” he said. “Mine. At first I thought there would be time to heal by ordinary means. There wasn’t. Then I thought knowing my pain would force one of you to choose before you could tell duty from fear.”

“So you let us think you were getting better.”

“Yes.”

“You lied.”

“Yes.”

She waited for the gentle qualification he usually found, the comparison to pruning a diseased branch or holding a frightened horse’s bridle. None came.

I asked, “Why aren’t you afraid?”

“I am afraid of hurting you. I am afraid you will punish each other afterward. I am not afraid of the stair happening again.” He opened his eyes and looked at us both. “I remember it. I know what follows. I am tired, and I want this interval to end tonight.”

My sister’s stack slipped sideways. “Then I’ll do it.”

“No,” I said.

She did not look at me. “I am the elder. The instruments already assume—”

“The instruments you wrote.”

“They follow the likely challenge. The council will accept my succession faster. Your college place can be protected by charter. I can appoint—”

“Listen to yourself.”

“I am trying to solve the immediate problem.”

“By becoming the answer before I can speak.”

“Then speak.”

I had nothing. That was the old trick between us: she ran ahead and built the bridge, and I criticized the shape after crossing.

Father pressed a hand against his side. The physician bent to him, but he shook his head.

“Neither of you owes me this,” he said. “And I will not rank your futures to make it easier.”

“You just said you want it tonight,” I said.

“I do.”

“That makes it ours to refuse and yours to suffer.”

“Yes.”

His literal answers were worse than reassurance. They left the choice where it was.


The physician gave us one hour before the next dose, though I suspected she had chosen the interval because a family needed a number to push against.

My sister went to have the throne chamber cleared. I stayed until Father slept, or pretended to. The attendant replaced his damp shirt, and I lifted him while she drew the clean one down his back. We discussed sleeves and buttons. The attendant asked whether he wanted the window latched. The physician counted drops into the blue cup. For ten minutes no one said prophecy, throne, death, or love.

His body said enough. Even asleep, he guarded each breath. When the clock shifted by a quarter hour, he opened his eyes as if the small sound had struck him.

“Is there anything you want?” I asked.

“My grey blanket. The blue one scratches.”

I found the grey blanket in his study, folded across the couch beneath my sister’s travelling coat.

She stood at the writing desk with her spring survey map rolled beside her. The western coast spread across the top sheet: soundings, inlets, a line of proposed beacons. In the corner, she had drawn three alternative routes around a reef. Of course she had.

“The chamber is empty,” she said. “I dismissed the court, guards, musicians, witnesses beyond the rite keeper. We can have the physician close enough without placing her inside. I checked the transfer wording against two reigns and the original stone inscription. There are three clear stops before acceptance. If I take the office, the council can meet at dawn. If I die before appointing—”

“Stop.”

She rolled the map too tightly. It bent near the eastern cape.

“I need to know this is correct.”

“You need to know every consequence except what it costs you.”

“I know what it costs.”

“Say one thing, then.”

“This is not helped by—”

“One thing you wanted next spring.”

She stared at the map.

“The western survey,” I said. “Did you want it?”

“Yes.”

“Was it an escape?”

“Partly.”

“From Father?”

“From being first.” She smoothed the bent corner with her thumb. “First into the council room. First asked when he coughs. First named in every plan. First expected to say it’s manageable.”

Her voice lost its edges. She turned away and tried to tie the map. The cord missed her fingers once, twice.

“I can take it,” she said.

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

“I know.”

Then she had no next option. The silence frightened me more than her columns had.

I laid the grey blanket on the desk. “I keep making you choose, then hating you for choosing.”

“Sometimes you hate me before.”

“Sometimes you make it easy.”

Her breath hitched into something that was not quite laughter. She sat on the couch and put her face in her hands.

I wanted her to tell me what to do. The wanting was so familiar I nearly mistook it for love.

Instead I picked up the blanket.

“I’m taking this to Father.”

She lowered her hands. “Then what?”

“I don’t know yet.”


Father was awake when I returned. I spread the grey blanket over him, tucked it around his feet, and sat beside the bed until the hour ran out.

I thought of the physicians’ college: the basement rooms that smelled of vinegar and boiled linen, the anatomy lectures I had fought to attend, the patients who did not care which chair my ancestors had occupied. I wanted the work. Her western coast did not cancel my basement wards.

I thought of Father’s hand steadying a child’s bowl at breakfast, Father listening to petitions until his ankles swelled, Father quietly removing onions from my plate even after I was old enough to do it myself. He had not become a mechanism when the throne kept his heart moving. His fear, secrecy, pain, and poor decisions were his. So was his request.

If neither of us acted, he would suffer. My sister would keep preparing to act until preparation wore her down into consent. I would keep objecting and leave her hand as the only one visible in the record.

Her regency drafts had protected courses and commissions. None made a place for Father’s next breath.

When the medicine clock rang, I stood.

Father watched me. “Have you decided?”

“I have.”

“Your sister?”

“Has her own decision.”

He nodded once.


The throne chamber looked smaller without the court in it.

No banners hung from the gallery. The candle stands had been pushed against the walls, leaving the black stone chair alone on its low platform. It was broad through the arms and worn pale along the front edge by generations of ceremonial hands. Nothing stirred around it. Nothing called.

My sister waited at the platform with our father’s other arm around her shoulders. She had brought him by the short passage and left her survey coat behind. When she saw me, she searched my face with the same concentration she had given the forecast.

“I’ll do it,” she said.

“I know.”

“There is still time.”

“Yes.”

I went to Father and took his weight from her. For a moment the three of us stood badly tangled at the foot of the throne, adjusting hands and elbows.

“Your foot,” my sister said.

“I know where my foot is.”

“It’s on my hem.”

I moved it. She freed her skirt and guided Father onto the low stool beside the throne. He breathed with his eyes closed until the spasm passed.

Then he said, “The first stop is before you sit.”

My sister stepped between me and the chair. “Why you?”

Not an accusation. She had run out of plans and needed a fact.

“Because I’m choosing it.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“It’s the one I have.” I touched her sleeve. “Move.”

She caught my wrist. “Not to free me.”

“Not only.”

“Not because you think I can’t bear it.”

“I know you can.”

Her grip tightened. Then she let go and stepped aside.

I sat.

The stone was cold through my clothes. No crown descended. No hidden voice tested my heart. The room remained a room, and my father remained alive on the stool to my left.

“Second stop,” he said. “Before you take my hand.”

I looked at him. “Do you still want this?”

All his gentle evasions were gone. “Yes.”

I reached down. His palm was warm, the fingers dry. He closed them around mine.

The contact ran through the stone beneath me—not a thought or judgment, only a gathered pressure answering two living bodies and the office between them. The pressure held, incomplete.

“Last stop,” Father said. “You may release me and rise.”

My sister knelt in front of him. He set his free hand against her cheek. She covered it with both of hers.

I could hear the physician moving once beyond the closed side door, and courtiers shifting much farther away in the passage. Waiting for a ruler. Waiting for a death. They were the same wait now.

Father looked from my sister to me. “I am ready.”

I held his hand and said, “I accept the office.”

The pressure entered me as heat, then weight: not wisdom, not desire, but every claim the throne made on the body that held it. Beside me, Father drew one startled breath. His shoulders folded.

My sister caught him before he struck the stone.

I left the throne at once and knelt with her. Acceptance had completed the transfer; standing could not undo it.

Father’s hand remained in mine. The physician came through the side door, listened, checked, and after a little while stopped checking.

My sister pressed her forehead to Father’s sleeve. I sat beside them with the throne’s new weight moving quietly through my pulse.


Near midnight, the medicine clock rang in Father’s room.

The court was still waiting beyond the long doors for me to receive them. The physician had taken Father’s body to be washed. My sister and I went instead to stop the clock.

The blue cup stood ready on its saucer. She picked it up, carried it to the basin, and paused.

“Do you want me to speak to them?” she asked.

Once, she would already have drafted the words.

I took the cup from her and rinsed the bitter medicine from it before it could dry around the rim. My hands shook. She held the basin steady, saying nothing.

“Come with me,” I said when the cup was clean.

She set the basin down. “All right.”

We left the medicine clock silent and went to open the doors.

stories.title: A Darkness Written Under Skin
stories.prompt: Everyone in the world is born with a tattoo. The tattoo can be made from any kind of ink-like fluid and creates various possible abilities. You are the first to be born without one. Or so they thought until a black light was shined on you.
stories.body:
# A Darkness Written Under Skin

"Keep it flat," the practitioner said. "You've moved twice."

You flattened your palm on the dye table. The wood was cold despite the steam that had lived in the workroom all night. Under your wrist, old stains made a dull geography: madder red in the knife cuts, walnut brown around a peg hole, one thumb-shaped island of blue that your mother claimed had been there before you were born.

The practitioner drew a glass rod through the vial meant for tomorrow's graft. The ink climbed after it in a gray thread, neither dripping nor quite holding. A good match, she had said twice already. Your mother still watched the gray thread as if it might answer something.

"Three days or five?" she asked. Her sleeves were rolled above the red-lake whorls at her elbows. Whenever she flexed her hands, the marks darkened and the damp cloth hanging behind her stopped bleeding color into color. "The clinic gave me both."

"Three if you sit still for a living. Five for the vats." The practitioner touched the thread to a square of test paper.

"Five," your mother said, and pulled the aftercare sheet closer.

Your younger brother snorted from the other end of the table. He had been told to hold the black-light inspection lamp and had spent the last ten minutes trying its violet beam on everything except the vial. White lint flared on his shirt. A smear of soap shone along the basin. His own birth mark, a loop of amber resin running from palm to forearm, disappeared under the strange light instead of brightening.

"The soap's glowing," your brother said.

The practitioner held out her empty hand. He took another look at the basin before bringing the lamp back over the table.

Every child was born carrying some ink-like fluid in a pattern beneath or across the skin. Soot, resin, metal suspended in oil, substances with no names outside the families who passed them down: the fluid varied, and the pattern shaped the faculty. No one before you had been found empty.

The practitioner lifted the paper. The artificial ink had spread into a narrow fork and stopped within the chalk ring. Tomorrow, under numbing salve, she would feed it into channels cut shallowly along your inner arm. Months later, if your body accepted it, the graft would let you hold a chosen color steady while you worked: no drift in the bath, no pale seam where cloth folded against itself. Not the broad, effortless command your mother's birth tattoo gave her. Something narrower. Something reliable. Something yours because you had signed for it and saved for it and spent six years saying you did not need it before admitting that you wanted it.

"Here," the practitioner said, tapping the test paper.

Your brother aimed it at the paper. His wrist bumped yours.

Violet light spilled across your hand.

The practitioner's glass rod halted against the paper.

At first you thought the gray graft ink had splashed. A black-violet stroke lay beneath the skin of your wrist, so dark it seemed cut into the bone. It curved once around the tendon. Fine branches broke from it and vanished at the edge of the beam.

Your brother moved the lamp.

The line moved with the light, appearing ahead of it and going invisible behind.

"Wait," the practitioner said.

"What?" your mother asked.

"Don't move the light."

"I'm not." Your brother's voice had risen. The beam shook over your hand. The buried line trembled with it, now black, now bruised purple. "I didn't spill anything."

"Spill what?" your mother said.

"The stand," the practitioner said. "Put the lamp in."

No one did.

You took your hand off the table. The practitioner reached after it. You pulled your arm out of reach.

"Don't," you said.

Her hands stopped in the air. You turned your wrist yourself.

At last your brother obeyed. The workroom changed under the fixed violet glow. Detergent flashed in the grain of the table. The boiled linen around the graft tools became painfully white. Where the light found your forearm, the hidden stroke divided and divided again, fine as frost under a windowpane, except frost lay on a surface and this did not. You turned your arm. The pattern turned inside it.

Your mother came around the table, passed you, and slid the bolt across the workroom door.

"Turn it off," she said.

"Not yet."

The refusal surprised you. All your life other people had leaned closer to the absence, as if enough attention might produce what they expected. Now there was finally something to look at, and your mother wanted darkness back. You held your arm nearer the lamp.

"Anyone could come down."

Your brother stared at your lit skin. "Does it hurt?"

You did not know whether he meant the line, the light, or finding it. "No."

The practitioner slid the graft vial away from the beam and stoppered it. She bent close to the light without reaching for you.

"Could the lamp have made it?" your mother asked.

The practitioner looked up at her. "I don't know what it is."

"Turn it off," you said.

The practitioner reached past the stand and clicked the switch. Ordinary yellow lamplight returned. Your skin was bare. Not faded, not pale: bare, as it had been in every mirror and every examination room of your life.

You rubbed your thumb over the place. Nothing rose under it.

The practitioner took a fresh cloth and held it up where you could see. "Water."

You kept your wrist against your chest. She poured from the covered pitcher into a clean bowl and waited. At last you laid your arm on the table. The cloth passed over your wrist once, cool and rough. No color came away. Under violet light, the line returned with the same branches.

The practitioner put a clear glass plate between the lamp and your arm. The pattern remained. She nodded toward your other wrist. You gave it to the light. More black-violet lines rose there, thinner but unmistakable. At the bend of your elbow, the pattern climbed past your rolled sleeve.

"Enough," you said.

She switched the lamp off at once.

The practitioner drew the dark cloth around the graft vial.

"Why are you packing it?" you asked.

"I'm not putting new ink through that."

"Tomorrow?"

She shook her head. The graft had been mapped for tissue everyone believed empty. Whatever lay under your skin turned every shallow channel into a crossing she had not planned.

You had spent months saving for tomorrow. Now the morning coach would leave without you, and the cancellation made no sound beyond the stopper pressed into the vial.

For weeks you had measured tomorrow in clean bandages and coach times. You knew which hand would lift the kettle, how long you could sleep without rolling onto the new channels, which vat you would try first when they healed. None of that preparation had included wanting the graft after someone found the thing you were supposed to have wanted instead.

"Thank God," your mother said.

"Don't."

"I didn't mean—"

"I wanted it," you said.

She had called you whole at clinic counters, at school meetings, in the kitchen after relatives tried to be kind. Now the edge of the aftercare sheet collapsed between her fingers.

"I know." She folded the aftercare sheet across the middle, missed the crease, and folded it again.

Behind her, a drop fell from the draining cloth into the stone trough. Then another.

"Can you tell what it does?" your brother asked.

"Couldn't tell you."

Your brother rubbed his palm. "That winter the wall froze. When you slept in my bed."

"What about it?"

"I couldn't warm your feet. Not properly. I thought you were kicking it away."

"You were eight."

"Nine. And you did kick."

Your mother looked sharply at the practitioner. "The stitches. The pain-worker kept saying you were fighting her."

"I remember the stitches," you said.

"And the naming oil," she went on. "It wouldn't stay on you. Then the fever—"

"The kettle burned me," you said.

The burn had blistered two of your fingers for a week. Your mother looked at your hand as if it had interrupted her.

"That was boiling water."

"I know."

Your brother looked at you. "Did mine work? Other times, I mean."

"Sometimes."

"Sometimes?"

The practitioner set the unused graft tools back into their case, piece by piece. Their little metal mouths clicked against the felt.

"Try it now," you said.

"No," your brother said.

You held out your hand anyway.

"I burned the cuff."

Until tonight he had told that story as a joke, changing whether the iron or the stove took the blame. Now he kept his thumb over the singed place as though it had become evidence against him.

"You said the iron did that," your mother said.

"I don't know what did it."

"You use your mark in the setting bath every day."

"That's cloth."

"Please," you said.

He looked at your hand, then rubbed his amber-marked palm hard against his trousers.

The practitioner sat opposite him and offered her palm. "On me first."

His amber loops darkened. Nothing came from them on their own. He drew a breath, pressed his fingers into hers, and warmth spread a pink flush up her hand.

"That's enough."

He let go. The practitioner rubbed her thumb across the warmed center of her palm, then moved out of your place at the table.

You put your palm against his. His skin was clammy.

"Your hand's freezing," he said.

"Start."

The amber deepened. Warmth flowed into your palm, as ordinary-seeming as sun through a window, then climbed to your wrist. You had expected resistance and found none. The surprise loosened something in your shoulders.

"Oh," you said.

"Too much?"

You shook your head. Warmth was still moving toward your wrist when the practitioner tapped the table at five. Your brother released you, looking relieved.

"Again," you said. "With the lamp."

"You felt it."

"I want to see."

The practitioner fitted the lamp into its stand. Black-violet branches appeared through your hand and ran up beneath your cuff. "Same hand," she told him.

You remembered the pain-worker leaning over your split chin when you were eleven, her blue mark open across her throat, telling you to stop fighting the quiet she was offering. You had not known how to stop. You had only known you did not want her inside your hurt while she spoke as if your fear were disobedience.

Not him, you reminded yourself. The warmth.

You set your feet under the table. You watched the amber lines in his palm. When he touched you, you imagined a door you had never seen and made no picture of closing it. You simply held the edge of yourself where it was.

His mark darkened.

Pressure. Damp skin. No warmth.

Under the violet light, the lines within your palm drew tight around each place his fingers met yours. They did not flare or reach for him. They held.

Your brother swallowed. "I'm doing it."

"Don't force it," the practitioner said.

"I'm not." His fingers tightened anyway. "It's warm on my side. It's just—"

He tore his hand away before five and tucked it under his opposite arm.

"I didn't want it," you said.

He looked at you.

"The heat," you said.

"I know."

He said it too quickly and did not offer his hand again. The places where his palm had pressed yours cooled in separate damp patches.

The practitioner leaned toward the dark lines. "Again."

"No," you said.

"They said no," your mother said.

The practitioner looked at you as if she had only just heard herself. Then she switched off the lamp.

Your brother fetched the little tin cup from beside the sink and held it between both palms. His amber loops darkened before he seemed to notice. The metal gave a soft tick.

He set it down too quickly. You moved it away from the edge of the table.

Heat entered your fingertips. Nothing beneath your skin answered it.

Your brother watched you put the cup down. Whatever had failed between your palms, it had not been warmth itself.

Afterward your brother tucked his hand under the other arm again.

Your mother reached for the inspection lamp. "The paper's upstairs. We take both to the registry."

"Leave it."

"They'll say we changed something. They'll say the lamp was wrong, or you moved, or—"

"I'm not going to the registry."

"You have to go somewhere."

"The clinic. For the appointment."

"And after?"

"I don't know."

She let go of the lamp. "It has already been twenty years."

You had no answer that would make twenty years shorter. Your mother pressed one fingertip after another against her thumb, making a count only she understood.

"I kept every receipt," she said. "Every stupid little bottle they told us to try."

Your brother rubbed his hidden palm against his trousers. "You said you didn't want it."

"The heat."

"I heard you."

"Then what?"

He picked at a loose thread on his cuff. "Nothing."

You wanted to tell him the first warmth had felt like relief. By the time the words arrived, he was worrying the thread loose, and saying them would have sounded like another correction.

The practitioner opened her case, took out the blank morning form, and wrote while the three of you watched. She turned it for you to read. Existing channel structure suspected. Planned graft contraindicated pending consultation. No claim about faculty. No description of the lamp.

"Does it have to say existing?" you asked.

"If it doesn't, they'll send another vial."

"Nothing about the lamp."

She drew a line through the blank space below the note.

You signed beneath her note. Your hand shook only when the pen left the paper.

Your mother noticed. "You've got ink."

A black smear from the pen crossed the side of your thumb. She set the damp cloth beside your hand. You wiped the ordinary ink away yourself.

Across the table, your brother busied himself wrapping the cold inspection lamp in its frayed cord. He made a knot too tight, picked at it, and finally left it tangled.

The practitioner packed the sealed graft vial in ice for return to the clinic. Your mother covered the unused aftercare food and put the kettle back on the stove. Nobody suggested waking the house.

The bolt stayed across the workroom door. Each time a floorboard sounded overhead, your mother looked up, but she did not move toward it.

By the time gray morning reached the high windows, the workroom looked almost ready for an ordinary day. Tools cased. Cloth folded. Consultation form tucked inside your coat. The tin cup had cooled beside the form; you carried it to the sink with the other dishes.

Your brother switched off the lamp at the wall, though it had already been dark for half an hour.

stories.title: The Night Harvest
stories.prompt: Out of the blue, monsters appeared in our world. They appear at night, never seem to run out. A whole industry to profit off their corpses start to appear. One day, odd people start to appear as well. They barely communicate, and only seem interested in fighting and kill these monsters.
stories.body:
# The Night Harvest

The first stranger ruined forty-three crowns' worth of lamp-grade throat node before Brelva could get off the weighing platform.

She knew the value because she had just chalked it on the carcass board. Two nodes, no punctures, good color, vibration holding north-northeast. The creature that had grown them lay across the intake rails with its six legs trussed and its wet hide steaming in the cold. Three months ago, people had screamed at the sight of such a thing. Now a hook crew was arguing over who had misplaced the small gut knife.

The stranger vaulted the rail.

She was lean beneath a patched coat of plates, her black hair hacked short. Her long blade had opened the monster below its jaw. Before Brelva could call to the guards, the woman set an iron wedge between the paired swellings in its throat and struck once with her hand.

Both nodes cracked.

Blue fluid ran into the sawdust. The faint tremor under Brelva's palm stopped.

“Forty-three,” Brelva said.

Perren, who had been holding the tally slate, looked at the ruined nodes and then at the woman. “You think she takes crowns?”

“She can take the consequence.” Brelva stepped down. “You. Those were ours.”

The stranger stared at her. Rain ticked on her shoulder plates. Gray monster ash filled the seams, and three healed cuts crossed the woman's cheek.

Brelva pointed to the chalkboard, then the nodes, then held out her hand.

The woman answered with a low cluster of sounds that had no edge Brelva could catch. She lifted one broken node. Its inner membrane, thin as an onion skin, shivered in the night air. She pointed along the north road, where the monster's living throat had faced when the hook crews brought it in. Then she pointed at the cold shed behind Brelva.

“Yes, we store them there,” Brelva said. “Very observant.”

Perren touched her elbow. “Brelva.”

Beyond the north lamps, something gave a long, hollow cry.

The stranger dropped the membrane into a brazier. It curled, flashed green, and went still. She tapped the dead flesh, pointed toward the cry, and then laid two fingers against the hard-packed ground between them.

One relation at a time. Flesh. Road. Ground.

Brelva understood none of it.

The stranger did not wait. She went over the rail again and ran north, coat plates clattering out of time with the rain.

The intake supervisor arrived after the lamps had been shuttered and the hook crew sent after the cry. He crouched over the blue stain with both hands tucked into his sleeves.

“Purchased batch,” he said.

“Ours until you pay it,” Brelva said.

“Purchased on the contract. Ruined on my floor. Your account will show the damage.”

Perren scraped sawdust over the stain with his boot. “Our account already shows an axle, two wheels, and a cart bed that leaks when it rains.”

“Then don't let foreign scavengers onto the rail.”

“I was grading,” Brelva said. “Your guards were eating.”

From behind the brine shed came the embarrassed clink of a spoon against a bowl.

The supervisor closed his eyes. “They get twenty minutes for supper.”

“They took twenty-four.”

“Then I will purchase four minutes back from the dead nodes.” He rose, knees cracking. “Forty-three crowns deducted. Bring me three full loads before sixth night and the cart is clear.”

Brelva looked at the chalkboard. Three loads meant no short routes, no turning back because the dark sounded busy. It meant the marsh road, where their partners had died in the second week.

Perren set the slate under his arm. “We'll bring them.”

Brelva said, “Two full, one mixed.”

“Three full,” the supervisor said. “The refiners bought fuel I promised them. The clinic bought tendon. Six crews have advances against that money, including yours.”

He did not sound greedy. He sounded tired, and the distinction annoyed her more.

“Three,” Perren repeated.

Brelva watched rain fill the stranger's footprint in the sawdust. “If the north road stays open.”

***

On the second night, two more strangers appeared. One fought beside the slaughterhouse ditch with a hooked spear; the other used a short bow that punched bolts through the monsters' knee joints. Neither answered questions. Both ignored hide, bone, heat sacs, and the pale liver combs the clinic rendered into fever wash. They killed until the street was quiet, broke every throat node they could reach, heated the membranes, and left.

The corpse industry had learned speed because rot did not care about grief. Roofers took the hides. Rope shops twisted tendon. Kilns ground the porous bones into hot-burning brick. In three months, the night harvest had put dismissed dockhands back on wages and given families a cheaper lamp than whale oil. The creatures kept coming. So did rent.

At the yard, Brelva began a second tally in the back of her ledger.

One wagon from the west ditch arrived untouched. Two creatures attacked behind it before the gate shut. A south-road load drew nothing until it passed a cold wagon carrying brined nodes; then three shapes abandoned the slaughterhouse pens and followed the wagon's iron wheels through the rain.

Perren saw a different pattern.

“The spear man stood here.” He put a finger on Brelva's map, on the row of cramped houses beyond the east drain. “Not where the thing came through. Here.”

“A person can stand anywhere.”

“He kept his back to the doors.”

“That is how you avoid being surrounded.”

“He had open road behind him.”

Brelva drew the wagon route in chalk. “And six houses ahead. I can count roofs too.”

Perren leaned across the cart tongue to inspect a split strap. “Didn't say you couldn't.”

“You meant it.”

“I meant he put his body in a place. Bodies are usually honest about what they expect.”

“Ours expected supper twenty minutes ago.”

Perren pulled the strap tight. “Stew or the heel of cheese?”

“Cheese tonight. Stew tomorrow if the west ditch pays.”

“That's a cruel order.”

It was not a joke so much as the shape of an old complaint. Brelva cut the cheese and gave him the larger piece. He accepted it without thanks, which was how they had thanked each other since childhood.

On the third night, the guards ringed the brine shed with pikes. The supervisor had bought shutters for its vents and hired two extra hands from the roof-hide crew.

“Protection for stock already purchased,” he told Brelva when she objected to the added gate fee.

“You put the fee on the crews whose stock you claim to own.”

“Because if it burns, I still owe the refiners. If a guard dies, I owe a widow. If I do not hire the guard, I owe everyone an explanation for why I preferred the cheaper funeral.”

Perren was beneath the cart, packing grease around the left hub. “We could take the nodes straight to the refinery.”

“Their vats are full,” the supervisor said. “I purchased capacity for seventh day.”

“It's third day.”

“Yes. That is why we have a cold shed.”

Brelva checked the brine barrels: thirty-two sealed, eight open, vibration faint but even beneath their waxed lids.

At midnight, a bolt struck the yard gate from outside. Not a monster bolt; one of the strangers' thick black shafts. It lodged above the latch.

The guards raised their pikes. The square-faced woman stood beyond the lamps with her empty hands spread. Behind her, shapes moved along the north road.

She pointed to the brine shed.

“No,” the supervisor said.

The word required no translation.

The woman pointed to the road. Then the shed. Then she drove the edge of one hand against her other palm.

“No,” he said again, louder. “Purchased stock.”

One of the new guards glanced at Brelva. “Should we move the barrels?”

“Hold your side of the gate,” the supervisor told him.

The woman waited, watching Brelva rather than the pikes. When no one copied her, she turned and ran toward the moving shapes alone.

The attack ended two streets north. None reached the yard.

Brelva wrote that down too.

***

On the fourth night, the left axle broke.

It happened on the marsh road, where reeds scraped the cart and black water covered both ditches. Brelva heard the crack, felt the load sag, and shouted before Perren could put his shoulder under it.

“Don't. Eleven hundredweight.”

“Wheel's in the ditch.”

“I can see the wheel.”

“Then count how long until the lamps go out.”

They had nine carcasses, sixteen sound nodes packed in two brine tubs, three bad hides, and one lantern with less than a finger of oil. Behind them, far down the road, came the scrape of many feet.

Perren pulled the jack from its bracket. “I lift. You seat the block.”

“We cut the nodes loose and leave the cart.”

“The cart is the promise.”

“A promise doesn't get to bury you.”

“Neither do you.”

He said it into the mud, already setting the jack. There was no room in the road for the answer Brelva wanted: I kept you alive after the marsh took them. I learned every weight, every safe turn, every sound that meant run. She had promised their dead partners' families that she would not make the same mistake twice. Somewhere in keeping that promise, she had started deciding which risks belonged to Perren before he could speak.

The scrape grew louder.

“Lift,” she said. “On three. One, two—”

The square-faced stranger dropped from the reeds before three.

Perren swung the jack handle at her. She caught it on a bracer, barked one sharp sound, and pointed at the tubs. Then she pressed her palm to the road.

Vibration hummed up through Brelva's boots.

Not footsteps. Not yet.

The sealed nodes were trembling hard enough to ring against the tubs.

The stranger ripped the waxed cloth from one. She took out a node, cracked it on the cart rim, and thrust the inner membrane over Brelva's lantern.

Green light ran across it. The membrane shrank. Under Brelva's fingers, the vibration vanished.

The remaining tub shook harder, each node seeming to lean north. The scrape behind them became a chorus. Ahead, beyond the bend, the dark answered.

Brelva looked from one tub to the other. “They weren't following us yesterday.”

Perren heard what she did: one group on the road behind, another moving from ahead. “They don't need to follow the same wagon. They only need the same road.”

The stranger pointed past them, toward the settlement. Then at the tubs.

Brelva cut the first lid open.

Perren cracked nodes while she held membranes to the lantern. The stranger stood between them and the approaching sounds, blade low. She did not supervise. When Brelva fumbled one slick membrane, the woman snatched it from the mud, burned it, and returned to the dark.

Eight nodes. Ten. The lamp oil guttered.

“Last two,” Perren said.

“One.”

He pushed the final membrane into the flame with his bare thumb. It flashed. He hissed and wrapped his hand in his shirt.

The pressure under Brelva's boots stopped.

The creatures did not disappear. They did not turn obediently or fall dead. One came out of the reeds on six bowed limbs, its pale mouth opening along its chest. The stranger met it. Perren dragged the jack clear. Brelva shoved the block beneath the axle, and together the siblings heaved the wheel onto the road while the fight thudded behind them.

When the cart rolled, they took the ordinary salvage and left the empty tubs.

The stranger followed only as far as the first streetlamp. She put up her palm. Stop.

Then she touched two fingers to the road and drew them toward herself.

Approach.

Brelva tried the motions. Palm. Two fingers drawn in.

The woman corrected the angle of her wrist, once. Then she went back into the reeds.

***

By morning, Brelva had six routes and nineteen attacks marked in her ledger. She put the cold wagons in blue and the unbrined loads in white. Perren put stones on the places where the strangers had chosen to stand.

The blue lines did not explain where the creatures came from or why the strangers knew how to kill them. They showed something smaller: preserved nodes passed near every cluster.
